case_summary.text: CL: Where there were allegations of manipulation of accounts by company which raised inference of misappropriation and diversion of funds with intent to defraud creditors, petition to direct Central Government to take steps to investigate into affairs of company was to be allowed
CL: Where circumstances suggested that business of company was being conducted with intend to defraud petitioner and its members, investigation into affairs of respondent No. 1 was to be ordered

COMPANY LAW : Where RoC failed to exercise its statutory and public duties in arresting pilferage, siphoning off of assets and safeguard legitimate interests of investors of company 'C', interim directions were to be passed directing RoC to initiate appropriate legal action against alleged directors and to inspect affairs of 'C'

COMPANY LAW: Where respondent, claiming to be a shareholder, alleged fraudulent transfer of shares and sought investigation, Tribunal validly exercised its inherent power under rule 43 of NCLT Rules, 2016 to appoint an independent auditor for forensic examination without requiring a specific application, such power being independently vested to ensure effective justice without causing unfair prejudice to appellants

COMPANY LAW/SEBI : Where investigation by SEBI revealed that companies floated by petitioner were involved in illegal mobilization of funds, which was in nature of Collective Investment Scheme and petitioner filed instant writ seeking directions to SEBI to liquidate attached assets for purpose of refund monies to investors, said petition was to be allowed and High-Powered Sale Committee (HPSC) was to be constituted to auction immovable assets of companies

COMPANY LAW : Where petitioner being Lead Manager for IPO issue of company and respondent directors of company had allegedly diverted IPO proceeds of company to their associates, there existed circumstances which prima facie suggests that business of company was being conducted with an intent to defraud its members, thus, it was necessary to investigate into affairs of company under provisions of section 213

SEBI : Where a committee was appointed to manage affairs of company and to make sure that sale of assets of company were to ensure that depositors be refunded their amounts, expert was to be appointed to assist committee in its task to evolve a feasible practicable method for disbursement of various amounts to depositors and investors

COMPANY LAW : Where petitioner/homebuyer alleged that promoters and directors of respondent company 'TCSPL' had misappropriated and siphoned off funds collected from innocent homebuyers into various shell/sister concerns and sought directions to respondents/Central Government to take cognizance, initiation and conduction of appropriate inquiries and investigation against management of 'TCSPL' as well as its shell/sister group of companies, in view of complexity of factual narrative and interwoven set of legal proceedings, Central Government was directed to entrust investigation to Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO)

COMPANY LAW/SEBI: Where winding-up of CRB Mutual Fund was prolonged despite the Special Committee’s mandate, with allegations of irregular payments to CRB Group entities emerging, yet no conclusive finding of manipulation or mala fide conduct was established, directions for a SEBI-led forensic audit and for SEBI to take over trustee functions were justified, and continued judicial oversight was warranted until full compliance with regulatory framework and investor protection was ensured.

SC admits writ plea; directs SEBI to auction assets of Companies running illegal ‘CIS’ and to refund monies to investors

HEADNOTE: Section 12(1B) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with article 142 of the Constitution of India - Collective Investment Scheme -Investigation into - Petitioners, who were shareholders of respondent-company, filed petition stating that investment made by investors in pursuance of certain scheme floated by company promising 1025 per cent return was unsafe and amount collected by company had disappeared from company - They prayed that an investigation was required to be carried out - Whether even in absence of statutory provision, since large number of investors were being defrauded by employing aforesaid corporate veil which might amount to criminal offence appropriate directions could be issued by court to search and seize property of company - Held, yes

FACT: The respondent-company had floated an investment scheme promising high return on investment. It was called 'Project Grapes' and the return mentioned in the brochure was 1025 per cent. On the basis of said scheme the company collected huge amount from public and its shareholders. The petitioners, who were shareholder of the company, filed petition stating that the investment of shareholders was totally unsafe in such company and the amount collected by the company had disappeared and, therefore, prayed that an investigation was required to be carried out.

HELD: There is no legislation which can effectively control the mushrooming of companies which tempt small investors to deposit or invest their life-savings in such companies, promising to pay fanciful returns on their investment but actually defrauding the investors after siphoning off large amounts from such investments. It is also unfortunate that nationalised banks are also advancing loans to such institutions without adequate security from such companies as well as their directors. The situation on the whole, prima facie, is not very happy and knowing fully well the parameters of the powers of the Court as well as the self-imposed restrictions under article 226 of the Constitution, the Courts, cannot be silent spectators to such piquant situations.

Prima facie, it appeared that respondents No. 1 and 2 and such other companies which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, were committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their life-long savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without there being any basis. Further, in agricultural production, this type of high returns are impossibility in this country, where, otherwise, the farmers of this country would have become multi-millionaires by this time. It appears that, because of these empty, false promises, investors are duped and the companies' monies are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

The Apex Court in case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Company (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401 held that the concept of corporate entity is evolved to encourage and promote trade and commerce but not to commit illegalities or to defraud people. The Court has also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court was exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties.

Applying the aforesaid ratio and taking into consideration the fact that large number of investors are being defrauded by employing the corporate veil which may amount to a criminal offence, and also the fact that under criminal law property acquired by fraud, cheating, etc., can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions could be issued by the Court to search and seize such property. Further, under article 226 the Court could issue appropriate directions for not only enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III but "for any other purpose", and 'any othe r purpose' would include such public interest purpose.

Considering all the facts disclosed from the material on record and taking into consideration the submissions, for combating exploitation and to retrieve hard-earned money and/or life savings of innumerable investors the Court passed order directing an enquiry, freezing of accounts of respondent-companies and attachment of their properties and assets.

HEADNOTE: Section 12(1B) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with article 142 of the Constitution of India - Collective investment scheme -Certificate of registration - SEBI filed petition in public interest stating that certain companies by issuing instrument like agro-bonds, plantation bonds, etc., were offering very high rates of return and collecting amounts from small investors and turning same amount to their sister-concern and other business instead of returning promised amount to investors and as such appropriate directions should be given by the Court to protect the interests of small investors - Whether even in absence of statutory provision since large number of investors were being defrauded by employing the aforesaid corporate veil, which might amount to a criminal offence, appropriate directions could be issued by Court to search and seize property of aforesaid companies - Held, yes

FACT: A petition was filed by the Securities & Exchange Board of India (SEBI) as a public interest litigation, wherein it was stated that it had come to the notice of the Government of India that there were entities which were issuing instruments such as agro bonds, plantation bonds, etc., offering very high rates of returns which were not consistent with the normal returns in such schemes.

In petition SEBI pointed out that respondent No. 1 had floated 18 Schemes and had collected approximately Rs. 16 crores from the small investors. Thereafter it was noticed that promoters of the schemes of respondent No. 1 were not traceable, respondent No. 1 had downed its shutters, the owners were not available, various offices of respondent No. 1 were closed and the said company was going through financial crises. Many investors were holding demonstrations outside the SEBI's office demanding action against the company and its directors.

Therefore, in petition SEBI prayed that in public interest, till regulations were framed under section 12(1B), appropriate directions be given to protect large amounts invested by middle-class people, and immediate action be taken against the directors who had siphoned off large amounts belonging to investors under the guise of corporate veil. It was further contended that the bank accounts and other assets, movable as well as immovable, of respondent No. 1 wheresoever situated required to be frozen and attached to protect the investor's money from being frittered away.

HELD: Unfortunately it appeared that there is no legislation which can effectively control the mushrooming of companies which tempt small investors to deposit or invest their life-savings in such companies, promising to pay fanciful returns on their investment but actually defrauding the investors after siphoning off large amounts from such investments. It is also unfortunate that Nationalised Banks are also advancing loans to such institutions without adequate security from such companies as well as their directors. The situation on the whole, prima facie, is not very happy and knowing fully well the parameters of the powers of the Court as well as the self-imposed restrictions under article 226 of the Constitution, the Courts, cannot be silent spectators to such piquant situations.

It, was appeared that respondent No. 1 and such other companies, which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, are committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their life-long savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without their being any basis. Further, in agricultural production, this type of high returns are impossibility in this country. It appears that, because of these empty, false promises, investors are duped and the company's monies are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

The Apex Court in case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Co. (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401, held that the concept of corporate entity is evolved to encourage and promote trade and commerce but not to commit illegalities or to defraud people.

The Court has also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court was exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties.

Applying the aforesaid ratio and taking into consideration the fact that large number of investors were being defrauded by employing the corporate veil, which may amount to a criminal offence, and also the fact that under Criminal Law property acquired by fraud, cheating, etc., can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions could be issued by the Court to search and seize such property. Further, under article 226 of the Constitution, the Court can issue appropriate directions for not only enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III of constitution but 'for any other purpose', and 'any other purpose 'would include such public interest purpose.

In this view of the matter the Court passed the order directing an enquiry freezing of accounts of respondent-company and attachment of its properties.

HEADNOTE: Article 226 of the Constitution of India - Writ petition - Whether where it prima facie appeared that investors were defrauded by respondent- company employing corporate veil and there was allegation of criminal offence of acquiring properties by fraud and cheating, appropriate directions for following properties and seizing these wherever these where lying, were required to be passed in exercise of Court's powers under article 226 of the Constitution -Held, yes

FACT: The respondent company (respondent No. 3), a residuary non-banking company, recorded a spurt in deposits from 1992-93. In 1995, on receiving complaints, the RBI conducted inspection of the respondent-company in which the RBI found an extremely unsatisfactory financial position, violation of the RBI directions and poor management. Therefore, the RBI issued prohibitory order restraining the company from accepting deposits from the public and also published notice in newspapers for the know- ledge of the general public. Receiving complaints about non-compliance of the prohibitory order, the RBI carried out a fresh inspection in 1997 in which it was found that the directors had no knowledge of and control over the affairs of the company. The registered office was not in operation and books of account had been shifted from there. Books of account had only been maintained upto 31-3-1995 and finalised upto 1993-94. Hence, the liabilities of the company to the depositors could not be determined. Substantial portion of liabilities, assets, properties and invest-ments of the company were transferred either to new companies or to its functionaries. These new companies where incorporated by officials agents and even field staff of the company. They were using premises of the assessee-company and were continuing deposit mobilisation activities violating prohibitory order of the RBI. In a branch the company itself collected deposit violating the order. The RBI also found that the company had substantial real estate, most of which had no complete documents and these were either repeatedly mortgaged or were in possession of the new companies. The RBI was also informed by the directors that investments of Rs. 152 lakhs were either realised or were encumbered.

The present writ petition under article 226 was filed by the agents and policy-holders of the respondent company. The petitioners sought appro-priate directions for protection of public interest.

HELD: There was great substance in the submission of the petitioners that the aforementioned state of affairs required immediate remedial attention. Prima facie, it was apparent that the third respondent had mobilised large deposits from the public and that innocent persons who had invested their money, had not been repaid The officials and other persons associated with the third respondent including the field-staff had formed new companies with the object of siphoning funds and assets of the third respondent to the detriment of the interest of the depositors.

Prima facie, it appeared that the respondents and such other companies, which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, are committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their lifelong savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without there being any basis. It appears that, because of these empty false promises, investors are duped and the Companies' monies are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

In the case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Company (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401, the Apex Court has referred to the discussion on the topic of corporate veil in Palmer's Company Law and has quoted with approval the observations that Courts have shown themselves willing to lifting the veil where the device of incorporation is used for some illegal or improper purpose.

The Courts have also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court is exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties. The Courts have also observed that in India, the Courts are not only Courts of law, but also the Courts of equity.

Considering the fact that a large number of investors prima facie appeared to have been defrauded, that the allegations of fraud and cheating if established would amount to a criminal offence and in view, of the fact that under the criminal law property acquired by fraud or cheating can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions were required to be issued by the Court to search and seize the property of the company. Under article 226 the Court can issue appropriate directions not only for enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III but 'for any other purpose' and 'any other purpose' would include a purpose for the protection of public interest. Therefore, order was passed directing the Commissioner, Police to appoint DC, Police to follow all assets and properties of respondent No. 3 company and to take necessary action for their seizure.

HEADNOTE: Section 12(1B) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 -Collective Investment Scheme-Respondent and certain other plantation companies were issuing instruments such as agro bonds, plantation bonds, etc., offering very high rate of returns which were not consistent with normal returns in such schemes - Cheques issued by respondent were dishonoured for want of fund and director/promoters of company were not traceable - SEBI filed petition in public interest stating that in order to ensure that investors make investment in such schemes only after they are fully acquainted with high risk factors involved in such schemes, it is necessary to decide an appropriate regulatory framework for regulating these companies - It was prayed that pending drafting of regulations appropriate directions be given to protect large amounts invested by middle class people - Whether in view of fact that large number of investors are being defrauded by employing corporate veil which may amount to a criminal offence and also fact that under criminal law property acquired by fraud, cheating, etc., can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions could be issued by Court to search and seize such property - Held, yes - Whether respondents should be restrained from operating their bank accounts and investigation by police with power to attach properties could be ordered - Held, yes

FACT: The respondent-company had floated various schemes by which it was offering fanciful returns which were highly disproportionate and com-mercially not viable. SEBI received several complaints from investors of the respondent-company to the effect that the cheques issued by the company had been dishonoured due to insufficient funds in the bank account of the respondent-company, that the office of the respondent- company had become non-functional, that directors of the respondent-company had gone defaulter and had more or less gone underground and that the funds received by the respondent had been diverted to the group companies. On the basis of these complaints, the SEBI filed petition in the interest of the members of public, stating that the Central Government was concerned with the high elements of risks associated with such schemes and hence, in order to ensure that investors make investment in such schemes only after they are fully acquainted with or made aware of the high risk factors involved in such schemes, it was felt necessary to decide an appropriate regulatory framework for regulating entities which issue such schemes.

It was prayed that in public interest, till regulations are framed, appropri- ate directions be given to protect large amounts invested by middle class people. It sought the bank accounts and other assets, movable as well as immovable, of respondent No. 1 wheresoever situated required to be frozen and attached to protect the investors’ moneys from being filtered away.

HELD: Prima facie it appears that respondent No. 1 and such other companies, which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, are committing fraud by tempting middle class persons to invest their lifelong savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without there being any basis. Further, in agriculture productions, this type of high returns are impossibility in this country, where, otherwise, the farmers of this country would have become multi-millionaires by this time. It appears that, because of this empty, false promises, investors are duped and the company’s moneys are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

As held in DDA v. Skipper Construction Co. (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401 where the corporate character is employed for the purpose of committing illegality or for defrauding others, the Court would ignore the entity with regard to corporate company and its association of men and women and will do justice between the real persons. The concept of corporate entity was evolved to encourage and promote trade and commerce but not to commit illegalities or to defraud people. Absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court while acting under article 142/226 from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties. In India, the Courts are not only Courts of law, but also the Courts of equity. In the aforesaid case, the Court passed an appropriate order attaching certain properties of the Directors of the company.

Applying the aforesaid ratio and taking into consideration the fact that large number of investors are being defrauded by employing the corporate veil, which may amount to a criminal offence, and also the fact that under Criminal Law property acquired by fraud, cheating, etc., can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions could be issued by the Court to search and seize such property. Further, under article 226 of the Constitution, the Court can issue appropriate directions for not only enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III but ‘for any other purpose’, and ‘any other purpose’ would include such public interest purpose.

In this view of the matter, following order was passed—

Code of Criminal Procedure

Sections 155 to 157 of the Code of Criminal Procedure would oblige the State to act on information received in non-cognizable cases and cognizable cases. Section 157 would lay down the procedure for investigation. Section 158 would suggest a procedure for submission of report. Section 159 onwards would lay down the procedure till the issue is brought to logical conclusion. [Para 53] On a combined reading of the law on the subject and applying it to the present context it is found, the depositors being citizens of the country were entitled to lodge complaint with regard to the non-refund of the deposits that they made with Saradha Group and police would be obliged to act upon such complaint and bring it to logical conclusion in accordance with the procedure laid down under the Code of Criminal Procedure. Similarly, the other Central Agency being SEBI was also empowered to look into the complaint as to whether there was any illegality committed by the company in contravention of the SEBI Act and the Regulations framed thereunder and suggest remedial and penal measures to be adopted by various agencies including State Police if the company failed to act upon their direction as contained in the order passed under Regulation 73. In the instant case, SEBI would contend, time was still there. Hence, it would be premature for them to take further steps in this regard. The company did not have any registration either under the Chit Funds Act or under the SEBI Act and, thus, would attract appropriate penal measures under the relevant provisions of law and Reserve Bank of India would be obliged to advise the State in case their assistance would be needed. [Para 54]

Sudipta's Letter to SEBI on 1-4-2013 and CBI on 6-4-2013

Sudipta offered explanation to SEBI pleading innocence. According to him, the fall of the group was a result of wrong business decision and recession in the market. He prayed for appointment of investigation agency. He would be also approaching the Court for appointment of retired High Court Judge or a Supreme Court Judge to conduct the investigation.[Para 61]

The subsequent letter to CBI was rather a detailed exercise to narrate his version from setting up his empire up to the fall. He blamed several persons including some of them having political clout. In his letter, he referred to various persons from business and political circle, sports circle, some having access up to the President of India, to assure him no interference in his business by the State agencies. He requested CBI to carry out appropriate investigation. He described the said letter as "his last wish" before his death either by way of suicide or otherwise. He referred to a list of persons that we did not get from any of the parties or the State Administration. The CBI would say, they forwarded the letter to the State for action. [Para 62]

The petitioners tried to get support from the letter establishing nexus of persons attached to corridors of power involved in this scam who in exchange of illegal gratification assured him trouble free business that would warrant an independent agency to take up the cause.[Para 63]

Sanchaita Episode

In later part of 1970s Sanchaita Investment, a partnership firm mostly operated in the urban part of the State based in Calcutta. They collected lump sum amounts as and by way of deposit refundable with high returns payable on monthly basis. The firm initially established credence by paying interest to the depositors on the firm date and obviously failed to sustain in absence of appropriate returns of investment that they made either in realty sector or film sector or otherwise. The matter reached up to the Apex Court level. The Apex Court passed an extraordinary order appointing a committee that would have an immense power including that of a Civil Court as well having summary jurisdiction. The committee would be headed by a retired District Judge to be nominated by the Chief Justice having other members on the Board. It had been stated that the company had assets worth Rs. 1500 crores as against liability of only Rs. 761 crores and the company was very much in a position to pay its dues. It was further stated that the company invited offers for sale of its certain properties but none of the buyers had shown any interest in view of the restraint imposed by the Mumbai High Court on 30-9-1999. Ultimately, the Mumbai High Court had appointed a retired Judge as private receiver for sale of 19 properties as set out in the schedule vide order dated 31-1-2000. [Para 11]

It was apparent from the above that there was no dispute as to the liability of the company towards the investors. It was the stand of the company that it had assets more than Rs. 1,000 crores which were sufficient to discharge the liability of the investors. It had come on record that the directors of the company were in custody since December, 2000 and the company had not been able to dispose of any of the properties for payment to the investors. It was also on record that private receiver appointed by the Mumbai High Court had also not been able to sell any property so far. Thus, a mechanism was required to be drawn so as to facilitate the sale of the property of the company at the earliest with a view to ensure payment to the investors without any further delay. The interest of such large number of creditors was required to be watched by the company court and the management of the company could not be permitted to take such investors for a ride. [Para 12]

With a view to protect the interest of the large number of creditors and shareholders of the company, it was just and appropriate to appoint provisional liquidator for control, management and sale of the movable and immovable properties so as to fetch maximum price thereof with a view to satisfy the claim of 25 lakh investors in a proper manner. However, the Official Liquidator attached to the High Court might not be able to take over the responsibility of management and sale of the properties of the company keeping in view the meagre resources at his command and inadequate infrastructure available. Therefore, instead of appointing Official Liquidator the responsibility of the provisional liquidator should be entrusted to such a person who would command respect and be able to discharge the onerous responsibility in a fair manner. Apart from vesting of the company with the provisional liquidator so as to facilitate the sale thereof to liquidate the claim of the investors, the affairs of the company were also required to be investigated by an independent agency. [Para 14]

Therefore, instead of winding-up of the company in the interest of creditors and shareholders of the company a provisional liquidator was appointed to control and manage the affairs of the company with certain directions. [Para 17]

On appeal:

HELD: Section 210 empowers the Central Government to investigate into the affairs of a company/(companies), if it is of the opinion that such investigation is necessary for the reasons mentioned therein, including public interest. For the purpose of the said provision, the Central Government may appoint one or more persons as inspectors to investigate into the affairs of the company and to report thereon in such manner as the Central Government may direct. The SFIO has been established under section 211 of the Companies Act, 2013, which has jurisdiction to investigate into the company/(companies), where the Central Government is of the opinion that it is necessary to investigate into the affairs of a company by the SFIO for different reasons, including the public interest. Where any case has been assigned by the Central Government to the SFIO for investigation under the Act, no other investigating agency of the Central Government or any State Government can proceed with investigation in such case in respect of any offence under the Companies Act and other cases before such agency are required to transfer the relevant documents and records in respect of such offences under the Companies Act to the SFIO. Sub-section (8) of section 211 empowers certain Officers of the SFIO to arrest any person, if on the basis of material in his possession there is reason to believe, which is to be recorded in writing, that any person has been guilty of any offence punishable under sub-section (6) of section 212. [Para 30]

Investigation into company's affairs in other cases can also be done under section 213 on an application made by the eligible members as mentioned in clause (a) of section 213 or on an application made by any other person or otherwise, if it is satisfied that there are circumstances suggesting that the business of the company etc. has been conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members etc. as mentioned in clause (b) of section 213. [Para 31]

From section 213, it is clear that the Tribunal on an application made to it or 'otherwise', if satisfied that there are circumstances suggesting that the business of the company is being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members etc. as mentioned in clause (b) of section 213, after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the parties, direct the Central Government to investigate. [Para 32]

From section 221, it is clear that the Tribunal has power to direct that the transfer, removal or disposal of funds, assets, or properties of the company shall not take place during such period not exceeding three years'. In case of any removal, transfer or disposal of funds, assets, or properties of the company in contravention of the order of the Tribunal under sub-section (1) of section 221, the company is punishable with fine and imprisonment as prescribed under sub-section (2) of section 221. [Para 34]

FACT: The Sanchaita in 70's acted in small urban area alluring people a high rate of interest.

They used to collect lump sum deposits from the depositors and pay them high rate of interest that they could not get from the market by reinvesting the said sums.

Very soon, the system collapsed. The small companies, operating in the same field, came under the Reserve Bank scanner. The Reserve Bank started taking action against those companies who were operating in the field as a non-banking financial company without any valid license. Sanchaita Saving was one of them.

In later part of the last decade, mushroom finance companies entered into the arena silently and were able to capture the rural market and Saradha was one of them.

Public interest litigations were filed by three advocates.

The petitioner made an enquiry and came to know, Saradha Group was one of the largest chit companies operating in Eastern India having diverse business in the field of construction, realty, tourism, hospitality, agriculture and media. The group was on the verge of collapse that would lead to a State level disaster.

The petitioner alleged, Kunal Ghosh, one Rajya Sabha M.P., was the Chief Executive Officer of the media run by Saradha Group. He was responsible to maintain liason between the group and the State, hence, an independent authority would be required to investigate, where she also referred to a letter of one Sudipta Sen the owner of the Saradha Group.

In the said letter addressed to CBI, Sudipta alleged, he paid huge sums to various politicians as also the persons connected with the administration to have his business free from any trouble.

According to the petitioner, the other chit fund companies were also responsible for collecting rupees fifteen thousand crores from the small investors in the State alone and, thus, funds were ultimately serving the interest of the political personnel.

The petitioner apprehended the ministers' intervention in the investment and, thus, demanded CBI investigation.

State in its affidavit in opposition expressed their helplessness in taking appropriate measures in the field as banking and corporate function would be under the Union List and State Government was not vested with the regulatory power or authority to oversee their activities that would be regulated by Reserve Bank of India, Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), National Housing Bank (NHB) and Department of Company Affairs (DCA).

The Reserve Bank contended chit funds did not come under their purview. Chit funds were within the statutory control of the State. Reserve Bank would have no role to play. The Reserve Bank also stated Saradha Group was not registered with the Reserve Bank.

HEADNOTE: Section 12(1B) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with article 142 of the Constitution of India - Collective investment scheme - Certificate of registration - SEBI filed petition in public interest stating that certain plantation companies by issuing instrument like agro bonds, plantation bonds, etc., were offering very high rates of return and collecting amounts from small investors and siphoned off amount to their sister concern and other business instead of returning promised amount to investors - SEBI sought appropriate directions to protect interests of small investors till regulation are framed under section 12(1B) - Directions were issued by court to conduct inquiry and search and seize of property and accordingly properties of directors were attached - Investigations were said to be still in progress - Whether no further directions viz., to direct RBI to issue orders to all commercial banks and/or cooperative banks, where Respondent No. 1 Plantation company had accounts, restraining Respondent Nos. 1 to 5 and 7 from withdrawing any money from the said accounts are required to be issued for present but Central Government or State Government would have to take appropriate action in framing appropriate regulations/enactment as early as possible - Held, yes

FACT: A petition was filed by the Securities & Exchange Board of India (SEBI) as a public interest litigation, stating that it had come to the notice of the Government of India that certain plantation companies were issuing instruments such as agro bonds, plantation bond, etc., offering very high rates of return which were not consistent with the normal returns in such schemes. In petition SEBI prayed that in public interest, till regulations were framed under section 12(1B), appropriate directions be given to protect large amounts invested by middle-class people, and immediate action be taken against the directors who had siphoned off large amounts belonging to investors under the guise of corporate veil. The Court ordered search and seizure and for an investigation by the Police into the affairs of the company with the assistance of the auditors and staff to be provided by the RBI. Consequently, investigations were made and prop- erties of directors of the company were attached. At this stage SEBI sought direction that till such regulations were framed and finalised, the Court may direct the RBI to issue orders to all commercial banks and/or cooperative banks, where Respondent No. 1 Plantation company had accounts, restraining Respondents No. 1 to 5 and 7 from withdrawing any money from the said accounts, and for certain other reliefs. The company opposed the prayer contending that it is the function of SEBI or the Central Government to frame the regulations at the earliest, if they think it necessary in the interests of investors/depositors in such plantation companies. It was contended that instead of moving the Central Govern- ment to frame and finalise the Regulations, they have approached the Court and it amounted to abuse of the process of law, because the court had issued various directions, including the direction to freeze the bank accounts of the directors.

HELD: On the basis of the earlier order of the Court the properties of the directors of Respondent No. 1 were attached. Further, the Deputy Commissioner of Police, Economic Offences Wing, Crime Branch, Mumbai, had carried out investigation which revealed that, out of Rs. 1,893.54 lakhs collected only Rs. 482.23 lakhs were expended fruitfully for business operations of the company. The investigation also revealed in detail the mismanagement by the directors of the respondent No. 1 company. As the investigation was still in progress, no further directions were required to be issued for the present.

However, considering the facts narrated above and various other similar petitions filed before the Court complaining against the mismanagement by such companies and their directors, the Central Government or the State Government would have to take appropriate action in framing appropriate Regulations/enactment as early as possible as suggested by the petitioner and respondent No. 6.

It would be open to the official liquidator to take physical possession of the premises located at Goregaon and Malad which were under his lock and key.

He had further submitted that assets of the company-in-liquidation had been transferred to other companies in a clandestine manner and therefore, it was a fit case to be referred to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for investigation into the matter. The Official Liquidator had stated that the office of the Official Liquidator did not have the resources or the expertise to undertake an investigation into the diversion of funds, etc.

HELD: Section 235 of the 1956 Act, enables the Central Government to appoint inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company and to report thereon in such manner as the Central Government may direct, in case where a report has been made by the Registrar of the company under sub-section (6) of section 234 or under sub-section (7) of that section read with sub-section (6) thereof. Under sub-section (2) of section 235, where an application has been received by the specified number of members or persons on the company's register of members, respectively, in case of a company having share capital and in case of a company having no share capital, the Tribunal may declare the investigation of the affairs of the company by an inspector, but, after giving the parties an opportunity of being heard. [Para 11]

HEADNOTE: Section 433 of the Companies Act, 1956, read with section 45-QA of Chapter III-B of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 - Winding-up - Circumstances in which a company may be wound-up - Whether there is no inconsistency between section 433 and any of provisions of Chapter IIIB of 1934 Act in relation to right of creditors to apply for winding-up of a company through Court under section 433 - Held, yes - Whether section 45-QA of 1934 Act giving creditors mode of recovery of amount deposited through Company Law Board, does not curtail their right of winding-up of company through Court nor ousts jurisdiction of Court to entertain such a petition of winding-up - Held, yes - Appellant-company failed to repay amount deposited by investors in accordance with fixed schedule - Investors, therefore, approached Company Law Board for recovery of said amount - Company Law Board issued a detailed order as to repayment of deposits - Appellant-company, however, did not pay amount in accordance with order issued by Company Law Board - On petitions filed by investors, Company Judge passed winding-up order under section 433(e) - Appellant, in instant appeal, raised objection that investors were not entitled to file winding-up petition as only remedy available to them was to approach Civil Court for execution of order passed by Company Law Board - Whether since inspite of detailed order being issued by Company Law Board, appellant-company neither repaid amounts deposited nor took any effective steps in that regard, investors in such a situation were well within their right to approach Company Court for winding-up of appellant-company - Held, yes - Whether, in view of conduct of appellant-company and its sister concern as to collecting money from public in general, utilization of that money for purchasing properties to detriment of investors, siphoning-off of appellant-company’s money to sister concern under loan agreement with no effective condition of repayment, it could be concluded that in reality properties of sister concern also belonged to appellant-company and, therefore, such properties could also be auctioned or proceeded with for realization of amount of creditors of appellant-company - Held, yes

FACT: The investors who had invested their money in the appellant-company, namely, ’IMFB’ Ltd. filed company petitions for its winding-up on account of its failure to repay the deposited amount in accordance with fixed schedule. The Company Judge, finding it to be a case of cheating and misappropriation of public funds with evil designs, allowed the petitions and ordered for winding-up of the appellant-company under section 433(e). The Official Liquidator was appointed and he was directed to exercise power under section 457, with authority to take into custody all movable and immovable properties of the appellant-company. He was further directed to auction properties of one of the sister concern of the appellant-company, i.e., ’IFCL’, also on ground that properties of said company were in reality properties belonging to the appellant-company.

Against aforesaid order, two sets of appeals were filed. First set of appeals was filed by the appellant-company wherein the order of its winding-up was challenged on various grounds. Second set of appeals was filed by the ’IFCL’ Ltd. on ground that there was no order of winding-up against it nor it was impleaded as a party in the company petitions and, therefore, even if the appellant-company was to be wound-up under the orders of the Court, no assets or properties of ’IFCL’ Ltd. could be taken possession of or could be put to auction.

HELD: The first submission of the appellant was that in view of provisions of Chapter III-B of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 and in particular that of sections 45-Q and 45-MC, the creditors could not have filed the company petition under section 433 as the provisions of this Chapter have got overriding effect as against any other law for the time being in force, wherein section 45MC gives the power to file winding-up petition to the Reserve Bank of India alone. [Para 6]

The non obstante clause in section 45Q would prohibit the Reserve Bank of India to file a company petition under section 433 as a specific provision for the purpose has been provided under section 45MC in Chapter III-B giving the grounds for moving for winding up of a non-banking financial company by the bank. The grounds (a) to (d) which are available to the RBI for filing winding-up petition against a non-banking financial company provide different grounds for winding-up except the ground (a ), namely, the non-banking financial institution is unable to pay its debts as against the grounds mentioned in section 433 of the Companies Act. [Para 13]

HEADNOTE: Regulation 73 of the SEBI (Collective Investment Schemes) Regulations, 1999 - Manner of repayment and winding up -  Applicant was National Investors Forum (NIF) and its members were investors of respondent-company GFIL - SEBI inquired into activities of GFIL group and noted financial and other irregularities committed by company - SEBI filed a writ petition in Bombay High Court, in which an order was passed against GFIL restraining it from alienating properties; a similar order was passed by High Court in same year - Thus, SEBI made an order prohibiting company from alienating its properties - However, GFIL, continued to accept deposits, carrying business and alienating properties - Therefore, winding up proceedings, were preferred before High Court - Company Judge by order directed appointment of a provisional liquidator to control and manage affairs of company in accordance with directions of company court - Thereafter, company petition and all other proceedings pending against GFIL in various High Courts throughout country were transferred to Supreme Court, in a transfer petition filed by SEBI - Supreme Court by its order constituted a committee to monitor affairs of GFIL and to make sure that sale of assets of GFIL were to ensure that depositors who had parted with sizeable amounts ought to be refunded their amounts - Committee had detailed figures of amounts invested from depositors in GFIL and its group companies from different States - Committee had so far been able to collect and put to sale and realize assets to tune of Rs. 400 crore - Possibilities of disbursements, regardless of total amount deposited resulted in an outgoing of Rs.309.60 crore - As on date, there was uncertainty with respect to litigation pending in regard to at least three properties - Committee was facing a possible reimbursement claim to tune of Rs.65 crore - Further, an income tax payment of Rs.32 crore towards capital gains had been made - Whether having regard to all these aspects, at this stage, it would not be appropriate to direct any claim - Held, yes - Whether in these circumstances an expert ought to be appointed to assist committee in its task of ensuring management of its funds and evolving a method of disbursing amounts whenever position became clear - Held, yes - Whether thus RBI was to be directed to nominate an expert to advise Committee in its task of managing funds available with it to optimise their returns having regard to previous orders of Court and to evolve a feasible practicable method for disbursement of various amounts to depositors and investors - Held, yes [Paras 15, 16  18]SEBI : Where a committee was appointed to manage affairs of company and to make sure that sale of assets of company were to ensure that depositors be refunded their amounts, expert was to be appointed to assist committee in its task to evolve a feasible practicable method for disbursement of various amounts to depositors and investors

FACT: The respondent-company Golden Forests (India) Ltd. (GFIL) was incorporated in 1987. Between the years 1991 and 1997, its promoters set up over 100 companies and introduced a number of investment schemes promising handsome returns, lured investors and depositors, and in 9-10 years collected several hundred crores of rupees. Huge tracts of lands and property were also acquired by it.

The applicant was National Investors Forum and its members were the investors of the respondent-company GFIL.

In 1997, the Securities Exchange Board of India (SEBI) inquired into the activities of GFIL group and a two member committee was constituted. The report of the committee highlighted financial and other irregularities committed by the company.

SEBI filed a writ petition in the Bombay High Court, in which an order was passed against GFIL restraining it from alienating the properties; a similar order was passed by this High Court in the same year. Thus, SEBI made an order prohibiting the company from alienating its properties. A retired judge was appointed as receiver and certain properties were earmarked for sale, but the receiver could not sell the properties.

GFIL, in the meanwhile continued to accept deposits, carrying business and alienating properties. In this background, winding up proceedings, were preferred before the Punjab & Haryana High Court. The Company Judge by order directed that all properties of the company would be managed, controlled, regulated by a provisional liquidator, who shall have power to sell the movable and immovable property. Thus, a provisional liquidator was appointed.

Section 207 enables the Registrar or the inspector to conduct inspection and inquiry and they are vested with all powers of the Civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure, while trying a suit in respect of; (a) the discovery and production of books of account; (b) summoning and enforcing the attendance of persons and examining them on oath; (c) inspection of any books, registers and other documents of the company at any place. [Para 19] The Registrar or inspector is mandated to submit a report in writing to the Central Government pursuant to an inquiry either under section 206 or 207, which may include a recommendation and further investigation into the affairs of the company is necessary along with reason. [Para 20]

The power to search and seizure is provided under section 209. Section 210 of the Act, 2013 empowers the Central Government, where it forms an opinion that it is necessary to investigate into the affairs of a company either, (a) on the receipt of a report of the Registrar or inspector under section 208; (b) on intimation of a special resolution passed by a company that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated; or (c) in public interest. Sub-section (2) thereof mandates the Central Government to order an investigation into the affairs of that company where an order is passed by a court or the Tribunal in any proceedings before it that affairs of a company ought to be investigated. [Para 21]

The establishment of SFIO is provided in section 211 of the Act, 2013, which also provides for its constitution by experts headed by a Director appointed by a notification by the Central Government. Section 212 provides for investigation into affairs of Company by SFIO. The procedure to be adopted by SFIO is also provided in this section. [Para 22]

Section 226 indicates that where winding up proceeding in respect of a company is pending before a Tribunal, that is to say, where winding up order has not been passed by a Tribunal, an investigation in the Chapter may be initiated, and no such investigation shall be stopped or suspended by reason only of the fact that such winding up proceeding is pending. However, where a winding up order is passed by the Tribunal in a proceeding referred to in clause (c) of section 226 of the Act, 2013, the Inspector shall inform the Tribunal about the pendency of investigation proceedings before him and the Tribunal shall pass such order as it may deem fit. [Para 27]

Once the provisions of Part VII of the Act, 1956 or Chapter XX of the Act, 2013 are brought into play, then the companies become subject to provisions of winding up and orders passed by the Tribunal. [Para 28]

The Official Liquidator under the Act, 1956 and the Company Liquidator under the Act, 2013 are empowered to take into custody the company's properties and are vested with wide powers in that regard. [Para 29]

Wide ranging powers have been given to the liquidator for taking custody of the company's property under section 456 of the Act, 1956. All the properties and effects of the companies are deemed to be in custody of the Court/Tribunal from the date of the order for winding up of the company. [Para 30]

Similar powers are vested in the liquidator in section 283 of the Act, 2013, which provision also creates a legal fiction with regard to the custody of the properties and effects of the company being deemed to be with the Tribunal from the date of the order for winding up of the company. Wide ranging powers are provided by the Act, 2013 to the Tribunal which orders winding up of the company. Therefore, the purpose of the first proviso to section 226 of the Act, 2013 appears to be that since the Inspector would have taken into his custody the books and papers of the company or would have examined the various persons in exercise of his power under section 217 of the Act, 2013, or he would require papers and books for purpose of investigation initiated, he would bring to the knowledge of the Tribunal the steps taken by him or requiredto be taken, to enable the Tribunal to pass such orders as it may deem fit. This is in view of the fact that under section 283 of the Act, 2013 all the property of the company is deemed to be in the custody of the Tribunal. [Para 31]

It is not denied by the Official Liquidator that it has a panel of Chartered Accountants through whom the inspection and inquiries may be ordered. The sole purpose for which the Official Liquidator has sought for referring the matter to the SFIO was for detection of diversion of assets/funds of the company-in-liquidation. It is not denied by the Official Liquidator that the balance sheet, other books of account and documents are in possession of the Official Liquidator as well as the statement of affairs filed by the ex-director on behalf of the company-in-liquidation. [Para 32]

HEADNOTE: Section 237, read with section 10, of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company’s affairs in other cases - Whether ‘Court’ referred to in section 237 is court having jurisdiction under section 10 and no other court - Held, yes - Whether under section 237(a)(ii), court can appoint directly inspector(s) to investigate into affairs of company - Held, no - Whether court can only make a declaration that affairs of company ought to be investigated by an inspector appointed by Central Government - Held, yes - Whether power of Company Law Board under section 237(b) is a bar to exercise of discretionary jurisdiction of court under section 237(a)(ii) - Held, no - Whether mere allegations are insufficient to support an application to court to act under section 237(1)(ii) and material placed before court should be such as to satisfy court that a deeper probe into affairs of company is desirable in interests of company itself - Held, yes - Whether court can pass a declaration under section 237(a) for a fishing expedition - Held, no - Whether an isolated instance of mismanagement is enough for court to declare that an investigation is required - Held, no - Whether existence of circumstances described under section 237(b) may sway court to pass an order under section 237(a)(ii) also but it is not always mandatory that court can pass a declaration only if conditions under section 237(b) exist - Held, yes - Whether power of court under section 237(a)(ii) is equal to power of CLB under section 237(b) - Held, no - Whether unlike CLB, there are no restrictions placed on Court even though Court will exercise its judicial discretion only on sufficient materials and only after it is convinced that situation warrants an investigation in interest of company as a whole - Held, yes - Whether when a discretionary order under section 237(a)(ii) is passed by proper court with jurisdiction, unless there are compelling grounds appellate court will not interfere - Held, yes

FACT: The respondent was an equity shareholder and the promoter of the appellant-company. He was also appointed as the Chairman of the company. Subsequently, the company came out with public issue which was subscribed in excess of 14 times the offer. Thereafter, the respondent filed petition under section 237(a)( ii ) before the Company Judge seeking to direct the Central Government to appoint inspectors to investigate into the affairs of the company. It was alleged that no first annual general meeting of the company was held as convened in time.

The managing director, ‘M’ had been fraudulently mismanaging the company in utter disregard of the interest of the shareholders and was acting in an autocratic and oppressive manner. He created false and fabricated documents with nefarious motive to oust the respondent and other members of the board of directors who opposed the misutilisation and misappropriation of public funds. He created documents and minutes purporting to remove the petitioner and others who opposed the mismanagement and oppression. Though on the public issue, shares were over subscribed to the tune of 14 times and huge amounts were collected from the public, shares were neither allotted properly nor amounts refunded to the applicants whose application for shares were not accepted.

It was further alleged that 1200 complaints had been filed against ‘M’ by the subscribers to whom the amounts were not refunded and that ‘M’ had misappropriated, misutilised and mismanaged the funds collected through public issue and diverted the funds for his private purposes. The company opposed the petition. The Company Judge found that the submission of the Central Government supported the respondent’s allegations and concluded that a deeper probe was necessary and passed an order declaring that affairs of the company ought to be investigated by an inspector appointed by the Court itself.

On appeal :

HELD: By virtue of the power under section 237(a )(ii), the Court cannot appoint directly inspector or inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company but only make a declaration that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated by an inspector appointed by the Central Government. Once such an order is passed it is mandatory for the Central Government to conduct such investigation by appointing competent persons as inspectors.

NCLAT was challenged before the Supreme Court and an interim directions was passed to maintain status quo including the assets of 'C'.

The petitioner filed the instant writ petition praying for certain directions in the nature of mandamus to Registrar of Companies (RoC) to initiate and carry out appropriate inquiries and investigation against the management of 'C' and its sister group of companies, for the acts of manipulating of records and siphoning off funds of the said company to its sister concern and freeze its assets. Further the petitioner submitted that after raising funds from the investors/home buyers without any intention to complete the project, the ex-management of 'C' had altogether abandoned the project and despite the fact that entire information was brought to the knowledge of RoC, it was failing to perform its statutory duties to the detriment of large homebuyers and financial institutions.

HELD: The petitioner referred to an e-mail by one of the promoters of 'C', a bare reading of which would show that he highlighted that about Rs. 500 crores having been siphoned off from 'C' to its sister concerns and there is tabular depiction of the names of the companies besides the trail of money/funds that have been siphoned off including the details as to the date of the transfers and amounts involved. It was also pointed out that there has been a conspicuous common connection between the promoters of the ace group and 'C' having common directors and likewise with 'bright buildtech pvt. ltd.' and other shell companies so much so that huge parcel of land in YEIDA area (Yamuna Expressway Industrial Development Area) and other places have been transferred to ace infracity for nominal value of Rs. 1 lakh. It is also submitted that ace infracity is a proxy of 'C'. [Para 13]

In the backdrop of the aforesaid scenario, despite the fact that the entire information having been brought to the knowledge of RoC it is failing to perform its statutory duties in terms of Chapter XIV of The Companies Act, 2013 to the detriment of large homebuyers and financial institutions. In this regard, it has been pointed out that the petitioner and several investors have already written to RoC and Union of India to initiate action against 'C' and its promoters and ex-directors but they are sitting over the matter. [Para 14]

During the course of arguments, it was also canvassed that although IRP is seized of the assets of 'C' but in view of the order passed by the NCLAT, which is now under challenge before the Supreme Court, the IRP is not able to take any further actions so as to inquire into the various facets of siphoning of the funds by the culprits and retrieving the funds since the entire CIRP proceedings have come to a complete halt. [Para 15]

Prima facie the facts and circumstances brought on the record demonstrate a sordid state of affairs at the behest of unscrupulous promoters/ex-directors running the affairs of 'C' and its group of companies who evidently, brazenly committing repeated or multiple acts of siphoning of funds from one end to another and thereby causing irreparable hardships to the petitioner and similarly placed investors. [Para 16]

It is unfathomable that the information about the state of affairs of 'C' and its group of companies have not reached the ears of RoC, and yet shockingly no action has been taken in terms of Chapter XIV of the Companies Act, 2013. It is but imperative that they must exercise their statutory and public duties in arresting pilferage, siphoning off of the assets of 'C' and its group of companies and safeguard the legitimate interests and rights of the petitioner and those similarly placed. It is surprising that despite issuance of advance notice and having a battery of lawyers on their panel, no one has bothered to even appear for RoC during the hearing. [Para 17]

Chapter XIV of the Act provides for a detailed mechanism to inspect, call for the accounts and record of the company, inquire and investigate into the financial affairs of the company. Further, where the Registrar or inspector has reasonable grounds to believe that the books or documents with regard to the company under investigation are likely to be destroyed, mutilated, altered, falsified or secreted, an order can be prayed for from the Special Court for the seizure of such books and papers in the manner provided vide section 209 and proceed for freezing of the accounts of the company under investigation. [Para 18]

There are compelling and justifiable grounds to pass certain directions so as to safeguard the paramount interests of the petitioner and those who are similarly placed in larger public interest. [Para 19]

. The company not only got the notice of the petitions but a complete opportunity to show the reasons against it in writing besides the hearing in the open Court. Therefore, this was not a case of breach of natural justice on account of the denial of the opportunity.

There was no doubt that the considerations enumerated by the company Judge for the appointment of provisional liquidator were abundantly available in the present case. Therefore, the Single Judge was justified in admitting the petitions and in appointing the provisional liquidator. The Judge had given the directions that the report forwarded by the RBI to the Additional Director General of Police, in-charge of the Economic Offence Wing, to whom the RBI had forwarded the report of the Special Auditor should be treated as the first information report with regard to the apparent fraud committed by the company and those in-charge of the company. This action, according to the Single Judge, would be in addition to any of the cases that might have been registered against the company. The Judge then directed that steps should be taken against those involved in the apparent conspiracy to siphon off or divert the funds of the company. The observations made by the Single Judge directing an investigation to be made had got nothing to do with sections 541 and 542. Section 543 also speaks about the assessment of damages for any mis-application, retainer, misfeasance or breach of trust by the directors. Even that section had got nothing to do with the directions given by the Single Judge. That is a general power of the court and there can be no doubt that every court has that power and the Single Judge also had the same power.

Section 443 provides for the powers of the court. Clause (c) of section 443(1) thereof speaks of the Court's powers to make any interim order which the Court thinks fit to order an investigation. This has got no connection with sections 541 to 543 and, therefore, the argument that that part of the order was without jurisdiction was to be rejected.

The Court has ample powers including the power under section 443 to recommend an investigation. After all, an investigation into the affairs of the company does not mean a final conviction of the Directors. This argument, therefore, was to be rejected. The criminal liability would be decided by the competent Criminal Court on the evidence tendered before it by the prosecution. The question of the bail and release would also be decided by the Criminal Court which was dealing with the matters. The release of a person on bail in this case was the exclusive right of the Criminal Court dealing with the accused persons, viz., the directors of the company. The payment of Rs. 50 crores might have been considered as one of the considerations for grant of bail but, that did not divest the Criminal Court of its powers to deal with the bail matter and to deal further with the criminal matter pending before it in its own rights.

Accordingly, the application was disposed of.

The blocking of substantial funds in another company when the main object was not investment, diversion of project money to various bodies incorporated or unincorporated, the laxity in the collection of loans, the unusual facility of allowing repayment of principal with interest still outstanding, payment of substantial commission to a private company, substantial increase in the cost of materials and wasteful expenses all went to show that the funds of the company had gone out to third parties and were not easily recoverable. An investigator under section 237(b ) would be clothed with sufficient powers to investigate not only into the affairs of the company in question, but also related companies and firms and to that extent this investigation had a wider coverage. In addition, information could also be called by the investigator from any other company with the previous approval of the Central Government. Only such a kind of investigation would establish the link, if any, between the ultimate beneficiary and those incharge of the management of the funds of the company. Ultimately, the investigation might not be able to establish any link. However, prima facie opinion could be formed on the basis of facts available to warrant the investigation. It might be only through a detailed probe that the intention, if any, behind the above acts resulting in substantial loss to various interests in society through the company could be established. If the above acts were done intentionally (mens rea), adverse consequences may follow including penalising the guilty. Establishing mens rea is the purpose behind any legal framework of this kind. It is essential to invoke such provisions where the funds of public and creditors are vested in the hands of a few individuals for the benefit of the former. Thus, the affairs of the company had to be investigated in respect of the years 1990-91, 1991-92 and 1992-93 including the role of any of financial institutions in this regard.

HEADNOTE: Section 213, read with section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013/ Section 237, read with section 394 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of Company's affairs - Appellant filed an application for holding meeting of shareholders for approval of scheme of amalgamation - Single Judge finding some irregularities directed investigation by various agencies - Appellant filed appeal contending that Single Judge was carrying on roving enquiry and he should either allow or dismiss its application - Whether Single Judge was competent to issue direction under section 237(a)(ii) and, therefore, Single Judge was justified in carrying on investigation - Held, yes - Whether however, it was for Central Government to decide which authority would investigate and, therefore, it was a fit and proper case for Central Government to consider as to whether an investigation should be carried out by appropriate agency having authority in law followed by action that would be permitted in law - Held, yes - Whether appellant could not be permitted to proceed with proposed scheme of amalgamation and, therefore, application for convening meeting of shareholders was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 12  13]CL : Single Judge while sanctioning scheme of amalgamation is competent to issue direction under section 237(a)(ii) and then it is for Central Govt. to decide which authority would investigate

FACT: The appellant filed an application before the Single Judge proposing a scheme of amalgamation with M.

The Judge initially directed the Registrar of Companies to conduct an investigation and file a report.

The report of Registrar would reveal, the company had issued share premium to large number of companies mostly private companies on the same day and used funds for investments to a small extent and made advances to others. There were crores of investments involving a large number of private companies.

The Judge directed the Director, Revenue Intelligence to conduct an enquiry as to whether there was any money trail. The company preferred an appeal.

The Single Judge directed Ministry of Corporate Affairs to carry investigation. Accordingly, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs asked the SFIO to conduct such investigation. SFIO submitted a report, inter alia, pointing out irregularity in the affairs of the company.

Then Single Judge asked RBI to submit its report, which submitted its preliminary report observing, that the company might have carried on business as non-banking financial company without obtaining registration with the Reserve Bank of India or complying with the other conditions set by the Reserve Bank of India for non-banking financial companies.

The appellant contended the Judge, despite the restrictions being imposed by the Division Bench continued to carry on roving enquiry that would be an unending process.

In appeal, the appellant contended that the Judge should either allow its petition for holding meetings of the shareholders to ascertain their wishes or dismiss it so that the appellant could take further steps in the matter.

HELD: Section 391 imposed wide discretion upon the Judge. The Judge expressed doubt as to the function of the company. Such doubt ultimately came true as is found from the reports particularly of the SFIO. Hence, before the company was permitted to go ahead with the scheme, the Court was duty bound to remove doubt if any, in its mind as to whether such scheme was being propounded for an oblique purpose. The Court was not a mere rubber stamp. [Para 10]

In the instant case, the Single Judge passed series of orders directing various agencies to carry out investigations. Looking to the facts the Single Judge is to be agreed with, there would certainly be a justification to carry on investigation. If one looks to the income tax assessment order one would find, for the assessment year 2007-08 the company earned net profit for Rs. 290. They suffered penalty. The total income that was assessed was Rs. 3400 only and the company paid tax for Rs. 1,046. Such an insignificant company proposed scheme of amalgamation involving crores through allotment of shares at a huge premium. However, the Single Judge was perhaps not correct in either directing Director, Revenue Intelligence or the Reserve Bank of India. He was competent to issue direction under section 237(a)(ii). The Single Judge was right in sending the issue to the Ministry of Corporate Affairs being the appropriate authority of the Central Government. However, it is for the Central Government to decide which authority would investigate. Be that as it may, the report of SFIO would clearly show, despite being informed, the company did not appear. Hence, appellant was not right in saying, opportunity was not given. It is a fit and proper case for the Central Government to consider as to whether an investigation should be carried out by appropriate agency having authority in law followed by action that is permitted in law. [Para 12]

Considering the backdrop, the appellant cannot be permitted to proceed with the proposed scheme of amalgamation. Hence, the application for convening meeting of the shareholders is dismissed. [Para 13]

HEADNOTE: Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 -Investigation of company’s affairs in other cases - In inspection conducted under section 209A against respondent-company by virtue of order of Department of Company Affairs, certain irregularities and violations of provisions of Act were pointed out - There was also a complaint by Small Investor Protection Forum against respondent- company - Respondent-company had made huge investment in certain companies within a short spell of 3-4 months though its main object was not to enter into share market - Within short spell of two months, respondent-company had raised its authorized capital from Rs. 50,000 to Rs. 12 crores - Whether genesis and origin of huge funds invested by respondent-company in share market when they were not in that business, needed to be probed into - Held, yes - Whether therefore, Central Government was to be directed to undertake investigation of respondent-company under section 237 - Held, yes

FACT: In the inspection conducted under section 209 against respondent-company, certain irregularities and violations of provisions of the Act were pointed out and necessary action had been initiated by the Registrar. The petitioner filed petition under section 237 seeking investigation into affairs of respondent-company on the ground that respondent-company had connection with ‘KP’ group of companies and there was also a complaint by Small Investor Protection Forum. The case of the petitioner was that as per the balance sheet of the company as on 31-12-2000, the huge funds of the company were used primarily in share market during the scam period and huge investments were made in the shares of certain companies, which was not the main object of the respondent-company; and that the management had conducted the business of the company with intent to defraud its creditors, members, etc.

HELD: The respondent submitted that whatever shares had been purchased by those companies, which formed part of the ‘K’, had been purchased through stock exchange or public issue or between shareholders of the company in the normal course of business. There were no direct transactions by the company and the ‘K’ for dealing with those shares. The respondent had also forwarded copies of index of folios of shares which had been purchased by various parties from time-to-time. It was difficult to make out any proposition out of those huge papers submitted by the respondent. [Para 12]

The irregularities/violations of the provisions of the Act had already been taken care of by the Registrar of Companies, but some revealing propositions came out from the documents and averments of the case. The company was incorporated as early as in 1982 and since then, the authorized share capital was Rs. 5 lakhs and paid up capital was Rs. 15,000 as on 13-12-1999; but huge investments in share capital had been made within a short spell of 3 to 4 months. It was also admitted position that the company made investment of Rs. 83,41,00,000 in the shares of the certain companies when the main object of the company was not to enter the business in share market. The lead to value of huge investment went down after stock scam took place in March, 2001. It was also interesting to note that within a spell of two months, the authorized capital was raised first from Rs. 50,000 to Rs. 11 crores and thereafter to Rs. 12 crores. The genesis and origin of this huge funds invested by the respondent-company in share market when it was not in the business, needed to be probed into. It was difficult to find from the documents placed on record as to whether there was any relationship in the transactions with the ‘KP’ group of companies or those were the normal transactions of the business. That could only be found out by investigating the matter in depth. [Para 13]

In the light of the above discussion, the petition was to be allowed. Accordingly, the Central Government was to be directed to undertake the investigation of respondent-company under section 237 and take suitable action on the basis of the report when received. [Para 14]
