On appeal :

In year 2008, respondent Nos. 1 and 2, on the representation of one Managing Director (MD) of respondent No. 3 company, invested in a commercial project called Festival City Mall, being launched by respondent No. 3 company. The respondent Nos. 1 and 2 were assured of returns, failing which respondent No. 3 and its directors were to be jointly and severally liable to pay interest at rate of 2.15 per cent per annum on the amount remaining unpaid to respondent Nos. 1 and 2. The respondent Nos. 1 and 2 were collectively allocated 17 shops in the project.

The project, however, ran into trouble and the construction was stalled. Neither the possession was offered nor was the assured return or the interest thereon given to respondent Nos. 1 and 2.

The respondent Nos. 1 and 2, in the year 2009 filed a winding up petition before the High Court, against respondent No. 3 company. During the course of the winding up proceedings, the Single Judge of the High Court directed the respondent No. 3 to deposit a sum of Rs. 1.5 crore with the Registrar of the High Court. However, the said direction was not complied with, and, therefore, vide order of Single Judge of the High Court, the respondent No. 3 company went into liquidation.

There were several other investors who too had invested in the project. Various complaints were filed against the respondent no. 3 company and its directors which resulted in an FIR being registered. Subsequently, the investigation thereon resulted in a charge sheet, wherein it was alleged that huge sums of money were diverted, defalcated and siphoned off from the corpus of respondent No. 3 company, which was meant to be utilized for the construction of the project.

It was alleged that respondent No. 3 company had, in fact, siphoned off the monies of investors to four intermediate companies who, in turn, further transferred the money to the consortium of six land owning companies. These six land-owning companies were, allegedly, related party companies of respondent No. 3. It was further alleged that these six related party companies had then purchased the subject land for the Project Mall extending to area admesuring to 115 acres. A development and management agreement was entered into between the appellant herein and a consortium of six land-owning companies for exclusive developmental rights over 11 properties extending to 115 acres of land in a real estate project launched by the consortium of six companies for a consideration of Rs. 43 crores. Vide interim orders, the Single Judge of the High Court restrained the six companies from transferring, selling or alienating the properties till further orders.

Aggrieved by the same, the appellant as well as respondent No. 4 preferred applications for vacation of the aforesaid interim orders which were allowed by the Single Judge

The Division Bench of the Delhi High Court, vide the impugned judgment and order, allowed the appeal, thereby restraining once again the transfer, selling or alienation of the properties purchased by the consortium of six companies.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

held.text:
Unfortunately it appeared that there is no legislation which can effectively control the mushrooming of companies which tempt small investors to deposit or invest their life-savings in such companies, promising to pay fanciful returns on their investment but actually defrauding the investors after siphoning off large amounts from such investments. It is also unfortunate that Nationalised Banks are also advancing loans to such institutions without adequate security from such companies as well as their directors. The situation on the whole, prima facie, is not very happy and knowing fully well the parameters of the powers of the Court as well as the self-imposed restrictions under article 226 of the Constitution, the Courts, cannot be silent spectators to such piquant situations.

It, was appeared that respondent No. 1 and such other companies, which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, are committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their life-long savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without their being any basis. Further, in agricultural production, this type of high returns are impossibility in this country. It appears that, because of these empty, false promises, investors are duped and the company's monies are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

The Apex Court in case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Co. (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401, held that the concept of corporate entity is evolved to encourage and promote trade and commerce but not to commit illegalities or to defraud people.

The Court has also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court was exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties.

Applying the aforesaid ratio and taking into consideration the fact that large number of investors were being defrauded by employing the corporate veil, which may amount to a criminal offence, and also the fact that under Criminal Law property acquired by fraud, cheating, etc., can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions could be issued by the Court to search and seize such property. Further, under article 226 of the Constitution, the Court can issue appropriate directions for not only enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III of constitution but 'for any other purpose', and 'any other purpose 'would include such public interest purpose.

In this view of the matter the Court passed the order directing an enquiry freezing of accounts of respondent-company and attachment of its properties.

The Reserve Bank of India was directed to appoint at least three auditors with other necessary staff to carry out the inquiry and assist the Deputy Commissioner of Police in carrying out such inquiry:

Respondent No. 2 was directed, inter alia, to state on oath in an affidavit the following:—

(i) The list of their movable and immovable properties and all assets and the location thereof;

(ii) The list of their bank accounts and the particulars thereof, including the names and addresses of the banks and the amounts therein.

There was great substance in the submission of the petitioners that the aforementioned state of affairs required immediate remedial attention. Prima facie, it was apparent that the third respondent had mobilised large deposits from the public and that innocent persons who had invested their money, had not been repaid The officials and other persons associated with the third respondent including the field-staff had formed new companies with the object of siphoning funds and assets of the third respondent to the detriment of the interest of the depositors.

Prima facie, it appeared that the respondents and such other companies, which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, are committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their lifelong savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without there being any basis. It appears that, because of these empty false promises, investors are duped and the Companies' monies are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

In the case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Company (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401, the Apex Court has referred to the discussion on the topic of corporate veil in Palmer's Company Law and has quoted with approval the observations that Courts have shown themselves willing to lifting the veil where the device of incorporation is used for some illegal or improper purpose.

The Courts have also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court is exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties. The Courts have also observed that in India, the Courts are not only Courts of law, but also the Courts of equity.

Considering the fact that a large number of investors prima facie appeared to have been defrauded, that the allegations of fraud and cheating if established would amount to a criminal offence and in view, of the fact that under the criminal law property acquired by fraud or cheating can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions were required to be issued by the Court to search and seize the property of the company. Under article 226 the Court can issue appropriate directions not only for enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III but 'for any other purpose' and 'any other purpose' would include a purpose for the protection of public interest. Therefore, order was passed directing the Commissioner, Police to appoint DC, Police to follow all assets and properties of respondent No. 3 company and to take necessary action for their seizure.

Code of Criminal Procedure

Sections 155 to 157 of the Code of Criminal Procedure would oblige the State to act on information received in non-cognizable cases and cognizable cases. Section 157 would lay down the procedure for investigation. Section 158 would suggest a procedure for submission of report. Section 159 onwards would lay down the procedure till the issue is brought to logical conclusion. Sudipta's Letter to SEBI on 1-4-2013 and CBI on 6-4-2013

Sudipta offered explanation to SEBI pleading innocence. According to him, the fall of the group was a result of wrong business decision and recession in the market. Sanchaita Episode

In later part of 1970s Sanchaita Investment, a partnership firm mostly operated in the urban part of the State based in Calcutta. They collected lump sum amounts as and by way of deposit refundable with high returns payable on monthly basis. The firm initially established credence by paying interest to the depositors on the firm date and obviously failed to sustain in absence of appropriate returns of investment that they made either in realty sector or film sector or otherwise. The matter reached up to the Apex Court level. The Apex Court passed an extraordinary order appointing a committee that would have an immense power including that of a Civil Court as well having summary jurisdiction. The committee would be headed by a retired District Judge to be nominated by the Chief Justice having other members on the Board. The committee would be entitled to attach any property either belonging to the firm or its agents or benamidars or anyone having nexus with Sanchaita, after forming an opinion, the property was acquired with Sanchaita money. The Commissioner would invite objection, in case any objection was put against the attachment, such objection would be considered and disposed of by a Division Bench of the High Court to be nominated by the Chief Justice and on a failure to sustain the objection by the objector the property would be sold and the proceeds would be distributed amongst the small objectors. The Civil Court was divested of the power to deal with the issue. The Apex Court passed such order presumably under Article 142. Such power, the High Court does not have. The other similar companies were wound up. In cases where companies were established under the Companies Act, 1956, the Official Liquidator disposed of the assets to pay off the dues of the creditors. [Para 64]

The petitioner submitted that once the petition was admitted, there was no discretion with the court but to pass the order of winding-up and appoint Official Liquidator as liquidator of the company. Admission of a petition for winding-up of the company is prima facie proof of the admitted liability. The object of publication of admission in the newspaper is to invite objections from the persons interested for and against the order of winding-up of the company. If there is no discretion with the court at that stage but to pass the order of winding-up, the very purpose of publication of the admission is rendered nugatory. The company court is required to examine whether the winding-up of the company is in the interest of shareholders, secured and unsecured creditors, workers as well as in public interest. It is natural consequence of admission of petition. Thus, there was no merit in the contention of the petitioner that the company court had no discretion after the admission of the petition but to pass the order of winding-up. [Para 8]

A perusal of the written statement filed by the company showed that the liability was not disputed. Rather, it had sought intervention of the High Court in whose supervision the investors might be repaid to prevent further loss of prestige to the company. It had been stated that the company had assets worth Rs. 1500 crores as against liability of only Rs. 761 crores and the company was very much in a position to pay its dues. It was stated that the company was set up in 1987 and till 1988, there had been no default in repayment of any maturity amounts and refunds of investors. The company disclosed that in 1998, SEBI filed writ petition No. 344 of 1998 before the Mumbai High Court seeking, inter alia, that the company might be prevented from conducting its business. Such writ petition was opposed on the ground that the petition was not maintainable as an instrumentality of a State without any statutory power, was not entitled to seek any relief against the private party. The respondent-company was called upon to satisfy the Mumbai High Court in the interest of investors with regard to its workability. The company got its assets valued which were assessed at Rs. 1,071.55 crores in addition to Rs. 33,880 crores on account of movable assets and bank balance as on 31-12-1997 against the total liability of 761 crores as on 31-12-1997. It was further stated that the company invited offers for sale of its certain properties but none of the buyers had shown any interest in view of the restraint imposed by the Mumbai High Court on 30-9-1999. Ultimately, the Mumbai High Court had appointed a retired Judge as private receiver for sale of 19 properties as set out in the schedule vide order dated 31-1-2000. [Para 11]

It was apparent from the above that there was no dispute as to the liability of the company towards the investors. It was the stand of the company that it had assets more than Rs. 1,000 crores which were sufficient to discharge the liability of the investors. It had come on record that the directors of the company were in custody since December, 2000 and the company had not been able to dispose of any of the properties for payment to the investors. Thus, a mechanism was required to be drawn so as to facilitate the sale of the property of the company at the earliest with a view to ensure payment to the investors without any further delay. The interest of such large number of creditors was required to be watched by the company court and the management of the company could not be permitted to take such investors for a ride. [Para 12]

With a view to protect the interest of the large number of creditors and shareholders of the company, it was just and appropriate to appoint provisional liquidator for control, management and sale of the movable and immovable properties so as to fetch maximum price thereof with a view to satisfy the claim of 25 lakh investors in a proper manner. In the present case, acts of managements which were prejudicial to the interest of the company and which aroused suspicion of foul play were already established. The blocking of substantial funds in another company when the main object was not investment, diversion of project money to various bodies incorporated or unincorporated, the laxity in the collection of loans, the unusual facility of allowing repayment of principal with interest still outstanding, payment of substantial commission to a private company, substantial increase in the cost of materials and wasteful expenses all went to show that the funds of the company had gone out to third parties and were not easily recoverable.

An investigator under section 237(b ) would be clothed with sufficient powers to investigate not only into the affairs of the company in question, but also related companies and firms and to that extent this investigation had a wider coverage. In addition, information could also be called by the investigator from any other company with the previous approval of the Central Government. Only such a kind of investigation would establish the link, if any, between the ultimate beneficiary and those incharge of the management of the funds of the company. Ultimately, the investigation might not be able to establish any link. However, prima facie opinion could be formed on the basis of facts available to warrant the investigation. It might be only through a detailed probe that the intention, if any, behind the above acts resulting in substantial loss to various interests in society through the company could be established. If the above acts were done intentionally (mens rea), adverse consequences may follow including penalising the guilty. Establishing mens rea is the purpose behind any legal framework of this kind. Thus, the affairs of the company had to be investigated in respect of the years 1990-91, 1991-92 and 1992-93 including the role of any of financial institutions in this regard.

The details of the outstandings from the group companies as also the details of the investments were available. It was seen that the company Judge had directed almost a detailed questionnaire and sought the information which was extremely relevant and which would give the complete picture regarding the financial status, etc., of the company. The information sought also appeared to be extremely relevant in coming to the conclusion as to whether the transactions were of bona fide nature or not. There was also a second affidavit filed on record before the order of the Court dated 17-8-2000 seeking further information and even in this affidavit, the financial scenario of the company and its dealings generally were highlighted. In fact, from a reading of those affidavits, it was clear that the company had access to all that was filed before the Court including the petitions. The Single Judge had painstakingly and studiously gone into the whole financial aspects giving a thorough picture of the financial status of the appellant-company itself as also vis-a-vis the other companies floated by it. The Judge had also taken stock of the various transactions with reference to the figures involved in those transactions. It was true that the Judge had made a reference to that report. However, he was completely convinced that there was no necessity of supplying the copy of every document on which the RBI had relied in support of its petitions. The company had a complete idea as to what was the stand of the RBI and what were the precise grounds on which the RBI was moving against it. The company not only got the notice of the petitions but a complete opportunity to show the reasons against it in writing besides the hearing in the open Court. Therefore, this was not a case of breach of natural justice on account of the denial of the opportunity.

There was no doubt that the considerations enumerated by the company Judge for the appointment of provisional liquidator were abundantly available in the present case. Therefore, the Single Judge was justified in admitting the petitions and in appointing the provisional liquidator.

The Judge had given the directions that the report forwarded by the RBI to the Additional Director General of Police, in-charge of the Economic Offence Wing, to whom the RBI had forwarded the report of the Special Auditor should be treated as the first information report with regard to the apparent fraud committed by the company and those in-charge of the company. This action, according to the Single Judge, would be in addition to any of the cases that might have been registered against the company. The Judge then directed that steps should be taken against those involved in the apparent conspiracy to siphon off or divert the funds of the company. The observations made by the Single Judge directing an investigation to be made had got nothing to do with sections 541 and 542. Section 543 also speaks about the assessment of damages for any mis-application, retainer, misfeasance or breach of trust by the directors. Even that section had got nothing to do with the directions given by the Single Judge. That is a general power of the court and there can be no doubt that every court has that power and the Single Judge also had the same power.

Section 443 provides for the powers of the court. Clause (c) of section 443(1) thereof speaks of the Court's powers to make any interim order which the Court thinks fit to order an investigation. This has got no connection with sections 541 to 543 and, therefore, the argument that that part of the order was without jurisdiction was to be rejected.

The Court has ample powers including the power under section 443 to recommend an investigation. After all, an investigation into the affairs of the company does not mean a final conviction of the Directors. This argument, therefore, was to be rejected. The criminal liability would be decided by the competent Criminal Court on the evidence tendered before it by the prosecution. The question of the bail and release would also be decided by the Criminal Court which was dealing with the matters. The release of a person on bail in this case was the exclusive right of the Criminal Court dealing with the accused persons, viz., the directors of the company. The payment of Rs. 50 crores might have been considered as one of the considerations for grant of bail but, that did not divest the Criminal Court of its powers to deal with the bail matter and to deal further with the criminal matter pending before it in its own rights.

Accordingly, the application was disposed of.

the decisions after the adjudication process is over but such bar is not absolute and in a given case if the petitions are filed on the ground that the authority who has initiated the proceedings lacks inherent jurisdiction, the Court may entertain such writ petition and may issue appropriate writ, order or direction under article 226 of the Constitution of India. In the instant case, it could not be said that the petition was not maintainable or that it was not required to be entertained at all. [Para 24] It is true, as argued by the petitioners, that while exercising powers under the Act, it is not open to the SEBI to encroach upon the powers vested with the Institute under the Chartered Accountants Act. However, it was required to be examined as to whether in substance by initiating the proceedings under the SEBI Act, the SEBI was trying to overreach or encroach upon the powers conferred under the Chartered Accountants Act. In that connection, it was required to be noted that the SEBI has powers under the Act and the Regulation to take remedial measures in connection with safeguarding the interest of investors and regulate the securities market. Under section 11, the SEBI has power to prohibit fraudulent and unfair trade practices relating to securities market. Under section 11(4), the SEBI is entitled to pass appropriate orders in the interest of investors or securities market and is entitled to take measures as prescribed in the said section. Under section 11B, powers have been conferred on the SEBI to give appropriate directions even to any person or class of persons referred to in section 12 or associated with the securities market. The powers available to the SEBI under the Act are to be exercised in the interest of investors and interest of securities market. In order to safeguard the interest of investors or interest of securities market, the SEBI is entitled to take all ancillary steps and measures to see that the interest of the investors is protected. Looking to the provisions of the SEBI Act and the Regulations framed thereunder, it cannot be said that in a given case if there is material against any chartered accountant to the effect that he was instrumental in preparing false and fabricated accounts, the SEBI has absolutely no power to take any remedial or preventive measures in such a case. It cannot be said that the SEBI cannot give appropriate directions in safeguarding the interest of the investors of a listed company. Whether such directions and orders are required to be issued or not is a matter of inquiry. The jurisdiction of the SEBI would also depend upon the evidence which is available during such inquiry. It is true, as argued by the petitioners, that the SEBI cannot regulate the profession of chartered accountants. That proposition could not be disputed in any manner. By taking remedial and preventive measures in the interest of investors and for regulating the securities market, if any steps are taken by the SEBI, it can never be said that it is regulating the profession of the chartered accountants. So far as listed companies are concerned, the SEBI has all the powers under the Act and the Regulations to take all remedial and protective measures to safeguard the interest of investors and securities market. So far as the role of auditors is concerned, it is a very important role under the Companies Act. As posited in section 227 of the Companies Act, every auditor of a company shall have a right of access at all times to the books and account and vouchers of the company, whether kept at the head office of the company or elsewhere, and shall be entitled to require from the officers of the company such information and explanations as the auditor may think necessary for the performance of his duties. The auditors in the company are functioning as statutory auditors. They have been appointed by the shareholders by majority. They owe a duty to the shareholders and are required to give a correct picture of the financial affairs of the company. It is not uncommon now-a-days that for financial gains even small investors are investing money in the share market. As was rightly pointed out by respondent, there are cases where even retired persons are investing their retiral dues in the purchase of shares and, ultimately, if such a person is defrauded, he will be totally ruined and may be put in a situation where his life savings are wiped out. With a view to safeguard the interests of such investors, it is the duty of the SEBI to see that maximum care is required to be taken to protect the interest of such investors so that they may not be subjected to any fraud or cheating in the matter of their investments in the securities market. Normally, an investor invests his money by considering the financial health of the company and in order to find out the same, one would naturally bank upon the accounts and balance-sheets of the company. If it is unearthed during inquiry before the SEBI that a particular chartered accountant, in connivance and in collusion with the officers/directors of the company has concocted false accounts, there is no reason as to why to protect the interests of investors and regulate the securities market such a person cannot be prevented from dealing with the auditing of such a public listed company. The SEBI has got inherent powers to take all ancillary steps to safeguard the interest of investors and securities market. The powers conferred under various provisions of the Act are wide enough to cover such an eventuality and it cannot be given any restrictive meaning as suggested by the petitioners

The petitioner had clearly brought out that the promoters of the company, after having mobilised enormous amount of about Rs. 7 crores, more particularly from NRIs, had not bothered to conduct the affairs of the company in accordance with the provisions of law and in a prudent manner. The petitioner having invested more than Rs. 50 lakhs, had been running from pillar to post to get some information on the functioning of the company without any success. The Regional Director, Dept. of Company Affairs had also in his report reported that the company had not filed balance sheets from 1994 onwards. Notwithstanding the various observations made by the Chartered Accountant who had inspected the books of account and the fact that the Regional Director had initiated prosecution against the company, the very fact that the company had not finalised its accounts from 1993-94 onwards and that no AGM had been held after 1993 in spite of the fact that it was a listed company to protect the interest of a large number of shareholders, suitable remedial action deserved to be taken especially when the respondents had not chosen to participate in the proceedings. Accordingly, the Central Government was directed to carry out an investigation into the affairs of the company and take appropriate further action on receipt of the investigation report.

Further, in exercise of powers under section 402, the Central Government was also directed to appoint a suitable professional person as a director on the board of the company for a period of 3 years from the date of appointment to effectively monitor the conduct of affairs of the company.

1992 as the cut off year for preparing the list, the argument that the line had been drawn out arbitrarily excluding companies which had issued capital prior to 1992, was also unsustainable. The list of 80 companies was not a rigid list as freedom had been given to add names to the list considered necessary and the SEBI had also submitted that the identification exercise was not a one-time exercise but a continuing process. The matter under inquiry was not hit by the provisions of the Limitation Act. It was incorrect to say that by using section 11B the SEBI was usurping the powers of Registrar of Companies or that they were interfering with the management of the company. Sections 11 and 11B are interconnected and co-extensive as both these sections are mainly focussed on investor protection. On a perusal of the said section 11 it could be seen that the SEBI had been in no uncertain terms mandated to protect the interests of investors in securities by such measures as it thought fit. The expression ‘measure’ has not defined in the Act. ‘Measure’ in its generic sense is of wider amplitude. While section 11 deals with the functions of the Board section 11B is on the powers of the Board. Section 11B is in a sense a functional tool in the hands of the Board. In effect section 11B is one of the executive measures available to the SEBI to enforce its prime duty of investor protection. SEBI is thus empowered to issue directions in the interest of investors to any person or class of persons referred to in section 12 or associated with the securities market. It could not be said that a company having its shares listed on the exchange was out of the reach of sections 11 and 11B. Since the company was operating through its board of directors, the directors of the company also could be considered as persons associated with the capital market, as long as the company’s shares were listed on the exchange. Thus, taking into consideration the scope and reach of sections 11 and 11B it could not be said that the SEBI was lacking authority to issue direction to the appellant. Further, the impugned direction was not one for violation of the Companies Act or the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act. It was issued in the interest of investors under section 11B independent of the provisions of the Companies Act and the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act. Further, there was nothing wrong in relying on a report submitted by an authority like stock exchange, as the information furnished by itself was only a starting point. An inquiry thereafter followed and the concerned persons were given sufficient opportunities to put across their views before the authorities. Similarly exclusion of public deposits and debt instruments from the scope of inquiry could not be considered to be in any way discriminatory, as the matter relating to public deposits etc., was taken care of by other regimes vested with powers for the purpose. For these reasons, the SEBI was justified in pursuing the course of action against the vanishing companies and its promoters and directors and the SEBI was legally invested with the requisite authority for the purpose.

The main reason based on which the impugned order had been issued was an inference, in the absence of relevant material before the SEBI, that the appellant had misused the fund collected from the public for purposes other than for which it was collected. In terms of section 11(2)(i ) the SEBI is empowered to call for information, etc. from the appellant-company also for the reason that it was also a person associated with the securities market. The fund utilisation by the appellant-company need be looked into with reference its records in the context of the charge of misuse of funds raised from the public issue. Since the appellants had expressed their willingness to make available the requisite information, in depth study of the same would be useful to reach at a definite conclusion and also to pursue the matter thereafter, if considered necessary, to protect the interest of the investors. Since the impugned order was based on inference and was ex parte, it was proper that the appellants should be given one more opportunity to furnish the information to the SEBI in a reasonable time frame and the SEBI in the light of that information, would pass appropriate orders in accordance with the provisions of the law. The Department of Company Affairs may also be requested, if so desired, to examine the books of account and other records of the appellant company to ascertain the utilisation of the funds and if necessary follow up the matter.

The impugned order did not in any way redress the grievances of the persons who had already invested in the shares of the appellant-company. The prohibition put in on the appellants was effective only prospectively. Since the appellants had come forward to furnish the details, and the impugned order was ex parte, it was felt that further inquiry on the lines embarked on by the SEBI and follow-up action thereafter would be in the interest of the investors. For the purpose it was felt that the matter should be remanded.

Hence, the impugned order was set aside and the matter was remanded with the above directions.

There was overwhelming material available pointing to the circumstances suggesting that the business of the company was conducted for a fraudulent and unlawful purpose. The persons concerned in the management of the company had been guilty of fraud, misfeasance or other misconduct towards the company. It was a case squarely covered under the provisions of section 235 as the pre-conditions for initiating such an action existed as was clear from the foregoing. [Para 15] The directors owe fiduciary duty to the shareholders and they have to function in not only good faith, but in utmost good faith. In the instant case, shareholders’ faith seemed to have been belied. The petitioner was on a very sound footing besides having come to the CLB bona fide. Only investigation under section 235 could bring out the true state of affairs. An order to investigate under section 235 in any case could not be prejudicial to the respondent. An order of the CLB under this section directing an investigation is only analogous to the issue of a fact finding commission. This particular power of the CLB is not of a judicial or quasi-judicial nature. It is a power of administrative nature and the CLB may even take the initiative suo motu or on the application or information supplied by any shareholder or other person. Under this section, directing an investigation is only analogous to the issue of a fact finding commission by a civil court for looking into accounts or making an investigation and does not amount to a judgment within clause 15 of the Letters Patent, so as to enable an aggrieved party to appeal. An order of investigation is not an end by itself; it is only a means to find out the full facts of the acts complained of. It is nothing, but an exploratory measure to be proved or disproved with reference to the facts later on ascertained. This discretionary power of the CLB has to be exercised in good faith. An investigation may be ordered when public interest is involved or detriment to the interests of shareholders had been caused surreptitiously. Such investigation should not be taken lightly. Unless proper grounds exist for investigation of the affairs of the company, investigation cannot be ordered. The allegations made in the petition were such matters which would require an investigation. [Para 16]

In view of above, there was reason to believe that there was likelihood of the existence of malpractices envisaged in the provisions of section 235. To prove the prima facie case of ‘intent to fraud’ and misfeasance on general public and specifically the investor in the instant case and conducting the business of the company otherwise for a fraudulent and unlawful purpose, the petitioner’s prayer could be granted for ordering an investigation under section 235. [Para 17]

The petition was, accordingly, to be allowed. [Para 18]

the payment is not made by a company, the winding-up of the company can be ordered, as the company would be said to be unable to pay its debts. In a case where no properties of the company are available, and the company has not taken any steps worth being effective for making the payment for a considerable period, despite the order of the CLB, the company petition for winding-up would not be either not maintainable nor it can be rejected on this ground. [Para 25] In the instant case, the order passed by the CLB indicated that the CLB on the basis of the admission of the company that a large number of deposits were outstanding for repayment on maturity, decided to invoke suo motu powers to order repayment of the amount deposited as provided under section 45QA of the 1934 Act. Accordingly, the company was directed to indicate reasons for default and also its proposals to meet the pending claims as well as those which might arise in future on maturity. The company furnished a detailed statement of its reasons for its failure to repay all the matured deposits and also a scheme for repayment of both outstanding matured deposits and also the deposits that would be maturing in future. The company submitted a scheme for repayment of deposits during the period of five years, the gist of which had been quoted in the order of the CLB itself. Another scheme was given on behalf of the depositors asking for repayment scheme of 48 months. The company submitted a revised repayment schedule for 48 months and had published the scheme in two newspapers. [Para 27]

Thereafter, various dates were fixed by the CLB in which the company absented though representatives of the depositors and a large number of depositors attended the proceedings. The CLB, therefore, after observing that due opportunity had been given to the company to make its submission on the suggestions given by the depositor but no one was present on behalf of the company and directors had also chosen to remain absent whereas large number of depositors were involved who had put in their hard earned money with the company, found that the matter could not be allowed to be dragged. The CLB on going through the revised scheme submitted by the company and suggestions made by the advocate on behalf of the depositors, and with a view to balance the interest of the company and the depositors and also the public interest at large issued a detailed order as to payment of deposited amount. [Para 28]

Despite that order, the record revealed that not a single penny was paid nor any effective step was taken by the company or its directors for making any payment to the depositors. Since the company failed to make the repayment even as per the directions and the scheme and the company did not take any interest in the proceedings nor the directors attended the proceedings despite themselves having come to the Board for getting the scheme approved for payment, the investors were well within their right to approach the Court for winding-up of the company on the ground that the company had failed to make the payment and it was unable to pay its debts. [Para 30]

For allowing the winding-up petition, it is essential that there are dues of the creditors against the company, namely, debt, and that the company has failed to make the payment at the given intervals or at such intervals in time when the depositors have asked for payment and that the company is unable to pay its debts. In case all the three ingredients aforesaid are established, besides other contents, if, at all, required to be proved, the creditors would be justified in asking the winding-up of the company. [Para 31]

The appellant-company had floated various attractive schemes giving dreams and illusions to lakhs of people for having better return of their deposits so made and had collected the deposits but instead of acting bona fidely in taking the investment and making payment of dues, it indulged in siphoning off its money in other companies of the same group having almost common directors under some loan agreements which money was never sought to be realized from the company. [Para 38]

Hence, the view taken by the Company Judge regarding conduct of the company and its directors in collecting huge amount from the depositors and not paying it back, and deliberate attempt to misguide and mislead the depositors by giving false assurance of making repayment on future dates, coupled by the failure on the part of the company to make payment as per the scheme approved by the CLB, gave full jurisdiction to the Company Judge to entertain the petition for winding-up and to order for winding-up of the company. [Para 41]

So far as the appellant’s contention as to the validity of the statutory notice under section 434 issued by the investors to the company was concerned, no substantial defect in the notice was found so as to make it invalid, the invalidity of the notice even if any in the instant case would not affect the order of the Company Judge allowing winding-up of the company as it was not being disputed by the appellant that the issuance or service of the notice under section 434 was not a condition precedent for filing a winding-up petition against the company under section 433. [Para 42]

SEBI is vested with powers of Civil Court

The Securities Appellate Tribunal ('SAT') which exercises powers under Section 15T of the SEBI Act, it is well settled, is the final adjudicator of facts. The Tribunal has, for the purpose of discharging its functions, the same powers as are vested in a Civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure. Broadly speaking, the Tribunal has trappings of a Court in the sense that it has to determine the appeal placed before it judicially and give a fair hearing to the parties, to accept evidence and also order for inspection and discovery of documents, compel attendance of witnesses and to pass a reasoned order which gives finality to the dispute, subject to the appeal to Supreme Court under Section 15Z of the SEBI Act. Findings of fact generally fall in the domain of the Tribunal provided it stays within its jurisdiction.

Situations may also be there, where the evidence taken as a whole is not reasonably capable of supporting the findings recorded by the Tribunal or the Tribunal could have reasonably recorded that conclusion.

Questions repeatedly posed in instant case before SEBI as well as before SAT, were with regard to the nature of OFCDs issued by Saharas. RHPs produced had disclosed that Saharas did not intend the proposed securities to be listed on any stock exchange and that the issues consisted of unsecured OFCDs with an option to convert the same to equity shares. Saharas had also disclosed that the issue was made on a private placement basis and that OFCDs would be offered also to such persons to whom IM would be circulated. But the fact remains that it was circulated to more than three crore people inviting them to subscribe. The same was circulated through ten lakh agents and more than 2900 branch offices and Saharas had a capital base of only 10 lakhs with no other assets or reserves and was a loss making company and had collected nearly 27,000 crores by way of private placement through unsecured OFCDs redeemable/convertible after 48/60/120 months. Fact finding authorities repeatedly asked for information regarding the names, addresses of investors in OFCDs and the amounts subscribed by them. The appellant claimed that it had furnished to SEBI a separate CD giving the details of names of investors, the amount invested etc. along with the password and keys, along with its letter dated 19.4.2011 which, according to the appellant, was never opened or checked.

SEBI, has been vested with the powers of a Civil Court under CPC, as per sub-section (3) of section 11 of the SEBI Act. Under Section 11C, the Board has also been vested with the powers to order investigation to examine whether any person associated with securities market has violated any provision of the Act or the rules or the regulations made or direction issued by the Board. [Para 50]

Money collected by Saharas would amount to collection of money by way of issue of securities to public

Saharas, along with additional documents, filed before the Supreme Court, gave certain details of the persons who have invested. Documents produced before the Supreme Court and before the fact finding authorities do not show the relationship Sahara Group had with the investors. Claim of Saharas was that the investors were their friends, associated group companies, workers/employees and other individuals who were associated/affiliated or connected with Sahara Group. Saharas, in the bonds, sought for a declaration from the applicants that they had been associated with Sahara Group.

No details had been furnished to show what types of association the investors had with Sahara Group. Bonds also required to name an introducer, whose job evidently was to introduce the company to the prospective investor. If the offer was made to those persons related or associated with Sahara Group, there was no necessity of an introducer and an introduction. Burden of proof is entirely on Saharas to show that the investors are/were their employees/ workers or associated with them in any other capacity which they have not discharged.

Fact finding authorities have clearly held that Saharas had not discharged their burden which is purely a question of fact. Facts are elaborately discussed by SEBI (WTM) and SAT, hence those factual details are not to be discussed. No perversity or illegality is found in those findings which call for interference by the Supreme Court sitting under Section 15Z of the SEBI Act. Therefore, the Tribunal is to be fully concurred with that the money collected by Saharas through their RHPs dated 13.3.2008 and 6.10.2009,through the OFCDs, were from the public at large and the same would amount to collection of money by way of issue of securities to the public, a finding which calls for no interference by the Supreme Court sitting under Section 15Z of the SEBI Act. [Para 51]

Section 210 empowers the Central Government to investigate into the affairs of a company/(companies), if it is of the opinion that such investigation is necessary for the reasons mentioned therein, including public interest. For the purpose of the said provision, the Central Government may appoint one or more persons as inspectors to investigate into the affairs of the company and to report thereon in such manner as the Central Government may direct. The SFIO has been established under section 211 of the Companies Act, 2013, which has jurisdiction to investigate into the company/(companies), where the Central Government is of the opinion that it is necessary to investigate into the affairs of a company by the SFIO for different reasons, including the public interest. Where any case has been assigned by the Central Government to the SFIO for investigation under the Act, no other investigating agency of the Central Government or any State Government can proceed with investigation in such case in respect of any offence under the Companies Act and other cases before such agency are required to transfer the relevant documents and records in respect of such offences under the Companies Act to the SFIO. Sub-section (8) of section 211 empowers certain Officers of the SFIO to arrest any person, if on the basis of material in his possession there is reason to believe, which is to be recorded in writing, that any person has been guilty of any offence punishable under sub-section (6) of section 212. [Para 30]

Investigation into company's affairs in other cases can also be done under section 213 on an application made by the eligible members as mentioned in clause (a) of section 213 or on an application made by any other person or otherwise, if it is satisfied that there are circumstances suggesting that the business of the company etc. has been conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members etc. as mentioned in clause (b) of section 213. [Para 31]

From section 213, it is clear that the Tribunal on an application made to it or 'otherwise', if satisfied that there are circumstances suggesting that the business of the company is being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members etc. as mentioned in clause (b) of section 213, after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the parties, direct the Central Government to investigate. [Para 32]

From section 221, it is clear that the Tribunal has power to direct that the transfer, removal or disposal of funds, assets, or properties of the company shall not take place during such period not exceeding three years'. In case of any removal, transfer or disposal of funds, assets, or properties of the company in contravention of the order of the Tribunal under sub-section (1) of section 221, the company is punishable with fine and imprisonment as prescribed under sub-section (2) of section 221. [Para 34]

In the instant case, the Central Government by letter dated 17-2-2018 has directed the SFIO to investigate into the affairs of the respondent company, among other 114 entities. The investigation is currently undergoing and as such, as on date, being satisfied if so required, it is always open to the Central Government to file application under section 241(2), read with section 242 before the Tribunal. [Para 37]

In the interest of regulating the conduct of the company's affairs the interim order cannot be restrictive to any particular or individual person, including the company/companies, existing or erstwhile Officers and employees of the companies if investigation for alleged fraud is pending. [Para 38]

For the purpose of passing interim order, the Tribunal cannot fix the personal liability of delinquent Directors or Managers or Officers or other employees in absence of any specific evidence. Therefore, during the process of investigation and pendency of an application under section 241(2), read with section 242 and in view of powers conferred under section 221, the Tribunal is not only empowered to pass appropriate interim order against the company but also against any person or individual, including the order to desist. [Para 39]

Chapter XVI relates to 'Prevention of Oppression and Mismanagement'. An application to the Tribunal for relief in cases of oppression, etc. can be made by any eligible member(s) of the company under sub-section (1) of section 241 of the Companies Act, 2013, who complains about the oppression and mismanagement as stipulated in clauses (a) & (b) of sub-section (1). [Para 40]

On the other hand, the Central Government, if it is of the opinion that the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interest, it may itself apply to the Tribunal under sub-section (2) of section 241 for an order under Chapter XVI of the Companies Act, 2013. [Para 41]

Under section 235(2) a power is given to the CLB in case where, Inter alia, an application is received from not less than 200 members, or members holding not less than one-tenth of the total voting power in a company, to declare, after giving the parties an opportunity of being heard, that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated by an Inspector or Inspectors. On such a declaration being made, the Central Government shall appoint one or more competent persons as inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company and to report thereon.

The power, therefore, to appoint Inspector to investigate the affairs of a company has to be exercised by the Central Government after a proper preliminary scrutiny by the Registrar or by the CLB as the case may be. It cannot be instituted simply on the basis of allegations made by one shareholder. Under section 237, there is a further power given to the Central Government to appoint Inspectors to investigate the affairs of a company if the company, by a special resolution, or the Court, by order declares that such investigation is necessary. Similarly, this may be done if in the opinion of the CLB there are circumstances suggesting that the business of the company is being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members or any other person or otherwise for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose or in a manner oppressive of any of its members or that the company was formed for any fraudulent or unlawful purpose. The CLB may also come to a conclusion that there are circumstances suggesting that the persons concerned in the formation of the company or management of its affairs have been guilty of fraud, misfeasance or other misconduct towards the company or towards any of its members; or that the members of the company have not been given all the information with respect to its affairs which they might reasonably expect. In these circumstances, on the basis of the opinion so framed by the CLB, the Central Government may order an investigation.

In the instant case no attempt had been made by the respondent to get the affairs of the company investigated in the manner provided under the Act. Neither the Central Government nor the CLB had been moved by the respondent in accordance with law for this purpose. Instead of moving the authorities prescribed under the Act the first respondent had chosen to resort to the writ jurisdiction of the High Court for a direction to have the affairs of the company investigated by the CBI.

The Single Judge before whom the present writ petition came up for hearing very rightly held that the Companies Act provides a forum to consider the grievances made out by the first respondent in the writ petition. When such a forum, statutorily constituted, exists, it is but appropriate that resort to article 226 should be discouraged There is an efficacious alternative remedy available under the statute. In fact under the Companies Act, a more satisfactory solution is available. The Single Judge was right in pointing out that some of the shareholders had initiated proceedings before the CLB. The only grievance of the petitioner in the writ petition was that no orders had been passed thereon. The Single Judge had rightly held that such a grievance could not constitute a ground for invoking the jurisdiction of the High Court under article 226.

Further no public interest was involved in disputes of the kind referred to in the writ petition. They basically dealt with mismanagement of the affairs of the company and oppression of the minority shareholders. The company was only a deemed public limited company. Its shareholding was very closely held The only other factor referred to in the writ petition to invoke the doctrine of so-called public interest, was the fact that the company had borrowed moneys from public institutions. This was no ground for not availing of the statutory remedies provided under the Act before the appropriate statutory forums which are designed for this very purpose.

Therefore, the order of the Single Judge could not be interfered with. The judgment of the Division Bench was set aside.

The petitioner had submitted that the huge public money had been siphoned off by the respondents and that could not be visible to the naked eye. Therefore, there were sufficient grounds to order an investigation under section 237(b). The siphoning-off of the huge amount by 250 front companies in fraudulent manner had been indicated by the income-tax authorities also. The petitioner had also submitted that the new management came much after the loan amounts had been siphoned off. The investigation conducted by the CBI was for trying the accused persons for criminal conspiracy and cheating as criminal offences. Without investigation under section 237(b), it was not possible to discover true and correct facts and modus operandi adopted by the respondents in cheating the petitioner and siphoning-off of the public money. [Para 11]

Therefore, the petition was allowed and an enquiry under section 237(b) was to be ordered with direction to the Central Government to appoint inspectors for the enquiry and take appropriate action on the enquiry report. [Para 12]

The respondent submitted that whatever shares had been purchased by those companies, which formed part of the ‘K’, had been purchased through stock exchange or public issue or between shareholders of the company in the normal course of business. There were no direct transactions by the company and the ‘K’ for dealing with those shares. The respondent had also forwarded copies of index of folios of shares which had been purchased by various parties from time-to-time. It was difficult to make out any proposition out of those huge papers submitted by the respondent. [Para 12]

The irregularities/violations of the provisions of the Act had already been taken care of by the Registrar of Companies, but some revealing propositions came out from the documents and averments of the case. The company was incorporated as early as in 1982 and since then, the authorized share capital was Rs. 5 lakhs and paid up capital was Rs. 15,000 as on 13-12-1999; but huge investments in share capital had been made within a short spell of 3 to 4 months. It was also admitted position that the company made investment of Rs. 83,41,00,000 in the shares of the certain companies when the main object of the company was not to enter the business in share market. The lead to value of huge investment went down after stock scam took place in March, 2001. It was also interesting to note that within a spell of two months, the authorized capital was raised first from Rs. 50,000 to Rs. 11 crores and thereafter to Rs. 12 crores. The genesis and origin of this huge funds invested by the respondent-company in share market when it was not in the business, needed to be probed into. It was difficult to find from the documents placed on record as to whether there was any relationship in the transactions with the ‘KP’ group of companies or those were the normal transactions of the business. That could only be found out by investigating the matter in depth. [Para 13]

In the light of the above discussion, the petition was to be allowed. Accordingly, the Central Government was to be directed to undertake the investigation of respondent-company under section 237 and take suitable action on the basis of the report when received. [Para 14]

Even if the first petitioner-Managing Director, including those connected with the offences, viz., past directors and promoters were sent to the prison, the question still remained whether the Court had done any justice to the depositors. Sentencing the offenders and committing them to the prison was one thing. Ensuring the return of deposits to the poor depositors who made deposits from every nook and corner of this country was an other thing. In the instant case, it was clear that the corporate character was employed by the first petitioner for the purpose of committing illegality and defrauding the others. In such an event, this Court, piercing the corporate veil, could look at the reality behind the corporate veil so as to pass appropriate orders to do substantial justice to the victims. The Managing Director not only incorporated the company but subsequently other companies were brought into effect and that too by the persons who were none other than the close relations and promoters of the first company. The Supreme Court treated all such companies as one entity belonging to one and controlled by one family. The Reserve Bank of India also submitted that the bank was taking steps to initiate prosecution proceedings and also for winding up of the company, as it was a confirmed case of non-refund of deposits. Dehors this submission, this Court also gave number of opportunities to the petitioner to refund the deposits as per their own schedule of payments. Even though the schedule of payment was changed twice on the request of the petitioner, yet there was not even a single case where the company deposited any amount in the account opened by the Advocate-Commissioners. Thus, it proved to be a clear case for winding up.

The fate of lakhs of defrauded depositors by the company was still uncertain. Their aspirations that goose would lay golden eggs for them proved to be costly dream - the goose was not even responding for laying normal eggs. Their sweat and blood invested in the company vanished and plunged them in miseries and frustration. Even the new Act introduced by the Government of Andhra Pradesh did not deal with non-banking companies who had already misused the deposits and it hadonly prospective effect. But the emotions and feelings of parties have no place in judicial proceedings. This Court was required to salvage the situation in accordance with law keeping in view the mandate of the Constitution. It spreads its arms of justice to identify and reach the injustice, and thereby remedy the cause. The efforts of this Court to save the depositors yielded microscopic results. But, at the same time, no offender should be allowed to gain an impression that courts lean towards them. The petitioner failed to respond to the opportunities granted by this Court. The endoscopy of the matter led to inevitable conclusion that physico- judicial therapy was not the cure, but the judicial surgery was the only solution.

Under these circumstances, in the wake of the details referred to above and in order to see that the companies did not defraud the innocent depositors, the writ petition was disposed of with the following directions :

(a )The State Government should constitute a separate cell in the office of the Director General of Police headed by an officer of the rank of Superintendent of Police and above for dealing with Non-Banking Financial Institutions who had already collected the amounts and failed to repay the deposits and which did not possess registration under the Reserve Bank of India Act. The cell should cause discreet enquiries in respect of all such institutions and take immediate action to seize the properties of the company and also the assets of the persons involved in the formation or administration of the company and also the persons who obtained illegal benefit out of the transactions or assets of the company to ensure that the payments were made to the depositors either in full or pro rata depending upon the circumstances of each case. The cell should initiate prosecution under various laws against all the offenders who were either directly or indirectly involved.

(b )In respect of the petitioner-company, the Government of Andhra Pradesh should order immediate investigation by the CBCID by an officer of the rank of Superintendent of Police and above into the irregularities traced out in this order apart from the complaints already made. The criminal prosecution should be launched under the provisions of Indian Penal Code, Reserve Bank of India Act and other laws against not only the Managing Director of the Company the first petitioner, but against all the promoters and also the past directors including other persons who were responsible for misuse of the funds of the company either directly or remotely. All the concerned governmental and non-governmental agencies should extend co-operation to the investigating team. The Depositors Association also shouldassist the investigating agency in this regard.

(c )The Reserve Bank of India should initiate criminal proceedings against the petitioners under section 45MC of the Reserve Bank of India Act forth with and also file an application for winding up of the second petitioner-company under the provisions of the Companies Act, 1956, treating the registered office at Hyderabad as the registered office as the registered office at Mumbai had ceased to work for number of years and Hyderabad office was the only being operated

(d )All the documents delivered by the petitioner to the Advocate- Commissioners, viz., title deeds, etc., should be deposited before the Registrar (Judicial) for safe custody. As and when any requisition was received from the winding up Court, they could be transmitted under proper receipt.

The petitioner held 14.25 per cent shares in the respondent-company and was, admittedly, given affirmative rights as per the agreement. The entire efforts of the respondents had been to justify one resolution passed on 5-1-2002. They had pointed out that all along there was unanimity on transfer of funds, even amounts, the mode of transfer, the investments, etc., and the minutes of resolution dated 5-1-2002 were in furtherance of the decision taken by the board of directors to send/transfer 1 million USD to the wholly owned subsidiary. That contention of the respondents was not borne out from the chronology of the events and the documents. It was an admitted position that when alleged remittance of USD 1 million was made to the subsidiary company, it did not even exist at the relevant time. In the name of unanimous decision, the funds were siphoned off to the three assets management companies. Documents were fabricated for the purpose of effecting the change in the authorized signatories in respect of the investments with the investment funds. The amounts from those deposits, on being received from the investment funds, were deposited in respondent No. 1’s HDFC bank account which should have been closed as per the board’s resolution dated 20-12-2000. Later on, by the signatures of respondent No. 9, who was illegally shown as a director, USD 1 million was illegally and unauthorisedly remitted on 4-2-2002 to a wholly owned subsidiary in the USA which did not even exist at the relevant time. Other facts, which falsified the respondents’ contentions and pointed towards their intention to defraud the creditors, members or any other person including the petitioner or otherwise for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose, were that despite the petitioner’s repeated request for inspection and audit and despite the CLB’s repeated orders, the respondents had not given the requisite information to the company’s members with respect to its affairs. It was true that the petitioner was only an investor-director. It was also true that non-allowing of inspection could not be a ground for considering a petition under section 235. But the entire facts, totality of the circumstances and the illegal, unlawful and fraudulent acts of the respondents led to the inference that there existed a prima facie case for investigation under section 235 as the respondents had been guilty of fraud and misfeasance towards the company as well as towards its members. The respondents had not complied with the articles of association and the legal provisions of the Act. Moreover, the respondent-company had become a disappearing company. It was reportedly not available at the registered office of the company nor were its statutory records available at its registered office. Statutory statements had not been sent to the RoC for several years. Instead of meeting the specific charges and making their case for non-investigation, the respondents had simply reiterated their contention that the resolution dated 5-1-2002 was not fabricated while the respondents’ subsequent acts - the false plea of supplementary agenda, the invalid circular resolution dated 29-4-2002, etc., revealed an unsuccessful effort to cover up the intent to defraud the creditors and members for a fraudulent and unlawful purpose which only made the petitioner’s prima facie case for investigation, by pointing out specific instances, stronger. [Para 14]

The CLB has an onerous duty to form an opinion with regard to the existence of the intent to defraud. The conditions stated in section 235 are to be satisfied before ordering an investigation under section 235. The facts and circumstances of the instant case, prima facie demonstrated and established the existence of pre-requisites which compelled the CLB to form an opinion in terms of section 235. The grounds for ordering an investigation did exist. There was overwhelming material available pointing to the circumstances suggesting that the business of the company was conducted for a fraudulent and unlawful purpose. The persons concerned in the management of the company had been guilty of fraud, misfeasance or other misconduct towards the company. It was a case squarely covered under the provisions of section 235 as the pre-conditions for initiating such an action existed as was clear from the foregoing. [Para 15]

Whether petition is maintainable for recovery of amounts by invoking sections 397-398, read with sections 406, 542 and 543? Whether such kind of relief (recovery of amounts) can be sought? Admittedly the instant petition was filed for recovery of amounts from the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 in the petition. The grievance of the Union of India that the applicant and the 3rd respondent were the directors of the company and acting in a fraudulent manner had retained the funds and had become liable and accountable for their illegal acts. The case of the Union of India was that they had ordered investigation on 23-3-2004 by appointing inspector. The inspector had investigated into the matter and submitted the detailed report pointing out various illegal and fraudulent acts of the respondents, thereby it was of the view that it was a fit case to file the instant petition before the CLB. The main allegations were that from October, 1998 to January, 1999 the management of the company created an equity capital of Rs. 7093 crores through dubious method of rotation of cheques and by swapping of shares among group associates. The management was found to have indulged in falsification of accounts of the company. Further the allegation of the petitioner that the company adjusted the application money in the form of deposit for software, rigging of share price through manipulation of working results in financial statements, shares reprinted and sold in the market and whole original jumbo share certificates were under seizure of Income-tax Department for contravention of section 41, read with sections 372/372A, 78, 293, 295,370 etc. of the Income-tax Act, 1961. From the pleadings, it was apparent that the petition was filed basing on the report of the Investigating Officer. In that regard the provision under which the Union of India approached the CLB was necessary to emphasize. Section 397 empowers the CLB to make such order as it thinks fit, may with a view to bringing to an end the matters complained off by any member of a company who complains that the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interests or in a manner oppressive to any member or members. Section 398 empowers the CLB in case of mismanagement in the affairs of a company and may apply any member of a company who complained that the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interest or that a material change not being a change brought about by or in the interests of any creditor including debenture holders or any class of shareholders of the company. The CLB may with a view to bringing to an end or preventing the matters complained of are apprehended make such order as it thinks fit. Section 399 provides for the right to apply under sections 397-398 by the category of persons as mentioned in that section. Admittedly, there were no complaints before the Bench by any member/members or creditors of the company alleging/complaining the acts of oppression and mismanagement in the affairs of the company and the nature of allegations of the Union of India required a detailed trial by examining the witnesses and the veracity of documents. The proceedings under sections 397-398 are summary in nature. Therefore, the nature of allegations could not be decided by the CLB. The contention of the respondents was that no notice was given for the inspection which was ordered under section 209 or even under section 234. The petitioner submitted that opportunity was given to the respondents. The inspection was carried out in the year 2004 and a final report was submitted to the Government. It was open to the respondents to challenge the investigation report if it would have violated the principles of natural justice in conducting the inspection. The petitioner alleged violation of various provisions of law in the instant petition. Prima facie the petitioner could initiate prosecution for the said contraventions in appropriate Court of law. Further, the CLB would not intrude the functions of the other statutory bodies such as SEBI, RBI and the civil court, company court and exercising powers under IPC. It is well settled law that to invoke the provisions of sections 397 and 398 by any member, creditor a case has to be made out that facts would justify the making of winding up order and that winding up would unfairly prejudice the members. In the instant case the petitioner had not made out any case for winding up of the company on just and equitable ground. The petitioner was not remediless. Most of the allegations were in the nature of grievances for which specific alternate course of action was available under various provisions of the Act and other laws which could be resorted to by the petitioner. The petitioner also invoked the provisions of sections 542 and 543. Section 543 is relevant provision to be applied by the petitioner. However, to apply under that provision, only a creditor or a member can make an application. In the instant case admittedly the petitioner was neither a member nor creditor of the company. Hence, the petitioner could not invoke the provision of section 543 where the CLB has the power to order for repayment or restore the money or property. The sole prayer in the petition was for recovery of money

What is Extraordinary/Exceptional Circumstance ? It would mean a situation that would lead to obvious conclusion, the process being frustrated; having either the State machinery deeply involved in the crime or their lackadaisical approach would result in an unsuccessful exercise. [Para 68]

Involvement of Kunal Ghosh/Srinjoy Bose :

The petitioner alleged, Kunal being an employee of Saradha group acted as a liason between the group and the State Government. If any one of them would have involvement in the crime, they must be proceeded with irrespective of their colour and creed, for that the entire State machinery could not be blamed. His personal involvement in the crime may not have nexus with the State machinery unless it is proved; he acted as a conduit that would bring him under the scanner. If one commits a crime, it would be his personal responsibility that must not have repercussion on the entire State judiciary unless such crime would relate to a mechanism involving the system. It would be too early to blame the State solely on the ground. [Para 69]

Investigation

The involvement of the State in the present context, did not feature in the pleadings. The investigation is still on. A cumulative reading of the provisions of the SEBI Act, 1992 and SEBI (Prohibition of Fraudulent and Unfair Trade Practices relating to Securities Market) Regulations, 2003 indicates that if the Board - as established under section 3 and managed under section 4 of the Act, 1992, has reasonable grounds to believe that transactions of securities in the market are dealt with in a manner detrimental to interest of shareholders, the Board is empowered under section 11-C to appoint any person as the investigating authority, to investigate into affairs of persons associated with the securities market, and thereafter to report them to the Board.[Para 8]

■

Section 19 of the Act, 1992 empowers the Board to further delegate to any member, officer of the Board, or any other person, all such powers except the power to make Rules as stipulated under section 29, including the power conferred on the Board under section 11-C, to order investigation into market securities. Additionally, sub-section (3) of section 4 of the Act, 1992, reserves with the Chairperson of the Board all powers of, ''general superintendence and direction of the affairs of the Board'', and further exercise all powers and do all acts which may be exercised or done by the Board, independent of any general or special order which may be passed under section 19. It may therefore be reasonably inferred that the Chairperson of the Board is statutorily empowered to exercise all such powers as may be exercised by the Board, save the limitations placed on such authority in the concerned regulations. A perusal of Regulation 5 of the Regulations, 2003 reveals that where there exists a reasonable ground to believe, the Executive Director is empowered to direct - by an order in writing, any officer (investigating authority), not below the rank of Division Chief to investigate any transactions in securities which are alleged to be carried in manner detrimental to the shareholders. [Para 8]

■

Therefore, upon conjoint reading of the delegation order dated 31-7-2019 passed in terms of section 4(3) of the Act, 1992, and Regulation 5 of the SEBI (PFUTP) Regulations, 2003, it is understood that the respondentNo.1/ Executive Director, SEBI, is a lawful authority under the statute to order an investigation, under section 11-C of the Act, 1992. Hence, the order of appointment of respondent No.3/ Deputy General Manager as investigating authority, as in the instant case, is not bad in law for want of jurisdiction. [Para 10]
