Introduction

The Supreme Court's recent judgment in National Spot Exchange Limited (NSEL) v. Union of India & Ors (Writ Petition (Civil) No. 995 of 2019) is a landmark in the domain of financial fraud litigation and asset recovery. The decision, delivered on 15 May 2025, addresses the complex interplay between the Maharashtra Protection of Interest of Depositors (MPID) Act, the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), and central statutes such as the SARFAESI Act, Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act (RDB Act), and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC).

At its core, this decision represents a careful recalibration of the legal hierarchy between secured creditors, government agencies, and public interest protections in cases involving tainted assets.

Background: The NSEL Scam and Legal Tangle

NSEL, a commodity trading platform promoted by 63 Moons Technologies Ltd. The collapse of the National Spot Exchange in 2013 triggered a Rs. 5,600 crore default, affecting about 13,000 traders and investors. The fallout led to multiple FIRs, civil suits, and the attachment of assets by both the Enforcement Directorate (under PMLA) and the State of Maharashtra (under the MPID Act). The NSEL itself secured decrees and arbitral awards worth around Rs. 3,365 crore against defaulting members, but faced significant hurdles in executing them due to overlapping attachments and competing claims from secured creditors (primarily banks) under SARFAESI/RDB Act. IBC proceedings also initiated against several entities.

Genesis of the Supreme Court Committee

To streamline the complex situation, involving execution of multiple decrees and avoid conflicting proceedings, the Supreme Court, invoking Article 142, constituted a high-powered committee chaired by Justice (Retd.). This committee was vested with the powers of a civil court to execute all decrees, orders, and arbitral awards obtained by NSEL, including the authority to sell properties attached under PMLA and MPID Act and oversee distribution to verified claimants. In short, Article 142 was used as a constitutional "safety valve" to harmonize conflicting statutory regimes, centralize execution, and prioritize investor restitution in a manner that ordinary statutory processes could not have achieved efficiently.

Power under Article 142 is extraordinary, discretionary, and unique to the Supreme Court. It allows the Court to:

Fill legal gaps where no statute provides an adequate remedy. It Complements statutory law, but does not override it—cannot be used to violate or contradict existing statutes

Issue binding directions, even if not strictly aligned with procedural law. Curative in nature—used to resolve issues when ordinary law falls short or causes injustice

Craft equitable solutions, especially in complex, multi-party, or sensitive matters.

However, Article 142 cannot be used to create a new law or override substantive rights conferred by legislation. It must be used judiciously and only when regular statutory or procedural remedies are inadequate or unjust. Article 142 cannot be used to achieve something indirectly what cannot be achieved directly.

While initially hailed as a pragmatic consolidation, the order's breadth brought it into direct strain with key statutory provisions of PMLA, SARFAESI, RDB Act, and IBC—particularly regarding the priority of secured creditors and the moratorium under insolvency law.

Key Legal Questions before the Supreme Court

Two main issues crystallized before the Court in the later stages of the litigation:

1.

Do secured creditors have priority over assets attached under the PMLA and MPID Act by virtue of SARFAESI and RDB Act?

2.

Are properties attached under the MPID Act immune from the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC?

These questions weren't just technical—they strike at the heart of India's recovery framework, challenging the hierarchy of creditor rights in fraud scenarios.

Supreme Court's Ruling on Secured Creditors' Priority

The Court held that the MPID Act and PMLA take precedence over the SARFAESI Act and RDB Act when it comes to assets attached as "proceeds of crime" or for the protection of depositors. The rationale is rooted in constitutional law: the MPID Act is a state law enacted to maintain public order and protect depositors, while SARFAESI and RDB Act are central laws focusing on banking and secured creditors' rights. Since these statutes operate in distinct legislative fields, the doctrine of repugnancy under Article 254 does not apply.

Based on report of forensic auditor and other financial transaction proof with them, Regional Director, Western Region on behalf of Ministry of Corporate Affairs filed Petition for Interim Reliefs against officials of company and board of directors of group companies.

Present Case :

Various Interim reliefs were sought i.e. to direct respondents to disclose their Properties, to direct NSDL/CDSL to freeze their securities account, to direct CBDT to freeze assets of the respondents of the petition etc. and further to initiate oppression and mismanagement case against the promoter and BOD of the corporate debtor to secure or restore the assets back to catch out the real fraud and the wrong doers of the fraud along with assets to the right victim of the fraud

The respondent companies argued that matter was stayed by Appellate Tribunal and which was confirmed by Supreme court. Hence, Company is still under CIR and therefore as per Section 14 of IBC, Moratorium is in effect and therefore no judicial action can be initiated during CIRP against the company.

Brief of Section 14 related to case :

Section 14 (1) says that "Subject to provisions of sub-sections (2) and (3), on the insolvency commencement date, the Adjudicating Authority shall by order declare moratorium for prohibiting all of the following, namely :—

(a)

the institution of suits or continuation of pending suits or proceedings against the corporate debtor including execution of any judgment, decree or order in any court of law, tribunal, arbitration panel or other authority;"

(b)

transferring, encumbering, alienating or disposing of by the corporate debtor any of its assets or any legal right or beneficial interest therein;

(c)

any action to foreclose, recover or enforce any security interest created by the corporate debtor in respect of its property including any action under the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002;

(d)

the recovery of any property by an owner or lessor where such property is occupied by or in the possession of the corporate debtor.

Moratorium Prohibits Petitioner to initiate Suit against company which is under CIRP. The very purpose of Moratorium is to stop multiplicity of cases, safeguarding assets pool and help resolution professional in focusing CIRP.

The argument of respondents was that the prohibitions are on both parties i.e. for and against the corporate debtor and hence these proceedings are bad in law and therefore should be set aside.

However, NCLT rejected this argument that proceedings are not proceedings against the corporate debtor but for corporate debtor. They agreed on contention that no suit or proceeding can be initiated against corporate debtor.

But in the instance case the efforts made by the Union of India were analysed and the spirit of them was seen to secure or restore the assets back to the ultimate victims of fraud and it is not any adversarial proceeding that is the proceeding in rem which has initiated by the Union of India to catch hold all the wrong doers and the fraudulent persons.

Audit simply means checking of records to establish accuracy

'Audit' is a systematic and independent examination of data, statements, records, operations and performance (financial or otherwise) of an enterprise for a stated purpose. In an auditing situation, the auditor perceives and recognises the propositions before him for examination, collects evidence, evaluates the same and on that basis, formulates the judgment which is communicated through his audit report [ICAI in General guidelines on Internal Auditing].

Auditing is a systematic process of objectively obtaining and evaluating evidence regarding assertions about economic actions and events to ascertain the degree of correspondence between those assertions and established criteria, and communicating results to interested user (Auditing Concepts Committee of American Accounting Association).

In service tax audit under EA-2000, 'audit' simply means verification of records to ensure correctness.

Introduction

1. India has very large rural population with low income and access to formal banking facilities. As a result web of parallel informal banking channels arose to fill the vacuum. At its centre were moneylenders, who used to charge exorbitant rates of interest. This practice was greatly curbed by the several Moneylenders Acts enacted by the State Governments in the early 1950s. However, the fundamental failure to overcome the role of moneylenders gave rise to fly-by-night financial operators who ran Ponzi schemes in various disguises. However, some commentators place the blame for mushrooming of these kinds of Ponzi schemes on greed rather than on inadequacy of formal banking systems.

The relatively prosperous rural economy of West Bengal had previously relied on small savings schemes run by the Indian Postal Service. However, low rates of interest in the 1980s and 90s encouraged and gave rise to several Ponzi schemes in speculative ventures such as Sanchayita Investments, Overland Investment Company, Verona Credit and Commercial Investment Company. Together, these scams garnered close to 10 billion INR of investor's wealth.

The Saradha Group financial scandal has been a financial scam which was caused by the collapse of a Ponzi scheme run by Saradha Group, a consortium of Indian companies which was believed to be running a wide variety of collective investment schemes (popularly but incorrectly referred to as chit funds) in the Eastern India. The group collapsed in April, 2013, causing an estimated loss of INR 200–300 billion (US$ 4–6 billion). In the aftermath of the financial scandal, the State Government of West Bengal set-up an inquiry Commission to investigate into collapse and also set-up a fund of INR 5 billion (92 million USD) to ensure that low income investors were not bankrupted. The Union Government also launched a multi-agency probe to investigate into the Saradha scam, as well as into other similar Ponzi schemes.

The Ponzi Schemes

2. The Saradha Group has gained notoriety in recent weeks with outstanding public deposits reportedly exceeding Rs. 200 billion. There was anger and panic. The State Government has stepped in with partial redressal system.

As we watch unfolding of this saga, there may be another crisis waiting to happen in the form of a pyramid scheme offered by Mavrodi Mondial Moneybox (MMM) that is taking rural India by storm. MMM claims to be a "social financial network" in which members voluntarily share money with each other by buying and selling MAVROS - a currency-like unit devised by the operators of the scheme. MMM claims to generate returns of over 40% per month, although the returns are not guaranteed. It may be a ponzi scheme: one where money collected from new investors is used to pay returns to old investors. The cycle will continue till inflows into the scheme exceed outflows.

Saradha and MMM are not isolated examples. Some of the recent schemes have promised unrealistic returns from investments in goats, pigs, emu, teak wood and potatoes.

The history of savings and investments in India is replete with tragedies where financial firms have failed to return deposits or investments. This is particularly problematic in a country where 70% of the people earn under 2 dollars a day and, hence, have small amounts of money saved up. If savings are not safe, the central objective of regulation - consumer protection - is not met. What we need is institutions that can take up deposits or run investment schemes to operate in a safe and sound manner, within the bounds of financial regulation.

How Saradha delayed investigation by SEBI

3. SEBI was investigating into Saradha for more than 3 years before the deposit schemes of the company collapsed. Saradha seems to have used following two methods to delay the investigation:

When SEBI asserted its authority to stop Saradha group from collecting money, Saradha challenged the jurisdiction of the SEBI in district courts. It quickly got orders to prevent SEBI from interfering in its businesses. These orders were eventually overturned by the High Court.

When SEBI requested information from Saradha about their schemes and investors, Saradha responded by providing large volumes of documentation without specifically answering SEBI's questions. This slowed down the entire investigation.

Limitations of the SEBI

4. In the course of three years Saradha took on new depositors and collected money from existing ones. All this money is now lost. Two years of investigation were required to stop what seems to be a run of the mill Ponzi scheme. The tactics employed by Saradha are not new. They are similar to those employed by Sahara in delaying investigations in the OFCD schemes and in many other white collar crime investigations. The disturbing fact is that they seem to succeed time and again.

of the CrPC states that the Magistrate can also issue a search warrant and direct that the search be conducted in his presence.10

In addition to this, the police officers who are making an investigation also have the power to search a place without a warrant if they have reasonable grounds to believe that something which is important for the investigation will be found in the place he wishes to search.11 The detailed procedure for all these searches has been laid down under Section 100 of the CrPC.12 Now under the PMLA, Section 17 allows the concerned authority to enter, search any place suspected of containing proceeds or records of a crime, break open any lock or door if the concerned authority has reasons to believe that records or proceeds are related to a criminal activity.13 There is no requirement of a warrant here but there are certain checks and balances as the authority must have reasons to believe that must be recorded and be sent to the Adjudicating Authority.

Seizure of property

Regarding property, Section 102 of the CrPC gives the Police the power to seize any property that is alleged or suspected to be stolen or part of commissioning an offence.14 The police officer seizing the property has to report the seized property to the nearest magistrate.15 However, the situation is different when it comes to the PMLA, Section 17 states that when the authorized person as a reason to believe that a person has with him money obtained from money laundering or records or property relating to money laundering, he may seize and make a note of such a record or property.16 The authority seizing such evidence is required to forward the reasons for the seizure, along with the records to the Adjudicating Authority.17

This seizure is only mandated for a period of thirty days as after thirty days, the seizing authority may request the Adjudicating Authority for continuing the seizure.18 This shows that there is a better safeguard under the PMLA as the investigating authority needs permission to keep the property in custody for more than 30 days. The same does not exist under the CrPC and the police can keep the seized property in possession for the whole period of investigation without any time imposition. The Magistrate can make decisions as they seem fit relating to such seized property under Section 457 of the CrPC.

The Delhi High Court in the case of Abdullah Ali Balsharaf v. Directorate of Enforcement, where the action of Enforcement Directorate seizing property under both Section 102 of the CrPC and Section 17(1)(a) of the PMLA was challenged, has discussed both provisions in detail and held that the Enforcement Directorate acting under the PMLA cannot issue orders under the CrPC.19

The Court noted that the scheme of seizure and the checks and balances in the PMLA are substantively different than what is enshrined in the CrPC. The authorized officer under the PMLA can only go ahead with seizing a property if (a) they have material in possession that provides a reason to believe that the property is related to a crime and (b) the seizing officer has to record the reasons. Both these checks do not exist under Section 102 of the CrPC. This clearly shows that Section 17(1)(a) of the PMLA is inconsistent with Section 102 of the CrPC and cannot be applied to a case relating to money laundering that is punishable under the PMLA as Section 65 of the PMLA states that the provisions of CrPC can only apply when they are not inconsistent with the provisions of the PMLA.

The Delhi High Court in this judgement also disagreed with the view of the Gujarat High Court where in the case of Paresha G. Shah v. State of Gujarat, it was held that an order under Section 102 of the CrPC can be said to be aiding the order of provisional attachment passed under Section 5(1) of the PMLA or an order for seizing/freezing property under Section 17(1A) of the PMLA.20

CONCLUSION

In a nutshell, the PMLA and CrPC even though are very similar in terms of the procedure that has been prescribed, there is a both, a bane, and a boon when it comes to applying to procedure. The PMLA procedure for search and seizure does put a higher onus on the authority as it must have reasonable grounds for searching and seizing that must be recorded in writing. This check goes a long way in preventing misuse of power by the authority as the Adjudicating Authority can easily ascertain if the search and seizure took place on a weak or no reasons at all.

On the other hand, as it was seen above, the PMLA shifts the onus of proof on the defendant to prove that he is not guilty which means taking away the legal doctrine of presumption of innocence. Due to these reasons, the nature, and the limits of the power of the Enforcement Directorate, the authority to enforce PMLA are under challenge right now in the Supreme Court in the case of Vijay Madan Lal C haudhary v. Union of India where all these issues are up consideration.21 The decision of the Supreme Court in this case would serve as a landmark judgement showcasing the debate relating to the checks and balances of the criminal justice system relating to money laundering as well as how the Supreme Court interprets the different sections of PMLA to limit the power of the Enforcement Directorate.

[1996] 10 SCL 70 (SC) In the above matter the scope and ambit of the Company Court and the broad contours had emerged in respect of sanctioning the Schemes by the Court. It was held that the Court had to see that all the requisite statutory procedure for supporting the scheme had been complied with and that the requisite meetings was held; that the scheme put up for sanction of the Court was backed up by the requisite majority vote as required and the concerned meetings of the creditors or members or any class of them had the relevant material to enable the voters to arrive at an informed decision for approving the scheme in question; That the majority decision of the concerned class of voters was just and fair to the class as a whole so as to legitimately bind even the dissenting members of that class and ;that all necessary material indicated as per the provisions were placed before the voters at the concerned meetings ;That all the requisite material contemplated were placed before the Court by the concerned applicant seeking sanction for such a scheme and the Court gets satisfied about the same. The Court has to further see that the proposed scheme of compromise and arrangement was not found to be violative of any provision of law and was not contrary to public policy. For ascertaining the real purpose underlying the Scheme the Court, if necessary, could pierce the veil of apparent corporate purpose underlying the scheme and could judiciously X-ray the same. Further the Court has also to satisfy itself that members or class of members or creditors or class of creditors, as the case may be, were acting bona fide and in good faith and were not coercing the minority in order to promote any interest adverse to that of the latter comprising of the same class whom they purported to represent; the Court must also ascertain that the scheme as a whole is found to be just, fair and reasonable from the point of view of prudent men of business taking a commercial decision beneficial to the class represented by them for whom the scheme is meant.

Once the aforesaid broad parameters about the requirements of a scheme for getting sanction of the Court were found to have been met, the Court would have no further jurisdiction to sit in appeal over the commercial wisdom of the majority of the class of persons who with their open eyes gave their approval to the scheme even if in the view of the Court there would be a better scheme for the company and its members or creditors for whom the scheme is framed. The Court cannot refuse to sanction such a scheme on that ground, as it would otherwise amount to the Court exercising appellate jurisdiction over the scheme rather than its supervisory jurisdiction. The aforesaid parameters of the scope and ambit of the jurisdiction of the Company Court which was called upon to sanction a Scheme of Compromise and Arrangement were not exhaustive but only broadly illustrative of the contours of the Court's jurisdiction.

Making a Case for a Securities Market Whistleblower Policy 3. The Satyam s candal shook the corporate world due to the extent of havoc and uncertainty it created and raised several concerns regarding corporate governance issues. But it is more than just a corporate governance concern. It is about protecting the interests of the public where their monies are directly impacted. One of the severe criticisms of the above mentioned scandal was the lack of a operational whistleblower policy to deduct the overstating of the company's financial matters.

With regard to the Indian securities market, SEBI as an independent regulator is vested with the duty to protect the interests of the investors and actively participate in regulating and improving the Indian capital market. The market regulator has made significant strides since its statutory inception in 1992 by bringing to the fore various regulatory checks and balances such as prohibition of insider trading, ensuring disclosure mechanisms and the corporate takeover regulations. Following the Supreme Court's judgment in the Sahara case32, SEBI's jurisdiction over all companies that make public issue of securities have been widened. Therefore, most of the investors are protected by the SEBI. The Board's investigative and enforcement powers have been furthered augmented by the Securities Law (Amendment) Ordinance, 2013. Despite these legislative safeguards, SEBI has to within its means ensure maximum protection. One way is to give opportunity to the public to come forward with their fears of any securities law violation. Therefore, the author is of the opinion that in furtherance of SEBI's objective to ensure and maximise investor protection, administering a whistleblower policy will complement its measures in the process.

The steps taken by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) of the United States (US) have been hailed by the countries around the world for incentivizing whistleblowers coming forward to report corporate frauds. To briefly state it The Dodd Frank Act of 2010 brought out monetary incentives for voluntary disclosures to the Securities Exchange Commission (SEC) by the amending Securities Exchange Act.33 By inserting Section 21F to SEC Act, the Commission has been armed with the power to grant monetary awards to eligible individuals who voluntarily provide original information to the SEC about violations of the US securities law that leads to enforcement actions resulting in the imposition of monetary sanctions over $1,000,000. Anti-victimization clauses are extensive and thorough. The amendment is a significant measure in the global corporate whistleblower policy-making, as it is unambiguous with regard to defining key terms such as who constitutes a whistleblower, what comprises original information and the conditions for applying for a monetary award.

The US securities market varies from that of India's not only in terms of its size but also in the fact that it is more distributed when it comes to market participation. Although this might be the case, yet anti-fraud provisions in India with respect to the capital market draws inspiration largely from the similar provisions in the SEC Act in the United States. Not only this, certain provisions on whistleblowing in the Companies Act, 2013 are on the lines of the Sarbanes Oxley Act, 2002. As much as we imbibe from the success of their laws, we must also learn from their lacunae and loopholes.

There are several questions one must address before SEBI takes up the responsibility of providing whistleblowers. Starting with the SEBI Act itself, s. 24B seeks to provide relief from prosecution of a person who has been alleged to have committed a violation of the Act during the course of proceedings. However, this a power that vests in the Central Government and SEBI has only non-binding recommendatory effect. This law has to be amended to vest SEBI with the power to grant this immunity. Moreover, the provision must also elaborate upon protection of the persons coming forward with the information on violation as their statements are liable to be used as a testimony against others involved in the violation. This is a step closer to tightening the law. Secondly, a dedicated whistleblower legislation within the framework of the SEBI has to address, more importantly, who will not be a whistleblower. Any member of the general public, on suspicion of a violation of the Act that has occurred, or will occur or is occurring should be allowed to come forward with his/her complaint to the SEBI. However, such a person cannot be entitled to a monetary reward if he/she is a part of the alleged violation. In such a scenario, section 24B of the Act will kick in and, accordingly, the law will take its due course. Another person who cannot be considered for a whistleblower's reward is any compliance officer within a company. As such, an officer will have first hand knowledge of any complaint brought to him, and he cannot be considered to be providing information that is original as a result of any independent analysis.

Towards Greater Depositors’ Protection

DR. V. BALACHANDRAN, K.S. RAVICHANDRAN AND R. KAMARAJ

Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) play a significant role in the economy of the nation. However, some unscrupulous elements among them have brought a bad name to the NBFC sector as a whole by cheating the investor’s of their hard-earned money. The CRB scam is a glaring and representative example of the same. Such dishonest conduct has forced the Government to put the activities of NBFCs under tight control In this article, the author discusses the measures adopted the RBI to protect the interest of depositors vis-a-vis NBFCs - EDITOR

Introduction

1. The role played by Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) in the national economy cannot be underestimated. They have been providing opportunities for better return to investors and flexibility in tapping resources. They extended retail services to small and middle level busi-nesses and road transport operators. The RBI has estimated that as at the end of March, 1996, regulated deposits of reporting non-banking compa-nies amounted to about Rs. 53,500 crores. Out of these NBFCs accounted for almost Rs. 45,500 crores. This represented about 10.8 per cent of the aggregate deposits of scheduled commercial banks. The rapid growth of NBFCs was facilitated by absence of restrictive legislative provisions. In fact most of the NBFCs did not even report about their operations to the RBI.

Post CRB scam scenario

2. Following the infamous CRB scam, suddenly black clouds have started gathering on the horizon creating an atmosphere of doubt and distrust. The industry was attacked from all sides. The most important critical problem confronting the industry is that of liquidity. New deposits have almost disappeared, the rate of renewal has fallen drastically and premature withdrawals have been heavy. To add salt to injury, banks and financial institutions have adopted a negative attitude of wait and watch;

Norms for unincorporated financial intermediaries

3. As stated by the Task Force Committee, one of the rudimentary factors contributing to distress in the NBFC sector is information asymmetry as between the depositors and NBFCs. The rationale for regulating the deposit-taking activities of unincorporated bodies essentially flows from the need to protect uninformed depositors. The first attempt to regulate the deposit-taking activities of unincorporated bodies was made in 1984 by inserting Chapter IIIC in the RBI, Act 1934. However, the newly introduced section 45S proved to be different to implement. Again, the RBI banned deposit-taking activities of unincorporated financial intermediaries by amending the RBI Act in 1997. These unincorporated entities were banned from, soliciting deposits by way of advertisements. This does not mean that section 45S prevents such entities from carrying on their operations. These regulations are intended to impel them towards acquiring a corporate status so that they operate within the regulatory framework created under the Companies Act arid Chapter IIIB of the RBI Act.

The unincorporated bodies engaged in non-banking financial business are not allowed to accept deposits except from the relatives, However, such entities could be allowed to access loans from bodies with corporate identity including NBFCs. Unauthorised deposit-taking by both NBFCs and unincorporated bodies is an offence. However, as regards NBFCs cognizance of this offence can be taken only on the complaint of an officer of the RBI. Such offences will now be made cognizable. Unauthorised deposit-taking by a financial sector intermediary automatically catapults these violations into the category of serious crimes.

The task force has advised the RBI to appoint depositors’ grievance redressal authorities with specified territorial jurisdiction. It suggested that a banking ombudsman could be a viable ‘option for such appointments. It has said that the authorities should be empowered to pass orders in regard to direct the unscrupulous and fraudulent companies to pay a part of the deposits to the depositors. To provide legal strength to the order of such authority, it has said, the order could be transmitted by this authority to the principal civil court of the district in which the registered office of the company is located.

Co-ordination mechanism with the RBI

4. The panel has suggested that the CLB must constitute a co-ordination mechanism with the RBI to ensure that default cases are speedily dealt with. The Task Force recognised the need for a decentralised machinery for inspection of smaller NBFCs. It has also suggested that stringent provisions be made for attachment of assets of finance companies engaged in fraudulent activities and the liquidation of NBFCs.

CHAPTER 385

COMPLAINT BY ANY PERSON TO COMPANY LAW BOARD FOR FINDING OUT FACTS ABOUT SHARES OR DEBENTURES OF A COMPANY *COMPLAINT BY ANY PERSON TO COMPANY LAW BOARD FOR FINDING OUT FACTS ABOUT SHARES OR DEBENTURES OF A COMPANY*

385.1 Background note385.1 Background note

The Central Government is empowered to appoint inspectors to investigate and report on the ownership of the company under certain circumstances.

385.2 Investigation into ownership of the company385.2 Investigation into ownership of the company

An investigation into the ownership of the company may be ordered under the following circumstances :

385.2-1 Investigation by Central Government on its own385.2-1 Investigation by Central Government on its own

The Central Government may, when it appears that there is good reason to do so, appoint one or more inspectors to investigate and report on the membership of any company and other matters relating to the company for the purpose of determining the true persons who are or have been—

u financially interested in the success or failure, whether real or apparent, of the company; or

u able to control or materially influence the policy of the company.

385.2-2 Investigation at the instance of Company Law Board385.2-2 Investigation at the instance of Company Law Board

Where in the course of any proceedings before it, the Company Law Board declares that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated, the Central Government shall appoint one or more investigators and report on the membership of any company and other matters relating to the company for the purpose of determining the true persons who are or have been—

u financially interested in the success or failure, whether real or apparent, of the company; or

u able to control or materially influence the policy of the company.

385.3 Scope of investigation385.3 Scope of investigation

While appointing inspectors, the Central Government may define the scope of investigation with regard to matters, period to which such inspection extends and limit the investigation to matters connected with particular shares or debentures.

385.4 Powers of Inspectors385.4 Powers of Inspectors

The inspectors shall have powers to examine persons on oath, inspect the books and papers. Refer para 384.9 for other provisions.

385.5 Inspector’s Report385.5 Inspector’s Report

The inspector shall forward his report to the Central Government. However, the Central Government shall not be bound to furnish the company or any other person with a copy of such report or any portion thereof, if there is a good reason for not divulging the contents thereof. In such a case, the Central Government shall require the Registrar to keep a copy of such report or parts of such report which could be divulged.

385.6 Expenses of Investigation385.6 Expenses of Investigation

The expenses of investigation shall be defrayed by the Central Government out of the moneys provided by the Parliament, unless it directs that the expenses or part thereof should be met by the applicants on whose application the investigation was ordered.

385.7 Imposition of restrictions385.7 Imposition of restrictions

Where it appears to the Company Law Board that for the purpose of investigation into ownership of the company, it is necessary to impose restrictions, it may by order direct that the shares shall be subject to the following restrictions for a period not exceeding three years as may be specified in the order viz.

u transfer of those shares shall be void;

u where shares are to be issued, they should not be issued and any issue thereof or transfer of any right to be issued therewith shall be void;

u no voting right shall be exercisable;

u no further shares shall be issued in right of those shares or in pursuance of any offer made to the holder thereof and any issue thereof or transfer of any right to be issued therewith shall be void ;

u except on liquidation no payment should be made for any sums due from the company on those shares, whether in respect of dividend or capital or otherwise.

385.8 Restriction on transfer of shares or debentures385.8 Restriction on transfer of shares or debentures

Where a transfer of shares or debentures in a company has taken place and as a result thereof a change in the composition of the Board of Directors is likely to take place which would be prejudicial to the public interest, the Company Law Board may, by order, direct that—

u the voting rights in respect of those shares or debentures shall not be exercisable for a period not exceeding three years as may be specified in the Order.

u no resolution passed or action taken to effect a change in the composition of the Board of Directors before the date of the order unless it is confirmed by the Company Law Board.

u the transfer of shares in the company during such period not exceeding three years as may be specified in the Order, shall be void.

Investigation on Registrar’s Report to Central Government [Sections 234 & 234A]

25.6 Section 234 assigns the role of a watch-dog of corporate affairs of companies to the Registrar, and for the purpose empowers him to call for any information or explanation in writing from any company as required by him in his opinion formed on perusing any document filed with him in compliance with the requirements of the Act. He can exercise the same power, also, on a representation or complaint received from any contributory or creditor or any other person interested in the company alleging that the business of the company is being carried on fraudulently. In relation to the Registrar’s demand for furnishing the specified information and explanations, a duty is cast statutorily on the companies requiring prompt response to the best of the power of the officers of the company, present and past. Any refusal, failure, negligence or deficiency in furnishing the information or explanations within the time stipulated by the Registrar in his demand leads to his issuing another such demand by way of an order calling for the production of books and papers before him for his inspection within the time specified in his order which the company and its officers are enjoined to comply by the provision in the section. If his order is neglected or refused, it attracts fine up to five thousand rupees plus five hundred rupees for each day of continuing non-compliance for the company and its officers in default if the Registrar prosecutes for the offence and imposition of the said fine as well as for the conversion of his demand for information or explanations or the production of the books and papers into an order of the Court, with due notice to the accused. On the Court passing its order against the accused company and it furnishing the information or explanation, the Registrar is entitled to record a note or attach any reply or paper received from the company to the relevant document while taking it on record, which means that it shall be open for public inspection which otherwise it is not.

Registrar's report to Central Government

25.6-1 If the information or explanation or the books and papers thus received by the Registrar when perused along with the document, if the overall disclosure falls short of a fair statement of any matter to which the document relates or it reveals an unsatisfactory state of the company’s affairs, the Registrar is bound to make a report in writing to the Central Government in terms of section 234(6) or (7), or conversely, if he concludes that the complaint received on which he raised the demand against the company is frivolous or vexatious, he shall inform the company accordingly disclosing the identity of the informant. This procedure is equally applicable to documents filed by the liquidator or by the foreign companies with the Registrar. Investigation on other counts

25.7 (1) Group Action: Under section 235(2) any group of not less than two hundred members or the group holding not less than one-tenth of the total voting power in the company having a share capital, or, in the case of the company having no share capital, the group not less in number than one-fifth of the persons on the company’s register of members, is entitled to present an application to the CLB 1/Tribunal, on the basis of such supporting evidence requisite to make out a good reason for the application made seeking the CLB 1 /Tribunal’s order declaring that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated by the Inspector(s)—competent individuals, that is, either the officials of DCA or Chartered Accountants—appointed by the Central Government and to report thereon to the Central Government. The CLB 1/Tribunal after giving an opportunity to the parties of being heard may pass the order accordingly, and thereupon the Central Government may require the applicants to give a security of not exceeding one thousand rupees as is fixed by it towards the costs of investigation (section 236) before appointing an Inspector. For the group action, the catch is in section 236 which lays down that such an application shall be supported by such evidence as the CLB/Tribunal may require to make out a case for investigation, and if such evidence is insisted upon to be one on the lines of section 237( b)(i), (ii) and (iii ) it will in all probability amount for the outsider group insurmountable, as we shall see in (3) below.

(2) Action by Company/Order of Court [Section 237 (a)] : Without prejudice to the power conferred under section 235, the Central Government has been vested with the power to appoint inspector(s) to investigate a company’s affairs forked in a two-way mode—one compulsory and the other optional under section 237(a) and (b), [the optional mode discussed in (3) below]. The compulsory mode under section 237(a) is again divided into two kinds, one the company passing a special resolution, and the other the High Court declaring that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated by an inspector appointed by the Central Government, under section 237(a)(ii ), in either of which case it becomes compulsory for the Central Government to do so.

Company passing the special resolution

25.7-1 The first case of the company passing the special resolution declaring that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated by an Inspector appointed by the Central Government should be the rarest of rare occurrences, probably when the minority controls the company and is confronted by the majority commanding 75% or more of the voting control preferring that option than dismissing the entire Board of directors which it could easily do under such circumstances, for some compelling reason or as a means of swearing by fire of Government Investigation for an honourable takeover on a clean slate of a dubious company.

Any shareholder may make an application

25.7-2 The second case comes into play in the case where the High Court [‘Court’ referred to in section 237(a)(ii ) is the Court having jurisdiction under section 10, Premier Plantations Ltd. v. M. Ebrahimkutty (2002) 37 SCL 804 (Ker.)], on an application of any shareholder aggrieved or anyone interested in the affairs of the company and adversely affected by the manner in which the company’s affairs had been conducted, declares so by its order. Where no legal injury has been caused to a person, he has no right to move the Court in this behalf, V.V. Purie v. E.M.C. Steel Ltd. (1980) 50 Comp. Cas. 127 (Delhi). Section 237( a)(ii) is not controlled by section 235 or 237, and the Court’s power is not circumscribed in any way by the Legislature, Alembic Glass Industries Ltd., In re (1972) 42 Comp. Cas. 63 (Guj.), and the power of Court under section 237(a)( ii) is not equal to the power of CLB/Tribunal under section 237(b), Premier Plantations Ltd. v. M. Ebrahimkutty (2002) 37 SCL 804 (Ker.). Though the order of CLB 1 is subjective, Court can review it and can find out as to whether the circumstances relied upon existed or whether order was not mala fide : reasons cannot be added later to justify the order of investigation, Hari Ganga Cements Ltd. v. CLB (1998) 3 Comp. LJ 323 (Bom.) (DB).

Ebrahimkutty (2002) 37 SCL 804 (Ker.).

Powers of CLB 25.7-10 The powers of CLB under section 237(b) is a matter of judicial consideration as to whether circumstances for drawing an inference contemplated by section 237(b) existed, Ashoka Marketing Ltd. v. Union of India (1981) 51 Comp. Cas. 634 (Delhi): the discretion controlled by matters referred to in section 237(b) is to be exercised if it is satisfied that at least a prima facie case has been made out, P. Sreenivasan v. Yoousuf Sagar Abdulla & Sons (P.) Ltd. (1983) 53 Comp. Cas. 485 (Ker.), and it must proceed reasonably according to the law, not actuated by bad faith or dishonesty, and excluding matters which are irrelevant from consideration, New Central Jute Mills Co. Ltd. v. Deputy Secretary, Ministry of Finance (1966) 36 Comp. Cas. 512 (Cal.). If CLB neglects to take into account very material and important documents while forming its opinion, such an opinion cannot be reasonable, Jiyajeerao Cotton Mills Ltd. v. CLB (1969) 39 Comp. Cas. 856 (MP). The petitioner holding 8.35% shares in the company filed a petition under section 235 read with section 237(b )—praying for an order to investigate the affairs of the company and to direct seizure of all books and records of the company. Petition under section 235 was found to be not maintainable since the capital held was less than 10% fixed in the Act. However, following the ratio determined in Alembic Glass Industries Ltd., In re (1972) 42 Comp. Cas. 63 (Guj.) to say that the Court may make an order to investigate, the view was taken that CLB can take information from any source including members and creditors or otherwise if the person providing the information has a stake or is an interested party in the company, the petition was treated as a petition under section 237(b), and the respondents were directed to file their reply within four weeks, and the petitioner his rejoinder, if any, within two weeks thereafter, Shree Rama Multi Tech Ltd., In re (2005) 63 SCL 154 (CLB - New Delhi).

Valid grounds under section 237( b) : Excessive declaration of dividend or a doubt that statutory auditors of the company are under obligation to the company and are not independent, form valid grounds prima facie: Ashoka Marketing Ltd. v. Union of India (1967) 37 Comp. Cas. 341 (Cal.), and New Central Jute Mills Co. Ltd. v. Deputy Secretary, Ministry of Finance (1966) 36 Comp. Cas. 512 (Cal.), respectively.

Existing facts not showing objectively a prima facie case of an offence of the type mentioned in section 237(b)( i) to (iii ), Modi Industries Ltd. v. Union of India (1982) 52 Comp. Cas. 589 (Delhi). 384.8 Appointment of inspectors384.8 Appointment of inspectors

On making of order by Company Law Board to appoint inspectors, the Central Government shall appoint one or more competent persons as inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company and to report thereon.

384.8-1 Prohibition384.8-1 Prohibition

No firm, body corporate or other associations shall be appointed as inspectors.

384.8-2 Continuance of investigation384.8-2 Continuance of investigation No investigation shall be stopped or suspended by reason of the fact that an application has been made for an order for prevention of oppression or mismanagement or a special resolution has been passed for voluntary winding up of the company.

384.9 Powers of inspectors384.9 Powers of inspectors

An inspector appointed to investigate the affairs of the company has the following powers :

384.9-1 Power to investigate other body corporates384.9-1 Power to investigate other body corporates

The inspector may also investigate the affairs of the following persons/body corporates which may be relevant to his investigation viz.,

u any other body corporate which is, or has at any relevant time been, the company’s holding or subsidiary company or a subsidiary of its holding company or a holding company of its subsidiary.

u any other body corporate which is or has at any relevant time been, managed by any person as managing director or manager of the company who is or was the managing director or manager of the company at the relevant time.

u any other body corporate which is or has at any relevant time been, managed by the company.

u any other body corporate whose board of directors comprises of nominees of the company.

u any other body corporate whose Board of directors are accustomed to act in accordance with the directions or instructions of the company or any of the directors of the company or any company whose directorships is held by the employees or nominees of those having the control and management of the first mentioned company. However, the prior approval of the Central Government is required in this case.

u any person who is or has at any relevant time been the managing director or manager of the company. However, the prior approval of the Central Government is required in this case.

384.9-2 Power to examine books and documents384.9-2 Power to examine books and documents

The inspector shall have powers to demand inspection of all books and papers relating to the company or other body corporate [referred to in para 384.9-1] and it is the duty of all officers and employees of the company to produce the said documents and provide all assistance to the inspector to carry out the duties. The inspector may, with the prior approval of the Central Government, require any other body corporate to furnish such information and produce such books and papers before which he considers it necessary for carrying out his duties as inspector. The inspector can keep the books under his custody for six months and thereafter return it to the person concerned. He may call back the books once again or obtain certified copies of the books and papers. If such certified copies are furnished, the inspector must return those books and papers to the concerned person.

384.9-3 Power to examine on oath384.9-3 Power to examine on oath

The inspector may examine on oath any officer, employee, agent of the body corporate(s) in respect of which the investigation is carried out. He may, with the prior approval of the Central Government, examine any other person on oath.

384.9-4 Power to seize documents384.9-4 Power to seize documents

If, during the course of investigation, the inspector apprehends that the books and papers are likely to be destroyed, mutilated, altered, falsified or secreted, he may make an application to the Presidency Magistrate 1 of the concerned jurisdiction and obtain an order for searching and seizing such documents. Such books can be retained by him until the conclusion of the investigation and should be returned to the concerned person on conclusion of the investigation.

384.10 Inspector’s report384.10 Inspector’s report

The inspector may, and if so directed by the Central Government shall, make interim reports to that Government and on conclusion of the investigation, shall make a final report to the Central Government. Such report shall be written or printed, as the Central Government may direct.

384.11 Authentication of Inspector’s Report384.11 Authentication of Inspector’s Report

The inspector’s report shall be authenticated either by the seal of the company whose affairs have been investigated or by a certificate of a public officer having the custody of the report, under and in accordance with the provisions of section 76 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. Such authenticated report shall be admissible as an evidence in any legal proceedings in relation to any matter contained in the report.

384.12 Forwarding of report by Central Government384.12 Forwarding of report by Central Government

The Central Government—

u shall forward a copy of any report [other than the interim report] to the company at its registered office and the other body corporate(s) dealt with in the report.

u may forward a copy of the report or furnish to any member of the company or other body corporate dealt with in the report on payment of prescribed fee of Re. 1 for every one hundred words or any part thereof.

u shall forward a copy of the report to the applicants who submitted an application for ordering investigation.

CHAPTER 389

APPOINTMENT OF INSPECTOR FOR INVESTIGATION INTO AFFAIRS OF A COMPANY BASED ON REPORT OF REGISTRAR OF COMPANIES *APPOINTMENT OF INSPECTOR FOR INVESTIGATION INTO AFFAIRS OF A COMPANY BASED ON REPORT OF REGISTRAR OF COMPANIES*

389.1 Background note389.1 Background note

The Central Government may appoint one or more Inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company based on the report of the Registrar of Companies under section 234 of the Act.

389.2 Power of Registrar to call for information or explanation389.2 Power of Registrar to call for information or explanation

The Registrar of Companies has the power under section 234 of the Act to call for information or explanations from any company under the following circumstances :

389.2-1 Requiring information on the basis of documents389.2-1 Requiring information on the basis of documents

The Registrar of Companies has the power to call, by written order, such information and explanations as may be necessary relating to any document filed in his office.

389.2-2 Requiring information on the application of creditors etc.389.2-2 Requiring information on the application of creditors etc.

If it is represented to the Registrar on materials placed before him by any contributory or creditor or any other person interested, that the business of the company is being carried on in fraud of its creditors or of persons dealing with the company or otherwise for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose, he may, after hearing the company, issue an order in writing asking for such informations and explanations as he may consider necessary.

389.3 Furnishing of explanation by company389.3 Furnishing of explanation by company

On receipt of such order, it shall be the duty of the company and all officers of the company to furnish such information and explanations within the time limit fixed by the Registrar of Companies.

389.3-1 Action by Registrar in case of failure389.3-1 Action by Registrar in case of failure

If no information or explanation is furnished within the prescribed time or if such information or explanation is inadequate, the Registrar may issue another written order calling for production of books and papers which are considered necessary and specify a time limit within which such books should be produced. On receipt of such order, the Company and every officer shall produce such books and papers within the specified time limit.

389.4 Penalty in case of default389.4 Penalty in case of default

If the company fails to furnish the information and explanations or produce books and paper, the company and every officer thereon shall be punishable with a fine which may extend up to five thousand rupees and in the case of continuing offence with an additional fine which may extend to rupees five hundred for everyday during which such default continues. The Registrar may also apply to the Court for issue of an order on the company to produce books and papers before the Registrar of Companies.

389.4-1 Production/Service of records389.4-1 Production/Service of records

The Registrar may also apply to the Court of Magistrate of the First class for issue of an order on the company to produce books and papers before the Registrar of Companies, under section 234(4). Further, under section 234A, he may move the said Court for seizure of the Company’s records if he has reasonable ground to believe that the books and papers of or relating to the company or other body corporate associated with it may be destroyed mutilated, attend falsified or secreted by the managing director or manager of the company.

389.5 Report by Registrar for investigation389.5 Report by Registrar for investigation

The Registrar shall make a report to the Central Government under the following circumstances :

u if the information or explanation sought for is not produced within the specified time;

u if on a perusal of the information or explanation or books and papers, the Registrar finds an unsatisfactory state of affairs ; or

u if on a perusal of the information or explanation or books and papers, the Registrar finds that they do not disclose a full and fair statement of any matter to which the document purport to relate.

389.6 Appointment of Inspectors389.6 Appointment of Inspectors

On receipt of the report from the Registrar of Companies, the Central Government may appoint one or more competent persons as Inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company and to report thereon.

389.7 Investigation by Inspector(s)389.7 Investigation by Inspector(s)

Investigation of company - Tribunal’s opinion basis for exercise of discretion

The Central Government exercises its discretion on the basis of the opinion of the Tribunal that the circumstances exist for ordering investigation. The Tribunal may take the initiative suo motu or on an inspection of or information supplied by any shareholder or other person. It must be satisfied as to whether the circumstances as provided in the Companies Act exist. Formation of the company or conduct of its affairs for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose, or the persons managing the affairs being guilty of fraud, misfeasance or misconduct or keeping the members uninformed of important matters, are the circumstances which may lead the Tribunal to form an opinion for investigation.

Circumstances should be brought to light to suggest that the business of the company is being carried on for fraudulent or unlawful purposes or in a manner oppressive to the minority, or that those in management had misconducted themselves towards the company or its members, no action can be ordered [P. Sreenivasan v. Yoosuf Sagar Abdulla & Sons (P.) Ltd. [1983] 53 Comp. Cas. 485 (Ker.)]. Such circumstances cannot be presumed, if a company has been incurring the losses. Investigation is ordered if such losses could be linked with fraud, misfeasance, mismanagement or oppression [see Mrs. U. A. Sumathy v. Digvijay Chit Fund (P.) Ltd. [1983] 53 Comp. Cas. 493 (Ker.)]

Unless any of such circumstances exist, the Central Government cannot order an investigation. Whether circumstances are existing for drawing contemplated inference is a matter of judicial consideration [see Ashoka Marketing Ltd. v. Union of India [1981] 51 Comp. Cas. 634 (Delhi)]. If the Tribunal neglects to take into account very material and important documents while forming its opinion, the opinion cannot be reasonable [see Jiyajeerao Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Company Law Board [1969] 39 Comp. Cas. 856 (MP)]. The term "opinion" is indicative of the existence of some material, which, at the outset, without deeper probe into the materials lead to an opinion that the complaint lodged is not frivolous, to be thrown out at the threshold. It is an opinion formed at the first impression. An order of investigation is not made on suspicion and surmises; there should be proper material to form an opinion that the affairs of the company need to be investigated [see Dwija Bandhu Sarkar v. D. N. Chakraborty [2004] 121 Comp. Cas. 712 (CLB)]. In that case the Company Law Board observed :

". . In respect of his complaints of siphoning off of funds by the respondent etc., they are all based on the balance - sheet figures/An order of investigation is not made on suspicion and surmises. There should be proper material to from an opinion that that the affairs of the company need to be investigated. The petitioner has not furnished sufficient particulars to enable me to form an opinion that the affairs of the company need to be investigated."

A mere statement of facts based on auditors report without any corroborative evidence would not be sufficient to form an opinion that the affairs of the company should be investigated. [see Andhra Pradesh State Civil Supply Corporation Ltd. v. Delta Oils and Fats Ltd. [1996] 96 Comp. Cas. 303 (CLB), Gopalakrishna Kamath v. M. T. Association [2004] 121 Comp. Cas. 191 (CLB) and Rohinten Mazda v. Hypoids (India) Pvt. Ltd. [2004] 121 Comp. Cas. 729 (CLB)]. No investigation can be ordered without particulars and on mere suspicion or surmises. The allegations must be substantiated with concrete material. There must be some material, something more than the mere statement of facts and allegations, suggesting deeper probe.

For example, allegation that there is doubt that statutory auditors of the company are under obligation to it and are not acting independently, makes out a prima facie case for investigation [New Central Jute Mills Co. Ltd. v. Deputy Secretary [1966] 36 Comp. Cas. 512 (Cal.)]. Unreasonable declaration of dividends could be a prima facie ground for ordering investigation [see Ashok Marketing Ltd. v. Union of India [1967] 37 Comp. Cas. 341 (Cal.)].

If the Tribunal is satisfied on the basis of the information and evidence in its possession with respect to any person who is or was a director or an officer or other employee of the sick company, that such person by himself or along with others had diverted the funds or other property of such company for any purpose other than the purposes of the company or had managed the affairs of the company in a manner highly detrimental to the interests of the company, the Tribunal shall, by order, direct the public financial institutions, scheduled banks and State level institutions not to provide, for a maximum period of ten years from the date of the order, any financial assistance to such person or any firm of which such person is a partner or any company or other body corporate of which such person is a director, by whatever name called, or to disqualify the said director, promoter, manager from being appointed as a director in any company registered under this Act for a maximum period of six years. No order shall be made by the Tribunal under this section against any person unless such person has been given a reasonable opportunity of being heard.

Punishment of certain offences (section 267)

As described under Section 267 in regard to the punishment of certain offences: whoever violates the provisions of this Chapter or any scheme, or any order, of the Tribunal or the Appellate Tribunal or makes a false statement or gives false evidence before the Tribunal or the Appellate Tribunal or attempts to tamper with the records of reference or appeal filed, he shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years and with fine which may extend to ten lakh rupees.

6.14

If a company has raised share capital from certain persons who are untraceable or fictitious, will it be a benami transaction under section 2(9)(D) of the PBPT Act, 1988?

A case in point is the kind of facts that came to light during enquiries by AO and CIT(A) in Commissioner of Income-tax, Chennai v. Midas Golden Distelleries (P.) Ltd. [2021] 130 taxmann.com 206 (Madras). The findings of AO and CIT(A) were upheld by the High Court. The High Court held that where Assessing Officer noted that share capital of assessee-company had been routed through two companies, existence and operation of which remained only on paper and enquiries conducted showed that intermediary companies acted as conduits and huge amount were brought in assessee's books as share application money through intermediary companies by shareholders, who could not properly explain their source and assessee had not established creditworthiness and genuineness of transaction to satisfaction of Assessing Officer, Assessing Officer was justified in holding that provisions of section 68 got attracted and that share application money had to be assessed in hands of assessee-company.

The Assessing Officer held that the enquiry with the past and the present directors would show that there was no transparency in the control and administration and even about the ownership of the company; that the share capital has been introduced in the company through two intermediary companies, which operated with the same pseudonymous address and there was no business activity in those companies; that the directors of the intermediary companies pleaded ignorance about the decision regarding the investment in the assessee-company; that the sources of the shareholders, who made their investment in the assessee-company through the intermediary companies were not properly explained; that the affairs of the two intermediary companies established the fact that those were only paper companies created with the sole intention to act as a conduit for facilitating transfer of funds; that the signatories to the agreement were between the assessee and another company, as per which, the shares of the assessee were to be allotted to the other company or its nominees in lieu of the alleged advance of Rs. 5.35 Crores, totally denied by stating that he did not have knowledge of such transaction and that transaction was not reflected by the erstwhile partnership firm M/s. Golden Distilleries; that the addresses of the share applicants namely M/s. D. Kumar Trading and Co., and M/s. Pooja Equitex and M/s. Pentium were not furnished.

The CIT(A), while confirming the order passed by the Assessing Officer, reexamined the entire facts and the discussions commenced from paragraph 4.1.3 in the order dated 21.7.2008. After noting the submissions, which were recorded by the Assessing Officer during the course of assessment proceedings, the CIT(A) held that the so-called directors basically discharged their functions in the honorary capacity during their tenure and they used to look after the routine matters pertaining to the assessee and that they categorically denied having every actively participated in the crucial decision making process of the assessee company. As former managing director of the assessee-company, he was stated to be in charge of civil work, erection of plant and machinery, purchases, etc., and expressed ignorance about the shareholding pattern of the assessee-company and other financial transaction entered into by the initial promoter – directors and the present directors. All of them appeared to have stated that the important decisions used to be taken by only one person, who was the main person behind the promotion of the assessee-company and its business operations. But, the main person pleaded that he and his family members had no role to play in the assessee's business activities apart from holding shares therein.

After noting the statements recorded by the Assessing Officer, the CIT(A) observed that the Assessing Officer was within his right to probe the genuineness and source of the share application money received by the assessee during the year. The statements recorded from the persons had clearly established that the needle of suspicion inevitably and inexorably pointed to one particular person and since the suspicion was so overwhelming, the Assessing Officer had no other option except to trace the origin of funds, which got channelized into the assessee-company through the corporate entities. Further, the CIT(A) pointed out that the Assessing Officer, while embarking upon such an enquiry, found that the share application money was primarily contributed by two companies and an aggregate sum of Rs. 3 Crores was found to be contributed by three Mumbai based companies.

CHAPTER 388

APPOINTMENT OF INSPECTOR FOR INVESTIGATION INTO AFFAIRS OF A COMPANY ON ORDER OF COMPANY LAW BOARD *APPOINTMENT OF INSPECTOR FOR INVESTIGATION INTO AFFAIRS OF A COMPANY ON ORDER OF COMPANY LAW BOARD*

388.1 Background note388.1 Background note

The Central Government may appoint one or more Inspectors to investigate the affairs of a company if in the opinion of the Company Law Board, there are circumstances suggesting the grounds specified in section 237(b).

388.2 Grounds for Investigation388.2 Grounds for Investigation

An investigation into the affairs of the Company may be done under the following circumstances :

u If the business of the company is being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members or any other persons, or otherwise for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose, or in a manner oppressive of any of its members, or that the company was formed for any fraudulent or unlawful purpose;

u If the persons concerned in the formation of the company or the management of its affairs have in connection therewith been guilty of fraud, misfeasance or other misconduct towards the company or towards any of its members; or

u If the members of the company have not been given all the information with respect to its affairs which they might reasonably expect, including information relating to the calculation of the commission payable to the managing or other director or the manager, of the company.

388.3 Appointment of Inspectors388.3 Appointment of Inspectors

The Central Government may appoint one or more competent persons as Inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company and to report thereon if it or the Tribunal is satisfied to form an option that it is warranted in the circumstances. This is the position after the modified clause that way comes into operation on the notification of the Second Amendment Act, 2002. Until then, it is the CLB that should be satisfied to from such an opinion.

388.4 Investigation by Inspector(s)388.4 Investigation by Inspector(s)

The Inspector(s) shall investigate the affairs of the company and submit a report thereon to the Central Government. A copy of the report should be sent by the Central Government to the Company Law Board. Refer paras 384.8 to 384.14 for provisions relating to appointment of Inspectors, powers of Inspectors, Inspector’s report, action by Central Government and expenses on investigation which are also applicable in case of appointment of Inspector at the instance of Company Law Board.

INVESTIGATION

Investigation of company can be carried out in one of following situations-

Order by Central Government - Central Government may order investigation into affairs of the company in following situations - (a) On receipt of report from Registrar or inspector under section 208 of Companies Act, 2013 (b) On intimation of a special resolution passed by a company that the affairs of the company be investigated (c) In public interest - section 210(1) of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding section 235(1) of the 1956 Act].

Central Government shall order investigation into affairs of the company if order is passed by a Court or NCLT in any proceedings before it - section 210(2) of Companies Act, 2013.

Order by NCLT on application from members - Section 213 of Companies Act, 2013 has been notified and is effective w.e.f. 1-6-2016.

NCLT can order investigation in specified cases.

Such order can be passed by NCLT only after giving reasonable opportunity of being heard to the concerned parties.

Security from applicants - Central Government (presently CLB) may require appellants to provide security upto Rs. 25,000 towards cost of investigation. The security will be refunded if investigation results in prosecution - section 214 of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding section 236 of the 1956 Act]

Applicability of provisions to foreign company - The provisions of investigation apply to foreign company also [section 228 of Companies Act, 2013].

Procedure for making application before NCLT - An application under section 213 of Companies Act, 2013 may be made in Form NCLT.1. The application shall be accompanied with such documents as are mentioned in Annexure B of NCLT Rules - Rule 80 of NCLT Rules, 2016.

39.3-1 Investigation cannot be ordered lightly

In Rohtas Industries Ltd. v. SD Agarwal 39 Comp Cas 781 = AIR 1969 SC 707 = (1969) 1 SCC 325 = (1969) 1 Comp LJ 350 = (1969) 3 SCR 108 (SC 3 member bench), it was held that standard required under section 237(b) is that of an expert and not of an ordinary citizen. An investigation may seriously damage the company and should not be ordered without proper material. Investigation is a serious matter. It should not be ordered except for good and satisfactory grounds. - . - Opinion formed by Government (for ordering investigation) is not amenable to review by Courts, but whether circumstances existed [as prescribed under section 237(b)] can be examined by Court.

39.3-2 Appointment of Inspector

Central Government can appoint one or more competent persons as inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company and report to Central Government - section 210(3) of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding section 235(1) of the 1956 Act].

If such report is on basis of request of company by special resolution, then security will have to be deposited by company (between Rs 10,000 to Rs 25,000) If investigation results in prosecution, the security will be refunded - Rule 5 of Companies (Inspection, Investigation and Inquiry) Rules, 2014.

Only an individual can be appointed as inspector. A firm or company or association cannot be appointed as inspector - section 215 of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding section 238 of the 1956 Act].

Such inspector may or may not be Government employee.

39.3-3 Investigation once continued cannot be stopped

Once investigation is ordered, the investigation can continue even if (a) special resolution for voluntary winding up is passed or (b) petition for oppression and mismanagement has been made under section 241 of Companies Act, 2013 or (c) any other proceeding for winding up is made before NCLT - section 226 of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding section 250A of the 1956 Act].

If winding up of company is ordered by NCLT, inspector shall inform NCLT about pending investigation - first proviso to section 226 of Companies Act, 2013.

Irrespective of any winding up order, the director or other employee is still required to participate in proceedings before inspector or any liability as a result of findings of the inspector - second proviso to section 226 of Companies Act, 2013.

30.39-7 (1) The Tribunal on its own or on the application of any person interested in the winding up (by the Tribunal), it may direct the liquidator either himself to prosecute the offender, or to refer the matter to the Registrar, where it appears to the Tribunal that any past or present officer, or member, of the company has been guilty of any offence in relation to the company. (2) If the needle of suspicion against any of the said persons being pointed to is discovered by the liquidator in the course of a voluntary winding up, he shall forthwith report the matter to the Registrar and to furnish him with the relevant evidence in the liquidator’s possession or control, as required; and in turn, the Registrar may refer the matter to the Central Government for further enquiry. In the case where in spite of a prima facie case arising in the course of voluntary winding up of any of the said persons being guilty the liquidator made no report to the Registrar, on the application to the Tribunal made by any one interested in the winding up, or on its own motion, the Tribunal may direct the liquidator to make such a report, whereupon the rest will follow as stated above.
