Jansen (1956) Ch 565. 26.26-6-3 STATE POLICY - The State Policy regarding company promoters, directors and managerial persons so far as their disqualifications or misconduct in relation to company affairs is concerned, it seems in an overview to have emerged as the concentration of Central Government’s power designed into a truly MCA-21 to protect the companies, not the investors, in the name of control as the mainstay. Whether it is in the nature of removal of the blot of a court conviction, increase in the number of directors on the Board beyond twelve, remuneration of directors or its increase, holding offices or places of profit by the directors and their qualification or disqualification or loans to them or loans and investments in their related companies (for return investment in the parent company’s shares as cross-holdings) or contracts or arrangements in which they are interested or sole-selling-buying agencies in which they are suspected to be interested or suspension of powers or supersession of the directors by those nominated in case of mismanagement/change in the constitution of the Board or investigation into the affairs of a company or the ownership of the shares as well as the appointment and remuneration of the managerial persons or changes in the company’s name or its situation from one State to another or unclaimed dividends, it is entirely at the highest level in the Ministry at New Delhi with the obligation of an Annual Report on its working being placed on the table of the Parliament on which there is hardly any debate. Public issues, listing and insider-trading, among others, is controlled by SEBI. Matters left to shareholders and investors include the fiduciary obligations of company promoters/directors/managerial persons, fund-raising and maintenance, dividends and bonus, political contributions, financial sickness and as contributories in winding up. The power of the general meeting is reserved for formal compliances connected with the yearly maintenance of companies and fund-raising and maintenance, with no way made visible to get back their investments robbed by the wrongdoers in control of companies. As to judicial review, as a result of the latest amendments to the Act, excepting the Supreme Court all High Court jurisdiction has been divested and transferred to the Tribunals and continued with the Criminal Courts for the levy of enhanced fines, many of them open for compounding out of court under section 621A, and imprisonment for infractions remaining only as a mere threat with the few of Government prosecutions bringing not much significant deterrence. The singular offence that is punishable with imprisonment alone extending up to five years under the Act is the application made for subscription of shares in a fictitious name by the investors, under section 68A(1).

26.26-6-4 COMPLAINTS BASED ON FIDUCIARY DUTIES - Complaints based on the fiduciary obligations per se of company promoters and directors or the managerial persons could be considered as covered by the general section 628/621 read with section 299(5) for false statements attracting imprisonment up to two years and also with fine with no limit specified. If in any return, report, certificate, balance sheet, prospectus, statement or other document required by or for the purposes of any of the provisions of the Act, any person making a statement that is false in any material particular knowingly, (not wilfully, as under section 438 of the English Act, thus widening the scope of the section) or which omits any material fact knowing it to be material, the person making the same incurs the liability to be punished under section 628. But to sustain a prosecution under the section, proof of guilty mind of knowledge of falsity is essential - P.P. Looke v. N.J. Mathew [1967] 37 Comp. Cas. 790 (Ker.).

26.26-6-4a DIRECTORS OWE THEIR DUTIES TO THE COMPANY - The directors owe their duties to the company, and it is the company or in the name of the company at the instance of shareholders where allowed or the creditors if the company’s solvency is not sufficient to pay its debts in full (for which reason the shareholders lose their power to ratify the acts of directors), that those duties can be enforced, but not at the instance of the employees as employees while the company is a going concern. A single shareholder will not succeed to bring an action for any recovery of profit made by the director, unless the action is brought as a derivative action, Prudential Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Newman Industries Ltd. (1982) 1 All ER 354 (CA). The Register of Directors’ Contracts required to be kept by the company under section 301is the open source for the shareholders as regards company contracts in which directors are interested. Filing a civil suit may be another option which is of considerable complexity, expense and time-consuming. But, such complaints are rare in our country.

Investor Help-lines

1.50 Ordinarily, in the absence of fraud or misfeasance in relation to the company or any breach of duty to the company alleged, there is no remedy in law against loss of investment in a company as a result of the company ceasing to be a going concern, it taken as an inherent risk in carrying on a business. In order to protect themselves from loss otherwise, the investors are expected generally to be aware of their rights with due recognition of their responsibilities to keep themselves informed about the developments in the affairs of the company where they have invested and to act, like participation in its meetings in person or by proxy individually or better still as a member in a kindred group of investors.

Investors’ rights

1.50-1 The investors’ rights in respect of shares include: (a) timely receipt of share certificates, whether on allotment or transfer/transmission, the abridged annual report each year and the notices for the general meetings and prompt refund of excess money paid with the share-application, dividend warrants, offers of rights shares on approval of the issue by the general body; (b) inspection of the statutory books and registers kept by the company as per the Act or to have copies in full or as extracts from the company; (c) to exercise the right of piloting members’ requisitioned resolutions/general meetings to force a change in the company’s course of affairs; (d) to commence civil and criminal proceedings against the company or the directors for defaults or infringements of their rights like oppression or mis-management; (e) to be the residual claimants or be liable as contributories on the company’s winding up; and (f) to prosecute the company and the directors for defaults under and offences against the Act or for the company to be wound-up by the Tribunal, if appropriate. Debenture or bond-holders’ rights are limited to receive the periodic returns and the return of the investment at maturity, to receive the debenture-trust-deed copy on request, and to seek the company’s winding up, if appropriate, before the Tribunal.

Trading and transfer of securities

1.50-2 As regards trading in and transfer of securities, the channels available to investors include :

(A) Trades - purchase and sale by private arrangement or via the trading floors established by the stock exchange where the securities are listed, the stock exchange route being free of the loss due to the risk of non-performance of delivery of securities and prompt payment of the consideration in the deals apart from getting the advantage of the market price at a little extra cost to the investors. While the securities are held, as owners they can raise finances against deposit of the securities.

(B) Grievances (to the low of which property rights of citizens in company or other securities have been summarily diluted as an administrative expedient to form part of Company Law)—the redressal channels available at present include the company and its Registrars first and foremost, besides the DCA and additionally in respect of listed companies, the SEBI/Stock Exchanges where the securities are listed, and the debenture-trustee in the case of debentures. Grievances in respect of Fixed Deposit Receipts in banks or financial institutions other than the Non-banking financial companies may be addressed to the RBI, but for company public deposits it is only the DCA to be approached.

Help-lines, minimal

1.50-3 Obviously, these help-lines are minimal at any rate for the vast domestic investors in a large country like India comprising of several States and divided controls to nurture investor confidence and encourage wider participation of common people in company securities, in the absence of well-known institutional remedies against wrongs available close at hand and at small cost, including provision of some measure of compensation against the perceived loss in investing in company shares compulsorily highlighted as a disclaimer in the offer documents, without it being an end in itself on its occurrence.

1.40 Administration of Law and Justice

Company Court

1.40-1 Primarily, Company Court is the High Court of the State in which the registered office of a given company is situated (it being reckoned by the longest time duration in the immediately preceding six months for winding up) section 10(1)(a) read with sub-section (3), or the jurisdictional District Court in the State to the extent the jurisdiction has been conferred by the Central Government in section 10(1)(b) read with sub-section (2) vide Notification GSR 663 of 29-5-1959 and GSR 1626 of 13.10.1966 conferring jurisdiction in respect of sections 89, 113, 118, 141, 144, 163, 196, 219, 234, 304, 307 and 614—generally—with some conditions. Consequent to the coming into force of Companies (Second Amendment) Act, 2002, which is yet to be notified, the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) and Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) would be established (sections 10FB and 10FQ), in replacement of the Company Law Board which was in operation since 1-1-1964 introduced by the 1963 Amendment Act (section 10FA), and ousted the jurisdiction of High Court altogether so far as companies are concerned. With this, all Civil Court jurisdiction is barred with the exception of Constitutional powers of the High Court. Appeal against the orders of the Appellate Tribunal lies to the Supreme Court on questions of law. As against this, Taxation laws provide for reference of questions of law to the High Court [since shifted to the National Tax Tribunal formed recently, but halted by the ad interim order of the Bombay High Court in P.C. Joshi v. Union of India [2006] 282 ITR 39/152 Taxman 285] while jurisdiction of the Civil Courts is barred otherwise.

Puzzling mis-joinder of executive, civil and criminal adjudication

1.40-2 Under the Taxation and the economic laws enormous discretionary powers are vested in the Executive, subject to review of special Tribunals. In the same token, though companies are no Government, these are more or less equated to it in the philosophy of self-regulation subject to the purview of State-controlled Regulators of which SEBI partakes of the character both of a Corporate Regulator as well as a quasi-judicial Tribunal with powers of a Civil Court conferred on it in respect of calling for information from, undertaking inspection, conducting enquiries and audits of stock exchanges, mutual funds, other persons associated with the securities market, intermediaries and self-regulatory organizations in the securities market [section 10(i) and (3) of SEBI Act] and imposing penalties and/or fastening cease and desist orders.

Civil Court’s jurisdiction

1.40-3 Civil Court jurisdiction lies still in matters falling outside the purview of the NCLT in respect of protection of the property or prevention of invasion of related rights of the investors in shares or compensation for loss or damage like the remedies provided under section 62 (read with section 10), civil liability for mis-statements in prospectus under the Act and other civil matters connected to meetings, appointments of directors, debts and commercial disputes and torts subject to the jurisdiction being vested in the Court by Government Notification under section 10 and the Civil Procedure Code, and otherwise companies have been distanced from the Civil Court in the largest ever measure so far as shareholders are concerned.

Dilatory part of court procedure is a dampener 1.40-13 In addition to the question on the proper Court of competent jurisdiction discussed above, companies and company affairs that happen to be brought before the courts for adjudication in whatever context are equally subject to the common curse of endemic court delays and related costs largely due to the archaic, outmoded and staid procedural laws made by the imperialist British regime around the 1850’s remaining firm at the core through six decades of India’s Independence to the present electronic era, as a consequence of the law-makers’ choice of creating multiple fast track courts or forums parallelly, to the exclusion of the jurisdiction of ordinary civil courts which are nearer to people and familiar to them in the view that those courts are super-saturated with other cases and allowing their jurisdiction over company cases to continue would only add to further delays, instead of overhauling the procedural laws to rid them off the dilatory parts for faster disposal of cases by the common law courts and creating more. Unfortunately, seeing the victims sapped by prolonged litigation for years lasting for a generation or over in many cases, there is a misgiving present generally as an aside in the minds of people on ‘who is watching what they do’ about the Judiciary in our system. These factors have contributed to encourage people at large to keep away from approaching the Courts on their disputes with others and swallow the losses unless compelled not for some little money alone as in the case of the common investors, or it forms the lesser evil faced by them, or it found advantageous to show as inescapable and vindicate their own position at any cost to the company or others. Overall, so far as companies are concerned, the combined incidence of these factors has gone in favour of the managements to do what they prefer rather than what they should under the laws in matters of the corporate investors or others.

CHAPTER 384

PETITION TO COMPANY LAW BOARD 1 FOR INVESTIGATION OF COMPANY’S AFFAIRS *PETITION TO COMPANY LAW BOARD1 FOR INVESTIGATION OF COMPANY’S AFFAIRS*

384.1 Background note384.1 Background note

The Company Law Board has been empowered to order investigation into the company’s affairs if a petition to this effect is made by the specified number of members.

384.2 Right of members to submit petition384.2 Right of members to submit petition

The right to make an application is available to the following members :

u in the case of a company having a share capital, not less than two hundred members of the company or member(s) holding not less than one-tenth of the total voting powers.

u in the case of a company not having a share capital, not less than one-fifth of the total number of its members.

The application should be supported by evidence to show the grounds for ordering investigation of the affairs of the company.

384.3 Providing security384.3 Providing security

The applicant(s) must provide security, for such amounts not exceeding one thousand rupees, which may be required by the Central Government for payment of the cost of investigation.

384.4 Submission of petition384.4 Submission of petition

A petition in Form No. 1 in Annexure II to the Company Law Regulations, 1991 shall be made to the Company Law Board for issue of order for investigation of the company’s affairs. The petition may be made by the members and presented by the petitioner(s) in person or through authorised representative to the concerned Bench Office or by registered post with acknowledgement due addressed to the Secretary or Bench Officer of the concerned Bench. A copy of the petition should be served on the Registrar of Companies.

384.4-1 Documents to accompany petition384.4-1 Documents to accompany petition

The petition should be accompanied by the following documents :

(a) Document and/or other evidence in support of the statements made in the petition, as are reasonably open to the petitioner(s).

(b) Documentary evidence in proof of the eligibility and status of the petitioner(s) with the voting power held by each of them.

(c) Affidavit verifying petition.

(d) Bank draft drawn in favour of pay and Accounts Officer, Ministry of Company Affairs evidencing payment of application fee of Rs. 2,500.

(e) Memorandum of appearance in Form No. 5 of CLB Regulations with copy of the Board Resolution or the executed Vakalatnama, as the case may be, if the petition is filed by the authorised representative or advocate.

(f) Index of documents.

(g) Acknowledgement from the Office of the Registrar of Companies for serving the petition.

(h) Three extra copies of the petition.

384.4-2 Contents of petition384.4-2 Contents of petition

The petition should set forth the name of the company, with its status, date of incorporation, the address of its registered office, authorised capital, paid-up capital with division of different classes of shares and terms of issue, if any, in the case of preference shares, main objects in brief, present business activities and should also set forth concisely under distinct heads the grounds for such petition and nature of relief sought for.

384.4-3 Attestation of documents384.4-3 Attestation of documents

The documents may be attested by the party or the authorised representative or by the advocate and shall be marked serially as Annexures A1, A2, A3 and so on.

384.5 Serving copy of the petition on respondent(s)384.5 Serving copy of the petition on respondent(s)

A copy of the petition, reference or application should be served on the respondent(s) and evidence for service of petition should be produced. Where the number of respondents is more than five, the Secretary or Bench Officer may permit the petitioner to file extra copies of the petition at the time of issue of notice to the respondents.

384.6 Serving copy of the petition on Central Government384.6 Serving copy of the petition on Central Government

A copy of the petition or reference should be served upon the Central Government.

384.7 Order of Company Law Board384.7 Order of Company Law Board

The Company Law Board shall pass an order declaring that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated by an inspector or inspectors.

384.8 Appointment of inspectors384.8 Appointment of inspectors

On making of order by Company Law Board to appoint inspectors, the Central Government shall appoint one or more competent persons as inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company and to report thereon.

384.8-1 Prohibition384.8-1 Prohibition

No firm, body corporate or other associations shall be appointed as inspectors.

384.8-2 Continuance of investigation384.8-2 Continuance of investigation

[Para 13]. In Asia Stone S.L. v. B. & G. Impex (P.) Ltd.197, the applicant-company was a shareholder in the first respondent-company holding up to 99.67 per cent of its paid-up capital. The first respondent company held its first board meeting on 17-7-2006 wherein 'V' was appointed as an additional director. The second respondent and the third respondent were also appointed as additional directors at subsequent board meetings. Subsequently, 'V' and the first directors of the first respondent-company, i.e., respondents 4 and 5 resigned from their posts and their resignations were accepted by the board at a meeting held on 24-11-2006. Consequently, the board was left with only two members comprising of respondent Nos. 2 and 3. The applicant alleged that the first respondent held the first AGM on 25-7-2007 without giving any notice to the applicant. When the applicant's authorized representatives visited registered office of the first respondent, it was found closed and there was no responsible person available to answer their questions. Thereafter, the applicant made all efforts for inspection and for obtaining the records but all went in vain. The applicant apprehended that all was not well with the first respondent and that it was kept in dark about the affairs of the company. The applicant was served with a copy of the plaint from where it was able to get a copy of the notice of first the AGM, dated 25-7-2007. From said notice, it was evident that the first respondent had not appointed any new director at the AGM. The only two members of the board were respondent Nos. 2 and 3 who could only hold office upto the date of AGM, i.e., up to 25-7-2007 in terms of section 260. Further, the inspection of documents with RoC revealed that many statutory documents were not filed in spite of the fact that due date for filing same had already expired. The applicant feared of action by the RoC for statutory violations and non-performance of statutory violation by the first respondent. In these circumstances, the applicant invoked the provisions of section 186 for passing appropriate orders/directions in the interest of justice and prayed that the board may appoint an independent Chairman and also give directions in relation to calling/holding and conducting the EGM of the company for the purpose of appointing two individuals to the board of directors of the company. He further prayed that a single member present in person or proxy would be deemed to constitute a valid quorum for the purpose of the EGM. Held, As per the provisions of section 260 it is crystal clear that the additional directors so appointed shall hold office only up to the date of the next AGM. In the instant case, the first AGM purportedly was held on 25-7-2007 at the registered office of the company and the agenda of the meeting was mentioned in the notice dated 25-6-2007, wherein no such agenda for re-appointment of additional directors, as regular directors was found. Therefore, the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 were no more directors of the company, hence, the respondents stand that respondent Nos. 2 and 3 were the current directors could not be accepted. The first directors, i.e., the respondent Nos. 4 and 5 and the other additional director 'V' had resigned and the same was accepted at the sixth board meeting held on 24-11-2006. In view of the resignation and the completion of tenure of the additional directors, the company was not having any directors on its board. The submission of the applicant that the company was not having the directors was valid and legal. The report of the RoC was taken on record which further strengthened the case of the applicant that the company had no directors on its board. Section 169 specifically gives powers to the board of directors of a company to call for an EGM on the requisition of such number of members of the company as are specified in section 169(4). In the instant case, there was no such board and the main grievance of the applicant was that no such board existed and the company was functioning without a proper board and the applicant could not approach the company for convening an EGM. The submissions of the applicant were to be fully agreed with. As the company was not having board of directors, the contention of the respondent that the applicant could have invoked the provisions of section 169 did not have any merit. Therefore, the applicant had no other alternate except to invoke provisions of section 186(1). In view of the observations and findings, the application was to be allowed with the following directions :—

(i)

A practicing company secretary should be appointed as the Chairman for the purpose of calling, holding and conducting the EGM of the first respondent-company.

39.3-5 Procedures and powers of inspector during investigation

It is duty of all officers and employees of the company to preserve and produce all books and papers and to provide all assistance to the inspector. Agreement with foreign Government on reciprocal basis to assist in enquiry - Central Government can enter into agreement with Government of foreign State on reciprocal basis to assist in inspection, inquiry or investigation under the Companies Act and corresponding foreign Act [section 217(10) of Companies Act, 2013].

Letter of request to foreign Court or authority to take statement - Inspector can make application to local Court to request to foreign Court or authority to record statement of a person in that Country and send that statement to Court in India. Similarly, if Court or authority in foreign country requests, the Court in India shall record the statement and send it to foreign Court or authority through Central Government [section 217(12) of Companies Act, 2013].

The letter of request shall be transmitted in such manner as specified by Ministry of Corporate Affairs - Rule 6 of Companies (Registration Offices and Fees) Rules, 2014.

39.3-6 Seizure of documents by inspector

Company can take copies of the documents at its cost. Search and seizure must be according to provisions of Code of Criminal Procedure. The seized papers can be kept till conclusion of investigation. The inspector can take copies of any document or place identification marks on them before returning the books and papers - section 220 of Companies Act, 2013. 20.3-10d Role of SEBI - By section 11(1) of the SEBI Act, it is the duty of SEBI to protect the interests of investors in securities by such measures as it deems fit; and section 11A of the said Act authorizes SEBI :

(1) to prescribe regulations on matters relating to issue of capital, transfer of securities and other incidental matters as well as the manner in which such matters shall be disclosed in the offer documents by the companies, without prejudice to the Companies Act provisions;

(2) by general or special orders, prohibit any company from issuing prospectus, any offer document, or advertisement soliciting money from the public for the issue of securities as also specify the conditions subject to which the prospectus, offer document or advertisement, if not prohibited, may be issued; and

(3) specify the requirements for listing and transfer of securities and other incidental matters, without prejudice to section 21 of the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act (that is, the mandatory requirement of complying with the conditions of the listing agreement).

Investigation of a company - Purpose

The purpose of investigation is to find out whether those in charge of the affairs of a company are guilty of illegal conduct or conduct trenching upon the breach of fiduciary obligations or oppression or misfeasance [see Kumaranunni v. Mathrubhumi Printing and Publishing Co. Ltd. [1983] 54 Comp. Cas. 370 (Ker.)]. Towards this end, an inspector merely probes into the affairs of the company and embodies in the report his opinion. The document is admissible in evidence only as a piece of opinion. The opinion, by itself does not affect the rights of the company. He does not write a judgment which binds the company nor does he penalize any body [see Aditya Sharda v. Rangoli Texdye Pvt. Ltd. [2005] 123 Comp. Cas. 390 (CLB)]. Investigation is only a fact-finding measure and has no quasi-judicial character [see New Central Jute Mills Co. Ltd. v. Deputy Secretary, Ministry of Finance [1966] 37 Comp. Cas. 341 (Cal.) and Ashoka Marketing Ltd. v. Union of India [1967] 37 Comp. Cas. 341 (Cal.)]

assessee company.

The equity share capital of this company is only Rs. 14 lakhs, which is apparently issued at a premium of Rs. 507 lakhs. Out of the funds so raised, Rs. 474 lakhs are invested in the share application money and Rs. 42.10 lakhs as advance. Once again, much more than 90% of funds are invested in the share application money with the assessee company-something typical of a conduit or shell company. An analysis of bank statement shows that Manbhawan Commercial receives Rs. 40 lakhs from one Nexcare Agency on 16 July 2010, Rs. 55 lakhs from Campus Impex on 16th July 2010, and, on that very day pays, by bank transfer, Rs. 95 lakhs to the assessee company. Similarly, on 23rd July and 24th July, Manbhawan Commercial receives Rs. 55 lakhs and Rs. 25 lakhs from Nexcare Agencies, and immediately thereafter, on 26th July 2010, pays Rs. 80 lakhs to the assessee-company. On 29th July, Manbhawan receives Rs. 20 lakhs from Bliss Dealcom and on 29 July 2010, receives Rs. 30 lakhs from Nexcare Agencies on 30 July 2010, and immediately thereafter, on 30 July 2010, pays Rs. 50 lakhs to the assessee company. On 12th August, Manbhawan receives Rs. 40 lakhs from Campus Impex and Rs. 60 lakhs from Nexcare Agencies, and, on the very next day, i.e. 13 August 2010, pays over Rs. 100 lakhs to the assessee company. The same is the position with respect to receipts of Rs. 50 lakhs each from Nexcare Agencies and Campus Impex on 17th August, and subsequent payment of Rs. 100 lakhs to the assessee-company.

The Tribunal further observed as under:

"31. Clearly, all these transactions are circular transactions with opacity about the ultimate owners as evident from the fact that even the financial statements and bank statements of Nexcare Agencies and Campus Impex show similar features- negligible revenues, shares issued at high premium and almost entire fund available passed on to other entities, and predominantly circular transactions, with low independent balances. It is a complex web of companies through which the investments in question are made, issued at unrealistic premium justified by academic and patently incorrect calculations far divorced from the realities of commercial world, and the transactions are deceptive inasmuch as each layer of companies has the source of funds in some other layer of companies operating at another level. As we have noted earlier, the premium justification lacks merits and is already rejected. The premium calculations are based on such premises as no independent investor would ever adopt, and even the fundamental assumptions are incorrect and unreal. The movement of funds is not transparent and the ultimate beneficial owners of this investment in the assessee company are not even known, leave aside the reason for their making such a risky investment, at unjustified premiums and without any participation or management control despite huge size of investment vis-à-vis the size of the company in which investment is made. The material on record does not reasonably evidence genuineness of the transactions."

The Tribunal held that "In view of our this understanding of the situation, we are unable to accept the plea of the assessee that the transaction is a bona fide transaction. In view of these discussions, as bearing in mind peculiar facts of this case, we reject the explanation of the assessee with respect to genuineness of this transactions of investment by MCPL as well."

Clearly, the facts of the case in Leena (supra) show that such cases should be investigated for benami transactions under section 2(9)(D), 2(9)(B) and 2(9)(A). Further investigations by MCA need to be carried out by invoking section 216 of the Companies Act, 2013 to find out who are the true beneficial owners who appear to be using these layers of companies as their benamidars.

Report to Tribunal by Official Liquidator [Section 455]

30.24 This Report is required only in a case where a winding up order is made by the Tribunal. In that case, and where the Statement of Affairs is dispensed with, as soon as practicable after the date of the order, the Official Liquidator should submit a preliminary report to the Tribunal, which he can do so in the case where the Statement of Affairs is received not later than six months from the date of the order or such extended period allowed by the Tribunal, covering the facts (a) as to the amount of capital issued, subscribed, and paid-up, and the estimated amount of assets and liabilities, the assets detailed into (i) cash and negotiable securities, (ii) debts due from the contributories, (iii) debts due to the company and the securities available, movable and immovable properties belonging to the company, and (iv) unpaid calls; (b) if the company has failed, as to the causes of the failure; and (c) whether in his opinion, further inquiry is desirable as to any matter relating to the promotion, formation, or failure of the company, or the conduct of its business. He may supplement by further report or reports submitted to the Tribunal on the manner of the company’s promotion or formation and whether in his opinion any fraud has been committed by any person, or by any of the company’s officers since its formation, and any other matters. If the Official Liquidator’s Reports refer to any fraud having been committed, the Tribunal shall have the further powers as set out in section 478 to order public examination of promoters, directors etc. mentioned in the preceding discussion.

Investigation of ownership of company

The powers under section 247 of the 1956 Act were exercised by the CLB. These have been transferred to the Tribunal in the 2013 Act.

The following provisions which were there in section 247 of the 1956 Act are no longer there in section 216 of the 2013 Act—

-

Central Government shall not be bound to furnish the company or any other person with a copy of any report by an inspector or with a complete copy thereof, if it is of opinion that there is good reason for not divulging the contents of the report or of parts thereof.

-

In such a case, the Central Government shall cause to be kept by the Registrar a copy of any such report or, as the case may be, of the parts thereof, as respects which it is not of that opinion.

-

The expenses of any investigation as above shall be defrayed by the Central Government out of moneys provided by Parliament, unless the Central Government directs that the expenses or any part thereof should be paid by the persons on whose application the investigation was ordered.

Powers of directors

26.4 The powers of the directors are co-extensive with the powers of the company as conditioned and controlled by the memorandum, the articles and the Act, cf. Oakbank Oil Co. v. Crum (1882) 8 AC 65; and so long as they do so, the Court should grant temporary injunction to restrain persons from interfering with the duly elected directors in the discharge of their duties - Gur Prasad Kapoor v. Rameshwar Prasad (1933) 3 Comp. Cas. 153 (All.).

Directors’ acts have to be consistent with the articles and subsisting contracts

26.4-1 Where the articles specify the powers of directors, they cannot go beyond the limits set out - Agriculturists Cattle Insurance Co., In re (1866) 1 Ch. App. 511, and in the exercise of such powers the directors should do so subject to the agreements and contracts subsisting - Nelson v. James Nelson & Son Ltd. (1914-15) All. ER 433 (CA).

Board strength below minimum fixed by articles

26.4-2 A Board comprising lesser number of directors than that fixed by the articles cannot exercise the functions of the Board - Vishwanath Prasad Jallan v. Holyland Cinetone Ltd. (1939) 9 Comp. Cas. 324 (All.); but if their number is not less than the quorum, they may act and if the number falls below the quorum, they can act only to increase their number (regulation 75 of Table ‘A’).

Members cannot interfere with day-to-day management of the company

26.4-3 Unless the articles permit, the shareholders cannot interfere in the day-to-day management of the company - Suburban Bank (P.) Ltd. v. Thariath (1968) 38 Comp. Cas. 13 (Ker.); and where the management of the company is vested in the Board of directors by the articles, such power can be withdrawn only by amending the articles - Murarka Paint & Varnish Work (P.) Ltd. v. Mohanlal Murarka (1961) 31 Comp. Cas. 301 (Cal.), and the company in general meeting cannot pass a resolution inconsistent with the articles - Salmon v. Quin Axtens Ltd. (1909) 1 Ch. 311 (CA). Accordingly, the directors are not bound to comply with the directions given by majority of shareholders at a general meeting unless the articles are altered - Automatic Self-Cleaning Filter Syndicate Co. Ltd. v. Cunningham (1906) 2 Ch. 34 (CA), John Shaw & Sons (Salford) Ltd. v. Shaw (1935) 2 KB 113 (CA) and Pothen v. Hindustan Trading Corpn. (P.) Ltd. (1967) 37 Comp. Cas. 266 (Ker.).

Board’s powers include the powers incidental to its powers specified in the articles

26.4-4 All matters and outcomes touching the business operations may not be found listed in the memorandum and articles and, therefore, decisions on related issues are within the powers of the board of directors. Thus, whether a debt is worth pursuing is a discretion of the management - Pydah Venkata-chalapathi v. Guntur Cotton, Jute & Paper Mills Co. Ltd. AIR 1929 Mad. 353; and the management of business includes in it the power to institute suits - H.M. Ebrahim Sait v. South Indian Industrials Ltd. (1938) 8 Comp. Cas. 308 (Mad.) so also the power to remove the managing director from office - Pyare Lal Gupta v. D.P. Agarwal (1983) 53 Comp. Cas. 586 (All.), or the power to change the method of accounting - CIT v. Eastern Bengal Jute Trading Co. Ltd. (1978) 48 Comp. Cas. 262 (Cal.), or the power to create a reserve - CIT v. Oswal Woollen Mills Ltd. (1981) 51 Comp. Cas. 733 (Punj. & Har.), or to invest the reserve fund in such securities as the directors select other than speculative transactions - Burland v. Earle (1902) AC 83.

A peculiar case

Where company passes special resolution that its affairs ought to be investigated

Section 210 of the 2013 Act empowers the Central Government to order an investigation into the affairs of a company on intimation of a special resolution passed by a company that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated.

Thus, ordering of investigation when such special resolution is passed is discretionary under the 2013 Act whereas under section 237(a)(i) of the 1956 Act it was binding on the Central Government to appoint inspectors to investigate when company passed such special resolution.

in office after the expiry of his term, or serious infighting amongst the Board members. Such instances were noticed by the Courts in Re Albert David. (1964) 68 CWN 163, 172; Sishu Ranjan Dutta v. Bhola Nath Paper House Ltd. (1983) 53 Comp. Cas. 883 (Cal.) and Suresh Kumar Sanghi v. Supreme Motors Ltd. (1984) 3 Comp. LJ 9. Similarly, collusive sale of the company’s assets at low prices, fraudulent deals, misappropriation of the company’s property, fabrication of documents etc. amount to mismanagement - Hemen D. Vakil v. RDI Print & Publishing (P.) Ltd. (1993) 2 Comp. LJ 113 (CLB-New Delhi). The Supreme Court gave relief in favour of the companies in respect of mismanagement in Rajahmundry Electric Supply Corporation v. A. Nageswara Rao AIR 1956 SC 213 and Richardson & Cruddas Ltd., In re (1959) 29 Comp. Cas 549 (Cal.). However, in Ramdas Motor Transport Ltd. v. Karedla Suryanarayana (2002) 110 CC 1093, the AP High Court ordered for the complaining minority to be bought out even where the allegation of mismanagement by way of misapplication of the company’s funds failed.

25.9-9a Relief under section 398 is not linked to the liability of the company to be wound up on just and equitable ground - Relief under section 398 has no relation to the condition that the circumstances for winding up the company on just and equitable ground should exist as a preliminary for the Court to take up the complaint, as in the case of prevention of oppression under section 397. The cases that came up before the judicial forums on mismanagement under section 398 have not been many, obviously, for the reason that there specific reliefs are provided in the Act to deal with the guilty at the hands of the regulators, or otherwise in other laws with respect to the major aspects of irregularities or mismanagement again at the hands of the regulators in the financial market deals in corporate financing or fund-raising. In any case, it is rather difficult to reach to the core of the matters, for example, in various foreign technology transfer agreements or generally with respect to matters connected with intellectual property or brand equity deals or in cornering deferred tax gains in which the companies are interested, and mismanagement occurs in the dark that does not come out in the open or before the Courts, and yet makes headlines in secondary take-over deals at big values, often. To that extent, though section 398 is a complete code in itself, its range of efficacy for relief seems to be highly limited, in comparison to the cases of oppression, in practical terms to the minority stakeholders.

Other remedies - Sections 397, 398 and 408 do not confer exclusive jurisdiction on the Company Court 1/CLB to grant reliefs against oppression and mismanagement, they only provide a convenient remedy for minority shareholders under certain conditions and no intendment can be inferred that the sections exclude all other remedies: the suits by the minority shareholders against oppression and mismanagement are maintainable in the civil courts : C.D.S. Financial Services (Mauritius) Ltd. v. BPL Communications Ltd. (2004) 121 Comp. Cas. 374/56 SCL 665 (Bom.). If the allegation is that the company’s act is mala fide and oppressive which could be made in a petition under sections 397 and 398 to the CLB, the High Court cannot entertain such a petition sought to be filed under section 81 read with section 10 of the Act, as the Court has to look at the substance of the allegations and averments made in the petition - Vijay M. Shaw v. Flex Industries Ltd. (1996) 7 SCL 156 (Delhi). If a member complains that the affairs of the company were conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interest and oppressive to him which falls under section 397, the Civil Court has no jurisdiction to entertain the petition - Jaiprakash Industries Ltd. v. Lalit Bhasin (2003) 45 SCL 31 (All.) At the stage of directions to convene meeting to consider the scheme, substantive issue like justification of constitution of class of ‘scheme lenders’—debenture holders to be a separate class—could not be considered - Essar Oil Ltd., In re (2005) 62 SCL 345 (Guj.).

Notice to Central Government

25.9-10 The CLB 1 /Tribunal is required to give notice to the Central Government of every application made under section 397 or 398 to it, and is required to take into consideration any representation made to it by the Central Government before passing a final order (section 400).

HEADNOTE: Section 12(1B) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with article 142 of the Constitution of India - Collective Investment Scheme -Investigation into - Petitioners, who were shareholders of respondent-company, filed petition stating that investment made by investors in pursuance of certain scheme floated by company promising 1025 per cent return was unsafe and amount collected by company had disappeared from company - They prayed that an investigation was required to be carried out - Whether even in absence of statutory provision, since large number of investors were being defrauded by employing aforesaid corporate veil which might amount to criminal offence appropriate directions could be issued by court to search and seize property of company - Held, yes

FACT: The respondent-company had floated an investment scheme promising high return on investment. It was called 'Project Grapes' and the return mentioned in the brochure was 1025 per cent. On the basis of said scheme the company collected huge amount from public and its shareholders. The petitioners, who were shareholder of the company, filed petition stating that the investment of shareholders was totally unsafe in such company and the amount collected by the company had disappeared and, therefore, prayed that an investigation was required to be carried out.

HELD: There is no legislation which can effectively control the mushrooming of companies which tempt small investors to deposit or invest their life-savings in such companies, promising to pay fanciful returns on their investment but actually defrauding the investors after siphoning off large amounts from such investments. It is also unfortunate that nationalised banks are also advancing loans to such institutions without adequate security from such companies as well as their directors. The situation on the whole, prima facie, is not very happy and knowing fully well the parameters of the powers of the Court as well as the self-imposed restrictions under article 226 of the Constitution, the Courts, cannot be silent spectators to such piquant situations.

Prima facie, it appeared that respondents No. 1 and 2 and such other companies which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, were committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their life-long savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without there being any basis. Further, in agricultural production, this type of high returns are impossibility in this country, where, otherwise, the farmers of this country would have become multi-millionaires by this time. It appears that, because of these empty, false promises, investors are duped and the companies' monies are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

The Apex Court in case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Company (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401 held that the concept of corporate entity is evolved to encourage and promote trade and commerce but not to commit illegalities or to defraud people. The Court has also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court was exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties.

Applying the aforesaid ratio and taking into consideration the fact that large number of investors are being defrauded by employing the corporate veil which may amount to a criminal offence, and also the fact that under criminal law property acquired by fraud, cheating, etc., can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions could be issued by the Court to search and seize such property. Further, under article 226 the Court could issue appropriate directions for not only enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III but "for any other purpose", and 'any othe r purpose' would include such public interest purpose.

Considering all the facts disclosed from the material on record and taking into consideration the submissions, for combating exploitation and to retrieve hard-earned money and/or life savings of innumerable investors the Court passed order directing an enquiry, freezing of accounts of respondent-companies and attachment of their properties and assets.

HEADNOTE: Section 12(1B) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with article 142 of the Constitution of India - Collective investment scheme -Certificate of registration - SEBI filed petition in public interest stating that certain companies by issuing instrument like agro-bonds, plantation bonds, etc., were offering very high rates of return and collecting amounts from small investors and turning same amount to their sister-concern and other business instead of returning promised amount to investors and as such appropriate directions should be given by the Court to protect the interests of small investors - Whether even in absence of statutory provision since large number of investors were being defrauded by employing the aforesaid corporate veil, which might amount to a criminal offence, appropriate directions could be issued by Court to search and seize property of aforesaid companies - Held, yes

FACT: A petition was filed by the Securities & Exchange Board of India (SEBI) as a public interest litigation, wherein it was stated that it had come to the notice of the Government of India that there were entities which were issuing instruments such as agro bonds, plantation bonds, etc., offering very high rates of returns which were not consistent with the normal returns in such schemes.

In petition SEBI pointed out that respondent No. 1 had floated 18 Schemes and had collected approximately Rs. 16 crores from the small investors. Thereafter it was noticed that promoters of the schemes of respondent No. 1 were not traceable, respondent No. 1 had downed its shutters, the owners were not available, various offices of respondent No. 1 were closed and the said company was going through financial crises. Many investors were holding demonstrations outside the SEBI's office demanding action against the company and its directors.

Therefore, in petition SEBI prayed that in public interest, till regulations were framed under section 12(1B), appropriate directions be given to protect large amounts invested by middle-class people, and immediate action be taken against the directors who had siphoned off large amounts belonging to investors under the guise of corporate veil. It was further contended that the bank accounts and other assets, movable as well as immovable, of respondent No. 1 wheresoever situated required to be frozen and attached to protect the investor's money from being frittered away.

HELD: Unfortunately it appeared that there is no legislation which can effectively control the mushrooming of companies which tempt small investors to deposit or invest their life-savings in such companies, promising to pay fanciful returns on their investment but actually defrauding the investors after siphoning off large amounts from such investments. It is also unfortunate that Nationalised Banks are also advancing loans to such institutions without adequate security from such companies as well as their directors. The situation on the whole, prima facie, is not very happy and knowing fully well the parameters of the powers of the Court as well as the self-imposed restrictions under article 226 of the Constitution, the Courts, cannot be silent spectators to such piquant situations.

It, was appeared that respondent No. 1 and such other companies, which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, are committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their life-long savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without their being any basis. Further, in agricultural production, this type of high returns are impossibility in this country. It appears that, because of these empty, false promises, investors are duped and the company's monies are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

The Apex Court in case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Co. (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401, held that the concept of corporate entity is evolved to encourage and promote trade and commerce but not to commit illegalities or to defraud people.

The Court has also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court was exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties.

Applying the aforesaid ratio and taking into consideration the fact that large number of investors were being defrauded by employing the corporate veil, which may amount to a criminal offence, and also the fact that under Criminal Law property acquired by fraud, cheating, etc., can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions could be issued by the Court to search and seize such property. Further, under article 226 of the Constitution, the Court can issue appropriate directions for not only enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III of constitution but 'for any other purpose', and 'any other purpose 'would include such public interest purpose.

In this view of the matter the Court passed the order directing an enquiry freezing of accounts of respondent-company and attachment of its properties.

HEADNOTE: Article 226 of the Constitution of India - Writ petition - Whether where it prima facie appeared that investors were defrauded by respondent- company employing corporate veil and there was allegation of criminal offence of acquiring properties by fraud and cheating, appropriate directions for following properties and seizing these wherever these where lying, were required to be passed in exercise of Court's powers under article 226 of the Constitution -Held, yes

FACT: The respondent company (respondent No. 3), a residuary non-banking company, recorded a spurt in deposits from 1992-93. In 1995, on receiving complaints, the RBI conducted inspection of the respondent-company in which the RBI found an extremely unsatisfactory financial position, violation of the RBI directions and poor management. Therefore, the RBI issued prohibitory order restraining the company from accepting deposits from the public and also published notice in newspapers for the know- ledge of the general public. Receiving complaints about non-compliance of the prohibitory order, the RBI carried out a fresh inspection in 1997 in which it was found that the directors had no knowledge of and control over the affairs of the company. The registered office was not in operation and books of account had been shifted from there. Books of account had only been maintained upto 31-3-1995 and finalised upto 1993-94. Hence, the liabilities of the company to the depositors could not be determined. Substantial portion of liabilities, assets, properties and invest-ments of the company were transferred either to new companies or to its functionaries. These new companies where incorporated by officials agents and even field staff of the company. They were using premises of the assessee-company and were continuing deposit mobilisation activities violating prohibitory order of the RBI. In a branch the company itself collected deposit violating the order. The RBI also found that the company had substantial real estate, most of which had no complete documents and these were either repeatedly mortgaged or were in possession of the new companies. The RBI was also informed by the directors that investments of Rs. 152 lakhs were either realised or were encumbered.

The present writ petition under article 226 was filed by the agents and policy-holders of the respondent company. The petitioners sought appro-priate directions for protection of public interest.

HELD: There was great substance in the submission of the petitioners that the aforementioned state of affairs required immediate remedial attention. Prima facie, it was apparent that the third respondent had mobilised large deposits from the public and that innocent persons who had invested their money, had not been repaid The officials and other persons associated with the third respondent including the field-staff had formed new companies with the object of siphoning funds and assets of the third respondent to the detriment of the interest of the depositors.

Prima facie, it appeared that the respondents and such other companies, which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, are committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their lifelong savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without there being any basis. It appears that, because of these empty false promises, investors are duped and the Companies' monies are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

In the case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Company (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401, the Apex Court has referred to the discussion on the topic of corporate veil in Palmer's Company Law and has quoted with approval the observations that Courts have shown themselves willing to lifting the veil where the device of incorporation is used for some illegal or improper purpose.

The Courts have also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court is exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties. The Courts have also observed that in India, the Courts are not only Courts of law, but also the Courts of equity.

Considering the fact that a large number of investors prima facie appeared to have been defrauded, that the allegations of fraud and cheating if established would amount to a criminal offence and in view, of the fact that under the criminal law property acquired by fraud or cheating can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions were required to be issued by the Court to search and seize the property of the company. Under article 226 the Court can issue appropriate directions not only for enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III but 'for any other purpose' and 'any other purpose' would include a purpose for the protection of public interest. Therefore, order was passed directing the Commissioner, Police to appoint DC, Police to follow all assets and properties of respondent No. 3 company and to take necessary action for their seizure.

HEADNOTE: Section 12(1B) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 -Collective Investment Scheme-Respondent and certain other plantation companies were issuing instruments such as agro bonds, plantation bonds, etc., offering very high rate of returns which were not consistent with normal returns in such schemes - Cheques issued by respondent were dishonoured for want of fund and director/promoters of company were not traceable - SEBI filed petition in public interest stating that in order to ensure that investors make investment in such schemes only after they are fully acquainted with high risk factors involved in such schemes, it is necessary to decide an appropriate regulatory framework for regulating these companies - It was prayed that pending drafting of regulations appropriate directions be given to protect large amounts invested by middle class people - Whether in view of fact that large number of investors are being defrauded by employing corporate veil which may amount to a criminal offence and also fact that under criminal law property acquired by fraud, cheating, etc., can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions could be issued by Court to search and seize such property - Held, yes - Whether respondents should be restrained from operating their bank accounts and investigation by police with power to attach properties could be ordered - Held, yes

FACT: The respondent-company had floated various schemes by which it was offering fanciful returns which were highly disproportionate and com-mercially not viable. SEBI received several complaints from investors of the respondent-company to the effect that the cheques issued by the company had been dishonoured due to insufficient funds in the bank account of the respondent-company, that the office of the respondent- company had become non-functional, that directors of the respondent-company had gone defaulter and had more or less gone underground and that the funds received by the respondent had been diverted to the group companies. On the basis of these complaints, the SEBI filed petition in the interest of the members of public, stating that the Central Government was concerned with the high elements of risks associated with such schemes and hence, in order to ensure that investors make investment in such schemes only after they are fully acquainted with or made aware of the high risk factors involved in such schemes, it was felt necessary to decide an appropriate regulatory framework for regulating entities which issue such schemes.

It was prayed that in public interest, till regulations are framed, appropri- ate directions be given to protect large amounts invested by middle class people. It sought the bank accounts and other assets, movable as well as immovable, of respondent No. 1 wheresoever situated required to be frozen and attached to protect the investors’ moneys from being filtered away.

HELD: Prima facie it appears that respondent No. 1 and such other companies, which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, are committing fraud by tempting middle class persons to invest their lifelong savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without there being any basis. Further, in agriculture productions, this type of high returns are impossibility in this country, where, otherwise, the farmers of this country would have become multi-millionaires by this time. It appears that, because of this empty, false promises, investors are duped and the company’s moneys are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

As held in DDA v. Skipper Construction Co. (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401 where the corporate character is employed for the purpose of committing illegality or for defrauding others, the Court would ignore the entity with regard to corporate company and its association of men and women and will do justice between the real persons. The concept of corporate entity was evolved to encourage and promote trade and commerce but not to commit illegalities or to defraud people. Absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court while acting under article 142/226 from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties. In India, the Courts are not only Courts of law, but also the Courts of equity. In the aforesaid case, the Court passed an appropriate order attaching certain properties of the Directors of the company.

Applying the aforesaid ratio and taking into consideration the fact that large number of investors are being defrauded by employing the corporate veil, which may amount to a criminal offence, and also the fact that under Criminal Law property acquired by fraud, cheating, etc., can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions could be issued by the Court to search and seize such property. Further, under article 226 of the Constitution, the Court can issue appropriate directions for not only enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III but ‘for any other purpose’, and ‘any other purpose’ would include such public interest purpose.

Code of Criminal Procedure

Sections 155 to 157 of the Code of Criminal Procedure would oblige the State to act on information received in non-cognizable cases and cognizable cases. Section 157 would lay down the procedure for investigation. Section 158 would suggest a procedure for submission of report. Section 159 onwards would lay down the procedure till the issue is brought to logical conclusion. [Para 53] On a combined reading of the law on the subject and applying it to the present context it is found, the depositors being citizens of the country were entitled to lodge complaint with regard to the non-refund of the deposits that they made with Saradha Group and police would be obliged to act upon such complaint and bring it to logical conclusion in accordance with the procedure laid down under the Code of Criminal Procedure. Similarly, the other Central Agency being SEBI was also empowered to look into the complaint as to whether there was any illegality committed by the company in contravention of the SEBI Act and the Regulations framed thereunder and suggest remedial and penal measures to be adopted by various agencies including State Police if the company failed to act upon their direction as contained in the order passed under Regulation 73. In the instant case, SEBI would contend, time was still there. Hence, it would be premature for them to take further steps in this regard. The company did not have any registration either under the Chit Funds Act or under the SEBI Act and, thus, would attract appropriate penal measures under the relevant provisions of law and Reserve Bank of India would be obliged to advise the State in case their assistance would be needed. Sudipta's Letter to SEBI on 1-4-2013 and CBI on 6-4-2013

Sudipta offered explanation to SEBI pleading innocence. According to him, the fall of the group was a result of wrong business decision and recession in the market. He prayed for appointment of investigation agency. He would be also approaching the Court for appointment of retired High Court Judge or a Supreme Court Judge to conduct the investigation.[Para 61]

The subsequent letter to CBI was rather a detailed exercise to narrate his version from setting up his empire up to the fall. He blamed several persons including some of them having political clout. In his letter, he referred to various persons from business and political circle, sports circle, some having access up to the President of India, to assure him no interference in his business by the State agencies. He requested CBI to carry out appropriate investigation. He described the said letter as "his last wish" before his death either by way of suicide or otherwise. He referred to a list of persons that we did not get from any of the parties or the State Administration. The CBI would say, they forwarded the letter to the State for action. [Para 62]

The petitioners tried to get support from the letter establishing nexus of persons attached to corridors of power involved in this scam who in exchange of illegal gratification assured him trouble free business that would warrant an independent agency to take up the cause.[Para 63]

Sanchaita Episode

In later part of 1970s Sanchaita Investment, a partnership firm mostly operated in the urban part of the State based in Calcutta. They collected lump sum amounts as and by way of deposit refundable with high returns payable on monthly basis. The firm initially established credence by paying interest to the depositors on the firm date and obviously failed to sustain in absence of appropriate returns of investment that they made either in realty sector or film sector or otherwise. The matter reached up to the Apex Court level. The Apex Court passed an extraordinary order appointing a committee that would have an immense power including that of a Civil Court as well having summary jurisdiction. The committee would be headed by a retired District Judge to be nominated by the Chief Justice having other members on the Board. The committee would be entitled to attach any property either belonging to the firm or its agents or benamidars or anyone having nexus with Sanchaita, after forming an opinion, the property was acquired with Sanchaita money. The Commissioner would invite objection, in case any objection was put against the attachment, such objection would be considered and disposed of by a Division Bench of the High Court to be nominated by the Chief Justice and on a failure to sustain the objection by the objector the property would be sold and the proceeds would be distributed amongst the small objectors. The Civil Court was divested of the power to deal with the issue. The Apex Court passed such order presumably under Article 142. Such power, the High Court does not have. The other similar companies were wound up. In cases where companies were established under the Companies Act, 1956, the Official Liquidator disposed of the assets to pay off the dues of the creditors. [Para 64]

View in the Present Context

The Courts would definitely have power to direct CBI to conduct the investigation coupled with a direction upon the State authorities to co-operate with the CBI. However, the Court should be slow in exercising such power that could only be used in an extraordinary/exceptional circumstance. [Para 67]

While the culture of secrecy should be broken and a culture of accountability and transparency be practised, the culture of questioning is also a desirable element. Also, there cannot be any difference of opinion by any of the parties that the Central Government can very well invoke section 212(1)(c), i.e. in the public interest and order investigation into the affairs of the petitioner company. It is an admitted fact that the petitioner is now, available with all the impugned proceedings including the report of the Registrar of Companies. Their grievance is that the Central Government did not follow the relevant provisions as mandated under the Companies Act and they did not form an opinion, before ordering investigation by SFIO. It is also significant to point out that the petitioner stated in the affidavit filed in support of the writ petition in WP No. 25236 of 2018 that they are always ready and willing to face any enquiry conducted in accordance with law, besides the counsel for the petitioner during the course of argument, fairly submitted that the petitioner is inclined to co-operate with any kind of investigation to be done by the official respondents. [Para 40]

A repeated argument was made on the side of the respondents that there are sufficient materials available on record to order investigation into the affairs of the petitioner by SFIO. Even as per the statute as well as suo motu power, this Court can order such investigation. However, this Court is not inclined to do so, as it is not sitting in appeal over the decision of the Central Government in ordering investigation into the affairs of the company under section 212(1)(a) and (c) of the Act and scope of this Court under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, with regard to judicial review, is limited to the examination of decision making process and not the decision. of winding-up, the very purpose of publication of the admission is rendered nugatory. The company court is required to examine whether the winding-up of the company is in the interest of shareholders, secured and unsecured creditors, workers as well as in public interest. It is natural consequence of admission of petition. Thus, there was no merit in the contention of the petitioner that the company court had no discretion after the admission of the petition but to pass the order of winding-up. [Para 8] A perusal of the written statement filed by the company showed that the liability was not disputed. Rather, it had sought intervention of the High Court in whose supervision the investors might be repaid to prevent further loss of prestige to the company. It had been stated that the company had assets worth Rs. 1500 crores as against liability of only Rs. 761 crores and the company was very much in a position to pay its dues. It was stated that the company was set up in 1987 and till 1988, there had been no default in repayment of any maturity amounts and refunds of investors. The company disclosed that in 1998, SEBI filed writ petition No. 344 of 1998 before the Mumbai High Court seeking, inter alia, that the company might be prevented from conducting its business. Such writ petition was opposed on the ground that the petition was not maintainable as an instrumentality of a State without any statutory power, was not entitled to seek any relief against the private party. The respondent-company was called upon to satisfy the Mumbai High Court in the interest of investors with regard to its workability. The company got its assets valued which were assessed at Rs. 1,071.55 crores in addition to Rs. 33,880 crores on account of movable assets and bank balance as on 31-12-1997 against the total liability of 761 crores as on 31-12-1997. It was further stated that the company invited offers for sale of its certain properties but none of the buyers had shown any interest in view of the restraint imposed by the Mumbai High Court on 30-9-1999. Ultimately, the Mumbai High Court had appointed a retired Judge as private receiver for sale of 19 properties as set out in the schedule vide order dated 31-1-2000. [Para 11]

It was apparent from the above that there was no dispute as to the liability of the company towards the investors. It was the stand of the company that it had assets more than Rs. 1,000 crores which were sufficient to discharge the liability of the investors. It had come on record that the directors of the company were in custody since December, 2000 and the company had not been able to dispose of any of the properties for payment to the investors. It was also on record that private receiver appointed by the Mumbai High Court had also not been able to sell any property so far. Thus, a mechanism was required to be drawn so as to facilitate the sale of the property of the company at the earliest with a view to ensure payment to the investors without any further delay. The interest of such large number of creditors was required to be watched by the company court and the management of the company could not be permitted to take such investors for a ride. [Para 12]

With a view to protect the interest of the large number of creditors and shareholders of the company, it was just and appropriate to appoint provisional liquidator for control, management and sale of the movable and immovable properties so as to fetch maximum price thereof with a view to satisfy the claim of 25 lakh investors in a proper manner. However, the Official Liquidator attached to the High Court might not be able to take over the responsibility of management and sale of the properties of the company keeping in view the meagre resources at his command and inadequate infrastructure available. Therefore, instead of appointing Official Liquidator the responsibility of the provisional liquidator should be entrusted to such a person who would command respect and be able to discharge the onerous responsibility in a fair manner. [Para 13]

Apart from vesting of the company with the provisional liquidator so as to facilitate the sale thereof to liquidate the claim of the investors, the affairs of the company were also required to be investigated by an independent agency. [Para 14]

Therefore, instead of winding-up of the company in the interest of creditors and shareholders of the company a provisional liquidator was appointed to control and manage the affairs of the company with certain directions. [Para 17]

The Tribunal while allowing the Union of India to file additional affidavit supporting the case mentioned in the company petition, passed the orders on 23-2-2018 injuncting the respondents and other companies, LLPs, Trusts and individuals from removal, transfer or disposal of funds, assets and properties of the entities and individuals mentioned above until further orders.

The order dated 23-2-2018 was under challenge in company appeal.

Some of the contesting respondents to the company petition, including individuals against whom the interim order was passed on 23-2-2018, preferred different miscellaneous applications to vacate the interim order passed on 23-2-2018. Those miscellaneous applications were taken up by the Tribunal and on hearing the other common impugned order dated 2-4-2018 was passed. By the said order, interim order of stay passed against some persons, were vacated.

On appeal:

HELD: Section 210 empowers the Central Government to investigate into the affairs of a company/(companies), if it is of the opinion that such investigation is necessary for the reasons mentioned therein, including public interest. For the purpose of the said provision, the Central Government may appoint one or more persons as inspectors to investigate into the affairs of the company and to report thereon in such manner as the Central Government may direct. The SFIO has been established under section 211 of the Companies Act, 2013, which has jurisdiction to investigate into the company/(companies), where the Central Government is of the opinion that it is necessary to investigate into the affairs of a company by the SFIO for different reasons, including the public interest. Where any case has been assigned by the Central Government to the SFIO for investigation under the Act, no other investigating agency of the Central Government or any State Government can proceed with investigation in such case in respect of any offence under the Companies Act and other cases before such agency are required to transfer the relevant documents and records in respect of such offences under the Companies Act to the SFIO. Sub-section (8) of section 211 empowers certain Officers of the SFIO to arrest any person, if on the basis of material in his possession there is reason to believe, which is to be recorded in writing, that any person has been guilty of any offence punishable under sub-section (6) of section 212. [Para 30]

Investigation into company's affairs in other cases can also be done under section 213 on an application made by the eligible members as mentioned in clause (a) of section 213 or on an application made by any other person or otherwise, if it is satisfied that there are circumstances suggesting that the business of the company etc. has been conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members etc. as mentioned in clause (b) of section 213. [Para 31]

From section 213, it is clear that the Tribunal on an application made to it or 'otherwise', if satisfied that there are circumstances suggesting that the business of the company is being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members etc. as mentioned in clause (b) of section 213, after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the parties, direct the Central Government to investigate. [Para 32]

From section 221, it is clear that the Tribunal has power to direct that the transfer, removal or disposal of funds, assets, or properties of the company shall not take place during such period not exceeding three years'. In case of any removal, transfer or disposal of funds, assets, or properties of the company in contravention of the order of the Tribunal under sub-section (1) of section 221, the company is punishable with fine and imprisonment as prescribed under sub-section (2) of section 221. [Para 34]
