HEADNOTE: Section 457 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Powers of liquidator - Whether Company Court while exercising jurisdiction in an application under sections 433, 434 and 439 has power to appoint a provisional liquidator giving him liberty to sell properties, not merely property standing in name of company but also properties standing in names of other companies on premise that such assets have been created with funds collected by company - Held, yes

FACT: On complaints of large scale commission of frauds by the directors of the company involving siphoning off the company funds for private ends and for purchasing all properties in the names of other front companies and, thus, stashing away large assets from the reach of the creditors, the respondent filed winding up application against the appellant-company. The Company Court, on the basis of prima facie material that the funds of the company were transferred to other companies formed by one of the directors concluded that the affairs of the company, including assets in the names of other companies which had been created with the funds collected by the company, were required to be investigated and that such systematic investigation would bring out the extent of assets owned by the company, legal and valid so as to make available the properties for discharge of debts of the investors. The Company Court, accordingly, passed an order appointing a provisional liquidator under whose control the property, effects and actionable claims to which the company claimed to be entitled to would vest. In the instant appeal, the appellant contended that the properties that were to be brought for sale did not belong to the company and that the company could not have offered to the liquidator to take possession of all the assets, including the assets that did not stand in the name of the company.

HELD: STATUTORY POWERS OF OFFICIAL LIQUIDATOR

The powers of provisional liquidator appointed by the Company Court under section 450(3) the same powers as that the liquidator himself has. The extensive powers of the liquidator are delineated under section 457. [Para 4]

EXTENT OF DIRECTIONS THAT THE COMPANY COURT COULD PASS

Even apart from the powers of the liquidator which are co-extensive with the powers of the provisional liquidator, the Court itself has the power under section 477 at the time of appointment of the provisional liquidator to summon before it any officer of the company or person knowing or suspected to have in his possession any property or books or papers of the company or known or suspected to be indebted to the company. This power which the Company Court has under section 477 is wide enough to pass even an ex parte order to secure the interest of the persons moving the application for winding up. Having regard to such wide powers of the Company Court, it is untenable to contend that the Company Court could not have directed as regards the properties which, on a prima facie finding, were also the assets of the company. The order of the Company Court was unexceptional if it was noticed that the Company Court had also given liberty to show that the assets standing in the name of other companies did not belong to the company against which liquidation proceedings had been initiated. Indeed, no prejudice could be said to be caused by such an order. Further, section 533 enables the liquidator to apply for disclaimer of onerous property. Section 535(4), while fastening the liquidator to disclaim certain properties, makes it possible for any third party for approaching the liquidator himself staking his claim to the property which is taken possession of by the liquidator or in respect of which proceedings are taken for sale. Having regard to the scheme of the Act protecting the interest of third parties and controlling the discretion of the liquidator by overall supervision of the Company Court, it would be untenable to contend that the directions given by the Company Court at the time of appointment of the provisional liquidator were not in conformity with law. [Para 5]

DISPOSITION

The sole contention raised by the appellant was, therefore, without any substance and the appeal was to be dismissed. [Para 6]

HEADNOTE: Section 446 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding-up - Suits Stayed on Winding-Up Order - Pursuant to a petition filed by one of creditors for winding-up of company for its failure to return huge deposits collected from thousands of depositors, court formulated a scheme for running business without allowing to receive fresh deposits and appointed provisional liquidator - Company had diverted a huge amount to its sister company, by unlawful means - Despite repeated directions, company and its directors failed to furnish books of account, registers, etc., to Official Liquidator - Registers which were produced, were found to be forged and fabricated with false entries - Therefore, Court directed crime branch police to register case against managing director and directors of company (accused) and to recover books of account, register etc. - Court also directed that all matters including bail matters of accused persons should be placed before company court - At that stage company court issued notice to all accused to cancel bail granted to them - Whether except in case of proceedings pending in appeal before Supreme Court, and High Court, in respect of all other proceedings, both civil and criminal, company court has jurisdiction to transfer all such proceedings or cases before it and to decide same - Held, yes - Whether since directors were at large, all records were with them and there was every possibility of creating bogus claims in names of men of their confidence or choice thereby defeating interests of real depositors, it was imperative to cancel bail and to keep accused in judicial custody till they produced registers and books of account - Held, yes

FACT: When the company failed to return nearly Rs. 18 crores collected from thousands of depositors, one of the creditors filed petition for winding-up of the company. In the meantime, the company filed an application under section 391 for obtaining sanction to a scheme of compromise, which was refused by the court. The court, however, formulated a scheme for running the business without allowing to receive fresh deposits and appointed provisional liquidator. The company had diverted a huge amount to its sister company by unlawful means in violation of the provisions of law and the directions issued by the Reserve Bank of India. Despite repeated directions of the court, the company and its managing director did not furnish the books of account, registers and the securities including the gold to the Official Liquidator, and even those registers which were produced before the Official Liquidator, were found to be forged and fabricated with false entries. The court, thereupon, passed an order directing the crime branch police to register a case and to recover the books of account, register, etc. It also issued certain directions to the effect that all the genuine registers, account books, etc., should be seized/recovered and that the investigating officer should further enquire whether any properties had been acquired by the directors in the name of others as benami with the company's funds. Further, it would be open to him to arrest the respondent-managing director as well as directors of the company. The police, accordingly, registered a criminal case against the directors of the company as well as accused 5 and 6 who had joined them in diverting considerable sum to a sister concern. Subsequently, the court directed that all matters including bail matters, should be placed before the company court. At that stage the company court found it necessary to give notice to all the accused, why the bail granted to all of them should not be cancelled. The case of the accused was that the company court had no jurisdiction to cancel the bail which was granted by another bench of the court and the petition for cancellation of bail should also go before the same bench which granted the bail.

HELD: When the court had found that it was impossible to proceed with the liquidation proceedings in accordance with law due to the violation of the lawful orders and directions of the court by the directors and the large scale forging of documents, misappropriation of money and the fraud committed by the directors of the company, by order dated 25-3-2003, it was directed that all the matters including bail matters relating to the company and its sister companies should be placed before the company court. The said order was fully in accordance with section 446 which empowers the court to transfer all cases or proceedings pending before all courts to the company court. The only restriction imposed by sub-section (4) of section 446 is that the provisions in sub-sections (1) to (3) would not apply to proceedings pending in appeal before the Supreme Court or the High Court. But in respect of all other proceedings, both civil and criminal, the company court has jurisdiction to transfer all such proceedings or cases before it and to decide the same. [Paras 9 and 10]

1992 as the cut off year for preparing the list, the argument that the line had been drawn out arbitrarily excluding companies which had issued capital prior to 1992, was also unsustainable. The list of 80 companies was not a rigid list as freedom had been given to add names to the list considered necessary and the SEBI had also submitted that the identification exercise was not a one-time exercise but a continuing process. The matter under inquiry was not hit by the provisions of the Limitation Act. It was incorrect to say that by using section 11B the SEBI was usurping the powers of Registrar of Companies or that they were interfering with the management of the company. Sections 11 and 11B are interconnected and co-extensive as both these sections are mainly focussed on investor protection. On a perusal of the said section 11 it could be seen that the SEBI had been in no uncertain terms mandated to protect the interests of investors in securities by such measures as it thought fit. The expression ‘measure’ has not defined in the Act. ‘Measure’ in its generic sense is of wider amplitude. While section 11 deals with the functions of the Board section 11B is on the powers of the Board. Section 11B is in a sense a functional tool in the hands of the Board. In effect section 11B is one of the executive measures available to the SEBI to enforce its prime duty of investor protection. SEBI is thus empowered to issue directions in the interest of investors to any person or class of persons referred to in section 12 or associated with the securities market. It could not be said that a company having its shares listed on the exchange was out of the reach of sections 11 and 11B. Since the company was operating through its board of directors, the directors of the company also could be considered as persons associated with the capital market, as long as the company’s shares were listed on the exchange. Thus, taking into consideration the scope and reach of sections 11 and 11B it could not be said that the SEBI was lacking authority to issue direction to the appellant. Further, the impugned direction was not one for violation of the Companies Act or the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act. It was issued in the interest of investors under section 11B independent of the provisions of the Companies Act and the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act. Further, there was nothing wrong in relying on a report submitted by an authority like stock exchange, as the information furnished by itself was only a starting point. An inquiry thereafter followed and the concerned persons were given sufficient opportunities to put across their views before the authorities. Similarly exclusion of public deposits and debt instruments from the scope of inquiry could not be considered to be in any way discriminatory, as the matter relating to public deposits etc., was taken care of by other regimes vested with powers for the purpose. For these reasons, the SEBI was justified in pursuing the course of action against the vanishing companies and its promoters and directors and the SEBI was legally invested with the requisite authority for the purpose.

The main reason based on which the impugned order had been issued was an inference, in the absence of relevant material before the SEBI, that the appellant had misused the fund collected from the public for purposes other than for which it was collected. In terms of section 11(2)(i ) the SEBI is empowered to call for information, etc. from the appellant-company also for the reason that it was also a person associated with the securities market. The fund utilisation by the appellant-company need be looked into with reference its records in the context of the charge of misuse of funds raised from the public issue. Since the appellants had expressed their willingness to make available the requisite information, in depth study of the same would be useful to reach at a definite conclusion and also to pursue the matter thereafter, if considered necessary, to protect the interest of the investors. Since the impugned order was based on inference and was ex parte, it was proper that the appellants should be given one more opportunity to furnish the information to the SEBI in a reasonable time frame and the SEBI in the light of that information, would pass appropriate orders in accordance with the provisions of the law. The Department of Company Affairs may also be requested, if so desired, to examine the books of account and other records of the appellant company to ascertain the utilisation of the funds and if necessary follow up the matter.

The impugned order did not in any way redress the grievances of the persons who had already invested in the shares of the appellant-company. The prohibition put in on the appellants was effective only prospectively. Since the appellants had come forward to furnish the details, and the impugned order was ex parte, it was felt that further inquiry on the lines embarked on by the SEBI and follow-up action thereafter would be in the interest of the investors. For the purpose it was felt that the matter should be remanded.

Hence, the impugned order was set aside and the matter was remanded with the above directions.

Considering the report submitted by the 5th respondent dated 24-2-2020 and also the decision of the Oversight Committee dated 25-2-2020, it is viewed that there are prima facie circumstances justifying the action taken by the 2nd respondent in forming opinion with regard to necessity for ordering investigation into the affairs of by the company by SFIO, as large public interest is involved. [Para 85]

For the foregoing reasons, the issue No. 2 is also answered in the affirmative. [Para 88]

The other contention of behalf of the petitioner is that as the matter is sub judice by SEBI, the present investigation has to await the result of inquiry by SEBI. [Para 89]

In the counter affidavit it is categorically stated that the authorities that deal with the inquiry, inspection or investigation under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs are altogether different and the scope of inquiry and the procedure that would be adopted by another regulator i.e., SEBI, is different, therefore, the case of the respondents is that the contention of the petitioner is incorrect and absolute false. [Para 90]

Sub-section (2) of section 212, mandates that where any case has been assigned by the Central Government to SFIO for investigation under this Act, no other investigating agency of Central Government or the State Government shall proceed with investigation in such case in respect of any offence under this Act and in case any such investigation has already been initiated, it shall not be proceed further with and the concerned agency shall transfer the relevant documents and records in respect of such offences under this Act to SFIO. In the light of sub-section (2) of section 212, the contention of the petitioner in this regard is rejected. [Para 91]

concluded transaction but it has recurring effect on the business of the R1 company. In view of it there is no bar for petitioner to challenge the diversion of the proceeds of the IPO. In these circumstances the petition filed by the petitioner is held to be maintainable under sections 397, 398 and 237(b), as it fulfilled the requirements prescribed under section 399. Accordingly, the issue of the maintainability is decided in favour of the petitioner and against the respondents. [Para 43] The powers conferred under section 237(b) on the Tribunal are administrative in nature and can be exercised on the basis of the existence of circumstances as specified in the clause. The existence of the circumstances is a condition precedent as stipulated under section 213(b), on the basis of which a prime facie honest opinion could be formed for ordering an investigation into the affairs of the company. In other words the order for investigation into the affairs of the company can only be made on the satisfactory grounds, which are available on the record of the case file. [Para 47]

It is worthwhile to mention that the respondents have also levelled similar kind of the allegations against the petitioner. [Para 53]

According to respondents the present petition was a counter-blast to the petition filed under section 111(4) by the R2 and R10 in respect of another company, 'LIL', where the petitioner herein had played a fraud on the stakeholders including the R1 company herein.

The respondent stated that one 'KSMR', who was a General Manager of the Union Bank of India and a friend of the R2 herein advised R2 to go for a public issue and accordingly introduced 'AA', to the R2. 'AA' was the director of the P1. The R2 and his associates had an elaborate discussion with 'AA', and 'AA' at the time of discussion had promised the R2 that he would convert the R1 into one Rs. 100 crore company. Accordingly, R1 had entered into a Memorandum Of Understanding (MoU) with CSPL (a company which was managed by the 'AA') by which CSPL was appointed as Book Running Lead Manager for the IPO issue of R1.

The respondents submitted that 'AA', who was the Managing Director and Director for CSPL Group of companies in the process of preparation of documents for the IPO issue had asked the R2 to sign blank letter heads, blank printed forms and blank cheques and that the R2, though in the liquor business for more than 35 years, was not well educated and had been successfully doing liquor business only on the experience that he had acquired. To further coerce the R2 into signing the documents and the cheques, 'AA' had made a payment of Rs. 2.20 crores into the account of R1 allegedly to show his bona fide, but the fact remains that the intent of the said 'AA' from the beginning was to hatch a plan to deceive the R1 company.

The respondents further submitted that reposing faith and confidence in 'AA', the R2, signed all the blank cheques, blank forms and blank letter heads and handed over the same to 'AA' on trust and subsequently the R2 realized that the said payment was only an eye wash to carry out a much larger conspiracy against R1, the R2 and other shareholders of the company.

The respondents submitted that by way of the above transactions a sum of Rs. 72.35 crores had been credited into the account of R1 adjusting the initial expenditure of Rs. 1.25 crores. It was alleged that after crediting the IPO amount into the R1 account, 'AA' systematically transferred a lot of money to his associates and other companies utilizing the signed blank cheques.

From the facts mentioned above, it has become clear that both, the P1 and the respondents have allegedly diverted the funds of the R1 company to their associates and companies and matters are pending before the different judicial forums. Thus, there exist the circumstances which prima facie suggest that the business of the company is being conducted with intent to defraud its members and the amount collected through IPO has been diverted to the associates and companies by the P1 and the respondents, which amounts to fraud played on the investors, which points out that the management of the R1 company along with P1 is guilty of fraud, misfeasance or other misconduct towards the company and its members. In the light of the circumstances stated, this tribunal is satisfied that it necessary to order the investigation into the affairs of the R1 company under the provisions of section 213(b). [Para 55]

Thus, the Tribunal in exercise of the power conferred under section 237(b) orders for conducting investigation into the affairs of the R1 company for the purpose of bringing out the true picture about the diversion of the funds and the amount of the IPO of the R1 company and to fix the responsibility of the person in management including others responsible for misfeasance of the funds and to bring them to books and to recover the amount siphoned off in order to do substantial justice to the investor/shareholders and creditors of the R1 company. [Para 57]

HEADNOTE: Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company’s affairs in other cases - Petitioner, a shareholder of third respondent-company, being aggrieved by non-receipt of annual report and notice of extraordinary annual general meeting of company and not getting any return on his investment, filed writ petition seeking direction to first respondent to appoint a competent person as investigator for investigating affairs of company - Whether since power has been conferred on CLB to order investigation, if there are circumstances necessitating same, it was incumbent on petitioner to approach CLB and there arose no reason for exercising discretionary power vested in Company Court to order such investigation - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, writ petition was not maintainable - Held, yes

FACT: The petitioner had purchased certain shares of third respondent-company. According to him, he had neither received any annual report nor notice of any extraordinary annual general meeting of the company since he purchased the shares of the company and further he could not get even a single rupee as return on his investment. Those facts were allegedly brought to the notice of the Registrar of Companies, but no action was taken on the matter. Therefore, the petitioner filed writ petition seeking a direction to the first respondent to appoint a competent person as investigator for investigating the affairs of the third respondent-company from 1995 onwards and to file a report in the High Court. The second respondent took stand that remedy, if any, available to the petitioner was to approach the CLB in accordance with provisions of the Act and, hence, writ petition was not maintainable.

HELD: Section 237(b ) empowers the CLB, if there are circumstances necessitating investigation, to order accordingly. This power has been granted to the CLB in terms of the amendment effected in the Act in 1988. Before the amendment, sanction had to be given in terms of such clause (b ) by the Central Government. When the power vested in the executive Government is invoked, one incumbent may perhaps feel that justice may not be meted out. But after the amendment in 1988, the power vested with the Central Government had been taken away and vested with the CLB. When the power is conferred on the CLB, it was incumbent on the petitioner to approach that statutory Board which would examine and do justice, as the circumstances would demand. In such circumstances, there arose no reason for exercising the discretionary power vested in the Company Court to direct such investigation or declare that it needed investigation by the Central Government. [Para 11]

As could be seen from the different provisions of the Act and also the scheme of the Act, since the petitioner was having a remedy to approach the CLB or to invoke such other remedies available to him under the law or under the provisions of the Act, the petitioner was to be given liberty to pursue the other legal remedies available to him in accordance with law. [Para 15]

Accordingly, the writ petition was disposed of. [Para 16]

HEADNOTE: Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company’s affairs in other cases - Petitioner, which had given huge loans to respondent- companies, sought for investigation under section 237(b) by Central Government into affairs of respondent-companies and their promoter-directors for fraudulently and unlawfully making wrongful gain and having committed misfeasance, thereby causing pecuniary losses to petitioner - Siphoning-off of huge amount by respondents through 250 front companies in fraudulent manner was indicated by income-tax authorities also - Whether since without investigation under section 237(b), it was not possible to discover true and correct facts and modus operandi adopted by respondents in cheating petitioner and siphoning-off of public money, enquiry under section 237(b) was to be ordered and Central Government was to be directed to appoint inspectors for enquiry - Held, yes

FACT: The total loan given by the financial institutions to the respondent was Rs. 45 billion and stake of the petitioner (IFCI) was Rs. 17 billion. In its petitions under section 237(b), the petitioner alleged that respondents had siphoned-off loan amounts in fraudulent manner through 250 front companies as informed by the Income-tax authorities; that it had also taken proceedings against respondents before Debts Recovery Tribunal and that the BIFR had rejected the reference filed before it by the respondents. Since huge amounts of public money were involved, the petitioner had no powers of access, search or seizure into the records of the company and, therefore, prayed for investigation under section 237(b), independent of the CBI inquiry in which charge-sheet had already been filed before the Special Judge.

The respondents, on the other hand, submitted that the company had suffered huge losses due to bad market conditions; and that since the source of filing the instant petitions was based on the information provided by the income-tax authorities and a settlement application filed under section 245C(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 was still pending, the petitions were not maintainable. According to the respondents, the petition was not maintainable on the sole ground that the respondents were not managing the day-to-day affairs of respondent No. 1-company and the management of the company had been taken over by the petitioner who had appointed persons of its own choice.

HELD: The petitioner had submitted that the huge public money had been siphoned off by the respondents and that could not be visible to the naked eye. Therefore, there were sufficient grounds to order an investigation under section 237(b). The siphoning-off of the huge amount by 250 front companies in fraudulent manner had been indicated by the income-tax authorities also. The petitioner had also submitted that the new management came much after the loan amounts had been siphoned off. The investigation conducted by the CBI was for trying the accused persons for criminal conspiracy and cheating as criminal offences. Without investigation under section 237(b), it was not possible to discover true and correct facts and modus operandi adopted by the respondents in cheating the petitioner and siphoning-off of the public money. [Para 11]

Therefore, the petition was allowed and an enquiry under section 237(b) was to be ordered with direction to the Central Government to appoint inspectors for the enquiry and take appropriate action on the enquiry report. [Para 12]

HEADNOTE: Section 210 of the Companies Act, 2013/Section 235 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation - Into affairs of company - Whether provisions of 1956 Act and 2013 Act though, do not prohibit investigation to be initiated where company has passed a special resolution for voluntary winding up or where other proceeding for winding of a company are pending before Tribunal, however, same may not applicable in case of company-in-liquidation, inasmuch as winding up order of company-in-liquidation is passed much prior to report of Official Liquidator filed before Court seeking investigation by SFIO - Held, yes [Para 38]COMPANY LAW : Provisions of 1956 Act and 2013 Act though do not prohibit investigation to be initiated where company has passed a special resolution for voluntary winding up or where other proceeding for winding of a company are pending before Tribunal, however, same may not applicable in case of company-in-liquidation, inasmuch as winding up order of company-in-liquidation is passed much prior to report of Official Liquidator filed before Court seeking investigation by SFIO  COMPANY LAW : Where there was no material in Official Liquidator's report to demonstrate that there was any intention of Ex-Director of campany-in-liquidation to defraud creditors, members or any other person or that management of company-in-liquidation was guilty of fraud and misfeasance or other misconduct towards company or towards any of its members, referring matter to SFIO was uncalled for

Section 210 of the Companies Act, 2013/Section 235 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation - Into affairs of company - Respondent company was ordered to be wound up and Official Liquidator (OL) took charge of assets and affairs of company - OL filed an application seeking an order for conducting an investigation into affairs of company-in-liquidation by SFIO alleging web of intrigue employed by company in-Liquidation and other group companies in defrauding investors and diversion of funds of company - It was also alleged that balance sheets and details of group companies were not furnished by ex-directors despite being asked to do so - Further, investigation was required into diversion of funds of company-in-liquidation for which expertise was not available with Official Liquidator - Said application was allowed by Writ Court - It was noted that balance sheet, other books of account and documents of Company-in-Liquidation were in possession of OL - All properties and effects of companies were deemed to be in custody of Court/Tribunal from date of order for winding up of company - Further, there was no evidence of any fraud conducted by Company or its ex-director that would merit referring matter to SFIO - As a matter of fact, allegation against company-in-liquidation regarding a web of intrigue employed by company could have been substantiated by specific references to entries made in balance sheet and other books of account of company-in-liquidation, which had not been done - To insinuate that office of OL did not have capacity or ability to detect diversion of funds, was not acceptable given fact that a panel of chartered accountant was admittedly available to assist OL in discharge of its duties - Whether under facts and circumstances of case, instant application to recall order by writ Court directing SFIO to commence investigation was to be allowed - Held, yes [Para 47]

HEADNOTE: Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company's affairs - Whether in view of power vested with Company Law Board to order investigation in appropriate circumstances under section 237(b), petitioner could approach CLB and Company Court has no reason for exercising its discretionary power to direct such investigation - Held, yes

FACT: The petitioner, a contributory of the respondent company, in a petition filed under section 237(a)(ii) sought a declaration that the company's affairs were such that they required investigation by an Inspector appointed by the Central Government in that regard, as the Company was not maintaining proper accounts and was doing several business activities without obtaining statutory sanction from the Central Government as enjoined by law.

HELD: Of course, the company court has got power which it can exercise in terms of section 237(a)(ii) but section 237 (b) empowers the CLB, if there are circumstances necessitating investigation, to order accordingly. This power has been granted to the CLB, in terms of amendment effected in the Act in 1988. When the power is conferred on the CLB, it was incumbent for the petitioner to approach that statutory Board which should examine and do justice, as the circumstances demanded In such circumstances, there was no reason for exercising the discretionary power vested in this Company Court to direct such investigation or declare that it needed investigation by the Central Government. Accordingly, the company petition was dismissed without prejudice to the right of the petitioner to move the CLB in terms of section 237 (b).

HEADNOTE: Section 388B, read with sections 397, 398 and 403, of the Companies Act, 1956 - Managerial Personnel - Reference to Company Law Board - CLB had suspended board of directors of respondent-company by its order dated 9-1-2009 and had authorized Central Government to constitute a fresh board - Central Government with a view to safeguard interests of company, its stakeholders and public at large, filed instant application, ex parte seeking interim reliefs viz.; (i) to implead ‘V’, being Chief Finance Officer of company as respondent No. 13; (ii) to direct concerned respondents to disclose bank accounts and both movable and immovable assets owned by them; and (iii) to restrain them from alienating, mortgaging, creating charge or lien or interest in those properties - Whether since Chief Finance Officer of company was legally and directly interested in respect of subject major controversies, he was to be arrayed as respondent to instant proceedings - Held, yes - Whether since object was to preserve status quo while disputes were being adjudicated, there existed a strong prima facie case and balance of convenience in favour of grant of ex parte restraint order, as urged by Central Government, to preserve public interest at large - Held, yes

FACT: The CLB had suspended the board of directors of the respondent-company by order dated 9-1-2009 and had authorized the Central Government to constitute a fresh board of the company. The Central Government had appointed six nominee directors on the board. In the meanwhile, the Central Government with a view to safeguard the interests of the company, its stakeholders and the public at large, filed instant application, ex parte seeking interim reliefs viz.; (i ) to implead ‘V’, being Chief Finance Officer as respondent No. 13; (ii) to direct the concerned respondents to disclose the bank accounts and both movable and immovable assets owned by them; and (iii) to restrain them from alienating, mortgaging, creating charge or lien or interest in those properties. In support, of the application, it was submitted that the Central Government had ordered investigation into the affairs of the company on consideration of the report of the RoC and that the Central Government might not be able to enforce the ultimate relief which might be granted under section 542, unless the concerned respondents were restrained from alienating any of their assets, thereby protecting the interests of the company and the stake-holders.

HEADNOTE: Section 212, read with sections 210 and 206, of the Companies Act, 2013 - Serious Fraud Investigation Office - Investigation by - 'TCSPL' was a real estate company, which was developing a project named 'Greenopolis' - Petitioner/homebuyer had purchased a plot in said project - Petitioner filed a writ petition alleging that promoters and directors of 'TCSPL', had misappropriated and siphoned off funds collected from innocent homebuyers, including petitioner, into various shell/sister concerns - Petitioner sought directions to Central Government and ROC to take cognizance, initiation and conduction of appropriate inquiries and investigation against management of 'TCSPL', as also any other sister/shell companies in accordance with law - Writ Court allowed said petition - Whether since ‘Greenopolis project’ had been abandoned by ex-promoters and directors after siphoning of funds generated directly through ‘TCSPL’ and petitioner as well as those who were similarly placed investors/claimants/homebuyers were victims at their hands, application moved by ex-promoters for recalling of order was to be dismissed - Held, yes - Whether further since, investigation by RoC was progressing at a snail's pace qua ‘TCSPL’ and its ex-promoters & directors, marked by tardiness and a lack of urgency, which was unacceptable in law and prejudicial to interests of homebuyers, Central Government was thus, hereby directed that investigation be conducted into affairs of ‘TCSPL’ besides its Ex-Promoters and Directors/Management through SFIO to unearth manner in which funds generated from petitioner and other homebuyers had been siphoned off to detriment of its secured and unsecured creditors including homebuyers - Held, yes [Para 68, 74, 75, 76 and 77]

FACT: ■

The petitioner, who was a homebuyer, claimed to have purchased a plot from ‘TCSPL’, in a real estate project named ‘Greenopolis’, which was envisioned to be developed in Gurugram, Haryana. Petitioner filed writ petition against TCSPL and its Ex-promoters / directors / management, accusing them of allegedly siphoning off approximately Rs. 1,664 crores collected from innocent homebuyers into its various shell/sister concerns. This misappropriation led to TCSPL being subjected to proceedings under the IBC before the NCLT with nearly 536 investors/claimants/homebuyers lodging their claims before the IRP.

■

While the matter was pending before the NCLT, three reports were submitted by the IRP and the Status Report, which, inter alia demonstrated as to how and in what manner the Ex promoters/directors/management of TCSPL had been siphoning off the funds.

■

The petitioner vide said petition was seeking invoking the extraordinary jurisdiction of Writ Court under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution of India, 1950, seeking certain directions against Registrar of Companies (RoC) and Union of India (UoI) through the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for taking cognizance, initiation and conduction of appropriate inquiries and investigation against the management of TCSPL, as well as its shell/sister group of companies, for alleged action of manipulation of records and siphoning of funds to shell/sister companies based in Kolkata and elsewhere. Additionally, the petitioner sought reliefs in the nature of freezing the assets of such unscrupulous companies and their promoters/directors to safeguard the legal rights of the investors/claimants/homebuyers like the petitioner.

■

This, to safeguard the interest of the petitioner, as well as other similarly placed investors/claimants /homebuyers, RoC and UoI, were conjointly directed to initiate action and ensure step-wise compliance in terms of Section 206 to 210 of the Companies Act, 2013 and other analogous provisions in Chapter XIV of the Companies Act, 2013, and thereby inspect the affairs of TCSPL and the related.

■

During the course of proceedings before Writ Court, an application was moved on behalf of the ACE Group, a renowned Real Estate Developer in Delhi and NCR for impleadment, which was allowed. Subsequently, ACE Group moved an application for the recall of the order. Prior to this, TCSPL had also moved an application to recall / modification of order.

■

The ACE Group submitted that although the order was directed at RoC and UoI to inspect the affairs of the TCSPL, they were directly affected, as the IRP had endeavoured to reclaim or repossess certain properties belonging to them, which have no nexus or connection with the TCSPL.

■

HEADNOTE: Section 456 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Official Liquidator - Custody of company's property - Official Liquidator of company under liquidation put under seal two godowns claimed as belonging to applicant trust on basis of documentry evidence and only given on rent for a period to company under liquidation - However, in a writ, Division Bench had directed Police Officials to investigate properties of certain persons including that of applicant to find out as to whether directors of company siphoned off company's property - Whether, it would be proper to order police to complete investigation within four weeks and if same would not be complied with, impugned properties should be handed over to applicant - Held, yes

FACT: The Official Liquidator, appointed for liquidation of the company put his seal on the godown which the applicant trust claimed as belonging to it. The applicant submitted that they had purchased these godowns in the year 1984 while company was incorporated only in 1993. The applicant had only allowed the company to use the said premises for a period and subsequently the company vacated the premises and handed over same to the applicant. It was, therefore, contended that since the applicant trust was the owner of the premises, the seal was required to be removed. However, in a separate writ petition, the Division Bench in relevant matter had directed the Dy. Commissioner of Police to find out whether the properties belonging to respondent company were siphoned off by its director and, therefore, directed him to verify and attach the properties belonging to the company.

HELD: In view of the documentary evidence, prima facie, the property did not belong to the company in liquidation as the applicants based on the documentry evidence had been able to establish that the property belonged to the trust. Hence, the Official Liquidator should communicate to the Deputy Commissioner of Police, in charge investigating the matter who should investigate the same and if need be, move the Division Bench for suitable orders including directions in terms of para 10(j ) of the order of the Division Bench.

If no directions were taken within the said period of four weeks by the Dy. Commissioner of Police in charge of investigation, the Official Liquidator should remove the seal and handover possession of the premises to the applicant herein and the books of account and documents if any in the premises would be taken in custody by the Dy. Commissioner of Police investigating into the matter with liberty to the Official Liquidator to examine the said documents as and when required.

F.E. Devitre, J.P. Sen and Mrs. U.S. Fadia for the Applicant. B.N. Vaishnava for the Company. S.C. Gupta, Dy. Official Liquidator.

upheld - Held, yes

Section 237, read with section 397/398, of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company affairs in other cases - Whether power of CLB under section 237(b) is administrative in nature which can be exercised even suo motu by CLB - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, CLB can in a petition under section 397/398 appoint an auditor to conduct an investigative audit under section 237(b) - Held, yes FACT: The company-in-question was incorporated in 1979 by six brothers. They were the original subscribers to the memorandum of association of the company. Two more private companies and four partnership firms were thereafter floated by the six brothers. Only one brother was surviving and rest of five were dead. Legal heirs of six brothers were directors, shareholders/members of the company. Under a Housing Board Scheme, two plots earmarked for cinema theatre and petrol Bunk, were allotted to the company. The company, accordingly, constructed a theatre complex and a petrol bunk on the respective plots. In the year 2002, appellants 1 and 2 and respondent 7 executed a registered lease deed in respect of the plot on which theatre complex was constructed in favour of son of appellant 1 for a period of 10 years on monthly rent of Rs. 50,000; similarly land on which petrol bunk was constructed was sold by them to appellant 1 and his wife by a sale deed for a sum of Rs. 60 lakhs. However, the possession of the petrol bunk could not be taken, on account of the refusal of the tenant occupying the same, to vacate.

One of the companies promoted by the six brothers, viz , Annai Flour Mills had availed a loan from Vysa bank. Apart from the first charge created on the movables of the borrower company in favour of the bank, the company-in-question also gave a corporate guarantee in favour of the said bank, in addition to mortgaging the theatre complex to the bank. The borrower company, Annai Flour Mills committed default and the bank initiated recovery proceedings under the Recovery of Debts Due to Bank and Financial Institutions Act, 1993. The bank also sought the appointment of a receiver to collect the income from the theatre complex. Accordingly, the Debt Recovery Tribunal appointed a retired justice as receiver.

The receiver so appointed filed reports before the DRT pointing out certain facts with regard to the management of the company. The respondents No. 1 to 5 on the basis of said facts, alleged that those facts in the reports established oppression and mismanagement on the part of management of the company. Consequently, respondents 1 to 5 who were members/shareholders of company moved instant company petition under sections 397, 398,402 and 403 read with sections 235 and 237 and Schedule XI, seeking various reliefs. The acts of oppression and mismanagement complained of by respondents 1 to 5 were (1) the leasing out of the theatre complex to the son of the first appellant for a rent far below the market value (2) the sale of the petrol bunk in favour of the first appellant and his wife for a consideration of Rs. 60 lakh (3) the receipt of Rs. 99,000 per month by the first appellant, as interest on the sale consideration fixed for the petrol bunk, on the ground that the possession of the property could not be taken (4) the appropriation of the rent (licence fee), paid by a cellular company for the tower installed in the terrace of the theatre complex building, by the son of the first appellant (5) the salary drawn unauthorizedly by the first appellant, claiming to be the managing director and (6) the failure to conduct the annual general meetings from the year 2001 and the failure to file the annual returns. After the appointment of the receiver by the DRT, the payment of Rs. 99,000 allegedly towards interest to the first appellant and his wife was stopped. Similarly, the receipt of the rent/licence fee by the son of the first appellant from the cellular company had also been stopped.

The respondents 1 to 5 further pointed out certain circumstances indicating mismanagement. According to them, the income of the company rose up to Rs. 4 crores immediately after the receiver took over, while it remained at Rs. 2 crores, when it was under the management of the appellants. The receiver also reported that the company had received Rs. 45.10 lakh as advance from the tenants of the shops, while the income-tax return filed by the appellants for the assessment year 2004-05 accounted only for a sum of Rs. 15 lakhs towards the advances, indicating that there was siphoning off of the funds.

The CLB considered each one of the acts of mismanagement and came to a prima facie conclusion that the business of the company had been conducted in a manner oppressive to the members of the company at the hands of persons in management. The CLB also came to the conclusion that the surplus income shown by the receiver prima facie supported the charge of mismanagement, requiring a detailed investigation by an independent agency. Accordingly, a Chartered-Accountant was authorized to carry out an investigative audit of the accounts of the company from 2000 to 2005. Aggrieved by the order of the CLB, instant appeal was preferred raising contentions.

HEADNOTE: Section 237(b) of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company's affairs - Whether power under section 237(b) is a discretionary power - Held, yes -Whether, when justifiable grounds exist, merely because communication from Department of Company Affairs to Secretary, CLB, was in form of letter without any proper affidavit and without any specific mention as to what action was prayed for, CLB should refuse to exercise jurisdiction under section 237(b) - Held, no - Whether investigation is to be ordered if a prima facie opinion is formed by CLB that business of company is being/has been conducted with intent to defraud creditors, members or any other persons or conduct of company is oppressive to any of its members or there is misfeasance or misconduct on part of management in carrying on affairs of company - Held, yes - Whether, where report filed by Regional Director in Department of Company Affairs under section 209A on complaints made by Employees' Union alleging mismanagement of affairs of company, established mismanagement of funds of company, further enquiry by ROC had to be ordered - Held, yes

Section 235 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of Company's affairs -Whether section 235 can be invoked only on a report made by Registrar of Companies under section 234(6) - Held, yes - Whether where report was made by Joint Director in office of Regional Director, facility of reference under section 237(b) was correctly availed of - Held, yes

FACT: On a complaint from Workers' Union of the company, Joint Director of the office of Regional Director of Companies made enquiries under section 209A. The report revealed that (i) the company had stopped feeding its factories with sufficient quantity of raw materials forcing the workmen to idle away most of the time which resulted the production coming to stand-still; (ii) there was shortage of working capital due to mismanagement of funds resulting in loss to the tune of Rs. 659 lakhs and company could not consequently declare dividend; (iii) funds raised by floating debentures for a specific project had been diverted for other uses shelving the project; (iv) a number of loans had been advanced to totally unrelated companies and the management did not recover the same though the company was in critical financial crisis and due to this company could not procure even the raw materials, an export order could not be executed and further the company lost another foreign order worth 20 crores; (v) a sum of Rs. 77.32 lakhs was spent on construction of a temple as against the approved amount of Rs. 50 lakhs; (vi) quantity of raw material per ton cable manufactured was the highest in the year in question compared to previous year for which no plausible explanation was forthcoming; and (vii) the company had unnecessarily paid commission of Rs. 5.08 lakhs to one 'S' for procuring orders from a company with which it had regular business.

Based on this report, the Central Government filed a reference application under section 237(b) in the form of a letter, without proper affidavit and without any mention as to what action was prayed for, stating that in the absence of a report of ROC under section 234(6), the Government could not invoke its powers under section 235(1).

HELD: Though the communication from the Department of Company Affairs was in the form of a letter addressed to the Secretary, CLB without any proper affidavit and without any specific mention as to what action was prayed for, the facts as presented by the Department of Company Affairs were to be considered in exercise of power under section 237(b) since: (a) section 237(b) of the Act clothes the CLB with the suo motu power to form an opinion on consideration of circumstances presented before it;(b ) the CLB Regulations, 1991 have not specifically prescribed any procedure to be followed with regard to proceedings under section 237(b); and (c) the company was a public company and the interests of a large number of shareholders and employees were involved besides the creditors. If justifiable grounds existed CLB should not shy away from exercising jurisdiction under this section for technical reasons.

Investigation is to be ordered if a prima facie opinion is formed by the CLB that the business of the company is being/has been conducted with intent to defraud creditors, members or any other persons or the conduct of company is oppressive to any of its members or there is misfeasance or misconduct on the part of the management in carrying on the affairs of the company.

2009 filed a winding up petition before the High Court, against respondent No. 3 company. During the course of the winding up proceedings, the Single Judge of the High Court directed the respondent No. 3 to deposit a sum of Rs. 1.5 crore with the Registrar of the High Court. However, the said direction was not complied with, and, therefore, vide order of Single Judge of the High Court, the respondent No. 3 company went into liquidation. There were several other investors who too had invested in the project. Various complaints were filed against the respondent no. 3 company and its directors which resulted in an FIR being registered. Subsequently, the investigation thereon resulted in a charge sheet, wherein it was alleged that huge sums of money were diverted, defalcated and siphoned off from the corpus of respondent No. 3 company, which was meant to be utilized for the construction of the project.

It was alleged that respondent No. 3 company had, in fact, siphoned off the monies of investors to four intermediate companies who, in turn, further transferred the money to the consortium of six land owning companies. These six land-owning companies were, allegedly, related party companies of respondent No. 3. It was further alleged that these six related party companies had then purchased the subject land for the Project Mall extending to area admesuring to 115 acres. A development and management agreement was entered into between the appellant herein and a consortium of six land-owning companies for exclusive developmental rights over 11 properties extending to 115 acres of land in a real estate project launched by the consortium of six companies for a consideration of Rs. 43 crores. Vide interim orders, the Single Judge of the High Court restrained the six companies from transferring, selling or alienating the properties till further orders.

Aggrieved by the same, the appellant as well as respondent No. 4 preferred applications for vacation of the aforesaid interim orders which were allowed by the Single Judge

The Division Bench of the Delhi High Court, vide the impugned judgment and order, allowed the appeal, thereby restraining once again the transfer, selling or alienation of the properties purchased by the consortium of six companies.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

HELD: A perusal of the order of the Single Judge of the High Court would reveal that while vacating the interim injunction/orders, it had directed the Official Liquidator to carry out an audit of the books of account of the respondent No. 3 company and look into the allegations. The Single Judge of the High Court had also observed that, in case anything contrary is discovered in the course of the audit, the Official Liquidator was free to file an appropriate application with regard to the properties which were subject matter of Company Petition No. 482 of 2009. [Para 13]

It is contended on behalf of the appellant and the respondent No. 4 that the claim of the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 is hardly of a few crores. [Para 15]

While passing an order of injunction, the Courts are required to be guided by the principles of prima facie case, balance of convenience and irreparable injury. Assuming for a moment that the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 along with the other claimants have a claim of around Rs. 31 crores, the entire project in an area of 115 acres cannot be stalled. If the Division Bench of the High Court found that, there was a prima facie case in favour of the respondent Nos. 1 and 2, they could have passed an appropriate order to protect the interests of the said respondents rather than stalling the entire project. [Para 17]

Therefore, a blanket order directing maintenance of status quo in respect of the all 11 properties admeasuring 115 acres is not justified. If such an order is allowed to continue, it will cause irreparable injury to the appellant and the respondent No. 4 inasmuch as the entire development would be stalled. Insofar as the interests of the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 are concerned, the same can be protected by directing the appellant and the respondent No. 4 to file an undertaking that until further orders are passed in company petition for winding up, they shall not create any third party rights in respect of the subject properties. [Para 19]

In the result, appeal is partly allowed. The impugned judgment and order passed by the Division Bench of the High Court in Company Appeal is set aside. The appellant and the respondent No. 4 are directed to file an undertaking before this Court within four weeks from the date of this judgment that they shall not create any third party rights in respect of the properties. After the final audit report is submitted by the Auditor/Chartered Accountants appointed by the Single Judge, the Single Judge of the High Court would pass final orders with regard to the properties in respect of which the undertaking is to be given by the appellant and the respondent No. 4.

HEADNOTE: Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company's affairs - Whether very fact that respondent company had not finalised the accounts from 1993-94 onwards and that no AGM had been held after 1993 in spite of fact that it was a listed company, was sufficient to order an investigation into affairs of company under section 237(b) - Held, yes - Whether Central Government should also appoint a director on board of company to effectively monitor conduct of affairs of company - Held, yes

FACT: The respondent, a listed company, in its efforts to mobilise funds from NRIs induced the petitioner to contribute towards its share capital. After mobilising funds, the respondent company completely neglected the petitioner by not sending annual reports, etc., which a shareholder is entitled to get. All attempts made by the petitioner to get information about the functioning of the company through SEBI, Bombay Stock Exchange, etc., having failed, the petitioner tried to get inspection done of the records of the company, which was also refused by the company. Only after persistent efforts, the petitioner could get balance sheets of the company for the year ended 31-3-1992 and 31-3-1993. The Department of Company Affairs had conducted an inspection of the records of the company which revealed several violations of the provisions of the Companies Act. A Chartered Accountant permitted to inspect the books of account and other records, made several observations revealing misutilisation of funds for personal benefits. On these facts the petitioner in its petition under section 397/398 alleged oppression and mismanage- ment in the affairs of the company and sought reliefs.

HELD: The petitioner had clearly brought out that the promoters of the company, after having mobilised enormous amount of about Rs. 7 crores, more particularly from NRIs, had not bothered to conduct the affairs of the company in accordance with the provisions of law and in a prudent manner. The petitioner having invested more than Rs. 50 lakhs, had been running from pillar to post to get some information on the functioning of the company without any success. The Regional Director, Dept. of Company Affairs had also in his report reported that the company had not filed balance sheets from 1994 onwards. Notwithstanding the various observations made by the Chartered Accountant who had inspected the books of account and the fact that the Regional Director had initiated prosecution against the company, the very fact that the company had not finalised its accounts from 1993-94 onwards and that no AGM had been held after 1993 in spite of the fact that it was a listed company to protect the interest of a large number of shareholders, suitable remedial action deserved to be taken especially when the respondents had not chosen to participate in the proceedings. While the petitioner had sought for appointment of an Administrator, there were sufficient prima facie materials to exercise powers under section 237(b ) to order an investigation into the affairs of the company. Accordingly, the Central Government was directed to carry out an investigation into the affairs of the company and take appropriate further action on receipt of the investigation report.

Further, in exercise of powers under section 402, the Central Government was also directed to appoint a suitable professional person as a director on the board of the company for a period of 3 years from the date of appointment to effectively monitor the conduct of affairs of the company.

K. Ravi and Vikas Dhawan for the Petitioner. Bhogubati Prasad for the Respondent.

headnotes.text: Section 12(1B) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with article 142 of the Constitution of India - Collective Investment Scheme -Investigation into - Petitioners, who were shareholders of respondent-company, filed petition stating that investment made by investors in pursuance of certain scheme floated by company promising 1025 per cent return was unsafe and amount collected by company had disappeared from company - They prayed that an investigation was required to be carried out - Whether even in absence of statutory provision, since large number of investors were being defrauded by employing aforesaid corporate veil which might amount to criminal offence appropriate directions could be issued by court to search and seize property of company - Held, yes

Article 226 of the Constitution of India - Writ petition - Whether where it prima facie appeared that investors were defrauded by respondent- company employing corporate veil and there was allegation of criminal offence of acquiring properties by fraud and cheating, appropriate directions for following properties and seizing these wherever these where lying, were required to be passed in exercise of Court's powers under article 226 of the Constitution -Held, yes

Section 12(1B) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 -Collective Investment Scheme-Respondent and certain other plantation companies were issuing instruments such as agro bonds, plantation bonds, etc., offering very high rate of returns which were not consistent with normal returns in such schemes - Cheques issued by respondent were dishonoured for want of fund and director/promoters of company were not traceable - SEBI filed petition in public interest stating that in order to ensure that investors make investment in such schemes only after they are fully acquainted with high risk factors involved in such schemes, it is necessary to decide an appropriate regulatory framework for regulating these companies - It was prayed that pending drafting of regulations appropriate directions be given to protect large amounts invested by middle class people - Whether in view of fact that large number of investors are being defrauded by employing corporate veil which may amount to a criminal offence and also fact that under criminal law property acquired by fraud, cheating, etc., can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions could be issued by Court to search and seize such property - Held, yes - Whether respondents should be restrained from operating their bank accounts and investigation by police with power to attach properties could be ordered - Held, yes

Section 12(1B) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with article 142 of the Constitution of India - Collective investment scheme -Certificate of registration - SEBI filed petition in public interest stating that certain companies by issuing instrument like agro-bonds, plantation bonds, etc., were offering very high rates of return and collecting amounts from small investors and turning same amount to their sister-concern and other business instead of returning promised amount to investors and as such appropriate directions should be given by the Court to protect the interests of small investors - Whether even in absence of statutory provision since large number of investors were being defrauded by employing the aforesaid corporate veil, which might amount to a criminal offence, appropriate directions could be issued by Court to search and seize property of aforesaid companies - Held, yes

Section 210 of the Companies Act, 2013/Section 235 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation - Into affairs of company - Respondent company was ordered to be wound up and Official Liquidator (OL) took charge of assets and affairs of company - OL filed an application seeking an order for conducting an investigation into affairs of company-in-liquidation by SFIO alleging web of intrigue employed by company in-Liquidation and other group companies in defrauding investors and diversion of funds of company - It was also alleged that balance sheets and details of group companies were not furnished by ex-directors despite being asked to do so - Further, investigation was required into diversion of funds of company-in-liquidation for which expertise was not available with Official Liquidator - Said application was allowed by Writ Court - It was noted that balance sheet, other books of account and documents of Company-in-Liquidation were in possession of OL - All properties and effects of companies were deemed to be in custody of Court/Tribunal from date of order for winding up of company - Further, there was no evidence of any fraud conducted by Company or its ex-director that would merit referring matter to SFIO - As a matter of fact, allegation against company-in-liquidation regarding a web of intrigue employed by company could have been substantiated by specific references to entries made in balance sheet and other books of account of company-in-liquidation, which had not been done - To insinuate that office of OL did not have capacity or ability to detect diversion of funds, was not acceptable given fact that a panel of chartered accountant was admittedly available to assist OL in discharge of its duties - Whether under facts and circumstances of case, instant application to recall order by writ Court directing SFIO to commence investigation was to be allowed - Held, yes [Para 47]

Section 206, read with section 210, of the Companies Act, 2013 - Investigations and inquiries - Power to - CIRP was initiated against a real estate company 'C' by NCLT, wherein, investor/homebuyers of 'C' including petitioner, lodged their claims before resolution professional - However, NCLAT passed an order setting aside entire CIRP - Said order was challenged before Supreme Court, which passed an interim direction to maintain status quo with regard to assets of 'C' - Petitioner filed instant writ petition praying for directions in nature of mandamus to Registrar of Companies (RoC) for initiating and carrying out appropriate inquires and investigation against management of 'C' and its sister group of companies, for acts of manipulating of records and siphoning off funds - It was noted that unscrupulous promoters/ex-directors running affairs of 'C' and its group of companies had committed repeated or multiple acts of siphoning off funds which had reached ears of RoC as several investors had already written to RoC to initiat action against 'C' and yet no action was taken - Whether RoC must exercise its statutory and public duties in arresting pilferage, siphoning off of assets of 'C' and its group of companies and safeguard legitimate interests and rights of petitioner - Held, yes - Whether since there were compelling and justifiable grounds to pass directions so as to safeguard interests of petitioner and those who were similarly placed in larger public interest, interim directions were to be passed directing RoC to initiate appropriate legal action against ex directors of 'C', to inspect affairs of 'C' and also to call for records of books of account of all related companies of 'C' - Held, yes [Paras 14, 16, 18, 19 and 20]COMPANY LAW : Where RoC failed to exercise its statutory and public duties in arresting pilferage, siphoning off of assets and safeguard legitimate interests of investors of company 'C', interim directions were to be passed directing RoC to initiate appropriate legal action against alleged directors and to inspect affairs of 'C'

Section 433 of the Companies Act, 1956, read with section 45-QA of Chapter III-B of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 - Winding-up - Circumstances in which a company may be wound-up - Whether there is no inconsistency between section 433 and any of provisions of Chapter IIIB of 1934 Act in relation to right of creditors to apply for winding-up of a company through Court under section 433 - Held, yes - Whether section 45-QA of 1934 Act giving creditors mode of recovery of amount deposited through Company Law Board, does not curtail their right of winding-up of company through Court nor ousts jurisdiction of Court to entertain such a petition of winding-up - Held, yes - Appellant-company failed to repay amount deposited by investors in accordance with fixed schedule - Investors, therefore, approached Company Law Board for recovery of said amount - Company Law Board issued a detailed order as to repayment of deposits - Appellant-company, however, did not pay amount in accordance with order issued by Company Law Board - On petitions filed by investors, Company Judge passed winding-up order under section 433(e) - Appellant, in instant appeal, raised objection that investors were not entitled to file winding-up petition as only remedy available to them was to approach Civil Court for execution of order passed by Company Law Board - Whether since inspite of detailed order being issued by Company Law Board, appellant-company neither repaid amounts deposited nor took any effective steps in that regard, investors in such a situation were well within their right to approach Company Court for winding-up of appellant-company - Held, yes - Whether, in view of conduct of appellant-company and its sister concern as to collecting money from public in general, utilization of that money for purchasing properties to detriment of investors, siphoning-off of appellant-company’s money to sister concern under loan agreement with no effective condition of repayment, it could be concluded that in reality properties of sister concern also belonged to appellant-company and, therefore, such properties could also be auctioned or proceeded with for realization of amount of creditors of appellant-company - Held, yes

Section 206, read with section 210, of the Companies Act, 2013 - Investigations and inquiries - Power to - CIRP was initiated against a real estate company 'C' by NCLT, wherein, investor/homebuyers of 'C' including petitioner, lodged their claims before resolution professional - However, NCLAT passed an order setting aside entire CIRP - Said order was challenged before Supreme Court, which passed an interim direction to maintain status quo with regard to assets of 'C' - Petitioner filed instant writ petition praying for directions in nature of mandamus to Registrar of Companies (RoC) for initiating and carrying out appropriate inquires and investigation against management of 'C' and its sister group of companies, for acts of manipulating of records and siphoning off funds - It was noted that unscrupulous promoters/ex-directors running affairs of 'C' and its group of companies had committed repeated or multiple acts of siphoning off funds which had reached ears of RoC as several investors had already written to RoC to initiat action against 'C' and yet no action was taken - Whether RoC must exercise its statutory and public duties in arresting pilferage, siphoning off of assets of 'C' and its group of companies and safeguard legitimate interests and rights of petitioner - Held, yes - Whether since there were compelling and justifiable grounds to pass directions so as to safeguard interests of petitioner and those who were similarly placed in larger public interest, interim directions were to be passed directing RoC to initiate appropriate legal action against ex directors of 'C', to inspect affairs of 'C' and also to call for records of books of account of all related companies of 'C' - Held, yes [Paras 14, 16, 18, 19 and 20]

Rule 9 of the Companies (Court) Rules, 1959 - Inherent powers of Court - During take over of assets of assessee-company, suspicion arose with regard to bona fide of certain transactions - Company Court ordered C.I.D. to investigate and file a report - Investigation revealed that persons named in report had committed offences punishable under sections 120B, 420, 467 and 468 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 - Whether Company Court is empowered to issue directions to prosecute accused under rule 9 - Held, yes

Section 4 of the Chit Funds Act, 1982 - Prohibition of chits not sanctioned or registered under Act - Petitioner filed public interest litigation against chit fund companies collecting crores of rupees from investors and serving interest of political personnel - Petitioner demanded CBI investigation - Whether Courts would definitely have power to direct CBI to conduct investigation coupled with a direction upon State authorities to co-operate with CBI, however, Court should be slow in exercising such power that could only be used in an extraordinary/exceptional circumstance - Held, yes - Whether State was to be given some time to bring investigation at a close and start prosecuting accused - Held, yes - Whether CBI, Enforcement Directorate, Ministry of Corporate Affairs, SFIO and all other organisations of like nature were to be directed to render all necessary assistance to State machinery as and when asked for, so that they could complete process of investigation and start prosecuting accused - Held, yes [Paras 67,72  73]CL : Direction to CBI, Enforcement Directorate, Ministry of Corporate Affairs, SFIO and others to render all necessary assistance to State machinery to complete process of investigation and prosecution of accused in collection of funds by chit fund companies

Section 210 of the Companies Act, 2013/Section 235 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation - Into affairs of company - Whether provisions of 1956 Act and 2013 Act though, do not prohibit investigation to be initiated where company has passed a special resolution for voluntary winding up or where other proceeding for winding of a company are pending before Tribunal, however, same may not applicable in case of company-in-liquidation, inasmuch as winding up order of company-in-liquidation is passed much prior to report of Official Liquidator filed before Court seeking investigation by SFIO - Held, yes [Para 38]  Section 210 of the Companies Act, 2013/Section 235 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation - Into affairs of company - Respondent company was ordered to be wound up and Official Liquidator (OL) took charge of assets and affairs of company - OL filed an application seeking an order for conducting an investigation into affairs of company-in-liquidation by SFIO alleging web of intrigue employed by company in-Liquidation and other group companies in defrauding investors and diversion of funds of company - It was also alleged that balance sheets and details of group companies were not furnished by ex-directors despite being asked to do so - Further, investigation was required into diversion of funds of company-in-liquidation for which expertise was not available with Official Liquidator - Said application was allowed by Writ Court - It was noted that balance sheet, other books of account and documents of Company-in-Liquidation were in possession of OL - All properties and effects of companies were deemed to be in custody of Court/Tribunal from date of order for winding up of company - Further, there was no evidence of any fraud conducted by Company or its ex-director that would merit referring matter to SFIO - As a matter of fact, allegation against company-in-liquidation regarding a web of intrigue employed by company could have been substantiated by specific references to entries made in balance sheet and other books of account of company-in-liquidation, which had not been done - To insinuate that office of OL did not have capacity or ability to detect diversion of funds, was not acceptable given fact that a panel of chartered accountant was admittedly available to assist OL in discharge of its duties - Whether under facts and circumstances of case, instant application to recall order by writ Court directing SFIO to commence investigation was to be allowed - Held, yes [Para 47]

Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company’s affairs in other cases - Petitioner, which had given huge loans to respondent- companies, sought for investigation under section 237(b) by Central Government into affairs of respondent-companies and their promoter-directors for fraudulently and unlawfully making wrongful gain and having committed misfeasance, thereby causing pecuniary losses to petitioner - Siphoning-off of huge amount by respondents through 250 front companies in fraudulent manner was indicated by income-tax authorities also - Whether since without investigation under section 237(b), it was not possible to discover true and correct facts and modus operandi adopted by respondents in cheating petitioner and siphoning-off of public money, enquiry under section 237(b) was to be ordered and Central Government was to be directed to appoint inspectors for enquiry - Held, yes

Section 456 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Official Liquidator - Custody of company's property - Official Liquidator of company under liquidation put under seal two godowns claimed as belonging to applicant trust on basis of documentry evidence and only given on rent for a period to company under liquidation - However, in a writ, Division Bench had directed Police Officials to investigate properties of certain persons including that of applicant to find out as to whether directors of company siphoned off company's property - Whether, it would be proper to order police to complete investigation within four weeks and if same would not be complied with, impugned properties should be handed over to applicant - Held, yes

Section 209A, read with sections 397/398 and 237, of the Companies Act, 1956 - Inspection of books of account, etc., of companies - Petitioners, in a petition under section 397/398, besides seeking a number of reliefs, sought for investigation into affairs of company in terms of section 237(b) on ground that respondent Nos. 2 and 3 and respondent-company having mobilized funds by way of issue of shares for purpose of expanding business, had diverted same to their own sister concerns and, thus, had defrauded shareholders - It was found that respondents had failed to furnish statements of year-wise loans and investments and chartered accountants in their report submitted that company had not utilized funds for purpose for which same were raised and that substantial amount had been either invested in group companies or had been lent as loans and advances - Whether deeper probe was necessary to find out relevant facts - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Central Government was to be directed to conduct an inspection of books of account of company in terms of section 209A - Held, yes
