Section 58A of the Companies Act, 1956 - Public deposits - Pursuant to an advertisement made by an investment company inviting general public to subscribe in various fixed deposits and saving schemes, appellants subscribed to scheme - As on date of maturity certificates issued were not honoured appellants lodged an fir with police station - On application of appellants, Magistrate directed attachment of said company’s properties - Thereafter, appellants filed criminal revision petition, alleging that notwithstanding order of attachment, properties were either disposed of or dealt with in a manner contrary to order of attachment - Additional District and Sessions Judge rejected said petition on ground that appellants had no locus standi to file a revision petition - Against said order, appellants filed petitions, but same were also dismissed by High Court - Whether, on facts, without entering into matter relating to contempt of court, concerned court was to be directed to work out details and modalities as to how properties of said company could be sold to get highest price so that dues of creditors and liabilities could be paid - Held, yes

Section 12(1B) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with article 142 of the Constitution of India - Collective investment scheme - Certificate of registration - SEBI filed petition in public interest stating that certain plantation companies by issuing instrument like agro bonds, plantation bonds, etc., were offering very high rates of return and collecting amounts from small investors and siphoned off amount to their sister concern and other business instead of returning promised amount to investors - SEBI sought appropriate directions to protect interests of small investors till regulation are framed under section 12(1B) - Directions were issued by court to conduct inquiry and search and seize of property and accordingly properties of directors were attached - Investigations were said to be still in progress - Whether no further directions viz., to direct RBI to issue orders to all commercial banks and/or cooperative banks, where Respondent No. 1 Plantation company had accounts, restraining Respondent Nos. 1 to 5 and 7 from withdrawing any money from the said accounts are required to be issued for present but Central Government or State Government would have to take appropriate action in framing appropriate regulations/enactment as early as possible - Held, yes

Regulation 73 of the SEBI (Collective Investment Schemes) Regulations, 1999 - Manner of repayment and winding up -  Applicant was National Investors Forum (NIF) and its members were investors of respondent-company GFIL - SEBI inquired into activities of GFIL group and noted financial and other irregularities committed by company - SEBI filed a writ petition in Bombay High Court, in which an order was passed against GFIL restraining it from alienating properties; a similar order was passed by High Court in same year - Thus, SEBI made an order prohibiting company from alienating its properties - However, GFIL, continued to accept deposits, carrying business and alienating properties - Therefore, winding up proceedings, were preferred before High Court - Company Judge by order directed appointment of a provisional liquidator to control and manage affairs of company in accordance with directions of company court - Thereafter, company petition and all other proceedings pending against GFIL in various High Courts throughout country were transferred to Supreme Court, in a transfer petition filed by SEBI - Supreme Court by its order constituted a committee to monitor affairs of GFIL and to make sure that sale of assets of GFIL were to ensure that depositors who had parted with sizeable amounts ought to be refunded their amounts - Committee had detailed figures of amounts invested from depositors in GFIL and its group companies from different States - Committee had so far been able to collect and put to sale and realize assets to tune of Rs. 400 crore - Possibilities of disbursements, regardless of total amount deposited resulted in an outgoing of Rs.309.60 crore - As on date, there was uncertainty with respect to litigation pending in regard to at least three properties - Committee was facing a possible reimbursement claim to tune of Rs.65 crore - Further, an income tax payment of Rs.32 crore towards capital gains had been made - Whether having regard to all these aspects, at this stage, it would not be appropriate to direct any claim - Held, yes - Whether in these circumstances an expert ought to be appointed to assist committee in its task of ensuring management of its funds and evolving a method of disbursing amounts whenever position became clear - Held, yes - Whether thus RBI was to be directed to nominate an expert to advise Committee in its task of managing funds available with it to optimise their returns having regard to previous orders of Court and to evolve a feasible practicable method for disbursement of various amounts to depositors and investors - Held, yes [Paras 15, 16  18]SEBI : Where a committee was appointed to manage affairs of company and to make sure that sale of assets of company were to ensure that depositors be refunded their amounts, expert was to be appointed to assist committee in its task to evolve a feasible practicable method for disbursement of various amounts to depositors and investors

Section 446 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding-up - Suits Stayed on Winding-Up Order - Pursuant to a petition filed by one of creditors for winding-up of company for its failure to return huge deposits collected from thousands of depositors, court formulated a scheme for running business without allowing to receive fresh deposits and appointed provisional liquidator - Company had diverted a huge amount to its sister company, by unlawful means - Despite repeated directions, company and its directors failed to furnish books of account, registers, etc., to Official Liquidator - Registers which were produced, were found to be forged and fabricated with false entries - Therefore, Court directed crime branch police to register case against managing director and directors of company (accused) and to recover books of account, register etc. - Court also directed that all matters including bail matters of accused persons should be placed before company court - At that stage company court issued notice to all accused to cancel bail granted to them - Whether except in case of proceedings pending in appeal before Supreme Court, and High Court, in respect of all other proceedings, both civil and criminal, company court has jurisdiction to transfer all such proceedings or cases before it and to decide same - Held, yes - Whether since directors were at large, all records were with them and there was every possibility of creating bogus claims in names of men of their confidence or choice thereby defeating interests of real depositors, it was imperative to cancel bail and to keep accused in judicial custody till they produced registers and books of account - Held, yes

Section 433 read with  section 443 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Circumstances in which company may be wound up - Petitioner challenged winding up order on ground that company was not given opportunity of hearing and as such order was in breach of principles of natural justice - Whether where company judge had painstaking and studiously gone into whole financial aspects through a questionnaire and information regarding relevant transactions was also sought and affidavits were filed showing company's financial position, order of company judge for winding up could not be challenged on ground of non-hearing of company - Held, yes - Whether Court has ample powers to recommend investigation and give directions for filing first information report with regard to any apparent fraud by company and those in-charge of company - Held, yes

Section 235 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of affairs of a company - Whether before ordering appointment of inspectors for investigating into affairs of a company, there must be material to prove prima facie that certain irregularities are committed or fraud has been played on company by its directors; such a decision has to be taken subject to satisfaction on material placed and not otherwise - Held, yes - Whether where material placed on record prima facie showed that fraud had been played by managing director as well as other directors not only to get benefit to themselves but also causing loss to company in question, which was evident from findings recorded by management auditor's report as well as statutory auditor's report, CLB was justified in rejecting appellant's application seeking for an order of investigation into affair of company - Held, no- Whether therefore, order of CLB was liable to be set aside and application of appellant was to be allowed - Held, yes

Section 213, read with section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013/ Section 237, read with section 394 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of Company's affairs - Appellant filed an application for holding meeting of shareholders for approval of scheme of amalgamation - Single Judge finding some irregularities directed investigation by various agencies - Appellant filed appeal contending that Single Judge was carrying on roving enquiry and he should either allow or dismiss its application - Whether Single Judge was competent to issue direction under section 237(a)(ii) and, therefore, Single Judge was justified in carrying on investigation - Held, yes - Whether however, it was for Central Government to decide which authority would investigate and, therefore, it was a fit and proper case for Central Government to consider as to whether an investigation should be carried out by appropriate agency having authority in law followed by action that would be permitted in law - Held, yes - Whether appellant could not be permitted to proceed with proposed scheme of amalgamation and, therefore, application for convening meeting of shareholders was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 12  13]CL : Single Judge while sanctioning scheme of amalgamation is competent to issue direction under section 237(a)(ii) and then it is for Central Govt. to decide which authority would investigate

Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company’s affairs - In other cases - Petitioners were shareholders of respondent No. 1 company - They alleged that directors of respondent No. 1 company and its ex-promoters had committed acts of fraud, cheating, oppression, mismanagement, misfeasance, diversion of company's funds including sale of company's fixed assets and creation of multiple charge on certain fixed assets of company - It was submitted that company had failed to maintain a quorum of minimum three directors as required under section 252 as out of three persons presently acting as board of directors, tenure of two had already expired; that company had failed to convene annual general meeting continuously for seven years and also failed to submit annual returns with Registrar of Companies, due to non-finalisation of annual accounts; that directors' report was silent on important issues such as comments on qualifications in audit report, directors' responsibility statement, proper reasons for non-conducting of seven years' annual general meeting, etc.; that directors failed to appoint a whole time company secretary as per procedure laid down under section 383A; and that directors misused funds of company for personal gain - Registrar of Companies addressed a letter to instant Bench submitting therein that company held only one annual general meeting for seven years instead of holding separate annual general meetings for each year; that no extension of time was obtained by company; that company's shareholding detail was stated to be given in CD whereas no CD was received in that regard by Registrar of Companies; and that there were several complaints received by Registrar against said company - Whether on facts, it could be said that affairs of company were being conducted with an intent to defraud its members and public which were oppressive and prejudicial to interest of members - Held, yes - Whether therefore, there were enough circumstances suggesting for an investigation into affairs of company and to take necessary action - Held, yes - Whether therefore, in exercise of powers conferred under section 237(b), Central Government would order for investigation into affairs of respondent No. 1 company and would take appropriate action if warranted on receipt of investigation report - Held, yes

Section 11B of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with Regulation 41 of the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996 - Power to issue directions - SEBI had initiated proceedings against a wealth management firm founded by C.R. Bhansali ‘CRB Mutual Fund’ and its ex-management for multiple regulatory violations and systemic deficiencies - Pursuant to said proceedings, Bombay High Court vide an interim order had imposed embargo against making any payments to CR Bhansali and his group companies - On other hand, a Co Petition for winding up of scheme launched by CRB Capital was filed by RBI before Delhi High Court - For ensuring administrative convenience, Official Liquidator of Delhi High Court had filed a transfer petition before Supreme Court seeking to transfer both cases to Delhi and same was allowed by Supreme Court - Thereafter, Delhi Court had passed a final order constituting a Special Committee to discharge functions of trustee and to oversee procedure for formal winding up of scheme - A bare perusal of final order revealed that, surprisingly, none of parties raised issue concerning embargo imposed by interim order - As a result, final order remained silent on aspect and did not contain any discussion signifying an intention to modify or lift earlier embargo - In effect, there was neither an express affirmation nor an implied setting aside of interim restraint against payments being released to CRB and connected individuals and entities - Thereafter, a total sum of approximately Rs.350 crores was realised by Special Committee through sale of all assets of CRB Mutual Fund - Out of this, an amount of Rs.211 crore had been disbursed to approximately 5,000 unit holders / investors of scheme and out of Rs.211 crores, a substantial amount of Rs.131.9 crores (Approx.) had been paid to C.R. Bhansali and his family members - Whether priority of Special Committee ought to have been to firstly disburse to individuals, small unit holders  non CRB corporate entities and thereafter by way of abundant caution approach Court seeking clarification as to whether any disbursements ought to be made to CRB Group or not - Held, yes - Whether however, Special Committee had not sought any clarification from Court and had remained silent over years, even before instant Court, by not highlighting fact that such substantial sums have been paid to CRB Group - Held, yes - Whether in view of manner of distribution adopted by Special Committee, SEBI was to be directed to conduct of a Forensic Audit of all records, bank accounts, documents etc., pertaining to mutual fund scheme and Special Committee in accordance with law by exercising its powers under Section 11 and 11B of SEBI Act - Held, yes [Paras 89, 100, 128, 136 and 140]

Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 -Investigation of company’s affairs in other cases - In inspection conducted under section 209A against respondent-company by virtue of order of Department of Company Affairs, certain irregularities and violations of provisions of Act were pointed out - There was also a complaint by Small Investor Protection Forum against respondent- company - Respondent-company had made huge investment in certain companies within a short spell of 3-4 months though its main object was not to enter into share market - Within short spell of two months, respondent-company had raised its authorized capital from Rs. 50,000 to Rs. 12 crores - Whether genesis and origin of huge funds invested by respondent-company in share market when they were not in that business, needed to be probed into - Held, yes - Whether therefore, Central Government was to be directed to undertake investigation of respondent-company under section 237 - Held, yes

Section 388B, read with sections 397, 398 and 403, of the Companies Act, 1956 - Managerial Personnel - Reference to Company Law Board - CLB had suspended board of directors of respondent-company by its order dated 9-1-2009 and had authorized Central Government to constitute a fresh board - Central Government with a view to safeguard interests of company, its stakeholders and public at large, filed instant application, ex parte seeking interim reliefs viz.; (i) to implead ‘V’, being Chief Finance Officer of company as respondent No. 13; (ii) to direct concerned respondents to disclose bank accounts and both movable and immovable assets owned by them; and (iii) to restrain them from alienating, mortgaging, creating charge or lien or interest in those properties - Whether since Chief Finance Officer of company was legally and directly interested in respect of subject major controversies, he was to be arrayed as respondent to instant proceedings - Held, yes - Whether since object was to preserve status quo while disputes were being adjudicated, there existed a strong prima facie case and balance of convenience in favour of grant of ex parte restraint order, as urged by Central Government, to preserve public interest at large - Held, yes

Section  213,  read with section  221,  of the Companies Act, 2013 - Investigation into company’s affairs - Petitioner/homebuyer booked a flat in 2011 in respondent-company’s project, possession whereof was due in 2014; however, company neither delivered possession nor paid delay interest - On petitioner’s complaint, TNRERA by order dated 30-5-2022, upon company admitting refund liability but citing internal delay, directed refund with interest and costs and created a charge on allotted flat till repayment - Petitioner thereafter sought investigation under section 213(b), freezing of assets under section 221, and directions for inquiry, alleging intent to defraud creditors, non-compliance with regulatory orders, delayed statutory filings, SEBI penalty, unauthorized constructions, and pendency of insolvency proceedings - It was observed that petitioner failed to produce any material evidence demonstrating diversion or siphoning of funds by company or its directors - Mere delay in handing over possession, non-compliance with TNRERA or consumer orders, delayed financial filings, AGM violations, regulatory penalty, or initiation of insolvency proceedings would not, by themselves, establish fraudulent intent warranting investigation under section 213(b) - Whether petitioner failed to make out a prima facie case, and reliefs seeking investigation and asset freezing were liable to be declined - Held, yes - Whether further, since affairs and management of company were presently with its directors, company was to be directed to complete statutory audits from financial year 2019-20 onwards, prepare annual reports, convene AGMs, and file requisite returns with Registrar of Companies forthwith - Held, yes [Paras 63, 70, 74, 77 and 78]

Section 339 of the Companies Act, 2013 - Winding up - Liability for fraudulent conduct of business - Respondents invested Rs. 4 crores in a commercial project launched by real estate developer - Project, however, ran into trouble and construction was stalled - Neither possession was offered nor was assured return given to respondents - Respondents, thus, filed a petition for winding up of developer - There were several other investors who too had invested in project - Various complaints were filed against developer and its directors, which resulted in an FIR being registered - Subsequently, investigation thereon resulted in a charge sheet, wherein it was alleged that said developer siphoned off monies of investors including respondents to consortium of six land owning companies which were, related party companies of developer - Subsequently, said consortium of six companies purchased 11 properties extending to 115 acres of land for project mall - High Court, vide impugned judgment restrained these six companies from alienating aforesaid properties - Whether for a paltry amount claimed by respondents project admeasuring 115 acres could not be stalled however, developer was directed to give an undertaking that until further orders were passed in company petition for winding up, they would not create any third party rights in respect of subject properties - Held, yes - Whether therefore, order of High Court was not justified and was to be set aside - Held, yes. [Paras 19 and 20]

Section 339 of the Companies Act, 2013 - Winding up - Liability for fraudulent conduct of business - Respondents invested Rs. 4 crores in a commercial project launched by real estate developer - Project, however, ran into trouble and construction was stalled - Neither possession was offered nor was assured return given to respondents - Respondents, thus, filed a petition for winding up of developer - There were several other investors who too had invested in project - Various complaints were filed against developer and its directors, which resulted in an FIR being registered - Subsequently, investigation thereon resulted in a charge sheet, wherein it was alleged that said developer siphoned off monies of investors including respondents to consortium of six land owning companies which were, related party companies of developer - Subsequently, said consortium of six companies purchased 11 properties extending to 115 acres of land for project mall - High Court, vide impugned judgment restrained these six companies from alienating aforesaid properties - Whether for a paltry amount claimed by respondents project admeasuring 115 acres could not be stalled however, developer was directed to give an undertaking that until further orders were passed in company petition for winding up, they would not create any third party rights in respect of subject properties - Held, yes - Whether therefore, order of High Court was not justified and was to be set aside - Held, yes. [Paras 19 and 20]COMPANY LAW : Where in commercial property project admeasuring 115 acres respondent had a claim of only Rs. 4 crores, High Court could not stall entire project with injunction order, however, no third party rights were to be created in respect of subject properties till orders were passed in winding up petition filed by respondent against developer

I Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company’s affairs in other cases It is not necessary that for passing an order under section 237(a)(ii) there should be a proceeding already before Court; even a petition simpliciter can be entertained Delhi Flour Mills Co. Ltd., In re [1975] 45 Comp. Cas. 33 (Delhi) There is nothing in the language of section 237(a)(ii) indicating that a petition simpliciter for an action under section 237(a)(ii) cannot be entertained by the Court, but that power can only be exercised by the Court against the company in respect of whom some other proceeding is pending in the Court and the Court considers it proper to direct appointment of an Inspector. Existence or pendency of some proceeding other than one for taking action under section 237(a)(ii) is not a sine qua non. On the contrary, even in the absence of a petition simpliciter for an action under section 237(a)(ii) for directing the Central Government to appoint an Inspector, the Court while hearing some other proceeding against a company in the course of which the Court is satisfied that an inspector to investigate the affairs of the company should be appointed, may without any application to that effect proceed to pass such an order. If the Court has such wide power to exercise jurisdiction under section 237(a)(ii) in another proceeding against the same company, there is no justification for holding that a petition simpliciter under section 237(a)(ii) cannot be entertained by the Court. It may also be pointed out that rule 11(9) of the Companies (Court) Rules, 1959, provides that the Court can be moved under section 237 by a petition. That, of course, is not decisive. But if the above construction put upon section 237 is correct, the fact that a petition is prescribed for moving the Court may also point in the same direction.

Section 235, read with sections 394 and 433, of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of affairs of a company - Petitioning - creditors had filed winding up petition against respondent-company for non-payment of their dues - In order to get out of situation, board of directors of respondent-company resolved to propose a scheme of amalgamation by which respondent along with two other companies were to merge with transferee-company - Scheme of amalgamation was sanctioned - However, by interim order, effect of amalgamation was stayed - Meanwhile, without disclosing filing of company petition and that amalgamation had been stayed, transferee-company was wound up - Ex-directors of transferee-company did not file statement of affairs and left country - Whether ex-directors of respondent-company with other companies had played fraud with creditors and with Court by taking advantage of proceedings of Court by firstly making defaults in payment of creditors, getting a scheme of amalgamation approved without informing fact of pendency of winding up petition and giving notice to all creditors and, thereafter, in getting transferee-company wound up without much contest and leaving country without filing statement of affairs - Held, yes - Whether Official Liquidator was to be directed to inform Central Government to cause an enquiry into affairs of those companies under sections 235 and 237 and to submit report to Court - Held, yes

Section 213 of the Companies Act, 2013/Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation into company's affairs in other cases - Whether Tribunal is empowerd under section 213 to investigate into affairs of a company on an application made by certain number of members of company; and, on an application made by any other persons - Held, yes - Applicant bank sanctioned Term Loan Facility to respondent company - Since, respondent company failed to repay, loan account of respondent company was classified as NPA - After scrutiny of audited balance sheets of respondent company, Bank found certain financial irregularities - Bank alleged that respondent company had given interest free loans and advances to its group companies, whereas it was paying interest to banks for money borrowed and there was no material on record to suggest that respondent company had taken steps to recover advances in order to revive cash flows and stability of company - Bank had also shown that there had been diversion of funds from short term sources to long term uses - It was further revealed that though there was realization of stock receivables but there had not been any corresponding reduction in working capital limits, which suggested mismanagement in affairs of company - Bank had placed on record details of adverse comments made by auditor in audited balance sheet of respondent company - Further, not only company had collected huge amount from creditors but also had failed to repay debts and facts prima facie showed that business of respondent company was being conducted to deceive its creditors - Whether material on record suggested that deeper probe in affairs of respondent company was necessary - Held, yes - Whether thus, instant petition was allowed by holding that it was a fit case to direct Central Government to take steps to investigate into affairs of respondent company - Held, yes [Para 53]CL: Where there were allegations of manipulation of accounts by company which raised inference of misappropriation and diversion of funds with intent to defraud creditors, petition to direct Central Government to take steps to investigate into affairs of company was to be allowed

Section  213  of the Companies Act, 2013 -  Investigation into affairs of company  - Respondents were shareholders of appellant company holding 10 per cent of total shareholding of company - Respondents filed a company petition before NCLT with allegations against appellant of committing oppression and mismanagement with regard to affairs of appellant company including violations of directions and guidelines issued by RBI, siphoning of funds by board of appellant company etc. - NCLT finding substance in allegations levelled by respondents took a decision of appointment of an administrator to manage functions and affairs of company - NCLT also directed investigation into affairs of appellant company - It was noted that there were serious allegations of siphoning of funds from company - Whether an order of investigation can be directed if there are prima facie evidence and satisfaction of Tribunal that there are good reasons to warrant such investigation - Held, yes -Whether to order an investigation under section 213 conclusive proof with regard to allegations was not required and it would be sufficient if Tribunal, on basis of taking into consideration material/evidence produced on record, formed an opinion subjectively to satisfy itself that there were good grounds and reasons and prima facie case to order such investigation and such satisfaction must also be reflected in order -Held,yes -Whether in instant case, sufficient satisfaction and reasons were shown by Tribunal with regard to material/evidence considered by it and same was sufficient to order investigation as contemplated under section 213 - Held, yes - Whether therefore, investigation into affairs of appellant company was to be directed - Held, yes [Para 118]

Section 213, read with section 221 of the Companies Act, 2013 - Investigation - Into company's affairs in other cases - Petitioner was buyer in real estate project developed by company 'VSPL' - Petitioner alleged that despite very damning observations made by NCLT with regard to conduct of business/affairs of company 'VSPL' by its directors, and thereby, defrauding investors, respondent i.e. Ministry of Corporate Affairs, had miserably failed to order an inquiry into such sordid affairs through SFIO - Petitioner, thus, filed instant writ, seeking directions to respondent to appoint an investigator and complete investigation under relevent provisions of law in a time bound manner - Respondent had assailed maintainability of instant writ petition on ground that High Court in Delhi had no territorial jurisdiction - It was noted that entire cause of action on part of company 'VSPL' had arisen in State of Karnataka and, hence, instant Court in Delhi had no territorial jurisdiction and merely because seat or main head office of respondent was located in Delhi would not be sufficient to confer jurisdiction upon Court in Delhi - There was no gainsaying that respondent had its Regional Office with necessary paraphernalia in State of Karnataka and, thus, petitioner had appropriate efficacious remedy to approach Karnataka High Court in order to seek appropriate reliefs - Further, there was no averment that any person or authority within territorial jurisdiction of writ Court in Delhi was substantially affected by affairs of company in question - Whether accordingly, instant writ was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 9  10]

Section 11AA of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with regulations 10 and 71 of the SEBI (Collective Investment Scheme) Regulations, 1999 - Collective Investment Scheme - Supreme Court in Subrata Chattoraj v. UOI [2014] 45 taxmann.com 200 had held specifically that investigation should be undertaken in similar cases and other companies, with reference to Sarada Investment Company and its subsidiaries - Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) conducted investigation and framed charges against petitioner company and its directors for their alleged involvement in said financial scam - Petitioner by filing instant writ sought for quashing of charge sheet on ground that it was not a party to said matter and same dealt with a chit fund scam, in respect of which it was not concerned at all - It was noted that irrespective of fact that petitioner was not party in said litigation, petitioner clearly came within broad sweep of Supreme Court's direction for investigation, since charges had been framed against petitioner long back and after due investigation, trial of case was going on at present - Further, trial of CBI case, on its completion would reveal whether source of money involved in chit fund scam and rerouting of huge sums involved could be traced to petitioner company, even if petitioner it was assumed was not a chit fund company in strict sense of terms - That apart, mere investigation by CBI, that too, when criminal proceedings were at stage of trial, could not be a violation of any legal or fundamental right of petitioners - Whether therefore, CBI investigation of petitioner and framing of charges were not vitiated in any manner and instant writ petition was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 20, 21 and 22]COMPANY LAW/SEBI : Where CBI registered a case and framed charges against petitioner company and its directors for their alleged involvement in chit fund scam and trial was going on, completion of trial would reveal whether source of money involved in chit fund scam and rerouting of huge sums involved could be traced to petitioner company and, hence, CBI investigation of petitioner and framing of charges were not vitiated in any manner

Section 433 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Circumstances in which a company may be wound up - Respondent-company had failed to file balance sheet with Registrar of Companies (RoC) for period 1998-99/ 1999-2000 and had also committed default in making payment to various investors - There were allegations against its directors to have cheated several thousands of investors, banks and financial institution, through forgery and illegal means - CBI which investigated matter recommended action for taking over possession of assets of company - Instant petition for winding up of company was filed after giving statutory notice - Petition was advertised under rule 24 of Companies (Court) Rules, 1959 to which no objection had been filed - Whether on such facts company was liable to be wound up under section 433(b), (c) and (f) - Held, yes

Section 213, read with section 241, of the Companies Act, 2013/Section 237, read with sections 397 and 398, of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation - Into company's affairs in other cases - Petitioner company holding 13.18 per cent of paid up capital of R1 company filed petition under section 397 alleging that R1 company had not utilized proceeds of IPO as per terms and conditions of IPO and diverted IPO proceeds for benefits of related entities - On contrary, R1 company also claimed that present petition was a counter-blast to petition filed under section 111(4) by R2 to R9 directors of R1 company in respect of another company where petitioner had played a fraud on stakeholders, including R1 company - It was also claimed that petitioner company was appointed as book running lead manager for IPO issue of R1 and petitioner, in process of preparation of documents for IPO, had asked R2 to sign blank letter heads and blank cheques and, after crediting IPO amount into account of R1, petitioner systematically transferred a lot of money to its associates and other companies utilizing signed blank cheques - According to respondents, petitioner did not approached NCLT with clean hands and thus, no case was made out for intervention of NCLT in affairs of company - From facts it becomes clear that both, petitioner and R2 to R9 directors had allegedly diverted funds of R1 company to their associates, thus, there existed circumstances which prima facie suggest that business of R1 company was being conducted with intent to defraud its members and amount collected through IPO had been diverted to associates by petitioner and R2 to R9 directors, which amounts to fraud played on investors - Whether in light of circumstances, it was necessary to investigate into affairs of R1 company under provisions of section 213 - Held, yes [Para 55]COMPANY LAW : Where petitioner being Lead Manager for IPO issue of company and respondent directors of company had allegedly diverted IPO proceeds of company to their associates, there existed circumstances which prima facie suggests that business of company was being conducted with an intent to defraud its members, thus, it was necessary to investigate into affairs of company under provisions of section 213

Section 403, read with section 10E, of the Companies Act, 1956 - Oppression and mismanagement - Whether it would be within inherent jurisdiction of CLB to take assistance of specialized agencies where having regard to nature of information required, it may lack specific expertise or infrastructural support - Held, yes - Whether, however, such investigation is to be directed only after a case is made out of prima facie mismanagement and oppression in connection with a company in relation to subject on which investigation is being directed - Held, yes - Whether if silhouettes of irregularities appear in financial statements of a company but actual identification of such irregularities becomes impossible from available materials, directions for disclosure of particulars or other legal methods akin to discovery proceeding may be undertaken - Held, yes [Para 29]

Section 11B of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with Regulation 41 of the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996 - Power to issue directions - SEBI had initiated proceedings against a wealth management firm founded by C.R. Bhansali ‘CRB Mutual Fund’ and its ex-management for multiple regulatory violations and systemic deficiencies - Pursuant to said proceedings, Bombay High Court vide an interim order had imposed embargo against making any payments to CR Bhansali and his group companies - On other hand, a Co Petition for winding up of scheme launched by CRB Capital was filed by RBI before Delhi High Court - For ensuring administrative convenience, Official Liquidator of Delhi High Court had filed a transfer petition before Supreme Court seeking to transfer both cases to Delhi and same was allowed by Supreme Court - Thereafter, Delhi Court had passed a final order constituting a Special Committee to discharge functions of trustee and to oversee procedure for formal winding up of scheme - A bare perusal of final order revealed that, surprisingly, none of parties raised issue concerning embargo imposed by interim order - As a result, final order remained silent on aspect and did not contain any discussion signifying an intention to modify or lift earlier embargo - In effect, there was neither an express affirmation nor an implied setting aside of interim restraint against payments being released to CRB and connected individuals and entities - Thereafter, a total sum of approximately Rs.350 crores was realised by Special Committee through sale of all assets of CRB Mutual Fund - Out of this, an amount of Rs.211 crore had been disbursed to approximately 5,000 unit holders / investors of scheme and out of Rs.211 crores, a substantial amount of Rs.131.9 crores (Approx.) had been paid to C.R. Bhansali and his family members - Whether priority of Special Committee ought to have been to firstly disburse to individuals, small unit holders  non CRB corporate entities and thereafter by way of abundant caution approach Court seeking clarification as to whether any disbursements ought to be made to CRB Group or not - Held, yes - Whether however, Special Committee had not sought any clarification from Court and had remained silent over years, even before instant Court, by not highlighting fact that such substantial sums have been paid to CRB Group - Held, yes - Whether in view of manner of distribution adopted by Special Committee, SEBI was to be directed to conduct of a Forensic Audit of all records, bank accounts, documents etc., pertaining to mutual fund scheme and Special Committee in accordance with law by exercising its powers under Section 11 and 11B of SEBI Act - Held, yes [Paras 89, 100, 128, 136 and 140]COMPANY LAW/SEBI : Where in winding up of mutual fund scheme, Special Committee instead of seeking clarification from Court, unilaterally made payments to CRB group i.e. individuals from CRB families, CRB group companies and related entities, SEBI was permitted to conduct forensic audit of all records, bank accounts, documents, etc. pertaining to such mutual fund scheme and Special Committee in accordance with law by exercising its powers under sections 11 and 11B of SEBI Act

Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company’s affairs in other cases - Petitioner, a shareholder of third respondent-company, being aggrieved by non-receipt of annual report and notice of extraordinary annual general meeting of company and not getting any return on his investment, filed writ petition seeking direction to first respondent to appoint a competent person as investigator for investigating affairs of company - Whether since power has been conferred on CLB to order investigation, if there are circumstances necessitating same, it was incumbent on petitioner to approach CLB and there arose no reason for exercising discretionary power vested in Company Court to order such investigation - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, writ petition was not maintainable - Held, yes

Section 213, read with section 221 of the Companies Act, 2013 - Investigation - Into company's affairs in other cases - Petitioner was buyer in real estate project developed by company 'VSPL' - Petitioner alleged that despite very damning observations made by NCLT with regard to conduct of business/affairs of company 'VSPL' by its directors, and thereby, defrauding investors, respondent i.e. Ministry of Corporate Affairs, had miserably failed to order an inquiry into such sordid affairs through SFIO - Petitioner, thus, filed instant writ, seeking directions to respondent to appoint an investigator and complete investigation under relevent provisions of law in a time bound manner - Respondent had assailed maintainability of instant writ petition on ground that High Court in Delhi had no territorial jurisdiction - It was noted that entire cause of action on part of company 'VSPL' had arisen in State of Karnataka and, hence, instant Court in Delhi had no territorial jurisdiction and merely because seat or main head office of respondent was located in Delhi would not be sufficient to confer jurisdiction upon Court in Delhi - There was no gainsaying that respondent had its Regional Office with necessary paraphernalia in State of Karnataka and, thus, petitioner had appropriate efficacious remedy to approach Karnataka High Court in order to seek appropriate reliefs - Further, there was no averment that any person or authority within territorial jurisdiction of writ Court in Delhi was substantially affected by affairs of company in question - Whether accordingly, instant writ was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 9  10]COMPANY LAW : Where writ petition in High Court of Delhi had been filed by petitioner seeking a direction to respondent-MCA to appoint an investigator and complete investigation under sections 213 and 221 in respect of company 'VSPL', in view of fact that company 'VSPL' had its Regional Office with necessary paraphernalia in State of Karnataka and petitioner had appropriate efficacious remedy to approach Karnataka High Court in order to seek appropriate reliefs, instant writ petition filed in Delhi High Court was to be dismissed

Section 12(1B) of the Securities & Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 - Collective Investment Scheme - About 37,000 Plantation Companies collected approximately Rs. 25,000 crores from poor investors - Investors having no platform for redressing, instant writ under public interest litigation was filed - By its earlier interim orders instant High Court empowered SEBI to publish advertisement for investors, stating non- viability of plantation companies in India - State Government was also directed to issue notices to all revenue officers to prevent transfer of agricultural land in favour of plantation companies - Court also ordered inquiry by police into affairs of such companies with assistance of SEBI and order attachment of assets of directors, promoters, etc., - It also further expected that proper Investor Protection Act be made by Central/State Government - During final hearing it was brought to notice that State Government decided to promulgate ordinance to protect interest of investors and SEBI had constituted a Committee to draft appropriate regulations -Whether in view of above no purpose would be served in keeping pending writ petition and same was to be disposed of with direction to Government to implement earlier directions and earlier interim orders would be in operation until promulgation of impugned ordinance - Held, yes

Section 213 of the Companies Act, 2013 - Investigation -  Into company's affairs in other cases - Petitioners, buyers of real estate units in project namely 'VSPL Pinnacle' developed by respondent company/filed a petition under section 213 alleging that despite having right to said only 82,216.30 sq. ft., respondent had sold an area of 2,43,037 sq. ft. which was almost 3 times of area, which company was entitled to sell - According to petitioner, by making fraudulent sales, which was almost three times, it was apparent that affairs of company had been conducted to commit fraud and cheating with buyers - Petitioners had given specific list of 164 such Sale Deeds/Agreement to Sell, along with details such as Date of Execution, name of Buyers, Sub-Registrar Document No. etc. - There was also an allegation of siphoning of funds arising from these sales by promoters of company and, thus, according to petitioners there was urgent need to conduct enquiry into affairs of company to track funds diverted from company - Respondent had not addressed to any of allegations of these irregularities and not responded to documents along with list of irregular sales listed in Company Petition, instead submitted that it was ordered to be liquidated and RP was appointed as Liquidator and liquidation process of company was still in progress and, therefore, petitioner could not seek to circumvent liquidation process and try to initiate parallel investigative proceedings against respondent - It was noted that investigation under section 213 is possible in respect of company which is undergoing process of liquidation - Whether therefore, exercising powers under section 213, instant petition was to be allowed - Held, yes [Paras 18 and 19]

Section 237(b) of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company's affairs - Whether power under section 237(b) is a discretionary power - Held, yes -Whether, when justifiable grounds exist, merely because communication from Department of Company Affairs to Secretary, CLB, was in form of letter without any proper affidavit and without any specific mention as to what action was prayed for, CLB should refuse to exercise jurisdiction under section 237(b) - Held, no - Whether investigation is to be ordered if a prima facie opinion is formed by CLB that business of company is being/has been conducted with intent to defraud creditors, members or any other persons or conduct of company is oppressive to any of its members or there is misfeasance or misconduct on part of management in carrying on affairs of company - Held, yes - Whether, where report filed by Regional Director in Department of Company Affairs under section 209A on complaints made by Employees' Union alleging mismanagement of affairs of company, established mismanagement of funds of company, further enquiry by ROC had to be ordered - Held, yes

Section 456 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Custody of company’s property - Respondent-company had collected huge sums of money by way of deposits from general public and by utilizing money so collected, various assets had been acquired by it which included land whereon superstructure had been constructed for housing registered office of company - Applicants’ case was that respondent-company had become nearly insolvent and with a view to tide over its financial distress, it, through one of its directors, viz., ‘D’, sold said land together with building standing thereon to applicants - Certain payment was made by applicants as advance and balance was to be paid at time of registration - Applicants contended that receipt of said balance amount and consequential execution of sale deed were delayed on one pretext or other and, therefore, they filed suit seeking specific performance of agreement of sale - Immediately, a compromise memo was filed before Court and, consequently, matter was referred to Lok Adalat which passed a decree duly recording compromise between parties - In terms of compromise decree, balance amount was paid and sale deed was executed - Subsequently, applicants entered into an agreement of sale of said property with ‘V’ - In meantime, respondent-company was ordered to be wound up on applications by some depositors of company to whom company had not repaid their deposits and possession of said property was taken over by Official Liquidator - Hence, applicants moved instant application seeking property to be released from custody of Official Liquidator on ground that title over property had been transferred by company in favour of applicants by way of sale deed executed between parties - It was found that market value of property was much higher than value for which property was offered for sale to applicants - There was no resolution passed by board of directors of company, in accordance with provisions contained in section 291, for undertaking sale of any of asset of company - No publicity was ever issued by company or by its directors for intended sale of said asset - It was not explained as to how applicants came to know of impending sale of said asset and how they got property valued before entering into transaction - There was no authorization issued by company in favour of ‘D’ to enter into a compromise or enter into a transaction of sale at first instance with applicants - Sale consideration was paid in cash instead of secured instruments like cheques or demand drafts and no entries were found in books of company about receipt of said amount - Applicants failed to demonstrate their financial capacity to have pooled up such a huge sum at one go, to pay to respondent in cash - Thousands of complaints had been lodged with police at various places in State by depositors alleging fraud and misrepresentation indulged in by respondent-company - Whether, on facts, it could be said that entire transaction was vitiated by fraud played by applicants on District Court as well as on Lok Adalat and ‘D’ on behalf of respondent-company had joined hands with them - Held, yes - Whether since no right or interest or title can ever pass in favour of beneficiary of fraud and further, no action can be maintained which is founded in fraud, decree passed by Lok Adalat pursuant to a compromise entered into by and between parties therein in civil suit on file of Additional District Judge was to be declared as a nullity - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, no rights of any kind would ever pass to hands of applicants vis-a-vis property in question owned and belonging to company and, as such, application filed by them was to be dismissed - Held, yes

Section 213 of the Companies Act, 2013/Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 read with rule 11 of the Companies (Court) Rules, 1959 - Investigation of Company's affairs in other cases - Petitioner shareholders had subscribed to shares in respondent-company based on assurance that they would get good returns on their shares and that their shares would also be listed on other stock exchanges - However, petitioners alleged that from beginning they had not received notice from respondent-company regarding convening of Annual General Meetings or Extraordinary General Meetings and were also not informed of any major activities of company like amalgamation, listing and de-listing of shares - Hence, court appointed chartered accountants to look into affairs of company to understand seriousness of allegations made by petitioners - However, respondents did not comply with directions given by Court to furnish relevant particulars to chartered accountants - Whether, conduct of business of respondent-company was oppressive to its members and non-cooperation of respondent-company with chartered accountants, despite series of orders of Court, clearly showed that respondents intended to thwart attempts of Court to do substantial justice to either parties - Held, yes - Whether facts, as presented, clearly made out a case for Court to direct Central Government to order investigation into affairs of respondent-company, more particularly in view of fact that respondent-company had not furnished information in respect of its affairs, which it was reasonably expected to furnish - Held, yes [Para 15]CL: Where respondent-company had not furnished information in respect of its affairs, to Chartered Accountants appointed by Court which it was reasonably expected to furnish, Central Government was to be directed to order investigation into affairs of respondent-company

Section 11 of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 - Powers and functions of board - Pursuant to Saradha Chit Fund scam Inspector General of Registration and Commissioner of Stamp Revenue imposed restrictions on sale of properties owned by petitioner-agro company - SEBI in its report indicated violation of several provisions, including petitioner company having resorted to obtaining funds from public without either applying for mandatory listing or having its offer documents vetted by appropriate authorities - Whether in view of SEBI's report, appropriate authorities were to be directed to take steps in accordance with law against petitioners and, particularly, officers of petitioner-company responsible for multiple defaults - Held, yes - Whether there would be an order of injunction restraining petitioner-company from dealing with or disposing of or alienating or encumbering any of its assets without previous leave of the SEBI and SEBI leave should not be granted without an Executive Director of SEBI approving same - Held, yes - Whether petitioners could cause all or any of their assets or properties be sold under aegis of SEBI under any asset sale committee that might be set up by SEBI for purpose of refund of money which had been illegally obtained from depositors - Held, yes [Paras 4, 5  6]SEBI: Petitioner agro company was restrained from dealing with or disposing of its assets without previous leave of SEBI on basis of report of SEBI indicating violation of various provisions of SEBI Act

Section 58A of the Companies Act, 1956 - Public deposits - First petitioner, along with his family members, by floating a company, received heavy deposits but did not return any amount to depositors on maturity -Petitioner diverted and misused funds so collected for purchase of various assets - RBI had also refused to grant registration certificate for operating as non-banking financial institution because of petitioner having grossly violated norms - Interim orders/directions of court were grossly violated inasmuch as petitioner did not comply with direction to deposit amount in depositors' account opened for that purpose - Whether in such circumstances and in order to see that such companies did not defraud innocent depositors, State Government should set up a separate cell for making discreet enquiries in respect of all such NBFCs, seizing their properties and assets, ensuring payments to depositors either in full or on pro rata basis and initiating prosecution against all offenders - Held, yes -Whether State Government should order immediate investigation by CBCID in respect of petitioner-company and launch prosecution under various criminal and other laws against promoters including past directors and other connected persons - Held, yes - Whether RBI should also initiate criminal proceedings and take steps - Held, yes

Section 397, read with section 398, of the Companies Act, 1956 - Oppression and mismanagement - Whether object of section 397 is not to rake up past but to redeem future and power of CLB under section 397/398, is primarily intended for preventive purposes - Held, yes - Petitioner and respondent Nos. 2 to 5 were directors of respondent-company which had obtained a contract for processing and filling of aravana prasadam in composite cans by using modern technologies at Sri Ayappa Temple, Sabarimala which was under governance of respondent No. 6 and accordingly entered into an agreement with latter in April 1999 - Under said agreement, company was required, to fill prepared aravana prasadam in cans and supply to devotees for a period of eight years at rates specified therein which would be payable by respondent No. 6 - Petitioners collectively holding in excess of 10 per cent of issued share capital of respondent-company filed petition invoking provisions of sections 397, 398 and 402 wherein main grievance of petitioners was that respondent Nos. 2 to 5 had mismanaged affairs of respondent-company and had misappropriated receivables realised from respondent No. 6 for their personal benefits without settling dues of banks, financial institutions, suppliers and other creditors - It was seen from records that respondents had not furnished any particulars regarding actual receivables and utilization of such receivables excepting a bald statement that liabilities of banks, financial institutions and suppliers had been settled from and out of receivables realised from respondent No. 6 - Whether conduct of respondent Nos. 2 to 5 lacked in probity, which was unfair to petitioners causing prejudice to them in exercise of their legal and proprietary rights as shareholders - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, a chartered accountant was to be appointed to scrutinize and verify books of account, vouchers and other connected accounts of respondent-company since its inception till date and respondent Nos. 2 to 5 were to be directed to reimburse, in favour of company, moneys, if any found diverted on verification by chartered accountant, from receivables realised from respondent No. 6 - Held, yes

Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company affairs in other cases -  Under section 237(a)( ii), power of Court is invoked for directing Central Government to order investigation by concerned inspectors

Section 11B of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 - Powers and functions of board - Power to issue directions - SEBI suggested that a chartered accountant be appointed to look into deposits obtained by petitioner-company before SEBI approved final list and determined mode of payment - Accordingly, a chartered accountant was appointed for purpose of identifying depositors who had put in deposits with petitioner-company and quantum of deposits - Whether petitioner-company was to be directed to furnish a comprehensive list of its immovable properties alongwith copies of title deeds to SEBI with an affidavit affirmed by principal person in control of petitioner-company that there was no other immovable property directly or indirectly owned or controlled by petitioner-company - Held, yes - Whether petitioners would also furnish to SEBI particulars of bank accounts of petitioner-company including amounts standing to credit of petitioner-company therein - Held, yes [Paras 6  7]SEBI : Direction to company to furnish comprehensive list of its immovable properties and particulars of bank accounts to SEBI before SEBI approved final list of depositors and determined mode of payment

facts.text: On complaints of large scale commission of frauds by the directors of the company involving siphoning off the company funds for private ends and for purchasing all properties in the names of other front companies and, thus, stashing away large assets from the reach of the creditors, the respondent filed winding up application against the appellant-company. The Company Court, on the basis of prima facie material that the funds of the company were transferred to other companies formed by one of the directors concluded that the affairs of the company, including assets in the names of other companies which had been created with the funds collected by the company, were required to be investigated and that such systematic investigation would bring out the extent of assets owned by the company, legal and valid so as to make available the properties for discharge of debts of the investors. The Company Court, accordingly, passed an order appointing a provisional liquidator under whose control the property, effects and actionable claims to which the company claimed to be entitled to would vest. In the instant appeal, the appellant contended that the properties that were to be brought for sale did not belong to the company and that the company could not have offered to the liquidator to take possession of all the assets, including the assets that did not stand in the name of the company.

A petition was filed by the Securities & Exchange Board of India (SEBI) as a public interest litigation, stating that it had come to the notice of the Government of India that certain plantation companies were issuing instruments such as agro bonds, plantation bond, etc., offering very high rates of return which were not consistent with the normal returns in such schemes. In petition SEBI prayed that in public interest, till regulations were framed under section 12(1B), appropriate directions be given to protect large amounts invested by middle-class people, and immediate action be taken against the directors who had siphoned off large amounts belonging to investors under the guise of corporate veil. The Court ordered search and seizure and for an investigation by the Police into the affairs of the company with the assistance of the auditors and staff to be provided by the RBI. Consequently, investigations were made and prop- erties of directors of the company were attached. At this stage SEBI sought direction that till such regulations were framed and finalised, the Court may direct the RBI to issue orders to all commercial banks and/or cooperative banks, where Respondent No. 1 Plantation company had accounts, restraining Respondents No. 1 to 5 and 7 from withdrawing any money from the said accounts, and for certain other reliefs. The company opposed the prayer contending that it is the function of SEBI or the Central Government to frame the regulations at the earliest, if they think it necessary in the interests of investors/depositors in such plantation companies. It was contended that instead of moving the Central Govern- ment to frame and finalise the Regulations, they have approached the Court and it amounted to abuse of the process of law, because the court had issued various directions, including the direction to freeze the bank accounts of the directors.

When the company failed to return nearly Rs. 18 crores collected from thousands of depositors, one of the creditors filed petition for winding-up of the company. In the meantime, the company filed an application under section 391 for obtaining sanction to a scheme of compromise, which was refused by the court. The court, however, formulated a scheme for running the business without allowing to receive fresh deposits and appointed provisional liquidator. The company had diverted a huge amount to its sister company by unlawful means in violation of the provisions of law and the directions issued by the Reserve Bank of India. Despite repeated directions of the court, the company and its managing director did not furnish the books of account, registers and the securities including the gold to the Official Liquidator, and even those registers which were produced before the Official Liquidator, were found to be forged and fabricated with false entries. The court, thereupon, passed an order directing the crime branch police to register a case and to recover the books of account, register, etc. It also issued certain directions to the effect that all the genuine registers, account books, etc., should be seized/recovered and that the investigating officer should further enquire whether any properties had been acquired by the directors in the name of others as benami with the company's funds. Further, it would be open to him to arrest the respondent-managing director as well as directors of the company. The police, accordingly, registered a criminal case against the directors of the company as well as accused 5 and 6 who had joined them in diverting considerable sum to a sister concern. Subsequently, the court directed that all matters including bail matters, should be placed before the company court. At that stage the company court found it necessary to give notice to all the accused, why the bail granted to all of them should not be cancelled. The case of the accused was that the company court had no jurisdiction to cancel the bail which was granted by another bench of the court and the petition for cancellation of bail should also go before the same bench which granted the bail.

The respondent-company Golden Forests (India) Ltd. (GFIL) was incorporated in 1987. Between the years 1991 and 1997, its promoters set up over 100 companies and introduced a number of investment schemes promising handsome returns, lured investors and depositors, and in 9-10 years collected several hundred crores of rupees. Huge tracts of lands and property were also acquired by it.

The applicant was National Investors Forum and its members were the investors of the respondent-company GFIL.

In 1997, the Securities Exchange Board of India (SEBI) inquired into the activities of GFIL group and a two member committee was constituted. The report of the committee highlighted financial and other irregularities committed by the company.

SEBI filed a writ petition in the Bombay High Court, in which an order was passed against GFIL restraining it from alienating the properties; a similar order was passed by this High Court in the same year. Thus, SEBI made an order prohibiting the company from alienating its properties. A retired judge was appointed as receiver and certain properties were earmarked for sale, but the receiver could not sell the properties.

GFIL, in the meanwhile continued to accept deposits, carrying business and alienating properties. In this background, winding up proceedings, were preferred before the Punjab & Haryana High Court. The Company Judge by order directed that all properties of the company would be managed, controlled, regulated by a provisional liquidator, who shall have power to sell the movable and immovable property. Thus, a provisional liquidator was appointed.

The company petition and all other proceedings pending against the GFIL pending in various High Courts throughout the country were transferred to the Supreme Court, in a transfer petition filed by SEBI. Company petition was also transferred to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court by its order constituted a committee consisting of a retired judge KT of the Supreme Court, an officer to be nominated by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and an officer to be nominated by SEBI, and further ordered the committee to take into its custody all assets of the company, wherever they may be, to issue advertisement in Newspapers calling upon all the creditors of the company to submit the claim(s) before the committee.

The committee had, during pendency of the matters before the Supreme Court, invited claims from the depositors/investors of GFIL by advertisement which period was extended. Nevertheless, the committee continued to receive the claims even after the expiry of that period and later the claims were received during the extended period. However, since claims from the depositors of GFIL continued, the Supreme Court directed that no deposit accepted by an Agent after 1-1-2001 is to be considered as GFIL had closed business in December, 2000 and the Directors of the company were in the Jail in December, 2000. The Court also directed that there should be clear proof of deposit of money with GFIL or its group.

The liabilities were to be discharged by sale of the properties of GFIL and its group. The payments to the depositors were to be made after the properties were sold and payment were to depend on the realisation of proceeds of sale. As per the committee, there were about 15 lakh investors who had not been paid.

After notice was issued on the application, seeking directions to disburse amounts collected due to sale of assets of GFIL and its group companies, the Committee filed a status report as a step to assist in framing a scheme for disbursement of amounts.

In compliance with the above order, the Committee placed relevant materials in the form of affidavits. The Court, after considering the issue of disbursement of the amounts lying with the committee, was of the opinion that the proposal (for disbursement of funds scheme framed by the Committee), giving preference to 'small' investors in distribution of process, was not entirely equitable. Thus the above revised scheme for disbursement of monies to depositors of GFIL or its group companies was further revised, the committee in its second revision proposed several alternatives. The committee disclosed a consolidated chart of all the holdings of GFIL. It also disclosed the status of various funds and the various sale transactions that were incomplete and in respect of which amounts had been received. The committee had so far been able to collect and put to sale and realise assets to the tune of Rs. 400 crore.

The applicant in its response and in the submissions urged that a complete picture as to the assets of the GFIL and its group companies had always remained unclear and that in these circumstances, it would be appropriate that an Advisory Board ought to be constituted which consists of one member of SEBI, a member of RBI and a representative of one of the investors. The Board should identify and ascertain the exact number of properties of the company spread throughout the length and breadth of the country and thereafter, every effort should be made to ascertain the actual liabilities of all the investors of GFIL Group of companies.

The investors who had invested their money in the appellant-company, namely, ’IMFB’ Ltd. filed company petitions for its winding-up on account of its failure to repay the deposited amount in accordance with fixed schedule. The Company Judge, finding it to be a case of cheating and misappropriation of public funds with evil designs, allowed the petitions and ordered for winding-up of the appellant-company under section 433(e). The Official Liquidator was appointed and he was directed to exercise power under section 457, with authority to take into custody all movable and immovable properties of the appellant-company. He was further directed to auction properties of one of the sister concern of the appellant-company, i.e., ’IFCL’, also on ground that properties of said company were in reality properties belonging to the appellant-company.

Against aforesaid order, two sets of appeals were filed. First set of appeals was filed by the appellant-company wherein the order of its winding-up was challenged on various grounds. Second set of appeals was filed by the ’IFCL’ Ltd. on ground that there was no order of winding-up against it nor it was impleaded as a party in the company petitions and, therefore, even if the appellant-company was to be wound-up under the orders of the Court, no assets or properties of ’IFCL’ Ltd. could be taken possession of or could be put to auction.

The CLB had suspended the board of directors of the respondent-company by order dated 9-1-2009 and had authorized the Central Government to constitute a fresh board of the company. The Central Government had appointed six nominee directors on the board. In the meanwhile, the Central Government with a view to safeguard the interests of the company, its stakeholders and the public at large, filed instant application, ex parte seeking interim reliefs viz.; (i ) to implead ‘V’, being Chief Finance Officer as respondent No. 13; (ii) to direct the concerned respondents to disclose the bank accounts and both movable and immovable assets owned by them; and (iii) to restrain them from alienating, mortgaging, creating charge or lien or interest in those properties. In support, of the application, it was submitted that the Central Government had ordered investigation into the affairs of the company on consideration of the report of the RoC and that the Central Government might not be able to enforce the ultimate relief which might be granted under section 542, unless the concerned respondents were restrained from alienating any of their assets, thereby protecting the interests of the company and the stake-holders.

The respondent-company had floated various schemes by which it was offering fanciful returns which were highly disproportionate and com-mercially not viable. SEBI received several complaints from investors of the respondent-company to the effect that the cheques issued by the company had been dishonoured due to insufficient funds in the bank account of the respondent-company, that the office of the respondent- company had become non-functional, that directors of the respondent-company had gone defaulter and had more or less gone underground and that the funds received by the respondent had been diverted to the group companies. On the basis of these complaints, the SEBI filed petition in the interest of the members of public, stating that the Central Government was concerned with the high elements of risks associated with such schemes and hence, in order to ensure that investors make investment in such schemes only after they are fully acquainted with or made aware of the high risk factors involved in such schemes, it was felt necessary to decide an appropriate regulatory framework for regulating entities which issue such schemes.

It was prayed that in public interest, till regulations are framed, appropri- ate directions be given to protect large amounts invested by middle class people. It sought the bank accounts and other assets, movable as well as immovable, of respondent No. 1 wheresoever situated required to be frozen and attached to protect the investors’ moneys from being filtered away.

The first petitioner, a Non-Banking Finance Company (NBFC) registered under the Companies Act, 1956 having its registered office in Madhya Pradesh, was promoted by the second respondent with the objectives of carrying on the business of financing, money-lending, bills discounting, hire-purchasing, leasing, etc. The company evolved a scheme known as SFDR whereunder deposits collected from the investors were to be utilized for allotment of shares to them and also to be invested in other companies. The petitioners alleged that they collected non-interest yielding/profit-sharing investments in the form of equity and invested in equity shares. According to them, there were baseless rumours of cheating against first petitioner and, therefore, some of the members of public filed complaints against them in various police stations. It was alleged that there were serious threats to their lives and in spite of repeated requests to the SHOs to extend proper protection, the police officer was instead of protecting the petitioners, were compelling them to repay deposits collected by the company, and that some investors had attacked the office of the second petitioner and threatened him with physical abuses. Therefore the petitioners sought protection from third respondent - police officer. The third respondent, on the other hand, denied all the allegations.

On writ, the petitioners sought for relief (i) to declare the action of the respondents in not taking necessary prohibitive steps for the safety of the petitioners as illegal and unconstitutional, (ii) to declare the action of respondents in calling upon the petitioners to make payments on the basis of civil transactions between petitioners and their investors/shareholders as arbitrary, illegal and unjust and violative of the fundamental rights guaranteed under articles 14, 19, 20 and 21 of the Constitution of India and constitutional guarantees under articles 50 and 300A of the Constitution of India; (iii) to issue a direction to first respondent, namely, Central Economic Intelligence Bureau (CEIB), New Delhi, to centralize all the alleged complaints against petitioners, if any, and carry out investigation in accordance with law, (iv) to issue a consequential direction to police to take such steps as were necessary for protection of petitioners and not to harass petitioners on the back of civil complaints; and (v) to direct respondents to carry out their investigations, if any, on the complaints against petitioners strictly in accordance with the procedure under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

The Court appointed an Advocate Commissioner to take charge of the movable and immovable properties, who after visiting various places, reported that there were no substantial money deposits in the name of the company but there were deposits in the name of the second petitioner’s wife and personal accounts. According to the report, properties were sold under Revenue Recovery Act by the bank, cold storage units were still under construction and the Indore office was seized by the police in some criminal case. A letter from a depositor informed that all the depositors belonged to New Delhi and Indore, and that they were cheated by the petitioners against whom FIR was lodged at New Delhi. The Inspector of Crime Branch, New Delhi, enclosed a list of 94 investors who were cheated and all of them did not belong to Andhra Pradesh.

During the CIRP, the CoC appointed Forensic Auditor to conduct a Forensic Audit and on receipt of the report, the RP filed application under section 66, read with sections 25(2), 69, 70 and other applicable sections inter alia seeking to attach the personal assets of three directors alleging that they were responsible for defrauding the creditors. Same was to be done in order to recover the total dues of Rs. 46.11 crores. By exercising power conferred on the Adjudicating Authority, the order was passed referring the matter to the Central Government for investigation through SFIO (Serious Fraud Investigation Office).

The appellant, a majority shareholder of the corporate debtor, contended that Adjudicating Authority was not conferred with power under section 213 of the Companies Act, 2013 in absence of any amendment made in Schedule XI of the Code and, thus, had no jurisdiction to pass order under section 213 of the Companies Act.
