[Para 24] It is true, as argued by the petitioners, that while exercising powers under the Act, it is not open to the SEBI to encroach upon the powers vested with the Institute under the Chartered Accountants Act. However, it was required to be examined as to whether in substance by initiating the proceedings under the SEBI Act, the SEBI was trying to overreach or encroach upon the powers conferred under the Chartered Accountants Act. In that connection, it was required to be noted that the SEBI has powers under the Act and the Regulation to take remedial measures in connection with safeguarding the interest of investors and regulate the securities market. Under section 11, the SEBI has power to prohibit fraudulent and unfair trade practices relating to securities market. Under section 11(4), the SEBI is entitled to pass appropriate orders in the interest of investors or securities market and is entitled to take measures as prescribed in the said section. Under section 11B, powers have been conferred on the SEBI to give appropriate directions even to any person or class of persons referred to in section 12 or associated with the securities market. The powers available to the SEBI under the Act are to be exercised in the interest of investors and interest of securities market. In order to safeguard the interest of investors or interest of securities market, the SEBI is entitled to take all ancillary steps and measures to see that the interest of the investors is protected. Looking to the provisions of the SEBI Act and the Regulations framed thereunder, it cannot be said that in a given case if there is material against any chartered accountant to the effect that he was instrumental in preparing false and fabricated accounts, the SEBI has absolutely no power to take any remedial or preventive measures in such a case. It cannot be said that the SEBI cannot give appropriate directions in safeguarding the interest of the investors of a listed company. Whether such directions and orders are required to be issued or not is a matter of inquiry. The jurisdiction of the SEBI would also depend upon the evidence which is available during such inquiry. It is true, as argued by the petitioners, that the SEBI cannot regulate the profession of chartered accountants. That proposition could not be disputed in any manner. By taking remedial and preventive measures in the interest of investors and for regulating the securities market, if any steps are taken by the SEBI, it can never be said that it is regulating the profession of the chartered accountants. So far as listed companies are concerned, the SEBI has all the powers under the Act and the Regulations to take all remedial and protective measures to safeguard the interest of investors and securities market. So far as the role of auditors is concerned, it is a very important role under the Companies Act. As posited in section 227 of the Companies Act, every auditor of a company shall have a right of access at all times to the books and account and vouchers of the company, whether kept at the head office of the company or elsewhere, and shall be entitled to require from the officers of the company such information and explanations as the auditor may think necessary for the performance of his duties. The auditors in the company are functioning as statutory auditors. They have been appointed by the shareholders by majority. They owe a duty to the shareholders and are required to give a correct picture of the financial affairs of the company. It is not uncommon now-a-days that for financial gains even small investors are investing money in the share market. As was rightly pointed out by respondent, there are cases where even retired persons are investing their retiral dues in the purchase of shares and, ultimately, if such a person is defrauded, he will be totally ruined and may be put in a situation where his life savings are wiped out. With a view to safeguard the interests of such investors, it is the duty of the SEBI to see that maximum care is required to be taken to protect the interest of such investors so that they may not be subjected to any fraud or cheating in the matter of their investments in the securities market. Normally, an investor invests his money by considering the financial health of the company and in order to find out the same, one would naturally bank upon the accounts and balance-sheets of the company. If it is unearthed during inquiry before the SEBI that a particular chartered accountant, in connivance and in collusion with the officers/directors of the company has concocted false accounts, there is no reason as to why to protect the interests of investors and regulate the securities market such a person cannot be prevented from dealing with the auditing of such a public listed company. The SEBI has got inherent powers to take all ancillary steps to safeguard the interest of investors and securities market. The powers conferred under various provisions of the Act are wide enough to cover such an eventuality and it cannot be given any restrictive meaning as suggested by the petitioners

HEADNOTE: Section 213, read with section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013/ Section 237, read with section 394 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of Company's affairs - Appellant filed an application for holding meeting of shareholders for approval of scheme of amalgamation - Single Judge finding some irregularities directed investigation by various agencies - Appellant filed appeal contending that Single Judge was carrying on roving enquiry and he should either allow or dismiss its application - Whether Single Judge was competent to issue direction under section 237(a)(ii) and, therefore, Single Judge was justified in carrying on investigation - Held, yes - Whether however, it was for Central Government to decide which authority would investigate and, therefore, it was a fit and proper case for Central Government to consider as to whether an investigation should be carried out by appropriate agency having authority in law followed by action that would be permitted in law - Held, yes - Whether appellant could not be permitted to proceed with proposed scheme of amalgamation and, therefore, application for convening meeting of shareholders was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 12  13]CL : Single Judge while sanctioning scheme of amalgamation is competent to issue direction under section 237(a)(ii) and then it is for Central Govt. to decide which authority would investigate

FACT: The appellant filed an application before the Single Judge proposing a scheme of amalgamation with M.

The Judge initially directed the Registrar of Companies to conduct an investigation and file a report.

The report of Registrar would reveal, the company had issued share premium to large number of companies mostly private companies on the same day and used funds for investments to a small extent and made advances to others. There were crores of investments involving a large number of private companies.

The Judge directed the Director, Revenue Intelligence to conduct an enquiry as to whether there was any money trail. The company preferred an appeal.

The Single Judge directed Ministry of Corporate Affairs to carry investigation. Accordingly, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs asked the SFIO to conduct such investigation. SFIO submitted a report, inter alia, pointing out irregularity in the affairs of the company.

Then Single Judge asked RBI to submit its report, which submitted its preliminary report observing, that the company might have carried on business as non-banking financial company without obtaining registration with the Reserve Bank of India or complying with the other conditions set by the Reserve Bank of India for non-banking financial companies.

The appellant contended the Judge, despite the restrictions being imposed by the Division Bench continued to carry on roving enquiry that would be an unending process.

In appeal, the appellant contended that the Judge should either allow its petition for holding meetings of the shareholders to ascertain their wishes or dismiss it so that the appellant could take further steps in the matter.

HELD: Section 391 imposed wide discretion upon the Judge. The Judge expressed doubt as to the function of the company. Such doubt ultimately came true as is found from the reports particularly of the SFIO. Hence, before the company was permitted to go ahead with the scheme, the Court was duty bound to remove doubt if any, in its mind as to whether such scheme was being propounded for an oblique purpose. The Court was not a mere rubber stamp. [Para 10]

In the instant case, the Single Judge passed series of orders directing various agencies to carry out investigations. Looking to the facts the Single Judge is to be agreed with, there would certainly be a justification to carry on investigation. If one looks to the income tax assessment order one would find, for the assessment year 2007-08 the company earned net profit for Rs. 290. They suffered penalty. The total income that was assessed was Rs. 3400 only and the company paid tax for Rs. 1,046. Such an insignificant company proposed scheme of amalgamation involving crores through allotment of shares at a huge premium. However, the Single Judge was perhaps not correct in either directing Director, Revenue Intelligence or the Reserve Bank of India. He was competent to issue direction under section 237(a)(ii). The Single Judge was right in sending the issue to the Ministry of Corporate Affairs being the appropriate authority of the Central Government. However, it is for the Central Government to decide which authority would investigate. Be that as it may, the report of SFIO would clearly show, despite being informed, the company did not appear. Hence, appellant was not right in saying, opportunity was not given. It is a fit and proper case for the Central Government to consider as to whether an investigation should be carried out by appropriate agency having authority in law followed by action that is permitted in law. [Para 12]

Considering the backdrop, the appellant cannot be permitted to proceed with the proposed scheme of amalgamation. Hence, the application for convening meeting of the shareholders is dismissed. [Para 13]

FACT: In the inspection conducted under section 209 against respondent-company, certain irregularities and violations of provisions of the Act were pointed out and necessary action had been initiated by the Registrar. The petitioner filed petition under section 237 seeking investigation into affairs of respondent-company on the ground that respondent-company had connection with ‘KP’ group of companies and there was also a complaint by Small Investor Protection Forum. The case of the petitioner was that as per the balance sheet of the company as on 31-12-2000, the huge funds of the company were used primarily in share market during the scam period and huge investments were made in the shares of certain companies, which was not the main object of the respondent-company; and that the management had conducted the business of the company with intent to defraud its creditors, members, etc.

HELD: The respondent submitted that whatever shares had been purchased by those companies, which formed part of the ‘K’, had been purchased through stock exchange or public issue or between shareholders of the company in the normal course of business. There were no direct transactions by the company and the ‘K’ for dealing with those shares. The respondent had also forwarded copies of index of folios of shares which had been purchased by various parties from time-to-time. It was difficult to make out any proposition out of those huge papers submitted by the respondent. [Para 12]

The irregularities/violations of the provisions of the Act had already been taken care of by the Registrar of Companies, but some revealing propositions came out from the documents and averments of the case. The company was incorporated as early as in 1982 and since then, the authorized share capital was Rs. 5 lakhs and paid up capital was Rs. 15,000 as on 13-12-1999; but huge investments in share capital had been made within a short spell of 3 to 4 months. It was also admitted position that the company made investment of Rs. 83,41,00,000 in the shares of the certain companies when the main object of the company was not to enter the business in share market. The lead to value of huge investment went down after stock scam took place in March, 2001. It was also interesting to note that within a spell of two months, the authorized capital was raised first from Rs. 50,000 to Rs. 11 crores and thereafter to Rs. 12 crores. The genesis and origin of this huge funds invested by the respondent-company in share market when it was not in the business, needed to be probed into. It was difficult to find from the documents placed on record as to whether there was any relationship in the transactions with the ‘KP’ group of companies or those were the normal transactions of the business. That could only be found out by investigating the matter in depth. [Para 13]

In the light of the above discussion, the petition was to be allowed. Accordingly, the Central Government was to be directed to undertake the investigation of respondent-company under section 237 and take suitable action on the basis of the report when received. [Para 14]

1. This is a petition under section 237(a)(ii) of the Companies Act, 1956 ('the Act'). The petitioner, a contributory of the 1st respondent company seeks a declaration that the company affairs are in such a position that it requires investigation by an Inspector appointed by the Central Government in that regard. It is submitted that the company is not keeping proper accounts and it had done several business activities without obtaining the statutory sanction from the Central Government as enjoined by the law. The Directors of the company including respondents 2 and 3 are now mismanaging the affairs of the company. Therefore, the entire affairs of the company require an investigation and this Court has power under section 237(a)(ii) to order so. If such an order is issued, necessarily, the Central Government will be bound by that order to investigate it. It is submitted, relying on the decision reported in Kumarannuni v. Mathrubhumi Printing & Publishing Co. Ltd. [1981] KLT (S.N.) 88 - Case No. 159 that when it is prima facie satisfied, such a declaration can be issued.

2. Of course, the company court has got power to exercise in terms of Section 237(a)(ii). But section 237(b) empowers the CLB, if there are circumstances necessitating investigation to order accordingly. This power has been granted to the CLB, in terms of the amendment effected in the Companies Act in 1988. Before the amendment sanction had to be given in terms of sub-clause (b) by the Central Government. When the power vested in the Executive Government is invoked, one incumbent may perhaps feel that justice may not be meted out. But now, after the amendment in 1988 the power vested with the Central Government had been taken away and vested with the CLB. When the power is conferred on the CLB, it is incumbent on the petitioner to approach that statutory Board which shall examine and do justice, as the circumstances demand. In such circumstances, there arise no reason for exercising the discretion ary power vested in this company court to direct such investigation or declare that it need investigation by the Central Government. Accordingly, the company petition fails and is dismissed without prejudice to the right of the petitioner to move the CLB in terms of section 237(b).

12. Section 235 of the Companies Act, 1956 deals with Investigation of affairs of a Company, which reads hereunder :

"Investigation of affairs of a company.—(1) The Central Government may, where a report has been made by the Registrar under sub-section (6) of section 234, or under sub-section (7) of that section, read with sub-section (6) thereof, appoint one or more competent persons as inspectors to investigate the affairs of a company and to report thereon in such manner as the Central Government may direct.

(2) Where—

(a )in the case of a company having a share capital, an application has been received from not less than two hundred members or from members holding not less than one-tenth of the total voting power therein, and

(b )in the case of a company having no share capital, an application has been received from not less than one-fifth of the persons on the company’s register of members,

the Tribunal may, after giving the parties an opportunity of being heard, by order, declare that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated by an inspector or inspectors, and on such a declaration being made, the Central Government shall appoint one or more competent persons as inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company and to report thereon in such manner as the Central Government may direct."

13. Likewise, section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 deals with Investigation of Company’s affairs in other cases, which reads as under :

"Investigation of company’s affairs in other cases.—Without prejudice to its powers under section 235, the Central Government—

(a )shall appoint one or more competent persons as inspectors to investigate the affairs of a company and to report thereon in such manner as the Central Government may direct, if—

(i )the company, by special resolution; or

(ii )the Court, by order,

declares that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated by an inspection appointed by the Central Government; and

(b )may do so if, in its opinion or in the opinion of the Tribunal, there are circumstances suggesting—

(i )that the business of the company is being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members or any other persons, or otherwise for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose, or in a manner oppressive of any of its members, or that the company was formed for any fraudulent or unlawful purpose;

(ii )that persons concerned in the formation of the company or the management of its affairs have in connection therewith been guilty of fraud, misfeasance or other misconduct towards the company or towards any of its members; or

So far as the transactions themselves are concerned, I am of prima facie view that mere involvement of the company in CBLO or MIBOR linked debentures or investment in mutual funds through the two finance companies per se would not warrant an order or investigation. It does not appear again that the CLB had examined that issue in detail but investigator was appointed on being satisfied that the company was conducting business through entities connected with one of the Directors. As regards overall jurisdiction of CLB to direct investigation into accounts of a company through an auditor, such jurisdiction can be derived from Section 403 of the Act read with Clause 46 of the 1991 Regulations. Such power or jurisdiction can also be traced to sub-Section (4C) of Section 10E of the Act, read with Rule 14 of Order 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It would be within the inherent jurisdiction of the CLB to take assistance of specialized agencies where having regard to nature of information required, it may lack specific expertise or infrastructural support. But such investigation is to be directed only after a case is made out of prima facie mismanagement and oppression in connection with a company in relation to the subject on which investigation is being directed, and only after such case is established, again prima facie by the petitioners, who seek investigation about large scale misapplication or unauthorized application of company's funds. Question, however, may arise as to what would be the course if silhouettes of irregularities appear in financial statements of a company but actual identification of such irregularities become impossible from available materials. In such circumstances, in a shareholders' action, in my opinion, directions for disclosures of particulars or other legal methods akin to discovery proceeding may be undertaken, and directions may follow such disclosures.

Can the thirst of the depositors be wiped out if these offenders are prosecuted and sent to prisons. The answer is emphatically 'no'. Similar situation came to light before the Supreme Court in Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Co. (P.) Ltd. [1996] 4 SCC 622. The Supreme Court clarified that "imposition of punishment for contempt would not denude the Court of its power to issue directions to remedy by the wrong done by the contemner including those so as not to enable the contemner to retain the benefit derived by the contempt." The Supreme Court further clarified that "it is open for the Court to lift the corporate veil to see the real men behind the veil who are involved in defrauding others by corrupt and illegal means in deliberate defiance of Court's order." The Supreme Court further held that "the courts have power to reach the illegally obtained property even in the hands of relatives and associates and restore it to the victims of the fraud or corruption." In this case, it is clear that the corporate character was employed by the first petitioner for the purpose of committing illegality and defrauding the others. In such an event, this Court, piercing the corporate veil, can look at the reality behind the corporate veil so as to pass appropriate orders to do substantial justice to the victims. It is seen that the Managing Director not only incorporated Midwest India Industries Ltd., and subsequently other companies were brought into effect and that too by the persons who are none else than the close relations and promoters of the first company. The Supreme Court treated all such companies as one entity belonging to one and controlled by one family. The learned counsel for Reserve Bank of India also submits that the bank was taking steps to initiate prosecution proceedings and also for winding up of the company, as it was a confirmed case of non-refund of deposits. The submission of the learned counsel appears to be very appropriate. De hors this submission, this Court also gave number of opportunities to the petitioners to refund the deposits as per their own schedule of payments. Even though the schedule of payment was changed twice on the request of the petitioners, yet, there was not even a single case where the company deposited any amount in the account opened by the Advocate-Commissioners. But the emotions and feelings of parties have no place in judicial proceedings. This Court is required to salvage the situation in accordance with law keeping in view the mandate of the Constitution. It spreads its arms of justice to identify and reach the injustice, and thereby remedy the cause. The efforts of this Court to save the depositors yielded microscopic results. But at the same time, no offender should be allowed to gain an impression that Courts lean towards them. The petitioner failed to respond to the opportunities granted by this Court. HELD: From a perusal of the documents submitted by the petitioners, it was clear that the directors had violated various provisions of the Act and committed various acts which were prejudicial to the interest of the company and its shareholders at large. It was also seen from the documents that the Registrar of Companies, issued notice dated to 2-9-2008 to its directors under section 234(1) directing the company to furnish information and explanation within ten days or else action would be initiated under sections 234(3A), 234(4). Further, the Registrar of Companies issued another letter dated 19-9-2008 to the directors to furnish the minutes book of the board of directors and general meetings, fixed asset register, register of debenture holders, index of debenture holders, shareholders' attendance register, register of investments, copy of the annual report and balance-sheets for the last two years. It was seen from the records that having not received any information from the company and its directors, the Registrar of Companies referred the matter to the Regional Director for prosecution. The Registrar of Companies, in response to the notice regarding the filing of the instant petition before the principal Bench, CLB, vide his letter dated 10-6-2009 mentioned the details of the company and its directors and the fund position on the basis of the balance-sheets and also the assets and liabilities. It was also stated that the company had not filed its balance-sheet as on 31-3-2001 and the company held only one annual general meeting on 1-12-2007 for the years 2001 to 2007 instead of holding separate annual general meetings for each year. No extension of time was obtained by the company. It was also mentioned that the shareholding detail was given in CD whereas no CD was received in that regard by the Registrar of Companies. It was also stated that there were several complaints received by the Registrar of Companies against the company. [Para 4]

From the above, it was evident that the allegations of the petitioners had some force and the same were also further strengthened from the letter of the Registrar of Companies to the instant Bench and also various letters addressed to the company. The instant Bench would not keep its eyes closed on such acts when they came before it with un-controverted facts against the directors. The affairs of the company were being conducted with an intent to defraud its members and public which were oppressive and prejudicial to the interest of the members. To protect the interest of the company and its shareholders and also to up keep the faith of the public in the judicial system (Quasi Judicial Bodies), the Bench certainly came to the rescue of the petitioners and its shareholders to do substantial justice by ordering an investigation by invoking the provisions of section 237(b). [Para 5]

The petitioners also brought to the notice that the Registrar of Companies ordered for inspection of the company's records under section 209A which was pending. The scope of inspection and the scope of investigation were entirely different and inspection does not prejudice investigation. In view of the reasons as stated above, it was concluded that there were enough circumstances suggesting for an investigation into the affairs of the company and to take necessary action. The fraudulent companies cannot run away from the clutches of law. The law must be enforceable in such cases to prevent the fraudulent acts and bring back the faith of the members. Therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred under section 237(b), the Central Government would order for investigation into the affairs of the company and would take appropriate action if warranted on receipt of the investigation report. The petitioners were directed to furnish all the information they possessed to the authorities during investigation. [Para 8]

HEADNOTE: Section 457 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Powers of liquidator - Whether Company Court while exercising jurisdiction in an application under sections 433, 434 and 439 has power to appoint a provisional liquidator giving him liberty to sell properties, not merely property standing in name of company but also properties standing in names of other companies on premise that such assets have been created with funds collected by company - Held, yes

FACT: On complaints of large scale commission of frauds by the directors of the company involving siphoning off the company funds for private ends and for purchasing all properties in the names of other front companies and, thus, stashing away large assets from the reach of the creditors, the respondent filed winding up application against the appellant-company. The Company Court, on the basis of prima facie material that the funds of the company were transferred to other companies formed by one of the directors concluded that the affairs of the company, including assets in the names of other companies which had been created with the funds collected by the company, were required to be investigated and that such systematic investigation would bring out the extent of assets owned by the company, legal and valid so as to make available the properties for discharge of debts of the investors. The Company Court, accordingly, passed an order appointing a provisional liquidator under whose control the property, effects and actionable claims to which the company claimed to be entitled to would vest. In the instant appeal, the appellant contended that the properties that were to be brought for sale did not belong to the company and that the company could not have offered to the liquidator to take possession of all the assets, including the assets that did not stand in the name of the company.

HELD: STATUTORY POWERS OF OFFICIAL LIQUIDATOR

The powers of provisional liquidator appointed by the Company Court under section 450(3) the same powers as that the liquidator himself has. The extensive powers of the liquidator are delineated under section 457. [Para 4]

EXTENT OF DIRECTIONS THAT THE COMPANY COURT COULD PASS

Even apart from the powers of the liquidator which are co-extensive with the powers of the provisional liquidator, the Court itself has the power under section 477 at the time of appointment of the provisional liquidator to summon before it any officer of the company or person knowing or suspected to have in his possession any property or books or papers of the company or known or suspected to be indebted to the company. This power which the Company Court has under section 477 is wide enough to pass even an ex parte order to secure the interest of the persons moving the application for winding up. Having regard to such wide powers of the Company Court, it is untenable to contend that the Company Court could not have directed as regards the properties which, on a prima facie finding, were also the assets of the company. The order of the Company Court was unexceptional if it was noticed that the Company Court had also given liberty to show that the assets standing in the name of other companies did not belong to the company against which liquidation proceedings had been initiated. Indeed, no prejudice could be said to be caused by such an order. Further, section 533 enables the liquidator to apply for disclaimer of onerous property. Section 535(4), while fastening the liquidator to disclaim certain properties, makes it possible for any third party for approaching the liquidator himself staking his claim to the property which is taken possession of by the liquidator or in respect of which proceedings are taken for sale. Having regard to the scheme of the Act protecting the interest of third parties and controlling the discretion of the liquidator by overall supervision of the Company Court, it would be untenable to contend that the directions given by the Company Court at the time of appointment of the provisional liquidator were not in conformity with law. [Para 5]

DISPOSITION

The sole contention raised by the appellant was, therefore, without any substance and the appeal was to be dismissed. [Para 6]

Section 58A of the Companies Act, 1956 - Public deposits - Pursuant to an advertisement made by an investment company inviting general public to subscribe in various fixed deposits and saving schemes, appellants subscribed to scheme - As on date of maturity certificates issued were not honoured appellants lodged an fir with police station - On application of appellants, Magistrate directed attachment of said company’s properties - Thereafter, appellants filed criminal revision petition, alleging that notwithstanding order of attachment, properties were either disposed of or dealt with in a manner contrary to order of attachment - Additional District and Sessions Judge rejected said petition on ground that appellants had no locus standi to file a revision petition - Against said order, appellants filed petitions, but same were also dismissed by High Court - Whether, on facts, without entering into matter relating to contempt of court, concerned court was to be directed to work out details and modalities as to how properties of said company could be sold to get highest price so that dues of creditors and liabilities could be paid - Held, yes

A petition was filed by the Securities & Exchange Board of India (SEBI) as a public interest litigation, wherein it was stated that it had come to the notice of the Government of India that there were entities which were issuing instruments such as agro bonds, plantation bonds, etc., offering very high rates of returns which were not consistent with the normal returns in such schemes.

In petition SEBI pointed out that respondent No. 1 had floated 18 Schemes and had collected approximately Rs. 16 crores from the small investors. Thereafter it was noticed that promoters of the schemes of respondent No. 1 were not traceable, respondent No. 1 had downed its shutters, the owners were not available, various offices of respondent No. 1 were closed and the said company was going through financial crises. Many investors were holding demonstrations outside the SEBI's office demanding action against the company and its directors.

Therefore, in petition SEBI prayed that in public interest, till regulations were framed under section 12(1B), appropriate directions be given to protect large amounts invested by middle-class people, and immediate action be taken against the directors who had siphoned off large amounts belonging to investors under the guise of corporate veil. It was further contended that the bank accounts and other assets, movable as well as immovable, of respondent No. 1 wheresoever situated required to be frozen and attached to protect the investor's money from being frittered away.

Section 12(1B) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with article 142 of the Constitution of India - Collective investment scheme - Certificate of registration - SEBI filed petition in public interest stating that certain plantation companies by issuing instrument like agro bonds, plantation bonds, etc., were offering very high rates of return and collecting amounts from small investors and siphoned off amount to their sister concern and other business instead of returning promised amount to investors - SEBI sought appropriate directions to protect interests of small investors till regulation are framed under section 12(1B) - Directions were issued by court to conduct inquiry and search and seize of property and accordingly properties of directors were attached - Investigations were said to be still in progress - Whether no further directions viz., to direct RBI to issue orders to all commercial banks and/or cooperative banks, where Respondent No. 1 Plantation company had accounts, restraining Respondent Nos. 1 to 5 and 7 from withdrawing any money from the said accounts are required to be issued for present but Central Government or State Government would have to take appropriate action in framing appropriate regulations/enactment as early as possible - Held, yes

HEADNOTE: Section 446 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding-up - Suits Stayed on Winding-Up Order - Pursuant to a petition filed by one of creditors for winding-up of company for its failure to return huge deposits collected from thousands of depositors, court formulated a scheme for running business without allowing to receive fresh deposits and appointed provisional liquidator - Company had diverted a huge amount to its sister company, by unlawful means - Despite repeated directions, company and its directors failed to furnish books of account, registers, etc., to Official Liquidator - Registers which were produced, were found to be forged and fabricated with false entries - Therefore, Court directed crime branch police to register case against managing director and directors of company (accused) and to recover books of account, register etc. - Court also directed that all matters including bail matters of accused persons should be placed before company court - At that stage company court issued notice to all accused to cancel bail granted to them - Whether except in case of proceedings pending in appeal before Supreme Court, and High Court, in respect of all other proceedings, both civil and criminal, company court has jurisdiction to transfer all such proceedings or cases before it and to decide same - Held, yes - Whether since directors were at large, all records were with them and there was every possibility of creating bogus claims in names of men of their confidence or choice thereby defeating interests of real depositors, it was imperative to cancel bail and to keep accused in judicial custody till they produced registers and books of account - Held, yes

FACT: When the company failed to return nearly Rs. 18 crores collected from thousands of depositors, one of the creditors filed petition for winding-up of the company. In the meantime, the company filed an application under section 391 for obtaining sanction to a scheme of compromise, which was refused by the court. The court, however, formulated a scheme for running the business without allowing to receive fresh deposits and appointed provisional liquidator. The company had diverted a huge amount to its sister company by unlawful means in violation of the provisions of law and the directions issued by the Reserve Bank of India. Despite repeated directions of the court, the company and its managing director did not furnish the books of account, registers and the securities including the gold to the Official Liquidator, and even those registers which were produced before the Official Liquidator, were found to be forged and fabricated with false entries. The court, thereupon, passed an order directing the crime branch police to register a case and to recover the books of account, register, etc. It also issued certain directions to the effect that all the genuine registers, account books, etc., should be seized/recovered and that the investigating officer should further enquire whether any properties had been acquired by the directors in the name of others as benami with the company's funds. Further, it would be open to him to arrest the respondent-managing director as well as directors of the company. The police, accordingly, registered a criminal case against the directors of the company as well as accused 5 and 6 who had joined them in diverting considerable sum to a sister concern. Subsequently, the court directed that all matters including bail matters, should be placed before the company court. At that stage the company court found it necessary to give notice to all the accused, why the bail granted to all of them should not be cancelled. The case of the accused was that the company court had no jurisdiction to cancel the bail which was granted by another bench of the court and the petition for cancellation of bail should also go before the same bench which granted the bail.

HELD: When the court had found that it was impossible to proceed with the liquidation proceedings in accordance with law due to the violation of the lawful orders and directions of the court by the directors and the large scale forging of documents, misappropriation of money and the fraud committed by the directors of the company, by order dated 25-3-2003, it was directed that all the matters including bail matters relating to the company and its sister companies should be placed before the company court. The said order was fully in accordance with section 446 which empowers the court to transfer all cases or proceedings pending before all courts to the company court. The only restriction imposed by sub-section (4) of section 446 is that the provisions in sub-sections (1) to (3) would not apply to proceedings pending in appeal before the Supreme Court or the High Court. But in respect of all other proceedings, both civil and criminal, the company court has jurisdiction to transfer all such proceedings or cases before it and to decide the same. [Paras 9 and 10]

1992 as the cut off year for preparing the list, the argument that the line had been drawn out arbitrarily excluding companies which had issued capital prior to 1992, was also unsustainable. The list of 80 companies was not a rigid list as freedom had been given to add names to the list considered necessary and the SEBI had also submitted that the identification exercise was not a one-time exercise but a continuing process. The matter under inquiry was not hit by the provisions of the Limitation Act. It was incorrect to say that by using section 11B the SEBI was usurping the powers of Registrar of Companies or that they were interfering with the management of the company. Sections 11 and 11B are interconnected and co-extensive as both these sections are mainly focussed on investor protection. On a perusal of the said section 11 it could be seen that the SEBI had been in no uncertain terms mandated to protect the interests of investors in securities by such measures as it thought fit. The expression ‘measure’ has not defined in the Act. ‘Measure’ in its generic sense is of wider amplitude. While section 11 deals with the functions of the Board section 11B is on the powers of the Board. Section 11B is in a sense a functional tool in the hands of the Board. In effect section 11B is one of the executive measures available to the SEBI to enforce its prime duty of investor protection. SEBI is thus empowered to issue directions in the interest of investors to any person or class of persons referred to in section 12 or associated with the securities market. It could not be said that a company having its shares listed on the exchange was out of the reach of sections 11 and 11B. Since the company was operating through its board of directors, the directors of the company also could be considered as persons associated with the capital market, as long as the company’s shares were listed on the exchange. Thus, taking into consideration the scope and reach of sections 11 and 11B it could not be said that the SEBI was lacking authority to issue direction to the appellant. Further, the impugned direction was not one for violation of the Companies Act or the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act. It was issued in the interest of investors under section 11B independent of the provisions of the Companies Act and the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act. Further, there was nothing wrong in relying on a report submitted by an authority like stock exchange, as the information furnished by itself was only a starting point. An inquiry thereafter followed and the concerned persons were given sufficient opportunities to put across their views before the authorities. Similarly exclusion of public deposits and debt instruments from the scope of inquiry could not be considered to be in any way discriminatory, as the matter relating to public deposits etc., was taken care of by other regimes vested with powers for the purpose. For these reasons, the SEBI was justified in pursuing the course of action against the vanishing companies and its promoters and directors and the SEBI was legally invested with the requisite authority for the purpose.

The main reason based on which the impugned order had been issued was an inference, in the absence of relevant material before the SEBI, that the appellant had misused the fund collected from the public for purposes other than for which it was collected. In terms of section 11(2)(i ) the SEBI is empowered to call for information, etc. from the appellant-company also for the reason that it was also a person associated with the securities market. The fund utilisation by the appellant-company need be looked into with reference its records in the context of the charge of misuse of funds raised from the public issue. Since the appellants had expressed their willingness to make available the requisite information, in depth study of the same would be useful to reach at a definite conclusion and also to pursue the matter thereafter, if considered necessary, to protect the interest of the investors. Since the impugned order was based on inference and was ex parte, it was proper that the appellants should be given one more opportunity to furnish the information to the SEBI in a reasonable time frame and the SEBI in the light of that information, would pass appropriate orders in accordance with the provisions of the law. The Department of Company Affairs may also be requested, if so desired, to examine the books of account and other records of the appellant company to ascertain the utilisation of the funds and if necessary follow up the matter.

The impugned order did not in any way redress the grievances of the persons who had already invested in the shares of the appellant-company. The prohibition put in on the appellants was effective only prospectively. Since the appellants had come forward to furnish the details, and the impugned order was ex parte, it was felt that further inquiry on the lines embarked on by the SEBI and follow-up action thereafter would be in the interest of the investors. For the purpose it was felt that the matter should be remanded.

Hence, the impugned order was set aside and the matter was remanded with the above directions.

of section 235. The grounds for ordering an investigation did exist. There was overwhelming material available pointing to the circumstances suggesting that the business of the company was conducted for a fraudulent and unlawful purpose. The persons concerned in the management of the company had been guilty of fraud, misfeasance or other misconduct towards the company. It was a case squarely covered under the provisions of section 235 as the pre-conditions for initiating such an action existed as was clear from the foregoing. [Para 15] The directors owe fiduciary duty to the shareholders and they have to function in not only good faith, but in utmost good faith. In the instant case, shareholders’ faith seemed to have been belied. The petitioner was on a very sound footing besides having come to the CLB bona fide. Only investigation under section 235 could bring out the true state of affairs. An order to investigate under section 235 in any case could not be prejudicial to the respondent. An order of the CLB under this section directing an investigation is only analogous to the issue of a fact finding commission. This particular power of the CLB is not of a judicial or quasi-judicial nature. It is a power of administrative nature and the CLB may even take the initiative suo motu or on the application or information supplied by any shareholder or other person. Under this section, directing an investigation is only analogous to the issue of a fact finding commission by a civil court for looking into accounts or making an investigation and does not amount to a judgment within clause 15 of the Letters Patent, so as to enable an aggrieved party to appeal. An order of investigation is not an end by itself; it is only a means to find out the full facts of the acts complained of. It is nothing, but an exploratory measure to be proved or disproved with reference to the facts later on ascertained. This discretionary power of the CLB has to be exercised in good faith. An investigation may be ordered when public interest is involved or detriment to the interests of shareholders had been caused surreptitiously. Such investigation should not be taken lightly. Unless proper grounds exist for investigation of the affairs of the company, investigation cannot be ordered. The allegations made in the petition were such matters which would require an investigation. [Para 16]

In view of above, there was reason to believe that there was likelihood of the existence of malpractices envisaged in the provisions of section 235. To prove the prima facie case of ‘intent to fraud’ and misfeasance on general public and specifically the investor in the instant case and conducting the business of the company otherwise for a fraudulent and unlawful purpose, the petitioner’s prayer could be granted for ordering an investigation under section 235. [Para 17]

The petition was, accordingly, to be allowed. [Para 18]

The respondent was an equity shareholder and the promoter of the appellant-company. He was also appointed as the Chairman of the company. Subsequently, the company came out with public issue which was subscribed in excess of 14 times the offer. Thereafter, the respondent filed petition under section 237(a)( ii ) before the Company Judge seeking to direct the Central Government to appoint inspectors to investigate into the affairs of the company. It was alleged that no first annual general meeting of the company was held as convened in time.

The managing director, ‘M’ had been fraudulently mismanaging the company in utter disregard of the interest of the shareholders and was acting in an autocratic and oppressive manner. He created false and fabricated documents with nefarious motive to oust the respondent and other members of the board of directors who opposed the misutilisation and misappropriation of public funds. He created documents and minutes purporting to remove the petitioner and others who opposed the mismanagement and oppression. Though on the public issue, shares were over subscribed to the tune of 14 times and huge amounts were collected from the public, shares were neither allotted properly nor amounts refunded to the applicants whose application for shares were not accepted.

It was further alleged that 1200 complaints had been filed against ‘M’ by the subscribers to whom the amounts were not refunded and that ‘M’ had misappropriated, misutilised and mismanaged the funds collected through public issue and diverted the funds for his private purposes. The company opposed the petition. The Company Judge found that the submission of the Central Government supported the respondent’s allegations and concluded that a deeper probe was necessary and passed an order declaring that affairs of the company ought to be investigated by an inspector appointed by the Court itself.

On appeal :

the payment is not made by a company, the winding-up of the company can be ordered, as the company would be said to be unable to pay its debts. In a case where no properties of the company are available, and the company has not taken any steps worth being effective for making the payment for a considerable period, despite the order of the CLB, the company petition for winding-up would not be either not maintainable nor it can be rejected on this ground. [Para 25] In the instant case, the order passed by the CLB indicated that the CLB on the basis of the admission of the company that a large number of deposits were outstanding for repayment on maturity, decided to invoke suo motu powers to order repayment of the amount deposited as provided under section 45QA of the 1934 Act. Accordingly, the company was directed to indicate reasons for default and also its proposals to meet the pending claims as well as those which might arise in future on maturity. The company furnished a detailed statement of its reasons for its failure to repay all the matured deposits and also a scheme for repayment of both outstanding matured deposits and also the deposits that would be maturing in future. The company submitted a scheme for repayment of deposits during the period of five years, the gist of which had been quoted in the order of the CLB itself. Another scheme was given on behalf of the depositors asking for repayment scheme of 48 months. The company submitted a revised repayment schedule for 48 months and had published the scheme in two newspapers. [Para 27]

Thereafter, various dates were fixed by the CLB in which the company absented though representatives of the depositors and a large number of depositors attended the proceedings. The CLB, therefore, after observing that due opportunity had been given to the company to make its submission on the suggestions given by the depositor but no one was present on behalf of the company and directors had also chosen to remain absent whereas large number of depositors were involved who had put in their hard earned money with the company, found that the matter could not be allowed to be dragged. The CLB on going through the revised scheme submitted by the company and suggestions made by the advocate on behalf of the depositors, and with a view to balance the interest of the company and the depositors and also the public interest at large issued a detailed order as to payment of deposited amount. [Para 28]

Despite that order, the record revealed that not a single penny was paid nor any effective step was taken by the company or its directors for making any payment to the depositors. Since the company failed to make the repayment even as per the directions and the scheme and the company did not take any interest in the proceedings nor the directors attended the proceedings despite themselves having come to the Board for getting the scheme approved for payment, the investors were well within their right to approach the Court for winding-up of the company on the ground that the company had failed to make the payment and it was unable to pay its debts. [Para 30]

For allowing the winding-up petition, it is essential that there are dues of the creditors against the company, namely, debt, and that the company has failed to make the payment at the given intervals or at such intervals in time when the depositors have asked for payment and that the company is unable to pay its debts. In case all the three ingredients aforesaid are established, besides other contents, if, at all, required to be proved, the creditors would be justified in asking the winding-up of the company. [Para 31]

The appellant-company had floated various attractive schemes giving dreams and illusions to lakhs of people for having better return of their deposits so made and had collected the deposits but instead of acting bona fidely in taking the investment and making payment of dues, it indulged in siphoning off its money in other companies of the same group having almost common directors under some loan agreements which money was never sought to be realized from the company. [Para 38]

Hence, the view taken by the Company Judge regarding conduct of the company and its directors in collecting huge amount from the depositors and not paying it back, and deliberate attempt to misguide and mislead the depositors by giving false assurance of making repayment on future dates, coupled by the failure on the part of the company to make payment as per the scheme approved by the CLB, gave full jurisdiction to the Company Judge to entertain the petition for winding-up and to order for winding-up of the company. [Para 41]

So far as the appellant’s contention as to the validity of the statutory notice under section 434 issued by the investors to the company was concerned, no substantial defect in the notice was found so as to make it invalid, the invalidity of the notice even if any in the instant case would not affect the order of the Company Judge allowing winding-up of the company as it was not being disputed by the appellant that the issuance or service of the notice under section 434 was not a condition precedent for filing a winding-up petition against the company under section 433. [Para 42]

According to respondents the present petition was a counter-blast to the petition filed under section 111(4) by the R2 and R10 in respect of another company, 'LIL', where the petitioner herein had played a fraud on the stakeholders including the R1 company herein.

The respondent stated that one 'KSMR', who was a General Manager of the Union Bank of India and a friend of the R2 herein advised R2 to go for a public issue and accordingly introduced 'AA', to the R2. 'AA' was the director of the P1. The R2 and his associates had an elaborate discussion with 'AA', and 'AA' at the time of discussion had promised the R2 that he would convert the R1 into one Rs. 100 crore company. Accordingly, R1 had entered into a Memorandum Of Understanding (MoU) with CSPL (a company which was managed by the 'AA') by which CSPL was appointed as Book Running Lead Manager for the IPO issue of R1.

The respondents submitted that 'AA', who was the Managing Director and Director for CSPL Group of companies in the process of preparation of documents for the IPO issue had asked the R2 to sign blank letter heads, blank printed forms and blank cheques and that the R2, though in the liquor business for more than 35 years, was not well educated and had been successfully doing liquor business only on the experience that he had acquired. To further coerce the R2 into signing the documents and the cheques, 'AA' had made a payment of Rs. 2.20 crores into the account of R1 allegedly to show his bona fide, but the fact remains that the intent of the said 'AA' from the beginning was to hatch a plan to deceive the R1 company.

The respondents further submitted that reposing faith and confidence in 'AA', the R2, signed all the blank cheques, blank forms and blank letter heads and handed over the same to 'AA' on trust and subsequently the R2 realized that the said payment was only an eye wash to carry out a much larger conspiracy against R1, the R2 and other shareholders of the company.

The respondents submitted that by way of the above transactions a sum of Rs. 72.35 crores had been credited into the account of R1 adjusting the initial expenditure of Rs. 1.25 crores. It was alleged that after crediting the IPO amount into the R1 account, 'AA' systematically transferred a lot of money to his associates and other companies utilizing the signed blank cheques.

From the facts mentioned above, it has become clear that both, the P1 and the respondents have allegedly diverted the funds of the R1 company to their associates and companies and matters are pending before the different judicial forums. Thus, there exist the circumstances which prima facie suggest that the business of the company is being conducted with intent to defraud its members and the amount collected through IPO has been diverted to the associates and companies by the P1 and the respondents, which amounts to fraud played on the investors, which points out that the management of the R1 company along with P1 is guilty of fraud, misfeasance or other misconduct towards the company and its members. In the light of the circumstances stated, this tribunal is satisfied that it necessary to order the investigation into the affairs of the R1 company under the provisions of section 213(b). [Para 55]

Thus, the Tribunal in exercise of the power conferred under section 237(b) orders for conducting investigation into the affairs of the R1 company for the purpose of bringing out the true picture about the diversion of the funds and the amount of the IPO of the R1 company and to fix the responsibility of the person in management including others responsible for misfeasance of the funds and to bring them to books and to recover the amount siphoned off in order to do substantial justice to the investor/shareholders and creditors of the R1 company. [Para 57]

The appellant filed an application before the Single Judge proposing a scheme of amalgamation with M.

The Judge initially directed the Registrar of Companies to conduct an investigation and file a report.

The report of Registrar would reveal, the company had issued share premium to large number of companies mostly private companies on the same day and used funds for investments to a small extent and made advances to others. There were crores of investments involving a large number of private companies.

The Judge directed the Director, Revenue Intelligence to conduct an enquiry as to whether there was any money trail. The company preferred an appeal.

The Single Judge directed Ministry of Corporate Affairs to carry investigation. Accordingly, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs asked the SFIO to conduct such investigation. SFIO submitted a report, inter alia, pointing out irregularity in the affairs of the company.

Then Single Judge asked RBI to submit its report, which submitted its preliminary report observing, that the company might have carried on business as non-banking financial company without obtaining registration with the Reserve Bank of India or complying with the other conditions set by the Reserve Bank of India for non-banking financial companies.

The appellant contended the Judge, despite the restrictions being imposed by the Division Bench continued to carry on roving enquiry that would be an unending process.

In appeal, the appellant contended that the Judge should either allow its petition for holding meetings of the shareholders to ascertain their wishes or dismiss it so that the appellant could take further steps in the matter.

Regulation 73 of the SEBI (Collective Investment Schemes) Regulations, 1999 - Manner of repayment and winding up -  Applicant was National Investors Forum (NIF) and its members were investors of respondent-company GFIL - SEBI inquired into activities of GFIL group and noted financial and other irregularities committed by company - SEBI filed a writ petition in Bombay High Court, in which an order was passed against GFIL restraining it from alienating properties; a similar order was passed by High Court in same year - Thus, SEBI made an order prohibiting company from alienating its properties - However, GFIL, continued to accept deposits, carrying business and alienating properties - Therefore, winding up proceedings, were preferred before High Court - Company Judge by order directed appointment of a provisional liquidator to control and manage affairs of company in accordance with directions of company court - Thereafter, company petition and all other proceedings pending against GFIL in various High Courts throughout country were transferred to Supreme Court, in a transfer petition filed by SEBI - Supreme Court by its order constituted a committee to monitor affairs of GFIL and to make sure that sale of assets of GFIL were to ensure that depositors who had parted with sizeable amounts ought to be refunded their amounts - Committee had detailed figures of amounts invested from depositors in GFIL and its group companies from different States - Committee had so far been able to collect and put to sale and realize assets to tune of Rs. 400 crore - Possibilities of disbursements, regardless of total amount deposited resulted in an outgoing of Rs.309.60 crore - As on date, there was uncertainty with respect to litigation pending in regard to at least three properties - Committee was facing a possible reimbursement claim to tune of Rs.65 crore - Further, an income tax payment of Rs.32 crore towards capital gains had been made - Whether having regard to all these aspects, at this stage, it would not be appropriate to direct any claim - Held, yes - Whether in these circumstances an expert ought to be appointed to assist committee in its task of ensuring management of its funds and evolving a method of disbursing amounts whenever position became clear - Held, yes - Whether thus RBI was to be directed to nominate an expert to advise Committee in its task of managing funds available with it to optimise their returns having regard to previous orders of Court and to evolve a feasible practicable method for disbursement of various amounts to depositors and investors - Held, yes [Paras 15, 16  18]SEBI : Where a committee was appointed to manage affairs of company and to make sure that sale of assets of company were to ensure that depositors be refunded their amounts, expert was to be appointed to assist committee in its task to evolve a feasible practicable method for disbursement of various amounts to depositors and investors

HEADNOTE: Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company’s affairs in other cases - Petitioner, a shareholder of third respondent-company, being aggrieved by non-receipt of annual report and notice of extraordinary annual general meeting of company and not getting any return on his investment, filed writ petition seeking direction to first respondent to appoint a competent person as investigator for investigating affairs of company - Whether since power has been conferred on CLB to order investigation, if there are circumstances necessitating same, it was incumbent on petitioner to approach CLB and there arose no reason for exercising discretionary power vested in Company Court to order such investigation - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, writ petition was not maintainable - Held, yes

FACT: The petitioner had purchased certain shares of third respondent-company. According to him, he had neither received any annual report nor notice of any extraordinary annual general meeting of the company since he purchased the shares of the company and further he could not get even a single rupee as return on his investment. Those facts were allegedly brought to the notice of the Registrar of Companies, but no action was taken on the matter. Therefore, the petitioner filed writ petition seeking a direction to the first respondent to appoint a competent person as investigator for investigating the affairs of the third respondent-company from 1995 onwards and to file a report in the High Court. The second respondent took stand that remedy, if any, available to the petitioner was to approach the CLB in accordance with provisions of the Act and, hence, writ petition was not maintainable.

HELD: Section 237(b ) empowers the CLB, if there are circumstances necessitating investigation, to order accordingly. This power has been granted to the CLB in terms of the amendment effected in the Act in 1988. Before the amendment, sanction had to be given in terms of such clause (b ) by the Central Government. When the power vested in the executive Government is invoked, one incumbent may perhaps feel that justice may not be meted out. But after the amendment in 1988, the power vested with the Central Government had been taken away and vested with the CLB. When the power is conferred on the CLB, it was incumbent on the petitioner to approach that statutory Board which would examine and do justice, as the circumstances would demand. In such circumstances, there arose no reason for exercising the discretionary power vested in the Company Court to direct such investigation or declare that it needed investigation by the Central Government. [Para 11]

As could be seen from the different provisions of the Act and also the scheme of the Act, since the petitioner was having a remedy to approach the CLB or to invoke such other remedies available to him under the law or under the provisions of the Act, the petitioner was to be given liberty to pursue the other legal remedies available to him in accordance with law. [Para 15]

Accordingly, the writ petition was disposed of. [Para 16]

Adducing proof of circumstances stated in section 237(b ) not easy 25.7-8 To succeed in proving the existence of the circumstances enumerated in section 237(b) for any complaining shareholders who are not insiders is way beyond their means in the absence of which the Central Government and the Tribunal can afford no relief rendering the proceeding almost of no avail, as it appears. But, in Panther Fincap & Management Services Ltd. v. Central Government, Union of India (2005) 61 SCL 33 (Bom.) it was held that for purposes of section 237(b)( i), where a company conducted business in a fraudulent or unlawful manner, the fact that it has since closed down its business is no bar, and also the existence of another investigation by SEBI parallelly also is no bar: SEBI’s finding after inspection under section 209A was that due to concerted transactions between appellants and ‘K’-who was the moving spirit behind companies that caused the ultimate collapse of the stock market as a result of which the Global Trust Bank (GTB) and UTI were subjected to serious financial difficulties necessitating their being bailed out by the Central Government, as reported by the inspector to SEBI—showed a strong prima facie case for the permission to investigate into the affairs of the company sought from CLB by the Central Government placing reliance on it and was justifiable.

Powers of Authorities under section 237(a) & (b) : Section 237(a)(i ) and (ii) involve Central Government and the Court, and section 237(b) involves the CLB 1/Tribunal and the Central Government, all vested with discretionary power about investigation of the affairs of a company. The powers conferred on the Central Government under sections 235 and 237 are discretionary, Indian Express (Madurai) (P.) Ltd. v. Chief Presidency Magistrate (1974) 44 Comp. Cas. 106 (Mad.), and it is not imperative for the Central Government to order investigation when it does not find it necessary even though the facts in its possession show the commission of an offence by an officer or person; and, the discretion vested in the Central Government is not total and unexaminable, it must have some complaint before it from a person having a stake in the company’s affairs, and where an order is made on several grounds of which some are non-existent and some irrelevant with nothing to show that the order could have been made on existing grounds, such an order cannot be sustained, Jiyajeerao Cotton Mills Ltd. v. CLB (1969) 39 Comp. Cas. 856 (MP)—the reasons for making the order must be available to the authority at the time of making order and not those found subsequently to justify the order, New Central Jute Mills Co. Ltd. v. Deputy Secretary, Ministry of Finance (1970) 40 Comp. Cas. 543 (Cal.), and the Central Government’s power to invoke section 237 is circumscribed by section 237(b), Modi Industries Ltd. v. Union of India (1982) 52 Comp. Cas. 589 (Delhi).
