Section 446 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding-up - Suits Stayed on Winding-Up Order - Pursuant to a petition filed by one of creditors for winding-up of company for its failure to return huge deposits collected from thousands of depositors, court formulated a scheme for running business without allowing to receive fresh deposits and appointed provisional liquidator - Company had diverted a huge amount to its sister company, by unlawful means - Despite repeated directions, company and its directors failed to furnish books of account, registers, etc., to Official Liquidator - Registers which were produced, were found to be forged and fabricated with false entries - Therefore, Court directed crime branch police to register case against managing director and directors of company (accused) and to recover books of account, register etc. - Court also directed that all matters including bail matters of accused persons should be placed before company court - At that stage company court issued notice to all accused to cancel bail granted to them - Whether except in case of proceedings pending in appeal before Supreme Court, and High Court, in respect of all other proceedings, both civil and criminal, company court has jurisdiction to transfer all such proceedings or cases before it and to decide same - Held, yes - Whether since directors were at large, all records were with them and there was every possibility of creating bogus claims in names of men of their confidence or choice thereby defeating interests of real depositors, it was imperative to cancel bail and to keep accused in judicial custody till they produced registers and books of account - Held, yes

Per K.S. Radhakrishnan, J.

SEBI is vested with powers of Civil Court

The Securities Appellate Tribunal ('SAT') which exercises powers under Section 15T of the SEBI Act, it is well settled, is the final adjudicator of facts. The Tribunal has, for the purpose of discharging its functions, the same powers as are vested in a Civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure. Broadly speaking, the Tribunal has trappings of a Court in the sense that it has to determine the appeal placed before it judicially and give a fair hearing to the parties, to accept evidence and also order for inspection and discovery of documents, compel attendance of witnesses and to pass a reasoned order which gives finality to the dispute, subject to the appeal to Supreme Court under Section 15Z of the SEBI Act. Findings of fact generally fall in the domain of the Tribunal provided it stays within its jurisdiction.

Situations may also be there, where the evidence taken as a whole is not reasonably capable of supporting the findings recorded by the Tribunal or the Tribunal could have reasonably recorded that conclusion.

Questions repeatedly posed in instant case before SEBI as well as before SAT, were with regard to the nature of OFCDs issued by Saharas. RHPs produced had disclosed that Saharas did not intend the proposed securities to be listed on any stock exchange and that the issues consisted of unsecured OFCDs with an option to convert the same to equity shares. Saharas had also disclosed that the issue was made on a private placement basis and that OFCDs would be offered also to such persons to whom IM would be circulated. But the fact remains that it was circulated to more than three crore people inviting them to subscribe. The same was circulated through ten lakh agents and more than 2900 branch offices and Saharas had a capital base of only 10 lakhs with no other assets or reserves and was a loss making company and had collected nearly 27,000 crores by way of private placement through unsecured OFCDs redeemable/convertible after 48/60/120 months. Fact finding authorities repeatedly asked for information regarding the names, addresses of investors in OFCDs and the amounts subscribed by them. The appellant claimed that it had furnished to SEBI a separate CD giving the details of names of investors, the amount invested etc. along with the password and keys, along with its letter dated 19.4.2011 which, according to the appellant, was never opened or checked.

SEBI, has been vested with the powers of a Civil Court under CPC, as per sub-section (3) of section 11 of the SEBI Act. Under Section 11C, the Board has also been vested with the powers to order investigation to examine whether any person associated with securities market has violated any provision of the Act or the rules or the regulations made or direction issued by the Board. [Para 50]

Money collected by Saharas would amount to collection of money by way of issue of securities to public

Saharas, along with additional documents, filed before the Supreme Court, gave certain details of the persons who have invested. Documents produced before the Supreme Court and before the fact finding authorities do not show the relationship Sahara Group had with the investors. Claim of Saharas was that the investors were their friends, associated group companies, workers/employees and other individuals who were associated/affiliated or connected with Sahara Group. Saharas, in the bonds, sought for a declaration from the applicants that they had been associated with Sahara Group.

No details had been furnished to show what types of association the investors had with Sahara Group. Bonds also required to name an introducer, whose job evidently was to introduce the company to the prospective investor. If the offer was made to those persons related or associated with Sahara Group, there was no necessity of an introducer and an introduction. Burden of proof is entirely on Saharas to show that the investors are/were their employees/ workers or associated with them in any other capacity which they have not discharged.

Fact finding authorities have clearly held that Saharas had not discharged their burden which is purely a question of fact. Facts are elaborately discussed by SEBI (WTM) and SAT, hence those factual details are not to be discussed. No perversity or illegality is found in those findings which call for interference by the Supreme Court sitting under Section 15Z of the SEBI Act. Therefore, the Tribunal is to be fully concurred with that the money collected by Saharas through their RHPs dated 13.3.2008 and 6.10.2009,through the OFCDs, were from the public at large and the same would amount to collection of money by way of issue of securities to the public, a finding which calls for no interference by the Supreme Court sitting under Section 15Z of the SEBI Act. [Para 51]

HEADNOTE: Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company’s affairs in other cases - Petitioner, which had given huge loans to respondent- companies, sought for investigation under section 237(b) by Central Government into affairs of respondent-companies and their promoter-directors for fraudulently and unlawfully making wrongful gain and having committed misfeasance, thereby causing pecuniary losses to petitioner - Siphoning-off of huge amount by respondents through 250 front companies in fraudulent manner was indicated by income-tax authorities also - Whether since without investigation under section 237(b), it was not possible to discover true and correct facts and modus operandi adopted by respondents in cheating petitioner and siphoning-off of public money, enquiry under section 237(b) was to be ordered and Central Government was to be directed to appoint inspectors for enquiry - Held, yes

FACT: The total loan given by the financial institutions to the respondent was Rs. 45 billion and stake of the petitioner (IFCI) was Rs. 17 billion. In its petitions under section 237(b), the petitioner alleged that respondents had siphoned-off loan amounts in fraudulent manner through 250 front companies as informed by the Income-tax authorities; that it had also taken proceedings against respondents before Debts Recovery Tribunal and that the BIFR had rejected the reference filed before it by the respondents. Since huge amounts of public money were involved, the petitioner had no powers of access, search or seizure into the records of the company and, therefore, prayed for investigation under section 237(b), independent of the CBI inquiry in which charge-sheet had already been filed before the Special Judge.

The respondents, on the other hand, submitted that the company had suffered huge losses due to bad market conditions; and that since the source of filing the instant petitions was based on the information provided by the income-tax authorities and a settlement application filed under section 245C(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 was still pending, the petitions were not maintainable. According to the respondents, the petition was not maintainable on the sole ground that the respondents were not managing the day-to-day affairs of respondent No. 1-company and the management of the company had been taken over by the petitioner who had appointed persons of its own choice.

HELD: The petitioner had submitted that the huge public money had been siphoned off by the respondents and that could not be visible to the naked eye. Therefore, there were sufficient grounds to order an investigation under section 237(b). The siphoning-off of the huge amount by 250 front companies in fraudulent manner had been indicated by the income-tax authorities also. The petitioner had also submitted that the new management came much after the loan amounts had been siphoned off. The investigation conducted by the CBI was for trying the accused persons for criminal conspiracy and cheating as criminal offences. Without investigation under section 237(b), it was not possible to discover true and correct facts and modus operandi adopted by the respondents in cheating the petitioner and siphoning-off of the public money. [Para 11]

Therefore, the petition was allowed and an enquiry under section 237(b) was to be ordered with direction to the Central Government to appoint inspectors for the enquiry and take appropriate action on the enquiry report. [Para 12]

Section 433 read with  section 443 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Circumstances in which company may be wound up - Petitioner challenged winding up order on ground that company was not given opportunity of hearing and as such order was in breach of principles of natural justice - Whether where company judge had painstaking and studiously gone into whole financial aspects through a questionnaire and information regarding relevant transactions was also sought and affidavits were filed showing company's financial position, order of company judge for winding up could not be challenged on ground of non-hearing of company - Held, yes - Whether Court has ample powers to recommend investigation and give directions for filing first information report with regard to any apparent fraud by company and those in-charge of company - Held, yes

HEADNOTE: Section 210 of the Companies Act, 2013/Section 235 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation - Into affairs of company - Whether provisions of 1956 Act and 2013 Act though, do not prohibit investigation to be initiated where company has passed a special resolution for voluntary winding up or where other proceeding for winding of a company are pending before Tribunal, however, same may not applicable in case of company-in-liquidation, inasmuch as winding up order of company-in-liquidation is passed much prior to report of Official Liquidator filed before Court seeking investigation by SFIO - Held, yes [Para 38]COMPANY LAW : Provisions of 1956 Act and 2013 Act though do not prohibit investigation to be initiated where company has passed a special resolution for voluntary winding up or where other proceeding for winding of a company are pending before Tribunal, however, same may not applicable in case of company-in-liquidation, inasmuch as winding up order of company-in-liquidation is passed much prior to report of Official Liquidator filed before Court seeking investigation by SFIO  COMPANY LAW : Where there was no material in Official Liquidator's report to demonstrate that there was any intention of Ex-Director of campany-in-liquidation to defraud creditors, members or any other person or that management of company-in-liquidation was guilty of fraud and misfeasance or other misconduct towards company or towards any of its members, referring matter to SFIO was uncalled for

Section 210 of the Companies Act, 2013/Section 235 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation - Into affairs of company - Respondent company was ordered to be wound up and Official Liquidator (OL) took charge of assets and affairs of company - OL filed an application seeking an order for conducting an investigation into affairs of company-in-liquidation by SFIO alleging web of intrigue employed by company in-Liquidation and other group companies in defrauding investors and diversion of funds of company - It was also alleged that balance sheets and details of group companies were not furnished by ex-directors despite being asked to do so - Further, investigation was required into diversion of funds of company-in-liquidation for which expertise was not available with Official Liquidator - Said application was allowed by Writ Court - It was noted that balance sheet, other books of account and documents of Company-in-Liquidation were in possession of OL - All properties and effects of companies were deemed to be in custody of Court/Tribunal from date of order for winding up of company - Further, there was no evidence of any fraud conducted by Company or its ex-director that would merit referring matter to SFIO - As a matter of fact, allegation against company-in-liquidation regarding a web of intrigue employed by company could have been substantiated by specific references to entries made in balance sheet and other books of account of company-in-liquidation, which had not been done - To insinuate that office of OL did not have capacity or ability to detect diversion of funds, was not acceptable given fact that a panel of chartered accountant was admittedly available to assist OL in discharge of its duties - Whether under facts and circumstances of case, instant application to recall order by writ Court directing SFIO to commence investigation was to be allowed - Held, yes [Para 47]

Section 210 empowers the Central Government to investigate into the affairs of a company/(companies), if it is of the opinion that such investigation is necessary for the reasons mentioned therein, including public interest. For the purpose of the said provision, the Central Government may appoint one or more persons as inspectors to investigate into the affairs of the company and to report thereon in such manner as the Central Government may direct. The SFIO has been established under section 211 of the Companies Act, 2013, which has jurisdiction to investigate into the company/(companies), where the Central Government is of the opinion that it is necessary to investigate into the affairs of a company by the SFIO for different reasons, including the public interest. Where any case has been assigned by the Central Government to the SFIO for investigation under the Act, no other investigating agency of the Central Government or any State Government can proceed with investigation in such case in respect of any offence under the Companies Act and other cases before such agency are required to transfer the relevant documents and records in respect of such offences under the Companies Act to the SFIO. Sub-section (8) of section 211 empowers certain Officers of the SFIO to arrest any person, if on the basis of material in his possession there is reason to believe, which is to be recorded in writing, that any person has been guilty of any offence punishable under sub-section (6) of section 212. [Para 30]

Investigation into company's affairs in other cases can also be done under section 213 on an application made by the eligible members as mentioned in clause (a) of section 213 or on an application made by any other person or otherwise, if it is satisfied that there are circumstances suggesting that the business of the company etc. has been conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members etc. as mentioned in clause (b) of section 213. [Para 31]

From section 213, it is clear that the Tribunal on an application made to it or 'otherwise', if satisfied that there are circumstances suggesting that the business of the company is being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members etc. as mentioned in clause (b) of section 213, after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the parties, direct the Central Government to investigate. [Para 32]

From section 221, it is clear that the Tribunal has power to direct that the transfer, removal or disposal of funds, assets, or properties of the company shall not take place during such period not exceeding three years'. In case of any removal, transfer or disposal of funds, assets, or properties of the company in contravention of the order of the Tribunal under sub-section (1) of section 221, the company is punishable with fine and imprisonment as prescribed under sub-section (2) of section 221. [Para 34]

In the instant case, the Central Government by letter dated 17-2-2018 has directed the SFIO to investigate into the affairs of the respondent company, among other 114 entities. The investigation is currently undergoing and as such, as on date, being satisfied if so required, it is always open to the Central Government to file application under section 241(2), read with section 242 before the Tribunal. [Para 37]

In the interest of regulating the conduct of the company's affairs the interim order cannot be restrictive to any particular or individual person, including the company/companies, existing or erstwhile Officers and employees of the companies if investigation for alleged fraud is pending. [Para 38]

For the purpose of passing interim order, the Tribunal cannot fix the personal liability of delinquent Directors or Managers or Officers or other employees in absence of any specific evidence. Therefore, during the process of investigation and pendency of an application under section 241(2), read with section 242 and in view of powers conferred under section 221, the Tribunal is not only empowered to pass appropriate interim order against the company but also against any person or individual, including the order to desist. [Para 39]

Chapter XVI relates to 'Prevention of Oppression and Mismanagement'. An application to the Tribunal for relief in cases of oppression, etc. can be made by any eligible member(s) of the company under sub-section (1) of section 241 of the Companies Act, 2013, who complains about the oppression and mismanagement as stipulated in clauses (a) & (b) of sub-section (1). [Para 40]

On the other hand, the Central Government, if it is of the opinion that the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interest, it may itself apply to the Tribunal under sub-section (2) of section 241 for an order under Chapter XVI of the Companies Act, 2013. [Para 41]

HEADNOTE: Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company's affairs - Whether in view of power vested with Company Law Board to order investigation in appropriate circumstances under section 237(b), petitioner could approach CLB and Company Court has no reason for exercising its discretionary power to direct such investigation - Held, yes

FACT: The petitioner, a contributory of the respondent company, in a petition filed under section 237(a)(ii) sought a declaration that the company's affairs were such that they required investigation by an Inspector appointed by the Central Government in that regard, as the Company was not maintaining proper accounts and was doing several business activities without obtaining statutory sanction from the Central Government as enjoined by law.

HELD: Of course, the company court has got power which it can exercise in terms of section 237(a)(ii) but section 237 (b) empowers the CLB, if there are circumstances necessitating investigation, to order accordingly. This power has been granted to the CLB, in terms of amendment effected in the Act in 1988. When the power is conferred on the CLB, it was incumbent for the petitioner to approach that statutory Board which should examine and do justice, as the circumstances demanded In such circumstances, there was no reason for exercising the discretionary power vested in this Company Court to direct such investigation or declare that it needed investigation by the Central Government. Accordingly, the company petition was dismissed without prejudice to the right of the petitioner to move the CLB in terms of section 237 (b).

HEADNOTE: Section 388B, read with sections 397, 398 and 403, of the Companies Act, 1956 - Managerial Personnel - Reference to Company Law Board - CLB had suspended board of directors of respondent-company by its order dated 9-1-2009 and had authorized Central Government to constitute a fresh board - Central Government with a view to safeguard interests of company, its stakeholders and public at large, filed instant application, ex parte seeking interim reliefs viz.; (i) to implead ‘V’, being Chief Finance Officer of company as respondent No. 13; (ii) to direct concerned respondents to disclose bank accounts and both movable and immovable assets owned by them; and (iii) to restrain them from alienating, mortgaging, creating charge or lien or interest in those properties - Whether since Chief Finance Officer of company was legally and directly interested in respect of subject major controversies, he was to be arrayed as respondent to instant proceedings - Held, yes - Whether since object was to preserve status quo while disputes were being adjudicated, there existed a strong prima facie case and balance of convenience in favour of grant of ex parte restraint order, as urged by Central Government, to preserve public interest at large - Held, yes

FACT: The CLB had suspended the board of directors of the respondent-company by order dated 9-1-2009 and had authorized the Central Government to constitute a fresh board of the company. The Central Government had appointed six nominee directors on the board. In the meanwhile, the Central Government with a view to safeguard the interests of the company, its stakeholders and the public at large, filed instant application, ex parte seeking interim reliefs viz.; (i ) to implead ‘V’, being Chief Finance Officer as respondent No. 13; (ii) to direct the concerned respondents to disclose the bank accounts and both movable and immovable assets owned by them; and (iii) to restrain them from alienating, mortgaging, creating charge or lien or interest in those properties. In support, of the application, it was submitted that the Central Government had ordered investigation into the affairs of the company on consideration of the report of the RoC and that the Central Government might not be able to enforce the ultimate relief which might be granted under section 542, unless the concerned respondents were restrained from alienating any of their assets, thereby protecting the interests of the company and the stake-holders.

HEADNOTE: Section 212, read with sections 210 and 206, of the Companies Act, 2013 - Serious Fraud Investigation Office - Investigation by - 'TCSPL' was a real estate company, which was developing a project named 'Greenopolis' - Petitioner/homebuyer had purchased a plot in said project - Petitioner filed a writ petition alleging that promoters and directors of 'TCSPL', had misappropriated and siphoned off funds collected from innocent homebuyers, including petitioner, into various shell/sister concerns - Petitioner sought directions to Central Government and ROC to take cognizance, initiation and conduction of appropriate inquiries and investigation against management of 'TCSPL', as also any other sister/shell companies in accordance with law - Writ Court allowed said petition - Whether since ‘Greenopolis project’ had been abandoned by ex-promoters and directors after siphoning of funds generated directly through ‘TCSPL’ and petitioner as well as those who were similarly placed investors/claimants/homebuyers were victims at their hands, application moved by ex-promoters for recalling of order was to be dismissed - Held, yes - Whether further since, investigation by RoC was progressing at a snail's pace qua ‘TCSPL’ and its ex-promoters & directors, marked by tardiness and a lack of urgency, which was unacceptable in law and prejudicial to interests of homebuyers, Central Government was thus, hereby directed that investigation be conducted into affairs of ‘TCSPL’ besides its Ex-Promoters and Directors/Management through SFIO to unearth manner in which funds generated from petitioner and other homebuyers had been siphoned off to detriment of its secured and unsecured creditors including homebuyers - Held, yes [Para 68, 74, 75, 76 and 77]

FACT: ■

The petitioner, who was a homebuyer, claimed to have purchased a plot from ‘TCSPL’, in a real estate project named ‘Greenopolis’, which was envisioned to be developed in Gurugram, Haryana. Petitioner filed writ petition against TCSPL and its Ex-promoters / directors / management, accusing them of allegedly siphoning off approximately Rs. 1,664 crores collected from innocent homebuyers into its various shell/sister concerns. This misappropriation led to TCSPL being subjected to proceedings under the IBC before the NCLT with nearly 536 investors/claimants/homebuyers lodging their claims before the IRP.

■

While the matter was pending before the NCLT, three reports were submitted by the IRP and the Status Report, which, inter alia demonstrated as to how and in what manner the Ex promoters/directors/management of TCSPL had been siphoning off the funds.

■

The petitioner vide said petition was seeking invoking the extraordinary jurisdiction of Writ Court under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution of India, 1950, seeking certain directions against Registrar of Companies (RoC) and Union of India (UoI) through the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for taking cognizance, initiation and conduction of appropriate inquiries and investigation against the management of TCSPL, as well as its shell/sister group of companies, for alleged action of manipulation of records and siphoning of funds to shell/sister companies based in Kolkata and elsewhere. Additionally, the petitioner sought reliefs in the nature of freezing the assets of such unscrupulous companies and their promoters/directors to safeguard the legal rights of the investors/claimants/homebuyers like the petitioner.

■

This, to safeguard the interest of the petitioner, as well as other similarly placed investors/claimants /homebuyers, RoC and UoI, were conjointly directed to initiate action and ensure step-wise compliance in terms of Section 206 to 210 of the Companies Act, 2013 and other analogous provisions in Chapter XIV of the Companies Act, 2013, and thereby inspect the affairs of TCSPL and the related.

■

During the course of proceedings before Writ Court, an application was moved on behalf of the ACE Group, a renowned Real Estate Developer in Delhi and NCR for impleadment, which was allowed. Subsequently, ACE Group moved an application for the recall of the order. Prior to this, TCSPL had also moved an application to recall / modification of order.

■

The ACE Group submitted that although the order was directed at RoC and UoI to inspect the affairs of the TCSPL, they were directly affected, as the IRP had endeavoured to reclaim or repossess certain properties belonging to them, which have no nexus or connection with the TCSPL.

■

The second petitioner together with his relatives and friends at the behest of the second respondent’s parents, had invested certain amount towards share capital of the respondent-company. Further, he became director of the company, with understanding that the second petitioner would not participate in the day-to-day affairs of the company on account of his critical physical condition. Accordingly, the second petitioner had kept with the second respondent signed blank cheques in advance for facilitating issuance of cheques in favour of the creditors or suppliers of the company. Similarly, the second petitioner had executed bank loan as well as security documents giving his personal guarantee and collateral security of his immovable property in favour of the respondent Nos. 6 and 7 for the credit facilities extended by them in favour of the company. However, later it transpired that the second respondent failed to conduct the affairs of the company on sound business principles and corporate practices, without settling the dues of creditors but embezzled substantial amounts of the company and deliberately committed acts of fraud and misfeasance with mala fide intentions, resulting in removal of the statutory records, furnitures, computer systems and other movable assets of the company and closure of the factory as well as the corporate office premises without any intimation to the staff members, workers and other members, including the petitioners, and absconded himself. The second petitioner had to face several of civil and criminal proceedings at the hands of the financial institutions, suppliers and other creditors on account of the fraudulent conduct of the second respondent in collusion with the officials of the respondent Nos. 6, 7 and 9. Therefore, the petitioner filed the instant petition under sections 235, 237, 397 and 398 read with sections 402 and 403 for appointment of one or more competent persons as inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company.

Section 235 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of affairs of a company - Whether before ordering appointment of inspectors for investigating into affairs of a company, there must be material to prove prima facie that certain irregularities are committed or fraud has been played on company by its directors; such a decision has to be taken subject to satisfaction on material placed and not otherwise - Held, yes - Whether where material placed on record prima facie showed that fraud had been played by managing director as well as other directors not only to get benefit to themselves but also causing loss to company in question, which was evident from findings recorded by management auditor's report as well as statutory auditor's report, CLB was justified in rejecting appellant's application seeking for an order of investigation into affair of company - Held, no- Whether therefore, order of CLB was liable to be set aside and application of appellant was to be allowed - Held, yes

Under section 235(2) a power is given to the CLB in case where, Inter alia, an application is received from not less than 200 members, or members holding not less than one-tenth of the total voting power in a company, to declare, after giving the parties an opportunity of being heard, that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated by an Inspector or Inspectors. On such a declaration being made, the Central Government shall appoint one or more competent persons as inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company and to report thereon.

The power, therefore, to appoint Inspector to investigate the affairs of a company has to be exercised by the Central Government after a proper preliminary scrutiny by the Registrar or by the CLB as the case may be. It cannot be instituted simply on the basis of allegations made by one shareholder. Under section 237, there is a further power given to the Central Government to appoint Inspectors to investigate the affairs of a company if the company, by a special resolution, or the Court, by order declares that such investigation is necessary. Similarly, this may be done if in the opinion of the CLB there are circumstances suggesting that the business of the company is being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members or any other person or otherwise for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose or in a manner oppressive of any of its members or that the company was formed for any fraudulent or unlawful purpose. The CLB may also come to a conclusion that there are circumstances suggesting that the persons concerned in the formation of the company or management of its affairs have been guilty of fraud, misfeasance or other misconduct towards the company or towards any of its members; or that the members of the company have not been given all the information with respect to its affairs which they might reasonably expect. In these circumstances, on the basis of the opinion so framed by the CLB, the Central Government may order an investigation.

In the instant case no attempt had been made by the respondent to get the affairs of the company investigated in the manner provided under the Act. Neither the Central Government nor the CLB had been moved by the respondent in accordance with law for this purpose. Instead of moving the authorities prescribed under the Act the first respondent had chosen to resort to the writ jurisdiction of the High Court for a direction to have the affairs of the company investigated by the CBI.

The Single Judge before whom the present writ petition came up for hearing very rightly held that the Companies Act provides a forum to consider the grievances made out by the first respondent in the writ petition. When such a forum, statutorily constituted, exists, it is but appropriate that resort to article 226 should be discouraged There is an efficacious alternative remedy available under the statute. In fact under the Companies Act, a more satisfactory solution is available. The Single Judge was right in pointing out that some of the shareholders had initiated proceedings before the CLB. The only grievance of the petitioner in the writ petition was that no orders had been passed thereon. The Single Judge had rightly held that such a grievance could not constitute a ground for invoking the jurisdiction of the High Court under article 226.

Further no public interest was involved in disputes of the kind referred to in the writ petition. They basically dealt with mismanagement of the affairs of the company and oppression of the minority shareholders. The company was only a deemed public limited company. Its shareholding was very closely held The only other factor referred to in the writ petition to invoke the doctrine of so-called public interest, was the fact that the company had borrowed moneys from public institutions. This was no ground for not availing of the statutory remedies provided under the Act before the appropriate statutory forums which are designed for this very purpose.

Therefore, the order of the Single Judge could not be interfered with. The judgment of the Division Bench was set aside.

The petitioner had submitted that the huge public money had been siphoned off by the respondents and that could not be visible to the naked eye. Therefore, there were sufficient grounds to order an investigation under section 237(b). The siphoning-off of the huge amount by 250 front companies in fraudulent manner had been indicated by the income-tax authorities also. The petitioner had also submitted that the new management came much after the loan amounts had been siphoned off. The investigation conducted by the CBI was for trying the accused persons for criminal conspiracy and cheating as criminal offences. Without investigation under section 237(b), it was not possible to discover true and correct facts and modus operandi adopted by the respondents in cheating the petitioner and siphoning-off of the public money. [Para 11]

Therefore, the petition was allowed and an enquiry under section 237(b) was to be ordered with direction to the Central Government to appoint inspectors for the enquiry and take appropriate action on the enquiry report. [Para 12]

'SEBI', in exercise of its power under sections 11(1), 11B and 11(4) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 read with Regulation 65 of the SEBI (Collective Investment Schemes) Regulations, 1999 passed the impugned order.

By the impugned order, SEBI found that the company was running a collective scheme without necessary approvals and registration with SEBI. Accordingly, SEBI had asked the company and its directors not to collect any more money from investors including under the existing schemes with immediate effect and had also restrained them from launching any new schemes, disposal or alienation of any properties and diversion of funds.

Hence, the petitioners by way of this petition have sought for interim reliefs.

Section 213, read with section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013/ Section 237, read with section 394 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of Company's affairs - Appellant filed an application for holding meeting of shareholders for approval of scheme of amalgamation - Single Judge finding some irregularities directed investigation by various agencies - Appellant filed appeal contending that Single Judge was carrying on roving enquiry and he should either allow or dismiss its application - Whether Single Judge was competent to issue direction under section 237(a)(ii) and, therefore, Single Judge was justified in carrying on investigation - Held, yes - Whether however, it was for Central Government to decide which authority would investigate and, therefore, it was a fit and proper case for Central Government to consider as to whether an investigation should be carried out by appropriate agency having authority in law followed by action that would be permitted in law - Held, yes - Whether appellant could not be permitted to proceed with proposed scheme of amalgamation and, therefore, application for convening meeting of shareholders was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 12  13]CL : Single Judge while sanctioning scheme of amalgamation is competent to issue direction under section 237(a)(ii) and then it is for Central Govt. to decide which authority would investigate
CL: Where circumstances suggested that business of company was being conducted with intend to defraud petitioner and its members, investigation into affairs of respondent No. 1 was to be ordered

HEADNOTE: Section 456 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Official Liquidator - Custody of company's property - Official Liquidator of company under liquidation put under seal two godowns claimed as belonging to applicant trust on basis of documentry evidence and only given on rent for a period to company under liquidation - However, in a writ, Division Bench had directed Police Officials to investigate properties of certain persons including that of applicant to find out as to whether directors of company siphoned off company's property - Whether, it would be proper to order police to complete investigation within four weeks and if same would not be complied with, impugned properties should be handed over to applicant - Held, yes

FACT: The Official Liquidator, appointed for liquidation of the company put his seal on the godown which the applicant trust claimed as belonging to it. The applicant submitted that they had purchased these godowns in the year 1984 while company was incorporated only in 1993. The applicant had only allowed the company to use the said premises for a period and subsequently the company vacated the premises and handed over same to the applicant. It was, therefore, contended that since the applicant trust was the owner of the premises, the seal was required to be removed. However, in a separate writ petition, the Division Bench in relevant matter had directed the Dy. Commissioner of Police to find out whether the properties belonging to respondent company were siphoned off by its director and, therefore, directed him to verify and attach the properties belonging to the company.

HELD: In view of the documentary evidence, prima facie, the property did not belong to the company in liquidation as the applicants based on the documentry evidence had been able to establish that the property belonged to the trust. Hence, the Official Liquidator should communicate to the Deputy Commissioner of Police, in charge investigating the matter who should investigate the same and if need be, move the Division Bench for suitable orders including directions in terms of para 10(j ) of the order of the Division Bench.

If no directions were taken within the said period of four weeks by the Dy. Commissioner of Police in charge of investigation, the Official Liquidator should remove the seal and handover possession of the premises to the applicant herein and the books of account and documents if any in the premises would be taken in custody by the Dy. Commissioner of Police investigating into the matter with liberty to the Official Liquidator to examine the said documents as and when required.

F.E. Devitre, J.P. Sen and Mrs. U.S. Fadia for the Applicant. B.N. Vaishnava for the Company. S.C. Gupta, Dy. Official Liquidator.

upheld - Held, yes

Section 237, read with section 397/398, of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company affairs in other cases - Whether power of CLB under section 237(b) is administrative in nature which can be exercised even suo motu by CLB - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, CLB can in a petition under section 397/398 appoint an auditor to conduct an investigative audit under section 237(b) - Held, yes FACT: The company-in-question was incorporated in 1979 by six brothers. They were the original subscribers to the memorandum of association of the company. Two more private companies and four partnership firms were thereafter floated by the six brothers. Only one brother was surviving and rest of five were dead. Legal heirs of six brothers were directors, shareholders/members of the company. Under a Housing Board Scheme, two plots earmarked for cinema theatre and petrol Bunk, were allotted to the company. The company, accordingly, constructed a theatre complex and a petrol bunk on the respective plots. In the year 2002, appellants 1 and 2 and respondent 7 executed a registered lease deed in respect of the plot on which theatre complex was constructed in favour of son of appellant 1 for a period of 10 years on monthly rent of Rs. 50,000; similarly land on which petrol bunk was constructed was sold by them to appellant 1 and his wife by a sale deed for a sum of Rs. 60 lakhs. However, the possession of the petrol bunk could not be taken, on account of the refusal of the tenant occupying the same, to vacate.

One of the companies promoted by the six brothers, viz , Annai Flour Mills had availed a loan from Vysa bank. Apart from the first charge created on the movables of the borrower company in favour of the bank, the company-in-question also gave a corporate guarantee in favour of the said bank, in addition to mortgaging the theatre complex to the bank. The borrower company, Annai Flour Mills committed default and the bank initiated recovery proceedings under the Recovery of Debts Due to Bank and Financial Institutions Act, 1993. The bank also sought the appointment of a receiver to collect the income from the theatre complex. Accordingly, the Debt Recovery Tribunal appointed a retired justice as receiver.

The receiver so appointed filed reports before the DRT pointing out certain facts with regard to the management of the company. The respondents No. 1 to 5 on the basis of said facts, alleged that those facts in the reports established oppression and mismanagement on the part of management of the company. Consequently, respondents 1 to 5 who were members/shareholders of company moved instant company petition under sections 397, 398,402 and 403 read with sections 235 and 237 and Schedule XI, seeking various reliefs. The acts of oppression and mismanagement complained of by respondents 1 to 5 were (1) the leasing out of the theatre complex to the son of the first appellant for a rent far below the market value (2) the sale of the petrol bunk in favour of the first appellant and his wife for a consideration of Rs. 60 lakh (3) the receipt of Rs. 99,000 per month by the first appellant, as interest on the sale consideration fixed for the petrol bunk, on the ground that the possession of the property could not be taken (4) the appropriation of the rent (licence fee), paid by a cellular company for the tower installed in the terrace of the theatre complex building, by the son of the first appellant (5) the salary drawn unauthorizedly by the first appellant, claiming to be the managing director and (6) the failure to conduct the annual general meetings from the year 2001 and the failure to file the annual returns. After the appointment of the receiver by the DRT, the payment of Rs. 99,000 allegedly towards interest to the first appellant and his wife was stopped. Similarly, the receipt of the rent/licence fee by the son of the first appellant from the cellular company had also been stopped.

The respondents 1 to 5 further pointed out certain circumstances indicating mismanagement. According to them, the income of the company rose up to Rs. 4 crores immediately after the receiver took over, while it remained at Rs. 2 crores, when it was under the management of the appellants. The receiver also reported that the company had received Rs. 45.10 lakh as advance from the tenants of the shops, while the income-tax return filed by the appellants for the assessment year 2004-05 accounted only for a sum of Rs. 15 lakhs towards the advances, indicating that there was siphoning off of the funds.

The CLB considered each one of the acts of mismanagement and came to a prima facie conclusion that the business of the company had been conducted in a manner oppressive to the members of the company at the hands of persons in management. The CLB also came to the conclusion that the surplus income shown by the receiver prima facie supported the charge of mismanagement, requiring a detailed investigation by an independent agency. Accordingly, a Chartered-Accountant was authorized to carry out an investigative audit of the accounts of the company from 2000 to 2005. Aggrieved by the order of the CLB, instant appeal was preferred raising contentions.

HEADNOTE: Section 237(b) of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company's affairs - Whether power under section 237(b) is a discretionary power - Held, yes -Whether, when justifiable grounds exist, merely because communication from Department of Company Affairs to Secretary, CLB, was in form of letter without any proper affidavit and without any specific mention as to what action was prayed for, CLB should refuse to exercise jurisdiction under section 237(b) - Held, no - Whether investigation is to be ordered if a prima facie opinion is formed by CLB that business of company is being/has been conducted with intent to defraud creditors, members or any other persons or conduct of company is oppressive to any of its members or there is misfeasance or misconduct on part of management in carrying on affairs of company - Held, yes - Whether, where report filed by Regional Director in Department of Company Affairs under section 209A on complaints made by Employees' Union alleging mismanagement of affairs of company, established mismanagement of funds of company, further enquiry by ROC had to be ordered - Held, yes

Section 235 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of Company's affairs -Whether section 235 can be invoked only on a report made by Registrar of Companies under section 234(6) - Held, yes - Whether where report was made by Joint Director in office of Regional Director, facility of reference under section 237(b) was correctly availed of - Held, yes

FACT: On a complaint from Workers' Union of the company, Joint Director of the office of Regional Director of Companies made enquiries under section 209A. The report revealed that (i) the company had stopped feeding its factories with sufficient quantity of raw materials forcing the workmen to idle away most of the time which resulted the production coming to stand-still; (ii) there was shortage of working capital due to mismanagement of funds resulting in loss to the tune of Rs. 659 lakhs and company could not consequently declare dividend; (iii) funds raised by floating debentures for a specific project had been diverted for other uses shelving the project; (iv) a number of loans had been advanced to totally unrelated companies and the management did not recover the same though the company was in critical financial crisis and due to this company could not procure even the raw materials, an export order could not be executed and further the company lost another foreign order worth 20 crores; (v) a sum of Rs. 77.32 lakhs was spent on construction of a temple as against the approved amount of Rs. 50 lakhs; (vi) quantity of raw material per ton cable manufactured was the highest in the year in question compared to previous year for which no plausible explanation was forthcoming; and (vii) the company had unnecessarily paid commission of Rs. 5.08 lakhs to one 'S' for procuring orders from a company with which it had regular business.

Based on this report, the Central Government filed a reference application under section 237(b) in the form of a letter, without proper affidavit and without any mention as to what action was prayed for, stating that in the absence of a report of ROC under section 234(6), the Government could not invoke its powers under section 235(1).

HELD: Though the communication from the Department of Company Affairs was in the form of a letter addressed to the Secretary, CLB without any proper affidavit and without any specific mention as to what action was prayed for, the facts as presented by the Department of Company Affairs were to be considered in exercise of power under section 237(b) since: (a) section 237(b) of the Act clothes the CLB with the suo motu power to form an opinion on consideration of circumstances presented before it;(b ) the CLB Regulations, 1991 have not specifically prescribed any procedure to be followed with regard to proceedings under section 237(b); and (c) the company was a public company and the interests of a large number of shareholders and employees were involved besides the creditors. If justifiable grounds existed CLB should not shy away from exercising jurisdiction under this section for technical reasons.

Investigation is to be ordered if a prima facie opinion is formed by the CLB that the business of the company is being/has been conducted with intent to defraud creditors, members or any other persons or the conduct of company is oppressive to any of its members or there is misfeasance or misconduct on the part of the management in carrying on the affairs of the company.

2009 filed a winding up petition before the High Court, against respondent No. 3 company. During the course of the winding up proceedings, the Single Judge of the High Court directed the respondent No. 3 to deposit a sum of Rs. 1.5 crore with the Registrar of the High Court. However, the said direction was not complied with, and, therefore, vide order of Single Judge of the High Court, the respondent No. 3 company went into liquidation. There were several other investors who too had invested in the project. Various complaints were filed against the respondent no. 3 company and its directors which resulted in an FIR being registered. Subsequently, the investigation thereon resulted in a charge sheet, wherein it was alleged that huge sums of money were diverted, defalcated and siphoned off from the corpus of respondent No. 3 company, which was meant to be utilized for the construction of the project.

It was alleged that respondent No. 3 company had, in fact, siphoned off the monies of investors to four intermediate companies who, in turn, further transferred the money to the consortium of six land owning companies. These six land-owning companies were, allegedly, related party companies of respondent No. 3. It was further alleged that these six related party companies had then purchased the subject land for the Project Mall extending to area admesuring to 115 acres. A development and management agreement was entered into between the appellant herein and a consortium of six land-owning companies for exclusive developmental rights over 11 properties extending to 115 acres of land in a real estate project launched by the consortium of six companies for a consideration of Rs. 43 crores. Vide interim orders, the Single Judge of the High Court restrained the six companies from transferring, selling or alienating the properties till further orders.

Aggrieved by the same, the appellant as well as respondent No. 4 preferred applications for vacation of the aforesaid interim orders which were allowed by the Single Judge

The Division Bench of the Delhi High Court, vide the impugned judgment and order, allowed the appeal, thereby restraining once again the transfer, selling or alienation of the properties purchased by the consortium of six companies.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

HELD: A perusal of the order of the Single Judge of the High Court would reveal that while vacating the interim injunction/orders, it had directed the Official Liquidator to carry out an audit of the books of account of the respondent No. 3 company and look into the allegations. The Single Judge of the High Court had also observed that, in case anything contrary is discovered in the course of the audit, the Official Liquidator was free to file an appropriate application with regard to the properties which were subject matter of Company Petition No. 482 of 2009. [Para 13]

It is contended on behalf of the appellant and the respondent No. 4 that the claim of the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 is hardly of a few crores. [Para 15]

While passing an order of injunction, the Courts are required to be guided by the principles of prima facie case, balance of convenience and irreparable injury. Assuming for a moment that the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 along with the other claimants have a claim of around Rs. 31 crores, the entire project in an area of 115 acres cannot be stalled. If the Division Bench of the High Court found that, there was a prima facie case in favour of the respondent Nos. 1 and 2, they could have passed an appropriate order to protect the interests of the said respondents rather than stalling the entire project. [Para 17]

Therefore, a blanket order directing maintenance of status quo in respect of the all 11 properties admeasuring 115 acres is not justified. If such an order is allowed to continue, it will cause irreparable injury to the appellant and the respondent No. 4 inasmuch as the entire development would be stalled. Insofar as the interests of the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 are concerned, the same can be protected by directing the appellant and the respondent No. 4 to file an undertaking that until further orders are passed in company petition for winding up, they shall not create any third party rights in respect of the subject properties. [Para 19]

In the result, appeal is partly allowed. The impugned judgment and order passed by the Division Bench of the High Court in Company Appeal is set aside. The appellant and the respondent No. 4 are directed to file an undertaking before this Court within four weeks from the date of this judgment that they shall not create any third party rights in respect of the properties. After the final audit report is submitted by the Auditor/Chartered Accountants appointed by the Single Judge, the Single Judge of the High Court would pass final orders with regard to the properties in respect of which the undertaking is to be given by the appellant and the respondent No. 4.

The respondent submitted that whatever shares had been purchased by those companies, which formed part of the ‘K’, had been purchased through stock exchange or public issue or between shareholders of the company in the normal course of business. There were no direct transactions by the company and the ‘K’ for dealing with those shares. The respondent had also forwarded copies of index of folios of shares which had been purchased by various parties from time-to-time. It was difficult to make out any proposition out of those huge papers submitted by the respondent. [Para 12]

The irregularities/violations of the provisions of the Act had already been taken care of by the Registrar of Companies, but some revealing propositions came out from the documents and averments of the case. The company was incorporated as early as in 1982 and since then, the authorized share capital was Rs. 5 lakhs and paid up capital was Rs. 15,000 as on 13-12-1999; but huge investments in share capital had been made within a short spell of 3 to 4 months. It was also admitted position that the company made investment of Rs. 83,41,00,000 in the shares of the certain companies when the main object of the company was not to enter the business in share market. The lead to value of huge investment went down after stock scam took place in March, 2001. It was also interesting to note that within a spell of two months, the authorized capital was raised first from Rs. 50,000 to Rs. 11 crores and thereafter to Rs. 12 crores. The genesis and origin of this huge funds invested by the respondent-company in share market when it was not in the business, needed to be probed into. It was difficult to find from the documents placed on record as to whether there was any relationship in the transactions with the ‘KP’ group of companies or those were the normal transactions of the business. That could only be found out by investigating the matter in depth. [Para 13]

In the light of the above discussion, the petition was to be allowed. Accordingly, the Central Government was to be directed to undertake the investigation of respondent-company under section 237 and take suitable action on the basis of the report when received. [Para 14]

Shamit Majumdar, Sanjay Agarwal and Sanjay Shorey for the Respondent.

HEADNOTE: Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company's affairs - Whether very fact that respondent company had not finalised the accounts from 1993-94 onwards and that no AGM had been held after 1993 in spite of fact that it was a listed company, was sufficient to order an investigation into affairs of company under section 237(b) - Held, yes - Whether Central Government should also appoint a director on board of company to effectively monitor conduct of affairs of company - Held, yes

FACT: The respondent, a listed company, in its efforts to mobilise funds from NRIs induced the petitioner to contribute towards its share capital. After mobilising funds, the respondent company completely neglected the petitioner by not sending annual reports, etc., which a shareholder is entitled to get. All attempts made by the petitioner to get information about the functioning of the company through SEBI, Bombay Stock Exchange, etc., having failed, the petitioner tried to get inspection done of the records of the company, which was also refused by the company. Only after persistent efforts, the petitioner could get balance sheets of the company for the year ended 31-3-1992 and 31-3-1993. The Department of Company Affairs had conducted an inspection of the records of the company which revealed several violations of the provisions of the Companies Act. A Chartered Accountant permitted to inspect the books of account and other records, made several observations revealing misutilisation of funds for personal benefits. On these facts the petitioner in its petition under section 397/398 alleged oppression and mismanage- ment in the affairs of the company and sought reliefs.

HELD: The petitioner had clearly brought out that the promoters of the company, after having mobilised enormous amount of about Rs. 7 crores, more particularly from NRIs, had not bothered to conduct the affairs of the company in accordance with the provisions of law and in a prudent manner. The petitioner having invested more than Rs. 50 lakhs, had been running from pillar to post to get some information on the functioning of the company without any success. The Regional Director, Dept. of Company Affairs had also in his report reported that the company had not filed balance sheets from 1994 onwards. Notwithstanding the various observations made by the Chartered Accountant who had inspected the books of account and the fact that the Regional Director had initiated prosecution against the company, the very fact that the company had not finalised its accounts from 1993-94 onwards and that no AGM had been held after 1993 in spite of the fact that it was a listed company to protect the interest of a large number of shareholders, suitable remedial action deserved to be taken especially when the respondents had not chosen to participate in the proceedings. While the petitioner had sought for appointment of an Administrator, there were sufficient prima facie materials to exercise powers under section 237(b ) to order an investigation into the affairs of the company. Accordingly, the Central Government was directed to carry out an investigation into the affairs of the company and take appropriate further action on receipt of the investigation report.

Further, in exercise of powers under section 402, the Central Government was also directed to appoint a suitable professional person as a director on the board of the company for a period of 3 years from the date of appointment to effectively monitor the conduct of affairs of the company.

K. Ravi and Vikas Dhawan for the Petitioner. Bhogubati Prasad for the Respondent.

Even if the first petitioner-Managing Director, including those connected with the offences, viz., past directors and promoters were sent to the prison, the question still remained whether the Court had done any justice to the depositors. Sentencing the offenders and committing them to the prison was one thing. Ensuring the return of deposits to the poor depositors who made deposits from every nook and corner of this country was an other thing. In the instant case, it was clear that the corporate character was employed by the first petitioner for the purpose of committing illegality and defrauding the others. In such an event, this Court, piercing the corporate veil, could look at the reality behind the corporate veil so as to pass appropriate orders to do substantial justice to the victims. The Managing Director not only incorporated the company but subsequently other companies were brought into effect and that too by the persons who were none other than the close relations and promoters of the first company. The Supreme Court treated all such companies as one entity belonging to one and controlled by one family. The Reserve Bank of India also submitted that the bank was taking steps to initiate prosecution proceedings and also for winding up of the company, as it was a confirmed case of non-refund of deposits. Dehors this submission, this Court also gave number of opportunities to the petitioner to refund the deposits as per their own schedule of payments. Even though the schedule of payment was changed twice on the request of the petitioner, yet there was not even a single case where the company deposited any amount in the account opened by the Advocate-Commissioners. Thus, it proved to be a clear case for winding up.

The fate of lakhs of defrauded depositors by the company was still uncertain. Their aspirations that goose would lay golden eggs for them proved to be costly dream - the goose was not even responding for laying normal eggs. Their sweat and blood invested in the company vanished and plunged them in miseries and frustration. Even the new Act introduced by the Government of Andhra Pradesh did not deal with non-banking companies who had already misused the deposits and it hadonly prospective effect. But the emotions and feelings of parties have no place in judicial proceedings. This Court was required to salvage the situation in accordance with law keeping in view the mandate of the Constitution. It spreads its arms of justice to identify and reach the injustice, and thereby remedy the cause. The efforts of this Court to save the depositors yielded microscopic results. But, at the same time, no offender should be allowed to gain an impression that courts lean towards them. The petitioner failed to respond to the opportunities granted by this Court. The endoscopy of the matter led to inevitable conclusion that physico- judicial therapy was not the cure, but the judicial surgery was the only solution.

Under these circumstances, in the wake of the details referred to above and in order to see that the companies did not defraud the innocent depositors, the writ petition was disposed of with the following directions :

(a )The State Government should constitute a separate cell in the office of the Director General of Police headed by an officer of the rank of Superintendent of Police and above for dealing with Non-Banking Financial Institutions who had already collected the amounts and failed to repay the deposits and which did not possess registration under the Reserve Bank of India Act. The cell should cause discreet enquiries in respect of all such institutions and take immediate action to seize the properties of the company and also the assets of the persons involved in the formation or administration of the company and also the persons who obtained illegal benefit out of the transactions or assets of the company to ensure that the payments were made to the depositors either in full or pro rata depending upon the circumstances of each case. The cell should initiate prosecution under various laws against all the offenders who were either directly or indirectly involved.

(b )In respect of the petitioner-company, the Government of Andhra Pradesh should order immediate investigation by the CBCID by an officer of the rank of Superintendent of Police and above into the irregularities traced out in this order apart from the complaints already made. The criminal prosecution should be launched under the provisions of Indian Penal Code, Reserve Bank of India Act and other laws against not only the Managing Director of the Company the first petitioner, but against all the promoters and also the past directors including other persons who were responsible for misuse of the funds of the company either directly or remotely. All the concerned governmental and non-governmental agencies should extend co-operation to the investigating team. The Depositors Association also shouldassist the investigating agency in this regard.

A complaint was registered against 'Birla Power' and its Directors for offence under sections 406, 420, 120B of IPC. After registration of FIR, an ECIR was recorded.

It was alleged that accused company 'Birla Power' and their group entities issued an advertisement to invite fixed deposits on an attractive interest. The accused in coalition with each other had accepted the amount of more than 260 crores from around 20,000 victims/investors in 'Birla Power', 'Birla Shlok', 'Zenith' and 'Birla Cotsyn' After maturity of the amount, the companies failed rather refused to return the amount deposited with it and accordingly an amount of 57.04 crores and Rs. 214 crores remains unpaid towards Fixed Deposit and ICD depositors.

During the course of Investigation, the statement of the complainant/investors were recorded.

The complainant apart from many invested their hard earned money but the amount deposited by them remained unpaid. Thus, they filed a complaint. The statement of other investors were also recorded. They made reference of 163 investors filed the complaint against 'Birla Power' and its Director. In the investigation, it was found that the money collected from the investors was siphoned off and laundered by transfer to other companies and mainly the entities of 'Birla Power'.

The statement of the accused were also recorded who submitted that the investment were invited to expand the business and to cover the shortage of capital. The deposits so received from the investors was transferred to the group of companies which includes 'Birla Surya' which alleged to have siphoned of the money thus, an offence of money laundering was found.

The respondent finding a case of money laundering sought to attach the properties to safeguard the interest of the investors during the pendency of the criminal case. They accordingly attached several properties of 'Birla Surya' to whom the money was transferred by 'Birla Power' and its Directors. It was to secure the proceeds of crime so transferred to 'Birla Surya'.

The attachment order was confirmed by the Adjudicating Authority finding a case of money laundering. It had been questioned by the appellant principally on three grounds.

According to the appellant the proceeding before the Adjudicating Authority was suffering from mis-joinder of parties. The appellant was not in possession of proceeds of crime and those who were in possession of the proceeds were not impleaded. Thus, the attachment of property becomes illegal. The investment received from different persons said to have been transferred to 'Birla Surya' was also not in possession of the proceeds of crime because 'Birla Surya' went in liquidation at the time of attachment. The said company was not in a possession and control over the proceeds of crime rather it was lying with the Official Liquidator who was appointed by the High Court in the petition for winding up of the company. The Official Liquidator was having the possession and control over the proceeds attached by the respondent. The official liquidator was not impleaded as defendant while impleading appellants having no control and possession of the proceeds. Thus, the appeal was suffering from mis-joinders of the parties. Yet, the provisional attachment order was confirmed without a notice to the Official Liquidator.

The second issue is regarding non-compliance of section 8(1). It submited that the notice under section 8 was to be given to a person who claims the possession and the control of the property. He was required to be afforded an opportunity of hearing. It was stated that the properties attached was under the control of Official Liquidator. The Adjudicating Authority passed the impugned order without an opportunity of hearing, to the Official Liquidator. Thus, also, the impugned order deserves to be set aside.

It was also submitted that section 8(2) and (3) of Act of 2002 have not been complied rather Adjudicating Authority recorded finding going beyond its power under those provisions. The Adjudicating Authority had no power to hold that a predicate offence had been committed by the defendants. In fact, the jurisdiction for it lies with the Special Court, yet a finding for commission of offence had been recorded. Thus, for the aforesaid reasons also, the order deserves to be set aside.

The petitioner held 14.25 per cent shares in the respondent-company and was, admittedly, given affirmative rights as per the agreement. The entire efforts of the respondents had been to justify one resolution passed on 5-1-2002. They had pointed out that all along there was unanimity on transfer of funds, even amounts, the mode of transfer, the investments, etc., and the minutes of resolution dated 5-1-2002 were in furtherance of the decision taken by the board of directors to send/transfer 1 million USD to the wholly owned subsidiary. That contention of the respondents was not borne out from the chronology of the events and the documents. It was an admitted position that when alleged remittance of USD 1 million was made to the subsidiary company, it did not even exist at the relevant time. In the name of unanimous decision, the funds were siphoned off to the three assets management companies. Documents were fabricated for the purpose of effecting the change in the authorized signatories in respect of the investments with the investment funds. The amounts from those deposits, on being received from the investment funds, were deposited in respondent No. 1’s HDFC bank account which should have been closed as per the board’s resolution dated 20-12-2000. Later on, by the signatures of respondent No. 9, who was illegally shown as a director, USD 1 million was illegally and unauthorisedly remitted on 4-2-2002 to a wholly owned subsidiary in the USA which did not even exist at the relevant time. Other facts, which falsified the respondents’ contentions and pointed towards their intention to defraud the creditors, members or any other person including the petitioner or otherwise for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose, were that despite the petitioner’s repeated request for inspection and audit and despite the CLB’s repeated orders, the respondents had not given the requisite information to the company’s members with respect to its affairs. It was true that the petitioner was only an investor-director. It was also true that non-allowing of inspection could not be a ground for considering a petition under section 235. But the entire facts, totality of the circumstances and the illegal, unlawful and fraudulent acts of the respondents led to the inference that there existed a prima facie case for investigation under section 235 as the respondents had been guilty of fraud and misfeasance towards the company as well as towards its members. The respondents had not complied with the articles of association and the legal provisions of the Act. Moreover, the respondent-company had become a disappearing company. It was reportedly not available at the registered office of the company nor were its statutory records available at its registered office. Statutory statements had not been sent to the RoC for several years. Instead of meeting the specific charges and making their case for non-investigation, the respondents had simply reiterated their contention that the resolution dated 5-1-2002 was not fabricated while the respondents’ subsequent acts - the false plea of supplementary agenda, the invalid circular resolution dated 29-4-2002, etc., revealed an unsuccessful effort to cover up the intent to defraud the creditors and members for a fraudulent and unlawful purpose which only made the petitioner’s prima facie case for investigation, by pointing out specific instances, stronger. [Para 14]

The CLB has an onerous duty to form an opinion with regard to the existence of the intent to defraud. The conditions stated in section 235 are to be satisfied before ordering an investigation under section 235. The facts and circumstances of the instant case, prima facie demonstrated and established the existence of pre-requisites which compelled the CLB to form an opinion in terms of section 235. The grounds for ordering an investigation did exist. There was overwhelming material available pointing to the circumstances suggesting that the business of the company was conducted for a fraudulent and unlawful purpose. The persons concerned in the management of the company had been guilty of fraud, misfeasance or other misconduct towards the company. It was a case squarely covered under the provisions of section 235 as the pre-conditions for initiating such an action existed as was clear from the foregoing. [Para 15]
