Whether petition is maintainable for recovery of amounts by invoking sections 397-398, read with sections 406, 542 and 543? Whether such kind of relief (recovery of amounts) can be sought? Admittedly the instant petition was filed for recovery of amounts from the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 in the petition. The grievance of the Union of India that the applicant and the 3rd respondent were the directors of the company and acting in a fraudulent manner had retained the funds and had become liable and accountable for their illegal acts. The case of the Union of India was that they had ordered investigation on 23-3-2004 by appointing inspector. The inspector had investigated into the matter and submitted the detailed report pointing out various illegal and fraudulent acts of the respondents, thereby it was of the view that it was a fit case to file the instant petition before the CLB. The main allegations were that from October, 1998 to January, 1999 the management of the company created an equity capital of Rs. 7093 crores through dubious method of rotation of cheques and by swapping of shares among group associates. The management was found to have indulged in falsification of accounts of the company. Further the allegation of the petitioner that the company adjusted the application money in the form of deposit for software, rigging of share price through manipulation of working results in financial statements, shares reprinted and sold in the market and whole original jumbo share certificates were under seizure of Income-tax Department for contravention of section 41, read with sections 372/372A, 78, 293, 295,370 etc. of the Income-tax Act, 1961. From the pleadings, it was apparent that the petition was filed basing on the report of the Investigating Officer. In that regard the provision under which the Union of India approached the CLB was necessary to emphasize. Section 397 empowers the CLB to make such order as it thinks fit, may with a view to bringing to an end the matters complained off by any member of a company who complains that the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interests or in a manner oppressive to any member or members. Section 398 empowers the CLB in case of mismanagement in the affairs of a company and may apply any member of a company who complained that the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interest or that a material change not being a change brought about by or in the interests of any creditor including debenture holders or any class of shareholders of the company. The CLB may with a view to bringing to an end or preventing the matters complained of are apprehended make such order as it thinks fit. Section 399 provides for the right to apply under sections 397-398 by the category of persons as mentioned in that section. Admittedly, there were no complaints before the Bench by any member/members or creditors of the company alleging/complaining the acts of oppression and mismanagement in the affairs of the company and the nature of allegations of the Union of India required a detailed trial by examining the witnesses and the veracity of documents. The proceedings under sections 397-398 are summary in nature. Therefore, the nature of allegations could not be decided by the CLB. The contention of the respondents was that no notice was given for the inspection which was ordered under section 209 or even under section 234. The petitioner submitted that opportunity was given to the respondents. The inspection was carried out in the year 2004 and a final report was submitted to the Government. It was open to the respondents to challenge the investigation report if it would have violated the principles of natural justice in conducting the inspection. The petitioner alleged violation of various provisions of law in the instant petition. Prima facie the petitioner could initiate prosecution for the said contraventions in appropriate Court of law. Further, the CLB would not intrude the functions of the other statutory bodies such as SEBI, RBI and the civil court, company court and exercising powers under IPC. It is well settled law that to invoke the provisions of sections 397 and 398 by any member, creditor a case has to be made out that facts would justify the making of winding up order and that winding up would unfairly prejudice the members. In the instant case the petitioner had not made out any case for winding up of the company on just and equitable ground. The petitioner was not remediless. Most of the allegations were in the nature of grievances for which specific alternate course of action was available under various provisions of the Act and other laws which could be resorted to by the petitioner. The petitioner also invoked the provisions of sections 542 and 543. Section 543 is relevant provision to be applied by the petitioner. However, to apply under that provision, only a creditor or a member can make an application. In the instant case admittedly the petitioner was neither a member nor creditor of the company. Hence, the petitioner could not invoke the provision of section 543 where the CLB has the power to order for repayment or restore the money or property. The sole prayer in the petition was for recovery of money

View in the Present Context

The Courts would definitely have power to direct CBI to conduct the investigation coupled with a direction upon the State authorities to co-operate with the CBI. However, the Court should be slow in exercising such power that could only be used in an extraordinary/exceptional circumstance. [Para 67]

What is Extraordinary/Exceptional Circumstance ? It would mean a situation that would lead to obvious conclusion, the process being frustrated; having either the State machinery deeply involved in the crime or their lackadaisical approach would result in an unsuccessful exercise. [Para 68]

Involvement of Kunal Ghosh/Srinjoy Bose :

The petitioner alleged, Kunal being an employee of Saradha group acted as a liason between the group and the State Government. The other petitioner went one step forward to allege involvement of Srinjoy, both Members of Parliament, belonging to the ruling party. The allegations are serious. More serious the allegation is, the proof must be stricter. The people connected with politics would have to deal with various persons at various level. A politician may have his own means of livelihood and his involvement in the work place may not have necessary involvement in political circle. Kunal was already examined by the police. If any one of them would have involvement in the crime, they must be proceeded with irrespective of their colour and creed, for that the entire State machinery could not be blamed. His personal involvement in the crime may not have nexus with the State machinery unless it is proved; he acted as a conduit that would bring him under the scanner. If one commits a crime, it would be his personal responsibility that must not have repercussion on the entire State judiciary unless such crime would relate to a mechanism involving the system. It would be too early to blame the State solely on the ground. [Para 69]

Investigation

The involvement of the State in the present context, did not feature in the pleadings. The investigation is still on. It would be too early to comment as to Kunal's involvement in the present case, at least, no definite assertion backed up by sufficient particulars is found. Same was the case of Srinjoy Bose. Even if, these two persons are found to be involved in the crime, the State must spring into action and proceed against them irrespective of their political colour and creed. Sufficient opportunity is to be given to the State machinery to take a decision on that score. Merely someone was an employee in a particular branch of the business belonging to the group, one cannot blame the entire State machinery, particularly when the Court is prima facie satisfied with the progress that the State machinery made in the instant case, since the magnitude is huge, the machinery should be extra cautious in proceeding as the people involved in it would try to scuttle the process or create as many hindrances as they could. [Para 70]

The CBI clearly mentioned they did not have any appropriate infrastructure. They may do it only with the State helping them. They were very candid on the issue. If the process is withdrawn from the State machinery and the CBI is asked to take it over and ask the State machinery to assist them, the result would not be as expected, at least, stage has not come, as is found from the fact situation. [Para 71]

Since no better course is found the State is given some more time. [Para 72]

The State machinery is given liberty to take suggestion or advice of any other agency as they feel like. The CBI, Enforcement Directorate, Ministry of Corporate Affairs, SFIO and all other organisations of the like nature are directed, to render all necessary assistance to the State machinery as and when asked for, so that they could complete the process of investigation and start prosecuting the accused. The State machinery would however, be obliged to submit periodical report to the Court that would be considered at the appropriate stage. Such direction would be given at the end. [Para 73]

INVESTIGATION OF OWNERSHIP OF A COMPANY

Central Government can order investigation into ownership to decide who are really financially interested and who are in real control of the company.

Section 216(1) of Companies Act, 2013 provides that where it appears to the Central Government that there is a reason so to do, it may appoint one or more inspectors to investigate and report on matters relating to the company, and its membership for the purpose of determining the true persons—

(a)

who are or have been financially interested in the success or failure, whether real or apparent, of the company; or

(b)

who are or have been able to control or to materially influence the policy of the company.

(c)

who have or had beneficial interest in shares of a company or who are or have been beneficial owners or significant beneficial owner of a company [clause (c) inserted w.e.f. 13-6-2018].

Section 90 of Companies Act, 2013 substituted w.e.f. 13-6-2018 provides for declaration and register of beneficial interest. To support this provision, section 216 is amended w.e.f. 13-6-2018 to provide for investigation into beneficial ownership.

Central Government can appoint inspectors to investigate and report matters relating to company and its membership for purposes of determining the true persons who have or had beneficial interest in shares of a company or who are or have been beneficial owners or significant beneficial owner of a company - section 216(1)(c) of Companies Act, 2013 inserted w.e.f. 13-6-2018

Investigation if NCLT directs - Without prejudice to its powers section 216(1), the Central Government shall appoint one or more inspectors under that sub-section, if NCLT, in the course of any proceeding before it, directs by an order that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated as regards the membership of the company and other matters relating to the company, for the purposes specified in section 216(1) - Section 216(2) of Companies Act, 2013.

Investigation under section 216 can be initiated or continued even if special resolution for voluntary winding up is passed or application in respect of oppression and mismanagement has been made or any winding up petition is filed or pending - section 226 of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding to section 250A of the 1956 Act].

Section 226 of Companies Act, 2013 has been notified and made effective on 15-12-2016. Of course, this section is not relevant now as provisions relating to voluntary winding up have been omitted vide Insolvency Code, 2016.

Imposition on restrictions during investigation on securities issued or to be issued by company - During investigation under section 216, NCLT can impose certain restrictions upon securities. Such restriction can be upto three years - section 222(1) of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding to section 250(1) of the 1956 Act].

If despite such order, there is issue or transfer of securities, company as well as every officer who is in default is liable for punishment of fine and imprisonment - section 222(2) of Companies Act, 2013.

Applicability of provisions to foreign company - The provisions of investigation of ownership apply to foreign company also [section 228 of Companies Act, 2013]

A cumulative reading of the provisions of the SEBI Act, 1992 and SEBI (Prohibition of Fraudulent and Unfair Trade Practices relating to Securities Market) Regulations, 2003 indicates that if the Board - as established under section 3 and managed under section 4 of the Act, 1992, has reasonable grounds to believe that transactions of securities in the market are dealt with in a manner detrimental to interest of shareholders, the Board is empowered under section 11-C to appoint any person as the investigating authority, to investigate into affairs of persons associated with the securities market, and thereafter to report them to the Board.[Para 8]

■

Section 19 of the Act, 1992 empowers the Board to further delegate to any member, officer of the Board, or any other person, all such powers except the power to make Rules as stipulated under section 29, including the power conferred on the Board under section 11-C, to order investigation into market securities. Additionally, sub-section (3) of section 4 of the Act, 1992, reserves with the Chairperson of the Board all powers of, ''general superintendence and direction of the affairs of the Board'', and further exercise all powers and do all acts which may be exercised or done by the Board, independent of any general or special order which may be passed under section 19. It may therefore be reasonably inferred that the Chairperson of the Board is statutorily empowered to exercise all such powers as may be exercised by the Board, save the limitations placed on such authority in the concerned regulations. A perusal of Regulation 5 of the Regulations, 2003 reveals that where there exists a reasonable ground to believe, the Executive Director is empowered to direct - by an order in writing, any officer (investigating authority), not below the rank of Division Chief to investigate any transactions in securities which are alleged to be carried in manner detrimental to the shareholders. [Para 8]

■

Therefore, upon conjoint reading of the delegation order dated 31-7-2019 passed in terms of section 4(3) of the Act, 1992, and Regulation 5 of the SEBI (PFUTP) Regulations, 2003, it is understood that the respondentNo.1/ Executive Director, SEBI, is a lawful authority under the statute to order an investigation, under section 11-C of the Act, 1992. Hence, the order of appointment of respondent No.3/ Deputy General Manager as investigating authority, as in the instant case, is not bad in law for want of jurisdiction. [Para 10]

An inspection under section 209A is an inspection with regard to the books of account and other books and papers of a company. The scope of this inspection is limited to the books and papers and that too to the particular company only. The report of this inspection is submitted to the Central Government. Consequent to this report, the Central Government may not be able to initiate action under section 242 or section 243, namely, prosecution or application for winding-up or for initiating action for prevention for oppression and mismanagement under section 397/398. Similarly, no proceedings for recovery of damages or property in the public interest can be brought by the Central Government consequent to the report under section 209A. In this case, the Central Government on its own could have appointed one or more inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company in exercise of the powers under section 235. However, there was a technical snag inasmuch as this section could be invoked only on a report made by the ROC under section 234(6), i.e., a report by the Registrar based on information called by him from the company in exercise of his powers. Since the present report was made by the Joint Director in the office of Regional Director, the Central Government had refrained from exercising its powers under section 235. On the other hand, it had made use of the facility available under section 237(b) to make a reference with all the particulars for the CLB to form an opinion as to whether an investigation was warranted. The power under section 237(b) is a discretionary power which is to be exercised very carefully after considering all the circumstances.

The appellant had filed company application against the order of the CLB, dated 23-6-2003 and filed an application for directing the promoter and erstwhile director of NFL company to provide funds for payment of the deposited amounts. In the said application, the appellant had filed another application seeking a direction to conduct investigation into the affairs of the company by independent agencies. The depositors had filed writ petition directing the Central Government to conduct enquiry by the Central Bureau of Investigation regarding the affairs of the NFL company. In the affidavits filed in the company application and writ petition, number of allegations were levelled against the promoter and erstwhile directors of the NFL company. The respondent promoter and erstwhile directors of NFL company had filed counter affidavits and denied all the allegations. The merits and demerits of the allegations were not to be gone into. The Act is a self-contained code containing relevant and adequate provisions right from incorporating the company till winding up of the company and payment of amounts to the creditors even after winding up of the company by the independent authority like the Official Liquidator. There are two sets of remedies available for the grievance against the company and its management. One set of procedure is provided for the depositors and another set is provided for the members of the company. [Para 22]

The depositor who is an unsecured creditor has to file application under sections 58A and 58AA for the purpose of refund of his money before the CLB. The CLB on the application filed by the creditor has to conduct enquiry and pass order directing the company to pay the amount to the said creditor. The order of the CLB passed under sections 58A and 58AA is enforceable under section 634A. As per the provisions of the said section, the order of the CLB is deemed to be a decree and executable under the provisions of the CPC. [Para 23]

Notwithstanding the right under sections 58A and 58AA, the depositor has the right to file a petition under section 433 for winding up of the company as the company failed to discharge its financial obligations/commitments towards its creditors. On filing the winding up petitions under section 433, the Court after giving an opportunity to the company may pass an order of winding up and appoint the Liquidator to the company. Once the Liquidator is appointed, the management of the company ceases to function and the Official Liquidator would take charge of the company. The Official Liquidator is entitled to recover the dues of the company or to do all the acts for discharging the liabilities of the company and distribute the sale proceeds among the creditors. The Official Liquidator is also entitled to go into the mismanagement of the company by present and past directors and appoint tax inspectors and other persons under section 538 for the purpose of investigation into the affairs of the company. The present and past management is liable for the offences, if any committed by them, as per sections 539 to 545. Hence, the provisions of sections 58A, 58AA and 634 will safeguard the interests of the depositors prior to winding up and sections 433, 538 to 545 would take care of the depositors. [Para 24]

Sections 235 to 242 provide for investigation into the affairs of the company either by the Central Government or by the Registrar of Companies or at the instance of the members of the company. Section 235 provides for investigation by the Central Government regarding the affairs of the company and the Central Government is entitled to appoint inspectors to investigate into the affairs of the company on the report of the Registrar. Section 237 provides for investigation on the recommendation of the CLB. Sections 239 and 240 provide for the powers and procedure for investigation and under section 241, the inspector has to submit the report. The Government is entitled to prosecute the persons responsible for the offences under section 242 and section 244 provides for recovery of damages. These provisions would safeguard the interest of the members of the company. Apart from the said provisions, the members of the company can file a winding up petition under the Act in case the management is not acting in the interest of the company. [Para 25]

The said provisions clearly show the safeguards provided under the Act. The depositor is entitled to approach CLB under sections 58A and 58AA and execute the same as per the decree under section 634A. The depositors in the writ petition without approaching the CLB for recovery of their amount, straightaway filed the writ petition seeking investigation into the affairs of the company. The petitioners in the writ petition having not availed of the effective remedies under the Act cannot ask for investigation into the affairs of the company by an independent agency. [Para 26]

The petitioners had come before this Court alleging that the impugned action of sealing by the District Authorities of the State of Jharkhand was without any authority of law and no notice was given to them to defend themselves against any alleged violation of law. However, this Court found it necessary to implead the statutory authorities, who are under the mandate of law to regulate the affairs of such companies and take action, if any violation are found out of such statutory enactments like SEBI Act and other allied Acts and their Rules and Regulations, the RBI Act, Companies Act, the Regulations/Guidelines framed thereunder as also Acts and Rules regulating the affairs of Multistate Co-operative Society. The Respondents-District Authorities had undertaken the act of sealing of the business premises of the petitioners in a preemptive exercise for protecting the interest of investors as it appeared to them that the provisions of the SEBI Act and the RBI Guidelines and other statutory enactment are not being complied by them. However, after appearance of the parties, it is properly viewed that the continuance of the sealing for indefinite length of time, is not going to serve purpose. The interest of the investors are to be protected and at the same time the affairs of the Companies are also to be inquired into by the regulating bodies. The petitioners also claim a fundamental right to carry on their business. In any case, the statutory authorities are also required to undertake an inquiry into the affairs of the Companies by examining documents and materials etc. which are presently lying within the sealing business premises of the petitioners' as also elsewhere. In the background of the aforesaid facts, it is considered just and proper to pass the following orders in the larger interest to protect the interest of the investors and the general public as also to ensure that the matter is properly inquired into by the respective statutory bodies and thereafter the petitioners may be allowed to carry out their business in accordance with law:

(i)

The business premises of the petitioners which are lying sealed, shall be unsealed subject to the conditions;

(ii)

The Registrar of Companies-cum-Official Liquidator shall, in each individual case, prepare an inventory of all such documents, materials, papers and books which are lying within the seized premises within a period of two weeks with the aid and help of the District Administration and keep in safe custody;

(iii)

The District Administration including the Superintendent of Police of concerned district shall extend all possible help for preparation of such inventory and keeping the same in safe custody. The Deputy Commissioner of the concerned district may nominate an officer not below the rank of Additional Collector with whom the Official Liquidator shall co-ordinate all such action. Copies of the inventory so prepared shall also be handed over to the petitioners' or their representatives, who shall ensure their presence during the preparation of the inventory.

(iv)

The respective statutory authorities like the Securities and Exchange Board of India, the Reserve Bank of India, the Department of Co-operative having control of the Multi state Co-operative Society as also the Registrar of Companies shall inquire into the affairs of the Companies in respect of the compliance of the respective statutory provisions thereafter within a period of eight weeks subject to any extension as may be allowed on their requests. The power to pass ex parte ad interim order, pending investigation, flows from sections 11 and 11B of the SEBI Act. A plain reading of sections 11 and 11B shows that SEBI has to protect the interests of the investors in securities and to regulate the securities market by such measures as it thinks fit and such measures may be for any or all of the matters provided in sub-section (2) of section 11 of the Act. SEBI has power to pass an interim order and such interim order can also be passed ex parte in order to prevent further possible mischief of tampering with the securities market. If during the course of investigation, it is found prima facie, that the person is violating the securities laws or is siphoning of the funds of the listed company to the detriment of its shareholders, it would be obligatory for SEBI to pass an interim order or for that matter an ex parte ad interim order in order to safeguard the interests of the investors and to maintain the integrity of the market. [Para 15]

Normally, while passing an interim order, the principles of natural justice has to be adhered to, namely, that an opportunity of hearing is required to be given. Procedural fairness embodying natural justice is to be applied whenever action is taken affecting the rights of the parties. However, at times, an opportunity of hearing may not be pre-decisional and may necessarily have to be post-decisional especially where the act to be prevented is imminent or where action to be taken brooks no delay. Thus, pre-decisional hearing is not always necessary when ex parte ad interim orders are made pending investigation or enquiry unless provided by the statute. In such cases, rules of natural justice would be satisfied, if the affected party is given a post-decisional hearing. [Para 16]

The contention of the appellant that the transaction related to 2017-19 and therefore there was no tearing hurry to pass an ex parte ad interim order at this stage is not acceptable. A detailed investigation has been carried out which report indicates the involvement of 226 persons who were found to be part of a fraudulent scheme devised by 'HS' and its accomplices in which buy recommendations in the scrip of 5 scrips were circulated through SMS and certain websites which resulted in the increase in the price and volume of the scrips during the SMS period. The investigation has revealed, creating artificial price and volume in these scrips to lure the retail investors before circulating SMS and thereafter Off loading the scrips to the unsuspecting investors. Considering the gravity of the charges leveled in the interim order cum show cause notice read with the investigation report such order was required to be passed in order to prevent the appellants and other noticees from further infiltrating the market. [Para 19]

The contention that no prima facie case existed in passing the impugned order is wholly erroneous. The impugned order read with the investigation report indicates that a prima facie finding was arrived at based on objective facts indicating manipulation in the price of the 5 scrips in question and the diversion of the proceeds to the ultimate beneficiaries. Insofar as appellant 'Econo' is concerned admittedly the said appellant has not traded in the scrip in question but has acted as conduit in transferring the profits to the mastermind 'HS' and its connected entities through layered transactions. Details regarding transfer of the funds finds place in the impugned order cum show cause notice and in the investigation report. Large sums of money have been transferred through layered transactions. [Para 20]

In addition to the aforesaid, there is a direction connection of the appellant broking firm with the mastermind 'HS'. Mother of the mastermind 'HS' was holding 55 per cent shareholding in the appellant Econo. In addition, a close entity of 'HS' was the Chief Executive Officer in the appellant Company. These facts at the moment have not been disputed and the only allegation made is that the connection shown in the impugned order of the appellant Company with 'HS' is irrelevant. Such contention is unacceptable as, the mastermind who has controlling stake in the appellant firm has a material bearing to the transfer of the ill-gotten gains to the ultimate beneficiaries. [Para 21]

The charges leveled against the appellant are serious and in the given facts and circumstances of the case the respondent was justified in passing the ex parte ad interim order cum show cause notice. instead of dealing with the issues raised by the appellants it would be appropriate that the appellants should file an appropriate reply for vacation/modification of the impugned order these is no reason to interfere in the impugned order at this stage. From a perusal of the documents submitted by the petitioners, it was clear that the directors had violated various provisions of the Act and committed various acts which were prejudicial to the interest of the company and its shareholders at large. It was also seen from the documents that the Registrar of Companies, issued notice dated to 2-9-2008 to its directors under section 234(1) directing the company to furnish information and explanation within ten days or else action would be initiated under sections 234(3A), 234(4). Further, the Registrar of Companies issued another letter dated 19-9-2008 to the directors to furnish the minutes book of the board of directors and general meetings, fixed asset register, register of debenture holders, index of debenture holders, shareholders' attendance register, register of investments, copy of the annual report and balance-sheets for the last two years. It was seen from the records that having not received any information from the company and its directors, the Registrar of Companies referred the matter to the Regional Director for prosecution. The Registrar of Companies, in response to the notice regarding the filing of the instant petition before the principal Bench, CLB, vide his letter dated 10-6-2009 mentioned the details of the company and its directors and the fund position on the basis of the balance-sheets and also the assets and liabilities. It was also stated that the company had not filed its balance-sheet as on 31-3-2001 and the company held only one annual general meeting on 1-12-2007 for the years 2001 to 2007 instead of holding separate annual general meetings for each year. No extension of time was obtained by the company. It was also mentioned that the shareholding detail was given in CD whereas no CD was received in that regard by the Registrar of Companies. It was also stated that there were several complaints received by the Registrar of Companies against the company. [Para 4]

From the above, it was evident that the allegations of the petitioners had some force and the same were also further strengthened from the letter of the Registrar of Companies to the instant Bench and also various letters addressed to the company. The instant Bench would not keep its eyes closed on such acts when they came before it with un-controverted facts against the directors. The affairs of the company were being conducted with an intent to defraud its members and public which were oppressive and prejudicial to the interest of the members. To protect the interest of the company and its shareholders and also to up keep the faith of the public in the judicial system (Quasi Judicial Bodies), the Bench certainly came to the rescue of the petitioners and its shareholders to do substantial justice by ordering an investigation by invoking the provisions of section 237(b). The petitioners had come before this Court alleging that the impugned action of sealing by the District Authorities of the State of Jharkhand was without any authority of law and no notice was given to them to defend themselves against any alleged violation of law. However, this Court found it necessary to implead the statutory authorities, who are under the mandate of law to regulate the affairs of such companies and take action, if any violation are found out of such statutory enactments like SEBI Act and other allied Acts and their Rules and Regulations, the RBI Act, Companies Act, the Regulations/Guidelines framed thereunder as also Acts and Rules regulating the affairs of Multistate Co-operative Society. The Respondents-District Authorities had undertaken the act of sealing of the business premises of the petitioners in a preemptive exercise for protecting the interest of investors as it appeared to them that the provisions of the SEBI Act and the RBI Guidelines and other statutory enactment are not being complied by them. However, after appearance of the parties, it is properly viewed that the continuance of the sealing for indefinite length of time, is not going to serve purpose. The interest of the investors are to be protected and at the same time the affairs of the Companies are also to be inquired into by the regulating bodies. The petitioners also claim a fundamental right to carry on their business. In any case, the statutory authorities are also required to undertake an inquiry into the affairs of the Companies by examining documents and materials etc. which are presently lying within the sealed business premises of the petitioners' as also elsewhere. [Para 3]

It is, thus, considered just and proper to pass the following orders in the larger interest to protect the interest of the investors and the general public as also to ensure that the matter is properly inquired into by the respective statutory bodies and thereafter the petitioners may be allowed to carry out their business in accordance with law:

(i)

The business premises of the petitioners which are lying sealed, shall be unsealed subject to the following conditions;

(ii)

The Registrar of Companies-cum-Official Liquidator shall, in each individual case, prepare an inventory of all such documents, materials, papers and books which are lying within the seized premises within a period of two weeks with the aid and help of the District Administration and keep in safe custody;

(iii)

The District Administration including the Superintendent of Police of concerned district shall extend all possible help for preparation of such inventory and keeping the same in safe custody. Copies of the inventory so prepared shall also be handed over to the petitioners' or their representatives, who shall ensure their presence during the preparation of the inventory.

(iv)

The respective statutory authorities like the Securities and Exchange Board of India, the Reserve Bank of India, the Department of Co-operative having control of the Multistate Co-operative Society as also the Registrar of Companies shall inquire into the affairs of the Companies in respect of the compliance of the respective statutory provisions. The petitioners shall cooperate in the said inquiry in all possible ways and it is made clear that if the petitioners fail to cooperate in the inquiry by the Statutory Authorities, it will be open to the Statutory Authorities to take any decision as are permissible in law.

(v)

During the aforesaid period of inquiry, the petitioners shall not undertake any new business of the company or enter into fresh instrument with any party/investor and they will also not advertise in respect of their business during the said period. Petitioners also undertake to give an undertaking to that effect by way of an affidavit.

(vi)

During the course of inquiry, in case any existing customers/investors of the company, intends to make any deposit or investment, the same shall be deposited in an interest bearing Escrow Account opened in a Nationalized Bank under the modalities laid down by the Official liquidator-cum-Registrar of Companies. The petitioners shall not be allowed to withdraw the said money during the course of inquiry. Any such withdrawal thereafter will be permissible only after NOC /Clearance Certificate granted by the statutory authorities or this Court. The petitioners' undertake to file an affidavit to that effect also.

(vii)

In order to protect the interests of the investors/customers of the petitioners' companies, it is further directed that the petitioners shall not be allowed to operate and withdraw their existing Accounts during the period of inquiry. Only upon NOC/Clearance granted by respective Statutory Authorities will the petitioners be allowed to operate the Accounts and subject to any order passed or conditions imposed upon them.

(viii)

The petitioners' shall not alienate any assets, movable or immovable of the Company during the aforesaid period and thereafter only subject to the same conditions as aforesaid in the previous sub para.

Sum placed with NSEIL constituted property of company

Section 456 itself makes it clear that the PL shall take into his custody or under his control 'all the property' to which the company is or appears to be entitled. There can be no manner of doubt, and it is in fact not denied, that the company did place with NSEIL Rs. 1.10 crore when it became a trading member. The said sum definitely, therefore, constitutes the property of the company.

Although upon passing of the winding up order by the Court, the assets and the properties of the company came to the custody of the PL, but, in fact, the properties did not vest in the PL. Therefore, the PL acts as an agent of the company, a trustee of the properties as also the officer of the Court. He acts under the directions of the Court. This explains why under section 457(1), it is the liquidator who has been given the powers thereafter to represent the company under liquidation in all the proceedings. [Para 14]

Claims of investors had not been met out of company's fund with Defaulter Committee

In the instant case, although the company was expelled as a trading member, prior to the order of winding up, resulting in the deposit made by it with NSEIL vesting in the Defaulters' Committee, the claims of the investors had not been met out of that fund by the Defaulters Committee. It, in fact, set aside Rs. 83,91,000 pursuant to the letter written to the NSEIL by the Official Liquidator. It has met the claims of 68 investors in part out of IPFT. Therefore, the deposit made by the company with NSEIL, which constitutes its property under section 456(1), remains intact. [Para 17]

Conclusion

With the process of liquidation of the company already in progress, the scheme of section 456 will have to be followed. The inevitable result would be that wherever any property of the company-in-liquidation is available, the possession of such property would have to come to the PL appointed by the Court. Investors, who are before the Defaulters' Committee, will now have the option of pursuing their claims before the Official Liquidator in accordance with law.

Consequently, the plea of NSEIL that its Defaulters' Committee should be allowed to continue to be in possession and control of the deposits of Rs. 1.10 crore lying with it to the credit of the company cannot be countenanced. [Para 18]

Consequently, company application is to be allowed and NSEIL is to be directed to remit to the Official Liquidator the sum of Rs. 1.10 crore together with interest, if any accrued thereon. [Para 19]

By virtue of the specific stipulation in the statute, the power to restrain fraudulent persons from managing the companies as provided in section 203 can be exercised only in the course of winding up of a company. As such, the basic question to be considered was whether the prayer for winding up was liable to be entertained. The prayer for winding up had been raised by the petitioners only as an 'alternative prayer'. The description of the sequence of events and the facts and figures related more to the alleged misappropriation, mismanagement, fraud and oppression of the minority sector, which would not constitute or warrant a 'winding up' on the ground of 'just and equitable reason', as envisaged under section 433(f). The terms 'just and equitable' as they appear under section 433(f) are not to be read as 'ejusdem generis' with the preceding words of the enactment. It is in the nature of 'last resort', when other remedies are not efficacious enough to protect the general interests of the company. In that context, it was also relevant to note the pleading of the petitioners in the company petition, as to the foundation laid for pressing the relief of winding up. [Para 9]

It was very much clear that the basic grievance of the petitioners in respect of the reliefs sought for and the prayer for 'winding up' had been raised stating that there was no other alternate remedy for the minority members, except to invoke the jurisdiction of the Court for appropriate reliefs as the last resort, however, same was to be granted only if circumstances warranted it. [Para 10]

Considering the moot question put forth by the petitioners, as to whether the circumstances warranted 'winding up', nothing else was pleaded specifically, so as to grant the remedy of 'winding up' on just and equitable grounds as the 'last resort'. In other words, was there any other alternate remedy for redressal of the grievance with regard to the reliefs sought for and if any such remedy was available, whether the same was efficacious enough or had any of the minority petitioners been prevented from availing the benefit thereunder, were not discernible from the pleadings on record. As such, it had become necessary to ascertain as to whether the contention of the petitioners that there was no other alternate remedy for them, was correct or sustainable. [Para 11]

Section 235(1) deals with the power of the Central Government to investigate the affairs of the company on receipt of a report from the Registrar under sub-section (6) or (7) of section 234. Sub-section (2)(b ) of the very same provision deals with such power conferred on the Tribunal in the case of a company having no share capital (as in the instant case) where an application is received from not less than one-fifth of the persons on the company's register of members. The petitioners had no case that they had moved the Tribunal by filing an application preferred by not less than one-fifth of the persons on the company's register of members or that such course was not available or had been turned futile due to some or other reason, so as to make it ineffective. [Para 12]

There was no case for the petitioners that they had resorted to any steps to persuade the Central Government to take appropriate steps under sections 235 and 237 for redressal of their grievances and that the same did not yield any positive result. [Para 14]

In the case of oppression of the minority, the power is vested with the 'Tribunal' under section 397 for granting necessary reliefs. Similar power is vested with the Tribunal to deal with the situation of mismanagement as well as is provided under section 398. By virtue of the power specifically conferred under sections 397 and 398, if necessary application is preferred in the manner as specified therein, after considering the facts and circumstances, the Tribunal, if satisfied as to the 'just and equitable' reason to have the company wound up, can pass appropriate orders to meet the situation. The circumstances under which a petition can be moved before the Tribunal under section 397 or 398 are stipulated under section 399. The petitioners, by virtue of section 399(1)(b) were very much entitled to agitate the matter before the 'Tribunal', if an application was preferred by one-fifth of the total number of members of the first respondent. Why the petitioners had not resorted to such an exercise and why they had shut their eyes against the alternate remedy provided under the statute, rather remained obscure. [Para 15]

On seeing the present petition filed by the Operational Creditor, it seems there was no correspondence between this Creditor and the Corporate Debtor in between 2013 and 2016 except giving a notice in the year 2016 under section 434 of the Companies Act, 1956. But if the present case is set against the background of SEBI orders, then an inference could also be drawn that an effort has been made to take out the company as well as the investment already frozen by SEBI from the claws of SEBI. [Para 12]

There is no conflict between SEBI Act and Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code because SEBI deals with investor protection issues whereas Bankruptcy code deals with creditor issues. The jural relationship between the parties is also different. In SEBI, it is between the investors and the company, whereas in Bankruptcy code, it is between the creditors and the debtor, therefore, there is no subject matter conflict in between the two statutes. [Para 18]

On perusal of section 238, it is evident that overriding effect under section 238 will have over other laws, only when the other laws are inconsistent with the Insolvency and Bankruptcy code, since SEBI Act has been dealing with investor protection issues, not with creditor and debtor issues, though section 238 has exhaustive mode in respect of the subject matter of creditor and debtor issues, it has no overlapping or overriding effect over investor protection issues dealt with under SEBI Act. [Para 20]

The case before SEBI is a case involving fraud by the debtor entering into agreements not recognised by law and raised funds for an amount of more than Rs. 7000 crores, thereby Bankruptcy code has no overriding effect over the order passed by SEBI, hence the jurisdiction under Bankruptcy code will not come into operation to nullify the order passed by SEBI, henceforth, no order can be passed in this case in conflict to the order passed by SEBI. [Para 22]

A non-obstante clause is a legislative device which is usually employed to give overriding effect to certain provisions over some contrary provisions that may be found either in the same enactment or some other enactment, that is to say, to avoid the operation and effect of all contrary provisions. [Para 23]

The asset is same. There it is the funds of the debtor company that has made SEBI pass an order, and here it is the creditor who wants an order on the same funds from a different angle. [Para 28]

In the given matter, before SEBI, it is in respect to illegal business running without Registration Certificate and cheating gullible victims, at the most it may be coined as relation in between investor and the company, and here it is on jural relationship in between creditor and debtor, which is entirely on different footing. [Para 29]

I Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company’s affairs in other cases It is not necessary that for passing an order under section 237(a)(ii) there should be a proceeding already before Court; even a petition simpliciter can be entertained Delhi Flour Mills Co. Ltd., In re [1975] 45 Comp. Cas. 33 (Delhi) There is nothing in the language of section 237(a)(ii) indicating that a petition simpliciter for an action under section 237(a)(ii) cannot be entertained by the Court, but that power can only be exercised by the Court against the company in respect of whom some other proceeding is pending in the Court and the Court considers it proper to direct appointment of an Inspector. Existence or pendency of some proceeding other than one for taking action under section 237(a)(ii) is not a sine qua non. On the contrary, even in the absence of a petition simpliciter for an action under section 237(a)(ii) for directing the Central Government to appoint an Inspector, the Court while hearing some other proceeding against a company in the course of which the Court is satisfied that an inspector to investigate the affairs of the company should be appointed, may without any application to that effect proceed to pass such an order. If the Court has such wide power to exercise jurisdiction under section 237(a)(ii) in another proceeding against the same company, there is no justification for holding that a petition simpliciter under section 237(a)(ii) cannot be entertained by the Court. It may also be pointed out that rule 11(9) of the Companies (Court) Rules, 1959, provides that the Court can be moved under section 237 by a petition. That, of course, is not decisive. But if the above construction put upon section 237 is correct, the fact that a petition is prescribed for moving the Court may also point in the same direction.

Section 235, read with sections 394 and 433, of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of affairs of a company - Petitioning - creditors had filed winding up petition against respondent-company for non-payment of their dues - In order to get out of situation, board of directors of respondent-company resolved to propose a scheme of amalgamation by which respondent along with two other companies were to merge with transferee-company - Scheme of amalgamation was sanctioned - However, by interim order, effect of amalgamation was stayed - Meanwhile, without disclosing filing of company petition and that amalgamation had been stayed, transferee-company was wound up - Ex-directors of transferee-company did not file statement of affairs and left country - Whether ex-directors of respondent-company with other companies had played fraud with creditors and with Court by taking advantage of proceedings of Court by firstly making defaults in payment of creditors, getting a scheme of amalgamation approved without informing fact of pendency of winding up petition and giving notice to all creditors and, thereafter, in getting transferee-company wound up without much contest and leaving country without filing statement of affairs - Held, yes - Whether Official Liquidator was to be directed to inform Central Government to cause an enquiry into affairs of those companies under sections 235 and 237 and to submit report to Court - Held, yes

The petitioner had purchased certain shares of third respondent-company. According to him, he had neither received any annual report nor notice of any extraordinary annual general meeting of the company since he purchased the shares of the company and further he could not get even a single rupee as return on his investment. Those facts were allegedly brought to the notice of the Registrar of Companies, but no action was taken on the matter. Therefore, the petitioner filed writ petition seeking a direction to the first respondent to appoint a competent person as investigator for investigating the affairs of the third respondent-company from 1995 onwards and to file a report in the High Court. The second respondent took stand that remedy, if any, available to the petitioner was to approach the CLB in accordance with provisions of the Act and, hence, writ petition was not maintainable.

Section 235 of the 1956 Act, enables the Central Government to appoint inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company and to report thereon in such manner as the Central Government may direct, in case where a report has been made by the Registrar of the company under sub-section (6) of section 234 or under sub-section (7) of that section read with sub-section (6) thereof. Under sub-section (2) of section 235, where an application has been received by the specified number of members or persons on the company's register of members, respectively, in case of a company having share capital and in case of a company having no share capital, the Tribunal may declare the investigation of the affairs of the company by an inspector, but, after giving the parties an opportunity of being heard. [Para 11]

Under Section 237, without prejudice to the powers of the Central Government under section 235, the Central Government is empowered to appoint inspector to investigate the affairs of the company and to report thereon in such manner as the Central Government may direct, if the company by special resolution or, the court by order declares that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated by an inspector appointed by the Central Government. Under clause (b) of section 237, the Central Government may appoint an inspector if, in its opinion or in the opinion of the Tribunal, there are circumstances suggesting that the business of the company is being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members or any other persons, or otherwise for fraudulent or for unlawful purpose, or in a manner oppressive to any of its members; where the persons concerned in the formation of the company or the management of its affairs have in connection therewith been guilty of fraud, misfeasance and other misconduct towards the company or towards any of its members; or, that the members of the company have not been given all the information with respect to its affairs which they might reasonably expect. [Para 12]

The powers of the inspector to investigate into an affair of the referred companies is provided under section 239 of the Act 1956. Under section 240, it is the duty of all officers and other employees and agents of the company, where its affairs are being investigated by virtue of section 239 to preserve and produce all papers and documents and render all assistance. Section 240A empowers the inspector to seize books and papers relating to any company where he has reasonable grounds to believe that they may be destroyed to the mutilated, altered, falsified or secreted to seize such books and papers. [Para 13]

Under section 241, the inspectors are required to make interim reports to the Central Government and on conclusion of the investigation to make final report to the Central Government. Section 242 provides for prosecution pursuant to a report furnished under section 241. Section 243 provides for winding up of a company which enables the Central Government to cause to be presented to the tribunal by any authorised person, a petition for winding up of the company on the ground that it is just and equitable that it should be wound up or on an application for an order under section 397 or 398, or both a petition and an application as aforesaid. [Para 14]

Section 250A permits an investigation to be initiated under section 235, 237, 239 or 247 notwithstanding that an application has been made for an order under section 397 or 398; or the company has passed a special resolution for voluntarily winding up and no investigation so initiated shall be stopped or suspended by reason only of the fact that an application or a special resolution referred aforesaid, has been passed. [Para 15]

Under the Act 2013, there is a separate chapter, Chapter XIV, that deals with inspection, inquiry, and investigation. [Para 16]

Under section 206 of the Act, 2013, the Registrar has power to call for further information or explanation or any further documents relating to the company by a written notice, where on a scrutiny of any document filed by a company or on any information received by him, the Registrar forms that opinion requiring the company to furnish in writing such information or explanation, or to produce such documents. Where no information or explanation is so furnished, or the Registrar finds the information or explanation inadequate on his satisfaction that unsatisfactory state of affairs exists in the company and does not disclose a full and fair statement of the information required, he may, by another written notice, call on the company to produce for his inspection such further books of account, books, papers and explanations as he may require. [Para 17]

The ex-directors of the respondent-company with other companies had played fraud with the creditors and with the Court. They took advantage of the proceedings of the Court by firstly making defaults in payment of the creditors, getting a scheme of amalgamation approved without informing the fact of pendency of the winding up petition and giving notice to all the creditors and, thereafter, in getting the transferee-company wound up without much contest. They did not file the statement of affairs and it was reported that they had left the country. They appeared to have succeeded. The law, however, is above all, must take stock of the situation, and punish those who were guilty of misappropriation of crores of rupees or might be transferring crores of rupees outside the country. The public money should not be allowed to be siphoned off without fixing accountability and if possible recovery should be made from the hands of all those, who possessed the same. [Para 11]

In the circumstances, the Official Liquidator was to be directed to make an application in special appeal, placing on record the order passed in the instant appeal. [Para 12]

The Official Liquidator would inform the Central Government to cause an enquiry into the affairs of those companies under sections 235 and 237 and to submit report to the Court. The Official Liquidator would call a meeting of the secured and unsecured creditors of the respondent-company and all the petitioning-creditors in the pending winding up petitions of those companies. The meeting might be called which would resolve regarding the steps to be taken by the Official Liquidator to recover the dues. [Para 13]

Section 213 of the Companies Act, 2013/Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation into company's affairs in other cases - Whether Tribunal is empowerd under section 213 to investigate into affairs of a company on an application made by certain number of members of company; and, on an application made by any other persons - Held, yes - Applicant bank sanctioned Term Loan Facility to respondent company - Since, respondent company failed to repay, loan account of respondent company was classified as NPA - After scrutiny of audited balance sheets of respondent company, Bank found certain financial irregularities - Bank alleged that respondent company had given interest free loans and advances to its group companies, whereas it was paying interest to banks for money borrowed and there was no material on record to suggest that respondent company had taken steps to recover advances in order to revive cash flows and stability of company - Bank had also shown that there had been diversion of funds from short term sources to long term uses - It was further revealed that though there was realization of stock receivables but there had not been any corresponding reduction in working capital limits, which suggested mismanagement in affairs of company - Bank had placed on record details of adverse comments made by auditor in audited balance sheet of respondent company - Further, not only company had collected huge amount from creditors but also had failed to repay debts and facts prima facie showed that business of respondent company was being conducted to deceive its creditors - Whether material on record suggested that deeper probe in affairs of respondent company was necessary - Held, yes - Whether thus, instant petition was allowed by holding that it was a fit case to direct Central Government to take steps to investigate into affairs of respondent company - Held, yes [Para 53]CL: Where there were allegations of manipulation of accounts by company which raised inference of misappropriation and diversion of funds with intent to defraud creditors, petition to direct Central Government to take steps to investigate into affairs of company was to be allowed

Section  213  of the Companies Act, 2013 -  Investigation into affairs of company  - Respondents were shareholders of appellant company holding 10 per cent of total shareholding of company - Respondents filed a company petition before NCLT with allegations against appellant of committing oppression and mismanagement with regard to affairs of appellant company including violations of directions and guidelines issued by RBI, siphoning of funds by board of appellant company etc. - NCLT finding substance in allegations levelled by respondents took a decision of appointment of an administrator to manage functions and affairs of company - NCLT also directed investigation into affairs of appellant company - It was noted that there were serious allegations of siphoning of funds from company - Whether an order of investigation can be directed if there are prima facie evidence and satisfaction of Tribunal that there are good reasons to warrant such investigation - Held, yes -Whether to order an investigation under section 213 conclusive proof with regard to allegations was not required and it would be sufficient if Tribunal, on basis of taking into consideration material/evidence produced on record, formed an opinion subjectively to satisfy itself that there were good grounds and reasons and prima facie case to order such investigation and such satisfaction must also be reflected in order -Held,yes -Whether in instant case, sufficient satisfaction and reasons were shown by Tribunal with regard to material/evidence considered by it and same was sufficient to order investigation as contemplated under section 213 - Held, yes - Whether therefore, investigation into affairs of appellant company was to be directed - Held, yes [Para 118]

Section 213, read with section 221 of the Companies Act, 2013 - Investigation - Into company's affairs in other cases - Petitioner was buyer in real estate project developed by company 'VSPL' - Petitioner alleged that despite very damning observations made by NCLT with regard to conduct of business/affairs of company 'VSPL' by its directors, and thereby, defrauding investors, respondent i.e. Ministry of Corporate Affairs, had miserably failed to order an inquiry into such sordid affairs through SFIO - Petitioner, thus, filed instant writ, seeking directions to respondent to appoint an investigator and complete investigation under relevent provisions of law in a time bound manner - Respondent had assailed maintainability of instant writ petition on ground that High Court in Delhi had no territorial jurisdiction - It was noted that entire cause of action on part of company 'VSPL' had arisen in State of Karnataka and, hence, instant Court in Delhi had no territorial jurisdiction and merely because seat or main head office of respondent was located in Delhi would not be sufficient to confer jurisdiction upon Court in Delhi - There was no gainsaying that respondent had its Regional Office with necessary paraphernalia in State of Karnataka and, thus, petitioner had appropriate efficacious remedy to approach Karnataka High Court in order to seek appropriate reliefs - Further, there was no averment that any person or authority within territorial jurisdiction of writ Court in Delhi was substantially affected by affairs of company in question - Whether accordingly, instant writ was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 9  10]

Section 11AA of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with regulations 10 and 71 of the SEBI (Collective Investment Scheme) Regulations, 1999 - Collective Investment Scheme - Supreme Court in Subrata Chattoraj v. UOI [2014] 45 taxmann.com 200 had held specifically that investigation should be undertaken in similar cases and other companies, with reference to Sarada Investment Company and its subsidiaries - Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) conducted investigation and framed charges against petitioner company and its directors for their alleged involvement in said financial scam - Petitioner by filing instant writ sought for quashing of charge sheet on ground that it was not a party to said matter and same dealt with a chit fund scam, in respect of which it was not concerned at all - It was noted that irrespective of fact that petitioner was not party in said litigation, petitioner clearly came within broad sweep of Supreme Court's direction for investigation, since charges had been framed against petitioner long back and after due investigation, trial of case was going on at present - Further, trial of CBI case, on its completion would reveal whether source of money involved in chit fund scam and rerouting of huge sums involved could be traced to petitioner company, even if petitioner it was assumed was not a chit fund company in strict sense of terms - That apart, mere investigation by CBI, that too, when criminal proceedings were at stage of trial, could not be a violation of any legal or fundamental right of petitioners - Whether therefore, CBI investigation of petitioner and framing of charges were not vitiated in any manner and instant writ petition was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 20, 21 and 22]COMPANY LAW/SEBI : Where CBI registered a case and framed charges against petitioner company and its directors for their alleged involvement in chit fund scam and trial was going on, completion of trial would reveal whether source of money involved in chit fund scam and rerouting of huge sums involved could be traced to petitioner company and, hence, CBI investigation of petitioner and framing of charges were not vitiated in any manner

Section 433 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Circumstances in which a company may be wound up - Respondent-company had failed to file balance sheet with Registrar of Companies (RoC) for period 1998-99/ 1999-2000 and had also committed default in making payment to various investors - There were allegations against its directors to have cheated several thousands of investors, banks and financial institution, through forgery and illegal means - CBI which investigated matter recommended action for taking over possession of assets of company - Instant petition for winding up of company was filed after giving statutory notice - Petition was advertised under rule 24 of Companies (Court) Rules, 1959 to which no objection had been filed - Whether on such facts company was liable to be wound up under section 433(b), (c) and (f) - Held, yes

During the investigations made by the CBI, in the matter of default in making payment to various investors by ‘C’ Ltd., the agency registered criminal cases against directors of ‘C’ Ltd. having cheated several thousands of investors, banks and financial institutions through forgery, fraud and by corrupt/illegal business. Banks and financial institutions had filed suits before the Debt Recovery Tribunal. The respondent-company being one of the many companies, wherein directors of ‘C’ Ltd. were involved, on recommendation of CBI for taking action, the Central Government examined the matter and after giving statutory notice, sanction was given to the Registrar of Companies to file winding up petition against the respondent-company. The petition was, accordingly, filed and was advertised under rule 24 of the Companies (Court) Rules, 1959.

Section 213, read with section 241, of the Companies Act, 2013/Section 237, read with sections 397 and 398, of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation - Into company's affairs in other cases - Petitioner company holding 13.18 per cent of paid up capital of R1 company filed petition under section 397 alleging that R1 company had not utilized proceeds of IPO as per terms and conditions of IPO and diverted IPO proceeds for benefits of related entities - On contrary, R1 company also claimed that present petition was a counter-blast to petition filed under section 111(4) by R2 to R9 directors of R1 company in respect of another company where petitioner had played a fraud on stakeholders, including R1 company - It was also claimed that petitioner company was appointed as book running lead manager for IPO issue of R1 and petitioner, in process of preparation of documents for IPO, had asked R2 to sign blank letter heads and blank cheques and, after crediting IPO amount into account of R1, petitioner systematically transferred a lot of money to its associates and other companies utilizing signed blank cheques - According to respondents, petitioner did not approached NCLT with clean hands and thus, no case was made out for intervention of NCLT in affairs of company - From facts it becomes clear that both, petitioner and R2 to R9 directors had allegedly diverted funds of R1 company to their associates, thus, there existed circumstances which prima facie suggest that business of R1 company was being conducted with intent to defraud its members and amount collected through IPO had been diverted to associates by petitioner and R2 to R9 directors, which amounts to fraud played on investors - Whether in light of circumstances, it was necessary to investigate into affairs of R1 company under provisions of section 213 - Held, yes [Para 55]COMPANY LAW : Where petitioner being Lead Manager for IPO issue of company and respondent directors of company had allegedly diverted IPO proceeds of company to their associates, there existed circumstances which prima facie suggests that business of company was being conducted with an intent to defraud its members, thus, it was necessary to investigate into affairs of company under provisions of section 213

COMPANY LAW: Where respondent, claiming to be a shareholder, alleged fraudulent transfer of shares and sought investigation, Tribunal validly exercised its inherent power under rule 43 of NCLT Rules, 2016 to appoint an independent auditor for forensic examination without requiring a specific application, such power being independently vested to ensure effective justice without causing unfair prejudice to appellants

The instant application had been filed by an Ex-Director of the Company-in-liquidation to recall the order dated 13-12-2019 passed by writ Court, whereby, writ Court had directed the Special Frauds Investigating Office, to recommence the investigation into the affairs of the company-in-liquidation that was started pursuant to an order dated 18-7-2008 passed by writ Court in the said company petition. As reflected in the order dated 13-12-2019, the Official Liquidator in its Report urged that the original sale deeds of the properties of the company-in-liquidation should be directed to be produced. He had further submitted that assets of the company-in-liquidation had been transferred to other companies in a clandestine manner and therefore, it was a fit case to be referred to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for investigation into the matter. The Official Liquidator had stated that the office of the Official Liquidator did not have the resources or the expertise to undertake an investigation into the diversion of funds, etc.

Section 403, read with section 10E, of the Companies Act, 1956 - Oppression and mismanagement - Whether it would be within inherent jurisdiction of CLB to take assistance of specialized agencies where having regard to nature of information required, it may lack specific expertise or infrastructural support - Held, yes - Whether, however, such investigation is to be directed only after a case is made out of prima facie mismanagement and oppression in connection with a company in relation to subject on which investigation is being directed - Held, yes - Whether if silhouettes of irregularities appear in financial statements of a company but actual identification of such irregularities becomes impossible from available materials, directions for disclosure of particulars or other legal methods akin to discovery proceeding may be undertaken - Held, yes [Para 29]

The respondent-company had floated an investment scheme promising high return on investment. It was called 'Project Grapes' and the return mentioned in the brochure was 1025 per cent. On the basis of said scheme the company collected huge amount from public and its shareholders. The petitioners, who were shareholder of the company, filed petition stating that the investment of shareholders was totally unsafe in such company and the amount collected by the company had disappeared and, therefore, prayed that an investigation was required to be carried out.

During the investigations made by the CBI, in the matter of default in making payment to various investors by ‘C’ Ltd., the agency registered criminal cases against directors of ‘C’ Ltd. having cheated several thousands of investors, banks and financial institutions through forgery, fraud and by corrupt/illegal business. Banks and financial institutions had filed suits before the Debt Recovery Tribunal. The respondent-company was one of the companies wherein directors of ‘C’ Ltd. were involved. On recommendation of the CBI for taking action, the Central Government examined the matter and after giving statutory notice, sanction was given to the Registrar of Companies to file winding up petition against the respondent-company. The petition, was, accordingly, filed and was advertised under rule 24 of the Companies (Court) Rules, 1959.

Though the order of CLB 1 is subjective, Court can review it and can find out as to whether the circumstances relied upon existed or whether order was not mala fide : reasons cannot be added later to justify the order of investigation, Hari Ganga Cements Ltd. v. CLB (1998) 3 Comp. LJ 323 (Bom.) (DB). No requirement that there should be a proceeding pending before the Court or that the applicant should have approached the Central Government first. The shareholder’s application may be on its own arising

25.7-3 It is not necessary that for passing an order under section 237(a)( ii) there should be a proceeding already before the Court, even a petition simpliciter can be entertained and there is nothing in section 237( a)(ii) to say that a person should first approach the Central Government before coming to the Court, and even a single shareholder can approach the Court, Alembic Glass Industries Ltd., In re (1972) 42 Comp. Cas. 63 (Guj.); but in the view of Kerala High Court no investigation can be ordered merely because a shareholder feels aggrieved about the manner in which the company’s business is being carried on, Mrs. U.A. Sumathy v. Dig Vijay Chit Fund (P.) Ltd. (1983) 53 Comp. Cas. 493 (Ker.). There should be some material sufficient in terms of section 242 (any person being guilty of any offence in relation to the company involving criminal liability), 243 (in the case of a company/body corporate, its liability to be wound up on the ground ‘just and equitable’ or to be proceeded against under sections 397/398) or 244 (liability in public interest to take out proceedings on behalf of the company or body corporate whose affairs are investigated for recovery of damages for fraud/misfeasance/other misconduct in connection with its promotion, formation or management, or for recovery of any property misapplied or wrongfully retained), before an investigation can be ordered by the Court, Delhi Flour Mills Co. Ltd., In re (1975) 45 Comp. Cas. 33 (Delhi).

Court’s order in minority action

25.7-4 The order of the Court also ensues in causes of action by the minority if it is relatable to the fiduciary legal duties of the majority, Kumaranunni v. Mathrubhumi Printing & Publishing Co. Ltd. (1983) 54 Comp. Cas. 370 (Ker.). Only persons interested in the company as a member/creditor/customer can apply to the Court, V.V. Purie v. E.M.C. Steel Ltd. (1980) 50 Comp. Cas. 127 (Delhi). According to the Allahabad High Court, a declaration under section 237(a)( ii) should only be granted either where a party having applied to the Central Government for an investigation has failed despite sufficient grounds for it existing, or, when the proceeding before the Court under section 397/398 cannot satisfactorily terminate without such an investigation, Raghunath Swarup Mathur v. Har Swarup Mathur (1970) 40 Comp. Cas. 282 (All.), and V.J. Thomas Vettom v. Kuttanad Rubber Co. Ltd. (1984) 56 Comp. Cas. 284 (Ker.) on the second proposition. The powers invested in the Court under section 237(a)( ii) are limited to declare that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated which will be a direction to the Central Government to appoint the inspector(s), and it has no power to investigate itself nor to order the compliance with the provisions of the Act, and such a declaration is not a judgment determining the rights of the parties, Uunet India Ltd. v. I.C. Rao (1998) 93 Comp. Cas. 41 (AP); an order of the Court directing investigation is not a judgment and is non-appealable, N.P.S.N. Ramaiah Nadar v. N.K.R.K. Amirtharaj (1962) 32 Comp. Cas. 52 (Mad.).
