Section 11B of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with Regulation 41 of the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996 - Power to issue directions - SEBI had initiated proceedings against a wealth management firm founded by C.R. Bhansali ‘CRB Mutual Fund’ and its ex-management for multiple regulatory violations and systemic deficiencies - Pursuant to said proceedings, Bombay High Court vide an interim order had imposed embargo against making any payments to CR Bhansali and his group companies - On other hand, a Co Petition for winding up of scheme launched by CRB Capital was filed by RBI before Delhi High Court - For ensuring administrative convenience, Official Liquidator of Delhi High Court had filed a transfer petition before Supreme Court seeking to transfer both cases to Delhi and same was allowed by Supreme Court - Thereafter, Delhi Court had passed a final order constituting a Special Committee to discharge functions of trustee and to oversee procedure for formal winding up of scheme - A bare perusal of final order revealed that, surprisingly, none of parties raised issue concerning embargo imposed by interim order - As a result, final order remained silent on aspect and did not contain any discussion signifying an intention to modify or lift earlier embargo - In effect, there was neither an express affirmation nor an implied setting aside of interim restraint against payments being released to CRB and connected individuals and entities - Thereafter, a total sum of approximately Rs.350 crores was realised by Special Committee through sale of all assets of CRB Mutual Fund - Out of this, an amount of Rs.211 crore had been disbursed to approximately 5,000 unit holders / investors of scheme and out of Rs.211 crores, a substantial amount of Rs.131.9 crores (Approx.) had been paid to C.R. Bhansali and his family members - Whether priority of Special Committee ought to have been to firstly disburse to individuals, small unit holders  non CRB corporate entities and thereafter by way of abundant caution approach Court seeking clarification as to whether any disbursements ought to be made to CRB Group or not - Held, yes - Whether however, Special Committee had not sought any clarification from Court and had remained silent over years, even before instant Court, by not highlighting fact that such substantial sums have been paid to CRB Group - Held, yes - Whether in view of manner of distribution adopted by Special Committee, SEBI was to be directed to conduct of a Forensic Audit of all records, bank accounts, documents etc., pertaining to mutual fund scheme and Special Committee in accordance with law by exercising its powers under Section 11 and 11B of SEBI Act - Held, yes [Paras 89, 100, 128, 136 and 140]COMPANY LAW/SEBI : Where in winding up of mutual fund scheme, Special Committee instead of seeking clarification from Court, unilaterally made payments to CRB group i.e. individuals from CRB families, CRB group companies and related entities, SEBI was permitted to conduct forensic audit of all records, bank accounts, documents, etc. pertaining to such mutual fund scheme and Special Committee in accordance with law by exercising its powers under sections 11 and 11B of SEBI Act

Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company’s affairs in other cases - Petitioner, a shareholder of third respondent-company, being aggrieved by non-receipt of annual report and notice of extraordinary annual general meeting of company and not getting any return on his investment, filed writ petition seeking direction to first respondent to appoint a competent person as investigator for investigating affairs of company - Whether since power has been conferred on CLB to order investigation, if there are circumstances necessitating same, it was incumbent on petitioner to approach CLB and there arose no reason for exercising discretionary power vested in Company Court to order such investigation - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, writ petition was not maintainable - Held, yes

Petitioner, thus, filed instant writ, seeking directions to respondent to appoint an investigator and complete investigation under relevent provisions of law in a time bound manner - Respondent had assailed maintainability of instant writ petition on ground that High Court in Delhi had no territorial jurisdiction - There was no gainsaying that respondent had its Regional Office with necessary paraphernalia in State of Karnataka and, thus, petitioner had appropriate efficacious remedy to approach Karnataka High Court in order to seek appropriate reliefs - Further, there was no averment that any person or authority within territorial jurisdiction of writ Court in Delhi was substantially affected by affairs of company in question - Whether accordingly, instant writ was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 9  10]COMPANY LAW : Where writ petition in High Court of Delhi had been filed by petitioner seeking a direction to respondent-MCA to appoint an investigator and complete investigation under sections 213 and 221 in respect of company 'VSPL', in view of fact that company 'VSPL' had its Regional Office with necessary paraphernalia in State of Karnataka and petitioner had appropriate efficacious remedy to approach Karnataka High Court in order to seek appropriate reliefs, instant writ petition filed in Delhi High Court was to be dismissed

In the inspection conducted under section 209 against respondent-company, certain irregularities and violations of provisions of the Act were pointed out and necessary action had been initiated by the Registrar. The petitioner filed petition under section 237 seeking investigation into affairs of respondent-company on the ground that respondent-company had connection with ‘KP’ group of companies and there was also a complaint by Small Investor Protection Forum. The case of the petitioner was that as per the balance sheet of the company as on 31-12-2000, the huge funds of the company were used primarily in share market during the scam period and huge investments were made in the shares of certain companies, which was not the main object of the respondent-company; and that the management had conducted the business of the company with intent to defraud its creditors, members, etc.

The promoters/members of the respondent company filed a section 241 petition against the respondent company, alleging numerous acts of oppression and mismanagement of the affairs of the respondent by its director.

The NCLT superseded the board of directors of the respondent and appointed an administrator to carry on the functions of the respondent.

The administrator submitted an interim application before the NCLT requesting the director of the respondent to make available all the documents of the respondent but the director failed to submit the same.

Since the directors were not co-operating with the administrator, he appointed a chartered accountant to review the available books of account and other available records of the respondent and a report was submitted by the chartered accountant listing out the irregularities noticed, to the administrator and the same was placed before the NCLT.

The NCLT passed the impugned order directing Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) to investigate the affairs of the respondent.

The RoC assailing the validity and the legality of the impugned order filed the instant appeal, contending that the NCLT without considering the ingredients of sections 210 & 212 passed the same and only the Central Government was authorized to accord sanction to initiate an investigation against the company and its officers who were in default as per section 210.

Section 12(1B) of the Securities & Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 - Collective Investment Scheme - About 37,000 Plantation Companies collected approximately Rs. 25,000 crores from poor investors - Investors having no platform for redressing, instant writ under public interest litigation was filed - By its earlier interim orders instant High Court empowered SEBI to publish advertisement for investors, stating non- viability of plantation companies in India - State Government was also directed to issue notices to all revenue officers to prevent transfer of agricultural land in favour of plantation companies - Court also ordered inquiry by police into affairs of such companies with assistance of SEBI and order attachment of assets of directors, promoters, etc., - It also further expected that proper Investor Protection Act be made by Central/State Government - During final hearing it was brought to notice that State Government decided to promulgate ordinance to protect interest of investors and SEBI had constituted a Committee to draft appropriate regulations -Whether in view of above no purpose would be served in keeping pending writ petition and same was to be disposed of with direction to Government to implement earlier directions and earlier interim orders would be in operation until promulgation of impugned ordinance - Held, yes

Section 213 of the Companies Act, 2013 - Investigation -  Into company's affairs in other cases - Petitioners, buyers of real estate units in project namely 'VSPL Pinnacle' developed by respondent company/filed a petition under section 213 alleging that despite having right to said only 82,216.30 sq. ft., respondent had sold an area of 2,43,037 sq. ft. which was almost 3 times of area, which company was entitled to sell - According to petitioner, by making fraudulent sales, which was almost three times, it was apparent that affairs of company had been conducted to commit fraud and cheating with buyers - Petitioners had given specific list of 164 such Sale Deeds/Agreement to Sell, along with details such as Date of Execution, name of Buyers, Sub-Registrar Document No. etc. - There was also an allegation of siphoning of funds arising from these sales by promoters of company and, thus, according to petitioners there was urgent need to conduct enquiry into affairs of company to track funds diverted from company - Respondent had not addressed to any of allegations of these irregularities and not responded to documents along with list of irregular sales listed in Company Petition, instead submitted that it was ordered to be liquidated and RP was appointed as Liquidator and liquidation process of company was still in progress and, therefore, petitioner could not seek to circumvent liquidation process and try to initiate parallel investigative proceedings against respondent - It was noted that investigation under section 213 is possible in respect of company which is undergoing process of liquidation - Whether therefore, exercising powers under section 213, instant petition was to be allowed - Held, yes [Paras 18 and 19]

COMPANY LAW/SEBI : Where investigation by SEBI revealed that companies floated by petitioner were involved in illegal mobilization of funds, which was in nature of Collective Investment Scheme and petitioner filed instant writ seeking directions to SEBI to liquidate attached assets for purpose of refund monies to investors, said petition was to be allowed and High-Powered Sale Committee (HPSC) was to be constituted to auction immovable assets of companies

Section 237(b) of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company's affairs - Whether power under section 237(b) is a discretionary power - Held, yes -Whether, when justifiable grounds exist, merely because communication from Department of Company Affairs to Secretary, CLB, was in form of letter without any proper affidavit and without any specific mention as to what action was prayed for, CLB should refuse to exercise jurisdiction under section 237(b) - Held, no - Whether investigation is to be ordered if a prima facie opinion is formed by CLB that business of company is being/has been conducted with intent to defraud creditors, members or any other persons or conduct of company is oppressive to any of its members or there is misfeasance or misconduct on part of management in carrying on affairs of company - Held, yes - Whether, where report filed by Regional Director in Department of Company Affairs under section 209A on complaints made by Employees' Union alleging mismanagement of affairs of company, established mismanagement of funds of company, further enquiry by ROC had to be ordered - Held, yes

Having allowed the inspector to conduct an enquiry extending full co-operation to him without challenging his appointment, it is not given to the company on the inspector rendering an adverse report against the company to challenge the decision on the investigation through a writ petition, Titagarh Paper Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1986) 59 Comp. Cas. 94 (Cal.).

Inspector’s Report 25.7-15 The Inspector may, and if so directed by the Central Government shall, make interim reports to it, and a final report on conclusion of the investigation; and such reports shall be admissible as evidence of the opinion of the Inspectors in any legal proceeding on any matter contained in them. It is not obligatory on the Central Government to prescribe the manner of making the inspector’s report or fix the time-limit of its submission, New Central Jute Mills Co. Ltd. v. Deputy Secretary, Ministry of Finance (1966) 36 Comp. Cas. 512 (Cal.).

25.7-15a Duty of Central Government to send copy of report to company - It is the duty of the Central Government to forward a copy of the final report to the company investigated as well as the applicants under section 235 (2) if the Inspectors were appointed at their instance, or, to the Court/Tribunal, and may also cause it to be published, or copies supplied to any member or creditor of the company or the entities dealt in the report. DCA publishes such reports only selectively in public interest as the report is a privileged document within the meaning of sections 123 and 124 of the Indian Evidence Act, Swadeshi Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Swadeshi Polytex (1982) 52 Comp. Cas. 483 (All).

25.7-16 Prosecution or winding up and proceedings for recovery of damages or property [Sections 242 & 243/244]

25.7-16a Prosecution - If it appears from the report, whether interim or final, to the Central Government that any person has been guilty of any offence attaching criminal liability, it may launch prosecution under section 242 against such person, and in that event, it becomes the duty of all officers, employees and agents of the company/other body corporate [other than the accused and as defined in section 240(6)] to give all assistance to the Central Government. Section 242 does not offend against Article 20(3) or Article 14 of the Constitution, Raja Narayan Bansilal v. Maneck Phiroz Mistry (1960) 30 Comp. Cas. 644 (SC), and section 242 does not divest the jurisdiction of a police officer under section 154, 156 or 157 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, M. Vaidyanathan v. Sub-Divisional Magistrate (1957) 27 Comp. Cas. 97 (Mad.); section 242 does not require a hearing to be given to the company before launch of prosecution, Titagarh Paper Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1986) 59 Comp. Cas. 94 (Cal.).

25.7-16b Act does not exclude CrPC - There is nothing in the Companies Act to exclude the Code of Criminal Procedure and the police in respect of cognizable offences under the Indian Penal Code committed in relation to the company’s affairs, Indian Express (Madurai) (P.) Ltd. v. Chief Presidency Magistrate (1974) 44 Comp. Cas. 106 (Mad.)

25.7-16c Winding up of the company - If from the Inspector’s report it appears to the Central Government that it is expedient to wind up the company or body corporate—if it is liable to be wound up under the Act—by reason of (a) the existence of circumstances that the company’s business was being conducted with intent to defraud the members/creditors or others or for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose or in a manner oppressive of any of its members, or if the company was formed for any fraudulent or unlawful purpose, or (b ) the persons connected with its formation or management of its affairs have been guilty of fraud, misfeasance or other misconduct towards the company or its members, the Central Government may cause a petition/application to be filed before the Tribunal for winding up on the ground that it is just and equitable or for an order under section 397/398 regarding oppression and mismanagement or for both. Under section 203, the persons found to be fraudulent may be restrained from being a director, promoter or manager of a company up to five years, by the Tribunal. However, the privileged communications or information in the possession of legal advisors and bankers, though they may be related to the matters covered by the investigation, are immune from disclosure, section 251.

25.7-16-1 RECOVERY OF DAMAGES OR PROPERTY [SECTION 244] - If warranted in public interest in the opinion of the Central Government on perusal of the Inspector’s report, that any proceedings should be initiated for the recovery of damages or property due to any fraud, misfeasance or other misconduct in connection with the promotion or management of the affairs of the company or body corporate investigated, the Central Government may itself bring the proceedings for the purpose.

Section 456 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Custody of company’s property - Respondent-company had collected huge sums of money by way of deposits from general public and by utilizing money so collected, various assets had been acquired by it which included land whereon superstructure had been constructed for housing registered office of company - Applicants’ case was that respondent-company had become nearly insolvent and with a view to tide over its financial distress, it, through one of its directors, viz., ‘D’, sold said land together with building standing thereon to applicants - Certain payment was made by applicants as advance and balance was to be paid at time of registration - Applicants contended that receipt of said balance amount and consequential execution of sale deed were delayed on one pretext or other and, therefore, they filed suit seeking specific performance of agreement of sale - Immediately, a compromise memo was filed before Court and, consequently, matter was referred to Lok Adalat which passed a decree duly recording compromise between parties - In terms of compromise decree, balance amount was paid and sale deed was executed - Subsequently, applicants entered into an agreement of sale of said property with ‘V’ - In meantime, respondent-company was ordered to be wound up on applications by some depositors of company to whom company had not repaid their deposits and possession of said property was taken over by Official Liquidator - Hence, applicants moved instant application seeking property to be released from custody of Official Liquidator on ground that title over property had been transferred by company in favour of applicants by way of sale deed executed between parties - It was found that market value of property was much higher than value for which property was offered for sale to applicants - There was no resolution passed by board of directors of company, in accordance with provisions contained in section 291, for undertaking sale of any of asset of company - No publicity was ever issued by company or by its directors for intended sale of said asset - It was not explained as to how applicants came to know of impending sale of said asset and how they got property valued before entering into transaction - There was no authorization issued by company in favour of ‘D’ to enter into a compromise or enter into a transaction of sale at first instance with applicants - Sale consideration was paid in cash instead of secured instruments like cheques or demand drafts and no entries were found in books of company about receipt of said amount - Applicants failed to demonstrate their financial capacity to have pooled up such a huge sum at one go, to pay to respondent in cash - Thousands of complaints had been lodged with police at various places in State by depositors alleging fraud and misrepresentation indulged in by respondent-company - Whether, on facts, it could be said that entire transaction was vitiated by fraud played by applicants on District Court as well as on Lok Adalat and ‘D’ on behalf of respondent-company had joined hands with them - Held, yes - Whether since no right or interest or title can ever pass in favour of beneficiary of fraud and further, no action can be maintained which is founded in fraud, decree passed by Lok Adalat pursuant to a compromise entered into by and between parties therein in civil suit on file of Additional District Judge was to be declared as a nullity - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, no rights of any kind would ever pass to hands of applicants vis-a-vis property in question owned and belonging to company and, as such, application filed by them was to be dismissed - Held, yes

Section 213 of the Companies Act, 2013/Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 read with rule 11 of the Companies (Court) Rules, 1959 - Investigation of Company's affairs in other cases - Petitioner shareholders had subscribed to shares in respondent-company based on assurance that they would get good returns on their shares and that their shares would also be listed on other stock exchanges - However, petitioners alleged that from beginning they had not received notice from respondent-company regarding convening of Annual General Meetings or Extraordinary General Meetings and were also not informed of any major activities of company like amalgamation, listing and de-listing of shares - Hence, court appointed chartered accountants to look into affairs of company to understand seriousness of allegations made by petitioners - However, respondents did not comply with directions given by Court to furnish relevant particulars to chartered accountants - Whether, conduct of business of respondent-company was oppressive to its members and non-cooperation of respondent-company with chartered accountants, despite series of orders of Court, clearly showed that respondents intended to thwart attempts of Court to do substantial justice to either parties - Held, yes - Whether facts, as presented, clearly made out a case for Court to direct Central Government to order investigation into affairs of respondent-company, more particularly in view of fact that respondent-company had not furnished information in respect of its affairs, which it was reasonably expected to furnish - Held, yes [Para 15]CL: Where respondent-company had not furnished information in respect of its affairs, to Chartered Accountants appointed by Court which it was reasonably expected to furnish, Central Government was to be directed to order investigation into affairs of respondent-company

During the year 2013, the respondent company 'V' entered into an arrangement with owners of a parcel of land measuring 41,702.873 sq. ft. to develop a commercial building upon the same.

In furtherance of the same, the Company developed the Property in the name of 'VSPL Pinnacle'. The Parties to the Agreement i.e., the Company and the Owners of the Land, to identify their respective shares in the building 'VSPL Pinnacle', executed a further Agreement in form of Supplementary Agreement whereby the Parties identified their respective shares in the Property in forms of total area available to them and their floor-wise locations. Accordingly, in terms of Supplementary Agreement the Company got an area of 82,216.30 sq. ft. in its share and the Owners got the same area in their share.

It was stated that with start of the Project, the company through its Directors started allotting and selling the Property in the Project to different Buyers of Commercial Units available on the said Project. Accordingly, the Company through its Directors convinced many buyers including the Petitioners to purchase the commercial property in the said Project and entered into Agreements to Sell whereby the Company undertook to sell and, in most cases, sold various commercial units to the Buyers.

From the above, it was apparent that the Company and its Directors have sold total area of 2,43,037 sq. ft. in 'VSPL Pinnacle', whereas the total available area in the Project was only 1,64,432 sq. ft. out of which the company had the right to sell only 82,216.30 sq. ft. Floor-wise details of total area available to the Company.

According to petitioners the affairs of the Company had been conducted to commit fraud and cheating with the ignorant buyers. By making fraudulent sales of the Property, which was almost three times the total area available for sale to the Company, the Company had collected a total sum of Rs. 136 crores by executing 164 Sale Deeds or Agreement to Sell to different persons and collected the abovementioned amount as sale consideration from them. In addition to the said amount the Company and its said Directors had collected huge amounts of money in cash also. In light of such conduct of affairs of the Company, there was urgent need to conduct enquiry into affairs of the Company and to freeze the assets of the Company, its Directors and the related Parties so that they did not conceal, dilute and divest the assets of the Company to make them unavailable for settlement of claims of the Creditors of the Company in terms of section 221 of the Companies Act, 2013.

Petitioner also stated that the affairs of the Company have not been conducted to do real estate business as mentioned in the Memorandum of Association but to collect huge amounts and thereafter to siphon them off. The Company and its Directors having malicious intention to cheat and defraud the purchasers have not only sold the area of 2,43,037 sq. ft. instead of 82,216.30 sq. ft. area available for sale, and collected money as stated supra. The money and assets of the Company have been so diverted that it is left with no funds to settle the claims of its Creditors, in case the liability is determined upon the Company.

Therefore, enquiry into affairs of the Company was required to be conducted to track funds diverted from the Company. The affairs of the Company had been conducted to defraud its Creditors/Buyers of the Units by conducting acts of forgery of the Sale Deed/Agreement to Sale. The Company, its Directors and connected persons have further committed offences under section 447 of the Companies Act, 2013.

This Petition had been filed by petitioners under sections 213 and 221 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with rules 11 and 74 of the National Company Law Tribunal Rules, 2016 seeking a direction for investigation into the affairs of the respondent company and those of the related parties.

In response to above, respondent company had filed his reply:

(a)

Vide order that NCLT had initiated the CIRP of the Company and appointed the RP for conducting the CIRP of Company.

(b)

Thus, on account of Company undergoing CIRP, all proceedings against company were hit by a moratorium under section 14 of the Code. Thus, any legal proceedings against company would automatically be not maintainable.

Petitioners company at three locations had been subjected to sealing by State Authorities.

Petitioner contended that impugned action of State Authorities was without any authority of law and as such impugned action was liable to be quashed leading to unsealing of business premises of petitioners company.

It was, however, disclosed on behalf of the petitioners that Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) vide an order dated 3-5-2011, had directed the petitioners company to wind up their operation and ensure return of the investors' money within a period of 3 months. Admittedly, the petitioners had not able to return the investors money by now. In the meantime, the petitioners' business premises had been sealed. Petitioners submitted that the final order of the SEBI, which had been brought on record, was under challenge in Kolkata High Court. However SEBI submitted that there was no interim protection granted to the petitioners in the said case and SEBI was fully entitled to take all steps as were available under the Act of 1992.

SEBI appeared on notice and vehemently submitted that the writ petitions should be dismissed at the outset as the petitioners had not come with clean hands and were in admitted breach of the final orders of the SEBI directing them to wind up their operations and ensure return of the investors' money within stipulated time which had elapsed much long ago.

It was further submitted that petitioners should be subjected to jurisdiction of the SEBI to undertake proper recourses available in law for refund of the investor's money by taking steps as were available in law.

Respondent submitted that the impugned actions had been taken only to ensure protection of the interest of investors, who admittedly appeared to have been duped by the petitioners and their money was not being returned in spite of the direction of the SEBI. Respondent also submitted that there was an F.I.R. registered in respect of one of the petitioners' Branch Office with an allegation that they were still in business despite the orders of SEBI. However, the petitioners were required to be subjected to the jurisdiction of the SEBI and SEBI was also entitled to take any action which were permissible in law under the Act of 1992 for ensuring the protection of the investors money and also for winding up operation of the business of such a company which was apparently operating in breach of the SEBI direction.

Section 11 of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 - Powers and functions of board - Pursuant to Saradha Chit Fund scam Inspector General of Registration and Commissioner of Stamp Revenue imposed restrictions on sale of properties owned by petitioner-agro company - SEBI in its report indicated violation of several provisions, including petitioner company having resorted to obtaining funds from public without either applying for mandatory listing or having its offer documents vetted by appropriate authorities - Whether in view of SEBI's report, appropriate authorities were to be directed to take steps in accordance with law against petitioners and, particularly, officers of petitioner-company responsible for multiple defaults - Held, yes - Whether there would be an order of injunction restraining petitioner-company from dealing with or disposing of or alienating or encumbering any of its assets without previous leave of the SEBI and SEBI leave should not be granted without an Executive Director of SEBI approving same - Held, yes - Whether petitioners could cause all or any of their assets or properties be sold under aegis of SEBI under any asset sale committee that might be set up by SEBI for purpose of refund of money which had been illegally obtained from depositors - Held, yes [Paras 4, 5  6]SEBI: Petitioner agro company was restrained from dealing with or disposing of its assets without previous leave of SEBI on basis of report of SEBI indicating violation of various provisions of SEBI Act

Section 58A of the Companies Act, 1956 - Public deposits - First petitioner, along with his family members, by floating a company, received heavy deposits but did not return any amount to depositors on maturity -Petitioner diverted and misused funds so collected for purchase of various assets - RBI had also refused to grant registration certificate for operating as non-banking financial institution because of petitioner having grossly violated norms - Interim orders/directions of court were grossly violated inasmuch as petitioner did not comply with direction to deposit amount in depositors' account opened for that purpose - Whether in such circumstances and in order to see that such companies did not defraud innocent depositors, State Government should set up a separate cell for making discreet enquiries in respect of all such NBFCs, seizing their properties and assets, ensuring payments to depositors either in full or on pro rata basis and initiating prosecution against all offenders - Held, yes -Whether State Government should order immediate investigation by CBCID in respect of petitioner-company and launch prosecution under various criminal and other laws against promoters including past directors and other connected persons - Held, yes - Whether RBI should also initiate criminal proceedings and take steps - Held, yes

Section 397, read with section 398, of the Companies Act, 1956 - Oppression and mismanagement - Whether object of section 397 is not to rake up past but to redeem future and power of CLB under section 397/398, is primarily intended for preventive purposes - Held, yes - Petitioner and respondent Nos. 2 to 5 were directors of respondent-company which had obtained a contract for processing and filling of aravana prasadam in composite cans by using modern technologies at Sri Ayappa Temple, Sabarimala which was under governance of respondent No. 6 and accordingly entered into an agreement with latter in April 1999 - Under said agreement, company was required, to fill prepared aravana prasadam in cans and supply to devotees for a period of eight years at rates specified therein which would be payable by respondent No. 6 - Petitioners collectively holding in excess of 10 per cent of issued share capital of respondent-company filed petition invoking provisions of sections 397, 398 and 402 wherein main grievance of petitioners was that respondent Nos. 2 to 5 had mismanaged affairs of respondent-company and had misappropriated receivables realised from respondent No. 6 for their personal benefits without settling dues of banks, financial institutions, suppliers and other creditors - It was seen from records that respondents had not furnished any particulars regarding actual receivables and utilization of such receivables excepting a bald statement that liabilities of banks, financial institutions and suppliers had been settled from and out of receivables realised from respondent No. 6 - Whether conduct of respondent Nos. 2 to 5 lacked in probity, which was unfair to petitioners causing prejudice to them in exercise of their legal and proprietary rights as shareholders - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, a chartered accountant was to be appointed to scrutinize and verify books of account, vouchers and other connected accounts of respondent-company since its inception till date and respondent Nos. 2 to 5 were to be directed to reimburse, in favour of company, moneys, if any found diverted on verification by chartered accountant, from receivables realised from respondent No. 6 - Held, yes

Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company affairs in other cases -  Under section 237(a)( ii), power of Court is invoked for directing Central Government to order investigation by concerned inspectors

Section 11B of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 - Powers and functions of board - Power to issue directions - SEBI suggested that a chartered accountant be appointed to look into deposits obtained by petitioner-company before SEBI approved final list and determined mode of payment - Accordingly, a chartered accountant was appointed for purpose of identifying depositors who had put in deposits with petitioner-company and quantum of deposits - Whether petitioner-company was to be directed to furnish a comprehensive list of its immovable properties alongwith copies of title deeds to SEBI with an affidavit affirmed by principal person in control of petitioner-company that there was no other immovable property directly or indirectly owned or controlled by petitioner-company - Held, yes - Whether petitioners would also furnish to SEBI particulars of bank accounts of petitioner-company including amounts standing to credit of petitioner-company therein - Held, yes [Paras 6  7]SEBI : Direction to company to furnish comprehensive list of its immovable properties and particulars of bank accounts to SEBI before SEBI approved final list of depositors and determined mode of payment

COMPANY LAW : Where petitioner being Lead Manager for IPO issue of company and respondent directors of company had allegedly diverted IPO proceeds of company to their associates, there existed circumstances which prima facie suggests that business of company was being conducted with an intent to defraud its members, thus, it was necessary to investigate into affairs of company under provisions of section 213

Facts

Four appellant companies, limited by shares, applied for sanction of scheme of amalgamation.

Raising objection on the share-exchange ratio, etc. the Central Government sought clarification, which the appellants failed to clarify satisfactorily.

The Central Government raised objection on ground that each of the appellants had issued shares with high premium which was highly disproportionate to the authorized capital as a means of evading duty.

The Court, therefore, directed that investigation in the affairs of the companies to be carried out by the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence.

The Division Bench, upheld the direction to carry out investigation.

The Companies, later on, withdraw its scheme. The Company Judge imposed costs of Rs. 17,000 and restrained these companies from filing such application for 5 years.

Against such orders of the Court, the companies went in appeal challenging cost imposed as well as on restraint order and direction for conducting investigations by a named agency.

Arguments of appellant

Under section 237 the Court, only on an application made therefor, can direct investigation to be carried out by the Central Government.

Naming an agency is overstepping the statutory power.

Share issue at premium is not prohibited in law and, thus, the Central Government could not have raised objections on it.

No litigant could be restrained from initiating any proceedings in accordance with law as per section 41(b), specific Relief Act, 1963.

Arguments of Central Government

Company's share exchange ratio was unusual and queries on it were not properly answered.

In case of share capital increase, it was entitled to appropriate duty that was evaded through issuance of shares with premium value.

Order of investigation was justified.

Issue Involved

Whether the investigation ordered by Court is to be continued and Court had named the agency correctly?

The case of the revision petitioners was that the first revision petitioner, being a foreign company, had applied to the Reserve Bank of India and as a matter of fact had applied to a foreign bank to invest in the share capital of the first respondent-company. Thereafter, the said foreign company had sent money by way of an inward remittance on two occasions totalling a sum of Rs. 5,87,00,000. After receipt of money, the first respondent/plaintiff-company had filed a return in Form II and had obtained certificates from the statutory auditor and the company secretary disclosing that the first respondent-company had allotted 5,87,000 shares to the first revision petitioner. The revision petitioners further submitted that within a month from the date of receipt of inward remittance by the first respondent-company, it had to allot shares to the first revision petitioner and, therefore, in accordance with the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 the first respondent-company had filed its return in the FGR Form. Out of the funds remitted by the first revision petitioner, the first respondent-company had purchased a land for a sum of Rs. 3,25,00,000 but the revision petitioners were not posted with information. The revision petitioners contended that to deprive the revision petitioners' investment in share capital of company, the second respondent and his family members had fabricated records as if no allotment was made to the first revision petitioner. The first respondent had also filed a suit filed before the civil court and obtained an interim injunction regarding fact that no shares had been allotted to the first revision petitioner.

On revision petition, the revision petitioners contended that the fraud had been played on the Court by the respondents as they had not disclosed either in the plaint or in the affidavit that the identical issue was pending before the CLB; that the order of the trial Court granting interim injunction was a non-speaking one and, therefore, the High Court could exercise its revisional powers under article 227 of the Constitution to set aside the same to promote substantial cause of justice. The respondent, however, submitted that the petitioners had got a remedy of appeal, in law, before the appropriate forum if they were aggrieved against the order of the trial court and, therefore, prayed for dismissal of the revision petition.

Petitioner Nos. 1 and 2 were the founder-directors of Company. The petitioners also floated various other companies, known as the Sai Group of Companies.

The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) received a complaint alleging illegal mobilisation of funds by companies floated by petitioners. After processing the said complaint and in furtherance of the orders passed by the High Court and the Department of Financial Services, Ministry of Finance, the SEBI (WTM) issued an interim order-cum-show cause notice inter alia, directing companies and its directors to refrain from collecting any more money from investors, under the existing schemes or any new schemes.

In addition, proceedings under Chapter VI-A of the SEBI Act, 1992 were also initiated, and an Adjudicating Officer was appointed to inquire into the violations.

Recovery proceedings for a sum of Rs. 30.56 crores were initiated; and all the immovable properties and jewelleries owned by the aforesaid companies were attached.

Thereafter, a series of FIRs were registered. Most of these FIRs had been registered under sections 406, 420 and 34 of IPC read with sections 3, 4, 5, 6 and 10 of the Prize Chits Act and section 3 of the Maharashtra Protection of Interest of Depositors (In Financial Establishment) Act, 1999 (MPID Act) and petitioner were arrested.

Petitioners' filed instant writ with a prayer seeking a direction to SEBI to liquidate the attached assets in a time-bound manner and disburse the sale proceeds to genuine investors as early as possible. In this regard, SEBI noted that the Forensic Audit conducted by the Economic Offence Wing (EOW) revealed that the companies floated by the petitioners were liable to refund Rs. 4700 crores, though as per the order passed by the SEBI the refund amount was initially Rs. 3049 crores only. It was also not in dispute that there were 498+13 immovable properties owned by the companies; the details whereof had been furnished before the MPID Court, Mumbai. The parties were broadly ad idem that the entire liability of each company regarding refund of the due amount to all the investors as well as various statutory, foreseen or unforeseen liabilities, could be extinguished from the sale proceeds of some of the immovable properties, if not all of them.

Since the immovable properties owned by the companies were spread over different parts of the country, it was sensed unachievable for either the SEBI or the MPID Court to liquidate all these assets through time-bound public auctions, for the reason that the process postulates various complex questions such as:

(i)

What was the exact location of the immovable property in metes and bounds;

(ii)

Whether or not such property was free from encumbrances;

(iii)

Whether the physical possession of the subject-property was with one of the companies or not;

(iv)

Whether any civil dispute regarding the title/ownership of such property was pending before a competent forum;

(v)

What was the market value of the property in the event of its sale in a transparent manner;

(vi)

Was there any lien of statutory tax, levy, duty, or any other charge attached to such property;

(vii)

What mechanism shall be evolved for the sale of each property, so as to fetch the best price; and

(viii)

What was the mandatory procedure to be followed in terms of local laws for the purpose of registration of the auctioned property and its mutation in favour of the auction purchaser, etc.

The company-in-liquidation, which was a ‘Nidhi’ started by the appellant, collapsed after collecting huge amounts of deposits from the public at large under certain schemes. On winding up petitions preferred by the affected persons, the Company Judge appointed an administrator, besides the Official Liquidator, to look into the affairs of the company. Since the Company Judge also made an observation to the effect that there was prima facie fraud of massive proportions having been committed by the appellants along with other board members of company-in-liquidation, the administrator appointed by the Court filed an application under sections 542 and 543 seeking for a declaration that those persons were liable to be prosecuted for the fraudulent diversion of the funds. The appellant contested the application denying all the allegations and also raised the question of maintainability of the same, but the Company Judge, while passing penal order against the appellant, also held that the application preferred by the administrator was maintainable.

On appeal to the Division Bench :

The petitioners were the shareholders of the respondent No. 1 company. They alleged that the directors of the respondent No.1-company and its ex-promoters had committed various acts of fraud, cheating, oppression, mismanagement, misfeasance, etc. It was submitted that (i) out of three persons presently acting as board of directors, tenure of two had already completed and, therefore, their act to continue as regular directors was violative of articles of company and also the company failed to maintain a quorum of minimum three directors as required under section 252; (ii) the company and its directors failed to convene and hold the annual general meeting continuously for seven years; (iii) the company failed to submit the annual returns with the Registrar of Companies, due to non-finalisation of annual accounts and, thus, there was contravention of sections 159, 166, 210 and 220; (iv) the directors failed to appoint a whole time company secretary as per the procedure laid down in section 383A; (v) the directors misused the company funds for personal gain, etc. (vi) the directors' report was silent on important issues such as comments on the qualifications in audit report, directors' responsibility statement, proper reasons for non-conducting of seven years' annual general meeting, etc. (vii) the directors sold some of property of company to different firms overlooking encumbrances of Court receiver and other secured creditors in those properties.

6. The Indian Financial Code, drafted by the Financial Sector Legislative Commission, would address these issues in the following ways:

The whole system of investigation is formalised under an investigator appointed by the regulator. The terms of reference for the investigator, the system of investigation and the time for investigation have to be written down at the onset. Since all incomplete investigations will require extensions, there will be system of raising alarms for an unusually long investigation – (see draft clause 394 of the IFC). The Code would allow the investigator to apply for a warrant for the search and seizure of documents. The investigator does not have to go to the area where the scheme is operating. He can apply for a warrant to the Magistrate where the head office of the regulator is situated. This allows the government to create a special Magistrate's office. This Magistrate can be trained in issues of finance and fraud and serve as a proper judicial check for warrants (see draft clause 396 of the IFC).

The Code also allows the financial agency to make an order preventing transfer of any money or assets pending an investigation, if there is a reasonable fear that the assets of clients are at risk. Any violation of such orders is also punishable by imprisonment up to five years (see draft clause 398 of the IFC).

The Code empowers the Central Government to set-up special Courts to try cases involving the violation of investment laws. This allows for far quicker and more efficient disposal of cases. These Courts will be district Courts and would follow all due process of law required under the Evidence Act and the Criminal Procedure Code. However, unlike general Criminal Courts, Judges in these Courts can be experts in securities and investment laws (see draft clause 417 of the IFC).

Finally, the Code envisages that the financial sector regulator appoints its own lawyers to prosecute cases of criminal offences. These lawyers will have the same powers as a prosecuting lawyers under the criminal procedure law. Since most financial regulators have legal officers on staff today, this allows specialised expertise to head the prosecution of these crimes, rather than a generalist public prosecutor.

The strategy used in the IFC is similar to that used in securities laws in the U.S., where dedicated federal Court benches are used to prosecute securities frauds. Even in India, special Courts and prosecutors have been created for the CBI and for prosecution of offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act. The longer a Ponzi scheme lingers on the more victims it would accumulate. The Indian Financial Code provides a system to effectively shut down schemes like these ones and a specialised criminal law system to prosecute violators.

The loss of critical savings by many people have raised demand for retribution. A hurried response to such demands can be bringing in laws which dilute the principle of 'innocent until proved guilty' or reduce the procedural and evidentiary standards. The Code scrupulously avoids this by placing the power of issuing warrants and convicting offences on the same standards as are envisaged in the laws of evidence and criminal procedure. However, it addresses the problems of a slow judicial system and dedicated expertise in resolving financial crimes.

Defining financial products and services

7. In the IFC, the definitions of financial products and services are broad ones and principles-based, with no statutory exemptions. All kinds of deposit-taking and investment schemes (including chit funds) are covered by these definitions. A deposit is defined as a contribution of money, made other than for the purpose of acquiring a security, which may be re-payable on the demand of the contributor. In section 2(90), an investment scheme means following:

"any arrangement with respect to property of any description, including money, the purpose or effect of which is to enable persons taking part in the arrangement, whether by becoming owners of the property or any part of it or otherwise, to participate in or receive profits or income arising from the acquisition, holding, management or disposal of the property or sums paid out of such profits or income, where:

persons participating in such schemes do not have day-to-day control over the management of the property, whether or not they have the right to be consulted or to give directions; and

the arrangement has either or both of the following characteristics:

the contributions of the participants and the profits or income out of which payments are to be made to them are pooled; or

the property is managed as a whole by or on behalf of the operator of the scheme."

Anyone in the business of accepting deposits or managing investment schemes would need to get authorisation from the UFA. Accordingly, both Saradha and MMM would be covered under the IFC, the former as a deposit-taking firm, and the latter one as an investment scheme. In case of the MMM scheme, a unit of MAVRO is the underlying property in which the members invest in. The other tests of the definition are also met as the member of the scheme do not have the ability to control the unit, which is managed by the operators of the scheme.

The IFC also empowers the Central Government to expand the definitions of financial products and services. When a new financial product or service is taken note of, instead of waiting for an amendment to the law, the Central Government can include the new product or service in the definition.

25.6 Section 234 assigns the role of a watch-dog of corporate affairs of companies to the Registrar, and for the purpose empowers him to call for any information or explanation in writing from any company as required by him in his opinion formed on perusing any document filed with him in compliance with the requirements of the Act. He can exercise the same power, also, on a representation or complaint received from any contributory or creditor or any other person interested in the company alleging that the business of the company is being carried on fraudulently. In relation to the Registrar’s demand for furnishing the specified information and explanations, a duty is cast statutorily on the companies requiring prompt response to the best of the power of the officers of the company, present and past. Any refusal, failure, negligence or deficiency in furnishing the information or explanations within the time stipulated by the Registrar in his demand leads to his issuing another such demand by way of an order calling for the production of books and papers before him for his inspection within the time specified in his order which the company and its officers are enjoined to comply by the provision in the section. If his order is neglected or refused, it attracts fine up to five thousand rupees plus five hundred rupees for each day of continuing non-compliance for the company and its officers in default if the Registrar prosecutes for the offence and imposition of the said fine as well as for the conversion of his demand for information or explanations or the production of the books and papers into an order of the Court, with due notice to the accused. On the Court passing its order against the accused company and it furnishing the information or explanation, the Registrar is entitled to record a note or attach any reply or paper received from the company to the relevant document while taking it on record, which means that it shall be open for public inspection which otherwise it is not.

Registrar's report to Central Government

25.6-1 If the information or explanation or the books and papers thus received by the Registrar when perused along with the document, if the overall disclosure falls short of a fair statement of any matter to which the document relates or it reveals an unsatisfactory state of the company’s affairs, the Registrar is bound to make a report in writing to the Central Government in terms of section 234(6) or (7), or conversely, if he concludes that the complaint received on which he raised the demand against the company is frivolous or vexatious, he shall inform the company accordingly disclosing the identity of the informant. This procedure is equally applicable to documents filed by the liquidator or by the foreign companies with the Registrar. Further, section 234A empowers the Registrar to carry out search and seizure of documents in a similar way that the Inspector appointed by the Central Government to investigate into the affairs of a company can do, discussed below.

25.7 (1) Group Action: Under section 235(2) any group of not less than two hundred members or the group holding not less than one-tenth of the total voting power in the company having a share capital, or, in the case of the company having no share capital, the group not less in number than one-fifth of the persons on the company’s register of members, is entitled to present an application to the CLB 1/Tribunal, on the basis of such supporting evidence requisite to make out a good reason for the application made seeking the CLB 1 /Tribunal’s order declaring that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated by the Inspector(s)—competent individuals, that is, either the officials of DCA or Chartered Accountants—appointed by the Central Government and to report thereon to the Central Government. The CLB 1/Tribunal after giving an opportunity to the parties of being heard may pass the order accordingly, and thereupon the Central Government may require the applicants to give a security of not exceeding one thousand rupees as is fixed by it towards the costs of investigation (section 236) before appointing an Inspector. For the group action, the catch is in section 236 which lays down that such an application shall be supported by such evidence as the CLB/Tribunal may require to make out a case for investigation, and if such evidence is insisted upon to be one on the lines of section 237( b)(i), (ii) and (iii ) it will in all probability amount for the outsider group insurmountable, as we shall see in (3) below.

(2) Action by Company/Order of Court [Section 237 (a)] : Without prejudice to the power conferred under section 235, the Central Government has been vested with the power to appoint inspector(s) to investigate a company’s affairs forked in a two-way mode—one compulsory and the other optional under section 237(a) and (b), [the optional mode discussed in (3) below]. The compulsory mode under section 237(a) is again divided into two kinds, one the company passing a special resolution, and the other the High Court declaring that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated by an inspector appointed by the Central Government, under section 237(a)(ii ), in either of which case it becomes compulsory for the Central Government to do so.

Company passing the special resolution

25.7-1 The first case of the company passing the special resolution declaring that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated by an Inspector appointed by the Central Government should be the rarest of rare occurrences, probably when the minority controls the company and is confronted by the majority commanding 75% or more of the voting control preferring that option than dismissing the entire Board of directors which it could easily do under such circumstances, for some compelling reason or as a means of swearing by fire of Government Investigation for an honourable takeover on a clean slate of a dubious company.

are concerned. Two other factors have made matters worse. The incursion of Big Business into the media and growing cross-media ownership, both of which lead to concentration and market dominance and work against competition and media freedom.

Cross-media ownership is an unhealthy phenomenon and is severely restricted in many countries, including the US, the UK, Germany, France and also South Africa. But in India there are no restrictions. The Administrative Staff College of India and Telecom Regulatory Authority of India have both examined cross-ownership. The 'conflict of interest' arising from this manifests itself in 'paid news', 'corporate and political lobbying', 'biased analysis and forecasts', and 'irresponsible reporting'. This is 'even more lethal where the ownership/control rests with entities which have both business and political interests.'

The need of the hour is more and more independent publications, which remain unaffected with such political and bureaucratic influences. Only then media will be able to play a fair role in identifying farudulent practices and stopping such schemes, and protect people at large.

Role of the SEBI

5. There are some indications that the Reserve Bank of India had warned the State Government on the mushrooming of chit funds in West Bengal. What is interesting is, that market regulator, SEBI has been investigating the Saradha Group since June, 2010. The Saradha Group had managed to delay the process by submitting voluminous documents. At various points of time in 2012, Saradha submitted 16 cartons, 19 cartons, 170 boxes and 35 cartons, as a strategy to avoid submitting the specific information being asked for by SEBI. After this Saradha Group was directed to provide information in Excel sheets. This helped SEBI to nail the group. As the SEBI order points out "On sample study of the data (in Excel) provided by the noticee (Saradha), veracity of which cannot be verified, it is noted that agreements for sale were entered into with two investors, namely, Dhruba Bose and Arindam Pani on January 01, 2010 for flats having number 1A and 1C, respectively, both admeasuring 1437 sq. ft. area in the same building, i.e., Ten Katha. It is further noted that the consideration amount for flat number 1A was Rs. 37,69,000 and for flat number 1C was Rs. 1,17,75,850. It is highly unlikely that in a real estate business the difference between consideration amounts for sale of two similar flats at the same building on the same day shall be in the ratio of 1:4. In view of these facts the possible inference will be that the allotment of plots/flats are simply a farce, and might have been done to mislead the regulatory authority." But by the time the SEBI's order came out, Saradha had already collapsed. What is intriguing is that the investigation against Saradha started in mid 2010, but it took the company more than two years to submit the relevant data. If SEBI had cracked the whip and acted a little faster, the situation might have been a little better.

Though everything written above evidences the reason why Saradha Group was able to defraud people, yet most important question, after all this discussion, is "Why such investors at the first place only invest in schemes like Saradha?" As already discussed, Saradha Group lured lakhs of investors to deposit money in its schemes with glossy brochures and the promise of abnormally high returns. It is true that such investors did not know that the scheme was a fraud, but it was evidently clear that such high returns were not possible and involved high risk. The upfront interest of 20% offered by the group as compared to 8% interest given by the banks made it crystal clear for investors to see the mala fide intent involved. The need of the hour is to encourage informed investors and discourage wanton pick and choose inter se such suicidal schemes.

Conclusion

6. It is distressing to see how the system can be hijacked by rogues without chances of any punishment. It is true that regulatory structure is riddled with holes, but surely some administrative measures could have been taken, provided the executive had the will to do so. Consistently the ruling parties, the Left or the Right, did not pay any heed as a portion of the loot helped in keeping its machine well-oiled. Keeping in mind all the relevant facts discussed above it will not be wrong to say that once the dust settles down, another Saradha like scam will emerge like a Phoenix.

In order to stop another Saradha like scam, it is very important to educate the masses regarding fundamentals of finances, the difference between reality and utopia.

The Securities & Exchange Board of India is monitoring the capital market and protecting the interest of investors. At the same time Ministry of Corporate Affairs is the executive head of company law administration in India. But again question is coming which agency had the absolute authority to control and restrict such type or financial disaster. In some cases SEBI has taken steps for prosecution of Collective Investment Schemes in various courts. The function of the SEBI is to regulate and register the workings of mutual fund, venture capital funds and collective investment schemes. But again sub-section (3) of section 11AA under SEBI Act, 1992 categorically mentioned that chit fund business shall not be collective investment scheme. Though as per RBI Governor it is 'misnomer' to call the West Bengal financial scam a chit fund scam, as chit funds are legal operations controlled by the central bank and what has been blown up in West Bengal is a Collective Investment Scam which is regulated by SEBI.4 All the Chit Funds should use the word 'chit fund' and chit business must register their name of fund before Registrar of chit funds.5 As per recent report of the Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission, India has a legacy of financial regulatory architecture. The present work allocation– between Reserve Bank of India, Securities & Exchange Board of India, Insurance Regulatory & Development Authority, Pension Fund Regulatory & Development Authority, and Forward Market Commission – was not designed; it evolved over the years, with a sequence of piecemeal decisions responding to immediate pressures from time to time. The present arrangement has gaps for which no regulator is in charge – such as the diverse kinds of ponzi schemes that periodically surface in India, which are not regulated by any of the existing agencies. It also contains overlaps where conflicts between regulators has consumed the energy of top economic policy makers and held back market development. Over the years, these problems will be exacerbated through technological and financial innovation. Financial firms will harness innovation to place their activities into the gaps, so as to avoid regulation. When there are overlaps, financial firms will undertake forum-shopping, where the most lenient regulator is chosen, and portray their activities as belonging to that favoured jurisdiction.6 The multiplicity of regulatory agencies and laws according to commission has generated difficulties in financial sector of India. 7

384.8 Appointment of inspectors384.8 Appointment of inspectors

On making of order by Company Law Board to appoint inspectors, the Central Government shall appoint one or more competent persons as inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company and to report thereon.

384.8-1 Prohibition384.8-1 Prohibition

No firm, body corporate or other associations shall be appointed as inspectors.

384.8-2 Continuance of investigation384.8-2 Continuance of investigation No investigation shall be stopped or suspended by reason of the fact that an application has been made for an order for prevention of oppression or mismanagement or a special resolution has been passed for voluntary winding up of the company.

384.9 Powers of inspectors384.9 Powers of inspectors

An inspector appointed to investigate the affairs of the company has the following powers :

384.9-1 Power to investigate other body corporates384.9-1 Power to investigate other body corporates

The inspector may also investigate the affairs of the following persons/body corporates which may be relevant to his investigation viz.,

u any other body corporate which is, or has at any relevant time been, the company’s holding or subsidiary company or a subsidiary of its holding company or a holding company of its subsidiary.

u any other body corporate which is or has at any relevant time been, managed by any person as managing director or manager of the company who is or was the managing director or manager of the company at the relevant time.

u any other body corporate which is or has at any relevant time been, managed by the company.

u any other body corporate whose board of directors comprises of nominees of the company.

u any other body corporate whose Board of directors are accustomed to act in accordance with the directions or instructions of the company or any of the directors of the company or any company whose directorships is held by the employees or nominees of those having the control and management of the first mentioned company. However, the prior approval of the Central Government is required in this case.

u any person who is or has at any relevant time been the managing director or manager of the company. However, the prior approval of the Central Government is required in this case.

384.9-2 Power to examine books and documents384.9-2 Power to examine books and documents

The inspector shall have powers to demand inspection of all books and papers relating to the company or other body corporate [referred to in para 384.9-1] and it is the duty of all officers and employees of the company to produce the said documents and provide all assistance to the inspector to carry out the duties. The inspector may, with the prior approval of the Central Government, require any other body corporate to furnish such information and produce such books and papers before which he considers it necessary for carrying out his duties as inspector. The inspector can keep the books under his custody for six months and thereafter return it to the person concerned. He may call back the books once again or obtain certified copies of the books and papers. u shall forward a copy of any report [other than the interim report] to the company at its registered office and the other body corporate(s) dealt with in the report.

u may forward a copy of the report or furnish to any member of the company or other body corporate dealt with in the report on payment of prescribed fee of Re. 1 for every one hundred words or any part thereof.

u shall forward a copy of the report to the applicants who submitted an application for ordering investigation.

The Central Government may appoint one or more Inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company based on the report of the Registrar of Companies under section 234 of the Act.

389.2 Power of Registrar to call for information or explanation389.2 Power of Registrar to call for information or explanation

The Registrar of Companies has the power under section 234 of the Act to call for information or explanations from any company under the following circumstances :

(2018-19) in its 70th Report on the Banning of Unregulated Deposit Schemes Bills, 2018,4 inter alia recommended removing the priority given to the IBC and the SARFAESI Act while undertaking refund to investors. This is in line with the earlier draft Bill that had been formulated by the Inter-Ministerial Group. The Committee noted that repaying depositors' money is the most critical part of the process of restitution of depositors. Where financial creditors, especially regulated businesses such as banks and financial institutions fail to exercise due diligence and give credit/lending to operators of unregulated securities schemes or schemes where fraudulent default is taken place, the law does not protect and give them priority and precedence. It does not incentivize lending to operators of unregulated schemes and those engaging in fraudulent default in regulated schemes. In this respect it may be noted that the US Bankruptcy Code is more explicit in excluding from the bankruptcy estate, "property in which the debtor holds, as of the commencement of the case, only legal title and not an equitable interest … becomes property of the estate … only to the extent of the debtor's legal title to such property, but not to the extent of any equitable interest in such property that the debtor does not hold."5 The property is part of the estate of the bankrupt only to the extent of his legal right, if he has any, and subject to the equitable interest of another. Thus, where the debtor holds bare legal title without any equitable interest, the estate acquires bare legal title without any equitable interest. Especially given the fact that in cases where the defaulter did not have the legal authorization to collect monies through the issuance of securities, the defaulter may not even have the prima facie legal right to create a security interest in the trust asset.

Collective Investment Schemes and the role of trust in insolvency

Generally, in a Collective Investment Scheme a trustee holds the pooled money on behalf of the beneficiary and in case the trust goes into insolvency the application of insolvency law poses certain important questions as to what happens to the pooled assets which the trustee has raised from the investors. In the famous international bankruptcy cases relating to Lehman Bros. Lehman Brothers International (Europe), In re6 the judge in that case explained the law on the above point maintaining that although the trust relationship may give rise to unsecured claims against the trustee for breach of trust or even negligence and may sometimes exist in a wider contractual framework, it remains at its core a different legal relationship. Subject to the terms of the trust instrument, the trustee holds the trust property for the benefit of those beneficially entitled to it and has a primary obligation to maintain those particular assets (or any which replace them) to the exclusion of all other claims. The trust property does not form part of the trustee's estate in the event of insolvency so as to be available to meet the claims of general creditors and the beneficiary is entitled to the property in specie free of any such claims.

Thus, where a trustee becomes insolvent, all the assets belonging to the trustee are divided up amongst his or her creditors. But if a beneficiary has an equitable property right to assets held by the trustee, it cannot be said that those assets belong to the trustee beneficially. Those assets are, therefore, removed from the pool of the trustee's assets, as they belong in equity to the beneficiary. Only the remaining assets that belong to the trustee beneficially are then distributed amongst the remaining creditors (generally paripassu, or proportionally). Clearly, this puts a beneficiary in a much stronger position than other creditors. The beneficiary is not a 'creditor' for the purposes of insolvency law; his position is higher than that of a creditor.

US Approach and the Berkeley Applegate Principle

Since the previous management of the company admitted to insolvency loses the power to deal with the company assets, it cannot discharge the burden of identifying the trust assets vis-à-vis the company assets. Under the IBC, the power to deal with the company assets, the right to manage the company and deal with its books of accounts primarily vest with the Insolvency professional. The Berkeley Applegate principle7 is useful for making the insolvency discharge the duty of differentiating the trust assets from other assets of the company and to be paid out of such funds. As a corollary of the rule that only the company's assets are available to the creditors, the liquidator has no power as the liquidator, to sell assets not beneficially owned by the company. But to apply this principle there needs to be some procedure to file this claim whereby the Insolvency Professional would then differentiate the assets. In civil matters, where property of a third party has been sequestered or a receiver has been appointed, a petition for examination pro interessesuo is permitted to prove the title and release of their assets.8 A petition for examination pro interessesuo would have to be filed under Section 60 of the IBC, for lack of a well-defined procedure under the IBC9. A well-defined procedure under the IBC at the outset would help in protecting the trust assets from being dissipated towards any creditor-oriented resolution or liquidation.

Investigation of company - Tribunal’s opinion basis for exercise of discretion

The Central Government exercises its discretion on the basis of the opinion of the Tribunal that the circumstances exist for ordering investigation. The Tribunal may take the initiative suo motu or on an inspection of or information supplied by any shareholder or other person. It must be satisfied as to whether the circumstances as provided in the Companies Act exist. Formation of the company or conduct of its affairs for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose, or the persons managing the affairs being guilty of fraud, misfeasance or misconduct or keeping the members uninformed of important matters, are the circumstances which may lead the Tribunal to form an opinion for investigation.

Circumstances should be brought to light to suggest that the business of the company is being carried on for fraudulent or unlawful purposes or in a manner oppressive to the minority, or that those in management had misconducted themselves towards the company or its members, no action can be ordered [P. Sreenivasan v. Yoosuf Sagar Abdulla & Sons (P.) Ltd. [1983] 53 Comp. Cas. 485 (Ker.)]. Such circumstances cannot be presumed, if a company has been incurring the losses. Investigation is ordered if such losses could be linked with fraud, misfeasance, mismanagement or oppression [see Mrs. U. A. Sumathy v. Digvijay Chit Fund (P.) Ltd. [1983] 53 Comp. Cas. 493 (Ker.)]

Unless any of such circumstances exist, the Central Government cannot order an investigation. Whether circumstances are existing for drawing contemplated inference is a matter of judicial consideration [see Ashoka Marketing Ltd. v. Union of India [1981] 51 Comp. Cas. 634 (Delhi)]. If the Tribunal neglects to take into account very material and important documents while forming its opinion, the opinion cannot be reasonable [see Jiyajeerao Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Company Law Board [1969] 39 Comp. Cas. 856 (MP)]. The term "opinion" is indicative of the existence of some material, which, at the outset, without deeper probe into the materials lead to an opinion that the complaint lodged is not frivolous, to be thrown out at the threshold. It is an opinion formed at the first impression. An order of investigation is not made on suspicion and surmises; there should be proper material to form an opinion that the affairs of the company need to be investigated [see Dwija Bandhu Sarkar v. D. N. Chakraborty [2004] 121 Comp. Cas. 712 (CLB)]. In that case the Company Law Board observed :

". . In respect of his complaints of siphoning off of funds by the respondent etc., they are all based on the balance - sheet figures/An order of investigation is not made on suspicion and surmises. There should be proper material to from an opinion that that the affairs of the company need to be investigated. The petitioner has not furnished sufficient particulars to enable me to form an opinion that the affairs of the company need to be investigated."

A mere statement of facts based on auditors report without any corroborative evidence would not be sufficient to form an opinion that the affairs of the company should be investigated. [see Andhra Pradesh State Civil Supply Corporation Ltd. v. Delta Oils and Fats Ltd. [1996] 96 Comp. Cas. 303 (CLB), Gopalakrishna Kamath v. M. T. Association [2004] 121 Comp. Cas. 191 (CLB) and Rohinten Mazda v. Hypoids (India) Pvt. Ltd. [2004] 121 Comp. Cas. 729 (CLB)]. No investigation can be ordered without particulars and on mere suspicion or surmises. The allegations must be substantiated with concrete material. There must be some material, something more than the mere statement of facts and allegations, suggesting deeper probe.

For example, allegation that there is doubt that statutory auditors of the company are under obligation to it and are not acting independently, makes out a prima facie case for investigation [New Central Jute Mills Co. Ltd. v. Deputy Secretary [1966] 36 Comp. Cas. 512 (Cal.)]. Unreasonable declaration of dividends could be a prima facie ground for ordering investigation [see Ashok Marketing Ltd. v. Union of India [1967] 37 Comp. Cas. 341 (Cal.)].
