A case in point is the kind of facts that came to light during enquiries by AO and CIT(A) in Commissioner of Income-tax, Chennai v. Midas Golden Distelleries (P.) Ltd. [2021] 130 taxmann.com 206 (Madras). The findings of AO and CIT(A) were upheld by the High Court. The High Court held that where Assessing Officer noted that share capital of assessee-company had been routed through two companies, existence and operation of which remained only on paper and enquiries conducted showed that intermediary companies acted as conduits and huge amount were brought in assessee's books as share application money through intermediary companies by shareholders, who could not properly explain their source and assessee had not established creditworthiness and genuineness of transaction to satisfaction of Assessing Officer, Assessing Officer was justified in holding that provisions of section 68 got attracted and that share application money had to be assessed in hands of assessee-company.

The Assessing Officer held that the enquiry with the past and the present directors would show that there was no transparency in the control and administration and even about the ownership of the company; that the share capital has been introduced in the company through two intermediary companies, which operated with the same pseudonymous address and there was no business activity in those companies; that the directors of the intermediary companies pleaded ignorance about the decision regarding the investment in the assessee-company; that the sources of the shareholders, who made their investment in the assessee-company through the intermediary companies were not properly explained; that the affairs of the two intermediary companies established the fact that those were only paper companies created with the sole intention to act as a conduit for facilitating transfer of funds; that the signatories to the agreement were between the assessee and another company, as per which, the shares of the assessee were to be allotted to the other company or its nominees in lieu of the alleged advance of Rs. 5.35 Crores, totally denied by stating that he did not have knowledge of such transaction and that transaction was not reflected by the erstwhile partnership firm M/s. Golden Distilleries; that the addresses of the share applicants namely M/s. D. Kumar Trading and Co., and M/s. Pooja Equitex and M/s. Pentium were not furnished.

The CIT(A), while confirming the order passed by the Assessing Officer, reexamined the entire facts and the discussions commenced from paragraph 4.1.3 in the order dated 21.7.2008. After noting the submissions, which were recorded by the Assessing Officer during the course of assessment proceedings, the CIT(A) held that the so-called directors basically discharged their functions in the honorary capacity during their tenure and they used to look after the routine matters pertaining to the assessee and that they categorically denied having every actively participated in the crucial decision making process of the assessee company. As former managing director of the assessee-company, he was stated to be in charge of civil work, erection of plant and machinery, purchases, etc., and expressed ignorance about the shareholding pattern of the assessee-company and other financial transaction entered into by the initial promoter – directors and the present directors. All of them appeared to have stated that the important decisions used to be taken by only one person, who was the main person behind the promotion of the assessee-company and its business operations. But, the main person pleaded that he and his family members had no role to play in the assessee's business activities apart from holding shares therein.

After noting the statements recorded by the Assessing Officer, the CIT(A) observed that the Assessing Officer was within his right to probe the genuineness and source of the share application money received by the assessee during the year. The statements recorded from the persons had clearly established that the needle of suspicion inevitably and inexorably pointed to one particular person and since the suspicion was so overwhelming, the Assessing Officer had no other option except to trace the origin of funds, which got channelized into the assessee-company through the corporate entities. Further, the CIT(A) pointed out that the Assessing Officer, while embarking upon such an enquiry, found that the share application money was primarily contributed by two companies and an aggregate sum of Rs. 3 Crores was found to be contributed by three Mumbai based companies.

In Rohtas Industries Ltd. v. Findings of the inspector's report

The sum and substances of the report submitted by the inspectors as per Section 207 are as follows:

1.

No registered office of the Company was located by the officer during physical inspection.

2.

No books of accounts were produced before the officer despite multiple notices and summons issued to the Company, its directors and statutory auditors.

3.

Shares of the Company were not listed on the stock exchange post its IPO in the year 1996.

4.

Company failed to file the Statutory Returns i.e. Annual financial statements and Annual Returns after the financial year 2015 – 16.

5.

The existing directors of the Company were dummy/shadow directors of the Chairman and were not traceable.

6.

Statement of one of the Directors of the Company proved that he was working as clerk and was induced by the auditor to join the Company as a Director.

7.

Statutory Auditor was not eligible to be appointed as an auditor under Section 141(3)(d) of the Act as his family members are shareholders of the Company.

8.

The Books of Accounts of the Company was signed by the Statutory Auditor without being audited. No internal audit system existed in the Company

9.

No working papers were maintained by the Statutory Auditor.

Analysis & Conclusion

Undoubtedly, the role of the auditor is very vital from the investors' as well as stakeholders' interest point of view as they implicitly trust the financials authenticated by him. The auditor must express his opinion on whether the financial statements give true and fair view of the state of the company's affairs. In reaching his opinion, the auditor must examine the company's books of accounts and related documents, conduct enquiries, collect evidences, detect frauds and so forth. Therefore, it is the duty of the auditor to perform all his statutory obligations with integrity and objectivity. The Tribunal also stated that the auditor owes a fiduciary duty towards the entire Nation.

In the present case, the statutory auditor lacked independence as his family members held shares in the Company which makes him ineligible to become auditor of the Company u/s 141(3)(d). Also, he was negligent in conducting audit and issued his report without proper inspection and examination to which he himself admitted.

Based on the inspection report, the Hon'ble Tribunal opined that the statutory auditor failed to exercise his duties and has certified the Profit & Loss Account and Balance Sheet of the company without even examining any of the records/ Books of the Account of the Company. Tribunal to prevent any further abuse of power, passed an interim order dated 03.01.2019 removing the auditor from function as statutory auditor of the Company and permitting the Company to replace him with an independent auditor. The Tribunal further held that:

"Statutory Auditor colluded with the Chairman/Director of company and has given a false Audit certificate relating to the Profit & Loss Account and Balance Sheet of the R-2 company, without even examining and verifying the books of accounts, and the Statutory Auditor has not given any plausible explanation for such irresponsible fraudulent activities"

The Tribunal, in exercise of its powers under sections 140(5) and 147(3)(i) of the Act, passed the following order as final stating that the statutory auditor:

1.

shall not be eligible to be appointed as an Auditor of any company for a period of 5 years from the date of passing this order;

2.

shall also be liable for action under Section 447 of the Companies Act, 2013; or

3.

to refund the remuneration received by him, during the period he acted as Auditor, back to the Company.

Evidently, the Hon'ble Tribunal stressed on how the role of statutory auditor is becoming important in detecting and preventing frauds. The Auditors are appointed by the shareholders with a view to report the true picture of the company which enables them to make a well-informed decision. However, if the same auditor gets involved in fraudulent instances it will erase their confidence. Therefore, how the Ministry and the Tribunal are exercising their powers to curb such activities is an appreciable move which is trying to reinstate the faith and confidence in the audit profession.

Jansen (1956) Ch 565. 26.26-6-3 STATE POLICY - The State Policy regarding company promoters, directors and managerial persons so far as their disqualifications or misconduct in relation to company affairs is concerned, it seems in an overview to have emerged as the concentration of Central Government’s power designed into a truly MCA-21 to protect the companies, not the investors, in the name of control as the mainstay. Whether it is in the nature of removal of the blot of a court conviction, increase in the number of directors on the Board beyond twelve, remuneration of directors or its increase, holding offices or places of profit by the directors and their qualification or disqualification or loans to them or loans and investments in their related companies (for return investment in the parent company’s shares as cross-holdings) or contracts or arrangements in which they are interested or sole-selling-buying agencies in which they are suspected to be interested or suspension of powers or supersession of the directors by those nominated in case of mismanagement/change in the constitution of the Board or investigation into the affairs of a company or the ownership of the shares as well as the appointment and remuneration of the managerial persons or changes in the company’s name or its situation from one State to another or unclaimed dividends, it is entirely at the highest level in the Ministry at New Delhi with the obligation of an Annual Report on its working being placed on the table of the Parliament on which there is hardly any debate. Public issues, listing and insider-trading, among others, is controlled by SEBI. Matters left to shareholders and investors include the fiduciary obligations of company promoters/directors/managerial persons, fund-raising and maintenance, dividends and bonus, political contributions, financial sickness and as contributories in winding up. The power of the general meeting is reserved for formal compliances connected with the yearly maintenance of companies and fund-raising and maintenance, with no way made visible to get back their investments robbed by the wrongdoers in control of companies. As to judicial review, as a result of the latest amendments to the Act, excepting the Supreme Court all High Court jurisdiction has been divested and transferred to the Tribunals and continued with the Criminal Courts for the levy of enhanced fines, many of them open for compounding out of court under section 621A, and imprisonment for infractions remaining only as a mere threat with the few of Government prosecutions bringing not much significant deterrence. The singular offence that is punishable with imprisonment alone extending up to five years under the Act is the application made for subscription of shares in a fictitious name by the investors, under section 68A(1).

26.26-6-4 COMPLAINTS BASED ON FIDUCIARY DUTIES - Complaints based on the fiduciary obligations per se of company promoters and directors or the managerial persons could be considered as covered by the general section 628/621 read with section 299(5) for false statements attracting imprisonment up to two years and also with fine with no limit specified. If in any return, report, certificate, balance sheet, prospectus, statement or other document required by or for the purposes of any of the provisions of the Act, any person making a statement that is false in any material particular knowingly, (not wilfully, as under section 438 of the English Act, thus widening the scope of the section) or which omits any material fact knowing it to be material, the person making the same incurs the liability to be punished under section 628. But to sustain a prosecution under the section, proof of guilty mind of knowledge of falsity is essential - P.P. Looke v. N.J. Mathew [1967] 37 Comp. Cas. 790 (Ker.).

26.26-6-4a DIRECTORS OWE THEIR DUTIES TO THE COMPANY - The directors owe their duties to the company, and it is the company or in the name of the company at the instance of shareholders where allowed or the creditors if the company’s solvency is not sufficient to pay its debts in full (for which reason the shareholders lose their power to ratify the acts of directors), that those duties can be enforced, but not at the instance of the employees as employees while the company is a going concern. A single shareholder will not succeed to bring an action for any recovery of profit made by the director, unless the action is brought as a derivative action, Prudential Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Newman Industries Ltd. (1982) 1 All ER 354 (CA). The Register of Directors’ Contracts required to be kept by the company under section 301is the open source for the shareholders as regards company contracts in which directors are interested. Filing a civil suit may be another option which is of considerable complexity, expense and time-consuming. But, such complaints are rare in our country.

(ix) If the existing legal framework is insufficient legislation akin to the Tamil Nadu Protection of Interests of Depositors (in Financial Establishments) Act, 1997, a State enactment could have been enacted. This State enactment had received the Presidential assent on August 7, 1997. It is an Act to protect the deposits made by the public in Financial Establishments and matters related thereto. The Act is penal in nature, and Special Courts are empowered to punish for defaults in the return of deposits or in the payment of interest on the deposits. The punishment prescribed is a term of imprisonment which may extend up to ten years and fine up to one lakh of rupees, for text of statute see All India High Court Reports, 1998 (4) statutes section p. 265.

(x) The Chit Funds Act, 1982, is itself a Central enactment, the result of a lot of discussion and deliberation, and a self-contained statutory Code for regulation of chit funds and for all matters connected therewith, consequently, issues indicated in the SOR of Bill 2000, pertaining to chit funds should have been incorporated as amendments to the Chit Funds Act, 1982, and not by inclusion of ‘chit funds’ in the Bill, 2000.

(xi) The Bill, 2000 seeking to include chit fund companies in the Statute of Financial Companies Regulation, 2000 and administer the same through Central Government directives, and Reserve Bank of India Rules and Regulations is administratively flawed, legally untenable and patently unjustified.

(xii) Chit Fund Companies are administered, controlled and supervised by the State Government, through the Registrar of Chit Funds under the Chit Funds Act, 1982, while if brought under the inclusive definition of section 2(e)( iv) ‘business of financial institution’ would entail administration by the Central Government and the Reserve Bank of India. The inevitable situation that results is Chit Fund Companies is Controlled by the State Government under the Chit Funds Act, 1982, and by the Central Government and the Reserve Bank of India under the Bill, 2000. Such dual administration apart from being legally impermissible, administratively incompatible is also unjustified.

(xiii) Dual procedure in administration both in substantive and procedural law is discriminatory and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution of India.

(xiv) From 1996, the Reserve Bank of India has been monitoring and following the functioning of NBFCs, which invite deposits and utilise them for their business activities, ceiling for acceptance of deposits, requirement of maintenance of certain liquidity of funds, borrowings not to exceed a certain percentage of net owned funds, are norms that have been provided in the corporate sector. Having regard to this policy backdrop the provision in the Bill to have a net working capital of Rs. 200 crores for NBFCs is wholly untenable and legally unjustified.

(xv) Protection of investors and depositors is the golden thread that runs through the Bill, 2000. Investor awareness and educational programmes have been initiated. The Government has enacted the Investor Education and Protection Fund (Awareness and Protection of Investors) Rules, 2001 in exercise of the powers conferred by clauses (a) and (b) of section 642, read with section 205C(3) of the Companies Act, 1956-GSR 750(E) dated October 1, 2001 [For Text of the Rules-see Taxman’s Consumer Protection Law Manual (2003) pp. 3.17 to 3.27] Rule 14 mandates the conditions for utilisation of Funds by the Committee for investor awareness, education, and projects for Investor Protection.

GVN Raju (2008) 88 SCL 65 (AP HC), it was held that while directing contributories and former directors to produce records or books of account, Court cannot ignore realities and issue directions even if it is proved that the records were lost/destroyed/damaged and whatever were available were already handed over.

28.11-7Recover Debts due by contributory

A contributory may be liable to pay any sum to company, besides the calls due. Company Court can order that the contributory or his estate should pay the amount due exclusive of any call payable by him or his estate - section 295(1) of Companies Act, 2013.

28.11-8 No powers to declare a court decree void

Under section 446 of the 1956 Act [section 280 of Companies Act, 2013] no power is conferred on Company Court (now NCLT) to declare a decree of competent court void. If appeal against court order is not filed by company or official liquidator, the decree becomes final and is binding on liquidator - Indian Bank v. Official Liquidator - AIR 1998 SC 2111 = (1998) 5 SCC 401 = 93 Comp Cas 76 (SC).

28.11-9 No powers to revive a claim which was time barred at commencement of winding up

As per section 358 of Companies Act, 2013, while computing limitation, period from date of commencement of winding order to till order of winding up is made plus one year has to be excluded.

If claim was time barred at the time of appointment of provisional liquidator or making of winding up order, it cannot be enforced. See case law under section 358 of Companies Act, 2013.

Any claim by or against the company is transferred to Company Court (now NCLT) under section 446(2)(b) of the 1956 Act [section 280 of Companies Act, 2013]. However, a claim which was time barred at the time of commencement of liquidation proceedings cannot be enforced by official liquidator - KTC Tyres (India) Ltd. v. Kavitha Auto Parts (1998) 97 Comp Cas 524 (Ker HC).

In Official Liquidator of Amfort Agro Finance v. Chittar Lohar (2003) 46 SCL 31 (Raj HC), loan was granted by company under liquidation to defendant in March 1994. Defendant did not pay any instalment of loan or interest. Company was ordered to be wound up in July 1995. Official Liquidator filed application in February 2000 for recovery of loan with interest @ 12%. It was held that there is no time limit prescribed under section 477 of the 1956 Act [section 299 of Companies Act, 2013] for taking proceedings thereunder. Hence, application is within time and loan with interest @ 12% can be recovered from defendant by Official Liquidator. [In this case, really, the claim was within time limit when winding up commenced. Hence, as per section 358 of Companies Act, 2013, demand is not time barred].

Investor Help-lines

1.50 Ordinarily, in the absence of fraud or misfeasance in relation to the company or any breach of duty to the company alleged, there is no remedy in law against loss of investment in a company as a result of the company ceasing to be a going concern, it taken as an inherent risk in carrying on a business. In order to protect themselves from loss otherwise, the investors are expected generally to be aware of their rights with due recognition of their responsibilities to keep themselves informed about the developments in the affairs of the company where they have invested and to act, like participation in its meetings in person or by proxy individually or better still as a member in a kindred group of investors.

Investors’ rights

1.50-1 The investors’ rights in respect of shares include: (a) timely receipt of share certificates, whether on allotment or transfer/transmission, the abridged annual report each year and the notices for the general meetings and prompt refund of excess money paid with the share-application, dividend warrants, offers of rights shares on approval of the issue by the general body; (b) inspection of the statutory books and registers kept by the company as per the Act or to have copies in full or as extracts from the company; (c) to exercise the right of piloting members’ requisitioned resolutions/general meetings to force a change in the company’s course of affairs; (d) to commence civil and criminal proceedings against the company or the directors for defaults or infringements of their rights like oppression or mis-management; (e) to be the residual claimants or be liable as contributories on the company’s winding up; and (f) to prosecute the company and the directors for defaults under and offences against the Act or for the company to be wound-up by the Tribunal, if appropriate. Debenture or bond-holders’ rights are limited to receive the periodic returns and the return of the investment at maturity, to receive the debenture-trust-deed copy on request, and to seek the company’s winding up, if appropriate, before the Tribunal.

Trading and transfer of securities

1.50-2 As regards trading in and transfer of securities, the channels available to investors include :

(A) Trades - purchase and sale by private arrangement or via the trading floors established by the stock exchange where the securities are listed, the stock exchange route being free of the loss due to the risk of non-performance of delivery of securities and prompt payment of the consideration in the deals apart from getting the advantage of the market price at a little extra cost to the investors. While the securities are held, as owners they can raise finances against deposit of the securities.

(B) Grievances (to the low of which property rights of citizens in company or other securities have been summarily diluted as an administrative expedient to form part of Company Law)—the redressal channels available at present include the company and its Registrars first and foremost, besides the DCA and additionally in respect of listed companies, the SEBI/Stock Exchanges where the securities are listed, and the debenture-trustee in the case of debentures. Grievances in respect of Fixed Deposit Receipts in banks or financial institutions other than the Non-banking financial companies may be addressed to the RBI, but for company public deposits it is only the DCA to be approached.

Help-lines, minimal

4. In the course of three years Saradha took on new depositors and collected money from existing ones. All this money is now lost. Two years of investigation were required to stop what seems to be a run of the mill Ponzi scheme. The tactics employed by Saradha are not new. They are similar to those employed by Sahara in delaying investigations in the OFCD schemes and in many other white collar crime investigations. The disturbing fact is that they seem to succeed time and again. While SEBI has wide powers in case of entities registered with it, if someone does not register with SEBI, the system of enforcement of law changes completely. The current system requires SEBI to approach the local courts for violations of the SEBI Act which constitute an offence. Moreover, SEBI cannot directly appoint lawyers for prosecuting the offenders and must rely on the State Government's prosecution machinery to get criminal prosecution started.

Weaknesses of the present system

5. The present system suffers from a number of weaknesses, main two of which are as follows:

The normal court systems do not have the time or expertise to enforce violations of investment and securities laws. This leads to confusing orders which sometimes exceed the jurisdiction of the courts. Even in the case of Saradha, the High Court set aside the orders preventing the SEBI from exercising its powers over Saradha, noting that the courts were out of jurisdiction when they prohibited SEBI. However, the High Court's orders take time, and in this time period the operator of the Ponzi scheme can continue to collect money or misappropriate the money already deposited. Expertise in deciding jurisdiction and applicability of SEBI laws is also not available in normal district courts. It will be extremely expensive and wasteful to train all district judges in securities laws for the once-in-a-decade case in financial laws.

The use of the State public prosecutors for violations of financial laws is problematic for two reasons-first, the normal public prosecutors office is flooded with normal criminal cases like theft, murder, etc. A complex financial law case will never be the priority of the normal public prosecutor's office. Secondly, the average public prosecutor who is extremely busy with the daily load of run of the mill criminal cases is not trained in investment and securities laws. Just like district judges, it would not be cost effective to train all public prosecutors in securities laws.

5.1 A fragmented regulatory system - Under the present system there are many institutions that offer deposit or investment services without any form of approval or regulation. Under a fragmented regulatory system, hazy lines of work have been drawn between financial regulators, the Central Government and the State Governments. This has led to the problem of under policing - anything that does not fall squarely within the lines tends to pass unnoticed from the radar of regulation. Saradha presents a good example - its activities could be argued to fall under any of the following categories: running a collective investment scheme (regulated by the SEBI); running a chit fund (regulated by the State Government); a private company taking deposits for its business (regulated by the Registrar of Companies) and taking public deposits as a non-banking financial company (regulated by the RBI). The Saradha Group chose to seek permission from none of these.

There is also inconsistency in the manner and extent of regulation of the financial institutions performing similar activities. For instance, 265 non-banking financial companies and 18 housing finance companies are allowed to take public deposits, but they don't enjoy the same deposit insurance protection that is available to banks. If the rationale for deposit insurance is to protect depositors from the risk of a financial institution becoming unable to make good its promise to refund public deposits, should the same logic not apply to all deposit takers?

Chit funds, which are governed by the State Governments, also suffer from the problem of inconsistent treatment. Differences in enforcement levels across the States have resulted in some States becoming more prone to ponzi schemes. In addition, most of the companies in this sector may be operating in the form of unregistered chit funds. It is estimated that registered chit funds have collected Rs. 300 billion worth of deposits while the collection of unregistered funds is much higher at Rs. 30 trillion.

The regulation of collective investment schemes that come under the SEBI's scanner has also left much to be desired. This is largely on account of the restrictive mandate. Section 11AA of the SEBI Act defines "collective investment schemes" in terms of principles to identify such schemes, but it contains exemptions for institutions such as chit funds, nidhis and co-operative societies. Pointing to the huge investment in the grey market that plagues the financial sector, the SEBI Chairman, U. K. Sinha observed that the loopholes in the existing laws are the primary cause for this type of situation. He pointed out towards the need for a single regulatory body to look into the regulation of all companies that take illegal deposits from the public.

Dilatory part of court procedure is a dampener 1.40-13 In addition to the question on the proper Court of competent jurisdiction discussed above, companies and company affairs that happen to be brought before the courts for adjudication in whatever context are equally subject to the common curse of endemic court delays and related costs largely due to the archaic, outmoded and staid procedural laws made by the imperialist British regime around the 1850’s remaining firm at the core through six decades of India’s Independence to the present electronic era, as a consequence of the law-makers’ choice of creating multiple fast track courts or forums parallelly, to the exclusion of the jurisdiction of ordinary civil courts which are nearer to people and familiar to them in the view that those courts are super-saturated with other cases and allowing their jurisdiction over company cases to continue would only add to further delays, instead of overhauling the procedural laws to rid them off the dilatory parts for faster disposal of cases by the common law courts and creating more. Unfortunately, seeing the victims sapped by prolonged litigation for years lasting for a generation or over in many cases, there is a misgiving present generally as an aside in the minds of people on ‘who is watching what they do’ about the Judiciary in our system. These factors have contributed to encourage people at large to keep away from approaching the Courts on their disputes with others and swallow the losses unless compelled not for some little money alone as in the case of the common investors, or it forms the lesser evil faced by them, or it found advantageous to show as inescapable and vindicate their own position at any cost to the company or others. Overall, so far as companies are concerned, the combined incidence of these factors has gone in favour of the managements to do what they prefer rather than what they should under the laws in matters of the corporate investors or others.

PETITION TO COMPANY LAW BOARD 1 FOR INVESTIGATION OF COMPANY’S AFFAIRS *PETITION TO COMPANY LAW BOARD1 FOR INVESTIGATION OF COMPANY’S AFFAIRS*

384.1 Background note384.1 Background note

The Company Law Board has been empowered to order investigation into the company’s affairs if a petition to this effect is made by the specified number of members.

384.2 Right of members to submit petition384.2 Right of members to submit petition

The right to make an application is available to the following members :

u in the case of a company having a share capital, not less than two hundred members of the company or member(s) holding not less than one-tenth of the total voting powers.

u in the case of a company not having a share capital, not less than one-fifth of the total number of its members.

The application should be supported by evidence to show the grounds for ordering investigation of the affairs of the company.

384.3 Providing security384.3 Providing security

The applicant(s) must provide security, for such amounts not exceeding one thousand rupees, which may be required by the Central Government for payment of the cost of investigation.

384.4 Submission of petition384.4 Submission of petition

A petition in Form No. 1 in Annexure II to the Company Law Regulations, 1991 shall be made to the Company Law Board for issue of order for investigation of the company’s affairs. The petition may be made by the members and presented by the petitioner(s) in person or through authorised representative to the concerned Bench Office or by registered post with acknowledgement due addressed to the Secretary or Bench Officer of the concerned Bench. A copy of the petition should be served on the Registrar of Companies.

384.4-1 Documents to accompany petition384.4-1 Documents to accompany petition

The petition should be accompanied by the following documents :

(a) Document and/or other evidence in support of the statements made in the petition, as are reasonably open to the petitioner(s).

(b) Documentary evidence in proof of the eligibility and status of the petitioner(s) with the voting power held by each of them.

(c) Affidavit verifying petition.

(d) Bank draft drawn in favour of pay and Accounts Officer, Ministry of Company Affairs evidencing payment of application fee of Rs. 2,500.

(e) Memorandum of appearance in Form No. 5 of CLB Regulations with copy of the Board Resolution or the executed Vakalatnama, as the case may be, if the petition is filed by the authorised representative or advocate.

(f) Index of documents.

(g) Acknowledgement from the Office of the Registrar of Companies for serving the petition.

(h) Three extra copies of the petition.

384.4-2 Contents of petition384.4-2 Contents of petition

The petition should set forth the name of the company, with its status, date of incorporation, the address of its registered office, authorised capital, paid-up capital with division of different classes of shares and terms of issue, if any, in the case of preference shares, main objects in brief, present business activities and should also set forth concisely under distinct heads the grounds for such petition and nature of relief sought for.

384.4-3 Attestation of documents384.4-3 Attestation of documents

The documents may be attested by the party or the authorised representative or by the advocate and shall be marked serially as Annexures A1, A2, A3 and so on.

384.5 Serving copy of the petition on respondent(s)384.5 Serving copy of the petition on respondent(s)

A copy of the petition, reference or application should be served on the respondent(s) and evidence for service of petition should be produced. Where the number of respondents is more than five, the Secretary or Bench Officer may permit the petitioner to file extra copies of the petition at the time of issue of notice to the respondents.

384.6 Serving copy of the petition on Central Government384.6 Serving copy of the petition on Central Government

A copy of the petition or reference should be served upon the Central Government.

384.7 Order of Company Law Board384.7 Order of Company Law Board

The Company Law Board shall pass an order declaring that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated by an inspector or inspectors.

384.8 Appointment of inspectors384.8 Appointment of inspectors

On making of order by Company Law Board to appoint inspectors, the Central Government shall appoint one or more competent persons as inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company and to report thereon.

384.8-1 Prohibition384.8-1 Prohibition

No firm, body corporate or other associations shall be appointed as inspectors.

[Para 13]. In Asia Stone S.L. v. B. & G. Impex (P.) Ltd.197, the applicant-company was a shareholder in the first respondent-company holding up to 99.67 per cent of its paid-up capital. The first respondent company held its first board meeting on 17-7-2006 wherein 'V' was appointed as an additional director. The second respondent and the third respondent were also appointed as additional directors at subsequent board meetings. Subsequently, 'V' and the first directors of the first respondent-company, i.e., respondents 4 and 5 resigned from their posts and their resignations were accepted by the board at a meeting held on 24-11-2006. Consequently, the board was left with only two members comprising of respondent Nos. 2 and 3. The applicant alleged that the first respondent held the first AGM on 25-7-2007 without giving any notice to the applicant. When the applicant's authorized representatives visited registered office of the first respondent, it was found closed and there was no responsible person available to answer their questions. Thereafter, the applicant made all efforts for inspection and for obtaining the records but all went in vain. The applicant apprehended that all was not well with the first respondent and that it was kept in dark about the affairs of the company. The applicant was served with a copy of the plaint from where it was able to get a copy of the notice of first the AGM, dated 25-7-2007. From said notice, it was evident that the first respondent had not appointed any new director at the AGM. The only two members of the board were respondent Nos. 2 and 3 who could only hold office upto the date of AGM, i.e., up to 25-7-2007 in terms of section 260. Further, the inspection of documents with RoC revealed that many statutory documents were not filed in spite of the fact that due date for filing same had already expired. The applicant feared of action by the RoC for statutory violations and non-performance of statutory violation by the first respondent. In these circumstances, the applicant invoked the provisions of section 186 for passing appropriate orders/directions in the interest of justice and prayed that the board may appoint an independent Chairman and also give directions in relation to calling/holding and conducting the EGM of the company for the purpose of appointing two individuals to the board of directors of the company. He further prayed that a single member present in person or proxy would be deemed to constitute a valid quorum for the purpose of the EGM. Held, As per the provisions of section 260 it is crystal clear that the additional directors so appointed shall hold office only up to the date of the next AGM. In the instant case, the first AGM purportedly was held on 25-7-2007 at the registered office of the company and the agenda of the meeting was mentioned in the notice dated 25-6-2007, wherein no such agenda for re-appointment of additional directors, as regular directors was found. Therefore, the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 were no more directors of the company, hence, the respondents stand that respondent Nos. 2 and 3 were the current directors could not be accepted. The first directors, i.e., the respondent Nos. 4 and 5 and the other additional director 'V' had resigned and the same was accepted at the sixth board meeting held on 24-11-2006. In view of the resignation and the completion of tenure of the additional directors, the company was not having any directors on its board. The submission of the applicant that the company was not having the directors was valid and legal. The report of the RoC was taken on record which further strengthened the case of the applicant that the company had no directors on its board. Section 169 specifically gives powers to the board of directors of a company to call for an EGM on the requisition of such number of members of the company as are specified in section 169(4). In the instant case, there was no such board and the main grievance of the applicant was that no such board existed and the company was functioning without a proper board and the applicant could not approach the company for convening an EGM. The submissions of the applicant were to be fully agreed with. As the company was not having board of directors, the contention of the respondent that the applicant could have invoked the provisions of section 169 did not have any merit. Therefore, the applicant had no other alternate except to invoke provisions of section 186(1). In view of the observations and findings, the application was to be allowed with the following directions :—

(i)

A practicing company secretary should be appointed as the Chairman for the purpose of calling, holding and conducting the EGM of the first respondent-company.

39.3-5 Procedures and powers of inspector during investigation

It is duty of all officers and employees of the company to preserve and produce all books and papers and to provide all assistance to the inspector. Agreement with foreign Government on reciprocal basis to assist in enquiry - Central Government can enter into agreement with Government of foreign State on reciprocal basis to assist in inspection, inquiry or investigation under the Companies Act and corresponding foreign Act [section 217(10) of Companies Act, 2013].

Similarly, if Court or authority in foreign country requests, the Court in India shall record the statement and send it to foreign Court or authority through Central Government [section 217(12) of Companies Act, 2013].

The letter of request shall be transmitted in such manner as specified by Ministry of Corporate Affairs - Rule 6 of Companies (Registration Offices and Fees) Rules, 2014.

Company can take copies of the documents at its cost. Search and seizure must be according to provisions of Code of Criminal Procedure. The seized papers can be kept till conclusion of investigation. The inspector can take copies of any document or place identification marks on them before returning the books and papers - section 220 of Companies Act, 2013. The learned counsel appearing on behalf of the Union of India relied heavily on the arguments of 'larger public interest' and submitted amongst other that -

(a)

the order passed by the learned Tribunal is absolutely in the larger public interest and absolutely in consonance with the provisions of Section 130 of the Companies Act;

(b)

there were very serious allegations of preparing the earlier accounts in a fraudulent manner, and also with respect to the mismanagement of the affairs of the company during the relevant period;

(c) all the three provisions, namely Sections 211/212, Sections 241/242 and Section 130 of the Companies Act are required to be considered and read conjointly;

(d)

the order passed under Section 130 of the Companies Act would be in the aid of the investigation going on by the SFIO under Section 212 of the Companies Act and the same shall be in the larger public interest;

(e)

the reopening of the books of accounts and recasting the financial statements is very much required and necessary, since the same shall be in the larger public interest, to find out the real truth;

(f)

the learned Tribunal has not received any objection from any regulatory body raising any concern for reopening/recasting books of accounts;

(g)

the impugned cannot be said to be in violation of the principles of natural justice as alleged; and

(h)

the report of the RBI dated 22-3-2019 demonstrates and establishes beyond any doubt about the complete correctness, validity and legality of the order under Section 130 of the Act.

Making the above submissions, it was prayed to dismiss the present appeal, more particularly, considering the larger public interest as, in the present case, thousands of crores of the public money is involved.

Observations by the Hon'ble Supreme Court

While considering the issue, the Hon'ble Supreme Court noted amongst others that -

(a)

in the preliminary SFIO report, there are specific findings with respect to mismanagement of the affairs and also with respect to preparing fraudulent accounts;

(b)

in the preliminary report, the ICAI has mentioned that "accounts for the post five years have been prepared in a fraudulent and negligent manner by the erstwhile auditors"; and

(c)

the Registrar of Companies prima facie concluded that mismanagement and compromise in corporate governance norms and risk management has been perpetuated indiscriminately raising long term and short-term loans/borrowings through public sector banks and financial institutions.

It was observed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court that -

(a)

on a fair reading of Section 130 of the Companies Act, if the Tribunal is satisfied that either of the conditions precedent is satisfied, the Tribunal would be justified in passing the order under Section 130 of the Companies Act;

(b)

it cannot be said that the conditions precedent while invoking the powers under Section 130 of the Act are not satisfied;

(c)

it was more than satisfied that in the facts and circumstances of the case, and also in the larger public interest and when thousands of crores of public money is involved, the Tribunal is justified in allowing the application under Section 130 of the Companies Act; and

(d)

it cannot be said that the order passed by the learned Tribunal is per se in violation of the principle of natural justice as alleged.

Further it was observed that the order passed by the Tribunal under Section 130 of the Companies Act does not suffer from any illegality and the same is passed in the larger public interest.

Final Order of the Hon'ble Supreme Court

The Hon'ble Supreme Court relied heavily on the merits of 'larger public interest', for passing the Order.

It was ordered that the Hon'ble Supreme Court had no reason to interfere with the impugned order dated 1-1-2019 passed by the learned Tribunal under Section 130 of the Companies Act for reopening of the books of accounts and recasting the financial statements for the last five years, viz. from Financial Year 2012-13 to the Financial Year 2017-18.

Accordingly, the present appeal was dismissed and order of the learned Tribunal was upheld.

Consequences of re-opening and re-casting of books of accounts

The books of accounts once reopened and recasted are deemed to be final under the provisions of Section 130(2) of the Companies Act, 2013. It means recasted books of accounts are to be considered as final for the relevant period for all purposes.

Recovery of remuneration

Section 199 of the Companies Act, 2013 permits the Company to recover remuneration from any managing director/whole-time director/manager/Chief Executive Officer (by whatever name called) who has received the remuneration (including stock option) in excess of what would have been payable to him as per the restated financial statements. This would be applicable for all the period(s) for which financial statements were restated.

Conclusion - some unanswered questions

There are many frontiers opens when an order is passed to re-open/re-cast the books of accounts and the law does not answer to all such questions in the statues. For example, recovery of dividend which was distributed based on previous accounts and claim of damages by the investors who have suffered losses.

Ministry of Corporate Affairs already ordered investigation of matters by Serious Fraud Investigation Order (SFIO) in July-November of 2012. Central Government and Ministry of Finance have said such types of activities are subject to examination by SEBI, RBI and Ministry of Corporate Affairs. Originally chit funds rendered yeoman service in providing cash to millions of families to solemnize marriages, to buy property, children's educations or contingencies when banking services had not reached rural India.8 Nowadays in the name of chit funds numerous companies are being mushroom every corner of the countries to collect monies mainly from the marginalized people. But these companies do not register with SEBI to avoid regulatory glare and stiff guidelines. At the same time these companies collect money as deposits but call them 'membership fees' to avoid coming under the purview of Reserve Bank of India. On the contrary, Insurance Regulatory & Development Authority (IRDA) cannot take any action because those monies are not collected for insurance purpose or not in the form of premium. Recently, the report of the Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission has recommended that a limited class of companies including banks and non- banking financial companies are allowed to accept deposits from public. This requires amending section 58A of the Companies Act, 1956. The proposed Companies Bill of 2011 is a step in this direction.9 At present, Indian law features tight connections between a particular agency (e.g. SEBI) and the functions that it performs (e.g. securities regulation). The draft Code does not provide for such integration. This is to ensure that from the outset, and over coming decades, decisions about the legal framework governing finance can proceed separately from decisions about the financial regulatory architecture. Changes in the work allocation of agencies would not require changes to the underlying law itself. This will yield greater legal certainty, while facilitating rational choices about financial regulatory architecture motivated by considerations in public administration and public economics.10 So recently the Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission has suggested for only 6 Regulatory Commissions for control of financial system in country and the Reserve Bank of India will have the wide functions including functions of SEBI and Forward Market Commission.

Many Laws But Little Justice

Though there are many laws existing but no appropriate law to solve the present problem. Not only to solve the problem it is very much clear that existing laws have some lacuna to prevent such type of scam generated by chit fund companies. But in the south Indian States, chit funds are being conducted for time immemorial and the first institutionalized chit fund11 was established in 1947 in Chennai.12 So in making of laws relating to chit funds south Indian states were pioneer also. Tamil Nadu was the first state to regulate chit fund business through the Madras Chit Fund Act, 1961 after independence followed by the Andhra Pradesh Chit Funds Act, 1971 for the State of Andhra Pradesh to protect the interest of investors. The Kerala enacted the Kerala Chitties Act, 1975 and also established the Kerala Financial Enterprise Corporation to regulate several chit funds throughout the State. In 1974, the Reserve Bank of India constituted a study group relating to non-banking financial companies under the chairmanship of James. S. Raj and the study group observed that the prize chit, benefit, saving schemes were beneficial for promoters but against the public policy as well as fiscal policy and did not serve any social purpose. Then Union Parliament passed the Prize Chits and Money Circulation Schemes (Banning) Act, 1978 to ban the promotion or conduct of prize chits and money circulation schemes within the country. Finally the Chit Funds Act, 1982, a central legislation, was made to regulate chit funds in India where previous sanction of the State Government is needed to conduct chit fund business13 and every chit agreement shall be filed to Registrar of Chits.14 Again to prevent the speculation of money, the Indian Parliament also enacted the Lotteries (Regulation) Act, 1998 which legalized only the State Government to organize, conduct or promote a lottery after following certain conditions15 otherwise the Central Government may prohibit any lottery16 and any company may also liable by such offences.17 In 2011 Ministry of Finance constituted one 'Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission' headed by former justice B.N. Srikrishna, to harmonise all the financial sector legislations which are more than 60 and very recently Commission suggested for synthesis of many laws and restructuring of regulating agencies.

28.2-3 Inspection of report of Company Liquidator

Report of Company Liquidator can be inspected by creditor or contributory or his agent and can obtain its copies - section 281(5) of Companies Act, 2013.

28.3 Directions by NCLT after receiving report of Company Liquidator Section 282 of Companies Act, 2013 enumerates steps to be taken by NCLT after receiving report of company liquidator. The steps include (a) fix time limit for completing winding up proceedings (b) Order sale of company or its assets as a going concern (c) Order action if fraud is suspected (d) Other order to protect, preserve and enhance value of assets of company (e) Other directions as NCLT may deem fit.

Thus, NCLT has very wide powers in winding up of company.

NCLT can review and modify its orders during winding up proceedings, on receiving quarterly report from Company Liquidator - section 288(2) of Companies Act, 2013.

NCLT has to grant hearing to Company Liquidator, Creditors, Contributories or other persons before passing order.

28.3-1 Fixing time schedule for dissolution of company

NCLT shall fix time limit to complete dissolution of company. The time limit can be revised on application of Company Liquidator, Creditor, Contributory or any other person - section 282(1) of Companies Act, 2013.

28.3-2 Sale of company or assets as going concern

NCLT can order sale of company or its assets as a going concern. NCLT may appoint sales committee for this purpose - section 282(2) of Companies Act, 2013.

If a unit is actually functional, sale as a 'going concern' may attract better price than sale of individual assets. This will also really speed up process of winding up.

Once NCLT sanctions sale as a going concern, the actual sale can be made by Company Liquidator as per powers under section 290(1)(d) of Companies Act, 2013.

Unit closed for long time may not be sold as going concern - If the unit is closed for long time, sale of machinery, plant and land separately will fetch a better price. The reason is that in case of sale as a going concern, employment of all employees will continue, which may cast a big liability.

In Allahabad Bank v. Arc Holding Ltd. 2000 AIR SCW 3498 = 28 SCL 394 (SC), it was held that if a unit is closed for a long time, sale as a going concern should not be normally ordered by High Court (now NCLT).

28.3-3 Action if Company Liquidator reports fraud

If Company Liquidator makes such report, NCLT shall order investigation under section 210 of Companies Act, 2013. On receipt of report of investigation, NCLT may give directions under sections 339 to 342 of Companies Act, 2013. NCLT may direct Company Liquidator to file criminal complaint against persons who were involved in the fraud - section 282(2) of Companies Act, 2013

If Company Liquidator reports that fraud has been committed in promotion, formation, business or conduct of affairs of company, NCLT can order examination of such promoters, directors or officers of the company - section 300(1) of Companies Act, 2013.

28.4 Custody of company's properties after order of winding up

Company Liquidator or Provisional Liquidator shall take custody of all properties, effects and actionable claims of the company. Even if actual possession is not taken, these will be deemed to be in custody of NCLT. NCLT can order any contributory, trustee, receiver, banker, officer or employee to pay or deliver or transfer any money, property or books and papers in his custody.

28.4-1 Taking over of company's property by Company Liquidator

After order of winding up is made or after a provisional liquidator has been appointed, the Company Liquidator or Provisional Liquidator shall take into his custody or under his control, all property, effects and actionable claims of the company - section 283(1) of Companies Act, 2013.

20.3-10c Action point against voilations - The action point comes out clear in the direction of the Lucknow Bench of the Allahabad High Court reported as having been given on October 23, 2003 to the Ministry of Finance, SEBI and the DCA to explain why the Orders issued by it on March 16, 1999 in the case of vanishing companies, (some 229 of them, a fraction of the whole lot, said to have been identified but with no arrests or recovery of the amounts embezzled out of collections from the public, made), have not been complied with for four and a half years, in spite of the assurance given by the additional solicitor-general on behalf of the Union of India, SEBI and the DCA, and to comply with the same before November 3, 2003, the next hearing date, in the PIL filed by Midas Touch Investors Association (Asian Age, 24th October, 2003). Functional overlaps seem to be the apparent reason for this regulator failure that goes to sap the investor confidence.

Role of Central Government - Such matters mentioned in section 55A entrusted to SEBI but related to other companies have been left to be administered by the Central Government, that is, matters relating to statement in lieu of prospectus, return of allotment, issue of shares and redemption of irredeemable preference shares and preference shares etc., the powers being exercisable by the Central Government/Tribunal/Registrar, as the case may be.

20.3-10d Role of SEBI - By section 11(1) of the SEBI Act, it is the duty of SEBI to protect the interests of investors in securities by such measures as it deems fit; and section 11A of the said Act authorizes SEBI :

(1) to prescribe regulations on matters relating to issue of capital, transfer of securities and other incidental matters as well as the manner in which such matters shall be disclosed in the offer documents by the companies, without prejudice to the Companies Act provisions;

(2) by general or special orders, prohibit any company from issuing prospectus, any offer document, or advertisement soliciting money from the public for the issue of securities as also specify the conditions subject to which the prospectus, offer document or advertisement, if not prohibited, may be issued; and

(3) specify the requirements for listing and transfer of securities and other incidental matters, without prejudice to section 21 of the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act (that is, the mandatory requirement of complying with the conditions of the listing agreement).

Investigation of a company - Purpose

The purpose of investigation is to find out whether those in charge of the affairs of a company are guilty of illegal conduct or conduct trenching upon the breach of fiduciary obligations or oppression or misfeasance [see Kumaranunni v. Mathrubhumi Printing and Publishing Co. Ltd. [1983] 54 Comp. Cas. 370 (Ker.)]. Towards this end, an inspector merely probes into the affairs of the company and embodies in the report his opinion. The document is admissible in evidence only as a piece of opinion. The opinion, by itself does not affect the rights of the company. He does not write a judgment which binds the company nor does he penalize any body [see Aditya Sharda v. Rangoli Texdye Pvt. Ltd. [2005] 123 Comp. Cas. 390 (CLB)]. Investigation is only a fact-finding measure and has no quasi-judicial character [see New Central Jute Mills Co. Ltd. v. Deputy Secretary, Ministry of Finance [1966] 37 Comp. Cas. 341 (Cal.) and Ashoka Marketing Ltd. v. Union of India [1967] 37 Comp. Cas. 341 (Cal.)]

Introduction

1. "Double your money in 90 days," promised Charles Ponzi, an Italian immigrant to the US, way back in 1919. That was the start of such fraudulent schemes. It seems that it has become immortal unlike its master. Every year hundreds & thousands of such schemes are floated in the market with an intent of defrauding innocent, or should we say, greedy investors who are easily trapped by their treacherous but very lucrative promises.

India saw its biggest Ponzi scheme in the name of Saradha scam in the State of West Bengal, which is slowly turning out to be the hot bed of fraudulent schemes in India. Data collected by the government shows more than 8 out of 10 multi-level marketing and finance schemes against which authorities have received complaints are running from West Bengal. As on March 14, 2013, the government had received complaints against 87 companies from across the country that were suspected of carrying out Ponzi or multi-level schemes. As many as 73 or 84% of these companies are from West Bengal and more than 30 or nearly half of these are believed to be related to the scam-scarred Sudipto Sen-promoted Saradha group. After seeing this data it will not be wrong to call "BENGAL-THE PONZI CAPITAL OF INDIA". The concern should be pinpointed towards eliminating the reason for mushrooming of such schemes and then set out the necessary regulatory set up enabling safeguarding of our ill informed citizens.

Modus Operandi of Saradha schemers

2. The group collected monies from the investors through agents promising them returns in the form of land or a flat, or an option for a refund with a rate of return ranging between 12% - 24% approximately. Most of the investors seem to have opted for the absolute return option rather than claiming land or a flat at the end of the investment tenure, as per the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) notice. The agents, in turn, were assured of a commission ranging from 15% to 20% on the funds mobilised by them, according to local media reports. In some of the schemes the group promised that on a deposit of Rs. 1 lakh an investor will get Rs. 10 lakhs after 14 years. If the same amount of money was kept in a fixed deposit in a bank for the same period, the amount at expiry would be Rs. 4 lakh. In other words, the rate of return promised by the group was exponential and completely shunned the idea of any other investment. According to some media estimates, the number of agents employed by Saradha group may run into thousands or even in lakhs, while the total amount of money mobilised by the group can run into thousands of crores. The huge collection of money from the agents was deposited with the main company which floated 160 companies (according to the letter submitted by Sudipto Sen to the CBI), including a large number of newspapers in various languages and TV channels in Bengali.

The companies that made up Saradha Group were incorporated in the year 2006. Initially, the front-line companies collected money from the public by issuing secured debentures and redeemable preferential bonds, but the entire exercise of mobilising the funds however, lacked procedural proprieties like-

None of the documents given to the Registrar of Companies by the Saradha Group, under statutory requirements, mentioned anything about mobilising such huge amount of money from the public.

Under Indian Securities Regulation and Section 67of the Companies Act, 1956 [now old Companies Act] a company cannot raise capital from more than 50 people without issuing proper prospectus and Balance Sheet, also requiring explicit SEBI clearance. No such clearance or approval was taken.

The promise of providing a plot of land or a flat after the maturity of the scheme was also a hoax.

The above were a few of the discrepancies that the Saradha Group Scheme had, though the list is not exhaustive one. It can be said that the Group's functioning was blatantly illegal. Survival of the scheme even after such manifest illegalities showed the failure of the regulatory authorities to take appropriate measures, at the centre and the State both and even hints at possible collusion with some of these authorities.

The premium calculations are based on such premises as no independent investor would ever adopt, and even the fundamental assumptions are incorrect and unreal. Powers of directors

26.4 The powers of the directors are co-extensive with the powers of the company as conditioned and controlled by the memorandum, the articles and the Act, cf. Oakbank Oil Co. v. Crum (1882) 8 AC 65; and so long as they do so, the Court should grant temporary injunction to restrain persons from interfering with the duly elected directors in the discharge of their duties - Gur Prasad Kapoor v. Rameshwar Prasad (1933) 3 Comp. Cas. 153 (All.).

Directors’ acts have to be consistent with the articles and subsisting contracts

26.4-1 Where the articles specify the powers of directors, they cannot go beyond the limits set out - Agriculturists Cattle Insurance Co., In re (1866) 1 Ch. App. 511, and in the exercise of such powers the directors should do so subject to the agreements and contracts subsisting - Nelson v. James Nelson & Son Ltd. (1914-15) All. ER 433 (CA).

Board strength below minimum fixed by articles

26.4-2 A Board comprising lesser number of directors than that fixed by the articles cannot exercise the functions of the Board - Vishwanath Prasad Jallan v. Holyland Cinetone Ltd. (1939) 9 Comp. Cas. 324 (All.); but if their number is not less than the quorum, they may act and if the number falls below the quorum, they can act only to increase their number (regulation 75 of Table ‘A’).

Members cannot interfere with day-to-day management of the company

26.4-3 Unless the articles permit, the shareholders cannot interfere in the day-to-day management of the company - Suburban Bank (P.) Ltd. v. Thariath (1968) 38 Comp. Cas. 13 (Ker.); and where the management of the company is vested in the Board of directors by the articles, such power can be withdrawn only by amending the articles - Murarka Paint & Varnish Work (P.) Ltd. v. Mohanlal Murarka (1961) 31 Comp. Cas. 301 (Cal.), and the company in general meeting cannot pass a resolution inconsistent with the articles - Salmon v. Quin Axtens Ltd. (1909) 1 Ch. 311 (CA). Accordingly, the directors are not bound to comply with the directions given by majority of shareholders at a general meeting unless the articles are altered - Automatic Self-Cleaning Filter Syndicate Co. Ltd. v. Cunningham (1906) 2 Ch. 34 (CA), John Shaw & Sons (Salford) Ltd. v. Shaw (1935) 2 KB 113 (CA) and Pothen v. Hindustan Trading Corpn. (P.) Ltd. (1967) 37 Comp. Cas. 266 (Ker.).

Board’s powers include the powers incidental to its powers specified in the articles

Cas. 586 (All.), or the power to change the method of accounting - CIT v. Eastern Bengal Jute Trading Co. Ltd. (1978) 48 Comp. Cas. 262 (Cal.), or the power to create a reserve - CIT v. Oswal Woollen Mills Ltd. (1981) 51 Comp. Cas. 733 (Punj. & Har.), or to invest the reserve fund in such securities as the directors select other than speculative transactions - Burland v. Technical Interpretation of 'Past Acts' covered ?

Respondent also argued that as per section 241(1) Central Government may itself apply tribunal only in case ,if it is of opinion that the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interest. Here "acts" in this case are past acts and not present acts.

The Hon'ble Bench have different view with contention raised by respondent, the reason being that company is alive and present acts covered under scope of section 241(2).

Bench said that "The use of words "are being conducted", does not mean it does not cover the past acts. It is to be interpreted that the acts so mentioned in the above proviso also indicates past acts of mis-management, the present acts of mis-management and also to contain the future acts, especially when it comes to dealing with fraudulent transactions. In this present case, the company is still in operation under the control of RP and hence all the acts so mentioned are not just past continuous but also present perfect continuous."

The rationale was held to be to be that Petitioner (R.D) did not sought any relief in petition which harms or goes against corporate debtor and the only relief which is sought is to save the public at large and provide them the best out of the fraud by freezing down the assets of the wrong doers.

Further, it held that it was fit case to grant interim relief as failure to do so shall have devastating effect, the wrongdoers and fraudulent persons would get away and the valuable assets of the companies would get depleted, bringing the irreparable loss to the stakeholders."

Obligations of financial institution and intermediaries

7.1 Maintaining record of certain transactions - Clause 11 of the Bill is considered to be the main cause of worry for financial institutions and other intermediaries. It proposes to make it obligatory for every financial institution and intermediary to maintain a record of all transactions or series of inter-connected transactions exceeding the value of rupees twenty-five lakhs held within a month.

7.2 Furnishing information about certain transactions to income-tax department - It is also proposed that they would be required to furnish information of these transactions to the Commissioner of Income-tax having jurisdiction over such financial institutions or the intermediaries. The financial institutions and intermediaries would also be required to verify and maintain the records of the identity of all of their clients in the prescribed manner for a period of five years from the date of cessation of transactions between the clients and financial institutions.

The provisions of the clause are likely to impose a severe burden on banks, financial institutions and other intermediaries. In view of the fact that the process of computerisation of banks may still take some time to complete, the compliance with these provisions may be very difficult, if not impossible. Even the Reserve Bank has criticised the provisions due to the fact that financial markets have significantly matured in recent years and the number of daily transactions exceeding Rs. 25 lakh runs into lakhs. Therefore, unless the limit is raised to Rs. 1 crore, it would be a nightmarish and back-breaking exercise for banks, financial institutions etc., to report every Rs. 25 lakh plus deal to the authorities.

Also, it is learnt that financial institutions etc. will be required to maintain the record of such transactions for a period of 5 years. This will further add to their headache as they would be required to preserve the records in their original forms. Thus, they would be under tremendous strain for not only maintaining the specified records but also for forwarding the same to the Commissioner of Income-tax. This information on financial trans-actions would be utilised by the enforcement agencies, in consultation with the Reserve Bank, to investigate offences under the Prevention of Money Laundering Legislation (after the Bill is enacted into an Act).

Clause 12 proposes to empower the Director to impose a fine on a financial institution if the institution has failed to maintain or retain records in accordance with the provisions of clause 11. The Director may levy a fine on such financial institution of not less than rupees ten thousand but not exceeding one lakh rupees. A copy of such order levying the fine will be forwarded to every financial institution or intermediary, or other person who is a party to the proceedings. However, clause 13 seeks to provide that the financial institutions, intermediaries and their offices will be provided immunity from any civil or criminal liability, under any existing law, arising out of disclosures of information under clause 11.

The Bill proposes to set up a directorate to administer the Act under the supervision of the Revenue department. The directorate would enjoy the same powers as a civil court enjoys. The officers of the directorate would enjoy powers similar to those conferred on the ITO. Apart from attachment of property, the directorate will have powers to summon, search, seize and arrest an offender. The authorities, such as the director, deputy director, assistant director or any other authorised officer, would have the power to search premises, vessels and aircrafts, seize documents and summon a company, individual or official with a 90 day notice.

Winding up order and its effects

26.1 Orders that can be passed by NCLT after receiving petition for winding up

After hearing the petition, NCLT can pass any of the following orders - section 273(1) of Companies Act, 2013 -

(a)

Dismiss petition with or without costs.

(b)

Make any interim order that it thinks fit.

(c)

Appoint a provisional liquidator of the company till the making of a winding up order.

(d)

Make an order for winding up the company with or without costs.

(e)

Make any other order that it thinks fit.

Thus, NCLT has wide powers in winding up petition.

NCLT can pass winding up order even if assets are mortgaged or there are no assets - NCLT cannot refuse to make a winding up order merely because all its assets are mortgaged to an amount equal to or more than the value of assets or company has no assets - third proviso to section 273(1) of Companies Act, 2013.

[This provision has been made, as, otherwise, company would argue that even if winding up is ordered, nobody is likely to get anything].

No Winding up order on just and equitable grounds if other remedy available - If petition is for winding up on the ground that it is 'just and equitable', NCLT can refuse winding up if it is of the opinion that some other remedy is available to the petitioners, and the petitioners are acting unreasonably in seeking winding up, instead of pursuing that other remedy - section 273(2) of Companies Act, 2013.

Winding up order can be recalled – If company in liquidation settles all claims and dues of creditors, winding up order can be recalled – Shekhar Electricals v. Falcon Retreat (2018) 147 SCL 559 = 93 taxmann.com 344 (Bom HC).

26.1-1 Wide powers or NCLT to pass any order as it deems fit

Section 273(1)(e) of 2013 Act states that NCLT can pass any order it deems fit, on receipt of winding up petition.

In NEPC Agro Food v. Hindustan Thompson (2001) 33 SCL 15 (Mad HC DB), it was held, 'In absence of any limitation or restriction in section 443 of the 1956 Act [parallel section 273(1)(e) of Companies Act, 2013] or elsewhere in the Act, it has to be taken that Court (Now NCLT) can pass any order it thinks fit or necessary in interest of justice and in implementing or giving effect to provisions of the Act'.

In the aforesaid case, it was held that company judge (Now NCLT) can issue interim order appointing auditor to verify extent of amount payable by the company. It was observed that since report of auditor is not binding on court (now NCLT), company would have opportunity to file its objections to it which would be considered by court before either accepting it or rejecting it.

NCLT can recommend investigation or filing FIR - Court (Now NCLT) has ample powers to recommend investigation and give directions for filing First Information Report (FIR) with regard to any apparent fraud by the company and those in-charge of company. - MCC Finance v. RBI (2002) 37 SCL 517 (Mad HC DB).

Appointment of company liquidator if winding up ordered - If winding up is ordered, Company Liquidator will be appointed by NCLT.

26.1-2 Submitting books of account and audited statement if winding up ordered

If NCLT orders winding up, the company is required to submit within 30 days, books of account duly audited upto date of winding up order to Company Liquidator, in the manner specified by NCLT - section 274(3) of Companies Act, 2013.

If Directors and officers of company fail to submit such audited report in 30 days, they are liable for punishment under section 274(4) of Companies Act, 2013. Complaint can be filed before Special Court by Registrar, Provisional Liquidator, Company Liquidator or any person authorized by NCLT - section 274(5) of Companies Act, 2013.

26.1-3 Powers of NCLT to entertain suits

NCLT can entertain all suits and proceedings by or against the company.
