Introduction

The Supreme Court's recent judgment in National Spot Exchange Limited (NSEL) v. Union of India & Ors (Writ Petition (Civil) No. 995 of 2019) is a landmark in the domain of financial fraud litigation and asset recovery. The decision, delivered on 15 May 2025, addresses the complex interplay between the Maharashtra Protection of Interest of Depositors (MPID) Act, the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), and central statutes such as the SARFAESI Act, Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act (RDB Act), and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC).

At its core, this decision represents a careful recalibration of the legal hierarchy between secured creditors, government agencies, and public interest protections in cases involving tainted assets.

Background: The NSEL Scam and Legal Tangle

NSEL, a commodity trading platform promoted by 63 Moons Technologies Ltd. The collapse of the National Spot Exchange in 2013 triggered a Rs. 5,600 crore default, affecting about 13,000 traders and investors. The fallout led to multiple FIRs, civil suits, and the attachment of assets by both the Enforcement Directorate (under PMLA) and the State of Maharashtra (under the MPID Act). The NSEL itself secured decrees and arbitral awards worth around Rs. 3,365 crore against defaulting members, but faced significant hurdles in executing them due to overlapping attachments and competing claims from secured creditors (primarily banks) under SARFAESI/RDB Act. IBC proceedings also initiated against several entities.

Genesis of the Supreme Court Committee

To streamline the complex situation, involving execution of multiple decrees and avoid conflicting proceedings, the Supreme Court, invoking Article 142, constituted a high-powered committee chaired by Justice (Retd.). This committee was vested with the powers of a civil court to execute all decrees, orders, and arbitral awards obtained by NSEL, including the authority to sell properties attached under PMLA and MPID Act and oversee distribution to verified claimants. In short, Article 142 was used as a constitutional "safety valve" to harmonize conflicting statutory regimes, centralize execution, and prioritize investor restitution in a manner that ordinary statutory processes could not have achieved efficiently.

Power under Article 142 is extraordinary, discretionary, and unique to the Supreme Court. It allows the Court to:

Fill legal gaps where no statute provides an adequate remedy. It Complements statutory law, but does not override it—cannot be used to violate or contradict existing statutes

Issue binding directions, even if not strictly aligned with procedural law. Curative in nature—used to resolve issues when ordinary law falls short or causes injustice

Craft equitable solutions, especially in complex, multi-party, or sensitive matters.

However, Article 142 cannot be used to create a new law or override substantive rights conferred by legislation. It must be used judiciously and only when regular statutory or procedural remedies are inadequate or unjust. Article 142 cannot be used to achieve something indirectly what cannot be achieved directly.

While initially hailed as a pragmatic consolidation, the order's breadth brought it into direct strain with key statutory provisions of PMLA, SARFAESI, RDB Act, and IBC—particularly regarding the priority of secured creditors and the moratorium under insolvency law.

Key Legal Questions before the Supreme Court

Two main issues crystallized before the Court in the later stages of the litigation:

1.

Do secured creditors have priority over assets attached under the PMLA and MPID Act by virtue of SARFAESI and RDB Act?

2.

Are properties attached under the MPID Act immune from the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC?

These questions weren't just technical—they strike at the heart of India's recovery framework, challenging the hierarchy of creditor rights in fraud scenarios.

Supreme Court's Ruling on Secured Creditors' Priority

The Court held that the MPID Act and PMLA take precedence over the SARFAESI Act and RDB Act when it comes to assets attached as "proceeds of crime" or for the protection of depositors. The rationale is rooted in constitutional law: the MPID Act is a state law enacted to maintain public order and protect depositors, while SARFAESI and RDB Act are central laws focusing on banking and secured creditors' rights. Since these statutes operate in distinct legislative fields, the doctrine of repugnancy under Article 254 does not apply.

No other investigating agency shall proceed with investigation in a case in respect of any offence under the Companies Act 2013, once the case has been assigned to SFIO. The SFIO has power to arrest individuals if it has reason to believe that he is guilty based on the material in possession. SFIO shall submit a report to the Central Government on conclusion of investigation. Central Government may direct SFIO to initiate prosecution against the company. This Article attempts to analyse the judgement passed in the matter of "Union of India v. Videocon Industries Ltd. [2021] 130 taxmann.com 52/[2022] 169 SCL 402 (NCLT - Mum.) wherein serious allegations of mismanagement has been taken against promoter/management of the company. The allegations were based on the forensic audit report which was conducted on directions of Resolution Professional during the insolvency process.

Brief History :

Videocon was large corporate performing in electronic hardware industry and as well as in telecom industry.

In 2018, State Bank of India, lead bank, which was Financial Creditor of the company, made an application under section 7 of Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 ('IBC')to initiated Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against company since there was default in repayment of debts.

During Corporate Insolvency Process , Resolution Professional filed application to tribunal based on avoidance transactions identified by forensic auditor. Various application were made under section 43 and 66 of IBC wherein serious allegations were made against Promoters for conducting fraudulent transaction.

In Forensic Audit, the independent Auditor made remarks based on the information available and provided that various fraudulent transactions occurred between group companies.

Based on report of forensic auditor and other financial transaction proof with them, Regional Director, Western Region on behalf of Ministry of Corporate Affairs filed Petition for Interim Reliefs against officials of company and board of directors of group companies.

Present Case :

Various Interim reliefs were sought i.e. to direct respondents to disclose their Properties, to direct NSDL/CDSL to freeze their securities account, to direct CBDT to freeze assets of the respondents of the petition etc. and further to initiate oppression and mismanagement case against the promoter and BOD of the corporate debtor to secure or restore the assets back to catch out the real fraud and the wrong doers of the fraud along with assets to the right victim of the fraud

The respondent companies argued that matter was stayed by Appellate Tribunal and which was confirmed by Supreme court. Hence, Company is still under CIR and therefore as per Section 14 of IBC, Moratorium is in effect and therefore no judicial action can be initiated during CIRP against the company.

Brief of Section 14 related to case :

Section 14 (1) says that "Subject to provisions of sub-sections (2) and (3), on the insolvency commencement date, the Adjudicating Authority shall by order declare moratorium for prohibiting all of the following, namely :—

(a)

the institution of suits or continuation of pending suits or proceedings against the corporate debtor including execution of any judgment, decree or order in any court of law, tribunal, arbitration panel or other authority;"

(b)

transferring, encumbering, alienating or disposing of by the corporate debtor any of its assets or any legal right or beneficial interest therein;

(c)

any action to foreclose, recover or enforce any security interest created by the corporate debtor in respect of its property including any action under the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002;

(d)

the recovery of any property by an owner or lessor where such property is occupied by or in the possession of the corporate debtor.

Moratorium Prohibits Petitioner to initiate Suit against company which is under CIRP. The very purpose of Moratorium is to stop multiplicity of cases, safeguarding assets pool and help resolution professional in focusing CIRP.

The argument of respondents was that the prohibitions are on both parties i.e. for and against the corporate debtor and hence these proceedings are bad in law and therefore should be set aside.

However, NCLT rejected this argument that proceedings are not proceedings against the corporate debtor but for corporate debtor. They agreed on contention that no suit or proceeding can be initiated against corporate debtor.

But in the instance case the efforts made by the Union of India were analysed and the spirit of them was seen to secure or restore the assets back to the ultimate victims of fraud and it is not any adversarial proceeding that is the proceeding in rem which has initiated by the Union of India to catch hold all the wrong doers and the fraudulent persons.

Audit simply means checking of records to establish accuracy

'Audit' is a systematic and independent examination of data, statements, records, operations and performance (financial or otherwise) of an enterprise for a stated purpose. In an auditing situation, the auditor perceives and recognises the propositions before him for examination, collects evidence, evaluates the same and on that basis, formulates the judgment which is communicated through his audit report [ICAI in General guidelines on Internal Auditing].

Auditing is a systematic process of objectively obtaining and evaluating evidence regarding assertions about economic actions and events to ascertain the degree of correspondence between those assertions and established criteria, and communicating results to interested user (Auditing Concepts Committee of American Accounting Association).

In service tax audit under EA-2000, 'audit' simply means verification of records to ensure correctness.

That audit need not be confused with 'statutory audit' which might be conducted under some specific provisions of Act, like section 73A of Finance Act, 1994. It seems this distinction was not properly brought out before High Court.

28.10-3 Binding nature of decisions taken at meeting of creditors, contributories or Advisory Committee

Section 292(1) of the 2013 states that Company Liquidator shall have regard to the directions given in the resolution at such meetings.

Section 354 of Companies Act, 2013 states that liquidator shall have regard to the wishes of creditors or contributories. Since creditors and contributories have different interests, their wishes may not tally. Even among contributories or creditors, views may differ as interest of each are different.

Thus, their resolutions cannot be binding on Company Liquidator or NCLT.

The resolutions passed at meeting of creditors or contributories have only persuasive value. Company Liquidator or NCLT are not bound by such resolutions.

If the Company Liquidator is not in agreement with the resolutions, he can bypass them for valid reasons. This is also obvious from the fact that any person can apply to NCLT against decision of Company Liquidator under section 292(4) of Companies Act, 2013.

However, in such cases, he should place the matter before NCLT for directions. NCLT will take final view considering totality of circumstances.

28.10-4 Company Liquidator to keep record of meetings

Company Liquidator should keep proper books in which he shall cause entries or minutes of proceedings of meetings and such other matters as may be prescribed. The 'books' are not 'books of account'. The 'books' only refer to records of meetings.

Introduction

1. India has very large rural population with low income and access to formal banking facilities. As a result web of parallel informal banking channels arose to fill the vacuum. At its centre were moneylenders, who used to charge exorbitant rates of interest. This practice was greatly curbed by the several Moneylenders Acts enacted by the State Governments in the early 1950s. However, the fundamental failure to overcome the role of moneylenders gave rise to fly-by-night financial operators who ran Ponzi schemes in various disguises. However, some commentators place the blame for mushrooming of these kinds of Ponzi schemes on greed rather than on inadequacy of formal banking systems.

The relatively prosperous rural economy of West Bengal had previously relied on small savings schemes run by the Indian Postal Service. However, low rates of interest in the 1980s and 90s encouraged and gave rise to several Ponzi schemes in speculative ventures such as Sanchayita Investments, Overland Investment Company, Verona Credit and Commercial Investment Company. Together, these scams garnered close to 10 billion INR of investor's wealth.

The Saradha Group financial scandal has been a financial scam which was caused by the collapse of a Ponzi scheme run by Saradha Group, a consortium of Indian companies which was believed to be running a wide variety of collective investment schemes (popularly but incorrectly referred to as chit funds) in the Eastern India. The group collapsed in April, 2013, causing an estimated loss of INR 200–300 billion (US$ 4–6 billion). In the aftermath of the financial scandal, the State Government of West Bengal set-up an inquiry Commission to investigate into collapse and also set-up a fund of INR 5 billion (92 million USD) to ensure that low income investors were not bankrupted. The Union Government also launched a multi-agency probe to investigate into the Saradha scam, as well as into other similar Ponzi schemes.

The Ponzi Schemes

2. The Saradha Group has gained notoriety in recent weeks with outstanding public deposits reportedly exceeding Rs. 200 billion. There was anger and panic. The State Government has stepped in with partial redressal system.

As we watch unfolding of this saga, there may be another crisis waiting to happen in the form of a pyramid scheme offered by Mavrodi Mondial Moneybox (MMM) that is taking rural India by storm. MMM claims to be a "social financial network" in which members voluntarily share money with each other by buying and selling MAVROS - a currency-like unit devised by the operators of the scheme. MMM claims to generate returns of over 40% per month, although the returns are not guaranteed. It may be a ponzi scheme: one where money collected from new investors is used to pay returns to old investors. The cycle will continue till inflows into the scheme exceed outflows.

Saradha and MMM are not isolated examples. Some of the recent schemes have promised unrealistic returns from investments in goats, pigs, emu, teak wood and potatoes.

The history of savings and investments in India is replete with tragedies where financial firms have failed to return deposits or investments. This is particularly problematic in a country where 70% of the people earn under 2 dollars a day and, hence, have small amounts of money saved up. If savings are not safe, the central objective of regulation - consumer protection - is not met. What we need is institutions that can take up deposits or run investment schemes to operate in a safe and sound manner, within the bounds of financial regulation.

How Saradha delayed investigation by SEBI

3. SEBI was investigating into Saradha for more than 3 years before the deposit schemes of the company collapsed. Saradha seems to have used following two methods to delay the investigation:

When SEBI asserted its authority to stop Saradha group from collecting money, Saradha challenged the jurisdiction of the SEBI in district courts. It quickly got orders to prevent SEBI from interfering in its businesses. These orders were eventually overturned by the High Court.

When SEBI requested information from Saradha about their schemes and investors, Saradha responded by providing large volumes of documentation without specifically answering SEBI's questions. This slowed down the entire investigation.

Limitations of the SEBI

4. In the course of three years Saradha took on new depositors and collected money from existing ones. All this money is now lost. Two years of investigation were required to stop what seems to be a run of the mill Ponzi scheme. The tactics employed by Saradha are not new. They are similar to those employed by Sahara in delaying investigations in the OFCD schemes and in many other white collar crime investigations. The disturbing fact is that they seem to succeed time and again.

28.4-11 Employees must vacate the quarters on issue of winding up order Winding up order acts as discharge of all employees. Hence, ex-employees have no right under Industrial Disputes Act and they must vacate possession of quarters occupied by them. Even otherwise, section 468 specifies that Court (now NCLT) may require any officer or employee of company to deliver, surrender or transfer property in his custody or control, to official liquidator. Upon passing of winding up order, section 630 immediately comes into operation. - Electronics Ltd. In re (2002) 39 SCL 585 = 2002 CLC 1457 (Del HC).

In Textile Labour Association v. Official Liquidator of Amruta Mills (2005) 58 SCL 452 (Guj HC), employees were in possession of chawls (residential complexes) of the company. The company went into liquidation. It was held that employer employee relationship comes to end as soon as company goes into liquidation. Hence, Court can order eviction of employees, as there is no tenancy right and occupation of residential accommodation is illegal and unlawful withholding of property of company is liquidation. The liquidator is not required to file any suit for eviction or initiate any other proceedings.

28.4-12 Lessor can terminate lease but possession of property only with permission of NCLT

In Phatu Rochiram Mulchandani v. Karnataka Industrial Areas Dev. Board (2015) 5 SCC 244, it has been held that lessor can terminate lease if less (company being wound up) for violation of terms of lease. Permission of Court (now NCLT) is not required. However, after winding up, possession of property cannot be taken by lessor without leave of Court.

28.4-13 NCLT cannot interfere when secured creditor has taken steps under SARFAESI Act

SARFAESI Act is a complete code. As per section 13 of SARFAESI Act, secured creditor has right to enforce security interest without intervention of Court. Hence, company judge (now NCLT) cannot interfere with proceedings by a secured creditor who has opted to stay outside winding up process to realise its secured assets as per SARFAESI Act - Pegasus Assets Reconstruction P Ltd. v. The magistrate can use force, if necessary, to take possession. He will then deliver its possession to NCLT or person authorized by NCLT [section 429 of Companies Act, 2013].

28.6 Promoters, directors, officers to co-operate with Company Liquidator

Section 284 of Companies Act, 2013 is a new provision under the Act, which provides that directors, promoters, officers and employees of company must co-operate with Company Liquidator in discharge of his duties.

If they fail to do so without reasonable cause, punishment of imprisonment and fine can be imposed.

Even without such specific provision, there is no doubt that directors, officers are required to co-operate with Company Liquidator appointed by NCLT.

It seems Company Liquidator himself has to file complaint in Special Court.

He may, instead of approaching criminal court, approach NCLT and seem suitable directions from NCLT. If despite such directions, director, promoter, officer or employee does not co-operate, criminal complaint may be filed.

Of course, evidence of specific instances of non-co-operation have to be stated and proved.

28.7 Settlement of list of contributory and application of assets

Section 285 of Companies Act, 2013 makes provision to settle list of contributories who are liable to pay some amounts to companies.

The title of section and words used in section 285(1) of Companies Act, 2013 are slightly misleading as though this section and title of section uses the words 'application of assets for discharge of liabilities', the other provisions of the section 285 of 2013 Act do not provide anything like application of assets' to discharge liabilities of company.

Of course these are provided in other sections like 280, 290, etc. of Companies Act, 2013.

12. It is very surprising to note that at a time when CSR activities are being promoted by government, due importance is not given to the transfer of amount to IEPF. Reporting relating to timely transfer of amount to IEPF has been done away with. Over the years, this clause has acted as a check point to ensure the timely transfer of unclaimed and unpaid amounts to IEPF. Reporting on accumulated losses would no longer be required

13. With a view to provide further ease of doing business, government has lifted another important reporting feature, under which auditor was to report on whether a newly incorporated company (Company registered for a period not less than 5 years) has accumulated losses at the end of financial year minimum 50% of its net worth. The clause was also required to report on cash losses in the financial year under review and in the immediately preceding financial year. Now the auditors are not at all required to report on these issues. However, this exemption is only allowed in case of newly incorporated companies. Probably the move is to see growth in the start-up companies.

Reporting on repayment of dues

14. Keeping in view rising debts and NPAs of the banks/financial institutions, the reporting format of auditors on the repayment of dues has been changed drastically. In addition to the earlier provisions of CARO applicable to the repayment of dues, now auditors are also required to report on lender-wise details. This move will surely act as an important check on further increase of NPAs and bad loans. Now the default in repayment of dues shall have its own language, as the name of the lenders and their respective amount shall be reported. It will be possible for all users of balance sheet to know/ascertain the dues to be paid to banks/financial institutions.

Default to government should also be specifically disclosed

15. Besides banks and financial institutions, now auditor shall also be required to report any default to the government. Thus, now onwards the government would also be construed as a party. In case of default to government, same type of lender-wise details have to be provided.

Corporate guarantee is no longer an item of CARO

16. CARO 2016 made another surprise move by deleting the clause for reporting of corporate guarantees given by the Company for loans taken by others from Bank or financial institutions. Subsequently, auditors are also not required to mention the interest of Company prejudicially affected by corporate guarantee.

Extensive and vast reporting on use of moneys raised through public issues as well as term loans

17. The recent scams of corporate sector seem to have widely effected the perception of the Ministry. The earlier CARO order was limited to the reporting on use of term loan for the purpose for which the loans were obtained. But keeping in view the public scams and frauds, the order is set to cover the whole gamut of fund raising in its coverage area.

Now onwards auditors have to be very cautious as they have to retain their identity of public trustees. Now they have to provide complete record for use of money raised through pubic issues and all other ways of raising finance, including debt instruments and term loans. Further reporting has to be on all kind of delays/defaults and subsequent rectifications, if any, and if applicable.

Two ways of fraud reporting

18. Earlier order was centered around reporting of fraud on or by the company. However, fraud on the company does not specifically mention the name of its officers/employees. Instead of that the new order specifically mentions the fraud on the company by its "officers/employees" as well as fraud by the Company. Thus, any kind of fraud, whether committed internally by the officers/employees or externally affecting public, shall have to be reflected in Auditor's report along with the nature of fraud and amount involved in the fraud.

Remuneration of managerial personnel would not be only a hidden item

19. Till now managerial remuneration has been reflected as a balance sheet item. But now onwards specific reporting by auditor has to be made on managerial remuneration. The auditor has to ensure that the remuneration paid to managerial personnel has been in accordance with section 197 and Schedule V of the Companies Act. Beyond that if amount paid or even amount provided has been in excess of section 197 and Schedule V of the Companies Act, 2013, the auditor has to mention the amount in excess of section 197, read with Schedule V and the steps taken by the company for recovery of the same. Thus, the Board or management shall have no right to waive off the amount to be recovered from managerial personnel.

Extensive exposure to related party transactions

20. The earlier order did not have any requirement of reporting on related party transactions. But the new one shall have extensive reporting feature, which shall cast direct responsibility on auditor and audit committee.

Auditor has to mention that all the related party transactions are in compliance with section 188 as well as in compliance with section 177. Section 177 which requires omnibus approval of audit committee, shall have to be counter reported in auditor's report. Thus, it should not be the prerogative of only audit committee to sanction the related party transactions as it will be counter checked by statutory auditor.

Under the Companies Act

Section 447 of the Companies Act, 2013 defines fraud as " any act, omission, concealment of any fact or abuse of positions with an intent to deceive, to gain undue advantage from or to injure the interests of the company or its shareholders or creditors or any other person, whether or not there is any wrongful gain or wrongful loss".

Some instances where Section 447 will trigger are:-

For untrue, misleading statement in prospectus or inclusion or omission of any matter.

For fraudulently inducing persons to invest money.

(d)

When auditor act in a fraudulent manner or abetted or colluded in any fraud.

(e)

When business of a company is carried on for a fraudulent or unlawful purposes or with intent to defraud creditors, members or any other person.

In addition to this, the police officers who are making an investigation also have the power to search a place without a warrant if they have reasonable grounds to believe that something which is important for the investigation will be found in the place he wishes to search.11 The detailed procedure for all these searches has been laid down under Section 100 of the CrPC.12 Now under the PMLA, Section 17 allows the concerned authority to enter, search any place suspected of containing proceeds or records of a crime, break open any lock or door if the concerned authority has reasons to believe that records or proceeds are related to a criminal activity.13 There is no requirement of a warrant here but there are certain checks and balances as the authority must have reasons to believe that must be recorded and be sent to the Adjudicating Authority.

Seizure of property

Regarding property, Section 102 of the CrPC gives the Police the power to seize any property that is alleged or suspected to be stolen or part of commissioning an offence.14 The police officer seizing the property has to report the seized property to the nearest magistrate.15 However, the situation is different when it comes to the PMLA, Section 17 states that when the authorized person as a reason to believe that a person has with him money obtained from money laundering or records or property relating to money laundering, he may seize and make a note of such a record or property.16 The authority seizing such evidence is required to forward the reasons for the seizure, along with the records to the Adjudicating Authority.17

This seizure is only mandated for a period of thirty days as after thirty days, the seizing authority may request the Adjudicating Authority for continuing the seizure.18 This shows that there is a better safeguard under the PMLA as the investigating authority needs permission to keep the property in custody for more than 30 days. The same does not exist under the CrPC and the police can keep the seized property in possession for the whole period of investigation without any time imposition. The Magistrate can make decisions as they seem fit relating to such seized property under Section 457 of the CrPC.

The Delhi High Court in the case of Abdullah Ali Balsharaf v. Directorate of Enforcement, where the action of Enforcement Directorate seizing property under both Section 102 of the CrPC and Section 17(1)(a) of the PMLA was challenged, has discussed both provisions in detail and held that the Enforcement Directorate acting under the PMLA cannot issue orders under the CrPC.19

The Court noted that the scheme of seizure and the checks and balances in the PMLA are substantively different than what is enshrined in the CrPC. The authorized officer under the PMLA can only go ahead with seizing a property if (a) they have material in possession that provides a reason to believe that the property is related to a crime and (b) the seizing officer has to record the reasons. Both these checks do not exist under Section 102 of the CrPC. This clearly shows that Section 17(1)(a) of the PMLA is inconsistent with Section 102 of the CrPC and cannot be applied to a case relating to money laundering that is punishable under the PMLA as Section 65 of the PMLA states that the provisions of CrPC can only apply when they are not inconsistent with the provisions of the PMLA.

The Delhi High Court in this judgement also disagreed with the view of the Gujarat High Court where in the case of Paresha G. Shah v. State of Gujarat, it was held that an order under Section 102 of the CrPC can be said to be aiding the order of provisional attachment passed under Section 5(1) of the PMLA or an order for seizing/freezing property under Section 17(1A) of the PMLA.20

CONCLUSION

In a nutshell, the PMLA and CrPC even though are very similar in terms of the procedure that has been prescribed, there is a both, a bane, and a boon when it comes to applying to procedure. The PMLA procedure for search and seizure does put a higher onus on the authority as it must have reasonable grounds for searching and seizing that must be recorded in writing. This check goes a long way in preventing misuse of power by the authority as the Adjudicating Authority can easily ascertain if the search and seizure took place on a weak or no reasons at all.

On the other hand, as it was seen above, the PMLA shifts the onus of proof on the defendant to prove that he is not guilty which means taking away the legal doctrine of presumption of innocence. Due to these reasons, the nature, and the limits of the power of the Enforcement Directorate, the authority to enforce PMLA are under challenge right now in the Supreme Court in the case of Vijay Madan Lal C haudhary v. Union of India where all these issues are up consideration.21 The decision of the Supreme Court in this case would serve as a landmark judgement showcasing the debate relating to the checks and balances of the criminal justice system relating to money laundering as well as how the Supreme Court interprets the different sections of PMLA to limit the power of the Enforcement Directorate.

[1996] 10 SCL 70 (SC) In the above matter the scope and ambit of the Company Court and the broad contours had emerged in respect of sanctioning the Schemes by the Court. It was held that the Court had to see that all the requisite statutory procedure for supporting the scheme had been complied with and that the requisite meetings was held; that the scheme put up for sanction of the Court was backed up by the requisite majority vote as required and the concerned meetings of the creditors or members or any class of them had the relevant material to enable the voters to arrive at an informed decision for approving the scheme in question; That the majority decision of the concerned class of voters was just and fair to the class as a whole so as to legitimately bind even the dissenting members of that class and ;that all necessary material indicated as per the provisions were placed before the voters at the concerned meetings ;That all the requisite material contemplated were placed before the Court by the concerned applicant seeking sanction for such a scheme and the Court gets satisfied about the same. The Court has to further see that the proposed scheme of compromise and arrangement was not found to be violative of any provision of law and was not contrary to public policy. For ascertaining the real purpose underlying the Scheme the Court, if necessary, could pierce the veil of apparent corporate purpose underlying the scheme and could judiciously X-ray the same. Further the Court has also to satisfy itself that members or class of members or creditors or class of creditors, as the case may be, were acting bona fide and in good faith and were not coercing the minority in order to promote any interest adverse to that of the latter comprising of the same class whom they purported to represent; the Court must also ascertain that the scheme as a whole is found to be just, fair and reasonable from the point of view of prudent men of business taking a commercial decision beneficial to the class represented by them for whom the scheme is meant.

Once the aforesaid broad parameters about the requirements of a scheme for getting sanction of the Court were found to have been met, the Court would have no further jurisdiction to sit in appeal over the commercial wisdom of the majority of the class of persons who with their open eyes gave their approval to the scheme even if in the view of the Court there would be a better scheme for the company and its members or creditors for whom the scheme is framed. The Court cannot refuse to sanction such a scheme on that ground, as it would otherwise amount to the Court exercising appellate jurisdiction over the scheme rather than its supervisory jurisdiction. The aforesaid parameters of the scope and ambit of the jurisdiction of the Company Court which was called upon to sanction a Scheme of Compromise and Arrangement were not exhaustive but only broadly illustrative of the contours of the Court's jurisdiction.

Making a Case for a Securities Market Whistleblower Policy 3. The Satyam s candal shook the corporate world due to the extent of havoc and uncertainty it created and raised several concerns regarding corporate governance issues. But it is more than just a corporate governance concern. It is about protecting the interests of the public where their monies are directly impacted. One of the severe criticisms of the above mentioned scandal was the lack of a operational whistleblower policy to deduct the overstating of the company's financial matters.

With regard to the Indian securities market, SEBI as an independent regulator is vested with the duty to protect the interests of the investors and actively participate in regulating and improving the Indian capital market. The market regulator has made significant strides since its statutory inception in 1992 by bringing to the fore various regulatory checks and balances such as prohibition of insider trading, ensuring disclosure mechanisms and the corporate takeover regulations. Following the Supreme Court's judgment in the Sahara case32, SEBI's jurisdiction over all companies that make public issue of securities have been widened. Therefore, most of the investors are protected by the SEBI. The Board's investigative and enforcement powers have been furthered augmented by the Securities Law (Amendment) Ordinance, 2013. Despite these legislative safeguards, SEBI has to within its means ensure maximum protection. One way is to give opportunity to the public to come forward with their fears of any securities law violation. Therefore, the author is of the opinion that in furtherance of SEBI's objective to ensure and maximise investor protection, administering a whistleblower policy will complement its measures in the process.

The steps taken by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) of the United States (US) have been hailed by the countries around the world for incentivizing whistleblowers coming forward to report corporate frauds. To briefly state it The Dodd Frank Act of 2010 brought out monetary incentives for voluntary disclosures to the Securities Exchange Commission (SEC) by the amending Securities Exchange Act.33 By inserting Section 21F to SEC Act, the Commission has been armed with the power to grant monetary awards to eligible individuals who voluntarily provide original information to the SEC about violations of the US securities law that leads to enforcement actions resulting in the imposition of monetary sanctions over $1,000,000. Anti-victimization clauses are extensive and thorough. The amendment is a significant measure in the global corporate whistleblower policy-making, as it is unambiguous with regard to defining key terms such as who constitutes a whistleblower, what comprises original information and the conditions for applying for a monetary award.

The US securities market varies from that of India's not only in terms of its size but also in the fact that it is more distributed when it comes to market participation. Although this might be the case, yet anti-fraud provisions in India with respect to the capital market draws inspiration largely from the similar provisions in the SEC Act in the United States. Not only this, certain provisions on whistleblowing in the Companies Act, 2013 are on the lines of the Sarbanes Oxley Act, 2002. As much as we imbibe from the success of their laws, we must also learn from their lacunae and loopholes.

There are several questions one must address before SEBI takes up the responsibility of providing whistleblowers. Starting with the SEBI Act itself, s. 24B seeks to provide relief from prosecution of a person who has been alleged to have committed a violation of the Act during the course of proceedings. However, this a power that vests in the Central Government and SEBI has only non-binding recommendatory effect. This law has to be amended to vest SEBI with the power to grant this immunity. Moreover, the provision must also elaborate upon protection of the persons coming forward with the information on violation as their statements are liable to be used as a testimony against others involved in the violation. This is a step closer to tightening the law. Secondly, a dedicated whistleblower legislation within the framework of the SEBI has to address, more importantly, who will not be a whistleblower. Any member of the general public, on suspicion of a violation of the Act that has occurred, or will occur or is occurring should be allowed to come forward with his/her complaint to the SEBI. However, such a person cannot be entitled to a monetary reward if he/she is a part of the alleged violation. In such a scenario, section 24B of the Act will kick in and, accordingly, the law will take its due course. Another person who cannot be considered for a whistleblower's reward is any compliance officer within a company. As such, an officer will have first hand knowledge of any complaint brought to him, and he cannot be considered to be providing information that is original as a result of any independent analysis.

Krishnamachari resigned. Scams made by stock market manipulators Harshad Mehta of 1990s and Ketan Parekh of 2000s are some prominent names in this regard. DR. V. BALACHANDRAN, K.S. RAVICHANDRAN AND R. KAMARAJ

Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) play a significant role in the economy of the nation. However, some unscrupulous elements among them have brought a bad name to the NBFC sector as a whole by cheating the investor’s of their hard-earned money. The CRB scam is a glaring and representative example of the same. Such dishonest conduct has forced the Government to put the activities of NBFCs under tight control In this article, the author discusses the measures adopted the RBI to protect the interest of depositors vis-a-vis NBFCs - EDITOR

Introduction

1. The role played by Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) in the national economy cannot be underestimated. They have been providing opportunities for better return to investors and flexibility in tapping resources. They extended retail services to small and middle level busi-nesses and road transport operators. The RBI has estimated that as at the end of March, 1996, regulated deposits of reporting non-banking compa-nies amounted to about Rs. 53,500 crores. Out of these NBFCs accounted for almost Rs. 45,500 crores. This represented about 10.8 per cent of the aggregate deposits of scheduled commercial banks. The rapid growth of NBFCs was facilitated by absence of restrictive legislative provisions. In fact most of the NBFCs did not even report about their operations to the RBI.

Post CRB scam scenario

2. Following the infamous CRB scam, suddenly black clouds have started gathering on the horizon creating an atmosphere of doubt and distrust. The industry was attacked from all sides. The most important critical problem confronting the industry is that of liquidity. New deposits have almost disappeared, the rate of renewal has fallen drastically and premature withdrawals have been heavy. To add salt to injury, banks and financial institutions have adopted a negative attitude of wait and watch;

Norms for unincorporated financial intermediaries

3. As stated by the Task Force Committee, one of the rudimentary factors contributing to distress in the NBFC sector is information asymmetry as between the depositors and NBFCs. The rationale for regulating the deposit-taking activities of unincorporated bodies essentially flows from the need to protect uninformed depositors. The first attempt to regulate the deposit-taking activities of unincorporated bodies was made in 1984 by inserting Chapter IIIC in the RBI, Act 1934. However, the newly introduced section 45S proved to be different to implement. Again, the RBI banned deposit-taking activities of unincorporated financial intermediaries by amending the RBI Act in 1997. These unincorporated entities were banned from, soliciting deposits by way of advertisements. This does not mean that section 45S prevents such entities from carrying on their operations. These regulations are intended to impel them towards acquiring a corporate status so that they operate within the regulatory framework created under the Companies Act arid Chapter IIIB of the RBI Act.

The unincorporated bodies engaged in non-banking financial business are not allowed to accept deposits except from the relatives, However, such entities could be allowed to access loans from bodies with corporate identity including NBFCs. Unauthorised deposit-taking by both NBFCs and unincorporated bodies is an offence. However, as regards NBFCs cognizance of this offence can be taken only on the complaint of an officer of the RBI. Such offences will now be made cognizable. Unauthorised deposit-taking by a financial sector intermediary automatically catapults these violations into the category of serious crimes.

The task force has advised the RBI to appoint depositors’ grievance redressal authorities with specified territorial jurisdiction. It suggested that a banking ombudsman could be a viable ‘option for such appointments. It has said that the authorities should be empowered to pass orders in regard to direct the unscrupulous and fraudulent companies to pay a part of the deposits to the depositors. To provide legal strength to the order of such authority, it has said, the order could be transmitted by this authority to the principal civil court of the district in which the registered office of the company is located.

Co-ordination mechanism with the RBI

4. The panel has suggested that the CLB must constitute a co-ordination mechanism with the RBI to ensure that default cases are speedily dealt with. The Task Force recognised the need for a decentralised machinery for inspection of smaller NBFCs. It has also suggested that stringent provisions be made for attachment of assets of finance companies engaged in fraudulent activities and the liquidation of NBFCs.

(l)

minimum networth on a continuous basis and shall inform the Board immediately of any shortfall;

(m)

been diligent in empanelling the marketing agents and in monitoring their activities.

(3) Where the trustee has reason to believe that the conduct of business of the 14[collective investment scheme] is not in accordance with these regulations, trust deed and the offer document of the 14[collective investment scheme], the trustee shall forthwith take such remedial steps as are necessary and shall immediately inform the Board of the action taken.

(4) The trustee shall be accountable for, and be the custodian of, the funds and property of the respective schemes and shall hold the same in trust for the benefit of the unit holders in accordance with these regulations and the provisions of trust deed.

(5) The trustee shall be responsible for the calculation of any income due to be paid to the 14[collective investment scheme] and also for any income received in the 14[collective investment scheme] to the unit holders.

(6) The trustee shall convene a meeting of the unit holders—

(a)

whenever required to do so by the Board in the interest of the unit holders; or

(b)

whenever required to do so on the requisition made by unit holders holding at least one-tenth of nominal value of the unit capital of any 14[collective investment scheme]; or

(c)

when any change in the fundamental attributes of any 14[collective investment scheme] which affects the interest of the unit holders is proposed to be carried out :

Provided that no such change shall be carried out unless the consent of unit holders holding at least three-fourths of nominal value of the unit capital of the 14[collective investment scheme] is obtained.

Explanation : For the purposes of this clause "fundamental attributes" means the investment objective and terms of a 14[collective investment scheme].

on a quarterly basis (i.e., by the end of March, June, September and December) every year all activities carried out by the Collective Investment Management Company;

periodically all service contracts relating to registrars to an issue and share transfer agents and satisfy itself that such contracts are fair and reasonable in the interest of the unit holders;

investor complaints received and the redressal of the same by the Collective Investment Management Company.

net worth of Collective Investment Management Company is not deployed in a manner which is detrimental to interest of unit holders;

property of each 14[collective investment scheme] is clearly identifiable as 14[collective investment scheme] property and held separately from property of the Collective Investment Management Company and property of any other 14[collective investment scheme];

for the purpose of satisfying itself as to the truth of the allegations made in the petition or application; or

reranked.text: Section 12(1B) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with article 142 of the Constitution of India - Collective Investment Scheme -Investigation into - Petitioners, who were shareholders of respondent-company, filed petition stating that investment made by investors in pursuance of certain scheme floated by company promising 1025 per cent return was unsafe and amount collected by company had disappeared from company - They prayed that an investigation was required to be carried out - Whether even in absence of statutory provision, since large number of investors were being defrauded by employing aforesaid corporate veil which might amount to criminal offence appropriate directions could be issued by court to search and seize property of company - Held, yes

HEADNOTE: Section 12(1B) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with article 142 of the Constitution of India - Collective investment scheme -Certificate of registration - SEBI filed petition in public interest stating that certain companies by issuing instrument like agro-bonds, plantation bonds, etc., were offering very high rates of return and collecting amounts from small investors and turning same amount to their sister-concern and other business instead of returning promised amount to investors and as such appropriate directions should be given by the Court to protect the interests of small investors - Whether even in absence of statutory provision since large number of investors were being defrauded by employing the aforesaid corporate veil, which might amount to a criminal offence, appropriate directions could be issued by Court to search and seize property of aforesaid companies - Held, yes

FACT: A petition was filed by the Securities & Exchange Board of India (SEBI) as a public interest litigation, wherein it was stated that it had come to the notice of the Government of India that there were entities which were issuing instruments such as agro bonds, plantation bonds, etc., offering very high rates of returns which were not consistent with the normal returns in such schemes.

In petition SEBI pointed out that respondent No. 1 had floated 18 Schemes and had collected approximately Rs. 16 crores from the small investors. Thereafter it was noticed that promoters of the schemes of respondent No. 1 were not traceable, respondent No. 1 had downed its shutters, the owners were not available, various offices of respondent No. 1 were closed and the said company was going through financial crises. Many investors were holding demonstrations outside the SEBI's office demanding action against the company and its directors.

Therefore, in petition SEBI prayed that in public interest, till regulations were framed under section 12(1B), appropriate directions be given to protect large amounts invested by middle-class people, and immediate action be taken against the directors who had siphoned off large amounts belonging to investors under the guise of corporate veil. It was further contended that the bank accounts and other assets, movable as well as immovable, of respondent No. 1 wheresoever situated required to be frozen and attached to protect the investor's money from being frittered away.

HELD: Unfortunately it appeared that there is no legislation which can effectively control the mushrooming of companies which tempt small investors to deposit or invest their life-savings in such companies, promising to pay fanciful returns on their investment but actually defrauding the investors after siphoning off large amounts from such investments. It is also unfortunate that Nationalised Banks are also advancing loans to such institutions without adequate security from such companies as well as their directors. The situation on the whole, prima facie, is not very happy and knowing fully well the parameters of the powers of the Court as well as the self-imposed restrictions under article 226 of the Constitution, the Courts, cannot be silent spectators to such piquant situations.

It, was appeared that respondent No. 1 and such other companies, which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, are committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their life-long savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without their being any basis. Further, in agricultural production, this type of high returns are impossibility in this country. It appears that, because of these empty, false promises, investors are duped and the company's monies are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

The Apex Court in case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Co. (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401, held that the concept of corporate entity is evolved to encourage and promote trade and commerce but not to commit illegalities or to defraud people.

The Court has also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court was exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties.

Applying the aforesaid ratio and taking into consideration the fact that large number of investors were being defrauded by employing the corporate veil, which may amount to a criminal offence, and also the fact that under Criminal Law property acquired by fraud, cheating, etc., can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions could be issued by the Court to search and seize such property. Further, under article 226 of the Constitution, the Court can issue appropriate directions for not only enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III of constitution but 'for any other purpose', and 'any other purpose 'would include such public interest purpose.

In this view of the matter the Court passed the order directing an enquiry freezing of accounts of respondent-company and attachment of its properties.

There was great substance in the submission of the petitioners that the aforementioned state of affairs required immediate remedial attention. Prima facie, it was apparent that the third respondent had mobilised large deposits from the public and that innocent persons who had invested their money, had not been repaid The officials and other persons associated with the third respondent including the field-staff had formed new companies with the object of siphoning funds and assets of the third respondent to the detriment of the interest of the depositors.

Prima facie, it appeared that the respondents and such other companies, which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, are committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their lifelong savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without there being any basis. It appears that, because of these empty false promises, investors are duped and the Companies' monies are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

In the case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Company (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401, the Apex Court has referred to the discussion on the topic of corporate veil in Palmer's Company Law and has quoted with approval the observations that Courts have shown themselves willing to lifting the veil where the device of incorporation is used for some illegal or improper purpose.

The Courts have also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court is exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties. The Courts have also observed that in India, the Courts are not only Courts of law, but also the Courts of equity.

Considering the fact that a large number of investors prima facie appeared to have been defrauded, that the allegations of fraud and cheating if established would amount to a criminal offence and in view, of the fact that under the criminal law property acquired by fraud or cheating can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions were required to be issued by the Court to search and seize the property of the company. Under article 226 the Court can issue appropriate directions not only for enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III but 'for any other purpose' and 'any other purpose' would include a purpose for the protection of public interest. Therefore, order was passed directing the Commissioner, Police to appoint DC, Police to follow all assets and properties of respondent No. 3 company and to take necessary action for their seizure.

HEADNOTE: Article 226 of the Constitution of India - Writ petition - Whether where it prima facie appeared that investors were defrauded by respondent- company employing corporate veil and there was allegation of criminal offence of acquiring properties by fraud and cheating, appropriate directions for following properties and seizing these wherever these where lying, were required to be passed in exercise of Court's powers under article 226 of the Constitution -Held, yes

FACT: The respondent company (respondent No. 3), a residuary non-banking company, recorded a spurt in deposits from 1992-93. In 1995, on receiving complaints, the RBI conducted inspection of the respondent-company in which the RBI found an extremely unsatisfactory financial position, violation of the RBI directions and poor management. Therefore, the RBI issued prohibitory order restraining the company from accepting deposits from the public and also published notice in newspapers for the know- ledge of the general public. Receiving complaints about non-compliance of the prohibitory order, the RBI carried out a fresh inspection in 1997 in which it was found that the directors had no knowledge of and control over the affairs of the company. The registered office was not in operation and books of account had been shifted from there. Books of account had only been maintained upto 31-3-1995 and finalised upto 1993-94. Hence, the liabilities of the company to the depositors could not be determined. Substantial portion of liabilities, assets, properties and invest-ments of the company were transferred either to new companies or to its functionaries. These new companies where incorporated by officials agents and even field staff of the company. They were using premises of the assessee-company and were continuing deposit mobilisation activities violating prohibitory order of the RBI. In a branch the company itself collected deposit violating the order. The RBI also found that the company had substantial real estate, most of which had no complete documents and these were either repeatedly mortgaged or were in possession of the new companies. The RBI was also informed by the directors that investments of Rs. 152 lakhs were either realised or were encumbered.

The present writ petition under article 226 was filed by the agents and policy-holders of the respondent company. The petitioners sought appro-priate directions for protection of public interest.

HELD: There was great substance in the submission of the petitioners that the aforementioned state of affairs required immediate remedial attention. Prima facie, it was apparent that the third respondent had mobilised large deposits from the public and that innocent persons who had invested their money, had not been repaid The officials and other persons associated with the third respondent including the field-staff had formed new companies with the object of siphoning funds and assets of the third respondent to the detriment of the interest of the depositors.

Prima facie, it appeared that the respondents and such other companies, which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, are committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their lifelong savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without there being any basis. It appears that, because of these empty false promises, investors are duped and the Companies' monies are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

In the case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Company (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401, the Apex Court has referred to the discussion on the topic of corporate veil in Palmer's Company Law and has quoted with approval the observations that Courts have shown themselves willing to lifting the veil where the device of incorporation is used for some illegal or improper purpose.

The Courts have also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court is exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties. The Courts have also observed that in India, the Courts are not only Courts of law, but also the Courts of equity.

Considering the fact that a large number of investors prima facie appeared to have been defrauded, that the allegations of fraud and cheating if established would amount to a criminal offence and in view, of the fact that under the criminal law property acquired by fraud or cheating can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions were required to be issued by the Court to search and seize the property of the company. Under article 226 the Court can issue appropriate directions not only for enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III but 'for any other purpose' and 'any other purpose' would include a purpose for the protection of public interest. Therefore, order was passed directing the Commissioner, Police to appoint DC, Police to follow all assets and properties of respondent No. 3 company and to take necessary action for their seizure.

HEADNOTE: Section 12(1B) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with article 142 of the Constitution of India - Collective investment scheme - Certificate of registration - SEBI filed petition in public interest stating that certain plantation companies by issuing instrument like agro bonds, plantation bonds, etc., were offering very high rates of return and collecting amounts from small investors and siphoned off amount to their sister concern and other business instead of returning promised amount to investors - SEBI sought appropriate directions to protect interests of small investors till regulation are framed under section 12(1B) - Directions were issued by court to conduct inquiry and search and seize of property and accordingly properties of directors were attached - Investigations were said to be still in progress - Whether no further directions viz., to direct RBI to issue orders to all commercial banks and/or cooperative banks, where Respondent No. 1 Plantation company had accounts, restraining Respondent Nos. 1 to 5 and 7 from withdrawing any money from the said accounts are required to be issued for present but Central Government or State Government would have to take appropriate action in framing appropriate regulations/enactment as early as possible - Held, yes

FACT: A petition was filed by the Securities & Exchange Board of India (SEBI) as a public interest litigation, stating that it had come to the notice of the Government of India that certain plantation companies were issuing instruments such as agro bonds, plantation bond, etc., offering very high rates of return which were not consistent with the normal returns in such schemes. In petition SEBI prayed that in public interest, till regulations were framed under section 12(1B), appropriate directions be given to protect large amounts invested by middle-class people, and immediate action be taken against the directors who had siphoned off large amounts belonging to investors under the guise of corporate veil. The Court ordered search and seizure and for an investigation by the Police into the affairs of the company with the assistance of the auditors and staff to be provided by the RBI. Consequently, investigations were made and prop- erties of directors of the company were attached. At this stage SEBI sought direction that till such regulations were framed and finalised, the Court may direct the RBI to issue orders to all commercial banks and/or cooperative banks, where Respondent No. 1 Plantation company had accounts, restraining Respondents No. 1 to 5 and 7 from withdrawing any money from the said accounts, and for certain other reliefs. The company opposed the prayer contending that it is the function of SEBI or the Central Government to frame the regulations at the earliest, if they think it necessary in the interests of investors/depositors in such plantation companies. It was contended that instead of moving the Central Govern- ment to frame and finalise the Regulations, they have approached the Court and it amounted to abuse of the process of law, because the court had issued various directions, including the direction to freeze the bank accounts of the directors.

HELD: On the basis of the earlier order of the Court the properties of the directors of Respondent No. 1 were attached. Further, the Deputy Commissioner of Police, Economic Offences Wing, Crime Branch, Mumbai, had carried out investigation which revealed that, out of Rs. 1,893.54 lakhs collected only Rs. 482.23 lakhs were expended fruitfully for business operations of the company. The investigation also revealed in detail the mismanagement by the directors of the respondent No. 1 company. As the investigation was still in progress, no further directions were required to be issued for the present.

However, considering the facts narrated above and various other similar petitions filed before the Court complaining against the mismanagement by such companies and their directors, the Central Government or the State Government would have to take appropriate action in framing appropriate Regulations/enactment as early as possible as suggested by the petitioner and respondent No. 6.

It would be open to the official liquidator to take physical possession of the premises located at Goregaon and Malad which were under his lock and key.

AIR 1996 SCW 2401, the Apex Court has specifically held that the concept of corporate entity was evolved to encourage and promote trade and commerce but not to commit illegali- ties or to defraud people. He prayed that immediate action be taken against the Directors who have siphoned off large amounts of investors under the guise of corporate veil.

7. Prima facie, it appears that respondent No. 1 and such other companies, which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, are committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their life- long savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without there being any basis. Further, in agricultural production, this type of high returns are impossibility in this country, where, otherwise, the farmers of this country would have become multi-millionaires by this time. It appears that, because of these empty, false promises, investors are duped and the company's monies are siphoned off either to sister-companies or firms of the Directors or their relatives

8. In the case of Skipper Construction Co. (P.) Ltd (supra ), the Apex Court has referred to the discussion on the topic of corporate veil in Palmer's Company Law and has quoted with approval the observations that Courts have shown themselves willing to lifting the veil where the device of incorporation is used for some illegal or improper purpose. The Court has also considered the concept of corporate entity and held that where the corporate character is employed for the purpose of committing illegality or for defrauding others, the Court would ignore the entity with regard to corporate company and its association of men and women and will do justice between the real persons. After discussing other authorities, the Court has observed that the concept of corporate entity was evolved to encourage and promote trade and commerce but not to commit illegal- ities or to defraud people and held as follows:

"Where, therefore, the corporate character is employed for the purpose of committing illegality or for defrauding others, the Court would ignore the corporate character and will look at the reality behind the corporate veil so as to enable it to pass appropriate orders to do justice between the parties concerned. The fact that Tejwant Singh and members of his family have created several corporate bodies does not prevent this Court from treating all of them as one entity belonging to and controlled by Tejwant Singh and family if it is found that these corporate bodies are merely cloaks behind which lurks Tejwant Singh and/or members of his family and that the device of incorporation was really a ploy adopted for committing illegalities and/or to defraud people."

The Court has also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court was exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appro-priate orders for doing complete justice between the parties. The Court has also observed that in India, the Courts are not only Courts of law, but also the Courts of equity and thereafter passed an appropriate order attaching certain properties of the Directors of the company in the aforesaid case.

HEADNOTE: Section 456 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Official Liquidator - Custody of company's property - Official Liquidator of company under liquidation put under seal two godowns claimed as belonging to applicant trust on basis of documentry evidence and only given on rent for a period to company under liquidation - However, in a writ, Division Bench had directed Police Officials to investigate properties of certain persons including that of applicant to find out as to whether directors of company siphoned off company's property - Whether, it would be proper to order police to complete investigation within four weeks and if same would not be complied with, impugned properties should be handed over to applicant - Held, yes

FACT: The Official Liquidator, appointed for liquidation of the company put his seal on the godown which the applicant trust claimed as belonging to it. The applicant submitted that they had purchased these godowns in the year 1984 while company was incorporated only in 1993. The applicant had only allowed the company to use the said premises for a period and subsequently the company vacated the premises and handed over same to the applicant. It was, therefore, contended that since the applicant trust was the owner of the premises, the seal was required to be removed. However, in a separate writ petition, the Division Bench in relevant matter had directed the Dy. Commissioner of Police to find out whether the properties belonging to respondent company were siphoned off by its director and, therefore, directed him to verify and attach the properties belonging to the company.

HELD: In view of the documentary evidence, prima facie, the property did not belong to the company in liquidation as the applicants based on the documentry evidence had been able to establish that the property belonged to the trust. Hence, the Official Liquidator should communicate to the Deputy Commissioner of Police, in charge investigating the matter who should investigate the same and if need be, move the Division Bench for suitable orders including directions in terms of para 10(j ) of the order of the Division Bench.

If no directions were taken within the said period of four weeks by the Dy. Commissioner of Police in charge of investigation, the Official Liquidator should remove the seal and handover possession of the premises to the applicant herein and the books of account and documents if any in the premises would be taken in custody by the Dy. Commissioner of Police investigating into the matter with liberty to the Official Liquidator to examine the said documents as and when required.

The investors who had invested their money in the appellant-company, namely, ’IMFB’ Ltd. filed company petitions for its winding-up on account of its failure to repay the deposited amount in accordance with fixed schedule. The Company Judge, finding it to be a case of cheating and misappropriation of public funds with evil designs, allowed the petitions and ordered for winding-up of the appellant-company under section 433(e). The Official Liquidator was appointed and he was directed to exercise power under section 457, with authority to take into custody all movable and immovable properties of the appellant-company. He was further directed to auction properties of one of the sister concern of the appellant-company, i.e., ’IFCL’, also on ground that properties of said company were in reality properties belonging to the appellant-company.

Against aforesaid order, two sets of appeals were filed. First set of appeals was filed by the appellant-company wherein the order of its winding-up was challenged on various grounds. Second set of appeals was filed by the ’IFCL’ Ltd. on ground that there was no order of winding-up against it nor it was impleaded as a party in the company petitions and, therefore, even if the appellant-company was to be wound-up under the orders of the Court, no assets or properties of ’IFCL’ Ltd. could be taken possession of or could be put to auction.

Section 210 empowers the Central Government to investigate into the affairs of a company/(companies), if it is of the opinion that such investigation is necessary for the reasons mentioned therein, including public interest. For the purpose of the said provision, the Central Government may appoint one or more persons as inspectors to investigate into the affairs of the company and to report thereon in such manner as the Central Government may direct. The SFIO has been established under section 211 of the Companies Act, 2013, which has jurisdiction to investigate into the company/(companies), where the Central Government is of the opinion that it is necessary to investigate into the affairs of a company by the SFIO for different reasons, including the public interest. Where any case has been assigned by the Central Government to the SFIO for investigation under the Act, no other investigating agency of the Central Government or any State Government can proceed with investigation in such case in respect of any offence under the Companies Act and other cases before such agency are required to transfer the relevant documents and records in respect of such offences under the Companies Act to the SFIO. Sub-section (8) of section 211 empowers certain Officers of the SFIO to arrest any person, if on the basis of material in his possession there is reason to believe, which is to be recorded in writing, that any person has been guilty of any offence punishable under sub-section (6) of section 212. [Para 30]

Investigation into company's affairs in other cases can also be done under section 213 on an application made by the eligible members as mentioned in clause (a) of section 213 or on an application made by any other person or otherwise, if it is satisfied that there are circumstances suggesting that the business of the company etc. has been conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members etc. as mentioned in clause (b) of section 213. [Para 31]

From section 213, it is clear that the Tribunal on an application made to it or 'otherwise', if satisfied that there are circumstances suggesting that the business of the company is being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members etc. as mentioned in clause (b) of section 213, after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the parties, direct the Central Government to investigate. [Para 32]

From section 221, it is clear that the Tribunal has power to direct that the transfer, removal or disposal of funds, assets, or properties of the company shall not take place during such period not exceeding three years'. In case of any removal, transfer or disposal of funds, assets, or properties of the company in contravention of the order of the Tribunal under sub-section (1) of section 221, the company is punishable with fine and imprisonment as prescribed under sub-section (2) of section 221. [Para 34]

In the instant case, the Central Government by letter dated 17-2-2018 has directed the SFIO to investigate into the affairs of the respondent company, among other 114 entities. The investigation is currently undergoing and as such, as on date, being satisfied if so required, it is always open to the Central Government to file application under section 241(2), read with section 242 before the Tribunal. [Para 37]

In the interest of regulating the conduct of the company's affairs the interim order cannot be restrictive to any particular or individual person, including the company/companies, existing or erstwhile Officers and employees of the companies if investigation for alleged fraud is pending. [Para 38]

For the purpose of passing interim order, the Tribunal cannot fix the personal liability of delinquent Directors or Managers or Officers or other employees in absence of any specific evidence. Therefore, during the process of investigation and pendency of an application under section 241(2), read with section 242 and in view of powers conferred under section 221, the Tribunal is not only empowered to pass appropriate interim order against the company but also against any person or individual, including the order to desist. [Para 39]

Chapter XVI relates to 'Prevention of Oppression and Mismanagement'. An application to the Tribunal for relief in cases of oppression, etc. can be made by any eligible member(s) of the company under sub-section (1) of section 241 of the Companies Act, 2013, who complains about the oppression and mismanagement as stipulated in clauses (a) & (b) of sub-section (1). [Para 40]

On the other hand, the Central Government, if it is of the opinion that the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interest, it may itself apply to the Tribunal under sub-section (2) of section 241 for an order under Chapter XVI of the Companies Act, 2013. [Para 41]
