The details of the outstandings from the group companies as also the details of the investments were available. It was seen that the company Judge had directed almost a detailed questionnaire and sought the information which was extremely relevant and which would give the complete picture regarding the financial status, etc., of the company. The information sought also appeared to be extremely relevant in coming to the conclusion as to whether the transactions were of bona fide nature or not. There was also a second affidavit filed on record before the order of the Court dated 17-8-2000 seeking further information and even in this affidavit, the financial scenario of the company and its dealings generally were highlighted. In fact, from a reading of those affidavits, it was clear that the company had access to all that was filed before the Court including the petitions. The Single Judge had painstakingly and studiously gone into the whole financial aspects giving a thorough picture of the financial status of the appellant-company itself as also vis-a-vis the other companies floated by it. The Judge had also taken stock of the various transactions with reference to the figures involved in those transactions. It was true that the Judge had made a reference to that report. However, he was completely convinced that there was no necessity of supplying the copy of every document on which the RBI had relied in support of its petitions. The company had a complete idea as to what was the stand of the RBI and what were the precise grounds on which the RBI was moving against it. The company not only got the notice of the petitions but a complete opportunity to show the reasons against it in writing besides the hearing in the open Court. Therefore, this was not a case of breach of natural justice on account of the denial of the opportunity.

There was no doubt that the considerations enumerated by the company Judge for the appointment of provisional liquidator were abundantly available in the present case. Therefore, the Single Judge was justified in admitting the petitions and in appointing the provisional liquidator.

The Judge had given the directions that the report forwarded by the RBI to the Additional Director General of Police, in-charge of the Economic Offence Wing, to whom the RBI had forwarded the report of the Special Auditor should be treated as the first information report with regard to the apparent fraud committed by the company and those in-charge of the company. This action, according to the Single Judge, would be in addition to any of the cases that might have been registered against the company. The Judge then directed that steps should be taken against those involved in the apparent conspiracy to siphon off or divert the funds of the company. The observations made by the Single Judge directing an investigation to be made had got nothing to do with sections 541 and 542. Section 543 also speaks about the assessment of damages for any mis-application, retainer, misfeasance or breach of trust by the directors. Even that section had got nothing to do with the directions given by the Single Judge. That is a general power of the court and there can be no doubt that every court has that power and the Single Judge also had the same power.

Section 443 provides for the powers of the court. Clause (c) of section 443(1) thereof speaks of the Court's powers to make any interim order which the Court thinks fit to order an investigation. This has got no connection with sections 541 to 543 and, therefore, the argument that that part of the order was without jurisdiction was to be rejected.

The Court has ample powers including the power under section 443 to recommend an investigation. After all, an investigation into the affairs of the company does not mean a final conviction of the Directors. This argument, therefore, was to be rejected. The criminal liability would be decided by the competent Criminal Court on the evidence tendered before it by the prosecution. The question of the bail and release would also be decided by the Criminal Court which was dealing with the matters. The release of a person on bail in this case was the exclusive right of the Criminal Court dealing with the accused persons, viz., the directors of the company. The payment of Rs. 50 crores might have been considered as one of the considerations for grant of bail but, that did not divest the Criminal Court of its powers to deal with the bail matter and to deal further with the criminal matter pending before it in its own rights.

Accordingly, the application was disposed of.

HELD: The financial position of the respondent-company as admitted by the second respondent was that the balance sheet carried as on 10-9-2008, (a ) inflated (non-existent) cash and bank balances, (b) accrued interest which was non-existent, (c) an understated liability on account of funds arranged by him, and (d) an overstated debtors position. The gap in the balance sheet had reportedly arisen on account of the inflated profits over a period of past several years. The desperate attempt of the second respondent to compensate the fictitious assets of the company by acquisition of ‘M’ miserably failed. In the words of respondent No. 11, the accounts of the company were unreliable. While considering the matters complained of on account of the massive financial fraud running into several thousands of crores of rupees, there would necessarily be need to examine the part played by the Chief Finance Officer of the company and, therefore, the proposed respondent, namely, the Chief Finance Officer, being interested in the subject-matter of the litigation, was a necessary party, without whom no order could effectively be made, in adjudicating the question of financial irregularities involved in the instant proceedings. Therefore, the Chief Finance Officer of the company was legally and directly interested in respect of the subject major controversies. The erstwhile directors and officers of the company were answerable for the whole of fraud unequivocally admitted by the second respondent. The Central Government, having satisfied with the prevailing state of affairs of the company, in exercise of powers under section 235, ordered investigation into the affairs of the company and further by virtue of section 240(1A) permitted the inspectors so appointed, to obtain information, books and papers related to MPL and MIL. Any order which might ultimately be passed against the delinquent officers, etc., under section 542 safeguarding the paramount interest of the company would be fruitful only if all their assets were maintained without any encumbrances whatsoever. The respondents, if on the other hand, were allowed to gain time to strip off their assets, there was no doubt that the company and its stakeholders would suffer irrepa-rable harm. The object was to preserve status quo, while the disputes were being adjudicated. There existed a strong prima facie case and the balance of convenience in favour of grant of the ex parte restraint order, as urged by the Central Government, to preserve the public interest at large. [Para 2] In view of the foregoing conclusions and in exercise of powers under section 403, it was deemed fit to order that (i) Chief Finance Officer ‘V’ of the company would be arrayed as respondent No. 13, to the instant proceedings; (ii) the respondents concerned should forward to the Bench Officer particulars of all their bank accounts, valuable movables and immovable properties owned in India or elsewhere outside India; (iii ) the concerned respondents should not alienate, charge, mortgage or sell any of their shares, securities and fixed assets, as the case may be, held and owned by them, without leave of the CLB, till disposal of the main petition. [Para 3]

One need not be hyper technical in dealing with cases as long as orders do not waive or alter the substantive rights of the parties. This order dated 23.02.2018 is only a temporary preventive relief to complete investigation effectively and expeditiously, if these kinds of orders are not passed, it will be like operation success, patient died. 20. Whenever any action or omission takes place in a company, though company is an independent entity equivalent to any other natural person, it will not get any momentum on its own for short of life in it, impetus will come into it only when it is driven by a natural person, so to the company, driver is a Board constituted with natural persons. Therefore, whenever company is involved in fraud, it will always point at the persons managing the affairs of the company. In this scenario, unless the persons (Directors and other key Managerial Personnel) involved are curtailed from dealing with not only the assets of the company but also the assets lying with the persons involved in committing fraud, it is next to impossible to claw back the proceeds of the fraud from the persons running the affairs of the companies. I need not say that fraud vitiates everything; therefore, to get off the hook, such persons cannot veil the situation with the doctrine of separate entity, because in a situation like this, hands of law are long enough to pierce the corporate veil and catch the culprits. Here money being secreted out by colluding with some Bank officials, Competent Authority is conferred with powers to search and seize them; this section is nothing but to aid the same.

21. In view of this reason, when action against company/companies for getting back the money fraudulently taken out is permissible, if such money is routed to the persons managing through these companies, then it is obvious to construe that such companies have come into existence to be used as conduits to gulp down everything that comes to the company. When this being the ground situation, can it be said that relief under section 221 is extendable only against the companies, not against the culprits hidden under it? That money is not in the books of at least companies in India. Linchpins in this fraud are not in India. Everybody knows it goes without saying that when granting consequential relief is imperative to attain the purpose of main relief, courts can reach out to pass such reliefs as well.

22. This relief u/s. 221 cannot be conceived as relief like in civil case asking for filing reply, rejoinder - the reason is, it is not on adjudication of rights of the parties, it is an aid to action under criminal law, because as I said earlier this procedure is akin to the procedure under CrPC, investigating officer of SFIO on the direction of Central Government will file its report before special court as police officer files charge sheet (final report) u/s. 173 of CrPC to prosecute the accused as mandated u/s. 212 of Companies Act, 2013, moreover it is a temporary injunction not culminating into a permanent order, therefore even for a moment, this order can't be seen as akin to an order in civil nature, when that being the intendment of the statute, for granting an aid to investigation, I don't believe it is imperative to hear such people who indulged in fraud or suspected to be involved in committing fraud or presumed to be participated in fraud before passing orders. This power being conferred upon this Bench, it can't be fought out that since this Bench has all trappings of civil court, unless all the procedure laid under civil law is complied with, no order could be passed. Law is law howsoever hard it is, which one is civil court, which one is criminal court, what order could be passed, what order could not be passed is in the domain of sovereignty of this country, not with the court dealing with a particular issue. For the reasons mentioned above, it is evident that this relief is an aid to investigation, so whatever principles applicable to conducting investigation under CrPC are equally applicable to the extent mentioned in this Act. For this, we have to read section 221 along with sections 212-220 of the Act.

When the power vested in the executive Government is invoked, one incumbent may perhaps feel that justice may not be meted out. But now, after the amendment in 1988, the power vested with the Central Government had been taken away and vested with the Company Law Board. When the power is conferred on the Company Law Board, it is incumbent on the petitioner to approach that statutory Board which shall examine and do justice, as the circumstances demand. In such circumstances, there arise no reason for exercising the discretionary power vested in this Company Court to direct such investigation or declare that it needs investigation by the Central Government.

12. Section 235 of the Companies Act, 1956 deals with Investigation of affairs of a Company, which reads hereunder :

"Investigation of affairs of a company.—(1) The Central Government may, where a report has been made by the Registrar under sub-section (6) of section 234, or under sub-section (7) of that section, read with sub-section (6) thereof, appoint one or more competent persons as inspectors to investigate the affairs of a company and to report thereon in such manner as the Central Government may direct.

(2) Where—

(a )in the case of a company having a share capital, an application has been received from not less than two hundred members or from members holding not less than one-tenth of the total voting power therein, and

(b )in the case of a company having no share capital, an application has been received from not less than one-fifth of the persons on the company’s register of members,

the Tribunal may, after giving the parties an opportunity of being heard, by order, declare that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated by an inspector or inspectors, and on such a declaration being made, the Central Government shall appoint one or more competent persons as inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company and to report thereon in such manner as the Central Government may direct."

13. Likewise, section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 deals with Investigation of Company’s affairs in other cases, which reads as under :

"Investigation of company’s affairs in other cases.—Without prejudice to its powers under section 235, the Central Government—

(a )shall appoint one or more competent persons as inspectors to investigate the affairs of a company and to report thereon in such manner as the Central Government may direct, if—

(i )the company, by special resolution; or

(ii )the Court, by order,

declares that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated by an inspection appointed by the Central Government; and

(b )may do so if, in its opinion or in the opinion of the Tribunal, there are circumstances suggesting—

(i )that the business of the company is being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members or any other persons, or otherwise for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose, or in a manner oppressive of any of its members, or that the company was formed for any fraudulent or unlawful purpose;

(ii )that persons concerned in the formation of the company or the management of its affairs have in connection therewith been guilty of fraud, misfeasance or other misconduct towards the company or towards any of its members; or

The respondent-company Golden Forests (India) Ltd. (GFIL) was incorporated in 1987. Between the years 1991 and 1997, its promoters set up over 100 companies and introduced a number of investment schemes promising handsome returns, lured investors and depositors, and in 9-10 years collected several hundred crores of rupees. Huge tracts of lands and property were also acquired by it.

The applicant was National Investors Forum and its members were the investors of the respondent-company GFIL.

In 1997, the Securities Exchange Board of India (SEBI) inquired into the activities of GFIL group and a two member committee was constituted. The report of the committee highlighted financial and other irregularities committed by the company.

SEBI filed a writ petition in the Bombay High Court, in which an order was passed against GFIL restraining it from alienating the properties; a similar order was passed by this High Court in the same year. Thus, SEBI made an order prohibiting the company from alienating its properties. A retired judge was appointed as receiver and certain properties were earmarked for sale, but the receiver could not sell the properties.

GFIL, in the meanwhile continued to accept deposits, carrying business and alienating properties. In this background, winding up proceedings, were preferred before the Punjab & Haryana High Court. The Company Judge by order directed that all properties of the company would be managed, controlled, regulated by a provisional liquidator, who shall have power to sell the movable and immovable property. Thus, a provisional liquidator was appointed.

The company petition and all other proceedings pending against the GFIL pending in various High Courts throughout the country were transferred to the Supreme Court, in a transfer petition filed by SEBI. Company petition was also transferred to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court by its order constituted a committee consisting of a retired judge KT of the Supreme Court, an officer to be nominated by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and an officer to be nominated by SEBI, and further ordered the committee to take into its custody all assets of the company, wherever they may be, to issue advertisement in Newspapers calling upon all the creditors of the company to submit the claim(s) before the committee.

The committee had, during pendency of the matters before the Supreme Court, invited claims from the depositors/investors of GFIL by advertisement which period was extended. However, since claims from the depositors of GFIL continued, the Supreme Court directed that no deposit accepted by an Agent after 1-1-2001 is to be considered as GFIL had closed business in December, 2000 and the Directors of the company were in the Jail in December, 2000. The Court also directed that there should be clear proof of deposit of money with GFIL or its group.

The liabilities were to be discharged by sale of the properties of GFIL and its group. The payments to the depositors were to be made after the properties were sold and payment were to depend on the realisation of proceeds of sale. As per the committee, there were about 15 lakh investors who had not been paid.

After notice was issued on the application, seeking directions to disburse amounts collected due to sale of assets of GFIL and its group companies, the Committee filed a status report as a step to assist in framing a scheme for disbursement of amounts.

In compliance with the above order, the Committee placed relevant materials in the form of affidavits. The Court, after considering the issue of disbursement of the amounts lying with the committee, was of the opinion that the proposal (for disbursement of funds scheme framed by the Committee), giving preference to 'small' investors in distribution of process, was not entirely equitable. Thus the above revised scheme for disbursement of monies to depositors of GFIL or its group companies was further revised, the committee in its second revision proposed several alternatives. The committee disclosed a consolidated chart of all the holdings of GFIL. It also disclosed the status of various funds and the various sale transactions that were incomplete and in respect of which amounts had been received. The committee had so far been able to collect and put to sale and realise assets to the tune of Rs. 400 crore.

The Board should identify and ascertain the exact number of properties of the company spread throughout the length and breadth of the country and thereafter, every effort should be made to ascertain the actual liabilities of all the investors of GFIL Group of companies.

The power to pass ex parte ad interim order, pending investigation, flows from sections 11 and 11B of the SEBI Act. A plain reading of sections 11 and 11B shows that SEBI has to protect the interests of the investors in securities and to regulate the securities market by such measures as it thinks fit and such measures may be for any or all of the matters provided in sub-section (2) of section 11 of the Act. SEBI has power to pass an interim order and such interim order can also be passed ex parte in order to prevent further possible mischief of tampering with the securities market. If during the course of investigation, it is found prima facie, that the person is violating the securities laws or is siphoning of the funds of the listed company to the detriment of its shareholders, it would be obligatory for SEBI to pass an interim order or for that matter an ex parte ad interim order in order to safeguard the interests of the investors and to maintain the integrity of the market. [Para 15]

Normally, while passing an interim order, the principles of natural justice has to be adhered to, namely, that an opportunity of hearing is required to be given. Procedural fairness embodying natural justice is to be applied whenever action is taken affecting the rights of the parties. However, at times, an opportunity of hearing may not be pre-decisional and may necessarily have to be post-decisional especially where the act to be prevented is imminent or where action to be taken brooks no delay. Thus, pre-decisional hearing is not always necessary when ex parte ad interim orders are made pending investigation or enquiry unless provided by the statute. In such cases, rules of natural justice would be satisfied, if the affected party is given a post-decisional hearing. [Para 16]

389.2-2 Requiring information on the application of creditors etc.389.2-2 Requiring information on the application of creditors etc.

If it is represented to the Registrar on materials placed before him by any contributory or creditor or any other person interested, that the business of the company is being carried on in fraud of its creditors or of persons dealing with the company or otherwise for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose, he may, after hearing the company, issue an order in writing asking for such informations and explanations as he may consider necessary.

389.3 Furnishing of explanation by company389.3 Furnishing of explanation by company

On receipt of such order, it shall be the duty of the company and all officers of the company to furnish such information and explanations within the time limit fixed by the Registrar of Companies.

389.3-1 Action by Registrar in case of failure389.3-1 Action by Registrar in case of failure

If no information or explanation is furnished within the prescribed time or if such information or explanation is inadequate, the Registrar may issue another written order calling for production of books and papers which are considered necessary and specify a time limit within which such books should be produced. On receipt of such order, the Company and every officer shall produce such books and papers within the specified time limit.

389.4 Penalty in case of default389.4 Penalty in case of default

If the company fails to furnish the information and explanations or produce books and paper, the company and every officer thereon shall be punishable with a fine which may extend up to five thousand rupees and in the case of continuing offence with an additional fine which may extend to rupees five hundred for everyday during which such default continues. The Registrar may also apply to the Court for issue of an order on the company to produce books and papers before the Registrar of Companies.

389.4-1 Production/Service of records389.4-1 Production/Service of records

The Registrar may also apply to the Court of Magistrate of the First class for issue of an order on the company to produce books and papers before the Registrar of Companies, under section 234(4). Further, under section 234A, he may move the said Court for seizure of the Company’s records if he has reasonable ground to believe that the books and papers of or relating to the company or other body corporate associated with it may be destroyed mutilated, attend falsified or secreted by the managing director or manager of the company.

389.5 Report by Registrar for investigation389.5 Report by Registrar for investigation

The Registrar shall make a report to the Central Government under the following circumstances :

u if the information or explanation sought for is not produced within the specified time;

u if on a perusal of the information or explanation or books and papers, the Registrar finds an unsatisfactory state of affairs ; or

u if on a perusal of the information or explanation or books and papers, the Registrar finds that they do not disclose a full and fair statement of any matter to which the document purport to relate.

389.6 Appointment of Inspectors389.6 Appointment of Inspectors

On receipt of the report from the Registrar of Companies, the Central Government may appoint one or more competent persons as Inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company and to report thereon.

CHAPTER 388

APPOINTMENT OF INSPECTOR FOR INVESTIGATION INTO AFFAIRS OF A COMPANY ON ORDER OF COMPANY LAW BOARD *APPOINTMENT OF INSPECTOR FOR INVESTIGATION INTO AFFAIRS OF A COMPANY ON ORDER OF COMPANY LAW BOARD*

388.1 Background note388.1 Background note

The Central Government may appoint one or more Inspectors to investigate the affairs of a company if in the opinion of the Company Law Board, there are circumstances suggesting the grounds specified in section 237(b).

388.2 Grounds for Investigation388.2 Grounds for Investigation

An investigation into the affairs of the Company may be done under the following circumstances :

u If the business of the company is being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members or any other persons, or otherwise for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose, or in a manner oppressive of any of its members, or that the company was formed for any fraudulent or unlawful purpose;

u If the persons concerned in the formation of the company or the management of its affairs have in connection therewith been guilty of fraud, misfeasance or other misconduct towards the company or towards any of its members; or

u If the members of the company have not been given all the information with respect to its affairs which they might reasonably expect, including information relating to the calculation of the commission payable to the managing or other director or the manager, of the company.

388.3 Appointment of Inspectors388.3 Appointment of Inspectors

The Central Government may appoint one or more competent persons as Inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company and to report thereon if it or the Tribunal is satisfied to form an option that it is warranted in the circumstances. This is the position after the modified clause that way comes into operation on the notification of the Second Amendment Act, 2002. Until then, it is the CLB that should be satisfied to from such an opinion.

388.4 Investigation by Inspector(s)388.4 Investigation by Inspector(s)

The Inspector(s) shall investigate the affairs of the company and submit a report thereon to the Central Government. A copy of the report should be sent by the Central Government to the Company Law Board. Refer paras 384.8 to 384.14 for provisions relating to appointment of Inspectors, powers of Inspectors, Inspector’s report, action by Central Government and expenses on investigation which are also applicable in case of appointment of Inspector at the instance of Company Law Board.

I Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company’s affairs in other cases It is not necessary that for passing an order under section 237(a)(ii) there should be a proceeding already before Court; even a petition simpliciter can be entertained Delhi Flour Mills Co. Ltd., In re [1975] 45 Comp. Cas. 33 (Delhi) There is nothing in the language of section 237(a)(ii) indicating that a petition simpliciter for an action under section 237(a)(ii) cannot be entertained by the Court, but that power can only be exercised by the Court against the company in respect of whom some other proceeding is pending in the Court and the Court considers it proper to direct appointment of an Inspector. Existence or pendency of some proceeding other than one for taking action under section 237(a)(ii) is not a sine qua non. On the contrary, even in the absence of a petition simpliciter for an action under section 237(a)(ii) for directing the Central Government to appoint an Inspector, the Court while hearing some other proceeding against a company in the course of which the Court is satisfied that an inspector to investigate the affairs of the company should be appointed, may without any application to that effect proceed to pass such an order. If the Court has such wide power to exercise jurisdiction under section 237(a)(ii) in another proceeding against the same company, there is no justification for holding that a petition simpliciter under section 237(a)(ii) cannot be entertained by the Court. It may also be pointed out that rule 11(9) of the Companies (Court) Rules, 1959, provides that the Court can be moved under section 237 by a petition. That, of course, is not decisive. But if the above construction put upon section 237 is correct, the fact that a petition is prescribed for moving the Court may also point in the same direction.

HEADNOTE: Section 446 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding-up - Suits Stayed on Winding-Up Order - Pursuant to a petition filed by one of creditors for winding-up of company for its failure to return huge deposits collected from thousands of depositors, court formulated a scheme for running business without allowing to receive fresh deposits and appointed provisional liquidator - Company had diverted a huge amount to its sister company, by unlawful means - Despite repeated directions, company and its directors failed to furnish books of account, registers, etc., to Official Liquidator - Registers which were produced, were found to be forged and fabricated with false entries - Therefore, Court directed crime branch police to register case against managing director and directors of company (accused) and to recover books of account, register etc. - Court also directed that all matters including bail matters of accused persons should be placed before company court - At that stage company court issued notice to all accused to cancel bail granted to them - Whether except in case of proceedings pending in appeal before Supreme Court, and High Court, in respect of all other proceedings, both civil and criminal, company court has jurisdiction to transfer all such proceedings or cases before it and to decide same - Held, yes - Whether since directors were at large, all records were with them and there was every possibility of creating bogus claims in names of men of their confidence or choice thereby defeating interests of real depositors, it was imperative to cancel bail and to keep accused in judicial custody till they produced registers and books of account - Held, yes

FACT: When the company failed to return nearly Rs. 18 crores collected from thousands of depositors, one of the creditors filed petition for winding-up of the company. In the meantime, the company filed an application under section 391 for obtaining sanction to a scheme of compromise, which was refused by the court. The court, however, formulated a scheme for running the business without allowing to receive fresh deposits and appointed provisional liquidator. The company had diverted a huge amount to its sister company by unlawful means in violation of the provisions of law and the directions issued by the Reserve Bank of India. Despite repeated directions of the court, the company and its managing director did not furnish the books of account, registers and the securities including the gold to the Official Liquidator, and even those registers which were produced before the Official Liquidator, were found to be forged and fabricated with false entries. The court, thereupon, passed an order directing the crime branch police to register a case and to recover the books of account, register, etc. It also issued certain directions to the effect that all the genuine registers, account books, etc., should be seized/recovered and that the investigating officer should further enquire whether any properties had been acquired by the directors in the name of others as benami with the company's funds. Further, it would be open to him to arrest the respondent-managing director as well as directors of the company. The police, accordingly, registered a criminal case against the directors of the company as well as accused 5 and 6 who had joined them in diverting considerable sum to a sister concern. Subsequently, the court directed that all matters including bail matters, should be placed before the company court. At that stage the company court found it necessary to give notice to all the accused, why the bail granted to all of them should not be cancelled. The case of the accused was that the company court had no jurisdiction to cancel the bail which was granted by another bench of the court and the petition for cancellation of bail should also go before the same bench which granted the bail.

HELD: When the court had found that it was impossible to proceed with the liquidation proceedings in accordance with law due to the violation of the lawful orders and directions of the court by the directors and the large scale forging of documents, misappropriation of money and the fraud committed by the directors of the company, by order dated 25-3-2003, it was directed that all the matters including bail matters relating to the company and its sister companies should be placed before the company court. The said order was fully in accordance with section 446 which empowers the court to transfer all cases or proceedings pending before all courts to the company court. The only restriction imposed by sub-section (4) of section 446 is that the provisions in sub-sections (1) to (3) would not apply to proceedings pending in appeal before the Supreme Court or the High Court. But in respect of all other proceedings, both civil and criminal, the company court has jurisdiction to transfer all such proceedings or cases before it and to decide the same. [Paras 9 and 10]

HEADNOTE: Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 -Investigation of company’s affairs in other cases - In inspection conducted under section 209A against respondent-company by virtue of order of Department of Company Affairs, certain irregularities and violations of provisions of Act were pointed out - There was also a complaint by Small Investor Protection Forum against respondent- company - Respondent-company had made huge investment in certain companies within a short spell of 3-4 months though its main object was not to enter into share market - Within short spell of two months, respondent-company had raised its authorized capital from Rs. 50,000 to Rs. 12 crores - Whether genesis and origin of huge funds invested by respondent-company in share market when they were not in that business, needed to be probed into - Held, yes - Whether therefore, Central Government was to be directed to undertake investigation of respondent-company under section 237 - Held, yes

FACT: In the inspection conducted under section 209 against respondent-company, certain irregularities and violations of provisions of the Act were pointed out and necessary action had been initiated by the Registrar. The petitioner filed petition under section 237 seeking investigation into affairs of respondent-company on the ground that respondent-company had connection with ‘KP’ group of companies and there was also a complaint by Small Investor Protection Forum. The case of the petitioner was that as per the balance sheet of the company as on 31-12-2000, the huge funds of the company were used primarily in share market during the scam period and huge investments were made in the shares of certain companies, which was not the main object of the respondent-company; and that the management had conducted the business of the company with intent to defraud its creditors, members, etc.

HELD: The respondent submitted that whatever shares had been purchased by those companies, which formed part of the ‘K’, had been purchased through stock exchange or public issue or between shareholders of the company in the normal course of business. There were no direct transactions by the company and the ‘K’ for dealing with those shares. The respondent had also forwarded copies of index of folios of shares which had been purchased by various parties from time-to-time. It was difficult to make out any proposition out of those huge papers submitted by the respondent. [Para 12]

The irregularities/violations of the provisions of the Act had already been taken care of by the Registrar of Companies, but some revealing propositions came out from the documents and averments of the case. The company was incorporated as early as in 1982 and since then, the authorized share capital was Rs. 5 lakhs and paid up capital was Rs. 15,000 as on 13-12-1999; but huge investments in share capital had been made within a short spell of 3 to 4 months. It was also admitted position that the company made investment of Rs. 83,41,00,000 in the shares of the certain companies when the main object of the company was not to enter the business in share market. The lead to value of huge investment went down after stock scam took place in March, 2001. It was also interesting to note that within a spell of two months, the authorized capital was raised first from Rs. 50,000 to Rs. 11 crores and thereafter to Rs. 12 crores. The genesis and origin of this huge funds invested by the respondent-company in share market when it was not in the business, needed to be probed into. It was difficult to find from the documents placed on record as to whether there was any relationship in the transactions with the ‘KP’ group of companies or those were the normal transactions of the business. That could only be found out by investigating the matter in depth. [Para 13]

In the light of the above discussion, the petition was to be allowed. Accordingly, the Central Government was to be directed to undertake the investigation of respondent-company under section 237 and take suitable action on the basis of the report when received. [Para 14]

The company court is required to examine whether the winding-up of the company is in the interest of shareholders, secured and unsecured creditors, workers as well as in public interest. It is natural consequence of admission of petition. Thus, there was no merit in the contention of the petitioner that the company court had no discretion after the admission of the petition but to pass the order of winding-up. [Para 8] A perusal of the written statement filed by the company showed that the liability was not disputed. Rather, it had sought intervention of the High Court in whose supervision the investors might be repaid to prevent further loss of prestige to the company. It had been stated that the company had assets worth Rs. 1500 crores as against liability of only Rs. 761 crores and the company was very much in a position to pay its dues. It was stated that the company was set up in 1987 and till 1988, there had been no default in repayment of any maturity amounts and refunds of investors. The company disclosed that in 1998, SEBI filed writ petition No. 344 of 1998 before the Mumbai High Court seeking, inter alia, that the company might be prevented from conducting its business. Such writ petition was opposed on the ground that the petition was not maintainable as an instrumentality of a State without any statutory power, was not entitled to seek any relief against the private party. The respondent-company was called upon to satisfy the Mumbai High Court in the interest of investors with regard to its workability. The company got its assets valued which were assessed at Rs. 1,071.55 crores in addition to Rs. 33,880 crores on account of movable assets and bank balance as on 31-12-1997 against the total liability of 761 crores as on 31-12-1997. It was further stated that the company invited offers for sale of its certain properties but none of the buyers had shown any interest in view of the restraint imposed by the Mumbai High Court on 30-9-1999. Ultimately, the Mumbai High Court had appointed a retired Judge as private receiver for sale of 19 properties as set out in the schedule vide order dated 31-1-2000. [Para 11]

It was apparent from the above that there was no dispute as to the liability of the company towards the investors. It was the stand of the company that it had assets more than Rs. 1,000 crores which were sufficient to discharge the liability of the investors. It had come on record that the directors of the company were in custody since December, 2000 and the company had not been able to dispose of any of the properties for payment to the investors. It was also on record that private receiver appointed by the Mumbai High Court had also not been able to sell any property so far. Thus, a mechanism was required to be drawn so as to facilitate the sale of the property of the company at the earliest with a view to ensure payment to the investors without any further delay. The interest of such large number of creditors was required to be watched by the company court and the management of the company could not be permitted to take such investors for a ride. [Para 12]

With a view to protect the interest of the large number of creditors and shareholders of the company, it was just and appropriate to appoint provisional liquidator for control, management and sale of the movable and immovable properties so as to fetch maximum price thereof with a view to satisfy the claim of 25 lakh investors in a proper manner. However, the Official Liquidator attached to the High Court might not be able to take over the responsibility of management and sale of the properties of the company keeping in view the meagre resources at his command and inadequate infrastructure available. Therefore, instead of appointing Official Liquidator the responsibility of the provisional liquidator should be entrusted to such a person who would command respect and be able to discharge the onerous responsibility in a fair manner. [Para 13]

Apart from vesting of the company with the provisional liquidator so as to facilitate the sale thereof to liquidate the claim of the investors, the affairs of the company were also required to be investigated by an independent agency. [Para 14]

Therefore, instead of winding-up of the company in the interest of creditors and shareholders of the company a provisional liquidator was appointed to control and manage the affairs of the company with certain directions. [Para 17]

If justifiable grounds existed CLB should not shy away from exercising jurisdiction under this section for technical reasons.

Investigation is to be ordered if a prima facie opinion is formed by the CLB that the business of the company is being/has been conducted with intent to defraud creditors, members or any other persons or the conduct of company is oppressive to any of its members or there is misfeasance or misconduct on the part of the management in carrying on the affairs of the company.

An inspection under section 209A is an inspection with regard to the books of account and other books and papers of a company. The scope of this inspection is limited to the books and papers and that too to the particular company only. The report of this inspection is submitted to the Central Government. Consequent to this report, the Central Government may not be able to initiate action under section 242 or section 243, namely, prosecution or application for winding-up or for initiating action for prevention for oppression and mismanagement under section 397/398. Similarly, no proceedings for recovery of damages or property in the public interest can be brought by the Central Government consequent to the report under section 209A. In this case, the Central Government on its own could have appointed one or more inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company in exercise of the powers under section 235. However, there was a technical snag inasmuch as this section could be invoked only on a report made by the ROC under section 234(6), i.e., a report by the Registrar based on information called by him from the company in exercise of his powers. Since the present report was made by the Joint Director in the office of Regional Director, the Central Government had refrained from exercising its powers under section 235. On the other hand, it had made use of the facility available under section 237(b) to make a reference with all the particulars for the CLB to form an opinion as to whether an investigation was warranted. The power under section 237(b) is a discretionary power which is to be exercised very carefully after considering all the circumstances.

It was a fact that production suffered, costs increased and losses were incurred because of bad management of the company. It was also a fact that substantial funds had been diverted to intercorporate loans after being raised for the purpose of a project. There was an unusual practice of accepting repayment of the principal amount of loans and leaving the interest on the loans as outstanding. It was also a fact that substantial foreign orders were lost due to apparently bad management and at the same time avoidable wasteful expenditure was incurred. Substantial funds were committed to a company and ultimately that company had gone into winding-up. The new management also conceded that it was not able to determine the facts and circumstances in which substantial commission was given to a party for procurement of business from an existing customer of the company. Consequent to all the above matters the company and in turn the public holding more than 40 per cent shares had all suffered.

If the above acts and consequent results were due to bad planning and lack of managerial skills it stood on a different footing. Probably the financial institutions which had a large stake could have checked this as apart of the continuous monitoring system. In any case, if it was mere poor management, courts might not intervene and impose an investigation. The matter to be investigated was whether the above deeds—in particular, diversion of funds and wasteful expenditure—was intentional and was to benefit any particular person or persons concerned with the management of the company. A strong suspicion arose in this direction particularly because the company was successful all along under the same management. Moreover, a normal prudential management would not involve the funds of the company in this manner. In order to establish whether the acts were intentional and had really gone to the benefit of one or a few at the expense of the investing public institutions and employees, appropriate action might have to be initiated. Courts have not hesitated in such instances to invoke the powers to order investigation.

View in the Present Context

The Courts would definitely have power to direct CBI to conduct the investigation coupled with a direction upon the State authorities to co-operate with the CBI. However, the Court should be slow in exercising such power that could only be used in an extraordinary/exceptional circumstance. [Para 67]

What is Extraordinary/Exceptional Circumstance ? It would mean a situation that would lead to obvious conclusion, the process being frustrated; having either the State machinery deeply involved in the crime or their lackadaisical approach would result in an unsuccessful exercise. [Para 68]

Involvement of Kunal Ghosh/Srinjoy Bose :

The petitioner alleged, Kunal being an employee of Saradha group acted as a liason between the group and the State Government. The other petitioner went one step forward to allege involvement of Srinjoy, both Members of Parliament, belonging to the ruling party. The allegations are serious. More serious the allegation is, the proof must be stricter. The people connected with politics would have to deal with various persons at various level. A politician may have his own means of livelihood and his involvement in the work place may not have necessary involvement in political circle. Kunal was already examined by the police. If any one of them would have involvement in the crime, they must be proceeded with irrespective of their colour and creed, for that the entire State machinery could not be blamed. His personal involvement in the crime may not have nexus with the State machinery unless it is proved; he acted as a conduit that would bring him under the scanner. If one commits a crime, it would be his personal responsibility that must not have repercussion on the entire State judiciary unless such crime would relate to a mechanism involving the system. It would be too early to blame the State solely on the ground. [Para 69]

Investigation

The involvement of the State in the present context, did not feature in the pleadings. The investigation is still on. It would be too early to comment as to Kunal's involvement in the present case, at least, no definite assertion backed up by sufficient particulars is found. Same was the case of Srinjoy Bose. Even if, these two persons are found to be involved in the crime, the State must spring into action and proceed against them irrespective of their political colour and creed. Sufficient opportunity is to be given to the State machinery to take a decision on that score. Merely someone was an employee in a particular branch of the business belonging to the group, one cannot blame the entire State machinery, particularly when the Court is prima facie satisfied with the progress that the State machinery made in the instant case, since the magnitude is huge, the machinery should be extra cautious in proceeding as the people involved in it would try to scuttle the process or create as many hindrances as they could. [Para 70]

The CBI clearly mentioned they did not have any appropriate infrastructure. They may do it only with the State helping them. They were very candid on the issue. If the process is withdrawn from the State machinery and the CBI is asked to take it over and ask the State machinery to assist them, the result would not be as expected, at least, stage has not come, as is found from the fact situation. [Para 71]

Since no better course is found the State is given some more time. [Para 72]

The State machinery is given liberty to take suggestion or advice of any other agency as they feel like. The CBI, Enforcement Directorate, Ministry of Corporate Affairs, SFIO and all other organisations of the like nature are directed, to render all necessary assistance to the State machinery as and when asked for, so that they could complete the process of investigation and start prosecuting the accused. The State machinery would however, be obliged to submit periodical report to the Court that would be considered at the appropriate stage. Such direction would be given at the end. [Para 73]

Commission - Its Function, Recovery and Distribution

As regards the residuary assets and the distribution of same amongst the depositors. The State already appointed Commission for the purpose. The Commission was empowered to provide hearing and receive complaint, examine the complaint and forward the same to SIT and/or any other appropriate authority, send directives if required to SIT, identify the key person responsible, enquire into the methodology adopted by the group of companies, quantify the estimated amount involved, assess the assets and liabilities, recommend means of providing compensation to the victims and to recommend remedial action. 28.2-3 Inspection of report of Company Liquidator

Report of Company Liquidator can be inspected by creditor or contributory or his agent and can obtain its copies - section 281(5) of Companies Act, 2013.

28.3 Directions by NCLT after receiving report of Company Liquidator Section 282 of Companies Act, 2013 enumerates steps to be taken by NCLT after receiving report of company liquidator. The steps include (a) fix time limit for completing winding up proceedings (b) Order sale of company or its assets as a going concern (c) Order action if fraud is suspected (d) Other order to protect, preserve and enhance value of assets of company (e) Other directions as NCLT may deem fit.

Thus, NCLT has very wide powers in winding up of company.

NCLT can review and modify its orders during winding up proceedings, on receiving quarterly report from Company Liquidator - section 288(2) of Companies Act, 2013.

NCLT has to grant hearing to Company Liquidator, Creditors, Contributories or other persons before passing order.

28.3-1 Fixing time schedule for dissolution of company

NCLT shall fix time limit to complete dissolution of company. The time limit can be revised on application of Company Liquidator, Creditor, Contributory or any other person - section 282(1) of Companies Act, 2013.

28.3-2 Sale of company or assets as going concern

NCLT can order sale of company or its assets as a going concern. NCLT may appoint sales committee for this purpose - section 282(2) of Companies Act, 2013.

If a unit is actually functional, sale as a 'going concern' may attract better price than sale of individual assets. This will also really speed up process of winding up.

Once NCLT sanctions sale as a going concern, the actual sale can be made by Company Liquidator as per powers under section 290(1)(d) of Companies Act, 2013.

Unit closed for long time may not be sold as going concern - If the unit is closed for long time, sale of machinery, plant and land separately will fetch a better price. The reason is that in case of sale as a going concern, employment of all employees will continue, which may cast a big liability.

In Allahabad Bank v. Arc Holding Ltd. 2000 AIR SCW 3498 = 28 SCL 394 (SC), it was held that if a unit is closed for a long time, sale as a going concern should not be normally ordered by High Court (now NCLT).

28.3-3 Action if Company Liquidator reports fraud

If Company Liquidator makes such report, NCLT shall order investigation under section 210 of Companies Act, 2013. On receipt of report of investigation, NCLT may give directions under sections 339 to 342 of Companies Act, 2013. NCLT may direct Company Liquidator to file criminal complaint against persons who were involved in the fraud - section 282(2) of Companies Act, 2013

If Company Liquidator reports that fraud has been committed in promotion, formation, business or conduct of affairs of company, NCLT can order examination of such promoters, directors or officers of the company - section 300(1) of Companies Act, 2013.

28.4 Custody of company's properties after order of winding up

Company Liquidator or Provisional Liquidator shall take custody of all properties, effects and actionable claims of the company. Even if actual possession is not taken, these will be deemed to be in custody of NCLT. NCLT can order any contributory, trustee, receiver, banker, officer or employee to pay or deliver or transfer any money, property or books and papers in his custody.

28.4-1 Taking over of company's property by Company Liquidator

After order of winding up is made or after a provisional liquidator has been appointed, the Company Liquidator or Provisional Liquidator shall take into his custody or under his control, all property, effects and actionable claims of the company - section 283(1) of Companies Act, 2013.

In Pradeshia Industrial & Investment Corpn of UP v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2003) 47 SCL 126 (All HC), Court had issued order of winding up. Even then, Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) ordered Official Liquidator (later Company Liquidator) to handover property to the company. It was held that order suffers from gross error of jurisdiction and beyond powers conferred on CJM under section 451 of CrPC.

In K & Co v. Aruna Sugars AIR 1999 Mad 45, it was held that disposition of property by company after commencement of winding up can be sanctioned if necessary for general interest of company, without causing harm to creditors.

Shri Chhibar has vehemently submitted that once the petition is admitted, there is no discretion with the court but to pass the order of winding up and appoint official liquidator as liquidator of the company. It was argued that the arrangement proposed by the company has been withdrawn by the company and the petition has been ordered to be admitted. In these circumstances, the order of winding up is a natural consequence. The reliance was placed upon the cases as Advent Corpn. (P.) Ltd., In re [1969] 39 Comp. Cases 463 (Bom.), Seksaria Cotton Mills Ltd., In re [1969] 39 Comp. Cas. 475 (Bom.) and Focus Advertising (P.) Ltd., In re [1974] 44 Comp. Cas. 567 (Bom.). However, I am unable to accept such a wide proposition. Admission of a petition for winding up of the company is prima facie proof of the admitted liability. The object of publication of admission in the newspapers is to invite objections from the persons interested, for and against the order of the winding up of the company. If there is no discretion with the court at that stage but to pass the order of winding up, the very purpose of publication of the admission is rendered nugatory. The company court is required to examine whether the winding up of the company is in the interest of shareholders, secured and unsecured creditors, workers as well as in public interest. It is natural consequence of admission of petition. Thus, I am unable to accept the argument raised by Shri Chhibar that the company court has no discretion after the admission of the petition but to pass the order of winding up. The judgments relied upon by the petitioner, no doubt, have taken a view that the Court has no discretion to refuse to make a winding up order ex debito justitiae if the company neglects to pay the sum demanded. However, the said judgments are distinguishable and not applicable to the facts of the present case. Here the company has stated on an affidavit that it has assets more than the due amount. The management of the company is not able to sell the property because of its physical disability being in custody, an FIR lodged by Vigilance Bureau, Punjab. Keeping in view the projected solvency of the company, it will not be fair and reasonable to pass an order of winding up but the interest of the creditors is required to be matched which will be best served by appointing a provisional liquidator for effecting sale of the property of the company. A Division Bench of this Court in Ambala Bus Syndicate (P.) Ltd. v. Bala Financiers (P.) Ltd. [1986] 59 Comp. Cas. 838, has quoted with approval the view of Division Bench of Calcutta High Court reported in Bengal Luxmi Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Mahaluxmi Cotton Mills Ltd. AIR 1955 Cal. 273 wherein it has been held that the basis of making an order of winding up against a company is that it has ceased to be commercially solvent and accordingly it is fit and proper in the interest of creditors and shareholders not to allow it to function further as a company. The basis of winding up order on the ground of company’s inability to pay its debts is always insolvency. In view of the above, it is not possible at this stage, to hold that the company is insolvent so as to discharge its liability towards the creditors.

387.1 Background note387.1 Background note

Sum placed with NSEIL constituted property of company

Section 456 itself makes it clear that the PL shall take into his custody or under his control 'all the property' to which the company is or appears to be entitled. There can be no manner of doubt, and it is in fact not denied, that the company did place with NSEIL Rs. 1.10 crore when it became a trading member. The said sum definitely, therefore, constitutes the property of the company.

Although upon passing of the winding up order by the Court, the assets and the properties of the company came to the custody of the PL, but, in fact, the properties did not vest in the PL. Therefore, the PL acts as an agent of the company, a trustee of the properties as also the officer of the Court. He acts under the directions of the Court. This explains why under section 457(1), it is the liquidator who has been given the powers thereafter to represent the company under liquidation in all the proceedings. [Para 14]

Claims of investors had not been met out of company's fund with Defaulter Committee

In the instant case, although the company was expelled as a trading member, prior to the order of winding up, resulting in the deposit made by it with NSEIL vesting in the Defaulters' Committee, the claims of the investors had not been met out of that fund by the Defaulters Committee. It, in fact, set aside Rs. 83,91,000 pursuant to the letter written to the NSEIL by the Official Liquidator. It has met the claims of 68 investors in part out of IPFT. Therefore, the deposit made by the company with NSEIL, which constitutes its property under section 456(1), remains intact. [Para 17]

Conclusion

With the process of liquidation of the company already in progress, the scheme of section 456 will have to be followed. The inevitable result would be that wherever any property of the company-in-liquidation is available, the possession of such property would have to come to the PL appointed by the Court. Investors, who are before the Defaulters' Committee, will now have the option of pursuing their claims before the Official Liquidator in accordance with law.

Consequently, the plea of NSEIL that its Defaulters' Committee should be allowed to continue to be in possession and control of the deposits of Rs. 1.10 crore lying with it to the credit of the company cannot be countenanced. [Para 18]

Consequently, company application is to be allowed and NSEIL is to be directed to remit to the Official Liquidator the sum of Rs. 1.10 crore together with interest, if any accrued thereon. [Para 19]

Section 235 of the 1956 Act, enables the Central Government to appoint inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company and to report thereon in such manner as the Central Government may direct, in case where a report has been made by the Registrar of the company under sub-section (6) of section 234 or under sub-section (7) of that section read with sub-section (6) thereof. Under sub-section (2) of section 235, where an application has been received by the specified number of members or persons on the company's register of members, respectively, in case of a company having share capital and in case of a company having no share capital, the Tribunal may declare the investigation of the affairs of the company by an inspector, but, after giving the parties an opportunity of being heard. [Para 11]

Under Section 237, without prejudice to the powers of the Central Government under section 235, the Central Government is empowered to appoint inspector to investigate the affairs of the company and to report thereon in such manner as the Central Government may direct, if the company by special resolution or, the court by order declares that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated by an inspector appointed by the Central Government. Under clause (b) of section 237, the Central Government may appoint an inspector if, in its opinion or in the opinion of the Tribunal, there are circumstances suggesting that the business of the company is being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members or any other persons, or otherwise for fraudulent or for unlawful purpose, or in a manner oppressive to any of its members; where the persons concerned in the formation of the company or the management of its affairs have in connection therewith been guilty of fraud, misfeasance and other misconduct towards the company or towards any of its members; or, that the members of the company have not been given all the information with respect to its affairs which they might reasonably expect. [Para 12]

The powers of the inspector to investigate into an affair of the referred companies is provided under section 239 of the Act 1956. Under section 240, it is the duty of all officers and other employees and agents of the company, where its affairs are being investigated by virtue of section 239 to preserve and produce all papers and documents and render all assistance. Section 240A empowers the inspector to seize books and papers relating to any company where he has reasonable grounds to believe that they may be destroyed to the mutilated, altered, falsified or secreted to seize such books and papers. [Para 13]

Under section 241, the inspectors are required to make interim reports to the Central Government and on conclusion of the investigation to make final report to the Central Government. Section 242 provides for prosecution pursuant to a report furnished under section 241. Section 243 provides for winding up of a company which enables the Central Government to cause to be presented to the tribunal by any authorised person, a petition for winding up of the company on the ground that it is just and equitable that it should be wound up or on an application for an order under section 397 or 398, or both a petition and an application as aforesaid. [Para 14]

Section 250A permits an investigation to be initiated under section 235, 237, 239 or 247 notwithstanding that an application has been made for an order under section 397 or 398; or the company has passed a special resolution for voluntarily winding up and no investigation so initiated shall be stopped or suspended by reason only of the fact that an application or a special resolution referred aforesaid, has been passed. [Para 15]

Under the Act 2013, there is a separate chapter, Chapter XIV, that deals with inspection, inquiry, and investigation. [Para 16]

Under section 206 of the Act, 2013, the Registrar has power to call for further information or explanation or any further documents relating to the company by a written notice, where on a scrutiny of any document filed by a company or on any information received by him, the Registrar forms that opinion requiring the company to furnish in writing such information or explanation, or to produce such documents. Where no information or explanation is so furnished, or the Registrar finds the information or explanation inadequate on his satisfaction that unsatisfactory state of affairs exists in the company and does not disclose a full and fair statement of the information required, he may, by another written notice, call on the company to produce for his inspection such further books of account, books, papers and explanations as he may require. [Para 17]

Under section 235(2) a power is given to the CLB in case where, Inter alia, an application is received from not less than 200 members, or members holding not less than one-tenth of the total voting power in a company, to declare, after giving the parties an opportunity of being heard, that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated by an Inspector or Inspectors. On such a declaration being made, the Central Government shall appoint one or more competent persons as inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company and to report thereon.

The power, therefore, to appoint Inspector to investigate the affairs of a company has to be exercised by the Central Government after a proper preliminary scrutiny by the Registrar or by the CLB as the case may be. It cannot be instituted simply on the basis of allegations made by one shareholder. Under section 237, there is a further power given to the Central Government to appoint Inspectors to investigate the affairs of a company if the company, by a special resolution, or the Court, by order declares that such investigation is necessary. Similarly, this may be done if in the opinion of the CLB there are circumstances suggesting that the business of the company is being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members or any other person or otherwise for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose or in a manner oppressive of any of its members or that the company was formed for any fraudulent or unlawful purpose. The CLB may also come to a conclusion that there are circumstances suggesting that the persons concerned in the formation of the company or management of its affairs have been guilty of fraud, misfeasance or other misconduct towards the company or towards any of its members; or that the members of the company have not been given all the information with respect to its affairs which they might reasonably expect. In these circumstances, on the basis of the opinion so framed by the CLB, the Central Government may order an investigation.

In the instant case no attempt had been made by the respondent to get the affairs of the company investigated in the manner provided under the Act. Neither the Central Government nor the CLB had been moved by the respondent in accordance with law for this purpose. Instead of moving the authorities prescribed under the Act the first respondent had chosen to resort to the writ jurisdiction of the High Court for a direction to have the affairs of the company investigated by the CBI.

The Single Judge before whom the present writ petition came up for hearing very rightly held that the Companies Act provides a forum to consider the grievances made out by the first respondent in the writ petition. When such a forum, statutorily constituted, exists, it is but appropriate that resort to article 226 should be discouraged There is an efficacious alternative remedy available under the statute. In fact under the Companies Act, a more satisfactory solution is available. The Single Judge was right in pointing out that some of the shareholders had initiated proceedings before the CLB. The only grievance of the petitioner in the writ petition was that no orders had been passed thereon. The Single Judge had rightly held that such a grievance could not constitute a ground for invoking the jurisdiction of the High Court under article 226.

Further no public interest was involved in disputes of the kind referred to in the writ petition. They basically dealt with mismanagement of the affairs of the company and oppression of the minority shareholders. The company was only a deemed public limited company. Its shareholding was very closely held The only other factor referred to in the writ petition to invoke the doctrine of so-called public interest, was the fact that the company had borrowed moneys from public institutions. This was no ground for not availing of the statutory remedies provided under the Act before the appropriate statutory forums which are designed for this very purpose.

Therefore, the order of the Single Judge could not be interfered with. The judgment of the Division Bench was set aside.

39.3-4 Inspection of related companies/persons An inspector can carry out investigation of (a) holding or subsidiary company (b) Any other body corporate which was managed at relevant time by Managing Director or Manager of the company or (c) Whose Board of directors comprises of nominees of the company under investigation or whose Board is accustomed to act in accordance with directions of the company or any director of the company or (d) Person who was Managing Director or Manager at relevant time. Powers in respect of (b), (c) and (d) above can be exercised only with prior approval of Central Government - section 219 of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding section 239 of the 1956 Act].

39.3-5 Procedures and powers of inspector during investigation

It is duty of all officers and employees of the company to preserve and produce all books and papers and to provide all assistance to the inspector. The inspector, with previous approval of Central Government, can ask any body corporate to supply information and produce books and papers as are necessary for investigation. These can be kept in his custody for six months and then returned. The inspector can examine a person on oath in relation to affairs of the company. Non-compliance in producing information or appearing before inspector is punishable with imprisonment upto 6 months and minimum fine of Rs. 25,000 which can extend upto Rs. one lakh, plus Rs. 2,000 for every day till default continues - section 217 of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding section 240 of the 1956 Act].

Agreement with foreign Government on reciprocal basis to assist in enquiry - Central Government can enter into agreement with Government of foreign State on reciprocal basis to assist in inspection, inquiry or investigation under the Companies Act and corresponding foreign Act [section 217(10) of Companies Act, 2013].

Letter of request to foreign Court or authority to take statement - Inspector can make application to local Court to request to foreign Court or authority to record statement of a person in that Country and send that statement to Court in India. Such statement will be admissible as evidence [section 217(11) of Companies Act, 2013].

Similarly, if Court or authority in foreign country requests, the Court in India shall record the statement and send it to foreign Court or authority through Central Government [section 217(12) of Companies Act, 2013].

The letter of request shall be transmitted in such manner as specified by Ministry of Corporate Affairs - Rule 6 of Companies (Registration Offices and Fees) Rules, 2014.

39.3-6 Seizure of documents by inspector

If the inspector has reasonable grounds to believe that books and papers relating to the affairs of company or other body corporate may be destroyed, mutilated, altered, falsified or secreted, he can enter into places or premises where books and papers are placed, to search the place and to seize the books and papers as necessary. Company can take copies of the documents at its cost. Search and seizure must be according to provisions of Code of Criminal Procedure. The seized papers can be kept till conclusion of investigation. The inspector can take copies of any document or place identification marks on them before returning the books and papers - section 220 of Companies Act, 2013. [corresponding to section 240A of the 1956 Act].

39.3-7 Inspector's report

Inspector can make interim as well as final report. The final report will be sent to Central Government. Copy of the report may be obtained by making application to Central Government [section 223(3) of Companies Act, 2013].

Copy of inspector's report made under section 223(1) may be obtained by members, creditors or any other person whose interest is likely to be affected, by making application to Central Government - section 223(3) of Companies Act, 2013. Words in italics inserted w.e.f. 9-2-2018.

39.3-8 Follow up action by Central Government

After the report of Inspector, Central Government can take action as specified in section 224 of Companies Act, 2013.

The public at large and the creditors in particular are being misled by all such exercises. All the investors including the petitioners are still craving for refund of their money. Merely because thousands of creditors have expressed their faith in the Chairman and reconstituted Board of Directors (appointed by the Company Law Board) is not enough to stay or keep in abeyance the winding up proceedings. The newly appointed Chairman Mr. Justice Ujjagar Singh has not yet concluded the repayment procedure, although he is seized of the matter for the last more than 1½ years. Also he has not sent any report either to this Court or the Company Law Board or the Official Liquidator of this Court. Incan Group of Companies are in liquidation and M/s. incan Greens has already been ordered to be wound up.

18. Keeping in view the discussions made above, I am of the decisive opinion that all these petitions deserve to be allowed and the company known as M/s. Incan Mutual Fund Benefit Limited is liable to be wound up.

He shall take into his custody all the movable and immovable properties, including the cash in custody with the District Magistrate, Rai Bareilly, under section 456(1) of the Act. He shall submit the statement of accounts and other necessary statements, within three months from today and also shall chalk out a plan for repayment of the petitioners/creditors’ dues in a just and reasonable manner.

of section 235. The grounds for ordering an investigation did exist. There was overwhelming material available pointing to the circumstances suggesting that the business of the company was conducted for a fraudulent and unlawful purpose. The persons concerned in the management of the company had been guilty of fraud, misfeasance or other misconduct towards the company. It was a case squarely covered under the provisions of section 235 as the pre-conditions for initiating such an action existed as was clear from the foregoing. [Para 15] The directors owe fiduciary duty to the shareholders and they have to function in not only good faith, but in utmost good faith. In the instant case, shareholders’ faith seemed to have been belied. The petitioner was on a very sound footing besides having come to the CLB bona fide. Only investigation under section 235 could bring out the true state of affairs. An order to investigate under section 235 in any case could not be prejudicial to the respondent. An order of the CLB under this section directing an investigation is only analogous to the issue of a fact finding commission. This particular power of the CLB is not of a judicial or quasi-judicial nature. It is a power of administrative nature and the CLB may even take the initiative suo motu or on the application or information supplied by any shareholder or other person. Under this section, directing an investigation is only analogous to the issue of a fact finding commission by a civil court for looking into accounts or making an investigation and does not amount to a judgment within clause 15 of the Letters Patent, so as to enable an aggrieved party to appeal. An order of investigation is not an end by itself; it is only a means to find out the full facts of the acts complained of. It is nothing, but an exploratory measure to be proved or disproved with reference to the facts later on ascertained. This discretionary power of the CLB has to be exercised in good faith. An investigation may be ordered when public interest is involved or detriment to the interests of shareholders had been caused surreptitiously. Such investigation should not be taken lightly. Unless proper grounds exist for investigation of the affairs of the company, investigation cannot be ordered. The allegations made in the petition were such matters which would require an investigation. [Para 16]

In view of above, there was reason to believe that there was likelihood of the existence of malpractices envisaged in the provisions of section 235. To prove the prima facie case of ‘intent to fraud’ and misfeasance on general public and specifically the investor in the instant case and conducting the business of the company otherwise for a fraudulent and unlawful purpose, the petitioner’s prayer could be granted for ordering an investigation under section 235. [Para 17]

The petition was, accordingly, to be allowed. [Para 18]
