384.8 Appointment of inspectors384.8 Appointment of inspectors

On making of order by Company Law Board to appoint inspectors, the Central Government shall appoint one or more competent persons as inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company and to report thereon.

384.8-1 Prohibition384.8-1 Prohibition

No firm, body corporate or other associations shall be appointed as inspectors.

384.8-2 Continuance of investigation384.8-2 Continuance of investigation No investigation shall be stopped or suspended by reason of the fact that an application has been made for an order for prevention of oppression or mismanagement or a special resolution has been passed for voluntary winding up of the company.

384.9 Powers of inspectors384.9 Powers of inspectors

An inspector appointed to investigate the affairs of the company has the following powers :

384.9-1 Power to investigate other body corporates384.9-1 Power to investigate other body corporates

The inspector may also investigate the affairs of the following persons/body corporates which may be relevant to his investigation viz.,

u any other body corporate which is, or has at any relevant time been, the company’s holding or subsidiary company or a subsidiary of its holding company or a holding company of its subsidiary.

u any other body corporate which is or has at any relevant time been, managed by any person as managing director or manager of the company who is or was the managing director or manager of the company at the relevant time.

u any other body corporate which is or has at any relevant time been, managed by the company.

u any other body corporate whose board of directors comprises of nominees of the company.

u any other body corporate whose Board of directors are accustomed to act in accordance with the directions or instructions of the company or any of the directors of the company or any company whose directorships is held by the employees or nominees of those having the control and management of the first mentioned company. However, the prior approval of the Central Government is required in this case.

u any person who is or has at any relevant time been the managing director or manager of the company. However, the prior approval of the Central Government is required in this case.

384.9-2 Power to examine books and documents384.9-2 Power to examine books and documents

The inspector shall have powers to demand inspection of all books and papers relating to the company or other body corporate [referred to in para 384.9-1] and it is the duty of all officers and employees of the company to produce the said documents and provide all assistance to the inspector to carry out the duties. The inspector may, with the prior approval of the Central Government, require any other body corporate to furnish such information and produce such books and papers before which he considers it necessary for carrying out his duties as inspector. The inspector can keep the books under his custody for six months and thereafter return it to the person concerned. He may call back the books once again or obtain certified copies of the books and papers. If such certified copies are furnished, the inspector must return those books and papers to the concerned person.

384.9-3 Power to examine on oath384.9-3 Power to examine on oath

The inspector may examine on oath any officer, employee, agent of the body corporate(s) in respect of which the investigation is carried out. He may, with the prior approval of the Central Government, examine any other person on oath.

384.9-4 Power to seize documents384.9-4 Power to seize documents

If, during the course of investigation, the inspector apprehends that the books and papers are likely to be destroyed, mutilated, altered, falsified or secreted, he may make an application to the Presidency Magistrate 1 of the concerned jurisdiction and obtain an order for searching and seizing such documents. Such books can be retained by him until the conclusion of the investigation and should be returned to the concerned person on conclusion of the investigation.

384.10 Inspector’s report384.10 Inspector’s report

The inspector may, and if so directed by the Central Government shall, make interim reports to that Government and on conclusion of the investigation, shall make a final report to the Central Government. Such report shall be written or printed, as the Central Government may direct.

384.11 Authentication of Inspector’s Report384.11 Authentication of Inspector’s Report

The inspector’s report shall be authenticated either by the seal of the company whose affairs have been investigated or by a certificate of a public officer having the custody of the report, under and in accordance with the provisions of section 76 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. Such authenticated report shall be admissible as an evidence in any legal proceedings in relation to any matter contained in the report.

384.12 Forwarding of report by Central Government384.12 Forwarding of report by Central Government

u shall forward a copy of any report [other than the interim report] to the company at its registered office and the other body corporate(s) dealt with in the report.

u may forward a copy of the report or furnish to any member of the company or other body corporate dealt with in the report on payment of prescribed fee of Re. 1 for every one hundred words or any part thereof.

u shall forward a copy of the report to the applicants who submitted an application for ordering investigation.

Introduction

The Supreme Court's recent judgment in National Spot Exchange Limited (NSEL) v. Union of India & Ors (Writ Petition (Civil) No. 995 of 2019) is a landmark in the domain of financial fraud litigation and asset recovery. The decision, delivered on 15 May 2025, addresses the complex interplay between the Maharashtra Protection of Interest of Depositors (MPID) Act, the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), and central statutes such as the SARFAESI Act, Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act (RDB Act), and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC).

At its core, this decision represents a careful recalibration of the legal hierarchy between secured creditors, government agencies, and public interest protections in cases involving tainted assets.

Background: The NSEL Scam and Legal Tangle

NSEL, a commodity trading platform promoted by 63 Moons Technologies Ltd. The collapse of the National Spot Exchange in 2013 triggered a Rs. 5,600 crore default, affecting about 13,000 traders and investors. The fallout led to multiple FIRs, civil suits, and the attachment of assets by both the Enforcement Directorate (under PMLA) and the State of Maharashtra (under the MPID Act). The NSEL itself secured decrees and arbitral awards worth around Rs. 3,365 crore against defaulting members, but faced significant hurdles in executing them due to overlapping attachments and competing claims from secured creditors (primarily banks) under SARFAESI/RDB Act. IBC proceedings also initiated against several entities.

Genesis of the Supreme Court Committee

To streamline the complex situation, involving execution of multiple decrees and avoid conflicting proceedings, the Supreme Court, invoking Article 142, constituted a high-powered committee chaired by Justice (Retd.). This committee was vested with the powers of a civil court to execute all decrees, orders, and arbitral awards obtained by NSEL, including the authority to sell properties attached under PMLA and MPID Act and oversee distribution to verified claimants. In short, Article 142 was used as a constitutional "safety valve" to harmonize conflicting statutory regimes, centralize execution, and prioritize investor restitution in a manner that ordinary statutory processes could not have achieved efficiently.

Power under Article 142 is extraordinary, discretionary, and unique to the Supreme Court. It allows the Court to:

Fill legal gaps where no statute provides an adequate remedy. It Complements statutory law, but does not override it—cannot be used to violate or contradict existing statutes

Issue binding directions, even if not strictly aligned with procedural law. Curative in nature—used to resolve issues when ordinary law falls short or causes injustice

Craft equitable solutions, especially in complex, multi-party, or sensitive matters.

However, Article 142 cannot be used to create a new law or override substantive rights conferred by legislation. It must be used judiciously and only when regular statutory or procedural remedies are inadequate or unjust. Article 142 cannot be used to achieve something indirectly what cannot be achieved directly.

While initially hailed as a pragmatic consolidation, the order's breadth brought it into direct strain with key statutory provisions of PMLA, SARFAESI, RDB Act, and IBC—particularly regarding the priority of secured creditors and the moratorium under insolvency law.

Key Legal Questions before the Supreme Court

Two main issues crystallized before the Court in the later stages of the litigation:

1.

Do secured creditors have priority over assets attached under the PMLA and MPID Act by virtue of SARFAESI and RDB Act?

2.

Are properties attached under the MPID Act immune from the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC?

These questions weren't just technical—they strike at the heart of India's recovery framework, challenging the hierarchy of creditor rights in fraud scenarios.

Supreme Court's Ruling on Secured Creditors' Priority

The Court held that the MPID Act and PMLA take precedence over the SARFAESI Act and RDB Act when it comes to assets attached as "proceeds of crime" or for the protection of depositors. The rationale is rooted in constitutional law: the MPID Act is a state law enacted to maintain public order and protect depositors, while SARFAESI and RDB Act are central laws focusing on banking and secured creditors' rights. Since these statutes operate in distinct legislative fields, the doctrine of repugnancy under Article 254 does not apply.

SEBI is vested with powers of Civil Court

The Securities Appellate Tribunal ('SAT') which exercises powers under Section 15T of the SEBI Act, it is well settled, is the final adjudicator of facts. The Tribunal has, for the purpose of discharging its functions, the same powers as are vested in a Civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure. Broadly speaking, the Tribunal has trappings of a Court in the sense that it has to determine the appeal placed before it judicially and give a fair hearing to the parties, to accept evidence and also order for inspection and discovery of documents, compel attendance of witnesses and to pass a reasoned order which gives finality to the dispute, subject to the appeal to Supreme Court under Section 15Z of the SEBI Act. Findings of fact generally fall in the domain of the Tribunal provided it stays within its jurisdiction.

Situations may also be there, where the evidence taken as a whole is not reasonably capable of supporting the findings recorded by the Tribunal or the Tribunal could have reasonably recorded that conclusion.

Questions repeatedly posed in instant case before SEBI as well as before SAT, were with regard to the nature of OFCDs issued by Saharas. RHPs produced had disclosed that Saharas did not intend the proposed securities to be listed on any stock exchange and that the issues consisted of unsecured OFCDs with an option to convert the same to equity shares. Saharas had also disclosed that the issue was made on a private placement basis and that OFCDs would be offered also to such persons to whom IM would be circulated. But the fact remains that it was circulated to more than three crore people inviting them to subscribe. The same was circulated through ten lakh agents and more than 2900 branch offices and Saharas had a capital base of only 10 lakhs with no other assets or reserves and was a loss making company and had collected nearly 27,000 crores by way of private placement through unsecured OFCDs redeemable/convertible after 48/60/120 months. Fact finding authorities repeatedly asked for information regarding the names, addresses of investors in OFCDs and the amounts subscribed by them. The appellant claimed that it had furnished to SEBI a separate CD giving the details of names of investors, the amount invested etc. along with the password and keys, along with its letter dated 19.4.2011 which, according to the appellant, was never opened or checked.

SEBI, has been vested with the powers of a Civil Court under CPC, as per sub-section (3) of section 11 of the SEBI Act. Under Section 11C, the Board has also been vested with the powers to order investigation to examine whether any person associated with securities market has violated any provision of the Act or the rules or the regulations made or direction issued by the Board. Applicants’ case was that respondent-company had become nearly insolvent and with a view to tide over its financial distress, it, through one of its directors, viz., ‘D’, sold said land together with building standing thereon to applicants - Certain payment was made by applicants as advance and balance was to be paid at time of registration - Applicants contended that receipt of said balance amount and consequential execution of sale deed were delayed on one pretext or other and, therefore, they filed suit seeking specific performance of agreement of sale - Immediately, a compromise memo was filed before Court and, consequently, matter was referred to Lok Adalat which passed a decree duly recording compromise between parties - In terms of compromise decree, balance amount was paid and sale deed was executed - Subsequently, applicants entered into an agreement of sale of said property with ‘V’ - In meantime, respondent-company was ordered to be wound up on applications by some depositors of company to whom company had not repaid their deposits and possession of said property was taken over by Official Liquidator - Hence, applicants moved instant application seeking property to be released from custody of Official Liquidator on ground that title over property had been transferred by company in favour of applicants by way of sale deed executed between parties - It was found that market value of property was much higher than value for which property was offered for sale to applicants - There was no resolution passed by board of directors of company, in accordance with provisions contained in section 291, for undertaking sale of any of asset of company - No publicity was ever issued by company or by its directors for intended sale of said asset - It was not explained as to how applicants came to know of impending sale of said asset and how they got property valued before entering into transaction - There was no authorization issued by company in favour of ‘D’ to enter into a compromise or enter into a transaction of sale at first instance with applicants - Sale consideration was paid in cash instead of secured instruments like cheques or demand drafts and no entries were found in books of company about receipt of said amount - Applicants failed to demonstrate their financial capacity to have pooled up such a huge sum at one go, to pay to respondent in cash - Thousands of complaints had been lodged with police at various places in State by depositors alleging fraud and misrepresentation indulged in by respondent-company - Whether, on facts, it could be said that entire transaction was vitiated by fraud played by applicants on District Court as well as on Lok Adalat and ‘D’ on behalf of respondent-company had joined hands with them - Held, yes - Whether since no right or interest or title can ever pass in favour of beneficiary of fraud and further, no action can be maintained which is founded in fraud, decree passed by Lok Adalat pursuant to a compromise entered into by and between parties therein in civil suit on file of Additional District Judge was to be declared as a nullity - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, no rights of any kind would ever pass to hands of applicants vis-a-vis property in question owned and belonging to company and, as such, application filed by them was to be dismissed - Held, yes

There is no conflict between SEBI Act and Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code because SEBI deals with investor protection issues whereas Bankruptcy code deals with creditor issues. The jural relationship between the parties is also different. In SEBI, it is between the investors and the company, whereas in Bankruptcy code, it is between the creditors and the debtor, therefore, there is no subject matter conflict in between the two statutes. [Para 18]

On perusal of section 238, it is evident that overriding effect under section 238 will have over other laws, only when the other laws are inconsistent with the Insolvency and Bankruptcy code, since SEBI Act has been dealing with investor protection issues, not with creditor and debtor issues, though section 238 has exhaustive mode in respect of the subject matter of creditor and debtor issues, it has no overlapping or overriding effect over investor protection issues dealt with under SEBI Act. [Para 22]

A non-obstante clause is a legislative device which is usually employed to give overriding effect to certain provisions over some contrary provisions that may be found either in the same enactment or some other enactment, that is to say, to avoid the operation and effect of all contrary provisions. 385.1 Background note385.1 Background note

The Central Government is empowered to appoint inspectors to investigate and report on the ownership of the company under certain circumstances.

385.2 Investigation into ownership of the company385.2 Investigation into ownership of the company

An investigation into the ownership of the company may be ordered under the following circumstances :

385.2-1 Investigation by Central Government on its own385.2-1 Investigation by Central Government on its own

The Central Government may, when it appears that there is good reason to do so, appoint one or more inspectors to investigate and report on the membership of any company and other matters relating to the company for the purpose of determining the true persons who are or have been—

u financially interested in the success or failure, whether real or apparent, of the company; or

u able to control or materially influence the policy of the company.

385.2-2 Investigation at the instance of Company Law Board385.2-2 Investigation at the instance of Company Law Board

Where in the course of any proceedings before it, the Company Law Board declares that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated, the Central Government shall appoint one or more investigators and report on the membership of any company and other matters relating to the company for the purpose of determining the true persons who are or have been—

u financially interested in the success or failure, whether real or apparent, of the company; or

u able to control or materially influence the policy of the company.

385.3 Scope of investigation385.3 Scope of investigation

While appointing inspectors, the Central Government may define the scope of investigation with regard to matters, period to which such inspection extends and limit the investigation to matters connected with particular shares or debentures.

385.4 Powers of Inspectors385.4 Powers of Inspectors

The inspectors shall have powers to examine persons on oath, inspect the books and papers. Refer para 384.9 for other provisions.

385.5 Inspector’s Report385.5 Inspector’s Report

The inspector shall forward his report to the Central Government. However, the Central Government shall not be bound to furnish the company or any other person with a copy of such report or any portion thereof, if there is a good reason for not divulging the contents thereof. In such a case, the Central Government shall require the Registrar to keep a copy of such report or parts of such report which could be divulged.

385.6 Expenses of Investigation385.6 Expenses of Investigation

The expenses of investigation shall be defrayed by the Central Government out of the moneys provided by the Parliament, unless it directs that the expenses or part thereof should be met by the applicants on whose application the investigation was ordered.

385.7 Imposition of restrictions385.7 Imposition of restrictions

Where it appears to the Company Law Board that for the purpose of investigation into ownership of the company, it is necessary to impose restrictions, it may by order direct that the shares shall be subject to the following restrictions for a period not exceeding three years as may be specified in the order viz.

u transfer of those shares shall be void;

u where shares are to be issued, they should not be issued and any issue thereof or transfer of any right to be issued therewith shall be void;

u no voting right shall be exercisable;

u no further shares shall be issued in right of those shares or in pursuance of any offer made to the holder thereof and any issue thereof or transfer of any right to be issued therewith shall be void ;

u except on liquidation no payment should be made for any sums due from the company on those shares, whether in respect of dividend or capital or otherwise.

385.8 Restriction on transfer of shares or debentures385.8 Restriction on transfer of shares or debentures

Where a transfer of shares or debentures in a company has taken place and as a result thereof a change in the composition of the Board of Directors is likely to take place which would be prejudicial to the public interest, the Company Law Board may, by order, direct that—

u the voting rights in respect of those shares or debentures shall not be exercisable for a period not exceeding three years as may be specified in the Order.

u no resolution passed or action taken to effect a change in the composition of the Board of Directors before the date of the order unless it is confirmed by the Company Law Board.

u the transfer of shares in the company during such period not exceeding three years as may be specified in the Order, shall be void.

HELD: From a perusal of the documents submitted by the petitioners, it was clear that the directors had violated various provisions of the Act and committed various acts which were prejudicial to the interest of the company and its shareholders at large. It was also seen from the documents that the Registrar of Companies, issued notice dated to 2-9-2008 to its directors under section 234(1) directing the company to furnish information and explanation within ten days or else action would be initiated under sections 234(3A), 234(4). Further, the Registrar of Companies issued another letter dated 19-9-2008 to the directors to furnish the minutes book of the board of directors and general meetings, fixed asset register, register of debenture holders, index of debenture holders, shareholders' attendance register, register of investments, copy of the annual report and balance-sheets for the last two years. It was seen from the records that having not received any information from the company and its directors, the Registrar of Companies referred the matter to the Regional Director for prosecution. The Registrar of Companies, in response to the notice regarding the filing of the instant petition before the principal Bench, CLB, vide his letter dated 10-6-2009 mentioned the details of the company and its directors and the fund position on the basis of the balance-sheets and also the assets and liabilities. It was also stated that the company had not filed its balance-sheet as on 31-3-2001 and the company held only one annual general meeting on 1-12-2007 for the years 2001 to 2007 instead of holding separate annual general meetings for each year. No extension of time was obtained by the company. It was also mentioned that the shareholding detail was given in CD whereas no CD was received in that regard by the Registrar of Companies. It was also stated that there were several complaints received by the Registrar of Companies against the company. [Para 4]

From the above, it was evident that the allegations of the petitioners had some force and the same were also further strengthened from the letter of the Registrar of Companies to the instant Bench and also various letters addressed to the company. The instant Bench would not keep its eyes closed on such acts when they came before it with un-controverted facts against the directors. The affairs of the company were being conducted with an intent to defraud its members and public which were oppressive and prejudicial to the interest of the members. To protect the interest of the company and its shareholders and also to up keep the faith of the public in the judicial system (Quasi Judicial Bodies), the Bench certainly came to the rescue of the petitioners and its shareholders to do substantial justice by ordering an investigation by invoking the provisions of section 237(b). [Para 5]

The petitioners also brought to the notice that the Registrar of Companies ordered for inspection of the company's records under section 209A which was pending. The scope of inspection and the scope of investigation were entirely different and inspection does not prejudice investigation. In view of the reasons as stated above, it was concluded that there were enough circumstances suggesting for an investigation into the affairs of the company and to take necessary action. The fraudulent companies cannot run away from the clutches of law. The law must be enforceable in such cases to prevent the fraudulent acts and bring back the faith of the members. Therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred under section 237(b), the Central Government would order for investigation into the affairs of the company and would take appropriate action if warranted on receipt of the investigation report. The petitioners were directed to furnish all the information they possessed to the authorities during investigation. [Para 8]

During the course of the winding-up proceedings of RPS Ltd., which was a financial company, the investigating committee found that the appellants had siphoned off the funds of RPS Ltd. and floated another company ‘A’ Ltd. The appellants were holding 81 per cent of shares in ‘A’ Ltd. and also had movable and immovable properties. On the basis of investigation report, the High Court directed the Official Liquidator to sell the shares of the appellants in ‘A’ Ltd. In the meanwhile, the High Court directed that money realised from the sale of ‘A’ Ltd.’s shares and some of the assets would be utilized exclusively for the payment to be made to the depositors of RPS Ltd. Simultaneously, the Economic Offences Wing also initiated action against RPS Ltd. under the provisions of the Criminal Law Amendment Ordinance, 1944 and attached the properties which were acquired out of the pecuniary sources that were believed to be procured from and out of the deposits collected from the depositors. The Tax Recovery Officer issued notice under section 222 to recover tax from the appellants towards capital gain out of the funds available with the Official Liquidator. On receipt of the said notice, the appellants filed applications. It was the common case of the appellants and the ITO that the capital gain tax was recoverable out of the funds available with the Official Liquidator from the sale of 81 per cent shares in ‘A’ Ltd. as per section 530(1)(a ) of the 1956 Act. But the Administrator objected to the same. The Single Judge dismissed application by holding that section 530 of the 1956 Act was not attracted for the disbursement of the sale consideration of 81 per cent of the shares of the appellants in ‘A’ Ltd.

From a perusal of the documents submitted by the petitioners, it was clear that the directors had violated various provisions of the Act and committed various acts which were prejudicial to the interest of the company and its shareholders at large. It was also seen from the documents that the Registrar of Companies, issued notice dated to 2-9-2008 to its directors under section 234(1) directing the company to furnish information and explanation within ten days or else action would be initiated under sections 234(3A), 234(4). Further, the Registrar of Companies issued another letter dated 19-9-2008 to the directors to furnish the minutes book of the board of directors and general meetings, fixed asset register, register of debenture holders, index of debenture holders, shareholders' attendance register, register of investments, copy of the annual report and balance-sheets for the last two years. It was seen from the records that having not received any information from the company and its directors, the Registrar of Companies referred the matter to the Regional Director for prosecution. The Registrar of Companies, in response to the notice regarding the filing of the instant petition before the principal Bench, CLB, vide his letter dated 10-6-2009 mentioned the details of the company and its directors and the fund position on the basis of the balance-sheets and also the assets and liabilities. It was also stated that the company had not filed its balance-sheet as on 31-3-2001 and the company held only one annual general meeting on 1-12-2007 for the years 2001 to 2007 instead of holding separate annual general meetings for each year. From the above, it was evident that the allegations of the petitioners had some force and the same were also further strengthened from the letter of the Registrar of Companies to the instant Bench and also various letters addressed to the company. The instant Bench would not keep its eyes closed on such acts when they came before it with un-controverted facts against the directors. The affairs of the company were being conducted with an intent to defraud its members and public which were oppressive and prejudicial to the interest of the members. To protect the interest of the company and its shareholders and also to up keep the faith of the public in the judicial system (Quasi Judicial Bodies), the Bench certainly came to the rescue of the petitioners and its shareholders to do substantial justice by ordering an investigation by invoking the provisions of section 237(b). [Para 5]

The petitioners also brought to the notice that the Registrar of Companies ordered for inspection of the company's records under section 209A which was pending. The scope of inspection and the scope of investigation were entirely different and inspection does not prejudice investigation. In view of the reasons as stated above, it was concluded that there were enough circumstances suggesting for an investigation into the affairs of the company and to take necessary action. The fraudulent companies cannot run away from the clutches of law. The law must be enforceable in such cases to prevent the fraudulent acts and bring back the faith of the members. Therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred under section 237(b), the Central Government would order for investigation into the affairs of the company and would take appropriate action if warranted on receipt of the investigation report. Investor Help-lines

1.50 Ordinarily, in the absence of fraud or misfeasance in relation to the company or any breach of duty to the company alleged, there is no remedy in law against loss of investment in a company as a result of the company ceasing to be a going concern, it taken as an inherent risk in carrying on a business. In order to protect themselves from loss otherwise, the investors are expected generally to be aware of their rights with due recognition of their responsibilities to keep themselves informed about the developments in the affairs of the company where they have invested and to act, like participation in its meetings in person or by proxy individually or better still as a member in a kindred group of investors.

Investors’ rights

1.50-1 The investors’ rights in respect of shares include: (a) timely receipt of share certificates, whether on allotment or transfer/transmission, the abridged annual report each year and the notices for the general meetings and prompt refund of excess money paid with the share-application, dividend warrants, offers of rights shares on approval of the issue by the general body; (b) inspection of the statutory books and registers kept by the company as per the Act or to have copies in full or as extracts from the company; (c) to exercise the right of piloting members’ requisitioned resolutions/general meetings to force a change in the company’s course of affairs; (d) to commence civil and criminal proceedings against the company or the directors for defaults or infringements of their rights like oppression or mis-management; (e) to be the residual claimants or be liable as contributories on the company’s winding up; and (f) to prosecute the company and the directors for defaults under and offences against the Act or for the company to be wound-up by the Tribunal, if appropriate. Debenture or bond-holders’ rights are limited to receive the periodic returns and the return of the investment at maturity, to receive the debenture-trust-deed copy on request, and to seek the company’s winding up, if appropriate, before the Tribunal.

Trading and transfer of securities

1.50-2 As regards trading in and transfer of securities, the channels available to investors include :

(A) Trades - purchase and sale by private arrangement or via the trading floors established by the stock exchange where the securities are listed, the stock exchange route being free of the loss due to the risk of non-performance of delivery of securities and prompt payment of the consideration in the deals apart from getting the advantage of the market price at a little extra cost to the investors. While the securities are held, as owners they can raise finances against deposit of the securities.

(B) Grievances (to the low of which property rights of citizens in company or other securities have been summarily diluted as an administrative expedient to form part of Company Law)—the redressal channels available at present include the company and its Registrars first and foremost, besides the DCA and additionally in respect of listed companies, the SEBI/Stock Exchanges where the securities are listed, and the debenture-trustee in the case of debentures. Grievances in respect of Fixed Deposit Receipts in banks or financial institutions other than the Non-banking financial companies may be addressed to the RBI, but for company public deposits it is only the DCA to be approached.

Help-lines, minimal

28.10-3 Binding nature of decisions taken at meeting of creditors, contributories or Advisory Committee

Section 292(1) of the 2013 states that Company Liquidator shall have regard to the directions given in the resolution at such meetings.

Section 354 of Companies Act, 2013 states that liquidator shall have regard to the wishes of creditors or contributories. Thus, their resolutions cannot be binding on Company Liquidator or NCLT.

The resolutions passed at meeting of creditors or contributories have only persuasive value. Company Liquidator or NCLT are not bound by such resolutions.

If the Company Liquidator is not in agreement with the resolutions, he can bypass them for valid reasons. This is also obvious from the fact that any person can apply to NCLT against decision of Company Liquidator under section 292(4) of Companies Act, 2013.

The 'books' are not 'books of account'. The 'books' only refer to records of meetings.

1.40 Administration of Law and Justice

Company Court

1.40-1 Primarily, Company Court is the High Court of the State in which the registered office of a given company is situated (it being reckoned by the longest time duration in the immediately preceding six months for winding up) section 10(1)(a) read with sub-section (3), or the jurisdictional District Court in the State to the extent the jurisdiction has been conferred by the Central Government in section 10(1)(b) read with sub-section (2) vide Notification GSR 663 of 29-5-1959 and GSR 1626 of 13.10.1966 conferring jurisdiction in respect of sections 89, 113, 118, 141, 144, 163, 196, 219, 234, 304, 307 and 614—generally—with some conditions. Consequent to the coming into force of Companies (Second Amendment) Act, 2002, which is yet to be notified, the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) and Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) would be established (sections 10FB and 10FQ), in replacement of the Company Law Board which was in operation since 1-1-1964 introduced by the 1963 Amendment Act (section 10FA), and ousted the jurisdiction of High Court altogether so far as companies are concerned. With this, all Civil Court jurisdiction is barred with the exception of Constitutional powers of the High Court. Appeal against the orders of the Appellate Tribunal lies to the Supreme Court on questions of law. As against this, Taxation laws provide for reference of questions of law to the High Court [since shifted to the National Tax Tribunal formed recently, but halted by the ad interim order of the Bombay High Court in P.C. Joshi v. Union of India [2006] 282 ITR 39/152 Taxman 285] while jurisdiction of the Civil Courts is barred otherwise.

Puzzling mis-joinder of executive, civil and criminal adjudication

1.40-2 Under the Taxation and the economic laws enormous discretionary powers are vested in the Executive, subject to review of special Tribunals. In the same token, though companies are no Government, these are more or less equated to it in the philosophy of self-regulation subject to the purview of State-controlled Regulators of which SEBI partakes of the character both of a Corporate Regulator as well as a quasi-judicial Tribunal with powers of a Civil Court conferred on it in respect of calling for information from, undertaking inspection, conducting enquiries and audits of stock exchanges, mutual funds, other persons associated with the securities market, intermediaries and self-regulatory organizations in the securities market [section 10(i) and (3) of SEBI Act] and imposing penalties and/or fastening cease and desist orders.

Civil Court’s jurisdiction

1.40-3 Civil Court jurisdiction lies still in matters falling outside the purview of the NCLT in respect of protection of the property or prevention of invasion of related rights of the investors in shares or compensation for loss or damage like the remedies provided under section 62 (read with section 10), civil liability for mis-statements in prospectus under the Act and other civil matters connected to meetings, appointments of directors, debts and commercial disputes and torts subject to the jurisdiction being vested in the Court by Government Notification under section 10 and the Civil Procedure Code, and otherwise companies have been distanced from the Civil Court in the largest ever measure so far as shareholders are concerned.

4. In the course of three years Saradha took on new depositors and collected money from existing ones. All this money is now lost. Two years of investigation were required to stop what seems to be a run of the mill Ponzi scheme. The tactics employed by Saradha are not new. They are similar to those employed by Sahara in delaying investigations in the OFCD schemes and in many other white collar crime investigations. The disturbing fact is that they seem to succeed time and again. While SEBI has wide powers in case of entities registered with it, if someone does not register with SEBI, the system of enforcement of law changes completely. The current system requires SEBI to approach the local courts for violations of the SEBI Act which constitute an offence. Moreover, SEBI cannot directly appoint lawyers for prosecuting the offenders and must rely on the State Government's prosecution machinery to get criminal prosecution started.

Weaknesses of the present system

5. The present system suffers from a number of weaknesses, main two of which are as follows:

The normal court systems do not have the time or expertise to enforce violations of investment and securities laws. This leads to confusing orders which sometimes exceed the jurisdiction of the courts. Even in the case of Saradha, the High Court set aside the orders preventing the SEBI from exercising its powers over Saradha, noting that the courts were out of jurisdiction when they prohibited SEBI. However, the High Court's orders take time, and in this time period the operator of the Ponzi scheme can continue to collect money or misappropriate the money already deposited. Expertise in deciding jurisdiction and applicability of SEBI laws is also not available in normal district courts. It will be extremely expensive and wasteful to train all district judges in securities laws for the once-in-a-decade case in financial laws.

The use of the State public prosecutors for violations of financial laws is problematic for two reasons-first, the normal public prosecutors office is flooded with normal criminal cases like theft, murder, etc. A complex financial law case will never be the priority of the normal public prosecutor's office. Secondly, the average public prosecutor who is extremely busy with the daily load of run of the mill criminal cases is not trained in investment and securities laws. Just like district judges, it would not be cost effective to train all public prosecutors in securities laws.

5.1 A fragmented regulatory system - Under the present system there are many institutions that offer deposit or investment services without any form of approval or regulation. Under a fragmented regulatory system, hazy lines of work have been drawn between financial regulators, the Central Government and the State Governments. This has led to the problem of under policing - anything that does not fall squarely within the lines tends to pass unnoticed from the radar of regulation. Saradha presents a good example - its activities could be argued to fall under any of the following categories: running a collective investment scheme (regulated by the SEBI); running a chit fund (regulated by the State Government); a private company taking deposits for its business (regulated by the Registrar of Companies) and taking public deposits as a non-banking financial company (regulated by the RBI). The Saradha Group chose to seek permission from none of these.

There is also inconsistency in the manner and extent of regulation of the financial institutions performing similar activities. For instance, 265 non-banking financial companies and 18 housing finance companies are allowed to take public deposits, but they don't enjoy the same deposit insurance protection that is available to banks. If the rationale for deposit insurance is to protect depositors from the risk of a financial institution becoming unable to make good its promise to refund public deposits, should the same logic not apply to all deposit takers?

Chit funds, which are governed by the State Governments, also suffer from the problem of inconsistent treatment. Differences in enforcement levels across the States have resulted in some States becoming more prone to ponzi schemes. In addition, most of the companies in this sector may be operating in the form of unregistered chit funds. It is estimated that registered chit funds have collected Rs. 300 billion worth of deposits while the collection of unregistered funds is much higher at Rs. 30 trillion.

The regulation of collective investment schemes that come under the SEBI's scanner has also left much to be desired. This is largely on account of the restrictive mandate. Section 11AA of the SEBI Act defines "collective investment schemes" in terms of principles to identify such schemes, but it contains exemptions for institutions such as chit funds, nidhis and co-operative societies. Pointing to the huge investment in the grey market that plagues the financial sector, the SEBI Chairman, U. K. Sinha observed that the loopholes in the existing laws are the primary cause for this type of situation. He pointed out towards the need for a single regulatory body to look into the regulation of all companies that take illegal deposits from the public.

How IFC would address the key issues

6. The Indian Financial Code, drafted by the Financial Sector Legislative Commission, would address these issues in the following ways:

The whole system of investigation is formalised under an investigator appointed by the regulator. The terms of reference for the investigator, the system of investigation and the time for investigation have to be written down at the onset. Since all incomplete investigations will require extensions, there will be system of raising alarms for an unusually long investigation – (see draft clause 394 of the IFC).

Section 397 empowers the CLB to make such order as it thinks fit, may with a view to bringing to an end the matters complained off by any member of a company who complains that the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interests or in a manner oppressive to any member or members. Section 398 empowers the CLB in case of mismanagement in the affairs of a company and may apply any member of a company who complained that the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interest or that a material change not being a change brought about by or in the interests of any creditor including debenture holders or any class of shareholders of the company. The CLB may with a view to bringing to an end or preventing the matters complained of are apprehended make such order as it thinks fit. Section 399 provides for the right to apply under sections 397-398 by the category of persons as mentioned in that section. Admittedly, there were no complaints before the Bench by any member/members or creditors of the company alleging/complaining the acts of oppression and mismanagement in the affairs of the company and the nature of allegations of the Union of India required a detailed trial by examining the witnesses and the veracity of documents. The petitioner submitted that opportunity was given to the respondents. The inspection was carried out in the year 2004 and a final report was submitted to the Government. It was open to the respondents to challenge the investigation report if it would have violated the principles of natural justice in conducting the inspection. Further, the CLB would not intrude the functions of the other statutory bodies such as SEBI, RBI and the civil court, company court and exercising powers under IPC. It is well settled law that to invoke the provisions of sections 397 and 398 by any member, creditor a case has to be made out that facts would justify the making of winding up order and that winding up would unfairly prejudice the members. The petitioner also invoked the provisions of sections 542 and 543. Section 543 is relevant provision to be applied by the petitioner. However, to apply under that provision, only a creditor or a member can make an application. In the instant case admittedly the petitioner was neither a member nor creditor of the company. Hence, the petitioner could not invoke the provision of section 543 where the CLB has the power to order for repayment or restore the money or property. The sole prayer in the petition was for recovery of money

Investigation of a company - Purpose

The purpose of investigation is to find out whether those in charge of the affairs of a company are guilty of illegal conduct or conduct trenching upon the breach of fiduciary obligations or oppression or misfeasance [see Kumaranunni v. Mathrubhumi Printing and Publishing Co. Ltd. [1983] 54 Comp. Cas. 370 (Ker.)]. Towards this end, an inspector merely probes into the affairs of the company and embodies in the report his opinion. The document is admissible in evidence only as a piece of opinion. The opinion, by itself does not affect the rights of the company. He does not write a judgment which binds the company nor does he penalize any body [see Aditya Sharda v. Rangoli Texdye Pvt. Ltd. [2005] 123 Comp. Cas. 390 (CLB)]. Investigation is only a fact-finding measure and has no quasi-judicial character [see New Central Jute Mills Co. Ltd. v. Deputy Secretary, Ministry of Finance [1966] 37 Comp. Cas. 341 (Cal.) and Ashoka Marketing Ltd. v. Union of India [1967] 37 Comp. Cas. 341 (Cal.)]

Introduction

1. "Double your money in 90 days," promised Charles Ponzi, an Italian immigrant to the US, way back in 1919. That was the start of such fraudulent schemes. It seems that it has become immortal unlike its master. Every year hundreds & thousands of such schemes are floated in the market with an intent of defrauding innocent, or should we say, greedy investors who are easily trapped by their treacherous but very lucrative promises.

India saw its biggest Ponzi scheme in the name of Saradha scam in the State of West Bengal, which is slowly turning out to be the hot bed of fraudulent schemes in India. Data collected by the government shows more than 8 out of 10 multi-level marketing and finance schemes against which authorities have received complaints are running from West Bengal. As on March 14, 2013, the government had received complaints against 87 companies from across the country that were suspected of carrying out Ponzi or multi-level schemes. As many as 73 or 84% of these companies are from West Bengal and more than 30 or nearly half of these are believed to be related to the scam-scarred Sudipto Sen-promoted Saradha group. After seeing this data it will not be wrong to call "BENGAL-THE PONZI CAPITAL OF INDIA". The concern should be pinpointed towards eliminating the reason for mushrooming of such schemes and then set out the necessary regulatory set up enabling safeguarding of our ill informed citizens.

Modus Operandi of Saradha schemers

2. The group collected monies from the investors through agents promising them returns in the form of land or a flat, or an option for a refund with a rate of return ranging between 12% - 24% approximately. Most of the investors seem to have opted for the absolute return option rather than claiming land or a flat at the end of the investment tenure, as per the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) notice. The agents, in turn, were assured of a commission ranging from 15% to 20% on the funds mobilised by them, according to local media reports. In some of the schemes the group promised that on a deposit of Rs. 1 lakh an investor will get Rs. 10 lakhs after 14 years. If the same amount of money was kept in a fixed deposit in a bank for the same period, the amount at expiry would be Rs. 4 lakh. In other words, the rate of return promised by the group was exponential and completely shunned the idea of any other investment. According to some media estimates, the number of agents employed by Saradha group may run into thousands or even in lakhs, while the total amount of money mobilised by the group can run into thousands of crores. The huge collection of money from the agents was deposited with the main company which floated 160 companies (according to the letter submitted by Sudipto Sen to the CBI), including a large number of newspapers in various languages and TV channels in Bengali.

The companies that made up Saradha Group were incorporated in the year 2006. Initially, the front-line companies collected money from the public by issuing secured debentures and redeemable preferential bonds, but the entire exercise of mobilising the funds however, lacked procedural proprieties like-

None of the documents given to the Registrar of Companies by the Saradha Group, under statutory requirements, mentioned anything about mobilising such huge amount of money from the public.

Under Indian Securities Regulation and Section 67of the Companies Act, 1956 [now old Companies Act] a company cannot raise capital from more than 50 people without issuing proper prospectus and Balance Sheet, also requiring explicit SEBI clearance. No such clearance or approval was taken.

The promise of providing a plot of land or a flat after the maturity of the scheme was also a hoax.

The above were a few of the discrepancies that the Saradha Group Scheme had, though the list is not exhaustive one. It can be said that the Group's functioning was blatantly illegal. Survival of the scheme even after such manifest illegalities showed the failure of the regulatory authorities to take appropriate measures, at the centre and the State both and even hints at possible collusion with some of these authorities.

Obligations of financial institution and intermediaries

7.1 Maintaining record of certain transactions - Clause 11 of the Bill is considered to be the main cause of worry for financial institutions and other intermediaries. It proposes to make it obligatory for every financial institution and intermediary to maintain a record of all transactions or series of inter-connected transactions exceeding the value of rupees twenty-five lakhs held within a month.

7.2 Furnishing information about certain transactions to income-tax department - It is also proposed that they would be required to furnish information of these transactions to the Commissioner of Income-tax having jurisdiction over such financial institutions or the intermediaries. The financial institutions and intermediaries would also be required to verify and maintain the records of the identity of all of their clients in the prescribed manner for a period of five years from the date of cessation of transactions between the clients and financial institutions.

The provisions of the clause are likely to impose a severe burden on banks, financial institutions and other intermediaries. In view of the fact that the process of computerisation of banks may still take some time to complete, the compliance with these provisions may be very difficult, if not impossible. Even the Reserve Bank has criticised the provisions due to the fact that financial markets have significantly matured in recent years and the number of daily transactions exceeding Rs. 25 lakh runs into lakhs. Therefore, unless the limit is raised to Rs. 1 crore, it would be a nightmarish and back-breaking exercise for banks, financial institutions etc., to report every Rs. 25 lakh plus deal to the authorities.

Also, it is learnt that financial institutions etc. will be required to maintain the record of such transactions for a period of 5 years. This will further add to their headache as they would be required to preserve the records in their original forms. Thus, they would be under tremendous strain for not only maintaining the specified records but also for forwarding the same to the Commissioner of Income-tax. This information on financial trans-actions would be utilised by the enforcement agencies, in consultation with the Reserve Bank, to investigate offences under the Prevention of Money Laundering Legislation (after the Bill is enacted into an Act).

Clause 12 proposes to empower the Director to impose a fine on a financial institution if the institution has failed to maintain or retain records in accordance with the provisions of clause 11. The Director may levy a fine on such financial institution of not less than rupees ten thousand but not exceeding one lakh rupees. A copy of such order levying the fine will be forwarded to every financial institution or intermediary, or other person who is a party to the proceedings. However, clause 13 seeks to provide that the financial institutions, intermediaries and their offices will be provided immunity from any civil or criminal liability, under any existing law, arising out of disclosures of information under clause 11.

The Bill proposes to set up a directorate to administer the Act under the supervision of the Revenue department. The directorate would enjoy the same powers as a civil court enjoys. The officers of the directorate would enjoy powers similar to those conferred on the ITO. Towards Greater Depositors’ Protection

DR. V. BALACHANDRAN, K.S. RAVICHANDRAN AND R. KAMARAJ

Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) play a significant role in the economy of the nation. However, some unscrupulous elements among them have brought a bad name to the NBFC sector as a whole by cheating the investor’s of their hard-earned money. The CRB scam is a glaring and representative example of the same. Such dishonest conduct has forced the Government to put the activities of NBFCs under tight control In this article, the author discusses the measures adopted the RBI to protect the interest of depositors vis-a-vis NBFCs - EDITOR

Introduction

1. The role played by Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) in the national economy cannot be underestimated. They have been providing opportunities for better return to investors and flexibility in tapping resources. They extended retail services to small and middle level busi-nesses and road transport operators. The RBI has estimated that as at the end of March, 1996, regulated deposits of reporting non-banking compa-nies amounted to about Rs. 53,500 crores. Out of these NBFCs accounted for almost Rs. 45,500 crores. This represented about 10.8 per cent of the aggregate deposits of scheduled commercial banks. The rapid growth of NBFCs was facilitated by absence of restrictive legislative provisions. In fact most of the NBFCs did not even report about their operations to the RBI.

Post CRB scam scenario

2. Following the infamous CRB scam, suddenly black clouds have started gathering on the horizon creating an atmosphere of doubt and distrust. The industry was attacked from all sides. The most important critical problem confronting the industry is that of liquidity. New deposits have almost disappeared, the rate of renewal has fallen drastically and premature withdrawals have been heavy. To add salt to injury, banks and financial institutions have adopted a negative attitude of wait and watch;

Norms for unincorporated financial intermediaries

3. As stated by the Task Force Committee, one of the rudimentary factors contributing to distress in the NBFC sector is information asymmetry as between the depositors and NBFCs. The rationale for regulating the deposit-taking activities of unincorporated bodies essentially flows from the need to protect uninformed depositors. The first attempt to regulate the deposit-taking activities of unincorporated bodies was made in 1984 by inserting Chapter IIIC in the RBI, Act 1934. However, the newly introduced section 45S proved to be different to implement. Again, the RBI banned deposit-taking activities of unincorporated financial intermediaries by amending the RBI Act in 1997. These unincorporated entities were banned from, soliciting deposits by way of advertisements. This does not mean that section 45S prevents such entities from carrying on their operations. These regulations are intended to impel them towards acquiring a corporate status so that they operate within the regulatory framework created under the Companies Act arid Chapter IIIB of the RBI Act.

The unincorporated bodies engaged in non-banking financial business are not allowed to accept deposits except from the relatives, However, such entities could be allowed to access loans from bodies with corporate identity including NBFCs. Unauthorised deposit-taking by both NBFCs and unincorporated bodies is an offence. However, as regards NBFCs cognizance of this offence can be taken only on the complaint of an officer of the RBI. Such offences will now be made cognizable. Unauthorised deposit-taking by a financial sector intermediary automatically catapults these violations into the category of serious crimes.

The task force has advised the RBI to appoint depositors’ grievance redressal authorities with specified territorial jurisdiction. It suggested that a banking ombudsman could be a viable ‘option for such appointments. It has said that the authorities should be empowered to pass orders in regard to direct the unscrupulous and fraudulent companies to pay a part of the deposits to the depositors. To provide legal strength to the order of such authority, it has said, the order could be transmitted by this authority to the principal civil court of the district in which the registered office of the company is located.

Co-ordination mechanism with the RBI

4. The panel has suggested that the CLB must constitute a co-ordination mechanism with the RBI to ensure that default cases are speedily dealt with. The Task Force recognised the need for a decentralised machinery for inspection of smaller NBFCs. It has also suggested that stringent provisions be made for attachment of assets of finance companies engaged in fraudulent activities and the liquidation of NBFCs.

17. Apart from management of the company and also auditors, the Independent directors are required to report their concerns about actual or suspected fraud. The Independentdirectors must also ascertain and ensure that the company has an adequate and functional vigilance mechanism and to ensure that the interests of a person who uses such mechanism are not prejudicially affected on account of such use.

As discussed, the auditors are required to report material fraud to the Central Government within 30 days. Immaterial fraud shall be reported to the board or the auditor of the company.

In case of listed companies, the constitution of Audit committee is required and the Audit Committee, to monitor by establishing a vigilance mechanism for directors and employees to report genuine concerns. The vigilance mechanism shall provide for adequate safeguards against victimization of persons who use such mechanism. It shall make provision for direct access to the Chairperson of the Audit Committee in appropriate cases.

Central Government can order investigation into the affairs of a company on the receipt of a report of the Registrar of Companies / inspector; on intimation of a special resolution passed by a company that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated; or in public interest.

Over and above, the provisions under section 211 of the Companies Act 2013, empowers the Central Government to establish an office called Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) to investigate frauds relating to companies. No other investigating agency shall proceed with investigation in a case in respect of any offence under the Companies Act 2013, once the case has been assigned to SFIO. The SFIO has power to arrest individuals if it has reason to believe that he is guilty based on the material in possession. SFIO shall submit a report to the Central Government on conclusion of investigation. Central Government may direct SFIO to initiate prosecution against the company. SFIO shall share information they possess regarding a case being investigated by the latter and vice versa.

Conclusion

18. As per the provisions of Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules 2014 amended from time to time read with the provisions of amended Companies Act 2013, the regulators have plugged almost all the loopholes which were existing earlier.

The role of Audit Committee in listed companies and also in unlisted specified class of public companies has become very crucial since the Audit Committee's primary purpose is to monitor and provide effective supervision of the company's financial reporting processes in order to ensure timely, accurate and proper disclosures and the transparency, integrity and quality of financial reporting.

The Audit Committee also review with the management, the annual financial statements and auditor's report thereon before submission to the board for approval. While reviewing the financial statements, the Audit Committee particularly take into account the following aspects amongst others.

(a)

Matters required to be included in the director's responsibility statement to be included in the board's report in terms of clause (c) of sub-section 3 of section 134 of the Companies Act, 2013

(b)

Changes, if any, in accounting policies and practices and reasons for the same.

(c)

Major accounting entries involving estimates based on the exercise of judgment by management.

(d)

Significant adjustments made in the financial statements arising out of audit findings.

The new Companies Act 2013 looks upon the auditors from being a watchdog to a whistle blower. Further, the stringent provisions relating to the fraud shows the seriousness to tackle this problem by the regulators and the provisions under the Companies Act 2013, would act as a deterrent and we can hope, none happens but if it does, there are enough legal recourses available to deal and counter them as discussed in the earlier paragraphs.

We can conclude that with the current Companies Act 2013 and the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules 2014 would greatly protect the interest of all stakeholders (especially minority shareholders) and bring improvement in the corporate governance practices in the company

The list of 80 companies was not a rigid list as freedom had been given to add names to the list considered necessary and the SEBI had also submitted that the identification exercise was not a one-time exercise but a continuing process. The matter under inquiry was not hit by the provisions of the Limitation Act. It was incorrect to say that by using section 11B the SEBI was usurping the powers of Registrar of Companies or that they were interfering with the management of the company. Sections 11 and 11B are interconnected and co-extensive as both these sections are mainly focussed on investor protection. On a perusal of the said section 11 it could be seen that the SEBI had been in no uncertain terms mandated to protect the interests of investors in securities by such measures as it thought fit. The expression ‘measure’ has not defined in the Act. ‘Measure’ in its generic sense is of wider amplitude. While section 11 deals with the functions of the Board section 11B is on the powers of the Board. Section 11B is in a sense a functional tool in the hands of the Board. In effect section 11B is one of the executive measures available to the SEBI to enforce its prime duty of investor protection. SEBI is thus empowered to issue directions in the interest of investors to any person or class of persons referred to in section 12 or associated with the securities market. It could not be said that a company having its shares listed on the exchange was out of the reach of sections 11 and 11B. Since the company was operating through its board of directors, the directors of the company also could be considered as persons associated with the capital market, as long as the company’s shares were listed on the exchange. Thus, taking into consideration the scope and reach of sections 11 and 11B it could not be said that the SEBI was lacking authority to issue direction to the appellant. Further, the impugned direction was not one for violation of the Companies Act or the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act. It was issued in the interest of investors under section 11B independent of the provisions of the Companies Act and the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act. Further, there was nothing wrong in relying on a report submitted by an authority like stock exchange, as the information furnished by itself was only a starting point. An inquiry thereafter followed and the concerned persons were given sufficient opportunities to put across their views before the authorities. Similarly exclusion of public deposits and debt instruments from the scope of inquiry could not be considered to be in any way discriminatory, as the matter relating to public deposits etc., was taken care of by other regimes vested with powers for the purpose. For these reasons, the SEBI was justified in pursuing the course of action against the vanishing companies and its promoters and directors and the SEBI was legally invested with the requisite authority for the purpose.

The main reason based on which the impugned order had been issued was an inference, in the absence of relevant material before the SEBI, that the appellant had misused the fund collected from the public for purposes other than for which it was collected. In terms of section 11(2)(i ) the SEBI is empowered to call for information, etc. from the appellant-company also for the reason that it was also a person associated with the securities market. Sections 11 and 11B are interconnected and co-extensive as both these sections are mainly focussed on investor protection. On a perusal of the said section 11 it could be seen that the SEBI had been in no uncertain terms mandated to protect the interests of investors in securities by such measures as it thought fit. The expression ‘measure’ has not defined in the Act. ‘Measure’ in its generic sense is of wider amplitude. While section 11 deals with the functions of the Board section 11B is on the powers of the Board. Section 11B is in a sense a functional tool in the hands of the Board. In effect section 11B is one of the executive measures available to the SEBI to enforce its prime duty of investor protection. SEBI is thus empowered to issue directions in the interest of investors to any person or class of persons referred to in section 12 or associated with the securities market. It could not be said that a company having its shares listed on the exchange was out of the reach of sections 11 and 11B. Since the company was operating through its board of directors, the directors of the company also could be considered as persons associated with the capital market, as long as the company’s shares were listed on the exchange. Analysis & Conclusion

Undoubtedly, the role of the auditor is very vital from the investors' as well as stakeholders' interest point of view as they implicitly trust the financials authenticated by him. The auditor must express his opinion on whether the financial statements give true and fair view of the state of the company's affairs. In reaching his opinion, the auditor must examine the company's books of accounts and related documents, conduct enquiries, collect evidences, detect frauds and so forth. Therefore, it is the duty of the auditor to perform all his statutory obligations with integrity and objectivity. The Tribunal also stated that the auditor owes a fiduciary duty towards the entire Nation.

In the present case, the statutory auditor lacked independence as his family members held shares in the Company which makes him ineligible to become auditor of the Company u/s 141(3)(d). Also, he was negligent in conducting audit and issued his report without proper inspection and examination to which he himself admitted.

Based on the inspection report, the Hon'ble Tribunal opined that the statutory auditor failed to exercise his duties and has certified the Profit & Loss Account and Balance Sheet of the company without even examining any of the records/ Books of the Account of the Company. Tribunal to prevent any further abuse of power, passed an interim order dated 03.01.2019 removing the auditor from function as statutory auditor of the Company and permitting the Company to replace him with an independent auditor. The Tribunal further held that:

"Statutory Auditor colluded with the Chairman/Director of company and has given a false Audit certificate relating to the Profit & Loss Account and Balance Sheet of the R-2 company, without even examining and verifying the books of accounts, and the Statutory Auditor has not given any plausible explanation for such irresponsible fraudulent activities"

The Tribunal, in exercise of its powers under sections 140(5) and 147(3)(i) of the Act, passed the following order as final stating that the statutory auditor:

1.

shall not be eligible to be appointed as an Auditor of any company for a period of 5 years from the date of passing this order;

2.

shall also be liable for action under Section 447 of the Companies Act, 2013; or

3.

to refund the remuneration received by him, during the period he acted as Auditor, back to the Company.

Evidently, the Hon'ble Tribunal stressed on how the role of statutory auditor is becoming important in detecting and preventing frauds. The Auditors are appointed by the shareholders with a view to report the true picture of the company which enables them to make a well-informed decision. However, if the same auditor gets involved in fraudulent instances it will erase their confidence. Therefore, how the Ministry and the Tribunal are exercising their powers to curb such activities is an appreciable move which is trying to reinstate the faith and confidence in the audit profession.

HEADNOTE: Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company's affairs - Whether very fact that respondent company had not finalised the accounts from 1993-94 onwards and that no AGM had been held after 1993 in spite of fact that it was a listed company, was sufficient to order an investigation into affairs of company under section 237(b) - Held, yes - Whether Central Government should also appoint a director on board of company to effectively monitor conduct of affairs of company - Held, yes

FACT: The respondent, a listed company, in its efforts to mobilise funds from NRIs induced the petitioner to contribute towards its share capital. After mobilising funds, the respondent company completely neglected the petitioner by not sending annual reports, etc., which a shareholder is entitled to get. All attempts made by the petitioner to get information about the functioning of the company through SEBI, Bombay Stock Exchange, etc., having failed, the petitioner tried to get inspection done of the records of the company, which was also refused by the company. Only after persistent efforts, the petitioner could get balance sheets of the company for the year ended 31-3-1992 and 31-3-1993. The Department of Company Affairs had conducted an inspection of the records of the company which revealed several violations of the provisions of the Companies Act. A Chartered Accountant permitted to inspect the books of account and other records, made several observations revealing misutilisation of funds for personal benefits. On these facts the petitioner in its petition under section 397/398 alleged oppression and mismanage- ment in the affairs of the company and sought reliefs.

HELD: The petitioner had clearly brought out that the promoters of the company, after having mobilised enormous amount of about Rs. 7 crores, more particularly from NRIs, had not bothered to conduct the affairs of the company in accordance with the provisions of law and in a prudent manner. The petitioner having invested more than Rs. 50 lakhs, had been running from pillar to post to get some information on the functioning of the company without any success. The Regional Director, Dept. of Company Affairs had also in his report reported that the company had not filed balance sheets from 1994 onwards. Notwithstanding the various observations made by the Chartered Accountant who had inspected the books of account and the fact that the Regional Director had initiated prosecution against the company, the very fact that the company had not finalised its accounts from 1993-94 onwards and that no AGM had been held after 1993 in spite of the fact that it was a listed company to protect the interest of a large number of shareholders, suitable remedial action deserved to be taken especially when the respondents had not chosen to participate in the proceedings. While the petitioner had sought for appointment of an Administrator, there were sufficient prima facie materials to exercise powers under section 237(b ) to order an investigation into the affairs of the company. Accordingly, the Central Government was directed to carry out an investigation into the affairs of the company and take appropriate further action on receipt of the investigation report.

Further, in exercise of powers under section 402, the Central Government was also directed to appoint a suitable professional person as a director on the board of the company for a period of 3 years from the date of appointment to effectively monitor the conduct of affairs of the company.
