This is in line with the earlier draft Bill that had been formulated by the Inter-Ministerial Group. The Committee noted that repaying depositors' money is the most critical part of the process of restitution of depositors. Where financial creditors, especially regulated businesses such as banks and financial institutions fail to exercise due diligence and give credit/lending to operators of unregulated securities schemes or schemes where fraudulent default is taken place, the law does not protect and give them priority and precedence. It does not incentivize lending to operators of unregulated schemes and those engaging in fraudulent default in regulated schemes. In this respect it may be noted that the US Bankruptcy Code is more explicit in excluding from the bankruptcy estate, "property in which the debtor holds, as of the commencement of the case, only legal title and not an equitable interest … becomes property of the estate … only to the extent of the debtor's legal title to such property, but not to the extent of any equitable interest in such property that the debtor does not hold."5 The property is part of the estate of the bankrupt only to the extent of his legal right, if he has any, and subject to the equitable interest of another. Thus, where the debtor holds bare legal title without any equitable interest, the estate acquires bare legal title without any equitable interest. Especially given the fact that in cases where the defaulter did not have the legal authorization to collect monies through the issuance of securities, the defaulter may not even have the prima facie legal right to create a security interest in the trust asset.

Collective Investment Schemes and the role of trust in insolvency

Generally, in a Collective Investment Scheme a trustee holds the pooled money on behalf of the beneficiary and in case the trust goes into insolvency the application of insolvency law poses certain important questions as to what happens to the pooled assets which the trustee has raised from the investors. In the famous international bankruptcy cases relating to Lehman Bros. Lehman Brothers International (Europe), In re6 the judge in that case explained the law on the above point maintaining that although the trust relationship may give rise to unsecured claims against the trustee for breach of trust or even negligence and may sometimes exist in a wider contractual framework, it remains at its core a different legal relationship. Subject to the terms of the trust instrument, the trustee holds the trust property for the benefit of those beneficially entitled to it and has a primary obligation to maintain those particular assets (or any which replace them) to the exclusion of all other claims. The trust property does not form part of the trustee's estate in the event of insolvency so as to be available to meet the claims of general creditors and the beneficiary is entitled to the property in specie free of any such claims.

Thus, where a trustee becomes insolvent, all the assets belonging to the trustee are divided up amongst his or her creditors. But if a beneficiary has an equitable property right to assets held by the trustee, it cannot be said that those assets belong to the trustee beneficially. Those assets are, therefore, removed from the pool of the trustee's assets, as they belong in equity to the beneficiary. Only the remaining assets that belong to the trustee beneficially are then distributed amongst the remaining creditors (generally paripassu, or proportionally). Clearly, this puts a beneficiary in a much stronger position than other creditors. The beneficiary is not a 'creditor' for the purposes of insolvency law; his position is higher than that of a creditor.

US Approach and the Berkeley Applegate Principle

Since the previous management of the company admitted to insolvency loses the power to deal with the company assets, it cannot discharge the burden of identifying the trust assets vis-à-vis the company assets. Under the IBC, the power to deal with the company assets, the right to manage the company and deal with its books of accounts primarily vest with the Insolvency professional. The Berkeley Applegate principle7 is useful for making the insolvency discharge the duty of differentiating the trust assets from other assets of the company and to be paid out of such funds. As a corollary of the rule that only the company's assets are available to the creditors, the liquidator has no power as the liquidator, to sell assets not beneficially owned by the company. But to apply this principle there needs to be some procedure to file this claim whereby the Insolvency Professional would then differentiate the assets. In civil matters, where property of a third party has been sequestered or a receiver has been appointed, a petition for examination pro interessesuo is permitted to prove the title and release of their assets.8 A petition for examination pro interessesuo would have to be filed under Section 60 of the IBC, for lack of a well-defined procedure under the IBC9. The petitioner, a contributory of the 1st respondent company seeks a declaration that the company affairs are in such a position that it requires investigation by an Inspector appointed by the Central Government in that regard. It is submitted that the company is not keeping proper accounts and it had done several business activities without obtaining the statutory sanction from the Central Government as enjoined by the law. The Directors of the company including respondents 2 and 3 are now mismanaging the affairs of the company. Therefore, the entire affairs of the company require an investigation and this Court has power under section 237(a)(ii) to order so. If such an order is issued, necessarily, the Central Government will be bound by that order to investigate it. It is submitted, relying on the decision reported in Kumarannuni v. Mathrubhumi Printing & Publishing Co. Ltd. [1981] KLT (S.N.) 88 - Case No. 159 that when it is prima facie satisfied, such a declaration can be issued.

2. Of course, the company court has got power to exercise in terms of Section 237(a)(ii). But section 237(b) empowers the CLB, if there are circumstances necessitating investigation to order accordingly. This power has been granted to the CLB, in terms of the amendment effected in the Companies Act in 1988. Before the amendment sanction had to be given in terms of sub-clause (b) by the Central Government. When the power vested in the Executive Government is invoked, one incumbent may perhaps feel that justice may not be meted out. But now, after the amendment in 1988 the power vested with the Central Government had been taken away and vested with the CLB. When the power is conferred on the CLB, it is incumbent on the petitioner to approach that statutory Board which shall examine and do justice, as the circumstances demand. In such circumstances, there arise no reason for exercising the discretion ary power vested in this company court to direct such investigation or declare that it need investigation by the Central Government. Accordingly, the company petition fails and is dismissed without prejudice to the right of the petitioner to move the CLB in terms of section 237(b).

The High Court held that where Assessing Officer noted that share capital of assessee-company had been routed through two companies, existence and operation of which remained only on paper and enquiries conducted showed that intermediary companies acted as conduits and huge amount were brought in assessee's books as share application money through intermediary companies by shareholders, who could not properly explain their source and assessee had not established creditworthiness and genuineness of transaction to satisfaction of Assessing Officer, Assessing Officer was justified in holding that provisions of section 68 got attracted and that share application money had to be assessed in hands of assessee-company.

The Assessing Officer held that the enquiry with the past and the present directors would show that there was no transparency in the control and administration and even about the ownership of the company; that the share capital has been introduced in the company through two intermediary companies, which operated with the same pseudonymous address and there was no business activity in those companies; that the directors of the intermediary companies pleaded ignorance about the decision regarding the investment in the assessee-company; that the sources of the shareholders, who made their investment in the assessee-company through the intermediary companies were not properly explained; that the affairs of the two intermediary companies established the fact that those were only paper companies created with the sole intention to act as a conduit for facilitating transfer of funds; that the signatories to the agreement were between the assessee and another company, as per which, the shares of the assessee were to be allotted to the other company or its nominees in lieu of the alleged advance of Rs. 5.35 Crores, totally denied by stating that he did not have knowledge of such transaction and that transaction was not reflected by the erstwhile partnership firm M/s. Golden Distilleries; that the addresses of the share applicants namely M/s. D. Kumar Trading and Co., and M/s. Pooja Equitex and M/s. Pentium were not furnished.

The CIT(A), while confirming the order passed by the Assessing Officer, reexamined the entire facts and the discussions commenced from paragraph 4.1.3 in the order dated 21.7.2008. After noting the submissions, which were recorded by the Assessing Officer during the course of assessment proceedings, the CIT(A) held that the so-called directors basically discharged their functions in the honorary capacity during their tenure and they used to look after the routine matters pertaining to the assessee and that they categorically denied having every actively participated in the crucial decision making process of the assessee company. As former managing director of the assessee-company, he was stated to be in charge of civil work, erection of plant and machinery, purchases, etc., and expressed ignorance about the shareholding pattern of the assessee-company and other financial transaction entered into by the initial promoter – directors and the present directors. All of them appeared to have stated that the important decisions used to be taken by only one person, who was the main person behind the promotion of the assessee-company and its business operations. But, the main person pleaded that he and his family members had no role to play in the assessee's business activities apart from holding shares therein.

After noting the statements recorded by the Assessing Officer, the CIT(A) observed that the Assessing Officer was within his right to probe the genuineness and source of the share application money received by the assessee during the year. The statements recorded from the persons had clearly established that the needle of suspicion inevitably and inexorably pointed to one particular person and since the suspicion was so overwhelming, the Assessing Officer had no other option except to trace the origin of funds, which got channelized into the assessee-company through the corporate entities. Further, the CIT(A) pointed out that the Assessing Officer, while embarking upon such an enquiry, found that the share application money was primarily contributed by two companies and an aggregate sum of Rs. 3 Crores was found to be contributed by three Mumbai based companies.

Originally chit funds rendered yeoman service in providing cash to millions of families to solemnize marriages, to buy property, children's educations or contingencies when banking services had not reached rural India.8 Nowadays in the name of chit funds numerous companies are being mushroom every corner of the countries to collect monies mainly from the marginalized people. But these companies do not register with SEBI to avoid regulatory glare and stiff guidelines. At the same time these companies collect money as deposits but call them 'membership fees' to avoid coming under the purview of Reserve Bank of India. On the contrary, Insurance Regulatory & Development Authority (IRDA) cannot take any action because those monies are not collected for insurance purpose or not in the form of premium. Recently, the report of the Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission has recommended that a limited class of companies including banks and non- banking financial companies are allowed to accept deposits from public. This requires amending section 58A of the Companies Act, 1956. The proposed Companies Bill of 2011 is a step in this direction.9 At present, Indian law features tight connections between a particular agency (e.g. SEBI) and the functions that it performs (e.g. securities regulation). The draft Code does not provide for such integration. This is to ensure that from the outset, and over coming decades, decisions about the legal framework governing finance can proceed separately from decisions about the financial regulatory architecture. Changes in the work allocation of agencies would not require changes to the underlying law itself. This will yield greater legal certainty, while facilitating rational choices about financial regulatory architecture motivated by considerations in public administration and public economics.10 So recently the Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission has suggested for only 6 Regulatory Commissions for control of financial system in country and the Reserve Bank of India will have the wide functions including functions of SEBI and Forward Market Commission.

Many Laws But Little Justice

Though there are many laws existing but no appropriate law to solve the present problem. Not only to solve the problem it is very much clear that existing laws have some lacuna to prevent such type of scam generated by chit fund companies. But in the south Indian States, chit funds are being conducted for time immemorial and the first institutionalized chit fund11 was established in 1947 in Chennai.12 So in making of laws relating to chit funds south Indian states were pioneer also. Tamil Nadu was the first state to regulate chit fund business through the Madras Chit Fund Act, 1961 after independence followed by the Andhra Pradesh Chit Funds Act, 1971 for the State of Andhra Pradesh to protect the interest of investors. The Kerala enacted the Kerala Chitties Act, 1975 and also established the Kerala Financial Enterprise Corporation to regulate several chit funds throughout the State. In 1974, the Reserve Bank of India constituted a study group relating to non-banking financial companies under the chairmanship of James. S. Raj and the study group observed that the prize chit, benefit, saving schemes were beneficial for promoters but against the public policy as well as fiscal policy and did not serve any social purpose. Then Union Parliament passed the Prize Chits and Money Circulation Schemes (Banning) Act, 1978 to ban the promotion or conduct of prize chits and money circulation schemes within the country. Finally the Chit Funds Act, 1982, a central legislation, was made to regulate chit funds in India where previous sanction of the State Government is needed to conduct chit fund business13 and every chit agreement shall be filed to Registrar of Chits.14 Again to prevent the speculation of money, the Indian Parliament also enacted the Lotteries (Regulation) Act, 1998 which legalized only the State Government to organize, conduct or promote a lottery after following certain conditions15 otherwise the Central Government may prohibit any lottery16 and any company may also liable by such offences.17 In 2011 Ministry of Finance constituted one 'Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission' headed by former justice B.N. Srikrishna, to harmonise all the financial sector legislations which are more than 60 and very recently Commission suggested for synthesis of many laws and restructuring of regulating agencies.

Introduction

1. India has very large rural population with low income and access to formal banking facilities. As a result web of parallel informal banking channels arose to fill the vacuum. At its centre were moneylenders, who used to charge exorbitant rates of interest. This practice was greatly curbed by the several Moneylenders Acts enacted by the State Governments in the early 1950s. However, the fundamental failure to overcome the role of moneylenders gave rise to fly-by-night financial operators who ran Ponzi schemes in various disguises. However, some commentators place the blame for mushrooming of these kinds of Ponzi schemes on greed rather than on inadequacy of formal banking systems.

The relatively prosperous rural economy of West Bengal had previously relied on small savings schemes run by the Indian Postal Service. However, low rates of interest in the 1980s and 90s encouraged and gave rise to several Ponzi schemes in speculative ventures such as Sanchayita Investments, Overland Investment Company, Verona Credit and Commercial Investment Company. Together, these scams garnered close to 10 billion INR of investor's wealth.

The Saradha Group financial scandal has been a financial scam which was caused by the collapse of a Ponzi scheme run by Saradha Group, a consortium of Indian companies which was believed to be running a wide variety of collective investment schemes (popularly but incorrectly referred to as chit funds) in the Eastern India. The group collapsed in April, 2013, causing an estimated loss of INR 200–300 billion (US$ 4–6 billion). In the aftermath of the financial scandal, the State Government of West Bengal set-up an inquiry Commission to investigate into collapse and also set-up a fund of INR 5 billion (92 million USD) to ensure that low income investors were not bankrupted. The Union Government also launched a multi-agency probe to investigate into the Saradha scam, as well as into other similar Ponzi schemes.

The Ponzi Schemes

2. The Saradha Group has gained notoriety in recent weeks with outstanding public deposits reportedly exceeding Rs. 200 billion. There was anger and panic. The State Government has stepped in with partial redressal system.

As we watch unfolding of this saga, there may be another crisis waiting to happen in the form of a pyramid scheme offered by Mavrodi Mondial Moneybox (MMM) that is taking rural India by storm. MMM claims to be a "social financial network" in which members voluntarily share money with each other by buying and selling MAVROS - a currency-like unit devised by the operators of the scheme. MMM claims to generate returns of over 40% per month, although the returns are not guaranteed. It may be a ponzi scheme: one where money collected from new investors is used to pay returns to old investors. The cycle will continue till inflows into the scheme exceed outflows.

Saradha and MMM are not isolated examples. Some of the recent schemes have promised unrealistic returns from investments in goats, pigs, emu, teak wood and potatoes.

The history of savings and investments in India is replete with tragedies where financial firms have failed to return deposits or investments. This is particularly problematic in a country where 70% of the people earn under 2 dollars a day and, hence, have small amounts of money saved up. If savings are not safe, the central objective of regulation - consumer protection - is not met. What we need is institutions that can take up deposits or run investment schemes to operate in a safe and sound manner, within the bounds of financial regulation.

When SEBI asserted its authority to stop Saradha group from collecting money, Saradha challenged the jurisdiction of the SEBI in district courts. It quickly got orders to prevent SEBI from interfering in its businesses. These orders were eventually overturned by the High Court.

When SEBI requested information from Saradha about their schemes and investors, Saradha responded by providing large volumes of documentation without specifically answering SEBI's questions. This slowed down the entire investigation.

Two years of investigation were required to stop what seems to be a run of the mill Ponzi scheme. The tactics employed by Saradha are not new. They are similar to those employed by Sahara in delaying investigations in the OFCD schemes and in many other white collar crime investigations. [1996] 10 SCL 70 (SC) In the above matter the scope and ambit of the Company Court and the broad contours had emerged in respect of sanctioning the Schemes by the Court. It was held that the Court had to see that all the requisite statutory procedure for supporting the scheme had been complied with and that the requisite meetings was held; that the scheme put up for sanction of the Court was backed up by the requisite majority vote as required and the concerned meetings of the creditors or members or any class of them had the relevant material to enable the voters to arrive at an informed decision for approving the scheme in question; That the majority decision of the concerned class of voters was just and fair to the class as a whole so as to legitimately bind even the dissenting members of that class and ;that all necessary material indicated as per the provisions were placed before the voters at the concerned meetings ;That all the requisite material contemplated were placed before the Court by the concerned applicant seeking sanction for such a scheme and the Court gets satisfied about the same. The Court has to further see that the proposed scheme of compromise and arrangement was not found to be violative of any provision of law and was not contrary to public policy. For ascertaining the real purpose underlying the Scheme the Court, if necessary, could pierce the veil of apparent corporate purpose underlying the scheme and could judiciously X-ray the same. Further the Court has also to satisfy itself that members or class of members or creditors or class of creditors, as the case may be, were acting bona fide and in good faith and were not coercing the minority in order to promote any interest adverse to that of the latter comprising of the same class whom they purported to represent; the Court must also ascertain that the scheme as a whole is found to be just, fair and reasonable from the point of view of prudent men of business taking a commercial decision beneficial to the class represented by them for whom the scheme is meant.

Once the aforesaid broad parameters about the requirements of a scheme for getting sanction of the Court were found to have been met, the Court would have no further jurisdiction to sit in appeal over the commercial wisdom of the majority of the class of persons who with their open eyes gave their approval to the scheme even if in the view of the Court there would be a better scheme for the company and its members or creditors for whom the scheme is framed. The Court cannot refuse to sanction such a scheme on that ground, as it would otherwise amount to the Court exercising appellate jurisdiction over the scheme rather than its supervisory jurisdiction. The aforesaid parameters of the scope and ambit of the jurisdiction of the Company Court which was called upon to sanction a Scheme of Compromise and Arrangement were not exhaustive but only broadly illustrative of the contours of the Court's jurisdiction.

Audit simply means checking of records to establish accuracy

'Audit' is a systematic and independent examination of data, statements, records, operations and performance (financial or otherwise) of an enterprise for a stated purpose. In an auditing situation, the auditor perceives and recognises the propositions before him for examination, collects evidence, evaluates the same and on that basis, formulates the judgment which is communicated through his audit report [ICAI in General guidelines on Internal Auditing].

Auditing is a systematic process of objectively obtaining and evaluating evidence regarding assertions about economic actions and events to ascertain the degree of correspondence between those assertions and established criteria, and communicating results to interested user (Auditing Concepts Committee of American Accounting Association).

In service tax audit under EA-2000, 'audit' simply means verification of records to ensure correctness.

That audit need not be confused with 'statutory audit' which might be conducted under some specific provisions of Act, like section 73A of Finance Act, 1994. It seems this distinction was not properly brought out before High Court.

Introduction

Recently, the broken down of chit fund in West Bengal is the latest financial scam which has generated lots of hue and cry throughout the India. Huge amounts of money were involved in this scam which has created an economic vacuum in the State where large portion of marginalized people have been affected. Apart from economic matter a social unrest is going on where depositors as well as agents are committing suicide, agents are being lynched by investors, some agents are absconding, company offices are attacked by public and so on. A total inter-class and intra-class conflicts has taken place. Such type of financial scam by corporate sector is a classic example of socio-economic offence against the public at large. Corporate crime is, therefore, a real social problem and represents a definite danger to society. They are no less morally reprehensible, and in terms of suffering inflicted or damage caused they are as bad, and often because of their magnitude, worse than conventional, run-of-the-mills crimes committed by individuals1. Though State Government has constituted one Commission by retired justice with economic experts, new law is going to be passed and one proposed fund will be generated, in spite all of these the collapse of the Saradha Group in West Bengal has exposed the regulatory gaps and overlap of various regulatory entities. While chit funds are governed by a central law, the regulatory oversight rests with the State Government.2 Financial scams are not new for Indian market and have been broken out many times in the past. Many Commissions were established, some amendments are made in regulations but it never come to an end. In 1957, scam made by Haridas Mundhra with State owned Life Insurance Corporation (LIC) was first major scam of India after independence.3 It raised questions in the Parliament and 'Chagla Commission' was constituted and finally then the Finance Minister T.T. Krishnamachari resigned. Scams made by stock market manipulators Harshad Mehta of 1990s and Ketan Parekh of 2000s are some prominent names in this regard. After such types of financial scams one or many Commissions are being set up by government through Ministry of Finance or Commerce or Corporate Affairs or by the Reserve Bank of India. But one thing was common in all those scams from experiences, i.e., public monies of poor and common people never retuned back to them. So these scams make poor people more poorer and financial instability in the country.

A reference was made above to section 21 of the Competition Act, which may provide a basis for interaction between the Competition Commission and the SEBI. A basis for interaction between the Competition Commission and the National Commission is provided by a unique provision under the Competition Act.

As is well known, the Competition Act is to replace the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act, 1969 (MRTP Act). Section 66(1) of the Competition Act clearly states that the MRTP Act, 1969 is hereby repealed and the MRTP Commission shall stand dissolved. One proviso to section 66, however, states that the pending enquiries before the MRTP Commission in respect of unfair trade practices only, would be transferred to the National Commission; and those involving both restrictive as well as unfair trade practices would be transferred to the Competition Commission which would dispose of these (transferred enquiries) in accordance with the provisions of the MRTP Act, as if that Act has not been repealed.

This particular provision, if invoked in due course, would provide another ground for interaction between the Competition Commission and the SEBI, in respect of unfair trade practices in the share markets.

A consumer had the choice of approaching either of the forums for relief. In fact, in many cases, the consumer approached both the forums. In all such cases, the MRTP Commission, on noticing the dual jurisdiction invoked by the complainant before it for the same cause of action, had decided not to entertain such complaints as a matter of judicial propriety. Regulatory provisions & Internal Auditors

Under the Companies Act

Section 447 of the Companies Act, 2013 defines fraud as " any act, omission, concealment of any fact or abuse of positions with an intent to deceive, to gain undue advantage from or to injure the interests of the company or its shareholders or creditors or any other person, whether or not there is any wrongful gain or wrongful loss".

The above definition is a very wide definition and covers "person".

Some instances where Section 447 will trigger are:-

(a)

Incorporation of company based on false or incorrect information.

(b)

For untrue, misleading statement in prospectus or inclusion or omission of any matter.

(c)

For fraudulently inducing persons to invest money.

(d)

When auditor act in a fraudulent manner or abetted or colluded in any fraud.

(e)

When business of a company is carried on for a fraudulent or unlawful purposes or with intent to defraud creditors, members or any other person.

Other aspects of Fraud

The offence of 'fraud' is non-compoundable. The Auditor and the Secretarial Auditor to report offence involving fraud to the Central Government and failure to do so will attract fine up to Rs25 lakhs. Further, provisions are also there for disgorgement of assets, property or cash if any Director, Key Managerial Personnel or other officer has derived undue advantage or benefit when fraud takes place in a company.

The provision is "Notwithstanding anything contained in this section, if an auditor of a company in the course of the performance of his duties as auditor, has reason to believe that an offence involving fraud is being or has been committed against the company by officers or employees of the company, he shall immediately report the matter to the Central Government within such time and in such manner as may be prescribed."

Further, in the cases where the fraud involves any amount lesser than the specified amount, the auditor shall report the matter to the audit committee constituted, if any or to the Board in other cases within the timeline and the manner prescribed in the above rules. Other remedies - Sections 397, 398 and 408 do not confer exclusive jurisdiction on the Company Court 1/CLB to grant reliefs against oppression and mismanagement, they only provide a convenient remedy for minority shareholders under certain conditions and no intendment can be inferred that the sections exclude all other remedies: the suits by the minority shareholders against oppression and mismanagement are maintainable in the civil courts : C.D.S. Financial Services (Mauritius) Ltd. v. BPL Communications Ltd. (2004) 121 Comp. Cas. 374/56 SCL 665 (Bom.). If the allegation is that the company’s act is mala fide and oppressive which could be made in a petition under sections 397 and 398 to the CLB, the High Court cannot entertain such a petition sought to be filed under section 81 read with section 10 of the Act, as the Court has to look at the substance of the allegations and averments made in the petition - Vijay M. Shaw v. Flex Industries Ltd. (1996) 7 SCL 156 (Delhi). If a member complains that the affairs of the company were conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interest and oppressive to him which falls under section 397, the Civil Court has no jurisdiction to entertain the petition - Jaiprakash Industries Ltd. v. Lalit Bhasin (2003) 45 SCL 31 (All.) At the stage of directions to convene meeting to consider the scheme, substantive issue like justification of constitution of class of ‘scheme lenders’—debenture holders to be a separate class—could not be considered - Essar Oil Ltd., In re (2005) 62 SCL 345 (Guj.).

Role of the SEBI

5. There are some indications that the Reserve Bank of India had warned the State Government on the mushrooming of chit funds in West Bengal. What is interesting is, that market regulator, SEBI has been investigating the Saradha Group since June, 2010. The Saradha Group had managed to delay the process by submitting voluminous documents. At various points of time in 2012, Saradha submitted 16 cartons, 19 cartons, 170 boxes and 35 cartons, as a strategy to avoid submitting the specific information being asked for by SEBI. After this Saradha Group was directed to provide information in Excel sheets. This helped SEBI to nail the group. As the SEBI order points out "On sample study of the data (in Excel) provided by the noticee (Saradha), veracity of which cannot be verified, it is noted that agreements for sale were entered into with two investors, namely, Dhruba Bose and Arindam Pani on January 01, 2010 for flats having number 1A and 1C, respectively, both admeasuring 1437 sq. ft. area in the same building, i.e., Ten Katha. It is further noted that the consideration amount for flat number 1A was Rs. 37,69,000 and for flat number 1C was Rs. 1,17,75,850. It is highly unlikely that in a real estate business the difference between consideration amounts for sale of two similar flats at the same building on the same day shall be in the ratio of 1:4. In view of these facts the possible inference will be that the allotment of plots/flats are simply a farce, and might have been done to mislead the regulatory authority." But by the time the SEBI's order came out, Saradha had already collapsed. What is intriguing is that the investigation against Saradha started in mid 2010, but it took the company more than two years to submit the relevant data. If SEBI had cracked the whip and acted a little faster, the situation might have been a little better.

Though everything written above evidences the reason why Saradha Group was able to defraud people, yet most important question, after all this discussion, is "Why such investors at the first place only invest in schemes like Saradha?" As already discussed, Saradha Group lured lakhs of investors to deposit money in its schemes with glossy brochures and the promise of abnormally high returns. It is true that such investors did not know that the scheme was a fraud, but it was evidently clear that such high returns were not possible and involved high risk. The upfront interest of 20% offered by the group as compared to 8% interest given by the banks made it crystal clear for investors to see the mala fide intent involved. The need of the hour is to encourage informed investors and discourage wanton pick and choose inter se such suicidal schemes.

Conclusion

6. It is distressing to see how the system can be hijacked by rogues without chances of any punishment. It is true that regulatory structure is riddled with holes, but surely some administrative measures could have been taken, provided the executive had the will to do so. Consistently the ruling parties, the Left or the Right, did not pay any heed as a portion of the loot helped in keeping its machine well-oiled. Keeping in mind all the relevant facts discussed above it will not be wrong to say that once the dust settles down, another Saradha like scam will emerge like a Phoenix.

In order to stop another Saradha like scam, it is very important to educate the masses regarding fundamentals of finances, the difference between reality and utopia.

Section 130, Sections 211-212 and Sections 241-242 Operate In Different Fields and Circumstances

The promoter argued that Section 130, Sections 211-212 and Sections 241-242 operate in different fields and circumstances and they are in the different Chapters and therefore any observation made while passing the order/orders with respect to a particular provision may not be considered while passing the order under relevant provisions is concerned. The apex court held that it is required to note that all the three provisions are required to be considered conjointly, while passing an order in a particular provision, the endeavour should be to see that the order/orders passed under other provisions of the Companies Act are given effect to, and/or in furtherance of the order/orders passed under other Sections. Therefore, the observations made while passing order under Section 241-242 of the Companies Act can be said to be relevant observations for passing the order under Section 130 of the Companies Act.

On 12th August, Manbhawan receives Rs. 40 lakhs from Campus Impex and Rs. 60 lakhs from Nexcare Agencies, and, on the very next day, i.e. 13 August 2010, pays over Rs. 100 lakhs to the assessee company. The same is the position with respect to receipts of Rs. 50 lakhs each from Nexcare Agencies and Campus Impex on 17th August, and subsequent payment of Rs. 100 lakhs to the assessee-company.

The Tribunal further observed as under:

"31. Clearly, all these transactions are circular transactions with opacity about the ultimate owners as evident from the fact that even the financial statements and bank statements of Nexcare Agencies and Campus Impex show similar features- negligible revenues, shares issued at high premium and almost entire fund available passed on to other entities, and predominantly circular transactions, with low independent balances. It is a complex web of companies through which the investments in question are made, issued at unrealistic premium justified by academic and patently incorrect calculations far divorced from the realities of commercial world, and the transactions are deceptive inasmuch as each layer of companies has the source of funds in some other layer of companies operating at another level. As we have noted earlier, the premium justification lacks merits and is already rejected. The premium calculations are based on such premises as no independent investor would ever adopt, and even the fundamental assumptions are incorrect and unreal. The movement of funds is not transparent and the ultimate beneficial owners of this investment in the assessee company are not even known, leave aside the reason for their making such a risky investment, at unjustified premiums and without any participation or management control despite huge size of investment vis-à-vis the size of the company in which investment is made. The material on record does not reasonably evidence genuineness of the transactions."

The Tribunal held that "In view of our this understanding of the situation, we are unable to accept the plea of the assessee that the transaction is a bona fide transaction. In view of these discussions, as bearing in mind peculiar facts of this case, we reject the explanation of the assessee with respect to genuineness of this transactions of investment by MCPL as well."

Clearly, the facts of the case in Leena (supra) show that such cases should be investigated for benami transactions under section 2(9)(D), 2(9)(B) and 2(9)(A). Further investigations by MCA need to be carried out by invoking section 216 of the Companies Act, 2013 to find out who are the true beneficial owners who appear to be using these layers of companies as their benamidars.

Making a Case for a Securities Market Whistleblower Policy 3. The Satyam s candal shook the corporate world due to the extent of havoc and uncertainty it created and raised several concerns regarding corporate governance issues. But it is more than just a corporate governance concern. It is about protecting the interests of the public where their monies are directly impacted. One of the severe criticisms of the above mentioned scandal was the lack of a operational whistleblower policy to deduct the overstating of the company's financial matters.

With regard to the Indian securities market, SEBI as an independent regulator is vested with the duty to protect the interests of the investors and actively participate in regulating and improving the Indian capital market. The market regulator has made significant strides since its statutory inception in 1992 by bringing to the fore various regulatory checks and balances such as prohibition of insider trading, ensuring disclosure mechanisms and the corporate takeover regulations. Following the Supreme Court's judgment in the Sahara case32, SEBI's jurisdiction over all companies that make public issue of securities have been widened. Therefore, most of the investors are protected by the SEBI. The Board's investigative and enforcement powers have been furthered augmented by the Securities Law (Amendment) Ordinance, 2013. Despite these legislative safeguards, SEBI has to within its means ensure maximum protection. One way is to give opportunity to the public to come forward with their fears of any securities law violation. Therefore, the author is of the opinion that in furtherance of SEBI's objective to ensure and maximise investor protection, administering a whistleblower policy will complement its measures in the process.

The steps taken by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) of the United States (US) have been hailed by the countries around the world for incentivizing whistleblowers coming forward to report corporate frauds. To briefly state it The Dodd Frank Act of 2010 brought out monetary incentives for voluntary disclosures to the Securities Exchange Commission (SEC) by the amending Securities Exchange Act.33 By inserting Section 21F to SEC Act, the Commission has been armed with the power to grant monetary awards to eligible individuals who voluntarily provide original information to the SEC about violations of the US securities law that leads to enforcement actions resulting in the imposition of monetary sanctions over $1,000,000. Anti-victimization clauses are extensive and thorough. The amendment is a significant measure in the global corporate whistleblower policy-making, as it is unambiguous with regard to defining key terms such as who constitutes a whistleblower, what comprises original information and the conditions for applying for a monetary award.

The US securities market varies from that of India's not only in terms of its size but also in the fact that it is more distributed when it comes to market participation. Although this might be the case, yet anti-fraud provisions in India with respect to the capital market draws inspiration largely from the similar provisions in the SEC Act in the United States. Not only this, certain provisions on whistleblowing in the Companies Act, 2013 are on the lines of the Sarbanes Oxley Act, 2002. As much as we imbibe from the success of their laws, we must also learn from their lacunae and loopholes.

There are several questions one must address before SEBI takes up the responsibility of providing whistleblowers. Starting with the SEBI Act itself, s. 24B seeks to provide relief from prosecution of a person who has been alleged to have committed a violation of the Act during the course of proceedings. However, this a power that vests in the Central Government and SEBI has only non-binding recommendatory effect. This law has to be amended to vest SEBI with the power to grant this immunity. Moreover, the provision must also elaborate upon protection of the persons coming forward with the information on violation as their statements are liable to be used as a testimony against others involved in the violation. This is a step closer to tightening the law. Secondly, a dedicated whistleblower legislation within the framework of the SEBI has to address, more importantly, who will not be a whistleblower. Any member of the general public, on suspicion of a violation of the Act that has occurred, or will occur or is occurring should be allowed to come forward with his/her complaint to the SEBI. However, such a person cannot be entitled to a monetary reward if he/she is a part of the alleged violation. In such a scenario, section 24B of the Act will kick in and, accordingly, the law will take its due course. Another person who cannot be considered for a whistleblower's reward is any compliance officer within a company. As such, an officer will have first hand knowledge of any complaint brought to him, and he cannot be considered to be providing information that is original as a result of any independent analysis.

Under said agreement, company was required, to fill prepared aravana prasadam in cans and supply to devotees for a period of eight years at rates specified therein which would be payable by respondent No. 6 - Petitioners collectively holding in excess of 10 per cent of issued share capital of respondent-company filed petition invoking provisions of sections 397, 398 and 402 wherein main grievance of petitioners was that respondent Nos. 2 to 5 had mismanaged affairs of respondent-company and had misappropriated receivables realised from respondent No. 6 for their personal benefits without settling dues of banks, financial institutions, suppliers and other creditors - It was seen from records that respondents had not furnished any particulars regarding actual receivables and utilization of such receivables excepting a bald statement that liabilities of banks, financial institutions and suppliers had been settled from and out of receivables realised from respondent No. 6 - The assessee, a public limited company, was registered on 27-4-1983. It had a share capital of Rs. 20 lakhs. Its accounts were closed for the first time on 30-6-1984, and a return for the assessment year 1985-86 was furnished covering the income from the date of incorporation. The object of the company was to deal in shares as well as financing. Before the ITO, the assessee had produced the bought-and-sold notes in support of share dealing. The company had also received income from interest, commission and discounting of bills and details regarding receipts and expenditure were also furnished before the ITO. A list of persons who had been allotted shares and confirmations from shareholders were furnished. The ITO, after considering all material placed before him, accepted the return and completed the assessment. However, the Commissioner set aside the assessment order under section 263 on grounds that the order was erroneous and prejudicial to the revenue on the basis that necessary and proper enquiries were not made in regard to the share capital raised by the company. The Commissioner observed that though details were furnished by the assessee, the ITO had not made any cross-verification or enquiry. He pointed out that a large number of investment companies were floated for laundering unaccounted money and that the ITO ought to have found out whether the shareholders were genuine and whether the monies introduced in the books of account actually belonged to shareholders. According to the Commissioner, it was the duty of the ITO to pierce the corporate veil and bring to tax unaccounted money without taking into account the fine and artificial distinction between the company on the one hand and the shareholders on the other.

26.4 The powers of the directors are co-extensive with the powers of the company as conditioned and controlled by the memorandum, the articles and the Act, cf. Oakbank Oil Co. v. Directors’ acts have to be consistent with the articles and subsisting contracts

26.4-1 Where the articles specify the powers of directors, they cannot go beyond the limits set out - Agriculturists Cattle Insurance Co., In re (1866) 1 Ch. App. 511, and in the exercise of such powers the directors should do so subject to the agreements and contracts subsisting - Nelson v. James Nelson & Son Ltd. (1914-15) All. ER 433 (CA).

Board strength below minimum fixed by articles

26.4-2 A Board comprising lesser number of directors than that fixed by the articles cannot exercise the functions of the Board - Vishwanath Prasad Jallan v. Holyland Cinetone Ltd. (1939) 9 Comp. Cas. 324 (All.); but if their number is not less than the quorum, they may act and if the number falls below the quorum, they can act only to increase their number (regulation 75 of Table ‘A’).

Members cannot interfere with day-to-day management of the company

26.4-3 Unless the articles permit, the shareholders cannot interfere in the day-to-day management of the company - Suburban Bank (P.) Ltd. v. Thariath (1968) 38 Comp. Cas. 13 (Ker.); and where the management of the company is vested in the Board of directors by the articles, such power can be withdrawn only by amending the articles - Murarka Paint & Varnish Work (P.) Ltd. v. Mohanlal Murarka (1961) 31 Comp. Cas. 301 (Cal.), and the company in general meeting cannot pass a resolution inconsistent with the articles - Salmon v. Quin Axtens Ltd. (1909) 1 Ch. 311 (CA). Accordingly, the directors are not bound to comply with the directions given by majority of shareholders at a general meeting unless the articles are altered - Automatic Self-Cleaning Filter Syndicate Co. Ltd. v. Cunningham (1906) 2 Ch. 34 (CA), John Shaw & Sons (Salford) Ltd. v. Shaw (1935) 2 KB 113 (CA) and Pothen v. Hindustan Trading Corpn. (P.) Ltd. (1967) 37 Comp. Cas. 266 (Ker.).

Board’s powers include the powers incidental to its powers specified in the articles

However, due to infighting in between the Patel brothers and also due to alleged improper management of the company, the company ran into serious financial difficulties. In such a scenario, the company could not repay the loan taken from UCO Bank. For the inability of the company to repay the loan, UCO Bank had issued notice under Scrutinization and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Security Interest Act, 2002. The management of the company had realized that it was not possible on the part of the management to continue the business of the company with such heavy financial liabilities on its head, more so, when the personal properties of the managerial persons were mortgaged to the bank and when such properties too were at huge stake. The then management of the company approached 'A' a Finance company urging the later to bail out the company from such hopeless condition. In 2008, a series of disputes arose between 'H' Director and 'Ha' Director and other Directors of the company in regard to running and management of the company and also in regard to some other ancillary matters which considerably crippled the running of the company. Worse still, such disputes resulted in filing of a suit before the Calcutta High Court, Kolkata, and such a suit was said to have been instituted at the behest of H. Since the management of the company was allegedly conducted in a very unsatisfactory way, the company suffered a series of consequences of extremely serious nature on all the fronts including availability of fund, required for continuance of the company as a viable entity. In such a hopeless scenario, it was that the company came into contact with 'A' Finance company. The 'A' on seeing the business prospects of the company, decided to rescue the company of its debts by infusing funds so that such amount could be utilized in liquidating the huge debt of the company. 12. It is very surprising to note that at a time when CSR activities are being promoted by government, due importance is not given to the transfer of amount to IEPF. Reporting relating to timely transfer of amount to IEPF has been done away with. Over the years, this clause has acted as a check point to ensure the timely transfer of unclaimed and unpaid amounts to IEPF. Reporting on accumulated losses would no longer be required

13. With a view to provide further ease of doing business, government has lifted another important reporting feature, under which auditor was to report on whether a newly incorporated company (Company registered for a period not less than 5 years) has accumulated losses at the end of financial year minimum 50% of its net worth. The clause was also required to report on cash losses in the financial year under review and in the immediately preceding financial year. Now the auditors are not at all required to report on these issues. However, this exemption is only allowed in case of newly incorporated companies. Probably the move is to see growth in the start-up companies.

Reporting on repayment of dues

14. Keeping in view rising debts and NPAs of the banks/financial institutions, the reporting format of auditors on the repayment of dues has been changed drastically. In addition to the earlier provisions of CARO applicable to the repayment of dues, now auditors are also required to report on lender-wise details. This move will surely act as an important check on further increase of NPAs and bad loans. Now the default in repayment of dues shall have its own language, as the name of the lenders and their respective amount shall be reported. It will be possible for all users of balance sheet to know/ascertain the dues to be paid to banks/financial institutions.

Default to government should also be specifically disclosed

15. Besides banks and financial institutions, now auditor shall also be required to report any default to the government. Thus, now onwards the government would also be construed as a party. In case of default to government, same type of lender-wise details have to be provided.

Corporate guarantee is no longer an item of CARO

16. CARO 2016 made another surprise move by deleting the clause for reporting of corporate guarantees given by the Company for loans taken by others from Bank or financial institutions. Subsequently, auditors are also not required to mention the interest of Company prejudicially affected by corporate guarantee.

Extensive and vast reporting on use of moneys raised through public issues as well as term loans

17. The recent scams of corporate sector seem to have widely effected the perception of the Ministry. The earlier CARO order was limited to the reporting on use of term loan for the purpose for which the loans were obtained. But keeping in view the public scams and frauds, the order is set to cover the whole gamut of fund raising in its coverage area.

Now onwards auditors have to be very cautious as they have to retain their identity of public trustees. Now they have to provide complete record for use of money raised through pubic issues and all other ways of raising finance, including debt instruments and term loans. Further reporting has to be on all kind of delays/defaults and subsequent rectifications, if any, and if applicable.

Two ways of fraud reporting

18. Earlier order was centered around reporting of fraud on or by the company. However, fraud on the company does not specifically mention the name of its officers/employees. Instead of that the new order specifically mentions the fraud on the company by its "officers/employees" as well as fraud by the Company. Thus, any kind of fraud, whether committed internally by the officers/employees or externally affecting public, shall have to be reflected in Auditor's report along with the nature of fraud and amount involved in the fraud.

Remuneration of managerial personnel would not be only a hidden item

19. Till now managerial remuneration has been reflected as a balance sheet item. But now onwards specific reporting by auditor has to be made on managerial remuneration. The auditor has to ensure that the remuneration paid to managerial personnel has been in accordance with section 197 and Schedule V of the Companies Act. Beyond that if amount paid or even amount provided has been in excess of section 197 and Schedule V of the Companies Act, 2013, the auditor has to mention the amount in excess of section 197, read with Schedule V and the steps taken by the company for recovery of the same. Thus, the Board or management shall have no right to waive off the amount to be recovered from managerial personnel.

Extensive exposure to related party transactions

20. The earlier order did not have any requirement of reporting on related party transactions. But the new one shall have extensive reporting feature, which shall cast direct responsibility on auditor and audit committee.

Auditor has to mention that all the related party transactions are in compliance with section 188 as well as in compliance with section 177. Section 177 which requires omnibus approval of audit committee, shall have to be counter reported in auditor's report. Thus, it should not be the prerogative of only audit committee to sanction the related party transactions as it will be counter checked by statutory auditor.

[Para 13]. In Asia Stone S.L. v. B. & G. Impex (P.) Ltd.197, the applicant-company was a shareholder in the first respondent-company holding up to 99.67 per cent of its paid-up capital. The first respondent company held its first board meeting on 17-7-2006 wherein 'V' was appointed as an additional director. The second respondent and the third respondent were also appointed as additional directors at subsequent board meetings. Subsequently, 'V' and the first directors of the first respondent-company, i.e., respondents 4 and 5 resigned from their posts and their resignations were accepted by the board at a meeting held on 24-11-2006. Consequently, the board was left with only two members comprising of respondent Nos. 2 and 3. The applicant alleged that the first respondent held the first AGM on 25-7-2007 without giving any notice to the applicant. When the applicant's authorized representatives visited registered office of the first respondent, it was found closed and there was no responsible person available to answer their questions. Thereafter, the applicant made all efforts for inspection and for obtaining the records but all went in vain. The applicant apprehended that all was not well with the first respondent and that it was kept in dark about the affairs of the company. The applicant was served with a copy of the plaint from where it was able to get a copy of the notice of first the AGM, dated 25-7-2007. From said notice, it was evident that the first respondent had not appointed any new director at the AGM. The only two members of the board were respondent Nos. 2 and 3 who could only hold office upto the date of AGM, i.e., up to 25-7-2007 in terms of section 260. Further, the inspection of documents with RoC revealed that many statutory documents were not filed in spite of the fact that due date for filing same had already expired. The applicant feared of action by the RoC for statutory violations and non-performance of statutory violation by the first respondent. In these circumstances, the applicant invoked the provisions of section 186 for passing appropriate orders/directions in the interest of justice and prayed that the board may appoint an independent Chairman and also give directions in relation to calling/holding and conducting the EGM of the company for the purpose of appointing two individuals to the board of directors of the company. He further prayed that a single member present in person or proxy would be deemed to constitute a valid quorum for the purpose of the EGM. Held, As per the provisions of section 260 it is crystal clear that the additional directors so appointed shall hold office only up to the date of the next AGM. In the instant case, the first AGM purportedly was held on 25-7-2007 at the registered office of the company and the agenda of the meeting was mentioned in the notice dated 25-6-2007, wherein no such agenda for re-appointment of additional directors, as regular directors was found. Therefore, the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 were no more directors of the company, hence, the respondents stand that respondent Nos. 2 and 3 were the current directors could not be accepted. The first directors, i.e., the respondent Nos. 4 and 5 and the other additional director 'V' had resigned and the same was accepted at the sixth board meeting held on 24-11-2006. In view of the resignation and the completion of tenure of the additional directors, the company was not having any directors on its board. The submission of the applicant that the company was not having the directors was valid and legal. The report of the RoC was taken on record which further strengthened the case of the applicant that the company had no directors on its board. Section 169 specifically gives powers to the board of directors of a company to call for an EGM on the requisition of such number of members of the company as are specified in section 169(4). In the instant case, there was no such board and the main grievance of the applicant was that no such board existed and the company was functioning without a proper board and the applicant could not approach the company for convening an EGM. The submissions of the applicant were to be fully agreed with. As the company was not having board of directors, the contention of the respondent that the applicant could have invoked the provisions of section 169 did not have any merit. Therefore, the applicant had no other alternate except to invoke provisions of section 186(1).
